en: Now begins the first section, the *Māheśvara-khaṇḍa*, in the glorious *Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa! *Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed Vāsudeva!* Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Jaya" (Victory). (1)
Vyāsa said: Salutations to that wielder of the Pināka bow, by whose command Viriñci is the creator of the world, Hari is its protector, and he who is called Kālarudra is its destroyer.

In that very Naimiṣa forest, the best of sacred fords and the most excellent of holy sites, dwell the ascetics headed by Śaunaka; performing a long sacrificial session, they are performers of the rite whose minds are fixed on ritual action.
Indeed, out of a desire to see them, the great ascetic, the highly wise disciple of Vyāsa known by the name Lomaśa, has arrived.
There, the sages performing long sacrificial sessions saw him arrive; all of them rose simultaneously, eager and with offerings of honor in their hands.
Having offered water for the feet and the guest-offering, and having honored him, the sages, who were free from stain and highly blessed, questioned him concerning the Dharma of Śiva in full detail.
The sages said: O one of great wisdom, O highly fortunate one, tell us of the majesty of the trident-bearing God of gods, together with the methods of meditation and worship.
What would be the fruit of sweeping, as well as of decorative paintings, and likewise of the offering of a mirror and a fly-whisk? (7)
What would be the fruit of giving a canopy as well as a fountain-house? What would be the fruit of offering a lamp, and what would be the fruit of worship? (8)
And let the various merits of worshipping Śiva be told: the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and likewise the study of the Vedas.
If men perform or cause to be performed [this rite] before Śiva, what is the fruit for those men? Please tell it in detail. (10)
O Sage, indeed there is no one else in the world besides you who is devoted to the narration of Śiva.
Having heard these words of those sages of purified souls, this disciple of Vyāsa spoke of the supreme majesty of Śiva.
Lomaśa said: In the eighteen Purāṇas, the Supreme Śiva is indeed sung of; therefore, no one is able to fully describe the majesty of Śiva.
Those people who shall utter the two-syllabled name "Śiva," for them there will be both heaven and liberation; it shall not be otherwise.
For Mahādeva is indeed sublime, the Lord and Master of the gods; since everything has been bestowed by him, he is therefore remembered as Sarva. || 15 ||
Blessed are they, those great-souled ones who always worship Śiva.
He who desires to cross the ocean of worldly existence without Sadāśiva is indeed a fool, a great sinner, and a hater of Śiva; of this there is no doubt. (17)
For by him poison was swallowed, by whom Dakṣa’s sacrifice was destroyed; by whom the burning of Kāla was performed and the king was liberated.
The sages said: Tell us how the poison was consumed and how the sacrifice of Dakṣa was destroyed; for our curiosity is indeed great. (19)
Sūta said: O Brahmins, in ancient times, Dakṣa gave his daughter, the daughter of Dakṣa (Dākṣāyaṇī), to the high-souled Śaṅkara at the command of Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
For once, that Dakṣa indeed arrived at the Naimiṣa forest; having come there by chance, he was honored by the sages.

Although Mahādeva remained there while being honored with hymns and prostrations by all the gods and asuras, he did not rise up nor offer a greeting; consequently, Dakṣa became enraged and spoke these words.

"Indeed, everywhere all the gods and asuras, as well as the most excellent brahmins, bow down deeply to me with great eagerness. How is it that this high-souled one—like a wicked person, accompanied by spirits and the like, ghosts and demons, a dweller of cremation grounds, and truly shameless—does not now offer salutation to me? (23)
Seeing a brahmin, heretics, wicked men, and those of sinful character become arrogant and intoxicated; such as these must be slain or abandoned by the virtuous. Therefore, I am prepared to curse him.
Having spoken thus, that great ascetic, filled with rage, then addressed Rudra in this manner.

"Let these most excellent of Brahmins now hear my words, for you ought to do this here: since this Rudra has been chosen by me as one excluded from the sacrifice, he is beyond the castes and superior to the castes. (26)
Having heard those words, Śailāda Nandī was indeed filled with rage; he quickly spoke to the highly effulgent Dakṣa, who had been cursed by him.
Nandin said: "How has my lord Maheśa been made outside the sacrifice? For by the mere remembrance of him, these sacrifices indeed become fruitful. (28)
How is it that he—by whose name sacrifices, charity, austerity, and various sacred fords are purified—is now cursed? (29)

"O evil-minded Dakṣa, this [Rudra] has been cursed by you in vain due to your Brahminical fickleness; for how can he, by whom this entire universe is protected and who is the Great Soul of all, be cursed? O sinner, lowest of Brahmins, this one is Rudra! (30)
Thus rebuked by Nandin, Prajāpati Dakṣa, filled with rage, then cursed Nandin.
All of you have indeed received boons from Rudra and are thoroughly outside the Vedic fold; you have been cursed by those following the Vedic path and likewise abandoned by the great seers.
Engaged in the doctrines of heretics and excluded from the conduct of the learned, these Kālamukhas are indeed skull-bearers (kapālins) addicted to drinking. || 33 ||
Thus were the servants of Śiva cursed by Dakṣa at that time; then Nandin, becoming enraged, proceeded to curse Dakṣa.
"O Brahmin, we virtuous servants of Śiva have been cursed by you in vain due to your brahmanical fickleness; I now bestow a curse upon you. (35)
"You are devoted to the mere recitation of the Vedas, asserting that there is nothing else; you are slaves to desire, intent upon heaven, and possessed by greed and delusion. (36)
And placing the Veda before them, Brahmins who officiate for Śūdras will become impoverished and will always be intent upon accepting gifts.
"Some Brahmins will become Brahmarākṣasas. Lomaśa said: "Those Brahmins were cursed by that Nandin, who was exceedingly enraged. (38)
Then, having heard the words of Nandin, Sadāśiva, as if smiling, spoke these sweet words, which were both enlightening and appropriate.
Mahādeva said: You ought never to direct anger toward Brāhmaṇas; for these Brāhmaṇas are indeed gurus, always devoted to the discourse of the Vedas.
The Veda is directly composed of mantras and is intensely composed of hymns (sūktas); for the Self of all embodied beings is indeed established within the hymn.

Therefore, those who know the Self are not to be censured; for I am the Self alone, and not anything else. Who is this? Who are you? And where indeed am I? For why have the twice-born been cursed? (42)

Abandoning the construction of conceptual proliferation, O Mahāmati, become a Buddha; having turned away from it through the knowledge of reality, remain established in yourself, free from anger and the like. (43)
Thus enlightened by that supreme lord Śambhu, Śailāda, the great ascetic, became devoted to discernment; having united with Śiva, he was flooded with supreme bliss. || 44 ||
For Dakṣa also, overcome with rage and surrounded by the sages, went to his own abode; there he entered, still filled with wrath.

Abandoning supreme faith, he became devoted to censuring the worshippers of Śiva; indeed, that lowest of men approached all the great sages and reviled the god Śarva, never becoming peaceful at any time. (46)
Lomaśa said: Once, a great sacrifice was commenced by him; then all were invited there by that ascetic who had been initiated for the rite.
Various sages, including Vasiṣṭha and others, assembled there: Agastya, Kaśyapa, Atri, Vāmadeva, and likewise Bhṛgu.
The venerable Dadhīca, Vyāsa, Bharadvāja, and Gautama—these and many other great sages assembled there. || 3 ||
Likewise, all the hosts of gods, the world-protectors, and others—the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and the throngs of Apsarases—[were there]. || 4 ||
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was brought from the seven worlds, and likewise Viṣṇu was brought from Vaikuṇṭha toward Maru.
For the radiant Lord of the Gods was brought there together with Indrāṇī, as was Candra with Rohiṇī, and Varuṇa with his beloved.
Kubera was mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot, and Māruta (the Wind-god) was mounted upon a deer; Pāvaka (the Fire-god) was mounted upon a goat, and Nirṛti was mounted upon a ghost.
All these twice-born ones arrived at the sacrificial enclosure; they were all received with hospitality by that evil-minded Dakṣa.
The palaces were highly precious, brilliantly radiant, and vast; they were divine structures fashioned with great skill by the high-souled Tvaṣṭṛ.
They were all stationed upon those celestial abodes according to their pleasure.
While that great sacrifice was being performed at the holy site of Kanakhala, Bhrigu and other ascetics rich in penance were appointed by him as the officiating priests.

Then Dakṣa, joined with the initiation ceremony, having performed the auspicious rites of the marriage-thread, accompanied by his wife and the Brahmins who had performed the necessary purificatory rites for him, [proceeded]. || 12 ||
Then, surrounded on all sides by his friends, he was honored with great magnanimity; in that interval, Dadhīci spoke these words there.

Dadhīci said: "These lords of the gods, these most eminent sages, and the guardians of the worlds have all assembled before you; nevertheless, this sacrifice does not shine at all without that high-souled wielder of the Pināka bow."
That very ancient man, the bull-bannered, blue-throated one with matted locks—the one by whom all auspicious things have arisen and whom the great sages praise—is not seen here. 15.
O Dakṣa, those very things which are inauspicious become auspicious when undertaken by Tryambaka; for even the most inauspicious things immediately become highly auspicious through him.
Therefore, you yourself must perform the invocation; it must be done swiftly by Parameṣṭhin, by Śakra, and by the powerful Viṣṇu.
For everyone must indeed go to where the god Maheśvara resides.
Bring him back with haste, accompanied by Dākṣāyaṇī; through that yogi Śambhu, everything shall become exceedingly pure.
Since by his remembrance and the utterance of his name all merit shall be attained, therefore the Bull-bannered Lord should be brought [to mind] with every effort.
Having heard those words of his, the evil-minded one said with a laugh: "Viṣṇu is indeed the root of the gods, wherein eternal dharma resides. (21)
He in whom the Vedas, the sacrifices, and all various ritual acts are established—he is that very Viṣṇu who has come here.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived from Satyaloka together with the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, and various Āgamas.
Likewise, the king of the gods himself has come along with the hosts of gods; and likewise you, O sages free from all stain, have arrived.
All those who are worthy of sacrifice and peaceful have assembled here; you are all knowers of the truth of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, and all are firm in your vows.
And what need have we here even for Rudra? O Brahmins, the maiden was indeed given away by me when urged by Brahmā. (26)
For he is of no noble lineage, O Brahmins; he is ruined, his beloved is always lost, and he is the singular, insurmountable lord of ghosts, spirits, and ghouls. || 27 ||
Self-conceited, foolish, arrogant, yet pretending to be silent, and full of envy—he is unfit for this task; indeed, he was not brought here by me now.
Therefore, O twice-born one, you must not speak such words again; all of you must ensure that my great sacrifice is made fruitful.
Having heard these words of his, Dadhīci spoke this speech: || 30 ||
Dadhīci said: "For all these best of sages and gods of purified souls, this great calamity has arisen because of that Great-souled One's absence."
"A great destruction will also immediately befall those residing here. Having spoken thus, that Dadhīca departed all alone.
He departed quickly from Dakṣa’s sacrificial enclosure for his own hermitage; once the sage had gone out, Dakṣa, laughing, spoke these words: || 33 ||
The hero named Dadhīci, beloved of Śiva, has departed; while the dull-witted, who are possessed by evil thoughts, delight in falsehood and are wicked. (34)
Those who are outside the Vedas and of evil conduct must be abandoned here in this rite; for you all, led by Viṣṇu, are merely devoted to the verbal recitations of the Vedas.
"O Brahmins, may you make my sacrifice fruitful without delay. Then all of them, together with the ṛṣis, performed the sacrificial rite for the gods.
In the meantime, on that Gandhamādana mountain, she was surrounded by her female companions in a celestial chariot within a fountain-house.
Then the great goddess Dākṣāyaṇī, situated within the celestial chariot, engaged in various sports by the thousands, such as playing with balls and other games.
Then, while the goddess was absorbed in play, the great virtuous lady saw the Lord Soma proceeding to the sacrifice accompanied by Rohiṇī.
"Where will this Candra go? Vijayā, ask him quickly! Thus addressed by her, the goddess Vijayā questioned him as was appropriate. (40)
He related all of that, beginning with the sacrifice of Dakṣa; having heard it, the goddess Vijayā was quickly filled with agitation and recounted everything exactly as it had been told by Śaśin.
Reflecting upon the cause, the Goddess thought: "Why does she not call out? My father Dakṣa and my mother—why have they forgotten me now? (42)
Having made a firm resolve and left my friends there, I have now come before Śaṅkara to ask him about the cause today. (43)
Then he beheld that three-eyed one stationed in the midst of the assembly hall, surrounded by all his attendants, Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and the others.
Bāṇa, Bhṛṅgin, as well as Nandin, Śailāda of great asceticism, Mahākāla, Mahācaṇḍa, Mahāmuṇḍa, and Mahāśiras; || 45 ||
Dhūmrākṣa, Dhūmraketu, and likewise Dhūmrapāda—these and many other hosts followed Rudra. || 46 ||
Some were terrifying and fierce, while others were headless trunks; some had bulging eyes, and others were devoid of chests. 47.
And all of them, numbering in the hundreds, were of such a nature: they were clad in animal skins, adorned with masses of matted hair, and all were decorated with rudrākṣa beads.

With their senses conquered and free from passion, all were enemies of the objects of the senses; surrounded by all these, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was seen by her seated upon a most wonderful throne.
With her mind captivated, she suddenly went into the presence of Śiva; her beloved was placed upon his lap by Śiva, who was filled with affection. (50)
Addressed with words of love and preceded by great respect, she said: "O slender-waisted one, tell me quickly: what is the purpose of your visit? (51)
Thus addressed by him at that time, the dark-eyed woman replied.
Satyuvāca said: "O Lord of the gods, O Master, why does your going to my father’s great sacrifice not please you? Tell me all of that. (53)
O Mahādeva, this indeed is the duty of friends: that they should form associations with one another which increase the joy of their friends. (54)
Therefore, O Sadāśiva, by all means go today to my father’s sacrificial enclosure at my word, even though you have not been invited.
Having heard those words of hers, he spoke these truthful words: "O blessed lady, you must not go to Dakṣa’s sacrifice."
All those who were proud toward him—the gods, serpents, and kinnaras—have undoubtedly come here to the sacrifice of your father. (57)
O fair-browed one, those who go to another's house uninvited incur an insult that is worse than death. (58)
"Even Indra would fall into insignificance upon reaching the temple of others; therefore, O auspicious one, you must not go to Dakṣa’s sacrifice."
Having been addressed thus by that high-souled Maheśa, she, the best among those skilled in speech, spoke these words filled with wrath.

For sacrifice is truth in this world, and you are that sacrifice, O Lord of the foremost gods. Therefore, you have been summoned today by my father, who has witnessed your deeds. I wish to know all of that—the disposition of that evil-minded one.
Therefore, I shall go this very day to my father’s sacrificial enclosure; grant me your permission, O Lord, God of gods, Master of the world. (62)
Thus addressed by that goddess, the Blessed Lord Rudra himself—the Blessed One who perceives all, the seer, and the creator of beings—replied. (63)
The Lord of Gods, Maheśa, the bestower of all perfections, said to her: "Go, O Goddess, with haste at my command, O lady of virtuous vows. (64)
Having mounted this Nandin, sixty thousand fierce Gaṇas, accompanied by various hosts, departed at the command of Śiva.
Surrounded by those hosts, the Goddess went to her father’s abode; beholding that entire army, Mahādeva was greatly amazed.
Then Mahadeva, the scorcher of foes, unperturbed, sent costly ornaments after them to the Goddess.

When the Goddess had indeed gone to her father’s house, the Lord Maheśa reflected upon everything and returned to his own city, thinking: "Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, being insulted by her father, will not return. (68)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Goddess Satī at Dakṣa’s Sacrifice," in the Kedāra-khaṇḍa of the first section, the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Lomaśa said: The daughter of Dakṣa went to that place where the great sacrifice had taken place; having gone to her father’s abode, which was filled with many wonders.
Then the highly fortunate gods, having descended from their own seats and gazed upon the world of the gods, stood at the gate of Nandī.
Having seen her mother, father, friends, relatives, and kinsmen, she joyfully saluted her father and mother.
Then the goddess spoke words appropriate to the occasion: "Why was the most auspicious Śambhu not invited by you? (4)

By whom all this entire universe, including the moving and the unmoving, is purified; he who is the sacrifice, the best among those who know the sacrifice, the limb of the sacrifice, and the sacrificial fee.
All substances, such as mantras and the like, as well as all offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya), consist of that [essence]; everything performed without it shall become impure.
"O father, how indeed can a sacrifice proceed without Śambhu? O sire, how have these arrived together with Brahmā?"
O Bhṛgu, you do not know; O high-minded Kaśyapa, you alone are distinguished among us; O Śakra, what has been done by you today? (8)
O Viṣṇu, you know Mahādeva, the Supreme Lord; O Brahmā, do you not know the prowess of Mahādeva?
Formerly, having become five-faced, you were arrogant toward Sadāśiva; he made you four-faced, and you have forgotten that wonder.
It was in the Dāruvana forest where the Lord formerly went begging for alms; at that time, he was cursed as a mendicant by you, his friends. 11.
And even though Rudra has been cursed by you, how have you forgotten him, by whose mere limb the entire world of moving and non-moving beings was filled?
Indeed, at that very moment, the entire world became the *liṅga*; for all the gods, including Indra, call it a *liṅga* because of its nature as a place of dissolution (*laya*).
Since all the gods have arisen from that god who wields the trident, that god, who has reached the end of the Vedas, cannot be known by you.
Having heard her words, Dakṣa, becoming enraged, spoke these words: "What is the use of your speaking at length? There is no business here for you at this time. (15)
"Go or stay, O blessed lady; for what purpose have you come? Indeed, your husband is inauspicious and ill-omened, O slender-waisted one. (16)
"O auspicious lady, O sweet-spoken one, he is of low birth, outside the Vedic fold, and a lord of ghosts, spirits, and piśācas; therefore, he was not invited for the sake of the sacrifice. (17)
"O lady of beautiful hips, you have been given by me, a sinner of dull intellect, to Rudra—who is ignorant of the truth, arrogant, and evil-minded. (18)
"Therefore, having abandoned this body, be at peace, O lady of pure smiles. Thus was Satī, who is honored by the world, addressed by Dakṣa at that time.
Seeing her father filled with reproach, the goddess became exceedingly enraged; she then reflected, "How shall I go to the palace? (20)
"Desiring to see Śaṅkara, what shall I say when questioned by him? Both he who reviles Mahādeva and he who listens to one being reviled go to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (21)
Therefore, I shall abandon this body and enter the fire.
Reflecting thus, she who had spoken the name "Śiva-Rudra," overcome by humiliation, entered the fire.
The space between the quarters was pervaded by a great cry of "Alas! Alas! All of them had ascended the platform, densely packed and covered with weapons.
With their own weapons they struck themselves and cut their own bodies; some, full of longing, took their own heads in the palms of their hands.
Waving the lights in haste, they were reduced to ashes; then they all spoke thus and roared most terrifyingly.
Those most terrifying beings cut their own limbs with blows from weapons; thus they met their destruction along with Dākṣāyaṇī at that time.
There were two ayutas of hosts there, and it was like a marvel; all those sages, gods led by Indra, together with the hosts of Maruts. (28)
Then all the Aśvins and the guardians of the worlds became silent; some, meanwhile, were praying from all sides to Viṣṇu, the most excellent one.
When the sacrifice of that evil-minded Dakṣa, that mere Brahmin in name, had thus come to pass, the sages were seized with fear.
In the meantime, O Brahmins, all these deeds of Dakṣa were related by the high-souled Nārada.
Having heard those words issuing from the mouth of Nārada, the Lord became exceedingly enraged, as if springing up from his seat.
And having loosened his matted locks, Rudra, the agent of the world's destruction, wrathfully slapped them upon the summit of the mountain.
And from that striking arose the highly illustrious Vīrabhadra; likewise Kālī was born, surrounded by millions of spirits.
From the very sigh of the high-souled Rudra in his anger, a hundred fevers and thirteen types of *sannipāta* disorders were born. (35)
Vīrabhadra informed Rudra, whose prowess is fierce: "O Lord, what is your business? Tell me quickly what must be done. (36)
Thus addressed, Lord Rudra quickly dispatched him, saying: "Go, O hero of mighty arms, and destroy the sacrifice of Dakṣa."

Having placed the command of the trident-bearing God of gods upon his head, the heroic Vīrabhadra, highly effulgent and beloved by Kālikā, set out toward Dakṣa’s sacrifice, surrounded by all the bhūtas.
At that very moment, ill omens suddenly appeared; a harsh wind then blew, filled with pebbles. (39)
The god rained down blood, and the quarters of the sky were shrouded in darkness; many meteors fell by the thousands upon the earth. (40)
The gods and others beheld such portents of death; Dakṣa, overcome with fear, sought refuge in Viṣṇu.
Protect me, protect me, O Great Viṣṇu! For you are our supreme preceptor; you are the sacrifice, O best of gods, so liberate me from fear. || 42 ||
Being thus entreated by Dakṣa, Madhusūdana said: "I must provide protection for you; of this there is no doubt."

Where those unworthy of worship are worshipped and he who is worthy of worship is not worshipped—there, O one ignorant of Dharma, three calamities prevail: famine, pestilence, and drought; and through the disregard for the Lord, everything shall become fruitless.
Where those unworthy of worship are worshipped, and he who is worthy of worship is not worshipped, there three things prevail: famine, death, and fear. (45)
Therefore, with every effort, the bull-bannered Lord must be honored; because you have failed to honor Maheśa, a great danger has approached you.
Right now we have all ceased to be powerful; this is due solely to your misconduct, there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (47)
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, Dakṣa became lost in thought; with a pale face, he remained silent, standing upon the ground.
The mighty-armed Vīrabhadra was impelled by Rudra himself; so too were Kālī, Kātyāyanī, Īśānā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Muṇḍamardinī.
Bhadrakālī, as well as Bhadrā, Tvaritā, and Vaiṣṇavī; together with the nine Durgās and others, there was a great host of spirits.
Śākinīs and Ḍākinīs, as well as Bhūtas, Pramathas, and Guhyakas, and likewise the circle of Yoginīs, accompanied by the sixty-four [deities]. || 51 ||

They suddenly emerged there at the sacrificial enclosure, which was of great splendor; all of them possessed the prowess of Hara, accompanied by Vīrabhadra, having ten arms, three eyes, matted hair, and adorned with the ornaments of Rudra. || 52 ||
All these attendants of Śaṅkara are of the nature of Rudra; they all have five faces, blue throats, and hold weapons in their hands.
All were endowed with the prowess of Hara; they possessed ten arms, three eyes, matted hair, and were adorned with the ornaments of Rudra, and were draped with umbrellas and chowries.
All of them bear crescent moons, and all possess great majesty; all are mounted upon bulls, and all are adorned with their characteristic attire and ornaments.

Surrounded by the lords of serpents, possessing a thousand arms, three eyes, and terrifying power, that high-souled Vīrabhadra, formidable and awe-inspiring, then approached the sacrifice accompanied by these [attendants].
His chariot was drawn by a thousand pairs of horses and also by a million lions.
In the same way, many armored lions served as his bodyguards, along with tigers, crocodiles, fish, and elephants by the thousands; there were likewise various kinds of umbrellas and chowries.
Held aloft upon their heads on all sides and in every direction, there arose the great sounds of kettledrums, conchs of various tones, drums, trumpets, and many kinds of horns.
Then they all played those very same solid and hollow instruments; all were intent on melodious singing, and all were players of the mṛdaṅga drum.
Engaged in various dances, they stood before Vīrabhadra; endowed with immeasurable splendor, they roared amidst the sounds of battle-instruments.
By that great roar, the three worlds were made to resound; thus all the Gaṇas, impelled by Rudra, arrived.
And for the purpose of destroying Dakṣa’s sacrificial enclosure, the assailants covered the sky with dust and the quarters of the horizon with darkness.
The earth, together with its mountains and forests, shook along with its seven islands; seeing that great wonder which portended the destruction of the world, they were struck with awe.
All the gods, Daityas, and night-stalkers rose up simultaneously; they beheld the terrifying army of Rudra approaching.
Some arrived from the earth, some came from the sky, and others likewise came having encompassed the cardinal and intermediate directions.

"Indeed, all these are infinite and inexhaustible; they are heroes equal to Rudra in battle. Seeing that army thus constituted and surrounded by the Rudras, they all spoke in amazement: 'Today, let us go forth with weapons in hand. (67)
For Indra is mounted upon an elephant, Sadāgati (Vāyu) is mounted upon a deer, and Yama is mounted upon a buffalo, accompanied by the staff of Yama.
Kubera was mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot, and Varuṇa (Pāśin) upon a crocodile; Agni was mounted upon a goat, and Nirṛti upon a corpse.
Likewise, other hosts of gods, as well as yakṣas, cāraṇas, and guhyakas, mounted their respective vehicles and set out.
Then Dakṣa, seeing the exertion of his own people and with a tearful face, prostrated himself on the ground like a staff and addressed them all.
"By your very power this great sacrifice has been commenced by me; for the successful completion of this virtuous deed, you, who possess great splendor, are the ultimate authority. (72)
O Viṣṇu, you are the direct witness of action and the protector of sacrifices; O Mādhava, you are devoted to Brahman and to Dharma, whose essence is the Veda.
"Therefore, protection must be provided for this sacrifice of the great lord Dakṣa. Having heard the words of Dakṣa, Madhusūdana spoke:
"I must provide protection for the preservation of the Dharma; that truth was indeed spoken by you, yet there has been a transgression of it. (75)
"Did you not remember what was said by you, the ever-auspicious one, today at the sacrifice in the Nimiṣa field of Naimiṣa? (76)
This Rudra, who is of great splendor, whose form is sacrifice, and who is Sadāśiva—O fool, that he was excluded from the sacrifice was a result of your evil counsel.
And due to the wrath of Rudra, who indeed here is capable of protecting you? O Brahmin, I do not see anyone who can protect you, for you are truly evil-minded.
"O evil-minded one, you do not perceive what is action and what is inaction; action alone shall always be efficacious. (79)
Know that action is possessed of a Lord, for it arises through His power; indeed, there can be no giver of the fruit of action other than the Lord.
And for those devotees of the Lord who are peaceful and whose minds are fixed upon Him, Sadāśiva always bestows the fruit of their actions.
Relying solely on ritual action and devoted to the doctrine of no Supreme Lord (nirīśvara), those people go to hell even after performing hundreds of millions of sacrifices.
Furthermore, bound again and again in birth after birth by the nooses consisting of karma, those who are of the very nature of karma are cooked in the hells.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Vīrabhadra," in the Kedāra-khaṇḍa of the first section, the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Lomaśa said: Having heard the words spoken by Viṣṇu, Dakṣa spoke these words: "O Madhusūdana, you have rendered the Vedas invalid."
Having abandoned Vedic ritual action, how can one attain the state of having a Lord? O Mahāviṣṇu, let that be told by which Dharma is established.
Addressed by Dakṣa, Mahāviṣṇu spoke, consoling him: "The Vedas have as their subject matter the three qualities (guṇas); they cannot be otherwise."
How can the rites prescribed in the Vedas bear fruit without the Lord? Indeed, they would be entirely fruitless.
"Therefore, with every effort, take refuge in the Lord. While Govinda was speaking thus, an ocean of an army arrived; the gods then beheld it, resembling Vīrabhadra himself.
Then Indra, laughing at Viṣṇu who was intent on self-praise, wielder of the thunderbolt, became desirous of fighting along with the gods.
For he had been swiftly incited by Bhṛgu, who was intent on his expulsion; then the Gaṇas, accompanied by their own hosts, fought with the gods.
They struck one another with arrows, spears, and maces; and many conchs were blown during that great festival of battle.
Likewise, kettledrums, tabors, ḍiṇḍimas, and other instruments resounded; praised by that great noise, the gods, together with the world-protectors, then struck down those servants of Śiva.
Some were struck down by swords, others crushed by maces; all the hosts, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, were utterly defeated by the gods.
Indeed, by the power of Bhṛgu’s mantra, Indra, the guardians of the world such as Dyaus, and those hosts were turned away from him in that very instant.
Then, for the sake of the sacrifice to the gods and for the satisfaction of the one initiated, Bhṛgu, the performer of sacrifices, carried out their eradication.
At that very moment, the gods indeed became victorious; seeing the defeat of his own people, Vīrabhadra was filled with wrath.

Having placed those very spirits, ghosts, and piśācas behind him, and having brought forward those mounted upon bulls, the exceedingly powerful one himself took up a sharp trident and struck them down in battle.
The gods, yakṣas, piśācas, guhyakas, and likewise the rākṣasas—all those hosts struck the gods with blows from their tridents.
Some were cut in two with swords, others were crushed with mallets, and some on the field of battle were hacked into pieces with battle-axes.
Pierced by spears by the hundreds, and some cut into pieces—thus utterly defeated, they all became intent on flight.
Having embraced one another, they too departed for heaven; only Indra and the other world-protectors remained anxious, questioning Bṛhaspati as to how victory might be ours.
Then Bṛhaspati quickly spoke this to the Lord of the Gods. Bṛhaspati said: "That which was previously spoken by Viṣṇu has indeed come true today."
If there were some Lord who is the creator of karma that takes the form of its fruit, even he would have to resort to another creator; for he has no power over one who is not his own creation.

Neither all mantras nor medicinal herbs, neither malevolent rites nor worldly practices; neither ritual acts nor the Vedas, and likewise not even the two systems of Mīmāṃsā [can protect one]. || 21 ||
He can be known through devotion; indeed, Sadāśiva is to be known through exclusive devotion, supreme tranquility, and perfect contentment. || 22 ||
By him everything that exists—the world consisting of pleasure and pain—is brought into being; nevertheless, I shall speak with a view toward what ought and ought not to be done. (23)
O Indra, having become a fool today along with the world-protectors, and having arrived as a fool, what will you do now? || 24 ||
These hosts, the companions of Rudra, are supremely beautiful; when enraged, O highly fortunate one, they leave nothing remaining.
Having thus heard the words of Bṛhaspati, all those celestial inhabitants—the world-protectors and great lords—fell into deep reflection.
Then Vīrabhadra, surrounded by his hosts, spoke vehemently: "You have all come here for the sake of slaughter out of sheer folly. (27)
"I shall give you avadānas for your satisfaction," he said, and in haste, filled with rage, he then struck them with sharp arrows.
Struck by those arrows, they all fled in the ten directions.
When the world-protectors had departed and the gods had fled, Vīrabhadra, accompanied by his hosts, arrived at the sacrificial enclosure.
Then all those sages, desiring to make a representation to the Lord of lords, suddenly spoke thus to Janārdana: || 31 ||
"Protect the sacrifice of Dakṣa, for you are the sacrifice itself; of this there is no doubt. Having heard these words of the sages, Janārdana [replied].
Desirous of fighting, standing ready for battle, the mighty-armed Vīrabhadra, who is Viṣṇu himself and the illuminator of the supreme self, spoke these words to Keśava: || 33 ||
Why have you come here, O Viṣṇu, knowing him to be of great strength? Tell me, how will you conquer him by taking recourse to the side of Dakṣa?

"O sinless one, have you not seen what was done by the daughter of Dakṣa? You too have come to the sacrifice of Dakṣa for the purpose of being offered as a victim; O mighty-armed one, I shall offer you up as a victim as well. (35)
Having spoken thus and first prostrated before Viṣṇu, who possessed a form similar to his own, Vīrabhadra stood before him and then addressed these words to Viṣṇu.

"As Śambhu is, so indeed are you; of this there is no doubt for me. Nevertheless, O mighty-armed one, since you stand before me desiring to fight, I shall send you to the state from which there is no return, if you persist with your own self."
Having heard those words of the wise Vīrabhadra, the god Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, spoke while laughing.
Viṣṇu said: "O high-minded one, you are born from the splendor of Rudra and you are pure; for this reason, he has previously entreated you again and again for the sake of the sacrifice. (39)
I am dependent on my devotees, and that Great Lord Maheśvara is likewise; for that very reason, [he did not attend] Dakṣa’s sacrifice here.
I have come, O Vīrabhadra, born from the wrath of Rudra; I shall restrain you, or you shall restrain me.
When Govinda had spoken thus, that mighty-armed one laughed and, bowing down with humility, said this to Janārdana: || 42 ||
For as Śiva is, so indeed are you; and as you are, so is Śiva. We are all your servants, or rather, the servants of Śaṅkara.
Having heard those words of his, the Imperishable One, the Supreme Lord, smiled and uttered this great mantra of Viṣṇu: "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ. (44)
"Fight with me without hesitation, O mighty-armed one! Being filled by your weapons, I shall go to my own abode. (45)
Having said "So be it," that heroic Vīrabhadra of great strength took up supreme weapons and roared with lion-like cries.
Viṣṇu also blew his conch with a great roar; hearing that, those gods who had fled, having abandoned the battle, returned once more.
Then all the world-protectors, together with Indra, formed a battle array; thereupon Nandin was struck by Indra with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
Śakra was struck in the chest with a trident by Nandī, and Bhṛṅgī was struck by Vāyu, while Vāyu was struck by Bhṛṅgin.
Equipped with a trident having white blades and wielding a staff, the powerful Mahākāla engaged in battle with Yama.
And having encountered Kubera himself, the lord of the Kūṣmāṇḍas engaged in battle with Varuṇa, as did the exceedingly powerful Muṇḍa.
Chanda, being exceedingly powerful, encountered the Nairṛta and fought with supreme strength, as if causing the three worlds to marvel.
The great leader Bhairava, joined by the circle of Yoginīs, fought with supreme weapons, emulating the god of the Nairṛtas.
Having torn asunder all the gods, he drank their wonderful blood; likewise the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) and others—the bhūtas, pramathas, and guhyakas.
The Sākinīs, Ḍākinīs, the fierce Raudrās, as well as the Navadurgās, the Yoginīs, the Yātudhānīs, and the Kūṣmāṇḍas and others, roared, drank blood, and devoured much flesh.
Then, beholding his army being devoured, the King of the Gods himself left Nandin behind and rushed toward Vīrabhadra.
Vīrabhadra, having left Viṣṇu, took his stand against the Lord of the Gods; a terrible battle ensued between them, like that between Mercury and Mars.
When Śakra, filled with haste, desired to slay Vīrabhadra, he then indeed filled Śakra, who was mounted upon his elephant, with arrows.
Vīrabhadra, possessed by rage, was difficult to restrain and possessed great strength; then he was swiftly struck by Indra with his hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
As he prepared to swallow Vāsava along with his elephant and his thunderbolt, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the beings watching there.
Then Viṣṇu, seeing Vīrabhadra—who had become such a being and was desirous of killing Purandara—stood before him, ready to strike.
Keeping Śakra at his back, he then indeed fought; at that time, there was a supreme battle between Vīrabhadra and Viṣṇu.
Then the two fought with various kinds of weapons and missiles; moreover, Śakra, who was skilled in battle, beheld Nandin once again.
A most tumultuous duel took place between the gods and the Pramathas; all those Pramathas, being crushed by the gods, fled from the battlefield.
Seeing the hosts turned away, all those diseases that had arisen from the wrath of Rudra fled in great haste, and the gods likewise ran away.
Seeing the gods afflicted by the fevers, Viṣṇu, as if laughing, seized those gods one by one, capturing them alive.
Then the gods, having summoned Aśvinī, gave them wages with great effort after calculating [the task], so that they might destroy diseases; for he was possessed of excellent intelligence. (67)
Then, having subdued all those fevers, the combined humors (sannipāta), and other malevolent spirits, the two Aśvins, filled with joy, made the gods free from fever and rejoiced for a long time.
By them the circle of Yoginīs was conquered and Bhairava was thrown into turmoil; with sharp-pointed arrows, they also struck down the hosts of spirits.
Beholding his army driven away by the gods and fallen upon the earth, Vīrabhadra, overcome with rage, addressed these words to Viṣṇu: || 70 ||
"You are a hero, O mighty-armed one; for you are indeed the protector of the gods. Fight me with diligence if such is your mind. (71)
Having spoken thus and approached Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra rained down sharp arrows upon him.
Then the Blessed One struck Vīrabhadra with his discus; seeing the discus approaching, Vīrabhadra swallowed it in that very instant.
Seeing the discus swallowed, Viṣṇu, the conqueror of enemy cities, wiped his mouth and swallowed it back again.

Then the one of great majesty, the sole lord of the world, took his own discus and ascended to heaven; and Viṣṇu, having understood all this—that which was done by others was difficult to withstand—was successful.
Lomaśa said: When Viṣṇu had departed, all the gods together with the sages were then utterly defeated by the hosts, as were all those who subsist upon sacrifices.
He caused Bhṛgu to fall and had his beard plucked out; he uprooted the teeth of the twice-born Pūṣan, thereby performing a deformed and cruel act.
There, the Svadhā offerings were mocked and the sages were also mocked; filled with rage, they rained excrement upon the sacrificial fire.
Then the hosts, filled with rage, made it impossible to describe; Dakṣa, indeed, having entered within the sacrificial altar, was seized by great fear.
Perceiving that he was hiding there, he, filled with rage, brought him forth; seizing him by the cheeks, he struck off his head with a sword.
Considering that head to be impenetrable, the powerful Vīrabhadra then stepped upon its shoulder with his feet and crushed it at the neck.

Then, as the head of the evil-minded Dakṣa was being severed by the wise Vīrabhadra from his body while it was being torn apart, that head was offered as a well-offered oblation into the blazing sacrificial pit.
And whatever other sages, gods, ancestors, yakṣas, and rākṣasas there were, all of them, harassed by the hosts, fled in every direction.
All the hosts of the moon and sun, as well as the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, were all shaken; indeed, they too were overwhelmed by those hosts.
Having gone to Satyaloka, Brahmā, afflicted by grief for his son, reflected with an undistracted mind: "What indeed must be done? What is the task to be performed today? (10)
With a tormented mind, the Grandfather found no peace; he learned through diligent effort of all the evil deeds committed by that sinner.
The one of great splendor, mounted upon a swan and accompanied by all the gods, set his mind on going toward Mount Kailāsa.
Having entered that best of mountains, he beheld Sadāśiva, Rudra dwelling in solitude, accompanied by Śailāda.
Beholding him with matted hair, endowed with splendor, and difficult for even the Vedāṅgas to comprehend, Brahmā became overcome with agitation.
Falling prostrate upon the ground like a staff, intent on seeking forgiveness and touching His lotus feet with the tips of his four crowns, he began to offer praise to Śiva, the Supreme Soul.
Brahmā said: Salutations to Rudra, the peaceful one, the Brahman, the Supreme Soul; for you are indeed the creator of the creators of the universe, the Sustainer, and the Great-Grandfather.
Salutations to the great Rudra, the blue-throated creator; to the universe, the seed of the universe, and the cause of joy for the world. || 17 ||
You are the syllable Oṃ, you are the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, and the initiator of all undertakings; you are the sacrifice, you are the sacrificial rite, and the promoter of sacrifices.
You alone are the protector of all performers of sacrifice; you are the refuge, O Mahādeva, for all living beings, O Lord. Protect, protect me, O Mahādeva, who am tormented by grief for my son! 19.
Mahādeva said: Listen attentively to my words, O Grandfather; this destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice was not brought about by me at all.
O Brahmana, Daksha was slain by his own karma; of this there is no doubt.
One should never perform an action that causes affliction to others; O Supreme Lord, what one does to others will eventually happen to oneself.
Having spoken thus, Rudra, accompanied by Brahmā and the gods, then went to the Kanakhala tīrtha, the sacrificial ground of Prajāpati.
Then Rudra beheld what had been done by Vīrabhadra, as well as Svāhā, Svadhā, Pūṣan, and Bhṛgu, the best among the wise.
Then all the other sages and likewise the ancestors, as well as many others there—the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras—[were present]. (25)
Some were torn apart, some were plucked out, and some even died upon the field of battle. || 26 ||
Seeing Śambhu arrived, Vīrabhadra, together with his attendants, stood before Sadāśiva, performing a prostration with his staff-like body.
Seeing the mighty Vīrabhadra standing before him, Rudra spoke these words with a smile: "O hero, what indeed has been done by you? (28)
"O, quickly bring Dakṣa here, by whom this was done; O dear one, he who has caused such a disturbance at the sacrifice as this, for which such is the fruit. (29)
Thus addressed by Śaṅkara, Vīrabhadra, filled with haste, brought the headless trunk and then cast it before Śambhu.
Then the high-minded Vīrabhadra was addressed by Śaṅkara himself: "By whom has the head of this evil-minded Dakṣa been carried away? (31)
"O hero, I shall grant life even to this crooked one now. When he was addressed thus by Śaṅkara, Vīrabhadra spoke again:
O Śaṅkara, at that very moment my head was offered into the fire; O Śambhu, what remains is the head of the sacrificial animal, with its distorted face.
Knowing this, Rudra then cast the head of the beast—deformed, possessed of a beard, and terrifying—upon the trunk.
By the grace of Śaṅkara, Dakṣa regained his life; then, seeing Rudra before him, Dakṣa, filled with shame, bowed down and praised Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world. (35)

Dakṣa said: I bow to the God who grants boons, the most excellent; I bow to the Lord of gods, the eternal; I bow to Hara, the sovereign of the gods; I bow to Śambhu, the sole kinsman of the world. (36)

I bow to the Lord of the Universe, whose form is the universe, the eternal Brahman, whose nature is one’s own self. I bow to all that exists as my own being; I am prostrate before the most excellent and the most venerable. 37.
Lomaśa said: Praised by Dakṣa, Rudra spoke, laughing privately.
Hara said: O best of the twice-born, virtuous people always worship me in four ways: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom. (39)
Therefore, all those who possess knowledge are dear to me; of this there is no doubt. Those who strive to attain me without knowledge are indeed foolish.
For you desire to cross over from saṃsāra by means of action alone. || 41 ||
Neither by the Vedas, nor by gifts, nor by sacrifices, nor by austerity at any time, can foolish men, who are under the sway of karma, attain me. || 42 ||
Therefore, becoming devoted to knowledge and composed in mind, perform your actions; having become equal toward pleasure and pain, be happy forever. || 43 ||
Lomaśa said: Having thus been instructed by that supreme lord Śambhu, Rudra established Dakṣa right there and departed for his own mountain.
Brahmā likewise consoled and enlightened all the great sages, Bhṛgu and the others; in an instant, they became possessors of knowledge.
The grandfather Brahmā then departed for his own abode.
And Dakṣa himself, having attained supreme awakening through those words, became intent on meditation upon Śiva and, being high-minded, performed austerities.
Therefore, with every effort, one should propitiate the Blessed Lord Śiva.
And those men who perform the sweeping of Śiva’s courtyard, having reached the city of Śiva, shall indeed become worthy of the world's veneration and blessed. (49)
Those men who offer a mirror of great luster to Śiva shall become his attendants in the presence of Śiva.
They shall offer chowries to the trident-bearing God of gods; they will become those whose feet are fanned with chowries throughout the three worlds. || 51 ||
Those men who offer lamps in the temple of Mahādeva will become radiant, serving as illuminators for the three worlds.
Those who indeed offer incense to Śiva, the Supreme Self, shall become illustrious and uplift both lineages.
Those men who offer food offerings with devotion before Hari and Hara indeed obtain the fruit of a sacrifice for every single mouthful.
Those best of men who restore a ruined temple of Śiva obtain twice the fruit; of this there is no doubt. || 55 ||

O best of the twice-born, those who construct something new, whether with bricks or even with stone, rejoice in heaven for as long as their stainless fame remains upon the earth; this is the conclusion one must reach.
Furthermore, those wise brahmins who cause a multi-storied temple to be built for Śiva attain the supreme goal.
Those who cleanse and whitewash the temple of Hara, whether it be their own or built by another, they too attain the supreme goal.
Those virtuous men who offer a canopy indeed deliver their entire lineage; having gone to the world of Śiva, they return once more.
And those who hang a bell made of sound in the temple of Śiva will become radiant and famous throughout the three worlds.
Whether once, twice, or thrice a day, one observes that whether wealthy or poor, one is liberated from suffering through happiness. (61)
He who, possessed of faith, worships Śiva as the Supreme Self, having uplifted ten million members of his lineage, rejoices together with Śiva.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between Indradyumna and the high-souled Yama.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Indrasena; he was a heroic ruler of Pratiṣṭhāna who was always fond of hunting.
Always hostile to Brahmins, ever cruel, and constantly intent on satisfying his own palate, that wicked man always nourishes his own life at the expense of the lives of others.
He was excessively lustful for the wives of others and greedy for the wealth of others; by him Brahmins were slain, and he was a constant drinker of liquor.
He was excessively heavy-handed in his punishments and was constantly a thief of gold; all the followers of that evil-minded king were likewise of such a nature.
In this way, that evil-minded one ruled his kingdom in many such ways; then, after a long time, that wicked-minded man met his death.
Then that evil-minded Indrasena, the sinful king, was led by the messengers of Yama and brought into the presence of Yama.
Seen there by Yama standing before Indrasena, he became intent on rising up and bowed his head to Śiva.
Yama, the best among the upholders of dharma, rebuked his messengers; and the King of Dharma, having released Candrasena who was bound with nooses, spoke to him.
Go to the most meritorious worlds and enjoy them, O best of kṣatriyas, as long as Indra remains in heaven and as long as the sun stays in the firmament.
"As long as the five elements endure, so long may you be happy; you are a man of merit, O Great King, for you are a constant devotee of Śiva. (73)
Having heard Yama’s words, Indrasena replied: "I do not know Śiva, for I am indeed a lover of the hunt. (74)
Having heard those words of his, Yama spoke this speech: "Bring it! Strike it!"—this has always been said by you. (75)
O giver of honor, by the ripening of that karma you have always been pure; therefore, go to Mount Kailāsa toward Śaṅkara.
While the high-souled Yama was speaking thus, those followers of Śiva arrived, mounted upon bulls and possessing great radiance.
They have blue throats, ten arms, five faces, and three eyes; they wear matted hair, possess earrings, and have their crests marked by the crescent moon.
Seeing them, Yama, the best among the upholders of dharma, rose up suddenly and then honored all of them, who were like Mahendra himself.

With great haste, they all spoke to Yama, the son of Vivasvat: "O illustrious one, Indrasena of immeasurable luster has arrived here; he is the eternal promoter of the name of the high-souled Rudra. (80)
Having heard their words and being escorted by Yama, Indrasena, seated in his celestial chariot, was indeed dispatched to the abode of Śiva.
Then he was brought there by those most excellent and foremost attendants; indeed, Śambhu then beheld Indrasena of immeasurable luster.
Then Rudra, having risen and approached, embraced the king; having seated Indrasena upon half of his throne, he then spoke to him.
"O best of kings, what should be given? I shall grant you whatever you desire. Having heard these words of Maheśa, the king then shed drops of tears of joy and, out of love, said nothing at all. (84)
Then Maheśa, the Great-Souled One, indeed made him his attendant; he was famous by the name Caṇḍa, the beloved friend of Muṇḍa. || 85 ||
Merely by the utterance of the name of Rudra, the Supreme Self, even the most sinful Indrasena, the lord of men, attained perfection.
By the name "Rahehara," Śiva, the wielder of the discus and the Supreme Soul, has indeed protected many mortals.
No deity other than Maheśa is seen in the three worlds; therefore, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with every effort.
Whether worshipped with leaves, flowers, fruits, or even pure water, Śaṅkara, when honored with karavīra blossoms, shall become the granter of boons. || 89 ||
The *arka* flower is ten times superior to the *karavīra*. By means of sacred ash (*vibhūti*) and other substances, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is sustained. (90)
Since it clings to the courtyard of Śiva, one should always wear it; therefore, O best of the twice-born, listen to the merit that resides in the *tripuṇḍra*.
O best of the twice-born, listen to that merit which removes all sins: a certain thief, a great sinner, was executed by the king's messengers.
Having arrived to devour him, the dog stood upon his head; the protective amulet remained stuck within the gaps between its claws, belonging to that very sinner.
On his forehead fell [the ash], marked with the sign of the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra), which clung solely to his body, devoid of consciousness.
Then, at that time, the thief was led to Kailāsa by the messengers of Rudra; for who can fathom the greatness of the glory of the Great Lord? (95)
There is no doubt that those men of meritorious deeds whose bodies are adorned with ashes and who have the five-syllabled mantra on their lips are indeed Rudras. (96)
Those who wear masses of matted hair and those who are adorned with rudrākṣa beads are indeed Rudras in human form; there is no doubt about this.
Therefore, Sadāśiva should indeed be worshipped constantly by men; at dawn, at midday, and especially at the evening twilight.

By beholding Śambhu at dawn, one’s nocturnal sin is dispelled; by beholding Śambhu at midday, the sins of men accumulated over seven lifetimes go to destruction; and [the merit of] the night is indeed not to be counted.
The two-syllabled name "Śiva" is the destroyer of great sins; this world is sustained by those men from whose mouths it has issued. 100.

Those people who are devoted to sin, even those heretics who hold false doctrines—even they attain the supreme goal when purified by the sound of the drum that has been installed in the courtyard of Śiva by those of meritorious deeds. (101)
That animal whose hide is connected to a drum, a mṛdaṅga, a muraja, or similar instruments placed by men in the temple of Śiva, attains proximity to Śiva; of this there is no doubt. (102)
Therefore, [he saw] woven and stretched-out [cloths], as well as thick and hollow ones; precious chowries, couches, and beds. (103)
One should arrange verses, historical narratives, and songs according to the prescribed rules; these, beginning with the *bahurūpa* hymn, are dear to Śambhu.
Having performed this rite, even sinners go to the world of Śiva; so too do those of virtuous conduct, the great-souled ones who are experts in the worship of Śiva. (105)

Those who have received [the teachings] from the mouth of the Guru and are devoted to the worship of Śiva, and who, having reached a firm conviction, perceive the entire universe as the form of Śiva; || 106 ||

Men belonging to the various castes and stages of life, endowed with right conduct through correct understanding—namely Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other men likewise—[attain their respective goals]. 107.
Even a dog-eater (outcaste) would become most excellent and most beloved to Śambhu; for this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, is presided over by Śambhu. 108.
Therefore, one should especially understand that everything is composed of Śiva, according to the Vedas, the Purāṇas, the Śāstras, and likewise the Upaniṣads.
Śambhu is to be known through various scriptures; there is no doubt in this matter. Sadāśiva is to be worshipped always by those both free from desire and possessed of desire.
Lomaśa said: I shall relate an ancient history, an account of events from the past. Formerly, there was indeed a Vaiśya named Nandī who dwelt in the city of Avantī.
Devoted to the meditation on Śiva, he performed the worship of Śiva; indeed, staying constantly in the penance grove, he worshipped a single Liṅga.
Rising every day at dawn after dawn, Nandin, the beloved of Śiva, became exceedingly devoted to the worship of the Liṅga of Śiva.
Surrounded by Brahmins who were constant masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, he consecrated the Liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) as prescribed.
He became devoted to the worship of the Liṅga according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures; having bathed it, he then honored it with flowers endowed with various wonders.
He worshipped [the deity] continuously with pearls, sapphires, gomedas, as well as lapis lazuli, emeralds, and rubies.
In this manner, the highly fortunate Nandī worshipped that Liṅga, which was situated in a secluded place and endowed with various enjoyments, for many years. || 117 ||
Once there was a Kirāta, addicted to hunting and a harmer of living beings, who was always devoted to the pleasures of the chase and intent upon a lack of discernment. (118)
A sinner of evil conduct, wandering through mountain caves crowded with many beasts of prey, was being struck down here and there. || 119 ||
Wandering in this manner, that Kirāta, a harmer of living beings, arrived by chance at the place where the well-worshipped Liṅga was located.
Looking for water while being severely afflicted by thirst, he then quickly saw a lake in the forest and entered its waters. (121)
Having left all those things, such as the hunting gear, on the bank, that evil-minded man spat out a mouthful of water, drank some water, and departed.
He beheld before him the abode of Śiva, adorned with many wonders; he saw the Liṅga, well-worshipped with various jewels set individually.
Likewise, when he performed worship upon observing the *liṅga*, all the jewels and all living beings were scattered here and there.
He performed the ceremonial bath of that Liṅga with the water from his mouth-rinsing; then, for the sake of worship, he offered bilva leaves with one hand.
With his second hand he offered the deer meat; bowing with a prostration like a staff, he made a mental resolve.
"From this day forward, O Śaṅkara, I shall indeed perform worship with great effort; you are my master and I am your devotee from this day forth. (127)
Thus, having become a Kirāta bound by his vow, he returned home; Nandin saw all of that [destruction] scattered here and there by the Kirāta.

Nandin became filled with anxiety: "What misfortune has arisen for me today? Those obstacles which were foretold for one devoted to the worship of Śiva have indeed arrived because of the reversal of my own fortune. (129)
Having reflected thus for a very long time and having cleansed the temple of Śiva, Nandin returned to his own home by the same path by which he had come.
Then the family priest, having approached Nandin whose mind was departed, spoke these words to him: "Why is your mind departed? (131)
Then Nandi spoke these words to the family priest.
"O Brahmin, today I saw an impure substance near Śiva; I have no idea at all by whom it was placed there. (133)

Then the priest spoke these words to Nandin: "He by whom the worship of the jewels and other offerings was neglected there is undoubtedly a fool, dull-witted regarding what ought and ought not to be done. (134)
Therefore, O Lord, you should not worry even for this; tomorrow morning, you must go to that abode of Śiva along with me.
"I shall perform that task for the sake of observing the wicked one. Having heard these words of his priest, Nandin—
Remaining in his own home during the night with a tormented heart, when that night had passed, he summoned his domestic priest.
Nandin went to the abode of Śiva together with that high-souled one; then he saw what had been done by that evil-minded man on the previous day.
Having performed the perfect worship, complete with various jewel ornaments, joined with the five types of offerings, and likewise accompanied by the Ekādaśī [rite], || 139 ||
Having praised Girīśa with manifold hymns together with the brahmins, two watches (yāmas) passed while Nandin continued his praise.
For Mahākāla has arrived, possessing the form of Time, endowed with great strength; he is the very embodiment of Time, most fierce, bow in hand, and full of majesty.
Seeing him, Nandin was terrified with fear and lamented; likewise, the priest suddenly became overcome by dread.
There, the Kirāta performed the worship exactly as before without error; having struck down that worship with the tip of his foot, he offered a bilva leaf.
Having performed the ceremonial bath for him with water from mouthfuls, the Kirāta then offered that palāśa leaf as a food offering (naivedya) to Śiva.
Having fallen to the ground like a staff, he rose and went to his own home; seeing that great marvel, he indeed reflected upon it for a long time. (145)
Then, together with the family priest whose mind was agitated by the sound of the drums, he summoned many Brahmins who were learned in the Vedas.
Having reported all of that which was done by the Kirāta to them, he said: "O Brahmins, tell me truly what must now be done. (147)
Then, having deliberated and gathered together according to the Dharmaśāstras, all those brahmins spoke to Nandin, who was filled with great apprehension.
"This obstacle has arisen, which cannot be warded off even by the gods; therefore, O best of Vaiśyas, take this liṅga back to your own home. (149)
Thinking "so be it," Nandin then uprooted that [liṅga] of Śiva, brought it to his own home, and installed it according to the prescribed rites.
Having fashioned a golden pedestal beautifully adorned with the nine gems, he then worshipped it with numerous ritual offerings.
Then on the following day, Kitarāta arrived at the temple of Śiva; however, upon looking about, he did not see the Linga of Īśvara.
Abandoning his silence, he suddenly cried out in reproach and said this: "O Śambhu, where have you gone? Show yourself truly today! (153)
Indeed, you have not been seen by me; therefore, I shall cast off my body this very day. O Śambhu! O Lord of the World! O Lord, Destroyer of Tripura! 154.
O Rudra, O Mahādeva, reveal yourself by means of your own self!
Thus rebuked by the Kirāta with words that were both reproachful and sweet, the heroic Sadāśiva then [opened] his own belly with [his] rays.
Then, suddenly tearing his arms apart and slapping them together, he spoke in fury: "O Śambhu! Show yourself! Why will you depart, abandoning me? (157)
Having spoken thus, the Kirāta then cut the entrails and flesh from all sides and suddenly threw them into that pit with his very hands.
Having made his heart steady, he certainly bathed in that lake; likewise, having quickly brought water and a bilva leaf, he acted with haste. (159)
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rule, he prostrated himself on the ground like a staff.
Then, while he was established in meditation there in the presence of Śiva, Rudra appeared, surrounded by his Pramatha attendants.
Taking him by the hand, Rudra, who is as white as camphor, radiant, with matted hair and the moon upon his crest, spoke while consoling him.
"O hero, O highly wise one, O great-minded one, you are my devotee; choose a boon for your own benefit, whatever great desire you have cherished. (163)
Thus addressed by Rudra, Mahākāla, filled with joy and endowed with supreme devotion, prostrated himself upon the ground like a staff.
Then he spoke to Rudra: "I am requesting a boon; O Rudra, I am your servant and you are my master, without a doubt. (165)
Grant me devotion to this Buddha-self in birth after birth; you are my mother and you are my father, you are my kinsman and indeed my friend. (166)
You are Guha; you are the Great Mantra; you are eternally the one to be known through mantras. Therefore, there is nothing else whatsoever other than you in the three worlds.
Having heard those disinterested words of the Kirāta, Bhava then granted him the status of a chief attendant as well as the office of gatekeeper.
Then the three worlds were made to resound by the blast of the hand-drum (ḍamaru), by the booming sound of kettledrums (bherī), and by the blare of conchs (śaṅkha). || 169 ||
Then kettledrums and thousands of drums resounded; hearing that noise, Nandin, overcome with wonder, went forth. || 170 ||
In that penance grove where Śiva was stationed, surrounded by his Pramathas, the Kirāta was indeed seen at that time by Nandin with great intensity.
Filled with wonder, Nandin spoke these humble words, desiring to praise the Kirāta with supreme concentration. (172)
"O scorcher of foes, Śambhu has been brought here by you; you are a supreme devotee. You are a devotee and I have arrived here; introduce me to Śaṅkara. (173)
Having heard those words of his, the Kirāta, filled with haste, took Nandin by the hand and approached Śaṅkara.
Laughing, the Blessed Lord Rudra spoke these words to the Kirāta: "Who is this that has been brought by you here into the presence of my attendants? (175)
The Kirāta said: This Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was informed by the Kirāta: "O God, he is always your devotee; indeed, he is ever intent upon your worship. (176)
Day after day, you have been worshipped with gems and rubies, with flowers both high and low, and even with life and wealth; of this there is no doubt. (177)
Therefore, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, know that Nandin is my friend.
Mahādeva said: "O highly fortunate one, I did not know that Nandin was honored by the Vaiśya; O Mahākāla of great intellect, you are my devotee and my friend. (179)
Those wise ones who are free from worldly attachments—they are exceedingly dear to me; they are my devoted ones, distinguished as the best among men.
"O dear one, I am indeed your devotee, and he is even more dear to me; both of them have been accepted by Śambhu as his attendants. (181)
Then many celestial chariots of great splendor arrived there; by that one of great splendor, the best of Kirātas, that best of Vaiśyas was indeed rescued.
They reached Mount Kailāsa by means of extremely swift celestial chariots; they attained a form identical to that of the high-souled Īśvara.
Then, having been consecrated with the lustration rite by Śiva along with Girijā, the goddess, who moves with the gait of an elephant, laughed and spoke this.
O Mahādeva, there is no doubt that these two are exactly like you in their essential nature, their gait, and their playful expressions; they are highly honored. (185)
"You were indeed served by me alone; of this there is no doubt. Having heard those words of the goddess, both the Kirāta and the Vaiśya [were filled with wonder]. (186)
"O Three-eyed One, having immediately turned our faces away while Śaṃkara looked on, we two, Bhava and Avastu, are indeed worthy of your compassion. (187)
They stand constantly at your gate; O Bhava, salutations again and again to you! || 188 ||
Having understood their state of being, the Blessed Lord Bhava, smiling, said: "By your supreme devotion, may your desire be fulfilled."
From that time forward, O brahmins, these two became gatekeepers; stationed at the door of Śiva, they behold Śiva at midday.
Nandī and Mahākāla—these two are dear to Śiva; filled with joy, they both said, "Sadāśiva is indeed one alone. (191)
Raising one finger, Mahādeva spoke; likewise, Nandin spoke this, raising two of his own fingers.
Thus endowed with such perceptions, those two stood at the gate of the high-souled Śaṅkara; O illustrious ones, let these sages listen. (193)
O Brahmins, in former times Śailāda proclaimed this infinite Śivadharma out of compassion for all living beings, even those of wicked nature. (194)
Even those men who are sinful and most unrighteous, the blind, the mute, the lame, those of low birth, the wicked-minded, and even the outcaste dog-cookers; || 195 ||
Others, too, of whatever kind they may be, who are distinguished by their devotion to Śiva, they also attain the presence of the trident-bearing God of gods. (196)
Those wise ones who worship a linga made of sand go to the world of Rudra; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (197)
The sages said: "How was the installation of the Linga carried out, bypassing Śiva? O highly fortunate one, let that be told to us, for we are eager to hear it."
Lomaśa said: When the Lord Śambhu wandered about in the Dāruvana forest for the sake of alms, [he was seen by the sages]. || 2 ||

Clad in the directions for raiment, with his mass of matted locks released, he is the one known through Vedānta, the sole lord of the world; that Īśvara, who assumes the form of Brahmā, is the supreme and transcendent master of all masters of yoga.

Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Great One of immense power, the Lord of the world—that Great Soul, the Sovereign, assumed the form of a mendicant and wandered for alms in the Dāru forest.
At midday, the brahmin sages departed from their own hermitage for the sacred ford; at that very moment, all those wives of the sages also arrived together.
Beholding Śambhu, they said to one another: "Who is this mendicant in disguise who has arrived, whose appearance is unprecedented? (6)
"Let us, together with our friends, give alms to him. Saying "So be it," they all went and joyfully brought [food] from their homes.
Various kinds of soft alms-food, along with respectful offerings, were given and begged according to his capacity by that trident-bearing God of gods.
A certain woman, filled with wonder, spoke to her beloved Śambhu: "Who are you that have come here in the guise of a mendicant, O high-minded one? (9)
"Why do you sit down in our pure hermitage of the sages? Though addressed thus by her, Śambhu then spoke as if laughing: 10.
"O lady of beautiful hair, I am the Lord, and I have attained this purifying [state]. Having heard the words of the Lord, the wife of the sage said to him: ||| 11 ||
"You are the Lord, O highly fortunate one, and indeed the master of Kailāsa; O God, how is it that you wander alone for the sake of alms? (12)
Thus addressed by her, Śambhu spoke these words to her again: "Separated from the daughter of Dakṣa, I wander about naked."
"O lady of beautiful hips, I am always free from desire when wandering for alms; without that Satī, O passionate one, no mere woman at all pleases me, O large-eyed one—I tell you this truly. (14)
Having heard those words spoken by him, the lotus-eyed woman said: "Women indeed provide a pleasant touch for a man; of this there is no doubt. (15)
O Śambhu, those women have been avoided by a wise man such as yourself.
And thus all the women gathered where Śaṅkara was, and that alms-bowl of Śambhu was filled with great virtues.
When Sambhu desired to go toward Mount Kailāsa, which was filled with four kinds of food and six flavors, then all the wives of the brahmins went along, filled with joy. (18)
Abandoning their household duties, they moved about with their minds fixed on her; when all those wives had departed, the best of sages remained.
Having arrived at the hermitage, they beheld it empty; then they said to one another, "Where have all our wives gone? (20)
"We do not know, indeed, by whom all of us have been carried off after being lost. Thus reflecting, they searched here and there.
Then they all beheld those women following after Śiva; and upon seeing Śiva, those sages arrived there filled with wrath.

Then, standing before Śiva, they all spoke with great urgency: "O Śambhu, what indeed has been done by you, the dispassionate Great Soul? Without a doubt, you are a stealer of the wives of the sages. (23)

Thus cast off, Śiva remained silent even as he was departing for the mountain; then Mahādeva, the imperishable one, was encountered by the sages, who said: "Since you are a stealer of wives, therefore become a eunuch immediately! (24)
Thus cursed by the sages, his linga fell to the earth; and once it reached the ground, that linga grew rapidly and immensely large.
Having covered the seven netherworlds in an instant, the Liṅga rose upward, pervaded the entire earth, and encompassed the intermediate space.
All the heavens were completely covered, and that which transcends heaven then came into being; there was no earth, nor the circle of the quarters, nor water, nor fire.
Nor is it wind, nor space, nor ego-consciousness, nor the Great Principle (mahat); nor is it the unmanifest (avyakta), nor time, nor likewise primordial nature (mahāprakṛti). || 28 ||

There was no longer any distinction between duality and non-duality, for everything was dissolved in that very instant; since the entire universe had dissolved into that *liṅga* of the Great-Souled One.
The wise declare that the *liṅga* is so called because it is a place of dissolution (*layana*); having seen it thus increasing, those divine sages [were amazed]. (30)
Then Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Agni, and the world-protectors, together with the serpents, their minds filled with wonder, spoke to one another.
"What is its length and breadth? Where is its end, and where is its pedestal?"—thus, filled with anxiety, all the gods then spoke to Viṣṇu.
The gods said: "O Viṣṇu, you must look for its root, and O Lotus-born one, you must look for its head; you two shall be the protectors in their respective places. (33)
Having heard this, those two illustrious ones, Viṣṇu born from the lotus of Vaikuṇṭha and Brahmā, went indeed to Pātāla and proceeded to the entire universe respectively.
Then, having gone to heaven, Brahmā, intent on observation, was unable to see the top of the Liṅga, despite his keen vision. || 35 ||
Then, returning by the same path as he had gone, the Lotus-born reached the summit of Mount Meru and was recognized there by Surabhī.
She who was standing in the shade of a *ketakī* tree spoke sweet words; having heard her speech, the Grandfather of all the worlds, laughing, addressed Surabhi with these words in a deceptive manner.
I have seen that most wonderful Liṅga by which the three worlds are pervaded; and for the sake of beholding its end, I have been sent here by the gods.
The head of that all-pervading Great Soul has not been seen; what shall I say before the gods? My anxiety is exceedingly great.
If you were to falsely say that the head of the Liṅga has been seen by the gods—even if all the hosts of deities, beginning with Indra, were to say so—[it would be a lie]. (40)
Those gods are witnesses; let them speak quickly on this matter. O lady of virtuous vows, together with Ketakī, you be a witness in this matter. (41)
Accepting those words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin with her head bowed, Surabhi, accompanied by Ketakī, brought them there.
Having thus arrived, Brahmā spoke in the presence of the gods.
Brahmā said: O gods, I beheld the wondrous top of the Liṅga, which was perfectly formed, polished, and adorned with a Ketakī petal.
It was vast, stainless, smooth, exceedingly serene, and wonderful; it was delightful, charming, beautiful to behold, and possessed of great splendor. || 45 ||
"Such a thing has been seen by me, but never before without him. Having heard these words of Brahmā, the gods were filled with wonder. (46)
While Indra and the other hosts of deities remained thus filled with wonder, Viṣṇu, the Lord of All and the lamp of the supreme self, appeared.
Having returned immediately from Pātāla, he quickly said to everyone: "Even though I was intent on searching, I did not see its end."
Great wonder has arisen in me as I travel beyond Pātāla—to Atala, Sutala, Nitala, and Rasātala. (49)
Likewise, he goes to the surface of the earth, to Pātāla, and to Atala; those Talātala regions are perceived by him as if they were empty.
Even from the empty, that which is empty has been thoroughly scrutinized; for it possesses neither root, nor middle, nor end.
Mahādeva, in the form of the Liṅga, by whom this world is sustained; through whose grace you and likewise the sages have been born.
Having heard his words, the gods and sages honored them; then Viṣṇu, as if smiling, spoke this to Brahmā.
O Brahman, if you have indeed seen the head from the perspective of ultimate reality, then who are the witnesses you have conceived of in this matter? (54)
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke quickly to the Ketakī flower, saying, "O Surabhi! (55)
"Know that those gods are my witnesses in the ultimate sense. Having heard the words of Brahmā, all the gods were filled with haste. (56)
They issued an invitation for Surabhi along with her; then, at the command of Brahmā, she arrived there for the sake of that task.
Then Surabhi was addressed by Indra and the other gods; she replied, "O gods, Brahmā has indeed seen me together with Ketakī."
When the gods worshipped the head of the Liṅga with Ketakī petals, a voice from the sky arose, heard by everyone present.
O gods, know that what was said regarding the *surabhī* and the *ketakī* is false; for his head has never been seen.
Then all the gods, including Indra and Viṣṇu, spoke in anger to Surabhi, who was intent on speaking falsehoods.
"O auspicious lady, since you have spoken such a falsehood this very day with your own mouth, may your mouth be impure and excluded from all dharma. (62)
"O beautiful woman, even the fragrant ketakī flower is unfit for the worship of Śiva; you shall become so as well, there is no doubt, for you have spoken a falsehood. (63)
Then a voice from the sky indeed cursed Brahmā: "O dull-witted one, why have you spoken falsely, for you are truly a fool! (64)
Together with Bhrigu, the sages, and likewise the family priest; therefore, you shall not be honored and shall instead become partakers of suffering.
Even the most righteous sages, though excluded from the words of truth, were fools devoted to disputation, ignorant of reality, and full of envy. (66)
They were both beggars and generous givers, yet they constantly destroyed their own knowledge; self-conceited and arrogant, they reviled one another.
Thus cursed by Śiva, all those sages as well as the deities beginning with Brahmā sought refuge in the Liṅga. || 68 ||
Lomaśa said: Then all those gods and even the sages, filled with fear, as well as Brahmā and the others overwhelmed by their lack of knowledge, praised the Linga of Īśa.
