Brahmā said: You are indeed the embodiment of the Liṅga, possessed of great majesty; you are the one to be known through Vedānta, the form of the Great Soul, by whom—ever intent on supreme bliss—the entire world was eternally made to have its root in the Self.
You are the witness of all worlds, and you are the wise destroyer; O Mahādeva, you are the protector, and you are Bhairava, O Lord of the Universe.
O Lord, these three worlds are pervaded by you in the form of the Liṅga; as for us, we are but insignificant beings whose minds are deluded by Māyā.
I am all the gods and asuras, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas, as well as these pannagas, piśācas, and vidyādharas.
For you are the creator of the creators of the universe; for you are the God, the Lord of the world. You are the maker of this world, and you are the supreme Puruṣa, its destroyer.
"Save us, O Mahādeva! O God of gods, salutations be unto you! Thus was Maheśvara, in the form of the Liṅga, indeed praised by the Creator (Brahmā).
Desiring to praise Maheśvara, the stainless one, those sages, full of reverence, extolled him with foremost words sung in the Vedas.
The sages said: "We are ignorant; due to our desires, we do not perceive his true nature. For you are indeed the Self and the Supreme Self, and you are the manifesting Prakṛti. (9)

You alone are my mother and you alone are my father; you alone are my kinsman and you alone are my friend. You are the Lord, the singular form known by the Vedas, contemplated by those of great majesty.
You are the self of all beings, the one like light among pieces of wood; since everything comes from you, therefore you are everything at all times.
And because this arises from him, the Lord is therefore called Śambhu.
We—all the gods and others, the sages, the celestial musicians, the Vidyādharas, and the great serpents—have come to your lotus feet.
Therefore, O Śambhu, Lord of the universe, protect us out of compassion.
Mahādeva said: "Listen now to my words; let it be done with haste. O you whose wealth is asceticism, all of you must urgently entreat Viṣṇu."
Having heard those words of the high-souled Śaṅkara, all the gods then paid homage to Viṣṇu and praised him.

The gods said: "O sole kinsman of the entire world, today you have become the savior of all the Vidyādharas, the hosts of gods, and the sages. Therefore, O Lord of the three worlds, O Ruler of the universe, O Abode of the world, protect these people with your compassion this very day. (17)
Then the Lord Viṣṇu, smiling, spoke these words: "In the past, you were oppressed by the Daityas and protected by me."
"O gods, even today a fear arising from this ancient liṅga has arisen; I am not able to protect you from this fear of the liṅga. (19)
When Acyuta had spoken thus, those gods became filled with anxiety; then a voice from the sky spoke, consoling the deities.

"O Janārdana, conceal this liṅga for the sake of worship; becoming a mass [of form], O mighty-armed one, protect all that is moving and unmoving. Having agreed, saying "So be it," the Blessed Lord Vīrabhadra performed the worship.

Then, that great-souled one, devoted to the performance of auspicious rites, was worshipped by the hosts of gods led by Brahmā; he was Virabhadra, the moon-crested one, beloved of Śiva, and equal to Rudra throughout the three worlds.
Then that Vīrabhadra became engaged in the worship of the Liṅga; indeed, by means of that very form of the Liṅga, this entire world [is sustained]. || 23 ||
It manifests, attains stability, and likewise undergoes dissolution; because of this process of dissolution (*layana*), those most proficient in the knowledge of reality call it *liṅga*. (24)
Pervaded by spheres of cosmic eggs and likewise adorned with rudrākṣas, a great liṅga was thus born, which is insurmountable for all.
Then all the gods and the sages of great luster praised the great Liṅga with various Vedic hymns. || 26 ||
O Lord, you are subtler than the subtlest, and likewise, you are greater than the greatest; therefore, the worship of the Liṅga must be performed by you for the sake of all these beings.
At that very moment, a Liṅga was fashioned many times over by everyone: the Brahmeśvara Liṅga in Satyaloka and Sadāśiva in Vaikuṇṭha. || 28 ||
In Amarāvatī is the well-established [liṅga] named Amareśvara; Varuṇeśvara is in Vāruṇī, and the Lord Kāleśvara is in the south.
Nairṛteśvara in the southwest, Pāvaneśvara in the northwest, Kedāra in the world of mortals, and likewise Amareśvara.
Oṃkāra at the Narmadā, and likewise Mahākāla; the god Viśveśvara at Kāśī, and Laliteśvara at Prayāga. (31)
Tiyambaka on Mount Brahmagiri, likewise Bhadreśvara in the Kali age, and the Drākṣārāmeśvara Liṅga at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Likewise, the Liṅga known as Someśvara is remembered in Saurāṣṭra; similarly, Sarveśvara is on the Vindhya [mountain], Śikhareśvara on Śrīśaila, Mallālanātha in Kāntī, and Siṃhanātha in Siṃhala.
Likewise, the Liṅga Virūpākṣa, Koṭiśaṅkara, Tripurāntaka, Bhīmeśa, and Amareśvara; || 34 ||
Bhogīśvara in Pātāla and Hāṭakeśvara as well—many such Liṅgas were then established by the gods throughout the three worlds for the sake of benefiting the universe. (35)
Thus, the three worlds became filled with all the lords of the Liṅgas; and likewise, portions of Vīrabhadra were established by the immortals for the purpose of worship.
In that regard, twenty ritual acts were taught by Śaṅkara himself as indicators for the worship of the Liṅga; of these, eight became additional [to the original twelve]. (37)
The eternal Śivadharmas were proclaimed by Rudra; Vīrabhadra is like Rudra, and others are likewise remembered as gurus. (38)
The gurus born from the Guru are renowned throughout the three worlds; however, Nandin alone knows the true majesty of the Liṅga in its essential reality.
For the Blessed Lord Skanda is indeed distinct from those other bearers of names who have been described as followers of the Śiva-dharma by Nandin. (40)
O highly fortunate one, by Śailāda, various bearers of the *liṅga* were established; and in ancient times, a *liṅga* was also placed upon a corpse.
Death together with the physical body, and life together with the physical body—these principles are well-established, having been established by Śailāda.
The Pāśupata dharma is supreme; it is protected by Skanda. || 43 ||
The pure five-syllable mantra is the Vidyā Prāsādī; immediately following that is the six-syllable Vidyā, which is the illuminator of the Prāsāda.
That [knowledge] was obtained from Skanda by the high-souled Agastya; subsequently, indeed, many traditions arose due to the division among teachers.
But what is the use of speaking at great length? Those who constantly utter these two syllables, "Śvi," are Rudras; of this there is no doubt. (46)

Those who, placing the path of the virtuous before them, have all become destroyers of the cities [of the senses]; they are to be known as heroic devotees of Maheśvara, who bring about the destruction of the sins of men. 47.
Those who indeed practice devotion to Śiva—whether by way of incidental association, through constant proximity, with faith, or even by chance—they attain the supreme goal.
Listen, I shall here relate an ancient history concerning how, in the past, a female moth constructed a temple for Śiva and performed its purification.
She had indeed come for the purpose of devouring; by whom was the sacrificial offering presented? Formerly, her dust was cleared away by the two wings.
By the ripening of that karma, she reached the highest heaven; having experienced the intense bliss of heaven, she has returned once more to saṃsāra. || 51 ||
Born as the daughter of the King of Kāśī, she became renowned by the name Sundarī; due to her former practice, she was a most auspicious and supreme virtuous woman.
Day after day, the slender-limbed woman, always devoted to the auspicious door, performs the sweeping with supreme devotion. (53)
Then the goddess Sundarī, the princess, herself became so; and seeing her in such a state, the seer Uddālaka said:
"O auspicious girl, you who are so delicate; O young maiden of pure smiles, why do you perform the sweeping yourself?"
"O Goddess, there are many male and female slaves before you; by your command, they shall perform all tasks, such as sweeping and so forth. (56)
Having heard those words of the sage, he laughed and spoke as follows.
Those men and women who perform service to Śiva and are distinguished by devotion to Śiva indeed go to the world of Śiva.
Sweeping with the hands and walking with the feet within the temple of Śiva [are forbidden]; therefore, I perform the sweeping without weariness.
"I know nothing else at all except for one thing: sweeping. Having heard those words and reflected upon them in his mind, the sage—
"What was done by her in the past? Who is she, and by whose grace [did this happen]? Then the sage, with his eye of knowledge, understood all of that; overcome with wonder, he then became silent.

Then, having understood that, Uddālaka—the foremost among the wise—was filled with wonder; reflecting upon the power of Śiva in his mind, he attained peaceful awakening, which transcends mere intellectual knowledge.
Lomaśa said: O Brahmin, in former times there was even a thief who was excluded from all righteous duties; he was a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, a drinker of liquor, and a stealer of gold.
He was always lustful for the wives of others, a great sinner, a gambler, ever dull-witted, and constantly associated with cheats.
Once, while playing, he lost a marvelous game of dice; though being tormented by the gamblers, he did not say anything at all.
Though tormented and addressed by them, that most wicked man remained silent; [they asked: "That wealth was lost by you at dice; what will you give? (4)
"Or else, O evil-minded one, let that which was pledged be told quickly and according to the truth; I shall give it back at night," he said. (5)
Released by those words of his, the gamblers and the others departed; then, at the time of midnight, he went to the temple of Śiva.
Having placed it upon his head, he prepared to seize the bell of Śambhu; at that moment, on the peak of Kailāsa, Śambhu spoke to his attendants.
Whatever he has performed today is superior on earth to that of all others; he is the most excellent among all devotees and is dear to me.
Having spoken thus, he dispatched him along with the Gaṇas headed by Vīrabhadra; they all went swiftly from Kailāsa, the beloved abode of Śiva.

The three worlds were made to resound by the sound of all their ḍamarus; seeing them, that wicked-souled thief suddenly leaped down from the top of the Liṅga and immediately became intent on flight. || 10 ||
Seeing him fleeing, Vīrabhadra challenged him to combat. || 11 ||
Why do you fear, O dull-witted one? The Great Lord, the God of gods, has become pleased with you today, for he is indeed of noble conduct.
Having spoken thus, he placed him upon his celestial chariot and went to Kailāsa; for that thief was indeed made an attendant by that high-souled one.
Therefore, devotion to Śiva should be cultivated by all embodied beings; for even animals would be worthy of worship, how much more so humans on this earth? (14)
Those logicians who are devoted to reasoning, as well as those Mīmāṃsakas, others who dispute with one another, and yet others who speculate about the self; || 15 ||
Those excluded from the worship of Śiva do not utter a single word [in his praise]; for what indeed can be achieved by those who engage only in mere reasoning, apart from Śiva? (16)
Likewise, what is the use of saying more? For even all living beings, both stationary and moving, are born merely as wearers of the *liṅga*. (17)
Just as the Liṅga was established together with the Piṇḍī, so too are men endowed with the Liṅga and women are the Piṇḍīs. || 18 ||
This entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is endowed with Śiva and Śakti; yet those fools who, out of delusion, abandon that Śiva and worship another, are truly ignorant. (19)
That which is material is ultimately hollow, perishable, and momentary; he who is Viṣṇu should be known as Śiva, and he who is Śiva is indeed Viṣṇu. (20)
The pedestal (pīṭhikā) shall be the form of Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara is the one whose form is the liṅga; therefore, O twice-born ones, the worship of the liṅga is indeed the most excellent of all.
Brahmā worships a beautiful liṅga made of jewels incessantly; Indra worships a liṅga made of gems, and likewise the Moon worships one made of pearls.
Bhānu worships a beautiful linga made of copper incessantly; Kubera worships one made of gold, and Varuṇa (the wielder of the noose) worships one that is indeed red.
Yama worships a linga made of sapphire, and Nairṛta likewise one of silver; Pavana constantly worships a linga of saffron belonging to the Lord.
Thus all those world-protectors, together with Indra, were embraced by him; likewise, all the gandharvas along with the kinnaras in the netherworld were also so embraced.
Among the Daityas, O twice-born ones, there were some Vaiṣṇavas headed by Prahlāda; likewise, among the Rākṣasas, there were those led by Vibhīṣaṇa.
Bali and Namuci, as well as Hiraṇyakaśipu; Vṛṣaparvan and Vṛṣa, Saṃhrāda and Bāṇa as well. (27)
These and many other disciples of the wise Śukra—all those Daityas and Dānavas—were likewise devoted to the worship of Śiva. || 28 ||
All those Rākṣasas were always engaged in the worship of Śiva: Heti, Praheti, Saṃyāti, Vighasa, and Praghasa. || 29 ||
Vidyujjihva with sharp fangs, Dhūmrākṣa of terrible prowess, as well as Mālin, Sumālin, and the exceedingly fearsome Mālyavat. || 30 ||
The immensely powerful Rāvaṇa, whose hair was like lightning and whose tongue was like a flash of thunder; and the invincible Kumbhakarṇa, who displayed great speed and possessed formidable majesty.
For these were the most excellent Rākṣasas, always devoted to the worship of Śiva; having worshipped the Liṅga, they attained perfection in ancient times.
Rāvaṇa performed a penance that caused suffering even to all [the gods]; then Mahādeva, the lord of asceticism, was greatly pleased.
Then he granted boons difficult for even all others to obtain; by him, knowledge together with realized wisdom was received from Sadāśiva.
There was invincibility in battle and even a doubling of their heads; [first] the great god with five faces, and then Rāvaṇa with ten faces.
Having conquered the gods, sages, and ancestors through his ascetic power, the Lord became superior to all by the grace of Maheśa.
The king, the lord of Trikūṭa, was made great by Maheśa; he has remained here as the supreme seat of all the Rākṣasas. (37)
O brahmins, that injury which was inflicted upon the sages by Rāvaṇa at that time was done for the purpose of testing ascetics.
For the great Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out, has been born invincible; by the grace of Śaṅkara, he has created another era.
By that ascetic, the world-protectors were conquered through his majesty; indeed, even Brahmā was defeated by him through supreme austerity.

O twice-born ones, he by whom the moon was conquered by becoming the bearer of nectar-rays, and by whom the Lord of Fire was surpassed through his power of burning, and Īśa was defeated by lifting Mount Kailāsa; (41)
Even Indra was conquered by his sovereignty, and likewise Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent; and by the grace of worshipping the Liṅga, the three worlds were brought under control.
Then all the hosts of gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, having reached the summit of Mount Meru, held a consultation.
"O gods, we have indeed been oppressed by Rāvaṇa through his difficult ascetic penance; listen to this most wonderful account on the mountain named Gokarṇa. (44)

By that great-souled one who has performed the direct worship of the Liṅga—whatever is knowledge, the object of knowledge, attainable through knowledge, supreme, and most wonderful—all that was accomplished by Rāvaṇa alone, which is difficult for all others to surpass. (45)
Having resorted to supreme detachment and even greater magnanimity, that high-souled Rāvaṇa abandoned all sense of possessiveness by means of that very [detachment]. 46.
And for a thousand years, O mighty-armed one, he indeed cut off his own head with his hand and offered it for the sake of worshipping the Liṅga.
And the headless trunk of Rāvaṇa was right there in front of him, close at hand, endowed with yogic concentration through supreme meditative absorption.

Having dissolved [his own head] into the Liṅga and remaining there by means of some subtle power (kalā), he likewise performed the worship of Śiva after cutting off another head; and it was not done in that same manner by any other sage, nor indeed by anyone else.
In this way, he offered many heads indeed for the sake of worshipping Śiva; for though he became a headless trunk again and again, that Śiva became the granter of boons.
"O descendant of Pulastya, in former times the Asura was there in a solid mass without me; choose boons as you desire, and I shall grant them. (51)
Then Rāvaṇa spoke to Śiva, the supreme auspicious one: "O Blessed One, if you are pleased, let an excellent boon be granted to me."
I desire no other boon; I take refuge in Your lotus feet. If You have compassion for me, let that which is appropriate be granted to me. 53.
Then Sadāśiva said to Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the worlds cry out: "And by my grace, you shall obtain everything desired by your mind. (54)
"Thus, O lords of the gods, everything was obtained from Śiva by Rāvaṇa; therefore, all of you must likewise [strive] with supreme austerity."
"This Rāvaṇa must be conquered"—this thought remained in my mind. Having heard these words of the one who had fallen [from his state], the hosts of deities headed by Brahmā [were moved]. (56)
All those who were attached to sense-objects fell into long reflection; even Brahmā, overcome by his senses, was intent on sporting with his daughter.
Indeed, Indra became so due to his state as a paramour; Candra because he violated the teacher's bed; Yama because of his miserliness; and Sadāgati (Vāyu) because of his fickleness. || 58 ||
Because he consumes everything, Pāvaka and likewise other hosts of deities were unable to conquer Rāvaṇa, who was empowered by his ascetic penance.
For Śailāda is of great splendor, the foremost of the Gaṇas from ancient times; he is wise, skilled in policy, and possessed of great strength and prowess.
The high-souled one, dear to Śiva and possessing the form of Rudra, spoke to all those headed by Indra: "Why have you come here in such agitation? Let all of this be told in detail."
Then, questioned by Nandin, they all spoke with great haste: || 62 ||
The gods said: "We have all been defeated by Rāvaṇa, along with the sages; we have come to propitiate Śiva, the Lord of the lords of the worlds. (63)

Laughing, the blessed Nandin indeed spoke to Brahmā: "Where are you, and where is Śiva, the source of bliss? He who is to be seen through supreme austerity dwells within the heart; he cannot be seen today."
For as long as there are manifold entities and likewise sense-objects, and as long as there is the state of "mine-ness," so long indeed is the Lord difficult to attain.

For those of great soul who have conquered their senses, who are tranquil, and who are established in that [state], the Lord in the form of the Liṅga is easily attained; indeed, for you, he is very difficult to reach.
Then Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the wise sages, bowed to Nandin and said: "Why do you have the face of a monkey? Tell us all of that, as well as the power of Rāvaṇa’s asceticism."
Nandīśvara said: Kubera was appointed by that high-souled Śaṅkara as the sovereign lord over all wealth; it was for the purpose of seeing him that Rāvaṇa came here.
Mounting his own vehicle, he arrived with great haste; and seeing me, he spoke in anger: "Kubera has indeed come here! (69)
"Or has he been seen by you here? Tell me without delay; what business do you have with Dhanada today?"—thus indeed was he questioned by me. (70)
Then Rāvaṇa, of great splendor, the one who makes the worlds cry out, spoke; he was full of self-conceit, devoted to sensual objects, and exceedingly arrogant, having become devoid of faith in me.
The Lord began to instruct him, saying, "Do not act in this way! O fool, may you become as endowed with fortune, as wealthy, and as powerful as I am; do not persist in such folly. (72)
I was rendered foolish by that high-souled Kubera; having been rejected by me out of anger, that Guhyaka performed austerities.
"O Nandin, has Kubera indeed come to your abode? Let Kubera be given [what he desires] today; no hesitation should be made in this matter. (74)
Having heard Rāvaṇa’s words, I spoke even in haste: "O illustrious one, you are a bearer of the Liṅga, and I am likewise. (75)
"O evil-minded one, knowing that both [of us] are equal, you prattle in vain! He, as described, spoke to me, arrogant as he was in his speech and power. (76)

Just as I was questioned by you great-souled ones for the sake of speaking, I have related this ancient account regarding the fruit of the rite of Śiva’s worship; at that time, the state of equality granted by Śiva was not accepted by me.
I requested the face of Śambhu from that of the monkey, and it was granted to me out of compassion by Śiva, who is full of mercy. (78)
Those who are free from pride, devoid of deceit, and without possessions—these should be known as beloved of Śambhu; others are excluded from Śiva.
Thus, by the power of his asceticism, Rāvaṇa spoke with me; and I, the wise one, requested that he grant me ten faces.
At that time, the gods [uttered] words of derision toward the descendant of Pulastya; for then I cursed that Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out.
When some excellent man of great asceticism, endowed with such faces as these, shall suddenly strike me down while placing me at the forefront, there is no doubt of it. (82)
O Brahmin, having been thus cursed by me, Rāvaṇa—the one who makes the world cry out—worshipped the Liṅga exclusively, except for that Great-Souled One (Śiva).
O best of gods, O highly fortunate ones, without Viṣṇu in the form of a pedestal, he will indeed accomplish everything. (84)
"May all of you pray to Viṣṇu, who dwells in the secret cave of all hearts—the God of gods, the Great God, Maheśvara in the form of Viṣṇu. (85)
"For I stand before all the gods; therefore," he said. Having heard Nandin’s words, they all, with joyful minds, went to Vaikuṇṭha and began to praise Viṣṇu with songs.
The gods said: "Salutations to you, O Blessed One, God of gods, Lord of the universe! This entire world, both moving and unmoving, has you as its support. (87)
O Viṣṇu, this very Liṅga was indeed borne by you in the form of a cosmic egg; in the form of Mahāviṣṇu, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were slain.
Likewise, Mount Mandara was indeed supported by you in the form of a tortoise; and having assumed the form of a boar, Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by you.
The Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by you in the form of Nṛhari, and the Daitya Bali was bound by you in the form of Vāmana.
"O Mahāviṣṇu, having been born in the lineage of the Bhṛgus as the son of Kṛtavīrya, he has been slain; protect me likewise from this [danger] as well. (91)
Out of fear of this roar, you ought to protect us quickly once again.
Thus entreated by the gods, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, Vāsudeva who pervades the universe, spoke to all the deities.
"O gods, listen to these great words worthy of the occasion: placing Śailādi at your head, all of you, filled with haste, shall manifest incarnations by assuming the bodies of monkeys. (94)

"For having become a human being, though shrouded in ignorance, I shall be born in Ayodhyā in the house of Daśaratha. With the knowledge of Brahman as my companion, I am here for the accomplishment of your purpose. (95)
In the house of Janaka, the Brahma-vidyā itself shall be born; for Rāvaṇa is truly devoted and entirely intent upon the meditation on Śiva.
When a person endowed with great austerity desires the knowledge of Brahman, then that man, conquered by dharma, becomes easily accomplished in his aim. || 97 ||
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu, the supreme auspicious one, said: "Vālin was born from a portion of Indra, and Sugrīva is the son of Aṃśumat. (98)
Likewise, Jāmbavān, the elephant among men and bears, was born from a portion of Brahmā; he is Nandin, the son of Śilāda and the beloved attendant of Śiva. (99)
He who is indeed the eleventh Rudra is that great monkey Hanumān; he has descended for the sake of assisting Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor.
Then Mainda and all those other monkeys, as well as all the best of the gods, descended exactly as they had been told. 101.
In that very same way, Viṣṇu was born as the increaser of Kauśalyā’s joy; and because he is the delight (ramaṇa) of the universe, he is called Rāma by the wise. (102)
The remainder also descended to earth through devotion to Viṣṇu and by means of ascetic penance.
The two powerful staff-like arms of Viṣṇu have also descended as the renowned Śatrughna and Bharata, famous throughout the three worlds. (104)

The daughter of the Lord of Mithilā, whom the exponents of Brahman spoke of, descended as Brahmavidyā for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose; she was born as Sītā from the furrowing of the earth by the plough. 105.
Therefore, that science of inquiry (anvīkṣikī) was then known as Sītā; having originated in Mithilā, it is called Māthitī.
Born in the lineage of Janaka, she was the renowned daughter of Janaka; formerly known as Vedavatī, she was the destroyer of the density of ignorance through the knowledge of Brahman.
She was given by Janaka himself to Viṣṇu, the Supreme Soul.
Then, together with that Vidyā, Viṣṇu, the God of gods and Lord of the universe, became absorbed in a most difficult and fierce austerity.
Desirous indeed of conquering Rāvaṇa, the lotus-eyed Rāma undertook residence in the forest for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Even though he was already a great incarnation, he performed most difficult austerities with supreme effort for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Both Śatrughna and Bharata performed supreme ascetic penance.

Then, endowed with ascetic power, Rāma, together with those hosts of deities, slew Rāvaṇa along with his followers within six months. Struck down by Viṣṇu’s weapons, he attained the same form as Śiva.
Furthermore, O you of excellent vows, that reunion with his kinsmen occurred immediately.

By the grace of Śiva, he indeed attained everything—both duality and non-duality. Even the sages are deluded in this matter regarding the discernment of duality and non-duality; however, men devoted to the worship of Śiva attain all of that here in this world. (115)

Those who constantly worship Śiva, even in the form of the Liṅga—whether they be women, Śūdras, outcastes, or those dwelling at the very fringe of society—they surely attain that Śiva, the destroyer of all suffering. (116)
Even animals have attained the supreme state, how much more so humans and others? || 117 ||
Those twice-born ones who, through celibacy, have established themselves in supreme austerity, they too, after many years, become intent upon heaven through sacrifices.
The Jyotiṣṭoma, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and these other sacrifices bestow heaven upon those who perform them; of this there is no doubt. (119)
Having enjoyed there the great heavenly bliss that exhausts merit, even when their merit is exhausted, those who performed sacrifices indeed fall back to the world of mortals.
O Brahmins, when those fallen into saṃsāra by fate develop an intellect consisting of the three guṇas, they are born here in various wombs.
O twice-born ones, just as beings arise from the quality of sattva and exist endowed with sattva, so too should those who are characterized by rajas and tamas be understood.
Thus, many people have wandered in this wheel of saṃsāra; yet, by chance and through the course of destiny, a man may serve Śiva.
For those men who are devoted to the meditation on Śiva and whose minds are restrained, the casting off of Māyā will occur immediately; it shall not be otherwise.
By the immediate dispelling of illusion, the triad of qualities perishes at once; when one transcends the three qualities, one becomes a partaker of liberation. 125.
Therefore, the worship of the *liṅga* should be performed by all embodied beings; having become Śiva in the form of the *liṅga*, he protects everything moving and unmoving. 126.
"O Brahmins, previously you asked me how Śiva exists in the form of a Liṅga; all of that has now been told by me exactly as it is."
How did Śiva, the Great Lord of the World, consume the poison? O brahmins, listen to all of that as I relate it to you exactly as it happened. (128)
Lomaśa said: Once, the King of the Gods himself was seated in the midst of the assembly hall, surrounded by the world-protectors, as well as by gods and sages.
Surrounded by hosts of Apsarases and preceded by Gandharvas, his victory was being sung even by Siddhas and Vidyādharas.
Then that illustrious Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the king of the gods, wise and noble-minded, arrived surrounded by his disciples.
Seeing him, the gods who had assembled there suddenly bowed down; Indra too beheld Vācaspati arrived there at that time.
The dull-witted one said nothing at all, neither offering a word of welcome, nor a seat, nor even a formal dismissal. || 5 ||
Then, perceiving Śakra to be negligent and wicked-minded due to intoxication with his sovereignty, Bṛhaspati, filled with anger, vanished from sight.
When that preceptor of the gods had departed, the deities became despondent; so too did the Yakṣas, Nāgas, along with the Gandharvas, the sages, and the twice-born.
When the Gandharva had finished speaking, Hari regained consciousness and quickly asked the gods, "Where indeed has that one of great asceticism gone?"
At that very moment, Śakra, the lord of the gods, was addressed by Nārada: "Indeed, you have shown contempt for your preceptor; there is no doubt about this."
"O slayer of Bala, because you showed disrespect toward your guru, your kingdom has been lost; therefore, he must indeed be propitiated by you with your whole being."
Having heard these words of the high-souled Nārada, Śakra rose suddenly from his seat and, surrounded by all of them, went with haste and unwearied diligence to the house of his preceptor.
Having first questioned Tārā and paid his respects, he asked, "Where has that one of great asceticism gone? Looking at Śakra, Tārā replied, "I do not know."
Then, filled with anxiety, Śakra returned to his own abode; in the meantime, indeed, ominous and wondrous portents appeared in heaven.
They existed for the sake of all suffering, as did those of the high-souled Śakra; and Bāli, residing in Pātāla, became aware of Śakra’s actions.
Surrounded by the Daityas, he went from Pātāla to Amarāvatī; then there was a most intense battle between the gods and the Dānavas.
The gods were defeated by the Daityas, and at that very moment, the entire kingdom of Śakra was seized by that foolish and evil-minded one.
Having been led to Pātāla with every effort, they departed in haste; through the grace of Śukra, they all likewise became victorious.
Śakra too became destitute of fortune and was utterly forsaken by the gods; then the lotus-eyed goddess vanished from sight.
The great elephant Airāvata, as well as the horse Uccaiḥśravas—many such jewels, indeed numerous and manifold—were suddenly carried off by the Daityas of wicked conduct out of greed. (19)

When those very same [offerings], which were meritorious, fell into the ocean, Bali, overcome with wonder, then spoke to his preceptor: 20. "Those very things, though meritorious, have fallen into the ocean. Then, filled with amazement, Bali spoke to his preceptor.
Having conquered the gods, we brought back many jewels, but they fell into the ocean; that was indeed a marvel.

Having heard those words of Bali, Uśanas replied to him: "By means of a hundred horse-sacrifices alone, the sovereignty of the gods shall be yours; for one who is consecrated, there is no doubt, and therefore he alone shall enjoy it."
Without the horse sacrifice, it is not possible to enjoy anything in heaven.
Having understood the words of his preceptor, Bali then became silent; together with the gods, he performed what was appropriate.
Indra too, having fallen into a state of lamentability, went to the Supreme Lord (Brahmā) and informed him of everything, including the fear for his kingdom and other matters. || 25 ||
Having heard the words of Śakra, Parameṣṭhin spoke.
Having assembled all the gods together with you, let us go in haste to propitiate Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords.
Saying "So be it," all those world-protectors, headed by Śakra, went forth; placing Brahmā at their head, they reached the shore of the Ocean of Milk, sat down, and all of them began to praise Hari.
Brahmā said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, saluted by gods and demons; O you of meritorious fame, imperishable, infinite Supreme Self, homage be to you! (29)

O Lord of Ramā, you are the sacrifice, you are the embodiment of the sacrifice, and you are the limb of the sacrifice; therefore, O Viṣṇu, by your grace today, become the bestower of boons upon the gods.
"Furthermore, today Śatakratu has been deprived of his kingdom due to his contempt for his guru; he has become [a pariah] along with the celestial sages. Therefore, deliver him. (31)

The Blessed Lord said: What wonder is there that everything perishes through the knowledge of one's own wickedness? For those who are sinful, most unrighteous, and solely devoted to sensual objects—who have reviled their parents and who are devoid of devotion to the Divine—of them there is no doubt [of destruction]. || 32 ||
O Brahmin, the fruit of what was done by him has arrived immediately; and because of this deed of Śakra, a state of peril has come upon them all.
When a person's time has become adverse, they then practice friendliness toward all beings for the sake of accomplishing every purpose.
For that very reason, O Indra, carry out my word; for the sake of our purpose, you must enter into an alliance with the Daityas.
Thus instructed by the Blessed One, Śakra, possessed of supreme intelligence, departed for Amarāvatī along with the deities, leaving Sutala behind.
Hearing that Indra had arrived, Indrasena, filled with rage, became desirous of slaying Purandara along with his army.
Then Nārada, with various kinds of words, restrained the Daityas and Bali, the best among the strong, from killing him.
Then, at the very word of that sage, Bali abandoned his anger; for Śatakratu had arrived together with his army.
Seen by Indrasena, surrounded by the world-protectors, the king of the Daityas spoke with haste, as if laughing: || 40 ||
"O Śakra, tell me why you have come here to Sutala. Having heard these words of his, he spoke to him with a smile:
We are the heirs of Kaśyapa, and you all are likewise; as we are, so are you—for this conflict is indeed meaningless. || 42 ||
By the power of fate, my kingdom was taken from me by you in a mere instant; for even those very many jewels, which you had indeed brought with great effort, vanished at that very moment.
Therefore, a wise person should engage in inquiry; from inquiry arises knowledge, and from knowledge liberation will come. || 44 ||
But alas, what is the use of my speaking before you? For I have come into your presence together with the gods, seeking refuge. (45)
Having heard these words of Śakra, the wise one, the best among those skilled in speech, laughed and spoke to Śakra.
O Lord of the Gods, I do not know for what purpose you have come here. || 47 ||
Having heard those words, Śakra’s eyes became clouded and filled with tears; he said nothing at all there, and Nārada spoke these words to him: ||| 48 ||
O Bala, do you not know how to discern what ought to be done and what ought not to be done? For this is the duty of the great: the protection of those who have come for refuge.
Those men who do not protect one who has sought refuge, a Brahmin, a sick person, or even an elderly person, are indeed slayers of Brahmins.

"By the word 'one who has come for refuge,' it means one who has come into your presence; such a person is worthy of protection by you, there is no doubt about this. When Nārada had spoken thus, the lord of the Daityas himself then [replied]: 51.
Having reflected with supreme intelligence upon the deliberation of what ought and ought not to be done, he honored Śakra with great respect, together with the world-protectors and the hosts of gods.
And for the sake of providing a pretext, that Purandara indeed caused many beings to adopt various vows as a means for the sacrificial offering.
Having thus made this agreement, Śakra, devoted to his own interests, dwelt together with Bali as a great master of the science of statecraft.
While Śatakratu was dwelling thus even in Sutala, many years passed; then, recollecting the words of Viṣṇu and reflecting upon them again and again, he formed a resolution.
Once, while seated in the midst of the assembly, the King of the Gods himself, being wise in policy, spoke these words with a smile, addressing Bali: (56)
O hero, you must obtain for us from that army many elephants and various other kinds of jewels. (57)
They have indeed fallen into the ocean at that very moment; therefore, an effort must certainly be made by us together with you.
O Daitya, for the sake of recovering those jewels from the ocean here, you must therefore perform churning for the accomplishment of your purpose. (59)
Bali was set in motion by that Śakra, the slayer of the gods; he spoke quickly to Śakra, "By what means shall this churning be accomplished? (60)
Then a voice from the sky, with a resonance as deep as a thundercloud, spoke to the gods and the Daityas: "Churn the Ocean of Milk!"
And there will be an increase in your strength, of this there is no doubt. || 62 ||
"Make Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope; then, having assembled both the gods and the Daityas, let it be churned. (63)
Then, having heard that voice coming from the sky, all those gods, rising up, made an effort together with the Daityas.
Then all those gods and asuras, having emerged from Pātāla, went together to Mandara, the incomparable and best of mountains.
And the Daityas, numbering in the tens of millions, as well as the gods, without a doubt, prepared themselves and quickly went to Mount Mandara, which shone with the luster of gold.
It was circular in shape, massive, and possessed great luster; it was encrusted with many jewels and frequented by various trees.
It was filled with sandalwood, pārijāta, nāga, punnāga, and campaka trees; it was teeming with various herds of deer and frequented by lions and tigers.
Having seen the great mountain, all those best of gods then spoke with their palms joined in reverence. || 69 ||
The gods said: "O mountain, we all, the gods, have come here to make a petition; listen to that, O great mountain, you who are a benefactor to others. (70)
Thus addressed by the gods and the Daityas, that mountain Mandara, having emerged in a supreme embodied form, spoke these words.
In that form, that mountain Mandara became possessed of material substance; let it be told why all of you have come into my presence. (72)
Then Bali spoke these words appropriate to the occasion, and Indra also, filled with haste, spoke truthful words.
O Mandarācala, for the sake of our common purpose, become our churning-stick for the production of the nectar of immortality; O you of noble vows, do so. (74)
Thinking "so be it" to those words for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, he spoke thus to the gods and asuras, and especially to Indra: || 75 ||
"And since my wings have been cut off by you with the hundred-jointed thunderbolt, how shall I be able to go for the sake of accomplishing your purpose? (76)
Then all the gods and asuras, being praised, might uproot that incomparable and wonderful great mountain Mandara. || 77 ||
Desiring to lead [him] to the Ocean of Milk, they indeed became powerless; then, the mountain suddenly fell firmly upon the gods and the Daityas. (78)
Some were broken, some died, and others fell into a state of unconsciousness; some became devoted to slander, while others fell into affliction.
Thus, their efforts shattered, the Asuras, Suras, and Dānavas regained their supreme composure and offered praise to the Lord of the Universe.
Protect, protect us, O Great Viṣṇu, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge! By you all this is pervaded—whatever is moving and whatever is unmoving. (81)
Then Hari manifested for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods; seeing them, Viṣṇu suddenly stood upon Garuḍa. (82)
Having effortlessly lifted that best of mountains and placed it upon Garuḍa in an instant, the Lord then granted fearlessness to all.
Then, rising up, he led those gods to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk; having cast that aged mountain into the waters, he then departed.
Then all the hosts of gods, having arrived together with the asuras and taking Vāsuki with them, made that agreement.
Having made Mount Mandara the churning rod, Vāsuki the rope, and [the ocean] itself the vessel, all the gods and demons together churned the ocean of milk for the sake of the divine nectar.

As the Ocean of Milk was being churned, the mountain indeed sank to the netherworld; at that very moment, the Lord of Ramā, having become a tortoise, lifted it up, and that very instant it became as if a marvel.
Then the mountain, being set in motion by the gods and dānavas, whirled about without support, like knowledge without a teacher.
Then Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, became the support for Mount Mandara; grasping it with his four arms, he churned the ocean which brought him ease.
Then all the gods and demons, having united and being exceedingly fierce in their strength, churned the ocean of milk with great force.

The back, neck, thighs, and knees of the great-souled tortoise were likewise struck by that best of mountains, which was firm and composed of the essence of diamond; from the friction of these two alone, the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni) arose.
Upon seeing that the Halāhala poison had arisen, the divine sage Nārada of immeasurable luster then spoke this to the gods: || 92 ||

"O gods, you must all now refrain from churning the ocean; instead, pray to Śiva for Dakṣa’s performance of the sacrifice. Furthermore, let Vīrabhadra’s act of causing you to forget that [sacrifice] be forgotten. (93)

Therefore, O gods, quickly remember Śiva—the highest even of the high, higher than the highest, whose nature is supreme bliss, who is the object of meditation for yogis, free from phenomenal expansion, and indeed formless. (94)
Being thus churned, all those gods, intent on their own desires and striving for the fulfillment of their self-interest, did not listen, for they were dull-witted.
They should never be instructed with many teachings; they are all masses of passion and hatred, turned away from Śiva. (96)
Clad in nothing but their exertion, they churned the ocean of milk; and from the ocean of milk, due to excessive churning, the Halāhala poison was born.

Having reached a state of maturity for burning the three worlds, it arrived to destroy the gods; thereafter, having pervaded all directions and the entire expanse of the sky, the Kālakūṭa poison approached to swallow all living beings.
Seeing that great king of serpents together with the mountain held by his own hand through his power, they abandoned it right there and then fled, joining with the asuras as they retreated.
In that very manner, all the sages, headed by Bhṛgu, became pacified by the hundreds; thus did Dakṣa’s sacrifice come to pass exactly as it had begun.

All have gone to Satyaloka, having been strongly urged by Bhaguṇa and by various Vedic utterances; O gods, Kālakūṭa has [been consumed] there hundreds of times—of this there is no doubt, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth. (101)
Having heard the words spoken by Bhṛgu, those afflicted by the Kālakūṭa poison reached Satyaloka and went to Brahmā for refuge. || 102 ||

Then, O Lord, seeing the blazing and intensely radiant Kālakūṭa, and seeing those gods and asuras who were ignorant of their own past actions, Brahmā began to curse them; however, he was restrained by Nārada.
Brahmā said: "O gods, what improper act has been committed, and why has this agitation arisen today against the Lord? My words cannot be otherwise."
Then, surrounded by the gods as well as the Vedas and Upaniṣads, and encompassed by various Āgamas, he departed out of fear of the Kālakūṭa poison.
Then the gods, filled with anxiety and enveloped by ignorance and desire, said this to one another: "Whom shall we make into Śaṅkara?"
Then, placing Brahmā at their head, all the gods, afflicted by the fear of Kālakūṭa, hastened toward Vaikuṇṭha. || 107 ||

Then Brahmā and the hosts of sages, along with all the multitudes of gods and asuras, sought refuge in Viṣṇu—the Supreme Lord, the Ancient Person, the Sovereign, the Mighty One, who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, who is beyond the senses (Adhokṣaja), and the Consort of Lakṣmī (Ādhava). || 108 ||
Having increased to such an extent, that great Kālakūṭa poison advanced; having first burnt the world of Brahmā, it indeed consumed Vaikuṇṭha as well.
Burned by the Kālakūṭa fire, Viṣṇu, who dwells in the secret cave of all, immediately assumed a complexion like that of the tamāla tree, accompanied by his attendants.
Vaikuṇṭha and Sunīla were completely surrounded by all the worlds; at that time, all the worlds became enveloped in the impurity of water.
He quickly reduced to ashes the entire cosmic egg, enveloped by its eight coverings along with Brahmā himself, performing a wondrous feat that cleansed the world of its impurities like water.

At that time, there was neither earth nor water, nor fire, nor wind, nor sky; there was no ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), nor the great principle (mahat), nor likewise root-ignorance (mūlāvidyā). Then, by the wrath of Śiva, the entire world became filled with ashes.
The sages said: O Brahman, you have told us how the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, was reduced to ashes by the fire of the Kālakūṭa poison through the wrath of Rudra.
However, we consider Rudra to be within the interior of the cosmic egg; at that time, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, was destroyed.
Once everything had been reduced to ashes by the wrath of Rudra, how was creation set in motion? From where did Brahmā and Viṣṇu arise, and from where did the gods led by Candra come forth?
Where did those other gods go, reduced to ashes and having met their dissolution? You ought to tell me everything that happened after that.
"By the grace of Vyāsa, you alone know this entirely, for no one else does; therefore, you know that scripture consisting of knowledge, and no other."
Thus questioned then by all those sages of purified souls, Sūta, having paid homage to Vyāsa, spoke these words.

Lomaśa said: When the gods situated within the cosmic egg—including Hari, Brahmā, and the others, as well as the world-protectors along with Indra—were pervaded by the poison-fire, then Śambhu was petitioned by the high-souled Heraṃba.
Heraṃba said: "O Rudra, O Mahādeva, O Sthāṇu, O Lord of the Universe! I have sportively created an obstacle for them that is very difficult to overcome."
Out of fear and delusion of intellect, they do not worship you nor even me; for those who exert themselves [in worldly efforts], their suffering becomes even greater.
Thus entreated by him—the lord of the Gaṇas, who was like a sun to the darkness of obstacles—the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose banner bears the bull, [responded] at that time.
Śambhu, who is formless, free from affliction, stainless, whose hair is the sky, who wears matted locks, and who is blue-and-red, spoke while in the form of a *liṅga*: || 11 ||
Maheśvara said: O Heraṃba, listen to my words with supreme faith; this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is composed of the nature of ego (ahaṃkāra).

O Lord of the Gaṇas, at the beginning of the world, the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) effects its own persistence, as well as its dissolution and origination, through the state of mere cognition (vijñaptimātratā).
It is free from illusion, eternally peaceful, always transcending both duality and non-duality; its nature is pure consciousness alone, and its sole defining characteristic is eternal bliss.
Gaṇapati said: "O scorcher of foes, if you are indeed the absolute Self characterized by supreme bliss, then there exists nothing else whatsoever other than you. (15)
How did this manifold form arise, distinct from gods and asuras, variegated, producing delusion, and characterized by the three deities? (16)
And by means of the four classes of beings, endowed with various distinctions, the wheel of saṃsāra has arisen, characterized as both eternal and non-eternal. || 17 ||
Deluded by the doctrine of knowledge which is mutually contradictory, some are devoted to the doctrine of action, while others rely upon their own particular qualities.
And those who are devoted to various forms of knowledge, which are mutually contradictory—save me, O Bull-bannered One, who have thus fallen into doubt. (19)
"O Lord, where do I and my host come from, and where is this bull? And whence have these others and so many more arisen, and where indeed do they belong? (20)
"All these illustrious ones have indeed been made composed of the qualities of sattva and rajas. Having laughed, the Blessed Lord Śambhu prepared to speak to Gaṇeśa.

Maheśvara said: By the power of Time (kāla-śakti), the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas) were produced; by them the entire world, including gods, spirits, and humans, was enveloped.
And know that all this which is perceived is impermanent from the perspective of ultimate reality; because it is produced, it is perishable despite the attainment of all supernatural powers. (23)
Lomaśa said: While Sadāśiva, who is endowed with Gaṇeśa, was speaking, he who is the universal form manifested from Sadāśiva in the form of a Liṅga.
The womb of the universe, whose form is Śiva and who consists of both cause and effect—that Blessed Lord, in the form of the Liṅga, became submerged at that very moment.
One supreme power stood there, characterized by the nature of the knowledge of Brahman; Gaṇeśa, filled with wonder, was intent on gazing at her. (26)
The sages said: "This entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is contained within Prakṛti; how then did the distinctness of Gaṇeśa arise? Let that be told. (27)
Lomaśa said: The Lord Gaṇeśa was born directly from Prakṛti; indeed, just as Śiva is manifest, so too is the Lord of Gaṇas of that same form.
Indeed, a battle took place between that great-souled one and Śiva; having become engaged through ignorance, it continued incessantly for a long time. (29)
Having seen his invincibility while mounted upon the elephant at that time, Śambhu struck him with a trident and felled him along with the beast.
Then Mahādeva, the scorcher of foes, being praised by the Supreme Śakti, said this to the Supreme Śakti: "Choose a boon, O beautiful one! (31)
Then Mahādeva was indeed chosen with the supreme boon: "O God, this one who has been slain by you is my son, without a doubt. (32)
"This fool, born from a portion of Prakṛti, does not know you; therefore, restore this son to life for the sake of my very satisfaction. (33)
Laughing, the Blessed Lord Rudra restored the son of Māyā to life; he joined him to his own mouth with a face like that of the ocean.
Then, by the grace of Śaṃkara, he became elephant-faced; though born of Māyā, he became free from illusion and possessed of knowledge.
Satiated eternally by the nectar of self-knowledge alone and free from all affliction, Raudra remained established in samādhi and became the destroyer of even Kāla, the god of death.

Having uprooted one of his own large teeth for the sake of the staff of yoga (yogadaṇḍa), the Lord of Gaṇas, holding it in his hand, transcends the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman); he shines with the singular unity of both supernatural power (ṛddhi) and perfection (siddhi). || 37 ||
Those who were his hosts and obstacles, and others who were even more numerous on earth—Śambhu then made him their lord as well.

Therefore, he beheld Prakṛti, who possesses universal form; standing apart before her, he recognized both the Liṅga and Prakṛti itself. He saw the stainless Liṅga abiding within Prakṛti by its very nature.

He saw that his own self, along with his attendants and likewise the entire three worlds, were all dissolved within the *liṅga*; even though Heramba was possessed of knowledge, he too was thus absorbed.
Having fainted and then regained consciousness with effort, that lord of the Gaṇas bowed his head to those two lords.
Then, right there, he beheld Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Sadāśiva, who are the agents of the destruction of the world.
He beheld millions of cosmic eggs, resembling the size of atoms, which were composed of the power of the Liṅga and Śakti, and were like unto departed spirits.
They dissolve and are absorbed into Maheśa, who exists in the form of the Liṅga; the Liṅga is contained within Prakṛti, and she is contained within the Liṅga.
Then the entire Liṅga was covered by the Śakti, and the Śakti was likewise covered by the Liṅga; they existed in mutual union.
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is supported by the two Śivas; even Gaṇeśa does not possess that knowledge, nor do others know it in such a manner.
Then the immensely radiant leader of the Gaṇas, together with his hosts and Śakti, being praised by them and by Śakti herself with supreme devotion, spoke as follows.

Gaṇeśa said: I bow to the God who is endowed with power, whose form is knowledge, who is gracious, who is beyond knowledge, the supreme embodiment of light; who is beyond form, the supreme essence, who is beyond the essence, the supreme auspiciousness, known as bliss, partless, and free from dejection.

From smoke, fire appears as if it were smoke; for you, who are born of knowledge, are perceived as being within Prakṛti. Indeed, you who have entered into Prakṛti are known as the manifestation of Māyā.

O Blessed One, being such as you are, you create, destroy, and protect the universe through your own māyā; yet by this poison, all this—along with Brahmā, the lords of the brahmins, and all that is moving and unmoving—has been utterly ruined.

Just as you were formerly the Lord Maheśvara, the sovereign of the three worlds and the self of all that is moving and unmoving, quickly restore that entire universe of moving and unmoving beings along with their vital essence, which has been consumed by fire.
Lomaśa said: Thus praised by Gaṇeśa, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings, [restrained] that Kālakūṭa poison which had arisen and was causing the destruction of the worlds.

In the form of a *liṅga*, he then swallowed that [poison] and made it pure; endowed with supreme compassion, he protected all the three worlds—including gods, asuras, and mortals—at that very moment. (53)

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Surendra, along with the world-protectors and the ṛṣis, the yakṣas, vidyādharas, siddhas, and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases—all of them rose up as if overcome by sleep. || 54 ||
Overcome with wonder and seized by awe, all the gods and asuras then spoke in amazement.
Where was that great Kālakūṭa poison by which we were put to flight, and these very guardians of the worlds were instantly rendered as if dead? (56)

Having spoken thus, the Daityas then remained silent; meanwhile, Śakra and the other world-protectors, placing Viṣṇu—the Lord of all lords—and Brahmā at their head, spoke these words with great enthusiasm.
"O Viṣṇu, by whom was this caused to be made? We of small intellect do not know. Then the Blessed One, laughing, [spoke] together with Brahmā and those gods.
Then all those twice-born ones attained samādhi with one-pointed minds, having eradicated desire, anger, and other passions through the knowledge of reality.
Then, not seeing the Liṅga situated within their own selves, Viṣṇu and the others, placing him at their head, praised [the Lord] according to the ultimate truth.
Through the self, yogis worship the Supreme Self.

The Liṅga alone is supreme knowledge; the Liṅga alone is supreme austerity; the Liṅga alone is the supreme dharma; the Liṅga alone is the supreme goal. Therefore, there exists nothing whatsoever that is superior to the Liṅga.

Speaking thus at that time, the gods and asuras, together with the world-protectors and the sages, placed Viṣṇu at their head and sought refuge in Śambhu, who is dark as the tamāla tree and the worthy protector.
Save us, save us, O Great God, compassionate Supreme Lord! Just as you previously saved us all, so too ought you to save us now.

Therefore, O God of gods, your lotus feet possess a greatness rooted in service that is infinite in form; they are those which, through your supreme compassion, take refuge in you. Salutations to you, O best of gods; be gracious! 65.
Standing in the midst of the very form of the Liṅga, the Lord, the creator of all beings and the husband of Ramā, spoke these words together with all the hosts of gods.
"You are the Lord in the form of the Liṅga, the bestower of fearlessness upon the worlds; you are the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God in the form of the Liṅga praised by Viṣṇu. (67)
All those who have died have been saved from poison; therefore, O Lord Mṛtyuñjaya, protect us, protect us! O Mahākāla, O Destroyer of Tripura, salutations be unto you! 68.
Then the god Maheśvara, in the form of a Liṅga, being praised by Viṣṇu, appeared together with Ambā, as if awakening those gods.
O Viṣṇu, O all you gods, O sages, listen to this: for even in this impermanent cycle of existence, one considers it to be filled with permanence.
O wise ones, for one who perceives the Self by means of the self, what is the use of sacrifices, what is the use of austerities, and what is the use of exertion in ritual actions? (71)
Whether as one or as many, there is no purpose whatsoever; for whatever difficult task has been accomplished by you all acting together, [that alone suffices]. (72)
How was that churning of the Ocean of Milk performed for the sake of the nectar, while always disregarding and setting aside Mṛtyuñjaya and me? (73)
Therefore, there is no doubt that we have all indeed fallen into the jaws of death; for this reason, we have fashioned the god Gaṇeśa for the sake of accomplishing our purpose.
Those who do not bow to Gaṇeśa and likewise to Durgā will become partakers of suffering; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (75)
All of you, however, are most unrighteous, arrogant, and merely fancy yourselves wise; ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, you are solely deluded by pride.
Therefore, all of you have fallen into the mouth of Kāla; of this there is no doubt. All of you, including Indra and the other hosts of deities, are devoted solely to the Vedas.
All those such as Indra and the others are petty and in vain, being intent only on self-glorification; for you, O Lord of Śacī, do not know yourself through this worldly manifestation.

O rogue, you have indeed made a great effort for the sake of immortality; yet, O evil-minded one, you do not realize that even this kingdom which you obtained by means of a hundred horse-sacrifices is dependent upon others.
O fool, those ascetics by whose words you have been praised are themselves fools; devoted to their respective passions, they seek only to gratify you.
O Viṣṇu, because of your partiality, you do not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful; some are supported by you, O Viṣṇu, while others are indeed protected as well.
"Endowed with desire, you always behave here like a child; as for all the other world-protectors, how could there even be news of them here? (82)
For if a matter is handled otherwise, there will be a change in the outcome; by that means, the accomplishment of the task will be achieved, though it has been forgotten by you. (83)
By whom all have been protected today from the great terror of the Kālakūṭa poison; by whom Viṣṇu was turned blue, and by whom all others were defeated. (84)
One should perform the rite of worship for that high-souled Gaṇeśa, by whom the worlds were reduced to ashes and yet by whom they were also protected.
But those who do not worship Gaṇādhipa Vighneśa at the commencement of an undertaking, their success in the task will certainly not come to pass, just as it has for you.
Having heard these words of Maheśa, the gods, asuras, kinnaras, and cāraṇas then questioned the Lord of the Mountain regarding the ritual procedure for worship according to its ultimate meaning.
Maheśvara said: On the fourth lunar day of the fortnight, the Lord of the Gaṇas should always be worshipped by men who have bathed with pure white sesame seeds during the bright fortnight.
Having performed all necessary duties, one should diligently carry out the rite of worship for Gaṇeśa with perfumes, garlands, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings.
First, meditation on Gaṇeśa must be performed according to the prescribed rule; for many Āgamas concerning Gaṇeśa have arisen, just as there are for me.
Since the lay devotees (upāsakas) were endowed with various degrees of darkness (tamas), goodness (sattva), and passion (rajas), those very names became manifold through the division of their groups.
He has five faces, is the leader of the Gaṇas, possesses ten arms and three eyes; he resembles beautiful crystal, has a blue throat, and the face of an elephant.
I shall describe his five faces exactly as they are.
The middle face, however, was fair-complexioned, four-tusked, and three-eyed; its trunk was beautiful, and its trunk-tip (puṣkara) held sweetmeats (modaka).
Likewise, another [form] has a yellow complexion, and one is blue with auspicious marks; another is tawny and bright white, possessing the auspicious face of Gaṇeśa.
Likewise, I shall describe to you the weapons for those with ten arms: the noose, the lotus, the goad, and the tusk.
One should meditate upon [the deity] holding a rosary, a plough, a pestle, and likewise granting a boon, as well as a vessel filled with sweetmeats in his hand.
With a protruding belly and distorted eyes, wearing a sacred thread and a girdle, seated in the yogic posture, with a crescent moon upon his matted hair; (11)

And meditation should be known as being of three types—sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa—just as it is for men. [The sāttvika meditation] has the luster of pure gold and possesses the extraordinary form of Gajānana (the Elephant-faced One). 12.
The god has four arms, three eyes, a single tusk, and a large belly; he holds a noose and a goad, and carries a bowl of modaka sweets in his hand.
The blue meditation is likewise said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa); thus it is described as threefold. Therefore, you must perform the worship immediately.
Twenty-one blades of dūrvā grass are offered individually under each name, while for the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇanāyaka), they are offered all together as one under all the names.
In that same manner, twenty-one modakas should be offered with their respective names. I shall now state ten names individually for the purpose of worship. (16)
O Lord of the Gaṇas, salutations to you, son of Umā, destroyer of sins; O Vināyaka, son of Īśa, bestower of all attainments. || 17 ||
O you who have a single tusk as your mouth, O you whose vehicle is a mouse, salutations to you, the preceptor of Kumāra; you are to be worshipped with great effort.
Having spoken thus to the gods and immediately embraced them with respect, Sadāśiva [then embraced] Viṣṇu, who dwells in the cave of the heart, and Brahmā.
The supremely resplendent Śambhu immediately vanished; having bowed to Śambhu, they all became intent upon the worship of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Then, having worshipped according to the prescribed rites, they were intent upon the adoration of Gaṇādhyakṣa with numerous offerings and with *dūrvā* grass, each separately.
For the leader of the Gaṇas, being well-pleased, became the bestower of boons upon the gods; having been circumambulated and saluted by them all, he was thoroughly gratified.
Endowed with the quality of darkness (tamas), all those foremost of asuras did not worship him; indeed, they were intent on mocking the gods.
Having worshipped Śāṅkarī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the sages, the gods, the Daityas, and the best of the deities went again to the Ocean of Milk.
Then the gods, having made Mount Mandara the churning-stick and Vāsuki the rope, churned [the ocean] while keeping Viṣṇu in close proximity.
And as the ocean was being churned, the Moon emerged first, filled with nectar for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of all the gods.
Śaunaka said: O observer of noble vows, why was the Moon formerly cast into the ocean, and by whom? You have previously described the jewels, such as the elephant and others. (27)
O Lord, tell us all this briefly at the outset; having understood it, O Sūta, we shall subsequently describe it in detail. (28)
Having heard those words of theirs, the charioteer took up speech.

O Brahmins, Candra, the son of Atri, endowed with all virtues, was born from Anasūyā; he originated from a portion of Brahmā. Durvāsas arose from a portion of Rudra, and Dattaka from a portion of Viṣṇu.
Seeing the ocean of milk being churned, Candra was filled with joy; and the ocean of milk, upon seeing Candra, also became eager.
And having entered with the delight of both parties, O best of the twice-born, the Moon, filled with nectar, stood before the presence of the gods while they listened.

And having seen that splendor, Candra was then quickly consecrated with the lustration rite (nīrājana) by the hosts of gods amidst the tumultuous sounds of many musical instruments, mṛdaṅgas, conchs, and various drums.
Then all of them, including the gods, asuras, and dānavas, paid homage to Garga and questioned him regarding the true extent of Candra’s strength.
Then Garga said: "Today indeed is the day for the strength of all; all your excellent planets have entered the quadrant positions. (35)
Muru arrived with Candra, and Budha also came; likewise Aditya, Śukra, Śani, and the great Aṅgāraka.
Therefore, the strength of the moon is most excellent for the accomplishment of your purpose; this moment, known by the name Gomanta, bestows victory. (37)
Thus consoled by the high-souled Garga, the gods—possessing great strength, roaring, and acting with haste—churned the ocean.
Having attained double their strength, those high-souled ones of firm vows repeatedly remembered Maheśa and Gaṇeśa.
From the ocean being churned and roaring on all sides, Surabhi herself emerged for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Satisfied, she, who was tawny-colored, with her great burden of udder-milk, then moved very slowly upon the waves.
Seeing the wish-fulfilling cow approaching, all the gods and demons showered a great rain of flowers upon her of immeasurable luster.
Then many musical instruments and various kinds of drums resounded; they had been brought from the midst of the water and were accompanied by hundreds of cows.
Among them were cows that were blue, black, tawny, pigeon-colored, brown, dark-grey, red, the color of rose-apple fruit, and tawny; Surabhi was then seen accompanied by these cattle.
At that very moment, the sages, filled with joy, requested Kāmadhenu—who was surrounded by both Asuras and Devas—from the gods and the Daityas alike.
To all the Brahmins, indeed, and to those of various lineages (gotras), cows together with Surabhi should be given; there is no doubt in this matter. || 46 ||
Requested by them, the gods and demons there gave those cows for the propitiation of Śiva; they were accepted by those most meritorious, highly auspicious, and noble-souled sages. 47.
Then all the sages caused those gods to proclaim an auspicious day for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the deities and for the destruction of the asuras. || 48 ||
Again, all of them, being greatly exerted, churned the ocean of milk; and from that ocean being thus churned, there then came forth—|| 49 ||
Having gathered together on one side the Kalpavṛkṣa, Pārijāta, Cūta, and Saṃtānaka trees—which resembled cities of the Gandharvas—the wise ones quickly churned the fierce Ocean of Milk once again.
From the ocean being churned, there arose the Kaustubha, the most excellent jewel among gems, possessing great luster and the brilliance of the sun.
Placing the cintāmaṇi jewel before them, they beheld the Kaustubha gem, which illuminates the three worlds with its own radiance.
Then all the gods indeed gave that Kaustubha gem to Viṣṇu; having placed the Cintāmaṇi in the middle, the gods and asuras, roaring with fierce strength, churned the ocean once again.
From that [ocean] being churned, the wonderful horse Uccaiḥśravas emerged, and furthermore, the elephant Airāvata appeared among the jewels.
In the same manner, he gave the jewel of an elephant accompanied by sixty-four others—white elephants with four tusks, full of rut. (55)
Having placed all of them in the middle, they churned once again; then, as the ocean was being churned, many things emerged.
Wine, Vijayā, Bhṛṅgī, as well as garlic and leeks, and likewise Dhattūra and Puṣkara, are extremely intoxicating.
They were stationed not all at once on the shore of the lord of rivers and streams; and again, those great lords of the asuras churned the ocean together with the best of the gods.
Then, from the ocean being churned, there arose that divine Lakṣmī, the sole mistress of the world; those who know Brahman call her Ānvīkṣikī, while others praise her as Mūlavidyā.

Some who are capable call it the knowledge of Brahman; others, perfection, prosperity, command, or even hope. Some yogins call it the power of Viṣṇu, while those ever-disciplined masters of illusion call it Māyā.
All those endowed with the power of knowledge speak of that Yogamāyā, which is joined with their respective philosophical tenets.
Then they beheld that Mahālakṣmī approaching slowly—a fair-complexioned young woman, affectionate, adorned with the filaments of lotuses.
She was beautifully smiling, with lovely teeth, dark-complexioned, adorned with fresh youth, and possessing the rising splendor of many wonderful garments, ornaments, and jewels. (63)
She had lips like the bimba fruit, a beautiful nose, was slender, possessed a lovely neck and charming eyes; she had a fine waist, shapely hips, and broad loins.
Her lotus-face was illuminated by lamps made of various jewels; her countenance was lovely and serene, and she was adorned with necklaces and anklets.
She was resplendent with a parasol being held over her head, and was being fanned with chowries as red as the surging waves of the Gaṅgā.
Mounted upon a pale white elephant, she was being praised by great sages; she bore garlands of celestial tree blossoms interspersed with jasmine flowers.
Seeing her held at the tip of his hand, the gods became intensely eager; while they were intent on gazing [at her], she indeed beheld them.
The virtuous Mahālakṣmī regarded the gods, the Dānavas, the Siddhas, the Cāraṇas, and the Pannagas just as a mother regards her own sons. 69.

Likewise, those gods who were looked upon by her with that splendor and fortune became endowed with it at that very moment, marked by the characteristics of sovereignty; whereas those Daityas who were not looked upon by her with that fortune became destitute of it.

And then, gazing upon Mukunda—dark as a tamāla tree, with beautiful cheeks and nose, resplendent with a supreme body, marked with the śrīvatsa, and casting a compassionate glance—[she beheld him]. (71)

Upon seeing this, Lakṣmī, adorned with a forest garland, suddenly descended from her elephant in great astonishment; she placed around the neck of the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu, the garland fashioned by Śrī and covered with bees.

Then, having observed both of them, she sat down there, taking her place on the left side of the Great-souled One; the gods along with the Daityas, as well as the Siddhas, Apsarases, Kinnaras, and Cāraṇas, experienced a wondrous joy.
Upon the arrival of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa there, a great joy arose among all the worlds simultaneously and in every way.
Mahāviṣṇu was surrounded by Lakṣmī, and Lakṣmī was likewise surrounded by him; thus, out of mutual affection, they were both intent upon gazing at one another.
Conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, flutes, and gomukhas, as well as bherīs and jharjharīs—there arose a tumultuous sound from them all. (76)
Then there was a magnificent performance by the singers, featuring stringed instruments, percussion instruments, wind instruments, and those with hollow bodies.
Thus, the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, skilled in beautiful song, propitiated Viṣṇu, Hari the Soul of All, with various kinds of musical instruments.
Thus sang Nārada, Tuṃburu, and others—the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and hosts of Suras and Siddhas—as they worshipped the god Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the Supreme Self and whose wisdom is unfathomable.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Lakṣmī," in the section on the Churning of the Ocean within the Kedāra-khaṇḍa, in the first part (Māheśvara-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 11 ||
Lomaśa said: Having bowed down to Janārdana, the Supreme Soul united with Ramā, the hosts of gods and asuras churned once again for the sake of the nectar.
And as the ocean was being churned, there emerged the highly illustrious one known as Dhanvantari, a youth who is the supreme conqueror of death.
Holding a full pitcher of nectar with both hands, all the gods indeed gazed upon that enchanting sight.
Then the Daityas went together, as if by force, desiring to seize the jar filled with nectar that was held in the hand of Dhanvantari.
Just as the best of physicians arrived, surrounded by a succession of waves, he was seen by Vṛṣaparvan as he approached very slowly.
The jar was in his hand, yet it was snatched away from him as if by force; thereupon, all the asuras roared most terrifyingly.
Taking the jar filled with nectar, those Daityas departed for Pātāla in great haste, while the gods were then filled with confusion.
Well-armored and desiring to fight, they followed along with them; then, beholding the gods, Bali spoke thus: || 8 ||
Bali said: "We gods, however, are satisfied solely by the nectar; therefore, you most excellent of gods must depart immediately."

"What need have we for heaven, filled with joy as you are? Formerly, friendship was shown to us by you who were intent only on your own interests; that is now known, and there is no need for further deliberation in this matter. (10)
Thus rebuked by that powerful one, the best of the gods departed for the Lord Nārāyaṇa by the same path they had come.
Seeing him, all the gods had their desires frustrated by Viṣṇu; they were then comforted with words and various skillful conciliations.
"Do not be afraid; I shall bring that nectar here. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Mukunda, the refuge of the helpless, [proceeded]. (13)
Having stationed all the gods right there, Madhusūdana assumed a deluding form and appeared before the face of the Daitya.
Then the Daityas, highly agitated, spoke to one another; at that time, a dispute among all the Daityas arose concerning the nectar.
While he was proceeding in this manner, by chance he then beheld a woman who had assumed a deluding form, enchanting to all living beings.
Overcome with wonder, their eyes became thirsty [to behold her]; then, having honored her, Bali, the king of the Daityas, spoke.
Bali said: "O highly fortunate one, the nectar must be distributed by you for the sake of providing a refuge for all; act quickly according to my word. (18)
Thus addressed, she spoke this with a smile to Bali: "A wise man should certainly never place his trust in women. (19)
Untruthfulness, rashness, deceit, folly, excessive greed, impurity, and cruelty—these are the faults inherent in women by their very nature. (20)
One should understand their lack of affection and their deceitfulness in accordance with reality; one should also recognize the faults of their own wives—of this there is no doubt. (21)

Just as wolves among beasts of prey are intent on violence, and as crows are among birds and jackals among wild animals, so should women always be known by the wise to be the rogues among human beings. (22)
"How can friendship proceed between me and you? In this matter, it is not at all to be understood who you are or who I am. (23)
Therefore, O best of Asuras, you who are discerning in what ought and ought not to be done, must act with supreme intelligence after due reflection. 24.
Bali said: "Today, distribute the nectar to all according to their due; we shall accept what is given by you. I tell you this in truth, indeed in truth. (28)
Thus addressed, the goddess Mohinī, the source of all auspiciousness, then spoke to all the Asuras, upholding the worldly order.
The Blessed One said: "By some divine power, you have all become ones who have achieved their purpose; today, joined with fasting, this is the consecration for immortality."

"O best of Asuras, let this auspicious desire be fulfilled; do you have any wish? Tomorrow morning you shall perform the breaking of the fast, and you must remain devoted to the worship of the vow. (31)
With wealth acquired through righteous means, the wise person should employ a tenth part for the purpose of pleasing the Lord.
Thinking "so be it," all those Daityas, deluded by the divine illusion and lacking sufficient discernment, did exactly as they were told.
And at that time, the Asura Maya indeed constructed dwellings that were charming, highly precious, radiant, and vast.
Having seated them all there, well-bathed and well-adorned, they, being highly excited, placed a full water-pot before them.
All kept a vigil throughout the night with supreme joy; then, when the dawn had arrived, they performed their morning ablutions.
The Asuras, headed by Bali, having formed themselves into rows in due order and performed all their necessary duties, then became intent on drinking.
Bali, Vṛṣaparvan, Namuci, and Śaṅkha; Sudaṃṣṭra, Saṃhlādin, Kālanemi, and Vibhīṣaṇa. || 38 ||
Vātāpi, Ilvala, Kumbha, Nikumbha, and likewise Pracchada; as well as Sunda and Upasunda, and Niśumbha and Śumbha. (39)
Mahiṣa, Mahiṣākṣa, the powerful Biḍālākṣa, the mighty-armed one named Cikṣu, Jṛmbhaṇa, and then the Asura Vṛṣa. || 40 ||
Vibāhu, Bāhuka, Ghora, and likewise Ghoradarśana—these and many other Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, as well as Rāhu and Ketu, sat down in their respective order. (41)
A row of those Daityas, numbering in the tens of millions, was stationed there.
Then, O twice-born ones, listen to what was done by that goddess for the sake of the nectar; indeed, a great deed was performed by her. (43)
Then, as soon as they were all informed, they took up their jars; endowed with supreme splendor, she was like the enchantress of Viṣṇu herself. 44.
