Then the Goddess, adorned with a water-pot held in her hand, shone with supreme splendor, she who is the most auspicious of all that is auspicious in the world. 45.
All those gods, bearing the halo [of light], arrived at that very moment in the presence of the Asuras, where those best of Asuras were.
Seeing them, Mohinī, that most excellent of women, immediately spoke.

Mohinī said: "These indeed should be known as guests, the means for accomplishing the entirety of dharma. To them, one should give according to one's ability, if my word is true. Let it be authoritative for you today; do not delay. (48)
Those who perform service for others according to their own ability should be known as blessed, pure, and protectors of the world. || 49 ||
Those who exert themselves solely for the sake of their own bellies should be known as partakers of suffering; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (50)
Therefore, O you of auspicious vows, I must divide this; give to the gods whatever is dear or not dear to yourselves. (51)
When these words were spoken by the goddess, they acted accordingly without delay; the Asuras summoned all the gods, including Indra.
And all those twice-born ones sat down for the sake of the nectar, O twice-born; while they were thus seated, Mohinī, who knew all dharmas, spoke these supreme words as if smiling at the Asuras.
Mohinī said: "Indeed, the Vedic revelation states that those who have arrived first are to be honored."

"Therefore, all of you who are devoted to the Vedas and dedicated to the gods, speak quickly: 'To whom shall I first give the nectar? O highly fortunate ones, let the leaders of the *balis* speak! (55)
Then Bali said to the goddess, "O lady of beautiful countenance, you are our mistress; of this there is no doubt—do whatever pleases your mind. (56)
Thus honored by that powerful one of purified soul, she quickly took up a water-pot for the purpose of serving the meal.

Therefore, with thighs like the trunks of lordly elephants, with eyes possessing a radiant luster, her gait slow due to the weight of her hips and her limbs slightly unsteady, she entered while making a sound with her tinkling golden anklets; she possessed jar-like breasts and held a water-pot in her hand. (58)
Then the enchanting goddess, serving the assembly of gods in person, repeatedly showered upon the deities the essence of nectar, like the flow of the nectar-nectar from the neck of the Moon. || 59 ||

Furthermore, those hosts of gods—the leaders of the *balis* along with the world-protectors (*lokapālas*), and the throngs of *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, and *apsarases*—were given the essence of nectar by that supreme Viśvamūrti.

All the Daityas remained seated on their thrones, while those hosts of gods were tormented by the nectar that had been offered; the eminent twice-born ones, headed by Bali, became silent and, being high-minded, became absorbed in meditation.
Then, seeing those Daityas thus fallen into delusion, Rāhu and Ketu—these two foremost of the Daityas—[acted].
Assuming the forms of gods and filled with haste for the sake of the nectar, those two seekers of immortality then sat down in the row of the gods.
When Rāhu, who was exceedingly difficult to conquer, desired to drink the nectar, he was pointed out to Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor by the Moon and the Sun.

Then the head of that Rāhu, who was difficult to withstand, was severed; the body of Śiva’s enemy ascended to the sky, while the trunk remained upon the surface of the earth. Wandering about at that time, it indeed crushed the mountains to powder.
Then the entire world of beings, along with the mountains, was pulverized; by her and by his body, all that is mobile and immobile was ground to dust.
Then Mahādeva, having seen her, stood upon her; she became the dwelling place for all the gods beneath the soles of his feet.
Its name is indeed "Affliction" (Pīḍana), because of dwelling in its vicinity.
Because her lotus feet are the abode of the great ones, she is renowned as Mahālayā, the enchantress of the three worlds.
And that Ketu, in the form of smoke, vanished into the sky; having offered nectar to the Moon, he became invisible.
Vāsudeva, the source of the universe and the supreme cause of all worlds, has through the grace of Viṣṇu brought this about, which grants the fulfillment of the purpose of the gods.
He was born for the destruction of the Asuras due to a reversal of fate; know that without destiny, even effort is indeed fruitless. (72)
All of them churned the Ocean of Milk simultaneously; success indeed accrued to the gods, while failure befell the asuras.
Then those Daityas, having provoked the best of gods and again deluded by Māyā, became equipped with many weapons and missiles, roaring as Viṣṇu had departed at that time.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Devas Consuming the Nectar," in the Section on Kedāra, within the First Part, the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 12 ||
Lomaśa said: Then, roaring and assailing the gods in battle—headed by Śatakratu and possessed of great strength and prowess—they [advanced]. || 1 ||

Then the high-souled son of Virocana, having ascended his celestial chariot together with his entire army and accompanied by various Daityas of great strength, rushed toward the gods, causing them great terror.
Assuming their own respective forms, they rushed forward by the thousands; some were mounted upon tigers, and others likewise upon buffaloes.
Some were mounted on horses, others likewise on elephants; still others were mounted upon lions, tigers, and śarabhas.
Others likewise mounted peacocks, royal swans, and cocks; some were mounted on horses, as well as camels and mules.
Others [mounted] elephants and donkeys, while still others were on carts; many Daityas were foot-soldiers, with swords, spears, and double-edged swords in their hands.
Some were armed with iron clubs, holding nooses, tridents, and mallets; others were equipped with swords and hair-tassels, while some carried *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles and iron bludgeons.
Other strikers were mounted on excellent elephants and chariots; and thousands of the leaders of the *bali* demons were mounted upon celestial palaces (*vimāna*).
Competing with one another and roaring again and again, Vṛṣaparvan indeed spoke thus to that powerful bull among the Daityas: ||| 9 ||
O mighty-armed one, you have brought about this encounter with Indra; however, one should never place trust in those who harbor ill intent.
For a wise person should somehow cultivate friendship even with one who is inferior, insignificant, or even an enemy; for such friendship does not fail even in times of adversity. (11)

One should never trust those who were previously enemies; for they might think, "We have now been defeated by you in battle," and how could those long-standing wicked ones not strive again to subvert your counsel? (12)
Thus spoke those invincible warriors, standing firm and desirous of battle; they adorned the field of combat with banners, parasols, and flags.
All the quarters were covered with yak-tail whisks and the battlefield was drenched; likewise, all the gods there were eager for the sake of the Daityas.

Having drunk the nectar, the illustrious ones mounted their mounts clad in armor; the majestic Mahendra, wielder of the thunderbolt, was mounted upon his elephant; Sūrya was mounted upon Uccaiḥśravas, and Candramas was mounted upon his deer. || 15 ||
Adorned with parasols and chowries, graced by the splendor of victory, all those beginning with Indra, desiring triumph, bowed down to Viṣṇu. (16)
Authorized by Viṣṇu, they indeed set out toward the Asuras in a rage; and those Asuras were of massive bodies, with terrifying eyes and fearsome prowess.
A battle took place between those gods and the Dānavas—tumultuous, most terrible, and bringing fear to all living beings. || 18 ||
Everything became filled with showers of arrows and was most wonderful; then, the sounds of "ṭacaṭa" arose in all ten directions.
Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, becoming struck by arrows, they fell to the earth, hit by shafts, tomara-spears, and iron bolts.
Some were being pierced in that manner, while others were struck down in battle; some fell broken by broad-headed arrows (bhallas), and others were mangled into pieces by iron shafts (nārācas).
Some Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas were struck by razor-sharp blows; some Dānavas were killed by arrows, while others were shattered. || 22 ||
Seeing the army of the Dānavas thus shattered, all the gods, roaring from every side and filled with joy, then gathered together and, having obtained victory in battle, praised it. || 23 ||
The three worlds were filled with the sound of conchs and musical instruments; those mighty Dānavas were filled with indignation toward the gods.
Bali and all the others rose up again in agitation, accompanied by many celestial chariots that resembled the sun. || 25 ||
A most tumultuous battle in pairs then broke out once more between the gods and the dānavas, each side desiring victory over the other.
Then Mahendra fought with the powerful lord of the Dānavas, and likewise the mighty-armed Yama encountered Namuci.
Nairṛta engaged in a truly great battle with Praghasa, while Pāśī, the subduer of enemies, fought with Kumbha and Nikumbha.
Rāhu waged a most terrible battle with Soma; at that time, Rāhu swallowed the nectar arising from the body of the Moon, and through contact with that very nectar, he became just like [the Moon]. (29)
All of those were seen by Śambhu, the Supreme Lord; and I am the refuge of all beings, of this there is no doubt, for I am beloved by all, both the Asuras and the Suras. (30)
Thus addressed, Rāhu then bowed his head to Śiva; meanwhile, the Moon, staying upon [Rāhu’s] crest, released nectar out of fear.
Indeed, by him [Brahmā], although his heads were very many, they were made into a single, enchanting garland all at once; then Śambhu bound it upon his own head as if it were a head-ornament.
Then, from consuming the Kālakūṭa poison, he became blue-throated; likewise, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, he wore a garland of skulls.
And Maheśvara bore that garland of skulls upon his head.

With that garland, the high-souled Hara—the god of gods, the destroyer of Tripura—shone resplendent; he by whom the great Gajāsura was struck down, and by whom Andhaka was likewise reduced to powder. (35)

By whom the Gaṅgā was held upon his head and the moon was placed as a crest-ornament—He who removes all fear; by whom the Vedas, Purāṇas, Āgamas, various Śrutis, and likewise the Śāstras [were upheld]. (36)

While they speak by means of various distinctions among the scriptures and remain silent when engaged in critical inquiry, the sole kinsman of the world is being discerned through the various divisions of the worship, doctrines, and tenets of those scriptures. (37)

For Śiva is eternal, the divine Supreme Self, to be known through the Vedas alone, the celestial Supreme Self; yet, having abandoned Him, deluded and heedless people do not recognize Śiva as the form of the Supreme Self. (38)

By whom alone it was created and by whom it is sustained; by whom it is supported and by whom this entire universe was made; he whose portion the world indeed is—the Supreme Self, Śiva, who is known through the Vedāntas—[is that one]. (39)
Whether wealthy or poor, whether high-born or lowly, one who is constantly devoted to Śiva is Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Or whoever, seeing an offering made by another that adorns Śiva, experiences satisfaction, obtains a gift equal to that [original offering]. (41)

Those who, endowed with faith, offer a garland of lamps on the full moon day of Kārttika—so long as those lamps burn before the Liṅga, for that many thousands of Yugas is the donor glorified in heaven. (42)
Those who have offered lamps combined with safflower oil in the temple of Śiva also rejoice in the presence of Śiva on Mount Kailāsa.
Lamps provided in the temple of Śiva, combined with linseed oil, lead those who offer them to Śiva together with a hundred of their lineages.
For even those who possess knowledge are indeed born as a result of the merit of giving lamps.
Those who have offered lamps combined with sesame oil in the temple of Śiva go to Śiva, accompanied indeed by a hundred generations of their lineage.
Those by whom lamps smeared with ghee are prepared and lit in the temple of Śiva go to the supreme abode, accompanied by a hundred thousand members of their lineage.

Those who always worship Sadāśiva with incense of camphor and aguru, and those who perform the waving of lights (ārārtikā) mixed with camphor day after day—they attain union (sāyujya); no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 48 ||
Those who, free from sloth, perform the worship of the Liṅga once, twice, or thrice a day, are indeed Rudras; of this there is no doubt. (49)

O twice-born ones, for those who wear Rudrākṣas while performing the worship of Śiva, and who do so without weariness during acts of charity, austerity, pilgrimage, and on festival days—all their merit becomes infinite. (50)

O best of the twice-born, listen to those rudrākṣas which were spoken of by Śiva: beginning with the single-faced and continuing up to sixteen faces. Among these, O brahmins, two should be known as the most excellent for the purpose of delivering [beings].

Among the rudrākṣas, the five-faced one and the single-faced one are likewise remembered. Those men who constantly wear the single-faced rudrākṣa go to the world of Rudra and rejoice in the presence of Rudra. (52)
Recitation, austerity, ritual action, yoga, bathing, giving gifts, worship, and whatever auspicious deed is performed, indeed becomes infinite through the wearing of the [sacred] thread.
Even if a Rudrākṣa is worn tied around the neck of a dog, that dog is also delivered by it; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Likewise, through association with the rudrākṣa, even sin goes to destruction; knowing this, one should perform auspicious deeds by wearing the rudrākṣa. (55)
Those who wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with sacred ash purified by mantra shall become Rudras in the world of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
And having collected the cow-dung of a tawny cow that has fallen from the sky, those dear to Śiva should dry it and then burn it for the sake of attaining *vibhūti*.
This is known as Vibhūti, the destroyer of all sins; first, the line on the forehead [formed by] the thumb must be meditated upon with effort. (58)

Excluding the middle finger, with the other two fingers [one should apply the ash]; thus, he on whose forehead three lines are seen should be known as a Śaiva, equal to Śiva himself, and the mere sight of him destroys sin. (59)
And those Śaivas who wear matted hair—whether seven, five, or nine—who shall establish these matted locks according to the Śaiva rite; || 60 ||
They attain auspiciousness here; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. Those devoted to Śiva, in particular, should wear rudrākṣa beads. (61)
Whether worshipped with flowers or through greatness, Sadāśiva, having delivered ten million members of his lineage, rejoices together with Śiva.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, there is nothing higher than Śiva; whatever is thus stated in the scripture has Śiva as its ultimate cause.
Śiva is indeed the giver, the creator, and the approver of the worlds; O best of the twice-born, know that the universe consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti.
The two-syllabled name "Śiva" protects one from great fear; therefore, O best of the twice-born, Śiva should indeed be meditated upon and remembered. (65)
The sages said: "Through his grace, the majesty of Somanātha has been understood; by the Supreme Lord, we have all been protected from the fear of Rāhu’s head. (66)
And what did Indra and the other gods do in that most terrible battle? Hereafter, let it be told what all the gods did. (67)
The entire majesty of Śiva has been heard by us as it issued from your mouth; now, let the account of the battle be told according to its true nature.
Lomaśa said: When the gods were indeed defeated by the Daityas, they all sought refuge with Śambhu; the best of gods suddenly bowed to Śiva, and then they all set their minds upon battle.
In the same way, all the Daityas as well, fighting with enthusiasm and possessing great strength, joined by the gods again and again engaged in battle, employing supreme missiles.

And thus all the asuras and the gods, seeking victory and filled with indignation, struck one another with spears, double-edged swords, tridents, iron clubs, and axes—like Himalayan lions difficult to overcome. Then the asuras, being slaughtered by the gods with the application of various supreme weapons, fell down.
They made the entire earth a mire of flesh and blood—this earth together with its trees and mountains, its oceans, forests, and mines.
And heads and headless trunks, great armor, standards, chariots, banners, and the heads of elephants and horses [lay scattered]. (73)

A marvelous sacrifice was performed by the son of Viśvakarman, by which even the gods and the sages of great splendor went to their destruction. || 15 ||
Therefore, O Lord, because of your assistance to others, we have all come from there to lead you to Amarāvatī.
While the gods were thus disputing, Brahmanicide, acting with haste, then said to Indra: "I choose you as my protector. (17)
Then Bṛhaspati suddenly spoke these words.
Bṛhaspati said: "We shall now prepare places for you to dwell; then, having been pacified by the gods out of regard for the gravity of that task, the slaughter [of the Brahmin] was appeased. (19)
Having reflected, all those wise gods, sages, yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, pataṅgas, as well as all the suras, siddhas, and cāraṇas, divided the slaughter into four parts. || 20 ||
Then all the inhabitants of heaven spoke to Kṣamā at the outset: "O Kṣamā, a portion of the slaughter must be accepted by you for the sake of accomplishing the task."
Having heard those words of the gods, the trembling Earth said: "Consider how this portion of the slaughter can indeed be accepted by me. (22)
"For I am the sustainer of all beings; I uphold the universe. I shall become impure, utterly overwhelmed by sin. (23)
Having heard those words of Pṛthvī, Bṛhaspati said to her: "Do not fear, O lady of beautiful limbs; you are sinless, and it shall not be otherwise."
Whenever the glorious Vāsudeva shall appear in the lineage of Yadu, at that time you shall become free from sin through the imprinting of his footsteps.
Follow our word; there is no need for deliberation in this matter.
Thus addressed, the sinless Earth carried out their word; then, having summoned the trees, all the gods spoke these words. (27)
"A portion of the slaughter must indeed be taken by you for the accomplishment of the task. Having been addressed thus, all the assembled trees spoke to the gods: || 28 ||
When we all become such givers of fruit to the ascetics, then all those ascetics will be possessed by the sin of slaughter.
"For those of great fortune are indeed sinners; therefore, let everything be deliberated. Then all the assembled trees were addressed by the family priest.
Let no anxiety be felt by anyone, for by the grace of Śatakratu, all [the arrows] have indeed been severed and have attained a state of being manifold fragments. (31)
"Therefore, you shall all eternally become trees. Having been addressed thus, they then all accepted their respective shares of the slaughter.
Then all the inhabitants of heaven, having summoned the waters, said: "O Waters, let a share of this slaughter be taken up by you today for the sake of accomplishing our purpose."
Then all the waters, having gathered together, spoke to the priest: "Whatever sins and whatever evil deeds there may be... (34)
Through contact with us, by means of bathing, purification, eating, and so forth, all living beings who are enveloped by sin are purified.
Having heard their words, Bṛhaspati said: "Let no fear be felt; for indeed, there is no sin that is difficult to overcome."
"May the waters purify all beings dwelling in the mobile and immobile worlds. Then, having summoned the women, Bṛhaspati spoke.

"Right this very day, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of all our undertakings, we must seize him who is the portion of the slaughter. Having heard those words of their preceptor, all the women spoke.
A woman who commits a sinful act is not tainted by that sin alone; rather, many parties are stained by it—such is the teaching of the Vedas. (39)
"Has nothing been heard by you? O priest, let it be reflected upon. Even though he was thus addressed by the women, Bṛhaspati then spoke.

"O fair-eyed ones, let no fear be felt regarding this sin; it shall likewise yield its fruit for others who are yet to come. For that portion of the slaughter belonging to all of you, as well as the fulfillment of your desires," (41)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, four portions and four Tīrthas were fashioned by the gods; he (Śiva) immediately took up residence in each of them.
For at that time Maheṃdra was born free from sin and was consecrated in the city of the gods by the hosts of deities as well as by the sages. || 43 ||
Accompanied by Śacī, the high-souled Purandara then became the sovereign of the universe, joined by the gods of great majesty, the lords of sages, and the hosts of Siddhas. || 44 ||

Then the fires were auspicious, all the winds and planets were radiant and endowed with peace; the earth immediately became beautiful, and likewise the mountains came to possess the luster of jewels. || 45 ||
For the minds of those wise ones were likewise serene.
The rivers flowed with nectar, the trees were always laden with fruit, and the medicinal herbs grew without cultivation and were like ambrosia.
Simultaneously, among all those dwelling in Indra’s world, there arose a supreme enthusiasm that brought great joy.
Lomaśa said: In the meantime, Tvaṣṭṛ, seeing the great festival of Indra, became exceedingly enraged, being tormented by grief for his son. || 49 ||
Overcome by despondency, he went to perform most severe penance; Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was satisfied by that austerity.

Being pleased, he said to Tvaṣṭṛ, "O you of noble vows, choose a boon. Then Tvaṣṭṛ chose a boon that would bring fear to all the worlds: "Indeed, let a son be granted to me who shall strike terror into the gods. (51)
"So be it," the boon was granted by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord; and immediately upon that granting of the boon, he then became a man.
There, indeed, was a most wonderful Daitya named Vṛtra; that Asura grew by a distance of a hundred bows every single day.
The Daityas who had emerged from Pātāla during the ancient churning for the nectar were slain by the hosts of gods, but were quickly brought back to life by Bhṛgu.
The entire surface of the earth was pervaded by that one Great-Souled One.
Then all the sages, those ascetics who were being slaughtered, quickly spoke to Brahmā regarding the calamity that had befallen them.
Likewise, Indra and the other gods, the Gandharvas, and the hosts of Maruts were told by Brahmā everything that Tvaṣṭṛ intended to do.
Indeed, for the purpose of slaying you, he who is named Vṛtra—possessing great splendor and the greatest of all Daityas—was produced through supreme ascetic penance.
"Nevertheless, let an effort be made so that he may be slain. Having heard the words of Brahmā, the gods, together with Indra, spoke.
The gods said: "When Indra was indeed released from the slaughter and established in heaven, we then committed an improper and difficult deed."
"O Brahmin, many weapons and missiles have indeed been gathered together through lack of wisdom in the hermitage of Dadhīci; what shall we do? (51)
Having heard that, Brahmā then spoke these words to the gods while smiling: "O gods, knowing that they have remained there for a long time, you must indeed go to them."
Then all the gods went there but did not see their respective weapons; they questioned Dadhīci, and he replied, "I do not know at all."
Then, having approached Brahmā once more, they all spoke the words of the sage.
Brahmā said: "Then, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of all the gods, you must beg for his very bones; he will grant them, of this there is no doubt."
Having heard those words of the Brahmin, Śakra spoke these words.
"O God, Viśvarūpa has been slain for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods; O Brahman, at that time I alone was made out to be the most wicked by the deities. (67)
Likewise, I was instantly rendered destitute of fortune by the family priest; yet, by supreme good fortune, I have now entered my own home.
Having indeed caused Dadhīca to be slain, those many bones of his were fashioned into weapons, O Blessed One; they are truly inauspicious.

"Indeed, this king of the Daityas named Vṛtra was begotten by Tvaṣṭṛ; how can I cause him to be slain, since Śakra is constantly afraid of sin? Having heard what was said, Brahmā then spoke these words.

He instructed him according to the very method prescribed in the treatises on statecraft (Arthaśāstra): "One may strike down an approaching assassin, even if he be a Brahmin or an ascetic, when he intends to kill; by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin. (71)
Indra said: "O Brahmin, I am undoubtedly afraid of the slaying of Dadhīca; therefore, from that killing of a Brahmin, a great sin will truly arise. (72)
Therefore, we must not commit an offense against the brāhmaṇas; from such an offense many evils will arise, and not otherwise.
Indeed, this supreme dharma, which is unseen, must be performed according to the highest rule by a wise man with his mind. (74)
Hearing those words of his, which were free from desire, Brahmā indeed said to him: "O Śakra, turn back by your own intelligence; go quickly to Dadhīci."
"Accompanied by your preceptor and joined by the gods, Śakra, you must request the bones of Dadhīci on account of the gravity of the task. (76)
Saying "So be it," they all went to the auspicious hermitage of Dadhīca, which was inhabited by various creatures and free from enmity.
Cats and mice were filled with mutual joy, as were lions, female elephants, and their calves, all moving together in unison.
Likewise, various species of animals were engaged in mutual play, and even snakes were engaged in mutual play with mongooses. (79)
Beholding many such wonders in that hermitage, all the gods were filled with the utmost amazement.
Then they beheld the best of sages seated upon his throne, blazing with supreme splendor like the sun.
Then, like Brahmā with Sāvitrī, that best of sages was likewise accompanied by Vibhāvasu or Suvarcas as his second.
Having bowed down to him, the gods then spoke these words: "You are the giver in the three worlds; we have come here into your presence. (83)
Having heard their words, the sage said to the gods: "O best of deities, tell me why you have all come here. (84)
"I shall give it, there is no doubt; my word cannot be otherwise. Then they all together, desiring their own ends, said to Dadhīci: (85)
O Brahmin, we are terrified and long for the sight of you; having heard that you are our protector, we have been sent by Brahmā.
Know that all of this has been obtained; therefore, O observer of noble vows, you ought to grant it.
Having heard their words, let it be said: what should be given? || 88 ||
Then the gods said, "O Brahmin, for the sake of destroying the Daityas and for the purpose of fashioning weapons, please give us your bones."
Laughing, the brahmin-sage said: "Wait but a moment, O gods; for today I myself shall cast off this body."
Having spoken thus to them, he then summoned his wife Suvarcas and said, "Listen, O Goddess of pure smiles, you of great splendor. (91)
"O gods, since you have requested my bones, I shall give up this body; today I shall go to the world of Brahmā through supreme meditative absorption. (92)
"When I have gone to the world of Brahmā, you shall surely reach me there by means of your own dharma; of this there is no doubt, so do not harbor vain anxiety. (93)
Having spoken thus to his wife, he sent her back to the hermitage; then, in front of the gods, the brahmin entered into meditative absorption.
Having cast off his own body by means of supreme meditative absorption (samādhi), he went immediately to the world of Brahmā, from which he does not return again. || 95 ||

Then that brahmin named Dadhīci, the best among the multitude of sages, beloved of Śiva and initiated into the Śaiva fold, quickly abandoned this body by his own will for the sake of helping others. 96.
Lomaśa said: Then all the hosts of gods, seeing that he had gone to destruction, began to reflect: "What shall we do? (1)
Then, having summoned Surabhi, the Lord of Śacī said to her: "At my command, you must lick the body of Dadhīci."
Having assented with the words "So be it," at that very moment, the cow immediately made the body fleshless by licking it.
The gods took those bones and fashioned them into weapons: from his backbone they made the thunderbolt (vajra), and likewise the Brahmaśiras weapon from his head.
Then the gods took many other bones of that sage; likewise, the gods, filled with enmity toward the Daityas, fashioned nooses from the network of his veins. || 5 ||
Having fashioned their weapons, they all, endowed with great strength and prowess, went forth from the gods in haste, intent upon the slaying of Vṛtra.
Then Suvarcā, the wife of Dadhīci, who had been sent there for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose, arrived and beheld everything; she saw her husband dead and observed his body.
Having understood all this deed of the gods at that time, the virtuous Satī became enraged; then Suvarcā, the wife of the eminent rishi, being exceedingly furious, uttered a curse.
"Aha! All the gods are most wicked; indeed, they are all powerless and likewise greedy. Therefore, let all the dwellers of heaven be childless from this day forward," she said. (9)
Having thus pronounced that curse upon those gods, that ascetic woman then entered the base of an Ashvattha tree and tore open her own belly.
The fetus emerged from the womb of the high-souled Dadhīca; he was the illustrious Piṅgalāda, a direct incarnation of Rudra. || 11 ||
Smiling, the mother, her eyes filled with anger, spoke to the embryo Suvarcas: "O Pippalāda, remain for a long time in his presence."
"O illustrious one, may you be fruitful for all [beings] like the Aśvattha tree. Speaking thus to her son, the virtuous Suvarcā followed her husband with supreme concentration.
In this manner, that wife of Dadhīca ascended to heaven together with her husband.
Those gods, having prepared their weapons and missiles, and being eager for the Daityas, arrived with Indra at their head, possessing great strength and prowess. || 15 ||
Then, placing their preceptor at their head and by his command, those many hosts of gods arrived on earth in the Middle Country; all of them, equipped with supreme weapons, spoke as follows. (16)
Having approached the assembled gods led by Indra, the great Daitya Vṛtra, surrounded by a host of Daityas, advanced.
Just as the summit of Mount Meru appears perfectly complete, so too did that great son of Viśvakarman, possessed of immense splendor.
By him Mahendra was seen, and by Mahendra the great Asura was seen; and the sight of both the gods and the Dānavas was most wonderful. (19)
Then those gods and Daityas, bound by mutual enmity and provoked against one another, roared most wonderfully.
And here, at the assembly of the gods, the deep and formidable sounds of musical instruments being played on all sides are heard.
While the musical instruments were being played, they all, filled with haste, struck one another with great force using various collections of weapons.
Then, in that battle between the gods and the asuras, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, became possessed by great fear and lost their senses.
Some were cut and split open, while others were severed in two by weapons; likewise, some were pierced by iron arrows and others were hacked to pieces by various missiles and arms.
Some of the denizens of heaven, struck by bhalla-arrows, wandered about maimed, like rays of light produced from clouds that shine within the skies. || 25 ||
Many heads indeed fell from the sky like stars, making it appear as tumultuous as the great dissolution of the universe.
It was set in motion in the Middle Country, bringing about the destruction of all beings; at that time, Namuci waged war against Śakra.
The King of the Gods himself swiftly struck Namuci with his thunderbolt; yet not even a single hair of the asura Tamucu was harmed.
Then, even with the thunderbolt, everyone—the asuras and the gods alike—was struck with supreme amazement, and Mahendra was then filled with shame.
He struck Namuci with his mace, yet that mace was shattered; though it remained stuck to Namuci's body, it fell to the surface of the earth.
Likewise, Purandara struck him with a great spear; that spear, having struck Namuci’s body, was shattered into a hundred pieces.
Thus the slayer of the enemies of the gods struck him with various weapons; yet, laughing and feeling prideful, Namuci did not strike Purandara.
Then Indra became silent, filled with profound anxiety; at that time, Indra did not know what should be done or what should not be done.
In the meantime, during that great battle of immense terror, a voice arose from the sky, quickly addressing Indra.

O Mahendra, slay this Daitya today at once—he who is most terrible and brings fear to the dwellers of heaven—using the foam near the waters, which is difficult to approach, against that great lord of Asuras.
Even when struck by another weapon, he is never subject to death; therefore, O Lord of Gods, make an effort for the sake of slaying this evil-minded Namuci.

Having heard these words, which were endowed with the supreme truth, divine, ever-joy-giving, and auspicious, that best among the diligent, possessed of infinite valor, went to the far shore of the ocean and exerted himself to the utmost.
Then, seeing him arrive there, Namuci, overcome with rage, struck the Lord of the Gods with a trident and, laughing, spoke these words: || 38 ||
O best of gods, why did you resort to the shore of the ocean, leaving the battlefield behind and casting away your weapons? (39)
O evil-minded one, what has been done to me by your very thunderbolt? (40)
Likewise, O dull-witted one, many other weapons and missiles were previously seized by you for the very purpose of killing me now. (41)
"What will you do to kill me, having arrived for battle? O dull-witted one, with what weapon do you wish to fight in this encounter? (42)
I shall cause you to go [to the next world] this very day, if you remain in battle; otherwise, depart, released by me—live long and be happy.
Having thus heard those arrogant words of him who shines in battle, Mahendra also, out of wrath, seized a wondrous mass of foam.
But seeing the foam in his hand, the asuras then laughed.
"Since my weapons have been exhausted by him alone, Purandara, the noble-minded Śatakratu, now desires to kill me. (46)
Having laughed thus at Purandara out of ignorance, Namuci, the preeminent among the Daityas, stood before him with contempt.
At that very moment, Indra swiftly struck him with foam.
When Namuci was slain, all the gods were filled with joy, and the sages honored him with shouts of "Excellent! Excellent! (sādhu-sādhu). || 49 ||
Then, having slain Namuci in battle, all those Daityas attained victory; filled with rage and imbued with joy, they were eager to fight.
Once again, the battle between the gods and the dānavas commenced, as they discharged various weapons and missiles, each desiring to slay the other.
When those Asuras were repeatedly struck down by the gods, then the highly resplendent Vṛtra approached Śatakratu.
Then, upon seeing Vṛtra, all the gods, asuras, and humans, overcome by great fear, fell down and lay upon the earth.
When all the gods and Siddhas were thus terrified, the powerful Indra, holding the thunderbolt in his hand, mounted Airāvaṇa.
Adorned with a held-up parasol and fanned by chowries, he was then attended by all the world-protectors and illuminated by their splendor.
Upon seeing Vṛtra, all those world-protectors and great lords were struck with fear, and they all sought refuge in Śiva. || 56 ||
Meditating in their minds upon Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, Maheṃdra, desiring victory, worshipped the Liṅga according to the prescribed rites.
Immediately recognized by his preceptor through supreme confidence, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati then spoke to Śakra.

Bṛhaspati said: If the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika falls on a Saturday, and it is obtained in its entirety, there is no doubt that all [desires] will be attained.
O Lord of the Gods, at the time of dusk on that [night], Sadāśiva in the form of a Liṅga should indeed be worshipped for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (60)
Having bathed at the time of midday, one should perform worship of Śiva with sandalwood paste, flowers, fruits, and other offerings, together with sesame seeds and *āmalaka* fruit.
Afterwards, at the time of dusk, one should worship a stationary linga—whether it be self-manifested (svayambhu), installed by oneself, or made by human hands.
Whether in a populated place, in a secluded spot, in a wilderness, or in a forest of asceticism, one should worship that Liṅga with devotion, especially during the evening twilight.
A Liṅga situated outside a village yields a hundredfold the fruit of one within the village; a wondrous Liṅga in the forest yields a hundredfold the merit of one in a Brahmin settlement.

Worship at a mountain shrine yields a hundredfold more merit than that at a forest shrine; and from a mountain *liṅga*, the fruit is known to be ten thousandfold. A *liṅga* situated in a penance grove, when worshipped, brings about even greater fruit.
Therefore, this worship and adoration of Śiva, as well as bathing in sacred fords and so forth, should be performed by the wise with discernment and skill. (66)
Having removed five lumps of earth, bathing alone is auspicious; one should perform bathing in a well especially with water that has been drawn out.
In a pond, one should perform the bath after removing ten lumps of earth; bathing in a river is superior, and especially so in a great river.
Of all sacred fords (tīrthas), bathing in the Gaṅgā is preeminent; one should perform the recommended bath in a natural pool (devakhāta), which is equal to that. 69.
Sadāśiva is to be illuminated by a thousand lamps, as well as by a hundred lamps or by a garland of thirty-two lamps.
One should light lamps with ghee for the complete satisfaction of Śiva, as well as with fruits, lamps, food offerings, perfumes, and incense.
Sadāśiva, in the form of the Liṅga, should always be worshipped with the sixteen types of offerings by men at the time of Pradoṣa for the attainment of all goals.
One should perform one hundred and eight circumambulations, and likewise, one should diligently perform prostrations that same number of times.
Sadāśiva is to be worshipped with circumambulations and prostrations; this Rudra is to be praised according to the prescribed rule by means of the hundred names.
Homage to Rudra, the Terrifying One, the Blue-throated, the Creator; homage indeed to the one with matted hair, the Lord of the Gods, whose hair is the sky.
Salutations indeed to the bull-bannered one, to Soma, to the blue-throated one; salutations to the sky-clad Bharga, the matted-haired beloved of Umā.
Salutations indeed to the one consisting of austerity, to the pervasive one, to Śipiviṣṭa; salutations to the lover of serpents, to the serpent, and to the lord of serpents. || 77 ||
Salutations to the mountain-dweller, to the tiger, to the lord of beasts; salutations to the lion who brought an end to Tripura, and to him whose roar is as fierce as that of a tiger.
Salutation to the Fish, to the Lord of Fish, to the Siddha, to the Supreme Being, to the Ender of Desire, to the Buddha, and to the Lord of Intellects. || 79 ||
Salutations indeed to the distinguished one, to the disciplined one, to the Supreme Self, to the Veda, to the seed of the Vedas, and to the secret of the gods. || 80 ||
Salutation to the Long One, to the exceedingly long, to the one of great value, and to the Great One; salutation indeed to the foundation of the world, whose form is space.
Salutations to the destroyer of the demon Gajāsura, the piercer of the demon Andhaka, who is blue, red, and white, and the beloved of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
Salutations to you, O Maheśa, the God who is fond of devotion, the imperishable source of all knowledge, the Great Lord, and the destroyer of Mahādeva.

Salutations again and again to the three-eyed one, to the three Vedas, and to the limbs of the Vedas; salutations indeed to the ultimate goal, to that whose form is the goal, and to the supreme reality.
Salutations indeed to the one of universal form, to the universal, to the creator of the universe; and to Śaṅkara, to Kāla (Time), who takes the form of the divisions of time. || 85 ||
Salutations indeed to the formless one, to the subtle, and to the most subtle; salutations to you who dwell in the cremation ground, salutations to you who are clothed in animal skins.
Salutations to the one who has the moon as his crest-jewel, to Rudra, the refuge of the universe; to Durga, the essence of the difficult-to-attain, the witness to the limbs of Durga.
Salutation to the one whose form is the *liṅga*, to the *liṅga*, and to the Lord of all *liṅgas*; salutation indeed to the one whose form is the *praṇava* and who is the meaning of the *praṇava*.

Salutations again and again to You, the cause of all causes, the conqueror of death, whose nature is the self-born [Brahmā]; salutations to the three-eyed one, the blue-throated Bharga, Lord of Gaurī, the source of all auspiciousness. (89)

Bṛhaspati said: Then, one observing the vow should recite the hundred names of Maheśa with effort, accompanied by circumambulations and prostrations of that same number, at the time of Pradoṣa for the sake of pleasing Saṃkara.
Thus has this vow been prescribed for you, O Śakra of great intelligence; perform it quickly, O illustrious one, and afterwards, O Lord, engage in battle. (91)
"By the grace of Śambhu, everything—victory and the rest—shall be yours."
For this Vṛtra, the son of Diti possessed of great splendor, formerly propitiated Śiva on Mount Gandhamādana through his ascetic penance.
"Know this, O Indra: the king named Citraratha [lived] there; that is the forest of Citraratha, located in the vicinity of Śivapurī. (94)

O highly fortunate one, in that forest the six waves of worldly existence do not exist; therefore, that most auspicious forest is named Caitraratha. To that king, a most wonderful vehicle was granted by Śiva himself. (95)
Moving at will, it was adorned with tinkling bells and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas; it was graced by Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, and Kinnaras.
Then, in former times, wandering the earth by that very same vehicle, he likewise [visited] the principal mountains and various islands.
Once, while wandering about, the great king named Citraratha arrived at Kailāsa; there he beheld a supreme wonder.
The assembly hall of Maheśa was resplendent with his attendants, and Maheśvara himself was graced by the Goddess, who was clinging to half of his body.
Having beheld Sadāśiva together with the Goddess, he spoke these words to the one accompanied by the Goddess.

O Śambhu, we as well as the ministers and others are possessed by sensual objects and even conquered by women; yet among people, we alone are ignorant, for out of shame we do not engage in the service of women.
Then, having heard these words, Maheśa, as if smiling, spoke words endowed with logic while everyone was listening.
Fear of public censure exists for everyone and not otherwise; likewise, the *kālakūṭa* poison was swallowed by all, yet it remained difficult for all to digest. (103)
Nevertheless, the mockery directed at me by the king was indeed difficult to digest; so Girijā summoned Citraratha and spoke these words. (104)
Girijā said: "O wicked soul, O fool, how is it that Śaṅkara has been mocked by you? O dull-witted one, you shall see the fruit of this deed along with me."
Whether he be a god or a mortal, whoever mocks those virtuous ones who possess equanimity of mind should be known as the lowest of the low. (106)

These lords of sages of great majesty, as well as these seers who embody the Vedas, and likewise all these beginning with Sanaka—indeed, they all, though ignorant [of his true nature], worship Śiva. (107)
"O fool! Among all people, you alone are truly wise today, and no others. Therefore, I shall indeed make you, O Daitya, who are excluded by both gods and the twice-born, truly wise. (108)
Thus cursed by the goddess Bhavānī, Citraratha, the best of kings, immediately fell suddenly from heaven. || 109 ||
Having entered an asuric womb, he then became known by the name Vṛtra; he was gradually endowed with supreme ascetic power by Tvaṣṭṛ.
By that great austerity, Vṛtra was said to be invincible; therefore, having now worshipped Śambhu at twilight according to the prescribed rite— || 111 ||

Having heard those words of his preceptor, Śatakratu, who had slain the great Daitya Vṛtra for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, then spoke: "Tell me now the procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana) of Pradoṣa."

Bṛhaspati said: When the month of Kārttika has arrived, on the thirteenth lunar day falling on a Saturday, the completion [of the vow] should take place there for the sake of achieving the perfection of the complete vow.
A silver bull should be fashioned, with a fine pedestal upon its back; upon that, one should place the three-eyed God, the beloved of Umā.
The wise man should have fashioned a golden image of Umā and Maheśvara, with five faces and ten arms, and the virtuous Girijā on his left side.
Having placed [the image] together with Śiva on a copper plate wrapped in cloth, accompanied by Umā and endowed with various enjoyments; || 116 ||
Endowed with faith, one should perform the night vigil according to the prescribed rite; first, the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) should be performed with great care.
O Lord of Gods, this bath with cow’s milk has been performed by me; O Supreme Lord, Master of the God of Gods, accept this ablution. (118)
"O Lord, the bathing is now being performed by me with curd; please accept what is offered by me today, and be truly well-pleased. (119)
"O Lord, a ceremonial bath with clarified butter is now being performed by me; please accept what is offered with faith, solely for the sake of your pleasure. (120)
"This honey has been offered by me for the sake of your pleasure alone; please accept it, O Lord of Gods, and be the bestower of peace upon me. (121)
O Lord of the gods of gods, the ceremonial bath is now being performed with sugar; accept this which is offered with faith, O Lord, and be well-pleased. (122)

In this manner, the bull-bannered Lord should be bathed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). Afterwards, the wise devotee should offer the arghya water in a copper vessel with this very mantra for the gratification of the beloved of Umā.
O Lord, beloved of Umā, you are worthy of the arghya offering; O Śaṅkara, be gracious and accept this arghya given by me.
I have offered you this water for the feet, accompanied by flowers and fragrance; accept it, O Lord of the gods, and being pleased, become the granter of boons.
O Lord, this seat has indeed been offered by me with a humble prostration; for the sake of your peace, O Lord of Gods, be forever a granter of boons to me. (126)
O Lord, Sovereign of the Universe, water for sipping has been offered by me; accept it, O Supreme Ruler, and be truly pleased with me today. (127)
O Lord, this golden sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), endowed with the *brahmagranthi* and the initiator of Brahmanic rites, has been given by me to you. (128)
"O Lord, O Śambhu, this fragrant sandalwood has indeed been offered by me with supreme devotion; O Bhava, make me fragrant. (129)
"O Śambhu, I have offered this supreme lamp kindled with ghee; accept it, O Lord of Gods, and become the bestower of knowledge upon me. (130)
O Supreme Lord, accept this distinguished and supreme lamp, expanded by all medicinal herbs, for the very sake of my peace. (131)
O Supreme Lord, accept this lamp-offering given by me; through the presentation of the *ārārtika*, become the bestower of splendor upon me. (132)
And on that night, those who know the ritual procedure should worship with effort, following the sequence of offerings such as fruit-lamps, food-oblations, and betel-leaf.

Thereafter, a vigil should be observed either at home or in a temple; having constructed a pavilion with a canopy adorned with various wonders, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with song, instrumental music, and dance. || 134 ||
O Śakra, by this very procedure, the rite for the concluding ceremony (udyāpana) of Pradoṣa should be performed by one who follows the rules, for the sake of accomplishing all purposes. 135.
Indra performed everything that was told by his preceptor; with him as his sole ally, Indra became intent upon battle.
Śatakratu fought against Vṛtra together with the gods; a tumultuous battle took place between the deities and the Dānavas. (137)
In that tumultuous and intense battle, which brought about the destruction of gods and demons, there was a most violent and exceedingly terrifying duel.
Vyoma fought with Yama, while Tīkṣṇakopana fought with Agni; Mahādaṃṣṭra fought with Varuṇa, and Mahābala with Vāyu. || 139 ||
All were intent on duels, each desiring to test the other's strength.
In that very manner, those best of gods, mighty-armed and heroic in battle, were then victorious; meanwhile, all the foremost Daityas suffered a supreme defeat on every side.
Seeing the foremost Daityas defeated by the gods and fleeing in all directions, utterly bewildered, the mighty Vṛtra, filled with supreme indignation, then spoke these words: || 142 ||
Vṛtra said: "O Daityas, why are you so deeply distressed and overcome with fear? Why are you all intent on flight, abandoning this wondrous battle?"
O heroes, firm in your resolve for battle, display each your own prowess; O hosts of gods, you who possess great strength, destroy [the enemy]! 144.
With maces, sharp-edged spears, swords, javelins, lances, and clubs; with scimitars, bhindipālas, nooses, tomara-darts, and fists. || 145 ||
Then the gods fought and, with supreme weapons and missiles produced from the bones of Dadhīci, they tore asunder the asuras.
Again the Daityas were slain by the gods and they too suffered defeat; yet once more, incited by that Vṛtra, they marched against the gods.

For when those foremost of Daityas were being struck down by the lords of the gods, they fled in all directions; some of those Dānavas, seeing [the situation] at that time, became terrified with fear and gradually assumed the appearance of eunuchs.
Thus reviled by the enraged Vṛtra, the preeminent Daityas said: "O illustrious Puloman! O Vṛṣaparvan! Salutations to you! (149)
O Dhūmrākṣa, O Mahākāla, O great Daitya Vṛkāsur, O Sthūlākṣa, O great Daitya Sthūladaṃṣṭra, salutations be unto you!
Having abandoned the very gateway to heaven, for what reason do you flee from this most excellent battlefield of the high-minded Kṣatriyas? 151.
Those for whom death occurs in battle go to the supreme state; therefore, a wise man should seek death in battle wherever it may be.
Those who indeed abandon their solemn pledge certainly go to hell. || 153 ||
Those men who, with weapons in hand, engage in battle for the sake of Brahmins, for the sake of their dependents, or indeed for their own sake, are great sinners. || 154 ||
Those who have indeed been struck by the blows of weapons or likewise died in battle, they go to the supreme abode; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 155 ||
Those whose bodies have been severed by weapons for the sake of cows or for the sake of their masters, and those who die or are wounded in battle—they indeed attain the supreme goal.
Therefore, even those sinful heroes who are slain first in battle attain the supreme abode, which is difficult to reach even for the wise. || 157 ||
Alternatively, visiting sacred fords, the study of the Vedas, the worship of deities, sacrifices, and various other such meritorious acts— || 158 ||
All those [other merits] together do not equal even a sixteenth part of that [merit], according to the unanimous teaching in all the scriptures regarding those fallen in battle. (159)
Therefore, you must perform heroic deeds in battle without hesitation; you must not act otherwise, for the word of the gods is authoritative.

All of you, endowed with the conduct of heroes and possessed of great majesty through your lineage and character, are now taking those very same steps as cowards who flee from the field of battle. (161)
Indeed, all those people surely go to the worlds of the wicked, according to both the word of scripture and traditional memory.
Those who are most wicked, established in unrighteousness, slayers of Brahmins, and violators of the teacher’s bed—they go to hell for their sin; likewise do those who flee from battle.
"Therefore, you must fight, being capable of bearing the burden of your master's task. Thus were they addressed at that time by the high-souled Vṛtra.
The Asuras accepted his word regarding the gods; they waged a tumultuous battle that struck fear into all the worlds. || 165 ||
When that tumultuous and deep conflict had commenced, Vṛtra, the sole lord of the great Daityas, spoke with extraordinary rage to Śatakratu, who was accompanied by the foremost of the gods.

Vṛtra said: "Listen to these words spoken by me, which are beneficial and consistent with dharma and artha; having become the lord of the gods, you do not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful. (167)
O Indra, having become intent on the power of what purpose was Viśvarūpa slain by you? Today, indeed, you have obtained the fruit of that very action.

O Lord of the Gods, consider this well with your mind: know that all those things which the dull-witted, the deluded, and those excluded from the Dharma—who lack the capacity for success—perform for the sake of accomplishing their goals, are entirely fruitless. (169)
Therefore, being devoted to dharma and freed from sin, fight! O Indra, you are indeed my brother-killer; for that reason, I shall cause you to be slain.
"Do not depart; remain firm, surrounded by the gods. Thus addressed by Vṛtra, Śakra was filled with extreme rage; mounting Airāvata, he went forth with the intent to slay Vṛtra.
Beholding Indra approaching, Vṛtra, the best among the powerful, spoke these words with a laugh, even as everyone was listening.
"Strike me first; therefore, I shall cause you to be slain. (173)
Thus addressed, the lord of the gods struck with great force the immensely powerful Vṛtra, the best among the strong, on the region of his knee with a mace.
He caught her as she was falling with a single hand as if in play; with that very mace, he swiftly struck the Lord of the Three Worlds.
That mace struck down Purandara along with his thunderbolt. Seeing Śakra fallen, Vṛtra spoke to the gods: || 176 ||
"O gods, lead your lord back to your own city, Amarāvatī. || 177 ||
Having heard these true words of the great-souled Vṛtra, all the gods, eager for battle, acted accordingly and withdrew Indra from the fight.
Having driven him away while he was mounted upon his elephant, and surrounding him, all the gods, overcome with fear, abandoned the battle and fled toward the celestial realm.
Then, when the gods had departed, the great asura Vṛtra danced and laughed most excessively; by that sound, the very horizons were filled.
And the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled; and then everything, both moving and stationary, was agitated.

Having heard that the Lord of the Gods had departed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, then approached Indra; he touched him with the water from his own water-pot, and at that very moment, Purandara regained consciousness.
Seeing the Grandfather (Brahmā) before him, Mahendra was then filled with shame; and to Mahendra, who was overcome with embarrassment, the Grandfather Brahmā spoke.

Brahmā said: "Vṛtra is indeed endowed with ascetic power and established in the vow of celibacy; this highly illustrious Vṛtra is also endowed with the ascetic power of Tvaṣṭṛ. He is invincible through his fierce asceticism; therefore, conquer him through asceticism."

"O Śakra, Vṛtrāsura, the lord of the Daityas, can be conquered by you only through supreme meditative concentration. Having heard these words of the Supreme Lord, Hari then called to mind the bull-bannered god.
Then the high-souled Purandara, urged by his preceptor, praised him with a hymn of praise.
Indra said: "Salutations to Bharga, the god who is most difficult for even the gods to approach. O Lord of gods, be a granter of boons for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. (187)
Thus, having become intent on existence, the noble-minded husband of Śacī—though skilled in his own affairs—is indeed dull-witted and devoted to worldly manifestation.
Even those fools who are devoted to Śiva, if they delight in worldly proliferation (prapañca) and remain full of passion, do not attain the supreme abode of the Lord.
Those people who, being stainless and free from egoism, worship Mṛḍa, the bestower of knowledge, the Lord, the Supreme Lord, and Śambhu himself; || 190 ||
To those others, Śarva, the bestower of boons and the bringer of welfare in this world and the next, was praised by Maheśvara, who was indeed supremely impassioned. 191.
For Śambhu is always difficult to attain for those possessed by passion; there is no doubt in this matter. Therefore, Sadāśiva is indeed ever-present before those who are free from passion.

For the king of the gods is indeed greatly passionate and highly skilled in the successful accomplishment of his own karmic deeds; therefore, the lord of Śacī is always devoted to affliction, for he is eternally intent upon his own sensual desires. (193)
Then, having perceived Indra as he was offering praise, Maheśa, the all-seeing witness who had assumed the form of a liṅga, spoke to him out of regard for the gravity of the task.
"O Indra, go together with the gods against the Dānava Vṛtra; for he can only be overcome through ascetic penance, O Śatakratu, and not conquered in battle. (195)
Indra said: "By what means can this great Vṛtra, the foremost of the Daityas, be subdued? O Śambhu, let it be told quickly so that victory may be mine. (196)
Rudra said: "He cannot be slain in battle even by the best of the gods; therefore, you must indeed perform a despicable deed this very day."
Formerly, in my presence, this curse was pronounced by Pārvatī: "This one shall be renowned in the three worlds by the name Citraratha. (198)
Wandering about in the radiant celestial chariot given by me, that foremost of Daityas has now attained this birth as a result of his derisive laughter.
"Therefore, O best among those skilled in battle, know him to be invincible in combat. Thus was Mahendra addressed by Śambhu, the great yogi. 200.
Thinking "So be it," Śakra undertook that vow.
Waiting for a vulnerability in Vṛtra, that illustrious one dwelt near him for a thousand years, setting his mind on slaying him.
Standing outside the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), Vajrapāṇi, by the permission of his preceptor and the family priest, zealously performed his own duties.
Once, Vṛtra, the preeminent among the Dānavas, surrounded by all the Daityas, arrived at the Narmadā by chance.
Indra met with defeat and was led back to heaven by the gods; "I alone have slain my enemies, and there is no one else equal to me. (205)
O Brahmins, always considering himself endowed with manly prowess, Vṛtra arrived at the Narmadā at the time of dusk.
Then, at the time of dusk, Indra beheld Vṛtra, the foremost among the powerful, surrounded by a vast multitude of asuras.
In that region, on the thirteenth day of the waning moon, when it was joined with Saturday, Indra was exhorted by Bṛhaspati, who took him by the hand.
Then, Oṃkāra, in the form of a Liṅga on the bank of the Narmadā, was worshipped according to the prescribed rite with circumambulations and prostrations.
By the greatness of the Pradoṣa vow, the powerful Vajrapāṇi became [so] at that very moment through the grace of Śaṅkara and Gaṇeśa.
Even the great Vṛtra, though endowed with ascetic power, became overcome by sleep there at the time of dusk; he was then awakened by Śuṇḍa.
The fruit earned through asceticism was destroyed at that very moment by falling asleep at the hour of dusk, and he fell into a state of misfortune.
And due to the goddess's curse, Vṛtra was born with his desires frustrated.
When the first quarter of twilight had passed, Vṛtra approached the sacred bathing place, surrounded by various Daityas equipped with diverse weapons.
The Lord of Śacī, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, seeking out a flaw in that deed, discovered a vulnerability and went slowly to slay his own enemy.
Then all those Daityas—furious, terrible, and of fearsome prowess—rose up simultaneously, unbearable even for Śatakratu.
Then a battle took place with those exceedingly powerful staff-bearers; at that time, all the gods came to the aid of Śatakratu.
Then the powerful Daityas and Devas fought; a battle took place at night, a crushing conflict between the Suras and Asuras.
Enveloped by many weapons, a most terrible conflict unfolded. While that fierce and dreadful battle was thus proceeding, Vṛtra then, having equipped himself for combat, seized a formidable trident.
Standing at the forefront with Indra, he let out an exceedingly terrifying roar; by the reverberation of that sound, the three worlds were struck with fear.
Having mounted Airāvaṇa, Mahendra then shone resplendent with a parasol being held over him, which was as beautiful as the orb of the moon.
Then, being fanned with yak-tail whisks, he spoke to the bull among the Daityas.
Indra said: "O Vṛtra, surrounded by my great army, engage me in battle; for you are a hero among heroes by virtue of your supreme asceticism. (223)
Thus addressed by him at that time, Vṛtra spoke these words: "O Indra, strike me first; afterwards, I shall slay you."

Thinking "so be it," Purandara then desired to release that extremely unbearable thunderbolt with its hundred edges; however, he was restrained by that highly radiant priest, the best among the wise. Accepting his words as "so be it," Indra did accordingly. || 225 ||
Seizing his mace, Indra struck Vṛtra; however, Vṛtra warded off that mace just as a wretched man wards off a guest.
And seeing his own mace rendered useless, Indra fell into deep anxiety.

While he was thus reflecting, Vṛtra then spoke to Purandara, reviling him: "O Śakra, have you forgotten that most wondrous and loathsome deed performed by you in the past, by which you were born with a thousand eyes through the curse of the great seer Gautama? (228)
Those heroes who indeed abide by restraining the collection of their senses attain victory in this world, but others such as you do not.
This battlefield is most terrible for sinners; of this there is no doubt. || 230 ||
Thus did the bull among the Daityas revile the lord of the gods; then the lord of the gods brandished his trident, which was like lightning.
With that great spear, Vṛtra of wondrous prowess shone like Rudra, the ender of the eon, with his intense ascetic heat.
Having observed him in such a state, Śatakratu, the king of the gods, advanced with the desire to slay Vṛtra, the bull among the Dānavas. || 233 ||
Beholding Purandara approaching with the intent to kill him, he laughed there most excessively, causing fear even to Śakra; for, having opened his mouth very wide, he had come toward Purandara.
Then the lord of the Daityas, possessed of great splendor and desiring to devour him, suddenly approached Śakra and swallowed him along with his elephant.
Bearing a vajra and a crown, he danced and roared; yet in the mere twinkling of an eye, that Purandara was swallowed up.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the gods as they looked on; for at that time there was an earthquake and thousands of meteors fell. (237)
The entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, was shrouded in darkness; yet at that time, Vṛtra, dancing about, became possessed of supreme splendor.
Then all the gods, being tormented, approached Brahmā and reported all these deeds of the demon Vṛtra.
Having heard that, Lord Brahmā was deeply distressed and utterly amazed: "How has this most extraordinary calamity befallen Mahendra? (240)
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, together with the gods, praised the god Giriśa with supreme concentration.
Brahmā said: Oṃ, salutations to Mahādeva in the form of the Liṅga; salutations indeed to the God who is the universal form, to Virūpākṣa. || 242 ||
"Save, save, O Lord of the Three Worlds, Purandara who is seized by Vṛtra! Then, while everyone was listening, a voice arose from the sky.
Satī spoke the procedure for the worship of the Liṅga to him who desired her welfare: "A transgression was committed by Indra while he was engaged in the Pradoṣa vow. (244)
By one who has performed circumambulation around the floral remains, the pedestal, and even the shadow of the temple, the transgression of stepping over the pedestal has been committed.

Those fools who leap over [the path] are indeed to be punished, there is no doubt; therefore, one should diligently perform circumambulation and prostration before Caṇḍa, the chief of the Gaṇas, accompanied by the worship of the Liṅga. || 246 ||
With the sole intention of attaining the highest good, those who have received initiation should always perform the worship of the Liṅga with effort for the sake of pacifying all sins. (247)
Having heard that disembodied voice, Brahmā and the other gods, with palms joined in reverence, questioned the auspicious celestial speech.
"How shall we worship the Liṅga, and by what ritual? At the time of dawn, at midday, and likewise in the evening? (249)
Which flowers are [appropriate] in the evening, and likewise at midday, as well as in the morning? Tell me those exactly as they are. (250)
Then a voice from the sky spoke in detail: || 251 ||
Karavīra, arka flower, and bṛhatī flower, as well as dhattūra blossom and likewise the śatapatra; || 252 ||
Āragvadha, punnāga, bakula, nāgakeśara, bradhna, utpala, kadamba, and likewise the mandāra flower; || 253 ||
Many excellent flowers and many lotuses are to be known by the wise as always pure during the three periods of the day. (254)

The *jātī* flower, the *mallikā* flower, the *mogaraka* flower, and likewise the blue flower; as well as the *kuṭaja*, the *karṇikāra*, that which is called *kausumbha*, and the red-colored lotus. || 255 ||
These very flowers that I have described as superior for the worship of the Liṅga at midday—I shall now speak of those for the evening.
And those that have ripened during the three times of day are undoubtedly pure; at night, the mogaraka flowers alone are undoubtedly pure. || 257 ||
Having thus understood these various modes of worship, those who know the ritual rules should always perform the prescribed procedure for the worship of that liṅga in the abode of Śiva.
Having passed between the bull and also between the pedestal, one should not perform a circumambulation; by doing so, one incurs sin.
For indeed, this Śakra performed the circumambulation while resorting to a rajasic disposition; therefore, it has become fruitless.
Indeed, Purandara, along with his elephant, has been seized by Vṛtra this very day; you yourselves must perform that task by which Indra may be liberated. (261)
By means of the ritual procedure of Mahārudra, one becomes liberated at that very moment; for this [man] is indeed Indra, O gods—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (262)
With those very words, the gods diligently worshipped Rudra according to the prescribed injunctions, with effort, using the Rudrasūkta.
And so, O best of the twice-born, having worshipped Rudra with the Ekādaśīrudriya, the gods performed the fire-oblation every day according to the ten-fold proportion.
Desiring to liberate Purandara, they suddenly performed recitations, worship, and oblations; then, by the grace of Śambhu, the king of the gods suddenly emerged, having burst through the womb.

Then, beholding him who had emerged—the lord of the gods of gods by his splendor, accompanied by his elephant and his thunderbolt, wearing a diadem and earrings, endowed with supreme glory, and possessed of great majesty—Puraṃdara; || 266 ||
The celestial drums resounded, as did conchs by the many; and the gandharvas, apsarases, yakṣas, and sages were filled with joy.
At that very moment, when Purandara was released, a great joy arose simultaneously among all the inhabitants of heaven; then Śacī arrived at the place where Purandara had been freed.
There, joined by Śacī, he was consecrated by the great sages; the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) was performed for him by everyone with great care.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, when Mahendra was consecrated again by the sages at that time, the earth became once more preeminent with auspiciousness.
The quarters became serene and the sky became stainless; the fires were then extinguished, as were the minds of the great-souled ones. (271)
Thus, many such auspicious events occurred thereafter; when Śatakratu was liberated, there arose a most wonderful marvel.
While such a great festival of the mighty was thus proceeding, the terrifying body of Vṛtra fell down.
Right there, the most sinful Brahman-slaughter fell upon the earth; that region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is called Antarvedī. || 274 ||
Renowned as a field of merit, famous, and a purifier of the world, that region where the slaying of Vṛtra was established is itself sinful.
Because of the great accumulation of impurity (*mala*), it is proclaimed as *Mālāva*; indeed, upon that ground of impurity lies the great head of Vṛtra.
Within six months, it was cut to pieces by all the gods together with Indra. Having thus slain Vṛtra, Śakra indeed attained victory.

Seated upon Indra’s throne, the Lord of Śacī remained free from all anxiety; meanwhile, in the meantime, the Daityas came and reported everything regarding Śakra’s activities to Bali, who dwelt in Pātāla.
Having heard those words of theirs, Vairocana, filled with rage, then asked Śukra: "How can that Indra be brought under control? (279)
He said to Bali, "O King, perform a great sacrifice today to obtain the chariot of Jayanta; by that, victory shall be yours. (280)
Thus addressed by Bhṛgu, Bali, the son of Virocana, who was intent on performing a sacrifice, being noble-minded, quickly gathered all those materials here that are suitable for the sacrifice. (281)
The great sacrifice was commenced by the high-souled Bhārgava; Bali, having entered the state of initiation, offered oblations into the sacrificial fire.
Then, while the fire was being offered oblations according to the ritual procedure, a most wonderful chariot emerged from that [fire] of Bali.
Yoked with four swift horses, bearing a lion-standard of great luster, the glorious one was equipped with weapons and missiles and adorned with white steeds.
Then, urged by Śukra, Bali performed the ritual bath of conclusion (avabhṛthasnāna); having honored the chariot, he then ascended it. || 285 ||
Surrounded by the Daityas and desiring immediately to fight Purandara, the great Bali, son of Virocana, instantly reached heaven.
Having arrived with his army, he ascended Amarāvatī. Seeing that city besieged, those best of gods then deliberated for a long time and all spoke to Bṛhaspati.
"O highly fortunate one, what shall we do today? The foremost of the Daityas have arrived; they are all most terrible, skilled in battle, and desirous of fighting. (288)
Having heard those words of theirs, Bṛhaspati spoke.
These terrible gods, whose mouths were filled with clarified butter, were incited by Bhṛgu; they were all invincible through both their ascetic power and their prowess.
Having heard these words endowed with such virtue, all the gods were overcome with shame; even Indra, his intellect clouded by anxiety, became filled with embarrassment as he was being reproached.
Lomaśa said: "Indeed, Mahendra, being overcome by his own karma, spoke to his preceptor: 'What is called karma that can be crossed over through suffering without effort? (1)
Bṛhaspati said this: "Having abandoned Amarāvatī, we shall all go elsewhere together with our families, desiring victory."
All the gods did exactly so, abandoning Amarāvatī; and Purandara, assuming the form of a peacock, departed immediately.
Yama became a crow, the Lord of Wealth became a chameleon, Agni became a pigeon, and Maheśvara became a frog. || 4 ||
At that very moment, Nairṛta became a pigeon and departed from there; Pāśī became a francolin partridge, and Vāyu became a dove.
Thus, having abandoned their various bodies, they went to the third heaven; then, overcome by fear, they arrived at the holy hermitage of Kaśyapa.
Everyone praised Aditi, their mother, regarding the deeds of the Daityas.

Having heard that unpleasant news, Aditi, who was longing for her sons, spoke to Kaśyapa regarding the great calamity of the gods: "O Great Sage, listen to my words; having heard them, you ought to act accordingly. (8)
Defeated by the Daityas, the gods have abandoned Amarāvatī and reached your hermitage; protect them, O Prajāpati! (9)

Having heard those words of hers, Kaśyapa spoke these words: "O slender-limbed one, O beautiful lady, you should know through your great ascetic power that the Asuras, O virtuous woman, are indeed invincible, for they have been favored by Bhṛgu. (10)
O beautiful lady, their victory will indeed come through fierce asceticism performed from this very day; therefore, act with the utmost speed for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
O highly fortunate one, I shall tell you this vow for the attainment of your goal; perform it with diligence according to the prescribed rite, O auspicious lady. (12)
O Goddess, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the tenth day, being self-restrained and pure, one should take a single meal solely for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu.
O fortunate one, O lady of excellent complexion, Hari himself—the Lord who grants all desires and boons—is to be prayed to by his devotees with this mantra.
"O Lord, I am your devotee; for three days beginning with the tenth day, O Viṣṇu, I shall observe a vow. You should grant me permission. (15)
With this very mantra, the Lord of the World should be entreated; one should observe a single meal, and that meal should consist of food alone.
One should eat from a plantain leaf, avoiding salt; and on the eleventh day, one should diligently observe a fast.

O slender-waisted one, one should diligently keep a vigil at night; on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī), the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) must be performed with care according to the rules, together with one's kinsmen, after having fed the most excellent twice-born brahmins.

In this manner, one should perform the vow diligently for twelve months. When the month of Bhādrapada arrives, on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), one should carefully worship Viṣṇu, who is seated upon a water-jar (kalaśa).

One should prepare [the image] out of gold or silver according to one's capacity; on the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, which destroys sins, the observer of the vow should diligently fast for the pacification of all defects.
Having thus heard what was spoken by Kaśyapa, Aditi then performed a vow for one year, being fully endowed with self-restraint.
O twice-born ones, at the end of the rainy season, Janārdana, being fully satisfied by that very vow, manifested himself on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) under the asterism of Śravaṇa.
The Lord of Śrī, assuming the form of a young brahmin, has two arms and lotus-like eyes; he resembles the flax flower and is adorned with a forest garland. || 23 ||
Seeing him, Aditi, filled with wonder, was then united with Kaśyapa in the midst of the worship; that lotus-eyed woman offered praise.

Aditi said: Salutations again and again to You, the cause of all causes, the Self of the universe, the creator of the universe, the essence of consciousness; salutations again and again to You, whose form is most excellent, the Self of both the high and the low, possessed of unimpeded awareness.
Thus addressed by the gods, the venerable Aditya, who never falls from his station, smiled and spoke to Aditi, the mother of the gods.
The Blessed Lord said: "O sinless one, I am pleased with your supreme austerity; and with this very body, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. (27)

Having heard the words of the Blessed One, Aditi said to him: "O Blessed One, the gods have been defeated by the more powerful Asuras; O Janārdana, protect all those Asuras who have come to you for refuge. (28)
Having heard those words of hers, Viṣṇu, the sole lord of Vaikuṇṭha, then understood all the machinations of the gods and everything that Bali intended to do.

"What task must indeed be performed by me this very day, by which the gods shall attain victory and all the foremost Daityas shall suffer defeat? Thus Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, reflected upon everything. (30)
The Blessed One said to Gada: "O illustrious lady, go today toward the slaughter; slay the son of Virocana with all haste. (31)
The beautiful woman, as if smiling, said to Hṛṣīkeśa: "Indeed, it was impossible for me to kill Bali, for he was a great devotee of Brahman. (32)
Then Viṣṇu, consoling him, said to the discus: "O Sudarśana, go at once to slay the powerful one."
Then he spoke with haste to Sudarśana, the wielder of the discus: "O Great Lord, that powerful one cannot be slain by me."

"O Viṣṇu, as you are devoted to Brahman, so too is that bull among the Daityas. Thus addressed by the bow, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow was astonished; having reflected for a very long time, he pondered deeply in many ways.
Atri said: "Then what did all those asuras do? Let that be told. (36)
Lomaśa said: Then all those asuras, headed by Bali, besieged the beautiful city in heaven, desiring to fight with Purandara.
For all the Asuras did not know that the gods had departed from heaven, having assumed various forms and taken refuge with Kaśyapa.
Then, having climbed the rampart in their agitation, the Daityas, desiring to slay the Lord of the Gods, entered Amarāvatī; but when they saw it empty, their minds were filled with satisfaction.
Then Bali was consecrated upon the throne of Indra by Śukra, surrounded by the asuras according to the ritual of consecration.
In that very manner, the great Bali Vairocana, having been established in the kingdom and appointed as the successor to Mahendra, then shone with supreme prosperity.
Served by the Nāgas and hosts of Asuras like Mahendra himself, he has conquered the celestial tree, the wish-fulfilling cow, and likewise the wish-granting gem.
