Among all those others who have attained the status of donors, the great Bali is the supreme donor of all beings through his gifts. (43)
Whatever desires he may wish for, the lord of the Dānavas bestows all of them upon every supplicant. (44)
Śaunaka said: "O highly fortunate one, it is indeed Indra, the lord of the gods, who never gives; how then is this Bali a giver? Tell me this exactly as it is. (45)
Lomaśa said: Whatever meritorious deed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is performed by men with effort, it must indeed be understood by the wise.
O Brahmins, Śakra, the performer of sacrifices, having indeed attained sovereignty over Amarāvatī through a hundred horse-sacrifices, was solely addicted to sensual enjoyments. || 47 ||
Know that the fruit sought after has been attained; yet, if he should again fall into miserliness, he will enter death once more and become devoid of merit.
O Indra, he who is a worm may indeed become a worm, and Indra himself may be born as a worm; therefore, there is no other liberation in this world superior to the act of giving.
For from giving, knowledge is obtained; from knowledge, liberation—of this there is no doubt. Indeed, O twice-born ones, devotion to the Trident-bearer is even superior to liberation.
Sadāśiva, the Lord of all, being pleased in spirit, bestows everything; Śaṅkara is satisfied with even a small amount of water. (51)
In this very context, they cite this ancient history; there is no doubt that this was performed by the son of Virocana.
For he was a gambler, a great sinner, a reviler of gods and brahmins, possessed of supreme deceit, and a great libertine devoted to the wives of others. (53)
Once, however, through great wickedness and deceit, wealth was won; and for the sake of a courtesan, flowers, betel, and sandalwood were likewise acquired.
Only his loincloth was visible; with both hands he formed the svastika gesture, and he offered perfumes, garlands, and other such things.
Running toward his home for the sake of the courtesan, he then stumbled on the ground and fell down at that very moment. || 56 ||
From falling, he then became possessed of a faint for a mere moment; thereafter, while that sinner, the doer of evil, remained in a state of unconsciousness—
Indeed, by virtue of his past actions, an immediate realization arose within him; overcome by supreme world-weariness and filled with suffering, he became like a gambler who has lost everything.
And whatever great offering of fragrant flowers and the like has fallen upon the ground, even if it was offered to Śiva by a rogue or one lacking intelligence; (59)
Citragupta declared: "Furthermore, you have given [this] to Śiva, the Supreme Self, at the end of your body's fall. (60)
"You are to be cooked by me, O dull-witted one, in the great hells!"—having been addressed thus by the King of Dharma, the gambler spoke these words: (61)
"O Blessed One, indeed no evil deed has ever been committed by me. O Yama, please examine my good deeds according to their true nature. (62)
Citragupta further declared: "Moreover, [this merit] was given by you at the end of your body's life and offered to Śiva, the Supreme Self. (63)
By the ripening of that karma, you shall undoubtedly attain the station of the Lord of Śacī for exactly three ghaṭikās; know this, there is no doubt.

At that very moment, the god [Indra], accompanied by all [his attendants] and mounted upon Airāvata, arrived; he was led to the abode of Śakra. Then Śakra was enlightened by that preceptor of purified soul.
O Purandara, for a period of three ghaṭikās, even a gambler must be seated upon my own throne by my command. (66)

Having heard the words of his preceptor and immediately placing them upon his head, Śakra went right there; for that gambler was ushered into the palace of the king of the gods, which was filled with various wonders.
He was consecrated upon the throne of Śakra and obtained the kingdom of Indra; and by offering fragrances, along with flowers and betel-leaf, to Śambhu, he attained that state. (68)
How much more so those endowed with faith who always offer with devotion great quantities of perfumes, flowers, and other such items to Śiva, the Supreme Self? (69)
Having attained union with Śiva and being accompanied by the army of Śiva, they experience great joy; indeed, Śakra is their servant.
The great happiness that belongs to those whose minds are peaceful and who are devoted to the worship of Śiva is difficult even for Brahmā, Śakra, and the other gods to attain.
Those fools, greedy for sense objects, do not understand; Mahādeva is indeed to be saluted, and Sadāśiva is to be worshipped.
Mahādeva is to be worshipped by living beings who know the truth; therefore, the gambler attained the status of Indra for three ghaṭikās.
Having been consecrated by the family priest, he was established in the position of Indra; at that time, Nārada spoke to that highly illustrious gambler.
"Bring Indrāṇī here so that the kingdom may be beautifully adorned. Then, laughing, the gambler who was dear to Śiva spoke.
"I have no business with Indrāṇī; you need not speak further, O high-minded one. Having said this, the gambler then proceeded to give [the gift].
The beloved of Śiva gave Airāvata to Agastya; the noble-minded gambler gave a horse to Viśvāmitra. (77)
The highly illustrious one then gave to Vasiṣṭha the horse named Uccaiḥśravas, the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu, and the Cintāmaṇi gem of great luster.
Then that one of great splendor gave the Kalpavṛkṣa tree to Gālava, and the illustrious one also gave Kitava his house to Kauṇḍinya.
Thus, filled with joy and solely for the sake of pleasing Śiva, he gave these and many other various kinds of jewels to the sages.
The Lord granted him a period of time lasting for three *ghaṭikās*; after those three *ghaṭikās* had passed, the former owner arrived.
Then Purandara, having seated himself upon his own throne in Amarāvatī, was praised by the sages and remained there together with Śacī.
The evil-minded one said to Śacī: "O beautiful lady, you have been enjoyed by this gambler; tell me the truth of the matter, O auspicious one. (83)
Then the stainless lady, smiling, spoke to Purandara: "O Purandara, you look upon all things through the analogy of yourself."

That great-souled one, appearing in the form of a gambler, was a knower of the supreme truth through the grace of Śiva; indeed, that noble being was endowed with dispassion, by whom everything has been attained as the Supreme. (85)
Having abandoned the snare of kingship and other such things consisting of delusion, he became victorious over others. || 86 ||
Having heard the words of Indrāṇī, Purandara, the lord of the gods, became filled with shame and remained silent while seated upon Indra’s throne.
The best among those skilled in speech spoke these words to Bṛhaspati: "Neither Airāvata nor the horse Uccaiḥśravas is to be seen. (88)
"By whom have all these objects, such as the *pārijāta* tree and others, been taken away? The Guru replied: "This great deed has been done by a gambler. (89)
Give this very day to the sages, for as long as his existence truly persists, so too do those who possess their own existence within that great existence of his. (90)

And those who are ever vigilant and devoted to the meditation on Śiva are indeed dear to Śaṅkara; having abandoned the fruits of action and relying solely upon knowledge, they go to the supreme state. || 91 ||
Having heard these words of his, Śakra spoke this speech to Bṛhaspati: "Yama will likely say all of this for the sake of his own prosperity, O Śakra. (92)
Thinking "so be it," the king went at once with his preceptor to the city of the gods; for, desiring his own purpose, Purandara likewise then departed for the city of Saṃyaminī.
Being honored by Yama, Śakra indeed spoke these words: "You have given my position to that wicked gambler! (94)
"By him this most loathsome deed has been committed; indeed, all my jewels have been given away by him to various people. Know this to be the truth regarding dharma. (95)
You are named Dharma; how could you have given it to a gambler? You have now brought about the destruction of my kingdom. (96)
"O highly fortunate one, bring quickly the elephants and other such things, as well as whatever other jewels have been given here and there. (97)
Having heard the words of Śakra, Yama spoke these words, overcome with anger toward the gambler: "What has been done by you, O sinner? (98)
Furthermore, that sovereignty over the realm of Śakra which was just now given by you for the sake of enjoyment has been bestowed upon the twice-born; indeed, a great wrong has been committed. (99)
"O fool, you have indeed committed an improper act by stealing another's property; because of that great sin, you shall go to hell. (100)
Having heard Yama’s words, the gambler spoke these words: "I am destined for hell; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (101)
O Lord, for as long as my sovereignty over the throne of Śakra has existed, whatever was given to the twice-born has indeed been bestowed exactly as prescribed.

Yama said: "Giving is praised on earth, and the fruit of one's actions is seen there; however, no one should ever give a gift in heaven to anyone at all. Therefore, you are to be punished, O fool! You have performed what is contrary to the scriptures."
The guru is the teacher of those who possess self-control; the king is the teacher of the wicked-minded; I am the teacher of all those of sinful character—of this there is no doubt. || 104 ||
Having thus rebuked that gambler himself, the King of Dharma said to Citragupta, "Let this man be cooked in hell. Then Citragupta, laughing, spoke to Yama: || 105 ||
How can a gambler go to hell, he by whom the great elephant Airāvata was indeed given to Agastya? (106)
Likewise, O Gālava, may there be prosperity for you; the horse born from the ocean was given to the high-souled Viśvāmitra, as was the immensely radiant cintāmaṇi gem.
Indeed, such jewels as these were given by him for a mere trifle; by the ripening of that karma, he is worthy of worship throughout the three worlds.

Whatever is given by men, whether in heaven or on earth, for the sake of Śiva—all that one should know to be imperishable; it is called a flawless deed. Therefore, there is no possibility of the gambler going to hell.
And whatever sins belonged to that high-souled gambler were all reduced to ashes simply by the act of remembering him.
By the grace of Śambhu, all their meritorious deeds were restored at that very moment; having heard those words of Citragupta, the King of the Pretas himself [acted accordingly].
Laughing and turning his face downward, he spoke thus to Śatakratu: "For you are the king of the lords of gods, an elder who is greedy for sovereignty."
"One hundred horse-sacrifices have been performed by you to earn a single birth; there is no doubt in this matter, for indeed a great merit has been earned by you. (113)

Indeed, by specifically entreating all the sages, beginning with Agastya, through wealth and prostration, those jewels—the elephant and others—shall be obtained by you, so that you may quickly become happy.
Thinking "so be it," Purandara, whose vision was clouded by a lack of discernment, departed for his own city; then, with his neck bowed low, he entreated the sages and obtained the Pārijāta tree.
In this very manner, having obtained the kingdom, Purandara then became the king in Amarāvatī together with the high-souled ones.
Indeed, rebirth was granted to Kitava by Vaivasvata; through the ripening of a certain karma, he became the son of Virocana. (117)
At that time, Suruci, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan and the chief queen of Virocana, became the mother of that gambler; he too remained within the womb of that high-souled woman.
From that time forward, he indeed remained highly devoted to righteousness and charity toward the son of that very Prahlāda as well as toward Suruci. (119)
While still residing within his belly, that gambler formed an unsurpassed resolve, O brahmins—a resolve difficult even for the wise to attain. (120)
Once upon a time, Śakra went toward Vairocana, desiring to slay the lord of the Daityas; he did so having become a brahmin beggar.

Having reached the house of Virocana, Indra spoke these words, having assumed the form of an elderly brahmin: "O you of noble vows, give this to me! You are wise, O Lord of Daityas, and a donor throughout the three worlds. (122)

O highly fortunate one, O observer of noble vows, the learned brahmins, remaining in assemblies, describe your most wonderful conduct and your stainless fame; and I am a petitioner, O Lord of Daityas—grant me the favor of a donor. (123)
Having heard those words of his, the lord of the Daityas spoke this speech: "O Lord, what should be given to you? Tell me quickly now. (124)
For Indra, indeed, having assumed the form of a Brahmin, spoke to Virocana: "O Lord of Daityas, I beg of you that which I have been longing for. (125)
"It should be given out of love for me; of this there is no doubt," said the Asura, the son of Prahlāda, speaking these words with a smile.

"O Brahmin, if you so desire now, I shall give you my own head; this kingdom is obtained without effort, and this royal fortune shall not go to another. I will surrender it all to you—of this there is no doubt. (127)
Having been addressed thus by that Daitya, Hari reflected for a moment and then said: "Give me your own head, adorned with its crown."
When these words had been spoken by Śakra in the form of a twice-born, the Asura Prahlāda’s son, acting with haste and joy, then cut off his own head and gave it to Mahendra with his own hand.
That dharma which was formerly performed by Prahlāda, which is extremely difficult to practice, was done by taking recourse solely in devotion to Viṣṇu with a mind entirely intent upon Him.
There exists no other thing anywhere superior to giving; that gift which is bestowed upon those who are afflicted brings great merit. (131)
Whatever one gives according to one's own capacity leads to infinity; there is nothing superior to giving found within the three worlds. (132)
It is proclaimed as being of three kinds: sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa. Furthermore, a gift given by this very person [in a specific manner] is characterized as sāttvika. (133)
Having cut off his own head, he gave it to Indra who was in the form of a brahmin; his crown fell there, along with its jewels of great luster.
They fell down all at once and became the maṇḍalas for the Daityas, the lords of men, and likewise for the Pannagas. || 135 ||
That gift of Virocana became renowned throughout the three worlds; even today, poets sing of it concerning that high-souled lord of the Daityas.
Virocana’s son was Kitava, who possessed great luster; he was born after his father had died, and his mother was devoted to her husband.
She then cast off her body and departed for the world of her husband; he, meanwhile, was consecrated by Bhārgava upon his own throne as king of Janaka.
There was one of great renown known by the name Bali; by him, all the hosts of gods, though possessed of immense strength, were terrified.
"Those [places] have already been described to you; now go to the auspicious hermitage of Kaśyapa. At that time, the highly illustrious Bali was Indra in the city of the gods."
Then that asura, having himself become the sun, scorched with his ascetic heat; and having himself become Īśa, he remained in the northeastern quarter, protecting it.

Likewise, having become Nairṛta himself, and likewise the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) himself, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) himself remained in the north; at that time, Bali himself remained thus as the direct enjoyer of the three worlds.
O twice-born ones, that gambler, solely devoted to the worship of Śiva, became intent on making great gifts through that very same former habit. (143)
Once, while seated in the midst of the assembly together with Bhṛgu and surrounded by the lords of the Daityas, the illustrious one spoke these words to Śaṇḍa and Marka: || 144 ||
"Let a dwelling be made here; let a dwelling be made here for me by the Asuras in my presence. Abandoning Pātāla this very day, you ought not to delay. (145)
Having heard that, Bhārgava laughed and said this: "One is glorified in the heavenly world by means of various sacrifices. (146)
O Great King, it is by the performers of sacrifice alone, and not otherwise, that heaven can indeed be enjoyed; O King, this which I have spoken is not otherwise.

Having understood the words of his preceptor, the lord of the Daityas spoke these words: "By whatever deed has been performed by me, let all the great Asuras dwell in heaven for a very long time; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (148)
Laughing, the Blessed One Śukra, the descendant of Bhṛgu and the greatest of the wise, who possesses great ascetic power, spoke these words, considering Bala to be a fool.
As for the words you have spoken, O Bala, they do not please me; if you wish to come and dwell right here, O observer of noble vows. (150)
Perform a hundred horse-sacrifices for the sake of Jātavedas; having come to this land of action, you ought not to delay. (151)
Thinking "so be it," the high-souled and wise Bali then abandoned heaven; accompanied by the Daityas, joined by his preceptor, and together with his followers, he went to the earth.
Then the high-souled lord of the Daityas, having conquered the entire surface of the earth, went to that great sacred site of magnificent splendor on the bank of the Narmadā known as Gurukulya. (153)
Then, impelled by his preceptor, that wise and highly illustrious Bali, the son of Virocana and the best among the truthful, underwent the supreme initiation and performed many horse-sacrifices.
Having appointed a Brāhmaṇa as the presiding Ācārya, there were sixteen officiating priests (Ṛtviks), all selected by that very high-souled Bhārgava after thorough examination.
He resolved to complete one hundred sacrifices—one short of the full number—by means of the horse-sacrifices, which were characterized by supreme consecration and great power. (156)
Until a full hundred sacrifices have been performed by that king, this supreme vow of Aditi, which was previously proclaimed by me here, shall remain in effect. (157)
Satisfied by that vow, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, became his son in the form of a great young ascetic.
Then the Lord was initiated by Kaśyapa, the son of Aditi; once he had been initiated, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived. || 159 ||
The sacred thread was given by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, and the wooden staff was indeed bestowed by the high-souled Soma.
The girdle was brought, as well as a most wonderful deer-skin; likewise, the sandals were given by Mahī to the high-souled one. (161)
There, alms were brought by Bhavānī for the sake of accomplishing her purpose; thus it was given to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, who was in the form of a young brahmin.

Having paid homage to Aditi and Kaśyapa, the glorious and most resplendent Vāmana, the Lord himself, went to the sacrificial enclosure of Bali, the performer of the sacrifice, in order to deceive him. (163)

Then that Maheśa, the dwarf in the form of a young brahmin, who was Viṣṇu himself, the Supreme Soul, went to heaven for the sake of the gods' mission, making the earth tremble with the weight of his forefeet. 164.

Praised with truthful words by the people, the lords of sages, and the hosts of gods, that high-souled one, the sole kinsman of the world, proceeded swiftly and then reached the sacrificial enclosure. || 165 ||

For it was while singing the Sāman that the Lord, assuming the guise of a young brahmin boy, directly manifested; that Lord being sung as the Udgītha is the Supreme Controller, Hari, the Lord, the Sovereign who is to be known through the Vedāntas. 166.
Then, standing at the gate, the immensely radiant Vāmana, assuming the form of a young brahmin student, beheld that great horse-sacrifice of Bala.
The quarters of space were pervaded by the great form of Brahmā, as well as by that of the high-souled Vāmana, the young student Pavamāna. || 168 ||
Having heard that, the wise Bali said to Śaṇḍa and Marka: "Let it be seen how many Brāhmaṇas have arrived. (169)
Thinking "so be it," O twice-born ones, those two, Śaṇḍa and Marka, then rose up in haste; having arrived, they stood at the entrance of the pavilion.
They beheld the high-souled Śrī Hari in the form of a young brahmin; then, they returned in haste to inform Bali of that.

"O Great King, a single celibate student has arrived here and no other; he has come into your presence for the purpose of study and such. We do not know for what reason; you alone, O high-minded one, must know. (172)
When these words had been spoken by the two of them, that high-minded one rose at that very moment to see the young brahmin.
The great and highly resplendent son of Virocana saw him and, prostrating himself on the ground like a staff, bowed his head to the young brahmin.
Having immediately brought the young brahmin and seated him upon his own throne, he honored that youth with a grand offering of water for the hands and feet.
Bowing his neck, he spoke with gentle words: "O Lord, from where, for what reason, and to whom do you belong? Let that be told quickly. (176)
Having heard those words of the son of Virocana, Vāmana, his mind filled with joy, began to speak.
The Blessed One said: "For you indeed are the king, the lord of the three worlds; it is not possible for anyone else to be so. He who would bring his own lineage to ruin is remembered as a base man."
It is said that a man who proceeds either equally or even superiorly [to his ancestors] has performed an action by you that was not performed by your predecessors. (179)
And those who were the most eminent among the Daityas, such as Hiraṇyakaśipu and others, performed great divine penance for a thousand years.
His body was being devoured by many ants and was completely covered with gadflies, even as he was devoted to great austerity.
Having learned of that, Surendra indeed went to his city in former times, surrounded by a great army. || 182 ||
In his presence, all the Asuras were slain by the enemy of the Daityas; moreover, his queen Vindhya, while being led away, was rescued.

O King, in former times, everything that Nārada, desiring to accomplish a certain task, had envisioned in his mind through the grace of Śambhu was entirely brought under control by the lord of the Daityas through his ascetic penance alone. (184)

Her son was of great splendor, by whom [the demon] was led to the assembly hall; his son, O fortunate one, was your father, devoted to his ancestors, the learned Virocana by name, by that high-souled one Indra was [conquered]. (185)
O King, gratified by that gift, he then said with his own head: "O King, you are indeed his son; you have achieved supreme glory. (186)
The gods have been consumed like moths by your great lamp of glory; even Indra has been conquered by you—of this there is no doubt. (187)
"O you of noble vows, I have heard all of your life's deeds; I have come here as one of little merit, established in the vow of celibacy. (188)
"And grant me land for the sake of a hut, O best of kings. Having heard those words of that very boy, Bali spoke:

"O boy, having become a scholar, you do not understand those words spoken previously because of your childhood; I believe that upon hearing them, you will grasp them according to their true meaning. (190)
"Speak quickly, O illustrious one, how much land shall I give to you? Let that be reflected upon with a swift mind. (191)
Then Vāmana, smiling, spoke these words with a sweet voice: "Those Brahmins who are devoted to discontent are lost, without a doubt. (192)

O King, those brahmins who are truly contented are the ones; these others are merely wearers of the dress. They are devoted to their own duty, free from hypocrisy, and unrestrained by worldly attachments.
O Mahāmati, those Brahmins who are free from envy, have conquered anger, and are generous—indeed, O fortunate one, it is by them that this earth is sustained. (194)
"You are wise and, because of your great wealth, you are a donor in the three worlds; nevertheless, land measured by three paces must be given to me. (195)
"O destroyer of the gods, I have no need for much space; let my hut be just large enough for my entrance. (196)
"Our three steps will be fulfilled; there is no doubt about this. O King Bali, if you are indeed a giver, you must grant me, step by step, as much land as shall exist. (197)
Laughing, Bali, the son of Virocana, said this to him: "I shall give you the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves. (198)
"O highly fortunate one, indeed accept this which has been given by me! You are a petitioner, O boy; look, O Daitya, at the gift you are requesting. (199)
Whether the supplicant be few or many, the donor indeed reflects upon everything; having thus examined himself, he bestows [gifts] upon those who seek them.
For he who, possessing a noble mind, gives everywhere by treating others as himself—to such a person, a petitioner of meager fortune should not even have to ask. (201)
"O boy, today I give to you the earth with its mountains, forests, and groves, along with its hills and oceans; my word shall not be otherwise. (202)
Again that young brahmin spoke to the son of Virocana: "O Lord of Daityas, my [debt] is indeed fulfilled by three steps taken in succession."

Having heard those words of Baṭu, Bali, the lord of the Asuras, then spoke these words while laughing and considering himself exceedingly powerful: "Let it be taken by me, granted as it is, adorned with three steps. (204)
Thus addressed, Vāmana replied with a smile to the asura: "O you of noble vows, having first resolved to give the entire earth, you ought to bestow it. (205)
Thinking "so be it," the great Vāmana, the son of Kaśyapa, was highly honored by Bali; at that time, Bali was suddenly being praised intensely by the ṛṣis and the lords of sages.
After he had worshipped him, just as Bali was about to bestow [the gift], he was restrained by his preceptor; at that moment, the great son of Virocana [Virocana] arrived.

"You must not give a gift to Viṣṇu in the form of a young brahmin; having come for the sake of Indra, he will immediately cause an obstacle to your sacrifice. Therefore, you must certainly not worship Viṣṇu, the illuminator of the supreme self. (208)
In the past, by this very one assuming the form of Mohinī, the nectar was given to the gods, and by him the great Rāhu was slain.
By him the Daityas were put to flight, and the powerful Kālanemi was slain.

Such is this Great-Souled One; he is the Lord, the Master of the Universe, he alone. Having reflected upon everything with your mind, O high-minded one, you ought to act for the sake of what is beneficial and what is harmful.
Lomaśa said: Thus instructed by his preceptor Bhārgava, the Daitya spoke these words with a laugh, in a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
I have been addressed by you for my own benefit with those words by which I have been moved; yet your speech, though intended for my pleasure and welfare, may prove to be harmful to me. (2)
I shall give whatever is begged from me to this Viṣṇu in the form of a young brahmin; for this Viṣṇu is the true recipient of offerings, the Lord of the fruits of all actions.
Those in whose hearts Viṣṇu resides are certainly the most worthy recipients; by his name alone, all this world is said to be as if purified.
He by whom these Vedas, sacrifices, mantras, tantras, and all others indeed attain their full completion—he is this very Hari, the Lord of the Universe.
Today the Lord Hari, the soul of all, has come out of compassion to deliver me; know this to be the truth without any doubt.
Having heard those words of his, Bhārgava became enraged and filled with wrath; he began to curse the lord of the Daityas, who was devoted to righteousness.
O subduer of enemies, you wish to give away [the bride] while transgressing my word; O dull-witted one, may you become devoid of merit, and therefore, may you be stripped of your fortune! (8)

Thus he then cursed his disciple, that high-souled knower of the supreme truth whose awakening was unfathomable. Thereupon, that great poet, the best among those who know the dharma, departed in haste for his own hermitage.
When that descendant of Bhṛgu had departed, Bali, the son of Virocana, having worshipped Vāmana, proceeded to give him the earth.
Vindhyāvalī, coming forward and graced by half of Bali’s body, washed the feet of the boy and offered the earth to Viṣṇu.
Then, according to the ritual preceded by formal resolve (saṃkalpa), the unborn Lord, who is skilled in rites, grew great through that very resolve alone.
When the earth was pervaded by the one powerful Viṣṇu, all the heavens were pervaded by that second high-souled one.
Having gone to Satyaloka, Viṣṇu’s foot was washed by the Supreme Lord with water taken from his water-pot.

From the water that came into contact with his feet was born the Bhāgīrathī, who is all-auspicious; by her the three worlds were made pure, by her all the sons of Sagara were uplifted, and by her the matted locks of Śambhu were indeed filled at that time by Bhagīratha.
The primordial of all sacred fords, known as Gaṅgā, was brought down; it was established by Brahmā, joined with the very foot of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, the Self who is beyond Trivikrama became known by the name Trivikrama; at that time, the three worlds were traversed by the strides of Trivikrama.

With just two steps, Janārdana, the God of gods, filled this entire world of moving and non-moving beings; yet, leaving behind that true form, he again assumed the guise of a young boy and sat down upon his own seat.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, sages, siddhas, and cāraṇas, arrived at Bali’s sacrifice to behold the Lord, the Master of Sacrifice.
Thereupon Brahmā arrived and offered praise to the Supreme Soul; at that very place, other lords of the Daityas also arrived in haste along with Bala.
Surrounded by all these, Vāmana sat upon his seat in the palace of Bali and then spoke to Garuḍa.
"Having become a fool, this Daitya gave me the earth; yet, by the mere act of taking three steps, he has seized two of them. (22)
"For that evil-minded one does not give even after promising a single step; therefore, you must take the third step as well. (23)
Thus addressed by that high-souled Vāmana, Garuḍa rebuked the son of Virocana and spoke these words.
"O fool, what loathsome thing have you done? For when an object does not truly exist, why do you offer it to the Supreme Self? What need is there for such meager magnanimity on your part now? (25)
Thus addressed, Bali, being possessed and trembling, then spoke these words that are about to be told to Garuḍa, the lord of birds.
O you of great wings, I am capable and I am not a beggar; what can I give to him by whom all this has been caused to be made? (27)
"O father, I have indeed been rendered powerless by this great-souled one. Then that high-minded son of Tārkṣya spoke to Bali: || 28 ||
O Lord of Daityas, even though you were aware [of the consequences] and were forbidden by your preceptor, you gave the earth to Viṣṇu; have you forgotten that great [deed]?
That third step of Viṣṇu which was promised must be given; O hero, why do you not give it? You shall fall into hell.
"You do not give me my third step, O Lord! I shall seize it by force, you fool!"—having spoken thus to that great asura, he then bound the son of Virocana with the nooses of Varuṇa.
Having become utterly ruthless, Garuḍa, the best among victors, beheld his own husband bound; Vindhyāvalī then approached him.
Having fixed a single arrow, she stood before Vāmana; then Vāmana asked, "Who is this standing here in front?"
Then the highly effulgent Prahlāda, the lord of the Asuras, said: "This virtuous Vindhyāvalī has come to you as the wife of Bali. (34)
Having heard the words of Prahlāda, Vāmana spoke these words: "Speak, O Vindhyāvalī; what must I do for you? Thus addressed by the Blessed One, Vindhyāvalī replied.
Vindhyāvalī said: "O illustrious Janārdana, why has my husband been bound by the high-souled Garuḍa? Tell me that quickly! Then the one of great splendor, wearing the guise of a young brahmin, spoke.
The Blessed One said: "By this very [gift], the earth characterized by three steps was given to me; and today, indeed, the three worlds have been traversed by me with two steps."
"He must give me the third step as well; therefore, O virtuous lady, your husband has been bound by me with the very form of Garuḍa."
Having heard the words of the Blessed One, he spoke these supreme words: "O Lord, that which was promised by him alone has not indeed been given to you. (39)
Today, the three worlds have been traversed by you in the form of valor; therefore, you may strike us down, whether in heaven or on earth.
"O Lord, O God of gods, O Master of the world, nothing at all has been given. Then the Blessed One, the Sovereign, smiling, spoke to Vindhyāvalī.
"Three steps must be given to me today; tell me quickly now, O large-eyed one, what it is that dwells in your mind. Then that virtuous woman, standing before him of wide strides, spoke.
O Lord of the universe, by whom was this triple world traversed by you of mighty strides? Likewise, O sole kinsman of the world, what can be given by us to you of incomparable form? (43)
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, abandon that [resolve] and act accordingly now. My husband has promised me three steps; my husband shall give them to me today—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
"O Lord, best of gods, place your foot upon my head; O Lord of the universe, place your second foot upon the head of my child. (45)
"And O Lord of the World, place the third step upon the head of my husband; thus, O Keśava, I shall give you three steps. (46)
Having heard those words of hers, Janārdana was well pleased and spoke in gentle tones to the son of Virocana.
The Blessed One said: "Go to Sutala, O Lord of Daityas; you should not delay. Live long with all the hosts of Asuras and be happy."
"I am well-pleased, my dear son; what task shall I perform for you? O high-minded one, you are the most excellent among all givers. (49)
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you; I shall grant you all your desires. Thus addressed by Trivikrama, the son of Virocana then [spoke].
For he was indeed embraced by the Discus-wielder, the God of gods; then Bali, who was skilled in speech, spoke these words.
"All this world, both moving and unmoving, has been created by you; therefore, O Lord, I desire nothing other than your lotus feet. (52)
O Lord Janārdana, may there be devotion to your lotus feet; O Lord of Gods, may that devotion be eternal, again and again. (53)
Thus entreated by him, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, being exceedingly pleased, then spoke to the son of Virocana.
The Blessed One said: "O Bala, go to Sutala surrounded by your kinsmen and relatives. Being thus addressed by him, the Asura then spoke these words: || 55 ||
"O God of gods, tell me what task I must perform on earth; I shall remain in your presence—do not speak otherwise. (56)
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, filled with compassion, said to Bali: "O King, I shall remain constantly by your side."

"O Lord, I dwell constantly at your gate; O best of asuras, O Bala, do not be distressed—listen to my words! O great one, you are a granter of boons today; I shall indeed resort to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha."
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor, he went to Sutala, O Daityas, surrounded by the asuras.
Then, with his hundred sons and his preeminent arrows, the mighty-armed one, who was the supreme refuge for those who give, quickly took up residence there. (60)
All those who are beggars in the three worlds come before Bali; Viṣṇu, standing at his gate, grants them whatever they desire.
And whatever Brahmins there may be who desire worldly enjoyment, as well as others who desire liberation—whichever of these are present at his sacrifice, he bestows [the fruits] upon them.
Such was the Bali who was born through the grace of Śaṅkara, because in former times he had given [his kingdom] to the Supreme Self while acting as a gambler.
Having reached an impure ground, he offered great quantities of perfumes, flowers, and other such items that had fallen, to Śiva, the Supreme Self.
How much more so those who worship Maheśvara with supreme devotion; they go to the presence of Śiva with flowers, fruits, and water. (65)
O twice-born ones, there is indeed no one more worthy of worship than Śiva; for even those who are mute, blind, lame, or dull-witted [attain their goals through him]. (66)
Even those of low birth—Caṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and other outcastes—who are constantly devoted to Śiva, attain the supreme goal.
Therefore, Sadāśiva is to be worshipped by all wise men; indeed, Sadāśiva is to be honored, to be fully adored, and to be revered. 68.
Those who know the supreme reality meditate upon Maheśa as abiding within the heart; wherever the individual soul (jīva) exists, there alone Śiva resides.
Without Śiva, whatever exists becomes inauspicious in an instant; for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are merely performers of actions resulting from the [three] qualities (guṇas).
Brahmā is endowed with the quality of rajas; Viṣṇu is endowed with the quality of sattva; Rudra rests upon the quality of tamas; and Maheśvara transcends the qualities.
Mahādeva in the form of the Liṅga is indeed to be worshipped by those seeking liberation; there is nothing higher than Śiva, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

The sages said: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra have been described by you as possessing attributes (saguṇa). Tell us, how is it that Īśa, who likewise exists in the form of the Liṅga, is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa)?"

This entire world, moving and unmoving, whether vast or minute, is pervaded by the three qualities (guṇas) and by the Great One (Mahat). All this shines forth as consisting of illusion (māyā); without the Liṅga, by what could it shine, and from where would it shine? || 2 ||
O Sūta, whatever is seen, whether great or small, is perishable because it is a product.
Therefore, O Sūta, having reflected, you ought to sever our doubt; by the grace of Vyāsa, you alone and no other know everything.

The son said: "Everything regarding this matter was told by Vyāsa to Śuka. Śuka said: "How is it that you describe Śambhu, who is beyond all attributes (nirguṇa), as having the form of a Liṅga? O father, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely. (5)
Vyāsa said: Listen, my child, for I shall tell you this which was formerly spoken by Nandin when he was questioned by Agastya, and by which everything was heard, O Śuka.
Know the Supreme Self to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) yet having the nature of a subtle mark (liṅga); likewise, the Supreme Power (parā śakti) should be known as quality-less, eternal, and true.
By her this entire creation, manifested through the three qualities, and this whole universe of moving and non-moving beings, is perishable from the perspective of ultimate reality.
For there is indeed only one supreme Self, stainless and in the form of the *liṅga*; all those [beings], along with *prakṛti*, have gone to dissolution within the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
Since that very thing was previously called a *liṅga* because of its dissolution (*layana*), the Supreme Power has attained dissolution in that *liṅga*; how then could there be others? (10)

O highly fortunate one, since the qualities (guṇas) are dissolved and this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is bound by them through the utterance of Rudra, one should therefore worship the Liṅga.
O best of the twice-born, know that the Liṅga is directly devoid of qualities; it is through its dissolution that the greatness of the qualities is proclaimed.
O Brahmins, Śaṅkara is indeed called the bestower of happiness by the wise; for he is said to be everything, as he is the refuge of all.
For, O Brahmins, Śambhu is so called because from him the origin of all auspiciousness arises. || 14 ||
Thus all the names of the Great-Souled One are meaningful; by that Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, the entire world is pervaded.
The sages said: When the highly fortunate Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, had cast herself into the fire during the sacrificial rite and had vanished from the sight of Dakṣa...
O Sūta, tell me now in truth: when did she manifest? And how, moreover, was she united with the supreme power of Maheśa? (17)
O highly fortunate one, all of this past history must be told to us exactly as it is; there is no other speaker whatsoever.
Sūta said: O Brahmin, when the daughter of Dakṣa was born with her limbs consumed by fire, Maheśa also performed supreme penance without Śakti.
On the Himavat mountain, he who had assumed a body through his divine play was accompanied by Bhṛṅgin, Viśva, and likewise by Nandin.
And thus he was surrounded by Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and many others, encircled by hosts multiplied ten million times over.
With ten million hosts and likewise sixty thousand, the bull-bannered god was thus surrounded there by the gaṇas.

Devoted to austerity, that great-souled one likewise stood at the summit of the Himalayas, surrounded by his hosts headed by Vīrabhadra; yet he was alone and devoid of the primordial knowledge (mūlavidyā). || 23 ||
In the meantime, the Daityas indeed appeared through ignorance; for Bali was bound by Viṣṇu, and so were those who were possessed of great strength.
Then, O brahmins, the Daityas were born—those who caused affliction to Indra; some were Kālakhañjas, others were extremely fierce Kālakāyas.
All the Nivātakavacas, those known as Rava-rāvaka, and many other Daityas who cause the destruction of living beings. || 26 ||
Tāraka, the son of Namuci, indeed gratified Brahmā through supreme austerity; Brahmā was truly pleased with him.
He granted boons as desired to the evil-minded Tāraka, saying: "Choose a boon—blessings upon you—I shall grant you all your wishes. (28)
Having heard those words of that Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, he then chose a boon that brought fear to the worlds.
"If you are pleased with me, O Lord, grant me freedom from old age and death, as well as invincibility, whatever you deem appropriate. (30)
Thus addressed at that time by that evil-minded Tāraka, he spoke these words with a smile: "Whence can immortality be yours? (31)
"Indeed, for one who is born, death is certain; know this according to reality. Laughing, Tāraka said, "And grant me invincibility. (32)
Brahmā said: "O sinless one, at that time your defeat by the Daityas will indeed be granted, except by a child; for a child shall conquer you. (33)
Then that Tāraka, bowing down, said to Brahmā, "O Lord, O Master of the Gods, I have indeed achieved my purpose now through your grace."
Having thus obtained the boon, the exceedingly powerful Asura Tāraka challenged the gods to battle and fought with them.
Having taken refuge in Mucukunda, those gods became victorious; yet those gods were repeatedly thwarted by Tāraka.
At that time, the gods achieved victory solely through the power of Mucukunda; for what indeed could be done by us, who were fighting incessantly? (37)
Remembering that "it must come to pass," they went to the abode of Brahmā; having stood before Brahmā, they, together with Indra, spoke.
The gods said: "That Madhusūdana dwells in Pātāla together with Bala; for without Viṣṇu, all those others, Vṛṣa and the rest, were defeated by their enemies. (39)

"O gods, let my words be carried out truly and swiftly; for when the son of Śiva becomes a god of great strength,"
Furthermore, in battle he will slay Tāraka; of this there is no doubt—by whatever means the Blessed Śambhu, who dwells in the cave of all hearts, [ordains].
"O gods, let the policy of taking a wife be thus established; you must exert the greatest effort, for my word shall not be otherwise. (43)
"O gods, you must understand," said an incorporeal voice. Having fallen into great astonishment, the gods spoke to one another. (44)
Having heard the voice from the sky, all the gods, placing Bṛhaspati at their head, arrived at the Himālaya and spoke these words. (45)
"O highly fortunate Himālaya, all of us [have come] because of the gravity of our purpose. O highly fortunate Himālaya, listen now to our words. (46)
"Tāraka terrifies us; provide assistance in his slaying! You are the refuge for all of us ascetics. Therefore, O Lord, we have all come together with Mahendra. (47)
Lomaśa said: Thus entreated by the gods, Himavat, the best of mountains and foremost among those skilled in speech, spoke these words to the gods with a smile.
Then, filled with derision toward Mahendra, they said: "We gods have all been rendered incapable by Mahendra. (49)
"What shall we do regarding the task of the gods and the slaying of Tāraka? We shall all become well-endowed with wings, O best of gods. (50)
Then we shall slay Tāraka along with his kinsmen; for he is as immovable as a mountain and is our adversary—what service can I perform for you?
Having heard those words of his, all the gods said to him: "O illustrious one, all of you and we ourselves are incapable of slaying Tāraka; let this matter be considered."
Then the immensely radiant Himavat spoke to the gods regarding that by which his enemy, the exceedingly powerful Tāraka, might be conquered.
"O gods, by what means do you wish to slay Tāraka? Tell me quickly, for I indeed desire to know this matter."
Then all this that had been previously spoken by the gods in their speech for the sake of the task was heard by the mountain; indeed, Himavat was the mountain who heard these words.
When the high-souled Daitya Tāraka is slain by the wise son of Śiva, then all the auspicious work of the gods shall be accomplished, and these words spoken shall become true.
Therefore, let this be done by you so that Maheśa may accept her; let a maiden suitable for that Śiva now be sought out quickly by the gods.
Having heard those words of his, the gods then laughed and said: "A daughter must be produced by you for the sake of Śiva, so that the purpose may be accomplished."
O high-minded one, quickly carry out the words of the gods; you shall undoubtedly become the support of the deities. (59)
Thus addressed by the gods, the King of Mountains then entered his own home and questioned his wife Menā regarding the important matter that had arisen.
"A single virtuous daughter must be brought forth for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, as well as for that of the ṛṣis and the ascetics. (61)
The birth of a daughter is not pleasing to women; nevertheless, O lady of beautiful countenance, one daughter must indeed be born. (62)
Laughing, Menā spoke to her husband Himālaya: "Listen now to me regarding the words that have been spoken by you."

O Lord of men, a daughter is always a source of suffering for men, and likewise, O high-minded one, she causes grief to women; therefore, O Lord of Mountains, reflect well for a long time by yourself with your own intellect and say what is beneficial.
Having heard those words of his beloved, the wise Himavat then spoke these words, which were filled with a desire to benefit others.
Indeed, by whatever means it may be, that which will serve as a livelihood for others must certainly be accomplished by a wise man. (66)
Even a woman must perform that duty accompanied by service to others. Thus impelled by that mountain, the fortunate Menā, his queen, then conceived a daughter in her womb. (67)
She is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), whose very nature is the Great Intellect (Mahāmedhā); she is Rudrakālī, Ambā, Satī, Dākṣāyaṇī, and the Supreme (Parā).
The highly fortunate Menā, of beautiful eyes and large vision, bore within her womb that supreme glory as a virtuous woman. (69)
Then the gods, sages, yakṣas, and kinnaras offered praise to the highly fortunate Menā and likewise to the mountain Himavat.
In the meantime, she was born and became known by the name Girijā; when the Goddess appeared, she bestowed happiness upon all.
The celestial drums resounded and the hosts of Apsaras danced; the lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Likewise, the gods rained down a great shower of flowers; at that moment, the entire three worlds became serene.

As soon as the great and virtuous Girijā descended, fear entered the hearts of the Daityas; meanwhile, the hosts of gods, the great sages, along with the Cāraṇas and the throngs of Siddhas, attained great joy.
Lomaśa said: Then that virtuous woman, growing day by day, shone brightly; when she had reached eight years of age in the home of Himālaya, she was a true satī.
Then Maheśa, surrounded by all his attendants, Vīrabhadra and the others, performed supreme austerity in a valley of the Himavat mountains.
The wise Himavat went together with Pārvatī to see that Maheśa, who was devoted to this austerity, in order to behold his sprout-like feet. || 3 ||
When he arrived to see him, he was stopped by Nandin; and as the gatekeeper stood there, he remained still for a single moment.
Then Mount Himavat made his request through Nandin; having been informed by Nandin, Śambhu [learned that] the mountain had come to see him.
Having heard those words of Nandin, the Supreme Lord spoke these words to Nandin: "Bring the Mountain here."
Thinking "so be it," Nandin brought that mountain Himācala as well, and likewise Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
Then, having seen the Lord, the sovereign of all, engaged in austerity with his eyes closed; || 8 ||

Then Himācala, possessed of undiminished strength, bowed his head to the one with matted hair, adorned with a digit of the moon, who is known through the Vedāntas and abides in the Supreme Self; and he attained supreme joy.
Himalaya, the foremost among those skilled in speech, spoke these words which are the singular blessing of the world.
"I am fortunate, O Mahādeva, by your grace, O Śaṅkara; O Lord, I shall come every day for the sake of beholding you. (11)
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to grant permission for her. Having heard his words, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [replied]. 12.
"O mountain, you must come to me constantly for the sake of my vision; having established the maiden in your home, there shall be no other way to behold me. (13)

Acala, with his neck bowed, replied thus to Giriśa: "Tell me, why should I not come along with her? And Śambhu, smiling, spoke these words to Acala: 14. [Śiva said: "Why should I not come along with her? Tell me that. And Śambhu, smiling, spoke these words to Acala.
"This maiden, with beautiful hips, slender and sweet-voiced, must not be brought into my presence; I forbid it again and again. (15)
Having heard these words of Śambhu—which were free from affliction yet harsh due to his lack of desire—and having listened to the speech uttered by the ascetic, Gaurī laughed and spoke to Śambhu.
Gaurī said: O Śambhu, endowed with the power of asceticism, you perform extensive penance; this thought has arisen in you, O Great-souled One, to practice such austerity. (17)
"Who are you, O Blessed One, and what is your subtle nature? Let that be reflected upon. Having heard those words of Pārvatī, Maheśa spoke these words: || 18 ||

By supreme austerity alone, I destroy my material nature; O fair-browed one, freed from nature, I abide in my true essence. Therefore, O Prakṛti, you should at times be united with the perfected ones (siddhas).
Pārvatī said: O Śaṅkara, is that which was spoken by you with supreme speech not indeed Prakṛti? How then could you have transcended it?
O Śaṅkara, whatever you hear, whatever you have heard, and whatever you see—O Lord, what further need is there for us to engage in verbal dispute now? (21)
All that is the work of Prakṛti; the doctrine of falsehood is useless. Having become superior to Prakṛti, for what purpose do you perform penance? (22)
O Śambhu, O Lord, you have now indeed united with Prakṛti on this Himavat mountain; for you do not realize it, O Śaṅkara. (23)
"And what need have we now for verbal debate, O Lord? If it is true that you are beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), then you, Śaṅkara, should not fear me at this time. (24)
Laughing, the Blessed Lord replied to Girijā.
Mahādeva said: "O Girijā, you who speak so well, perform service for me every single day."
Having spoken thus to Girijā, Maheśa then addressed these words to Himālaya: "Right here on this earth, I, whose nature is the supreme reality, shall practice the highest austerity. (27)
"O Lord of Mountains, permission must be granted to me to perform penance; without such permission, it is not possible to perform any austerity whatsoever. (28)
Having heard these words of the trident-bearing God of gods, Himavat laughed and spoke these words to Śambhu: || 29 ||
For this entire world, including the gods, asuras, and humans, belongs to you; O Mahādeva, being so insignificant, what indeed can I give to you? (30)
Thus addressed by Himavān, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, laughed and respectfully said to that king of mountains, "Go."
Permitted by Śaṅkara, Himavat went to his own home; he remained there with Girijā, intent on seeing [him] every day.
In this manner, some time passed as they performed their service to one another.
Right there, Śaṅkara, who is difficult to overcome, appeared before his daughter and parents; and right there, the gods fell into anxiety regarding Pārvatī.
While reflecting thus, those gods then said: "How will Maheśa unite with Girijā? What should we do this very day? O Bṛhaspati, tell us that without delay! (35)
Bṛhaspati spoke these virtuous words to Mahendra: "O Mahendra, listen then; this must be done by you in this very manner. (36)

"O King, this task can be accomplished by Madana alone; no one else in the three worlds will be capable of it. For the asceticism of the penance-performers has been overwhelmed; therefore, Māra must be entreated with haste. (37)
Having heard the words of his preceptor, Hari summoned Madana; then, at that summons, Madana arrived to accomplish the task.
Accompanied by Rati and together with Mādhava, that flower-bowed god approached Mahendra in the assembly hall and spoke these words, which were both full of pride and captivating to the world.
"Why have I been summoned? Tell me now, O Lord of Śacī! What task must I perform today? Let it be told; do not delay. (40)
Indeed, by my mere remembrance, the ascetics have fallen away; you alone, O Hari, know my prowess and valor.
Parāśara, the son of Śakti, knows my prowess, as do these many sages, Bhṛgu and the others, both here and in the other world.
The preceptor also recognized that she was indeed the wife of Utathya; Bharadvāja was born from her, for he was a product of a mixture [of castes] with his preceptor.
Then the preceptor said, "O highly fortunate one, Bharadvāja, the Lord of Creatures knows both my prowess and my valor. (44)

For Krodha is indeed my kinsman, possessing great strength and prowess; by both of us, the entire universe—great, moving and unmoving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—has been put to flight and overwhelmed.

The gods said: "O Madana, you are indeed always capable of conquering us; go quickly toward Maheśa for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. O high-minded one, unite Śambhu with Pārvatī this very day. (46)
Thus entreated by the gods, Madana, the deluder of the universe, departed in haste, accompanied by the Apsarases.

Then, having drawn his great bow adorned with flowers, that hero—the sole conqueror of the world and the best among warriors—quickly departed, grasping likewise his beautiful arrows; he was seen upon the earth on that Himalayan mountain, like the god of love himself.
Then Rambhā, Urvaśī, Puñjikasthalī, Sumlocā, Miśrakeśī, Subhagā, and Tilottamā arrived there.
And various other Apsarases were seen by the hosts, born for the assistance of Madana, together with Madana himself. || 50 ||
All the Gaṇas were suddenly deluded by Madana; at that time, Raṃbhā was with Bhṛṅgin and Urvaśī was with Caṇḍa.
Menakā was with Vīrabhadra, and Puñjikasthalī with Caṇḍa; Tilottamā and the others were then surrounded there by the Gaṇas.
The surface of the earth was filled with many intoxicated sages who had cast aside all shame, as well as with cuckoos out of season. (53)
Aśoka trees, Caṃpaka trees, mango trees, Yūthī trees, and Kadaṃba trees; Nīpa trees, Priyāla trees, Panasa trees, Rājavṛkṣa trees, and Carāyaṇa trees. || 54 ||
Abundant grapevines and nāgakeśara trees are visible, as well as plantains and ketaka flowers adorned by bees.
Intoxicated by the embrace of passion, the kalahamsa geese played with their female mates; the elephants frolicked with their female elephants, and the peacocks with their peahens.

"For they were indeed free from desire and afflicted by illness; how then did they suddenly become such as they are through the qualities born of contact with Śiva? Having reflected thus, [he asked]. 57.
For Śailāda, possessed of great splendor and Nandin of immeasurable prowess, reflected that there was some task to be performed for either the Rākṣasas or the gods.
In the meantime, O twice-born ones, Madana, the wielder of the bow, having fixed his five arrows upon his own bow, then took refuge in the shade of a tree made of devadāru wood.

He beheld Śambhu seated upon the supreme throne, performing austerities as the Lord of the highest beings—Gaṅgādhara, with a neck as dark as the blue tamāla tree, wearing matted hair and adorned with the crescent moon.

With all his limbs marked by the coils of serpents, five-faced, possessing the vast prowess of a lion, and joined by his supreme consort who was white as camphor—Madana desired to pierce that ascetic.

While [Śiva], the invincible, the most excellent among the radiant, the Great Lord, and the Fierce One, was together with Mādhava and desiring to pierce Śiva with his arrow, the Daughter of the Mountain, the Mother of the Universe, arrived—surrounded by her circle of friends—to worship Sadāśiva, the auspiciousness of all auspicious things. (62)

She placed a garland of golden flowers upon the blue-throated Lord; at that time, she—delightful with white rays and difficult to attain—became one whose eyes blossomed with smiles as she gazed upon the beautiful face of Śiva, the progenitor of all beings. (63)
Pierced at that moment from the crossroads by the very arrow named Mohana, Śambhu then slowly opened his eyes and beheld the Daughter of the Mountain, just as the Ocean beholds a digit of the moon.

She possessed a beautiful and serene countenance, lips like the bimba fruit, and eyes filled with smiles; she was born from fire, had excellent teeth, was slender, and brought great joy to her broad face. (65)
Gaurī, who possesses the gesture of serenity, the enchantress of the enchanters of the universe, by whom the creation of the three worlds was performed along with Brahmā and the other gods. 66.

She who brings about creation, preservation, and destruction, having placed the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas before her—she, the enchantress and the sole auspiciousness among all that is auspicious, was beheld by Hara standing face to face with his consciousness.
Beholding that Girijā, the purifier of the world, Lord Bhava was infatuated by the mere sight of her; made sick by Madana, Śiva suddenly became one whose eyes were wide with wonder. (68)
Beholding thus, that God of gods, the Lord of the universe, Sadāśiva, spoke these words with a grieving mind.
"Deluded by her, why do I remain here established in penance, free from ailment? From where, for what reason, and by whom has this unpleasant thing been done to me? (70)
Then Śambhu respectfully surveyed all directions; at that moment, he was seen in the southern quarter, having taken up his bow.
O twice-born ones, as soon as Madana drew his bow into a circle and prepared to pierce Sadāśiva, and while he was yet aiming at the destroyer of Madana, he was then beheld by Maheśa with great wrath.
Beheld indeed by the supreme third eye, Madana was instantly enveloped in garlands of flames; a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the gods who were watching there.
The gods said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, become the bestower of boons upon the gods! Madana has now been sent for the sake of assisting Girijā."
Indeed, that Madana of great splendor has been burnt by you in vain. || 75 ||

O sole kinsman of the world, you must indeed perform this task with supreme splendor for the sake of the gods; O Lord Śambhu, from her a son shall be born, and by him alone will every purpose here be accomplished.
O Great Lord, the gods were severely oppressed by Tāraka; for their sake, O Master, you gave up even your life and bestowed Girijā upon him.
Choose [a boon], O highly fortunate one; be capable of performing the work of the gods. We all, the inhabitants of heaven, were rescued by you from the demon Gajāsura. (78)
Indeed, we have certainly been protected from Kālakūṭa and not otherwise; O Lord of All, we have all been saved by you from Bhasmāsura, without a doubt. (79)
"This Madana has arrived for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods; therefore, he must be protected by you, for he is our supreme benefactor. (80)
"O Śaṅkara, without him the entire world will go to destruction; O Śambhu, you are free from desire—reflect upon this with your own intellect. (81)
Then Maheśvara, overcome with wrath, spoke to the gods: "O gods, it must happen without Kāma; it cannot be otherwise."
When all the gods, including Indra, having placed desire before them, fell from their positions and were overwhelmed by suffering, they resorted to a state of wretchedness.
For desire leads all living beings inevitably to hell; know this word of mine: that this bodiless one (Kāma) is indeed the very form of suffering. (84)
Even the wicked Tāraka will today become free from desire; for how can a man commit sin without desire? (85)
Therefore, Kāma has been burnt by me for the sake of the peace of all of you—of all the gods, the asuras, and the great sages. || 86 ||
Let other living beings here apply their minds to asceticism; by me, the entire world has been rendered free from desire and anger.

Therefore, O gods, wait; I shall not allow this sinner, the root of suffering, to live. [I shall instead manifest] that which is characterized by bliss, consisting of the constant awakening of one's own self, unfathomable, and of a unique nature.
Thus addressed then by Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, all the great sages spoke to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world: 89.
O Śambhu, that which has been spoken by you is indeed most conducive to our supreme welfare; however, O Lord of Gods, let us speak further—please listen and give it due consideration. (90)
Just as this entire universe was created, endowed with desire and anger, all that is indeed of the nature of desire; for that desire cannot be destroyed.
O Mahādeva, that desire which has been brought to a state of oneness with the four goals—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—is not destroyed.
How indeed was Kāma, who is so difficult to overcome, burnt away by you—he by whom the entire universe, from Brahmā down to the immovable world, was brought into being? (93)
By desire the universe is diminished; by desire it is protected; by desire the universe is produced; therefore, desire is of great power.
Since fierce anger has arisen by which you have been brought under its control, therefore, O Mahādeva, you ought to awaken Kāma.
"O Lord, Madana has indeed been brought forth by you; for he is possessed of great power, and by virtue of that capability, he will surely exercise his power. (96)
Although addressed thus by the sages, Hara then assumed a twofold form, desiring to burn [him] with his third eye.
Sadāśiva—Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow and the one whose vehicle is the bull—was praised and worshipped by the sages, the Cāraṇas, the Siddhas, and the Gaṇas as well. 98.
Having thus burnt Madana and abandoned that mountain in anger, he immediately vanished from the one named Himavān.
O Goddess, seeing that Manmatha had been consumed and had vanished, along with the cuckoo, the mango tree, the bee, and the campaka flower; || 100 ||
Seeing Madana thus consumed and hearing Rati’s lamentation, the high-minded woman, dejected and with long-drawn sobs, reflected: "How might that Rudra come under my control? (101)

Having reflected thus for a very long time, the daughter of the mountain then fell into a state of confusion; yet the virtuous Satī spoke in that manner to the high-minded and beautiful-eyed lady who was weeping in her bewilderment.
"Do not despair, my friend; I shall restore Madana to life. For your sake, O large-eyed one, I shall propitiate him through ascetic penance. (103)
"Hara, Rudra, Virūpākṣa, God of gods, Teacher of the world—do not worry, O fair-hipped one; I shall restore Madana to life. (104)
Having thus quickly consoled that virtuous Girijā, the slender-waisted Rati performed very great penance in order to obtain him as her husband.
At that place where Madana had been consumed by Rudra, the Supreme Soul, Nārada then beheld her performing austerities.
Having approached the beautiful woman Rati nearby, he suddenly said: "Whose daughter are you, O large-eyed one, and for whom do you perform this ascetic penance? (107)
A young woman, endowed with beauty and supreme good fortune, having heard Nārada’s words, then spoke with great anger some words that were both sweet and somewhat harsh. (108)
Rati said: "I have recognized you as Nārada; you are indeed Kumāra, there is no doubt. O observer of noble vows, it behoves you to reveal your true form."
"Go by the path you came; do not delay! O boy, you know nothing at all; you are merely a great maker of strife. (110)
Those who lust after the wives of others, the base, the lechers, and those addicted to vices—as well as the inactive and the obstinate—you are the foremost among them. (111)
Thus rebuked by Rati, Nārada, the best of sages, went himself in haste to Śambara, the foremost of the Daityas.
He reported to the king of the Daityas that Madana himself had been burnt by the wrathful Rudra, as well as his high-minded wife. || 113 ||

"O highly fortunate one, O mighty one, bring her back and make her your wife! O sinless one, she who was brought by you is exceedingly endowed with beauty; among them all, that beautiful woman is Rati, the beloved of Madana. (114)
Having thus heard the words of the celestial sage of purified soul, he went quickly to that place where she, so beautiful, was staying.
Seeing her, the large-eyed Rati who infatuates Madana, Śambara, who was besieged by the gods, spoke these words with a smile: || 116 ||
"Come, O slender one; together with me, O goddess, enjoy the kingdom and pleasures as you desire through my favor. What is the use of asceticism? (117)
Thus addressed then by that great-souled Śambara, that slender queen of Madana spoke sweetly.
"I am a widow, O mighty-armed one; you ought not to speak thus. You are the king of all the Daityas, surrounded by your attendants. (119)
Having heard these words, Śambara, deluded by passion, desired to seize her by the hand, but he was then restrained by Rati.
Having reflected with his mind upon all this and indeed upon his invincibility, [he said]: "O fool, do not touch me, for [the power] born from my touch—" (121)
"You have been consumed by contact [with me], and not otherwise; such is my word. Then the immensely radiant Śambara spoke, as if laughing: 122.
"O proud woman, you frighten me with many terrifying threats; go quickly to my house—what is the use of so much talk? (123)
While she was speaking thus, that slender and high-minded woman was then forcibly led by Śambara to his own supreme city.
She was appointed as the superintendent of the kitchen, and her name was Māyāvatī.

The sages said: "Everything concerning Pārvatī regarding the bringing of Madana has been told. That slender lady, the virtuous beloved of Madana, was abducted by Saṃbara. After that, O Sūta, what happened there? Please describe it."
Sūta said: Having seen that Śiva had departed after burning Madana with his splendor, the beautiful Pārvatī remained right there, engaged in ascetic penance.
Then that slender girl was addressed by her father and mother: "Child, come quickly home; you should not undergo such exhaustion."
Then, having been addressed by those two, the virtuous Girijā spoke these words.
Pārvatī said: "O Mother, I am not going home; O Father, hear my words from the truth, which are endowed with righteousness and purpose, so that you may attain satisfaction. (130)
Śambhu is supreme even among the supreme; by him the mighty Madana was consumed. I shall bring that Śiva here into my presence.
"For Śambhu is difficult to obtain for living beings who desire a home; therefore, O Mother, I shall not go home—let all this be well-considered. (132)

Then the immensely radiant Himavat spoke to his daughter: "Śiva is directly difficult to propitiate and is worshipped by all the gods; he truly cannot be attained by you, therefore, return to your own home."
With her throat choked with tears, Menā said to her daughter: "O slender-limbed one, go quickly toward home."
Then Pārvatī, smiling, spoke to her mother: "O Mother, listen to my vow, for it is through supreme asceticism. (135)
Having brought that wise one right here, O lady of excellent complexion, I shall destroy the very Rudra-hood of Rudra.
Having renounced her own form of happiness, the wise Girijā performed the propitiation of Śambhu through supreme meditative absorption.
Jayā, Vijayā, Mādhavī, Sulocanā, Suśrutā, Śrutā, and likewise Śukī, the supreme one. (138)
Pramlocā, Subhagā, Śyāmā, Citrāṅgī, Cāruṇī, and Svadhā—these and many other female companions attended upon the Daughter of the Mountain, as did that beautiful lady, the daughter of the gods.
Practicing most fierce austerity, she of the lovely smile established an altar right there and stood firmly upon it—precisely where Madana had been consumed by the high-souled Rudra.
Having abandoned the consumption of water, that young woman became an eater of leaves; then, having abandoned fresh leaves, she took up dry ones.
When she had consumed even the withered leaves, that slender-waisted woman became celebrated as Aparṇā.
After subsisting on water, she became devoted to drinking air; and in the course of great time, the virtuous Satī became Girijā. Then, with a single toe, she supported her own body. (143)
Thus, with supreme satisfaction, Satī performed the propitiation of Śaṅkara through such fierce asceticism, solely for the sake of pleasing Śambhu. (144)
Relying upon the Supreme Being, she who is the most auspicious of all auspicious things in the world performed supreme penance for the sake of pleasing Maheśa. || 145 ||
In this manner, he indeed performed austerities for thousands of divine years; then Himālaya, having approached Pārvatī who was firm in her resolve, [spoke].
Accompanied by his wife, he spoke to his daughter, the great virtuous lady: "Do not be distressed by this austerity, O great goddess, O beautiful woman."
"O young girl, where is Rudra seen? He is dispassionate; of this there is no doubt. You are slender, youthful, and young, and have been deluded by asceticism. (148)
It will come to pass, there is no doubt; I tell you this as the truth. Therefore, arise and go quickly to your own home, O lady of excellent complexion.
O sinless one, what have you to do with that Rudra by whom Madana was consumed long ago? Since he is free from all passion, how will you entreat him? (150)
Just as the moon situated in the sky cannot be grasped, even so, O lady of pure smiles, know that Śarabhu is difficult to reach. 151.
In the same way, she was addressed by Menā, as well as by Sahyādri, and likewise by Meru, Mandara, and Maināka. || 152 ||
Thus addressed by them while she was engaged in ascetic penance, the slender Pārvatī, with a pure smile, spoke as if laughing to Himavat: || 153 ||
"O father, was what you said previously forgotten by you, O mother? Now, O kinsmen, hear my vow! (154)
"That Great God is dispassionate, he by whom Madana was indeed destroyed; I shall propitiate that Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, through ascetic penance. (155)
"All of you must go; there is no need for deliberation here. For by him Madana was burnt, and by him the forest of the mountain was burnt. (156)
I shall bring him right here by means of pure asceticism alone; for Sadāśiva is always well-pleased by the great power of penance. 157.
Know that, O highly fortunate ones; I speak the truth, the absolute truth. || 158 ||

Then, conversing with her mother, as well as with Himālaya and Menā, and likewise with Meru, that daughter of the king of mountains, speaking measuredly, departed along that same path by which the mountains had come, looking back at them as they went.
When they had all departed, Satī, surrounded by her female companions, then performed austerities right there for the sake of the supreme goal.
By that great asceticism, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings was scorched; then all the gods and asuras went to Brahmā for refuge.
The gods said: "O God, this entire world, including all that is mobile and immobile, was created by you. You ought to protect us, O Lord; no one other than you is capable. (162)
Having heard those words, "He is capable of protecting us," Brahmā then reflected upon them with his supreme mind.
Knowing that a most great and supreme forest fire had arisen from the penance of Girijā, Brahmā quickly went to the most wonderful Ocean of Milk.
There, he was sleeping upon an exceedingly beautiful couch named Śeṣa, his pair of feet being constantly served by Lakṣmī.

He was being served by Tārkṣya, though standing at a distance, with his neck bowed in reverence; and he was attended by Śrī (Prosperity), Kānti (Beauty), Kṣānti (Forbearance), Vṛtti (Conduct), Dayā (Compassion), and other such qualities.
Viṣṇu, endowed with the nine powers and surrounded by his attendants—Kumuda, Kumudvān, Sanaka, and Sanandana—[was worshipped]. (167)
Sanātana, the illustrious Mahābhāga, the sleeping Vijaya who conquers his enemies, Jayanta, Jayatsena, and the highly resplendent Jaya. || 168 ||
Sanatkumāra, Sutapas, Nārada, and Tumburu; likewise, the great conch Pāñcajanya and the mace Kaumodakī.
Likewise, the Sudarśana and the most wonderful Śārṅga bow—these indeed were seen by the Supreme Lord in their embodied forms.
Then, having all gathered together in the presence of Viṣṇu, the supreme soul, all the gods and dānavas spoke to Viṣṇu, the lord of the creators, on the shore of the great-souled ocean at that time.
"Save us, save us, O Great Viṣṇu! We have come to you for refuge, tormented by the fierce and great asceticism of Pārvatī. Seated upon the Śeṣa-throne, the Supreme Lord spoke thus.
Accompanied by you all, I shall go to the Supreme Lord; O gods, let us pray to Mahādeva regarding Girijā. (173)
"Now, we shall act in such a way that the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, will take her hand right there. (174)
Therefore, we shall go to where Rudra, the great lord, dwells, endowed with fierce austerity and being the supreme auspiciousness.
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, all the gods and asuras said: "We shall not all go to the one of great splendor who has three uneven eyes. (176)
Since Madana, who is otherwise so difficult to overcome, was previously consumed by him, he will likewise consume us; there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (177)
Laughing, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Sovereign, said: "Let no fear be felt by any of you; Sadāśiva is the very form of Śiva. (178)
He, the destroyer of the fear of all the gods, shall not burn you; therefore, O wise ones, you must go along with me.

I go for refuge to that Śambhu, the ancient Puruṣa, the sovereign lord of supreme form, who is higher than the highest, who practices austerity, whose nature is the ultimate reality, and who is beyond the transcendent. 180.
Sūta said: Having been thus addressed by Viṣṇu, the supreme lord, all the gods then departed, desiring to see Maheśa, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
On the further shore, by means of the supreme meditative absorption, he beheld Śambhu seated upon the seat of yoga, surrounded by his attendants. || 2 ||
Wearing upon his chest the serpent king Vāsuki and likewise Kambala and Aśvatara, arranged according to the ritual of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). || 3 ||
He was wearing Karkoṭaka on both ears, and Pulaha as bracelets upon his two arms.

They beheld the most excellent of gods, white as camphor, with a blue throat, wondrous, accompanied by his bull, shining brilliantly as he held two conchs and lotuses in his hands and wore beautiful anklets.
Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the sages, gods, and dānavas praised him with various hymns accompanied by the Vedas and Upaniṣads.
Brahmā said: Salutations to the divine Rudra, the destroyer of Madana; to Bharga, the possessor of abundant fortune, the three-eyed one, and the lord of the three worlds.
Salutation to Śipiviṣṭa, to the Terrifying One, to the one who reclines upon Śeṣa; salutation indeed to the Three-eyed One, the Sustainer of the World, who possesses the universal form.
You are the sustainer of all worlds, you are the father and the mother, you are the Lord; endowed with supreme compassion, protect us, O Maheśvara!
While the gods were thus offering praise, Nandin spoke to them: "For what purpose have you come, or what is in your minds? (10)

They came before Śambhu to petition him for the sake of the gods' mission. That high-souled Nandin, the son of Śilāda, informed [him]; meanwhile, Mahādeva remained absorbed in meditation for the successful accomplishment of the purpose of the gods.

O best of gods, Brahmā and the other noble hosts, along with the multitudes of Suras and Siddhas, are especially eager to behold you; they have come seeking your aid, being threatened by the foremost of Asuras and suddenly oppressed by their enemies. (12)
"Therefore, O Lord of Gods, the deities must now be protected by you. Thus, O twice-born ones, was Śambhu then petitioned by Nandin.
Gradually withdrawing from his meditation, Śambhu, the supreme Lord and Great Controller, who is exceedingly prone to wrath, spoke as the Supreme Self.
Mahādeva said: "O highly fortunate ones, why have you come into my presence? O gods, beginning with Brahmā, tell me truly the reason for this today."
Then Brahmā indeed spoke these words: "O Śambhu, Tāraka has performed a most extraordinary deed against the gods, which constitutes a very great task for the deities. (16)

"O Lord, we have come here to report that which is more painful than pain itself: O Śambhu, the enemy of the gods, Tāraka, has been slain by your own legitimate son; my words shall not be otherwise. (17)
Therefore, O Lord Śambhu, you must take Girijā with your right hand; having been given by the Lord of Mountains through that very act of taking her hand, O noble one, accept her.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Śiva, smiling, said: "When the goddess Girijā, the most beautiful of all, was created by me... (19)
Then all the lords of the gods, as well as the ṛṣis and munis, shall have their desires fulfilled and become incapable of proceeding on the higher path.
Indeed, Madana was burnt by me for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of all; and the slender-waisted Girijā has been entrusted by me to you.
