At that very moment, O gods, Pārvatī shall restore both Madana and me to life; O Brahmā, there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Having reflected thus, O gods, you must deliberate upon what ought to be done; for by Madana himself, though he was consumed by fire, a great service to the gods has been performed.
All of you are free from desire; there is no doubt about this. O gods, you must strive with diligence just as I have.
"Endowed with supreme austerity, we shall accomplish that which is exceedingly difficult; for all of us are indeed happy, being united with supreme bliss. (25)
Through that meditative absorption and through passion, you have forgotten; for desire leads surely to hell, and from it, anger is born. (26)
From anger arises delusion; from delusion the mind wanders astray. O best of gods, having abandoned desire and anger, all of you must reflect upon my words, and never otherwise.
Having thus proclaimed this, the Blessed One, that god whose banner bears the bull, awakened the gods as well as the hosts of sages and ascetics.
Śambhu became silent once more, resorting to meditation; he remained just as before, surrounded by his attendants.
Seeing him established in meditation, Nanda dismissed all those gods, including Brahmā and Indra, and spoke as if laughing: || 30 ||
"Go by the path you have come; do not delay. Having agreed, saying "So be it," they all then departed for their respective places. (31)
When they had all departed, Bhava became established in meditative absorption; having made himself one with his own self, he remained contemplating within himself.
It is clearer than the clearest, more transcendent than the most transcendent, stainless, unimpeded, untainted, and without appearance—in which even the wise are bewildered.

Neither the sun, nor fire, nor the moon shines there, nor indeed light, nor even the wind; for that [Reality] alone, when investigated through the analysis of things, is subtler than the subtle and higher than the highest. (34)
Indeed, those who have renounced the world go there—to that which is indescribable, inconceivable, changeless, and free from affliction, whose very nature is pure consciousness alone.

That reality which is beyond words, devoid of qualities, changeless, pure existence, accessible through knowledge yet otherwise unapproachable, is indeed always proclaimed by the scriptures that transcend the Vedas and consist of mantras.

The Blessed One is that very reality; he is the Lord, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull. He is that Supreme Lord who, while engaged in ascetic penance, directly destroyed the one whose banner is the sea-monster (Kāmadeva).
Lomaśa said: At that time, the goddess Girijā performed supreme austerity; by that austerity, even Rudra was struck with great fear.

Having indeed conquered Śambhu—the bestower of all aims, the immovable Sthāṇu, who is absolute and possesses his own true nature—by means of supreme ascetic power, the goddess Pārvatī [attained him]. (39)
When the bull-bannered god was conquered by that goddess through her asceticism, he became shaken from his meditative absorption and went to where Pārvatī was staying.
The god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, went with great haste; there he beheld the goddess standing, surrounded by her female companions.
Just as the crescent of the moon is placed upon the altar, that god beheld her; and then, at that very moment, he became a young brahmin student (baṭu).

The Lord Bhava, the Great Ishvara, assuming the form of a celibate student (brahmacārin) and taking his place among the female companions, spoke while in the guise of a youth: "For what reason does this slender girl, beautiful in all her limbs, stand in the midst of her friends? (43)
"Who is she? Whose is she? From where has she come? For what purpose does she perform this penance? O friends, tell me everything now exactly as it is."
Then Jayā spoke to Rudra, the supreme cause of asceticism.
"Indeed, this daughter of the Himālaya, desiring to obtain the Lord Rudra as her husband through ascetic penance, has sat down here. (46)
He performed very great penance that was difficult for all to overcome. "O boy, know my word; what I have spoken cannot be otherwise. (47)
Having heard those words of hers, Maheśa, in the form of a young brahmin student, laughed and spoke this while her friends were listening.

"O friends, this Pārvatī is deluded; she does not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful. And for what purpose should penance be performed? It is surely only for the sake of attaining Rudra. (49)
He is inauspicious, a wearer of skulls, and has his abode in the cremation ground; he is inauspicious, yet he is indeed called by the name "Śiva" in vain.
For when Rudra, chosen by her, comes together with you as friends, then this slender girl will undoubtedly become auspicious. (51)
He who, deformed by the curse of Dakṣa, became an outcast excluded from sacrifice; and those serpents of great venom who were indeed the limbs of Śarva.
Rudra is indeed covered in the ashes of corpses, clad in a hide, and inauspicious; he is constantly surrounded by piśācas, pramathas, and bhūtas.
"What business has that Rudra with this delicate woman? Let her, who desires to die like a female ghoul, be restrained by her friends. (54)
Having abandoned Indra, who is pleasing to the mind, as well as Yama of great splendor, Nairṛta of wide eyes, and Varuṇa, the lord of the waters; || 55 ||
The Supreme Lord spoke such words as these to Kubera, Pavana, and Vibhāvasu, while his friends were listening, at the place where she was established in ascetic penance.
Having heard these words of Rudra in the form of a young brahmin student, the virtuous Śivā became enraged at Maheśa who was disguised as a student.
Victory to you, O virtuous Vijayā! And likewise, O beautiful Pramlocā! O noble Sulocanā, you have indeed done what is right for me.
"What business does this boy have with you here now? Having assumed the form of a boy, he has come as a reviler of the gods. (59)
"Friends, let this one be released; what need is there for him? Enraged, she then spoke to Rudra, who was in the form of a young brahmin boy. (60)
"O boy, go quickly with haste; you must not remain here now. What is the use of this idle chatter? You have no business here. (61)
Then, having been thus rebuked by her there, the young ascetic laughed, steadied himself, and spoke these words once more: (62)
Gradually and without falsehood, [he spoke] with haste regarding Vijayā: "O slender one, why has anger been shown by her? For what reason at all? (63)
"The words spoken by all of them were indeed well-spoken; yet why was the slender maiden provoked to anger by the speech as it was delivered? (64)
"He who is called Śambhu in the world, the mendicant beloved of mendicants—if what I have said to him were indeed false, then anger would be appropriate here. (65)
"She is indeed beautiful, while he, Sadāśiva, is deformed; this young woman has large eyes, whereas Bhava has deformed eyes. (66)
"How could this woman be deluded by such a Rudra? For a husband who is always fond of pleasure must indeed be considered fortunate by women. (67)
"How is it that this [goddess], who embodies the Yugas, has been deluded by the one devoid of qualities? By whom has Śiva not been heard of, nor known, nor seen? (68)
For Sadāśiva is indeed difficult for beings with worldly desires to attain; this slender-waisted woman has become proud only through her supreme asceticism.
"For how shall Sthāṇu, who is eternally devoid of pride, obtain him as his husband? She said, "O large-eyed one, why have you now become angry with me? (70)
To whatever extent there may be anger among men, and especially among women, by that very anger all of that will be reduced to ashes.
"O slender one, what you have said is well-done, powerful, and indeed true, O virtuous lady: lust, anger, greed, hypocrisy, and even envy. (72)
And by that conceptual proliferation, everything is destroyed; therefore, it is fitting for ascetics to abandon desire, anger, and the like. (73)

If the Lord, who is pure consciousness, is always to be meditated upon in the center of the heart by the wise, then He should be meditated upon by all through the conduct of a sage; He is not to be contemplated in any other way.
Having heard these words of Śambhu, Vijayā then said to him everything: "Go there; you have no business here, nor should you speak any other foolish word. (75)
Then Vijayā, who was skilled in speech, dismissed Sadāśiva, who was in the form of a young brahmin and was thus disputing.
The Supreme Lord Maheśa immediately vanished from the sight of Girijā, becoming invisible to all her companions.
Then, while the Goddess remained absorbed in meditation, devoted to her own contemplation, he suddenly appeared, assuming his own form. 78.

Then the Lord of Gods, who resided within her heart, became visible outside as he moved through her joy; opening her eyes, that virtuous Girijā, possessed of long eyes, beheld the God of gods, the Great Lord of all the worlds. (79)
He has two arms and one face, is wondrously clad in an animal skin, possesses matted hair marked by the crescent moon, and is draped with an elephant hide.
At that time, the two great serpents Kambala and Aśvatara were stationed at his ears, and Vāsuki, the king of snakes, of great splendor, formed his sacred thread.
Then, those highly precious bracelets made of serpents were fashioned by that Rudra, and they were likewise beautiful to behold.
Śambhu, being thus situated before Pārvatī at that time, spoke with urgency: "O beautiful lady, choose a boon."
Filled with supreme shame, the virtuous lady spoke to Śaṅkara: "O Lord of Gods, you are my protector; what was forgotten by you previously? (84)
O Lord, for the sake of which you brought about the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, I have been born from Menā as that very same person, so that the purpose may be accomplished. (85)
O Lord of the gods of gods, regarding the slaying of Tāraka, I have indeed conceived a son for you, O God. (86)
Therefore, O Maheśvara, you must indeed carry out my word; you must go to the side of the Himalayas—no hesitation should be made in this matter.
"O Mahādeva, surrounded by the sages, entreat me; my father will undoubtedly carry out your word. (88)
Formerly, when I was indeed the daughter of Dakṣa and given to you by my father, you did not perform the marriage ceremony there according to the prescribed injunctions.
Neither were the planets worshipped by that wise and high-souled Dakṣa; because he treated the planets as mere objects of sensory perception, this great flaw arose. (90)
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, you ought to perform your own marriage according to the prescribed rite, O illustrious one, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. (91)

Then, O mighty-armed one, he spoke to Girijā as if laughing: "All this great world of moving and non-moving beings has arisen by its very nature; yet it is deluded by you and enveloped by the three qualities. (92)
O Pārvatī, from the ego (ahaṃkāra) the principle of Mahat arose; from the principle of Mahat, Tamas was born, and the sky was enveloped by Tamas.
From space, wind was produced; from wind, fire was born; from fire, water was produced; and from water, the earth then arose. 94.
O fair-faced one, O proud lady, know that all this which is visible—the stable earth and so forth, as well as the moving beings—is transitory. 95.

The One who has attained manifoldness, who is indeed devoid of qualities yet enveloped by qualities; he who shines eternally as his own light and has become endowed with the supreme radiance; he who is both independent and dependent—O Goddess, a great deed has been performed by you.

This entire world has been understood by you with your supreme intellect to be composed of illusion and grasped in its totality; yet it is surrounded by the hosts of sense-faculties, which are attached to objects that appear as ultimate realities to all beings, even those of virtuous deeds.
"Which planets and which hosts of stars were created by you to be afflicted? And now, O Goddess of excellent complexion, they have been released for the sake of Śarva. (98)

In connection with the manifestation of the qualities (guṇas) and their effects, we two have appeared; for you indeed are the subtle primordial nature (prakṛti), composed of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas). 99.
O slender-waisted one, I too am always skilled in my duties; therefore, I shall not go to the Himalaya, nor shall I beg for anything under any circumstances.
"By the mere word 'give,' a man immediately incurs insignificance; knowing this, O Goddess, tell us indeed what [is the remedy] for us. (101)
"O auspicious lady, you ought to tell me all that task which must be done by your command. Thus addressed by him, the virtuous lotus-eyed woman then spoke.
"You are the Self and I am Prakṛti; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Nevertheless, O Śambhu, my great marriage must be performed."
For the body is projected by ignorance, whereas you, the Supreme, are indeed bodiless; nevertheless, O Mahādeva, assume such a bodily covering.
O Śambhu, O Lord, compose a discourse at my request; O Mahādeva, ask for me and grant me good fortune as well. (105)
Having been addressed thus by her, that Great-Souled One, Maheśvara, thinking "So be it" for the sake of deceiving the world, went to his own abode laughing, well-honored by the best of gods.
In the meantime, Himavat arrived there in great haste, accompanied by his wife Menā and various mountains.
Surrounded by his sons, he went for the purpose of seeing Pārvatī; there he beheld the Great Goddess surrounded by her female companions.
Then Pārvatī saw Himavat along with the mountains; the virtuous lady, intent on rising to greet them, then bowed her head to her parents, as well as to all her brothers and kinsmen.

Then the highly illustrious Himālaya, having placed his daughter upon his own lap and embraced her while filled with tears, spoke these sweet words: "O virtuous lady, what indeed has been done by you, however it may be? (110)
"O highly fortunate one, let all that be told to us who are indeed desirous of hearing it. Having heard those sweet words, she spoke in reply to her father: || 111 ||
The destroyer of Madana was entreated by means of supreme austerity: "My great task must be pacified, a task that is difficult for all others to achieve. (112)
Thereupon, Mahādeva, being pleased, arrived for the purpose of choosing [a bride]. I then said to Śambhu: "How can there be the taking of my hand in marriage? (113)
And then, O Śambhu, that destroyer of Tripura departed by the same path by which he had come, leaving my father behind now. (114)
Having heard those words of hers, the righteous-souled one attained supreme joy; together with his kinsmen, he spoke again to his daughter.
Today we all, including the mountains, shall go to our own homes; by her, the god Pinākin, whose banner is the bull, has been propitiated.
Thus spoke all those gods, led by Himālaya; together with Pārvatī, they all praised [him] with respectful words. || 117 ||

While she was being thus praised, Himālaya placed that woman of excellent complexion upon his shoulder; then all the mountains, surrounding her with eager anticipation, escorted her to their own abode.
The celestial drums resounded, as did conchs and trumpets in great numbers; indeed, many musical instruments were being played everywhere.
She was brought back toward the home by that great Puṣparṣi.
Being honored by many at that time, that ascetic woman shone with great splendor; likewise, she was surrounded on all sides by gods, Cāraṇas, great ṛṣis, and hosts of Siddhas.
Then, being honored, the Goddess spoke to the lotus-seated Brahmā, to the gods, the ṛṣis, the ancestors, the yakṣas, and all the others who had assembled there.
"All of you who have gathered here, depart for your respective abodes as you please; let the Supreme Lord be served."
Thus, having then gone to her father’s house, Pārvatī, shining with supreme splendor and well-honored by the best of gods, meditated upon Sadāśiva in her mind.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Manifestation of His Own Form to Pārvatī by Śaṅkara," in the first section, the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Lomaśa said: In the meantime, impelled by Maheśa, the sages also arrived suddenly and immediately at Himālaya.
Seeing them, Himādri, whose mind was like a mirror, rose up suddenly; bowing his neck, he honored them all and spoke.
"For what purpose have you come? Tell us the reason for your arrival. Then the seven sages said, "We have been sent by Maheśa."
"O Mountain, know that we have come into your presence for the purpose of beholding your daughter; show us your daughter without delay."

Having said "So be it," Pārvatī was brought there by the hosts of sages; then the lord of mountains, Himavat, who is affectionate toward his children, quickly took her onto his own lap and spoke as if smiling.
This is indeed my daughter; listen again to my words: he is the best among ascetics, dispassionate, and the ender of passion.

How could he who desires marriage be one by whom Smara was rendered bodiless? Giving a daughter in marriage is not recommended to one who is too near or too far, to one who is very wealthy or destitute of wealth, to one who lacks a livelihood, or to a fool. (7)

One should not give a daughter in marriage to one who is foolish, nor to one who is dispassionate, nor to one who is self-conceited, nor to one who is afflicted by illness, nor to one who is negligent. || 8 ||
Therefore, O best of sages, you must give her to Maheśa only after I have deliberated; this is my supreme vow.
Having heard those words of the King of Mountains, those great ṛṣis laughed and spoke to Himālaya all at once.
By her severe austerity was performed, and by her was Śiva propitiated; today Sadāśiva, satisfied by that penance, has become gracious.
"O Mountain, you do not know anything at all regarding her or him, nor their supreme majesty; therefore, indeed, bestow her upon him."
"Give this Menā, daughter of the mountain, to Śiva; indeed, carry out our word. Having heard those words of the sages of purified souls, [he acted accordingly].
Filled with haste, the Lord of Mountains spoke to the mountains: "O Meru, O Nishadha, O Gandhamadana, Mandara, and Mainaka! Let it be done this day; speak the truth as it is."
Then Menā, skilled in speech, spoke these words: "Why is deliberation being made now? Indeed, that very task should have been done at that time."
This highly fortunate one has arisen solely for the sake of the work of the gods; she is to be given to Śiva, having been brought down for the purpose of Śiva.
"Rudra was propitiated by her, and she was meditated upon by Rudra; let this highly fortunate woman be given back for the sake of Śiva. (17)
She indeed made a mere pretext for the worship of Śiva; having heard these words spoken by that Enā, [he said: 18.
And the Himalaya mountain, being highly pleased, spoke these words while looking toward the sages: "This girl is now mine. (19)

Then, having brought that beautiful Sulocanā—dark-complexioned, with a girdle resting upon her hips, wearing bracelets of lapis lazuli and pearls, and possessing a radiant luster like a crescent of the moon—[he spoke].

Upon seeing her—a fair-complexioned, beautiful-faced maiden, a pool of the nectar of loveliness, well-dressed and auspicious—even those sages fell into a state of delusion, bewildered by their agitation. Those wise men did not utter a single word; they were as if intoxicated, paralyzed, and utterly transfixed by her radiant and exceedingly beautiful form, the beloved of the Lord of the Three Worlds.
Thus, at that time, even those sages were deluded by her beauty, let alone the gods; likewise, they all gazed upon the slender Satī, the daughter of the lord of mountains and the beloved of Śiva.
Then, at that time, the sages, who were dear to Śiva, further praised the auspicious Caitya for him.
The sages said: "Your daughter has indeed been adorned by the Lord of Mountains; of this there is no doubt. O Lord of Gods, go forth, surrounded by the gods, to marry her."
"Go quickly, Mahādeva, to Pārvatī for the sake of procreating a son. Having heard those words of theirs, he laughed and spoke this.
"O highly fortunate sages, this marriage has never been seen nor even heard of by me before; please describe it to me in detail. (26)
Then all the sages, laughing, said to Sadāśiva: "O Lord, summon Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śatakratu. (27)
Likewise, [he saw] the hosts of ṛṣis, as well as yakṣas, gandharvas, and pannagas; siddhas and vidyādharas, and also kinnaras and throngs of apsarases. || 28 ||
"Bring these and many others quickly! Having heard those words spoken by the sage, he who was skilled in speech [responded].
The Lord said to Nārada: "Bring Viṣṇu quickly; bring Brahmā, Mahendra, and others as well. (30)
Taking the words of Śambhu upon his head, the purifier of the worlds, who is beloved by Viṣṇu, departed quickly for Vaikuṇṭha.

He beheld the God seated upon a supreme throne, being served by the goddess Śrī; the four-armed, most excellent of gods, of great splendor, with a body dark as a blue lotus, and most worthy of praise.

Nārada beheld him, the peerless beauty of the world, adorned with charming earrings set with precious gems, radiant with the supreme jewels of his great crown, and graced by a beautiful Vaijayantī garland of forest flowers.
Then Nārada, the omniscient and best of sages, approached and spoke these words with reverence to Śambhu, while playing his divine lute and his musical lute. (34)
"Come, come, O Mahāviṣṇu! Hurry to Mahādeva for the purpose of his marriage; you alone are the accomplisher of this task. (35)
Then the Blessed One, smiling, spoke to Nārada: "How did the thought of marriage arise in that wielder of the trident? Although the Blessed One already knew the matter, he questioned Nārada.
Nārada said: Rudra was gratified by the great austerity of Pārvatī; he himself came to that place where the virtuous Girijā resided.
Śambhu, gratified by Pārvatī, said, "I am your slave"; and having entreated Pārvatī, he added, "Choose a boon, O beautiful lady. (38)
"Śambhu has spoken in haste: 'He summons you now. Having heard those words of his, Janārdana, the God of gods, joined by Nārada and surrounded by his attendants, [set forth]. (39)
Then the high-souled Acyuta, the great lord of the masters of yoga, having mounted Suparṇa, himself departed by way of the sky together with Nārada and the best of gods. (40)
Seeing him, the Lord, whose lotus feet are meditated upon by yogis, quickly rose up filled with joy and embraced the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then the two gods, Hari and Hara, stood together as one and spoke to each other concerning their well-being and welfare.
Īśvara said: O Viṣṇu, I have been conquered by the penance of Girijā; there is no doubt about this. Today, I am desirous of going to Himālaya for the sake of taking her hand in marriage.
And I shall speak according to the truth before you, O Viṣṇu: when in former times Satī was given away by Dakṣa, O Viṣṇu... [44]
Nor was the taking of her hand performed by me according to the rite of formal resolve; I must now perform a great expansion of ritual acts.
"I do not know what task is required for all that is appropriate for taking her hand in marriage. Having heard those words of Śambhu, Madhusūdana laughed.
Just as he began to speak, Brahmā arrived in haste along with Indra and all the guardians of the world.
In the same way, the gods, asuras, yakṣas, dānavas, nāgas, pataṅgas, apsarases, and great ṛṣis—all having assembled and bowed their heads, spoke then to the Lord in order to speak against him.
"Go, go, O Great God, together with us, O Lord. Then Viṣṇu spoke these words, appropriate to the occasion:
O Śambhu, you ought to perform the rite here according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.
Perform the Nāndīmukha rite and the installation of the pavilion in accordance with the Dharma; some learned in the Vedas perform these even while avoiding the confluence of great rivers.
"O Lord, let the erection of the pavilion be performed now. Thus addressed by Viṣṇu, Śambhu indeed acted for his own benefit.
Therefore, everything appropriate for prosperity was performed by Brahmā and the others; Kaśyapa, joined by Brahmā, carried out the worship of the planets.
Likewise, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, the preceptor Bhṛgu, Kaṇva, Bṛhaspati, Śakti, Jamadagni, and Parāśara; || 54 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya, Śilāvāka, Śūnyapāla, Akṣataśrama, Agastya, Cyavana, Garga, Śilāda, and the great sage [Kāśyapa]. || 55 ||
These and many others indeed arrived in the presence of Śiva; urged by Brahmā, they performed the rites there according to the prescribed rules.

All those who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas performed the protective rite for Maheśa according to the injunctions prescribed in the Vedas, after the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony had been completed.
Likewise, the seers who know the truth [performed] various kinds of hymns from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as numerous auspicious rites.
They performed all the services for that Supreme Self, beginning with the application of unguents; indeed, Kaparda is the renowned name of that very Śiva, the Supreme Self. (59)
Then a garland of severed heads appeared, adorned with many pearls; and those serpents who had been his limbs all instantly became ornaments made of gold.
Adorned with all ornaments, Maheśvara, the God of gods, went toward the city of the King of Mountains, surrounded by the deities.
Then Caṇḍikā became his formidable sister; seated upon a corpse, the fierce goddess was adorned with ornaments of serpents.
Taking a golden pitcher full [of water] upon her head, the immensely radiant Mahācaṇḍī, with a blazing face and fierce eyes, was accompanied by her attendants.
There, accompanied by many thousands of various and hideous spirits, Caṇḍī, with her distorted face, went forth at their head.
Behind her were all the most terrible hosts, numbering eleven crores—those fierce ones who are dear to Rudra.
Then the three worlds were filled with the roar of the hand-drum (ḍamaru), the booming sound of the kettledrums (bherī), and the blaring of conch shells.
Likewise, a tumultuous roar arose from the sounds of kettledrums; all the gods, filled with eagerness, followed behind the hosts, accompanied by all the Siddhas and the guardians of the worlds.
Then, traveling through the midst [of the assembly], Mahendra arrived mounted upon Airāvata, indeed with a supreme, brilliant umbrella being held aloft.
Fanned with yak-tail whisks and surrounded by many gods, those numerous sages were then proceeding along.
The Brahmins, such as Bharadvāja and others, as well as Śākinīs, Yātudhānas, Vetālas, and Brahmarākṣasas, [were present] for the wedding of Śiva. (70)
Then the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and likewise other Pramathas and the like, following behind Caṇḍī, pursued her as they questioned her.
"Where has that fierce woman gone now, who was then running so swiftly? Having approached her as she was departing, they bowed down to that lady of great splendor.
Then they all said to Caṇḍī, who was accompanied by Bhairava: "O Caṇḍī, tell us how it is that you are going away without us; where are you going? (73)
Laughing, Caṇḍī said there in the hearing of all beings: "For the sake of marrying Śambhu, I am departing mounted upon a corpse."
Taking a golden pitcher and carrying it herself upon her head, Caṇḍī then personally assumed the form of Karavālī.
Surrounded by all the bhūtas, she went at the forefront of everyone; those hosts followed her, and behind the hosts were the gods.
Indra and the other guardians of the world, as well as the sages, were at his front and rear; and behind the sages stood the attendants of great splendor.

They were knowers of Viṣṇu’s immeasurable nature and were as charming as Mukunda; all were like clouds, wearing garlands and forest wreaths, all bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and clad in yellow garments. (78)

All of these were four-armed and adorned with earrings, crowns, bracelets, armlets, necklaces, anklets, threads, waist-bands, and finger-rings; they were all endowed with the marks of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa). || 79 ||
Among them stood Viṣṇu, accompanied by Śrī, the slayer of the enemies of the gods.

Then Hari, the Supreme Self, the sole kinsman of the world, who bestows the ultimate truth, shone forth; he who brings auspiciousness to the three worlds, who is established in the hearts of those of great majesty, and who dwells together with Śiva. (81)
Seated upon the son of Tārkṣya, the great Lord Hari, the sole sustainer of the world, was endowed with splendor; he was fanned by chowries and accompanied by all the lords of sages.

Likewise, Viriñci, seated upon his own vehicle, accompanied by the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), and surrounded by the Āgamas together with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, became the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha).

Then, surrounded by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and encompassed by the lords of the gods and the sages, he—mounted upon his bull, bearing the bull as his emblem, difficult to attain even for all the lords of yogis, and inaccessible to anyone—[proceeded]. (84)
Resembling pure crystal, the bull, who is devoted to Dharma, was accompanied by his mothers and cows, and was marked with auspicious signs. (85)
Accompanied by these asuras and dānavas, and adorned by the gods, Maheśa then went to Himālaya, the best of mountains, for the purpose of taking the hand of that most excellent of women.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Śrī Śiva," in the Kedāra-khaṇḍa of the first section, the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Lomaśa said: In that very manner, the Lord of Mountains, filled with supreme joy, placed Garga at the forefront and, being of great majesty, performed everything for the sake of his daughter with the highest splendor upon the auspicious ground.
Having summoned Viśvakarman, he respectfully had him construct a very extensive pavilion, beautiful with its sacrificial altars.
O best of the twice-born, the pavilion was ten thousand yojanas in extent, endowed with excellent qualities and filled with various wonders.
Both the stationary and the moving were alike and enchanting; yet even there, the moving was likewise conquered by the stationary.
There, the mobile was conquered by the immobile, and at that time, the dry land was overcome by the water.
People there do not truly distinguish whether it is water or land; in some places there are lions, and in others there are swans and highly resplendent cranes.
In some places there were very beautiful artificial peacocks, as well as artificial elephants, horses, and deer.
Which are true and which are false among those constructed by Viśvakarman? In that same manner, according to the prescribed rule, the wondrous gatekeepers were fashioned.
Having drawn their bows, the stationary [objects] became like moving beings; likewise, the horses along with their riders, and the elephants along with their mahouts.
Some were being fanned with yak-tail whisks and were adorned with flower buds; and some men there likewise shone, wearing garlands.
Likewise, many artificial banners were fashioned; and Mahālakṣmī, who arose from the Ocean of Milk, stood at the gateway.
Indeed, there were well-adorned artificial elephants that were like real ones; likewise, there were horses with their riders and elephants with their mahouts.
For indeed, chariots yoked with horses were there—artificial yet resembling those that are not made; they were fashioned thus for the purpose of deluding everyone, as well as the assembly.
Nandin was stationed by him at the great gate within that pavilion; resembling pure crystal, he was exactly like Nandin.
Above that was the great divine Puṣpaka chariot, adorned with jewels, shining with leaf-patterned parasols, and beautifully embellished with chowries. || 15 ||
On the left side were two elephants resembling pure saffron, possessing four tusks, sixty years of age, great-souled, and of great splendor.
In the same way, on the right side, two armored horses were fashioned, as well as the world-protectors (Lokapālas) adorned with jewel ornaments. || 17 ||
By that wise Viśvakarman, all sixteen types of deities were indeed fashioned according to their true nature and in accordance with reality.
In the same way, all the sages, Bhṛgu and the others whose wealth is austerity, and Indra along with all his attendants, are indeed [subordinate] in the ultimate sense. (19)
All these great-souled beings were created according to their true nature by that wise one; thus was this pavilion of divine form fashioned by him.
Born of many wonders, divine, and enchanting to the gods—at that moment, Nārada arrived there in front of him.
Urged by Brahmā toward the abode of Himālaya, Nārada then beheld before him his own self, endowed with humility.
For that reason, the highly illustrious Nārada was indeed deluded; intent on observation, he witnessed there the work of Viśvakarman.
He entered that pavilion of Himavat, which was variegated with jewels, adorned with golden pitchers, and graced by plantain trees and other ornaments.
Then the mountain, overcome with sudden paralysis and surrounded by his own attendants, honored that sage and asked, "What must be done? (25)

Nārada said: Those high-souled gods, led by Indra, have arrived; likewise, all the great sages have come, surrounded by their hosts. Indeed, Mahādeva, mounted upon his bull, has arrived for the wedding procession.
Then, having heard those words, Himavat, the best of mountains, spoke these great, praiseworthy, and sweet words to Nārada.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rule, go toward Śaṅkara.
Then, having heard those words, the sage, considering the speech of the mountain Himavat to be exactly so, spoke to the kings of mountains, together with Mena, Kena, Sahya, and Mount Meru.

O Mahāmati, since you are now joined with these, strive quickly and bring about auspiciousness here; [bring him] whose lotus feet are worshipped by the gods, the great sages, and the Suras and Asuras.
Thinking "so be it," he departed swiftly together with those kings of mountains; and having arrived in haste, that high-souled one, the foremost of sages, reached Śambhu in a single stride.
At that moment, Mahādeva was seen surrounded by the gods; likewise, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra were there together with the deities.
All those others who were followers of Rudra questioned Nārada intensely: "Tell us, for we are asking; why indeed is it not being told? (33)
Will Sahya, Maināka, and Meru each give their own daughters to Śambhu, or what else is happening now? (34)
Then the highly effulgent Nārada, the best of sages, placing Brahmā before him, spoke with reason concerning Viṣṇu.
Then, having retired to a secluded place, Nārada spoke these words to the Lord of the Gods: "Tvaṣṭṛ has indeed constructed a most magnificent palace, by which we have all been utterly deluded."
O Lord of Śacī, have you forgotten everything that was done for that high-souled one by you in the past? Therefore, desiring to conquer you, he dwells in the house of that great-souled mountain.
"Oh, he has been utterly deluded by that radiant semblance; thus was Viṣṇu made to appear by him, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and other weapons. (38)
And Brahmā, having become such as he was, performed that very same act.

O Lord of the Immortals, know that by means of this [power], a bull made of illusion was created from his own form, and likewise an elephant and an ass; furthermore, know that all other things were also fashioned here by him.
Having heard those words of his, the Lord of the Gods spoke this speech: || 41 ||
"O sir, having seen Viṣṇu, I shall go there quickly; you may dwell here. Tormented by grief for his son, he has acted thus either under some pretext or otherwise. (42)
Having heard those words of his, Janārdana, the god of gods, then spoke these words with a smile to Śakra, who was filled with fear.
O Lord of Śacī, you were previously deluded by the Nivātakavacas; there, the Vidyā-amṛtā was brought by me for your service.
Having now entered the pavilion by the very power of the Great Vidyā, this Himavat mountain as well as other excellent mountains [are present]. (45)
"O Vāsava, by my word all the obstacles have been overcome; however, Tvaṣṭṛ, remembering the cause, has indeed fashioned this through his illusory power."
Indeed, fools desire victory, yet they should not fear even the slightest bit.
While the gods, led by Śakra, were thus disputing, Viṣṇu consoled them; they then spoke to Nārada.
"Does the Lord of Mountains give his own daughter or not? Let it be told quickly! Tell me everything—was she seen by him today, and what was done? O Nārada, salutations to you!"

Having heard that, Śambhu laughed and then spoke these words: "If Himālaya, the mountain, will indeed give his daughter to me, then what need have I for your illusion? Tell me this truly, O Viṣṇu. (50)

"Indeed, it is said by the wise who know the principles of logic that a goal must be accomplished by whatever means possible; therefore, let all those seeking their purpose proceed with speed, led by Indra."
Then even Śiva, the soul of the universe and lord of beings, was deluded by the Great Being, the five-arrowed one; what then need be said of others?
And yet, while he exists in this way, Śambhu, who is supremely beautiful, has been brought under the sway of Anaṅga, just like any other ordinary person.
For Madana is indeed powerful in the world, by whom—through his own maturity—all this universe, including the gods and sages, has been conquered. (54)
For among all beings, and especially among the gods, the King is indeed powerful and bodiless; his command is most potent.
In the form of a woman, Pārvatī was invincible throughout the three worlds; for upon seeing her as a woman, even all the wise sages were overcome. (56)
Gods, humans, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas—all were non-transgressors of the command of the high-souled Madana. || 57 ||
O twice-born ones, Madana cannot be overcome even by the great power of asceticism or the power of charity without humility. || 58 ||
Therefore, the anger of Anaṅga is indeed exceedingly powerful. Having thus seen the Lord deluded by Madana, Mādhava—
The knower of speech spoke these words: "O Lord, do not indeed worry about everything that was said by Nārada regarding the pavilion."
All that was fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ was made diverse through the power of the Lord's passion; then Śaṅkara spoke these words to Madhusūdana.
"Indeed, this pavilion was constructed by Tvaṣṭṛ and enveloped by ignorance; however, O Viṣṇu, what shall we say of the pavilion alone? (62)
"O illustrious one, marriage indeed has its root in ignorance; therefore, let us all go now for the sake of the wedding. (63)

Placing Nārada at their head, all the gods together with Indra and accompanied by the Himālaya mountain went to that most wonderful palace, which was filled with many marvels and fashioned in diverse ways by Viśvakarman.

And today he has completed that most excellent, purifying [sacrificial ground], which is honored by many; the wise one made that sacrificial ground variegated with diverse patterns and captivating to the mind. (65)
As all those lords of the gods were about to enter together with the sages, they were seen there by Himādri, who rose up to meet them.

In the same manner, he constructed for them enchanting palaces; there, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Pramathas, Siddhas, gods, and hosts of Nāgas and Apsarases dwell in happiness, and for their sake, he created groves here and there.
For their sake, magnificent palaces with flowing water-courts, most wonderful and beautiful, have been constructed by that Great-Souled One. (68)
There indeed were spacious dwellings prepared for the sake of residence for all the gods and for the sages of purified souls. (69)
In this manner, Viśvakarman constructed many temples as well, appropriately located here and there for those who were to dwell therein. (70)
The Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, and others who dwell in sacred fields (kṣetra), those who dwell in cremation grounds, and others who dwell in banyan trees; || 71 ||
Others were worshippers of the Aśvattha tree, and others likewise were sky-dwellers; whomever was seated wherever, by that very act, they remained right there.
And Viśvakarman constructed vast and beautiful palaces, perfectly suited to those very beings.
Right there, the Himālaya mountain himself settled all those hosts together: the gods including Indra, along with the multitudes of yakṣas, piśācas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and apsarases.
Lomaśa said: There, all those gods, together with their retinues, their mounts, and filled with joy, sat down after being honored by the Himālaya mountain.
And right there, Viśvakarman fashioned a great minister, endowed with supreme radiance, for the purpose of serving as a residence for the Self-Existent One.

In that very same way, he himself indeed created another abode for Viṣṇu—resplendent, most wonderful, and delightful—which Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned; and likewise, he himself created a charming residence for Vaṇḍin.

In that very manner, he made that palace white, supremely charming, of great luster, well-worshipped by the best of gods, and beautifully adorned with the great splendor of the glory of Kailāsa. || 4 ||
Right there, Śambhu was indeed installed by that Himādri with supreme majesty.
In the meantime, Menā arrived with her circles of female companions and the sages, surrounding Śambhu for the purpose of performing the lustration rite (nīrājana).
Then the three worlds were made to resound with the long-continued music of instruments, and Menā performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for that ascetic.
Beholding him, the virtuous Menā then recognized Hara; recollecting what the Mountain’s daughter had said, Menā was filled with wonder.

Indeed, whatever was previously described by Pārvatī in my presence, I now perceive the beauty of Maheśa, the Supreme Lord, to be even greater than that—an indescribable beauty witnessed by me this very moment.
Thus filled with wonder and surrounded by the wives of the brahmins, that woman of excellent complexion was adorned with a pair of unwashed garments.
The most divine bodice, adorned with various jewels, was then accepted by the Goddess; it shone with supreme splendor.
And at that time, she wore a necklace adorned with divine jewels, as well as costly bracelets made of pure gold.
Seated there, the fortunate woman meditated upon the Supreme Lord while being attended by her female friends and the wives of the brahmins.
In the meantime, Garga spoke these words there: "O wise ones, bring Śambhu to your own home for the sake of the marriage ceremony; do so with great haste at this very hour."
Having heard those words of the high-souled Garga, all the mountains, together with their wives, rose up in attendance.
Endowed with great magnificence, all of them held auspicious objects in their hands; at that time, their wives were likewise adorned with ornaments and beautifully decorated.
With affectionate eyes, they accepted many gifts; then, amidst the great sound of musical instruments and the loud chanting of the Veda, [the king departed].
They all arrived there where Lord Maheśvara was, surrounded by his attendants (pramathas) and attended upon by Caṇḍī.
Likewise, the illustrious Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was surrounded there by the great sages as well as by the hosts of gods. (19)
Upon hearing the sound of the musical instruments, all the attendants of Śaṅkara, surrounded by gods and sages, rose up simultaneously.

Thus prepared, the yogins joined with their circles, and the hosts of hosts, whose splendor was singular—the Lord of the hosts (Gaṇeśa) at their head, as well as all the leaders of the Gaṇas—stood there, honoring Śiva and manifesting his majesty.

Then that exceedingly fierce circle of yoginīs, with the sound of the clanging of ṭaṅkas and the roar of kettledrums, placed the terrifying Caṇḍī at their head, who was then adorned with great majesty.
She made the serpent Karkoṭaka into a necklace for her neck, and she wore a breast-ornament of scorpions and venomous serpents.
She wore as ear-ornaments the hands and feet of heroes slain in battle, and others she placed upon her breast.
Clad in a leopard skin, she is joined by a circle of yoginīs; likewise, she is surrounded by kṣetrapālas and encircled by bhairavas.

Likewise, she was surrounded by ghosts, spirits, and deceivers, as well as the most formidable hosts such as Vīrabhadra and others, who had been commanded by Śiva at that time for the purpose of destroying Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Likewise, Kālī, Bhairavī, and Māyā who is indeed terrifying; Tripurā, Jayā, and the auspicious Kṣemakarī. || 27 ||
And all the others likewise, placing Sadāśiva at their head, were most fierce and desirous of going forth, surrounded by bhūtas and pretas.
Then, having beheld all these, Janārdana, the devotee of Śiva, placed the great sages at his head, as well as the immortals, and likewise Anasūyā and Arundhatī.
Viṣṇu said: "O Lord, place Caṇḍī nearby, she who is saluted by the world-protectors."
Having heard those words spoken by Viṣṇu, Sadāśiva, the Lord of the Universe, spoke with a smile toward Caṇḍī.
"Stay right here until the marriage to Caṇḍī takes place; you know my intentions regarding what ought and ought not to be done, O beautiful one. (32)
Having thus heard the words of Śambhu, who possesses immeasurable splendor, Caṇḍī spoke respectfully, addressing Viṣṇu with anger.
Likewise, all the other Pramathas, being provoked to anger, said to Viṣṇu: "O Lord, wherever Śiva shines, there we [must follow]. (34)
"Why have you prevented us from this supreme prosperity? Having heard those words of theirs, Keśava spoke these words:
Addressing Caṇḍī and likewise the other Pramathas of that kind, I say to you all: "You ought not to give way to anger. (36)
Thus addressed by him at that time, all those hosts headed by Caṇḍī withdrew to a secluded place, their hearts aflame due to Viṣṇu’s words.
Then all the ministers of the lord of mountains arrived in haste toward Maheśa with their wives, in a state of great agitation.
There they were surrounded by women amidst the loud sound of the five musical instruments, the frequent chanting of the *brahmaghoṣa*, and the great resonance of song.

Thus they arrived where Śambhu was surrounded by his entire retinue; having come with water-pots, Sadāśiva was indeed bathed by the women with auspicious songs, while he was adorned with all ornaments.
The sages, gods, gandharvas, and others from the best of mountains, as well as highly honored women, then proceeded at the very front of Śambhu. He shone with a great umbrella held over his head.
Being fanned with chowries and resplendent with a crown, he was likewise attended by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Candra, and the guardians of the world.
For even those moving at the front shone, endowed with supreme splendor; likewise were the conchs, kettledrums, tabors, drums, and gomukhas.
In that very same way, during the great festival, all the singers and musicians repeatedly played instruments of supreme auspiciousness.
The highly blessed Arundhatī and likewise Anasūyā, as well as Sāvitrī and Lakṣmī, were surrounded by their mothers.

Accompanied by these, the sole kinsman of the world then shone with supreme splendor, surrounded by the moon, the sun, the wind, and the air, as well as by the foremost of the world-protectors and the great sages.
Fanned by the wind, he was shaded by a parasol personally held over him by Śaśin; the Sun stood before him as his illuminator, and Viṣṇu, endowed with splendor, remained in his presence.

Then the gods, together with the sages, rained down flowers and scattered them about. Śambhu then went to his great palace, which had golden floors and was adorned with magnificent splendor; he entered while being honored with supreme worship by kings, gods, and dānavas.
Thus arrived Śambhu, the Supreme Lord, entered the sacrificial pavilion while being extolled with hymns of praise by the gods.
The best of mountains helped Maheśa descend from the elephant; then, having seated him upon a throne, he performed a great lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
Together with his wife, his friends, and likewise his family priest, everything that was performed there, such as the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and so forth, was indeed accomplished.
Prompted by Brahmā, the lordly priest immediately performed much auspicious and propitious ceremony, appropriate for the occasion.
Having led her into the inner altar where that Pārvatī was stationed, [he saw] the slender-limbed woman, adorned with all ornaments, upon the sacrificial altar.
There, Hara was brought in person by Viṣṇu together with Brahmā; they, led by Vācaspati, remained watching for the auspicious moment.
The sage Garga sat right there in that very water-clock pavilion; as soon as the full hour had elapsed, the recitation of the Praṇava began.
Uttering "Oṃ Puṇya," Garga placed his joined palms toward the bride; Pārvatī, for her part, showered a handful of unbroken rice grains upon Śiva.
Rudra was worshipped by her with curd, unbroken grains, kusha grass, and other offerings; Pārvatī, whose face was radiant, was filled with supreme joy.
She gazed upon that Śambhu, for whose sake the Great Goddess had formerly performed supreme and most great penance, the highest of all.
Through that asceticism, he attained the one who is the life of the life of the world; then Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull, was addressed by Nārada.

"Likewise, O Three-eyed One, quickly perform a reciprocal worship for Pārvatī along with Gaṅgā and other sages such as Sanaka. Then that slender lady was honored by Śiva with offerings of water (arghya), unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other items.
Thus, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, who are identical with the universe, shone forth at that time as they were being honored by one another.

Clad in the splendor of the three worlds and gazing at one another, that divine couple was then consecrated with the lustration rite (nīrājana) by Lakṣmī, and especially by Sāvitrī; and then by Arundhatī as well.
Then Anasūyā, her eyes overflowing with affection upon seeing Śambhu and the illustrious Pārvatī, performed the lustration ceremony for them.
In that very manner, all the wives of the twice-born performed the lustration ceremony again and again; and all of them, looking upon Satī and Śambhu, were likewise joyful and laughing.
Lomaśa said: In the meantime, urged by Garga Ācārya, Himavat, together with Menā, proceeded to give away his daughter.
Taking a golden pitcher, the highly fortunate Menā, adorned with all ornaments, took her place on the flank of the Himalaya mountain.
Then Viśvanātha, the bestower of boons, having been addressed by Himādri, came together with Brahmā and likewise with Viṣṇu.
Together with the high-souled family priest Garga, I shall today perform the gift of my daughter to the trident-bearing God of gods.
"O Brahman, let the ritual procedure be told now that this time has arrived. Thinking "So be it," all those best of the twice-born, who were knowers of the proper time, [prepared]. (69)

"O dear one, let your own lineage and family be told, especially in detail; speak, O illustrious one! Having heard these words, Vimukha immediately became Sumukha, for he who was beyond grief had fallen into a state of lamentation. (70)

At that time, the Blessed Maheśa, seeing the excellent gods, sages, as well as the hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, munis, and siddhas with their faces rendered speechless, laughed most heartily; and Nārada likewise did so.
Then Nārada, the son of Brahmā, brought forth his lute; at that time, the wise one was restrained: "O Lord, do not play the lute. (72)
Thus addressed by Parvata, Nārada spoke these words: "Bhava himself has been questioned by you regarding the declaration of his own lineage. (73)
O Mountain, his lineage and family are indeed Nāda alone; Śambhu is established in Nāda, for Nāda is established in him. (74)
Therefore, Śambhu consists of sound (nāda), and he is obtained through sound; for this reason, O scorcher of enemies, the lute has been played by me today.
O Parvata, indeed even the gods beginning with Brahmā do not know his lineage, family, or name; what then can be said of others? (76)
For you have fallen into a state of delusion and do not know anything at all; what should and should not be said regarding Maheśa, for sense-objects are directed toward the external.
Whosoever among those who follow the scriptures have perished on this mountain, of that there is no doubt; for this Virūpākṣa is formless and is said to be of no noble lineage.
O best of mountains, this son-in-law of yours is without lineage; of this there is no doubt. You, O wise one, must certainly not entertain any hesitation in this matter. (79)
O my Lord, O highly fortunate one, they do not know Hara; what is the use of much speaking on my part? For it is by his ignorance that these sages have indeed been deluded.
Even Brahmā does not know that head of Parameṣṭhin; for Viṣṇu went to the netherworld (pātāla), yet he likewise did not see it.
Know this: by that great and unfathomable mark, the three worlds are indeed pervaded; what need is there for anything else? (82)
"O Himālaya, this daughter of yours has surely propitiated me; for how else, O great mountain, could you not know this in truth? (83)
"By these two the universe is produced, and by these two it is sustained. Having heard these words of that high-souled Nārada, [the king spoke]. (84)
Led by Himādri and likewise headed by Indra, they all, with minds filled with wonder, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (85).
But having recognized the profundity of the Lord, all those wise ones, overcome with wonder, spoke to one another: (86)

The sages said: By whose command this vast universe came into being, which is higher than the highest and consists of the nature of his own consciousness; he who is accessible through the independent Supreme Lord, that Great Soul is endowed with the very form of the three worlds. (87)
Lomaśa said: Then those foremost of mountains, Meru and the others, filled with agitation, spoke in unison to Himavat, the great mountain.

The mountains said: "O Mountain, let the gift of your daughter be performed this very day; by good fortune, the glorious Śambhu has been obtained by you today. Indeed, no hesitation should be made here in your heart; therefore, let her be given to the Lord."
Having heard those words of his friends, Himālaya, then urged by Brahmā, formed a firm resolve: "O Supreme Lord, I give this maiden to you. (3)
"Accept her as a wife," he said, and gave her with these words: "To this great Rudra, the god of gods, to Śambhu; the maiden has been given to Maheśa by the high-souled Lord of Mountains. (4)
And having been brought outside to the sacrificial altar, the lotus-eyed couple, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, were seated upon the outer altar as if they were a married pair.
Then, O twice-born ones, the high-souled preceptor Kaśyapa himself performed the invocation of the fire for the purpose of the oblation right there.
Brahmā took his place upon the Brahma-throne in the presence of Śiva, while the learned sages proceeded with the oblation.
There, those who were conversant with various philosophical systems spoke to one another; some, devoted to the discourse of the Vedas, spoke indeed with mutual agreement.
In this very way, it is neither thus nor otherwise; it is indeed an effect, or rather not an effect—such is the "effect and non-effect" according to others. (9)

Thus, while they were speaking, their voices were heard in the presence of Śiva; adhering to their own respective opinions, they spoke to one another—devoid of knowledge of reality, possessed only of Vedic intellect.
Having heard those words of theirs, who were each desirous of victory over the other, Nārada laughed and spoke these words in the presence of Śiva: || 11 ||
"All of you, O Brahmins, though you are disputants and devoted to Vedic discourse, should maintain silence, keeping Sadāśiva in your hearts. (12)

Salutations to that Soul of All, who is the individual self, the supreme self, and the highest of all; by whom this universe was caused to be made, from whom everything proceeds, and into whom the universe dissolves. 13.
O twice-born ones, he now resides here in the abode of the lord of mountains; all of you wise ones have been born from his very mouth.
Thus addressed by Nārada at that time, those best of the twice-born were enlightened by his instructive words. || 15 ||
And while the sacrifice was proceeding, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, beheld the feet of the Goddess and her enchanting moon-like nails.
Upon seeing her, the lotus-born Brahmā immediately faltered; overcome by passion, he discharged his semen onto the ground as before.
As his semen was flowing, the Grandfather (Brahmā) became ashamed; he then crushed with his two feet that great secret which is difficult to overcome.
Then many thousands of Vālakhilya ṛṣis were born; they all approached him and said, "O Father! (tāta-tāta). || 19 ||
Then, being provoked, Nārada said to those Vālakhilyas: "O young brahmins, you must go to Mount Gandhamādana."
"You must not remain here, nor is there any need for you to stay. Thus addressed by Nārada, all those Vālakhilyas, having been so instructed, departed from the mountain with great haste.
Then Nārada consoled Brahmā with auspicious words, and at that moment, the sacrifice of that high-souled one was completed.
Likewise, O Brahmins, the priests became intent upon the recitation of peace-mantras; the space between the quarters was pervaded by the great sound of the Veda. (23)
Then the supreme god was honored with the *nīrājana* rite by the wives of the gods, and likewise worshipped and venerated by the wives of the sages.

Likewise, beautiful and auspicious women from the king of mountains performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with songs; and others, great sages skilled in the art of fine singing, likewise honored him with hymns of praise. || 25 ||
And the high-minded Himalaya, the great mountain, being greatly delighted, gave them precious jewels as a token of his satisfaction. (26)

Then that Lord, accompanied by his wife and surrounded by all his own attendants and hosts, shone upon the altar with the throngs of gods and Siddhas; his heart was filled with joy as he gazed upon those who were the most beautiful beings in the world.
In the meantime, Brahmā and Viṣṇu at their head, along with the sages, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and whoever else had gathered there, [were present]. (28)
Then the high-souled Mahāgirīśa, with supreme splendor, having honored them all, duly gave them fine jewels, garments, and ornaments, as well as betel and fragrant water.
Then, placing Śiva at their head, the lords of the gods entered; likewise, all of them, having gathered together, rejoiced with one accord.
Arranged in rows, they ate together with the ascetics and the horned ones; some groups, gathered separately, [amused] the Lord with various humorous sentiments.
Nārada and the others, accompanied by many celestial nymphs, were not satisfied; likewise, all the hosts of Caṇḍīs partook of their meals with prepared vessels.
The Vaitālas and Kṣetrapālas ate from prepared vessels, as did the Śākinīs, Ḍākinīs, Yakṣiṇīs, Mātṛkās, and others. (33)
Then there were sixty-four yoginīs, as well as other yogins; and ten crores of gaṇas and one crore of great-souled ones.
Thus have all the sages, as well as the gods and others, been described; indeed, other yogins as well have already been mentioned by me previously.
The Yoginīs have indeed been described; now I shall tell you what is to be eaten by them: some bring the pure flesh of rhinoceroses. (36)
Hungering, they ate even that which was joined with bones, as well as intestines; some, having brought the heavy heads of buffaloes, [ate them]. (37)

Likewise, some were dancing at that time, while others among the Pramathas were wailing loudly; some remained silent, possessing the form of Rudra, and others were likewise looking about at one another.
Bhairava, standing in the midst of the circle of Yoginīs, indeed danced; likewise, other spirits and vetālas cried out, "Come to me! (39).
Thus, having observed their agitation, Madhusūdana, smiling, spoke these words to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world: 40.
"O, restrain these hosts here who are currently intoxicated; and whatever task must be done at this time, let that indeed be performed by all. (41)
"Therefore, O Mahādeva, ward them off by means of your wisdom. Having heard that, the Blessed Lord Rudra spoke to Vīrabhadra.
Rudra said: "Restrain those who are intoxicated, and especially those who are drunk. Thus was Vīrabhadra addressed by Śambhu, the Supreme Lord.
Commanded by the wise Vīrabhadra, the Pramathas were restrained; having been silenced by him, they remained standing there in silence.
Within the midst of the Yoginīs were the Bhūtas, Pramathas, and Guhyakas, as well as Śākinīs, Yātudhānas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and Kopikarpaṭas; they remained motionless. || 45 ||
Likewise, other spirits, vetālas, field-protectors (kṣetrapālas), and the terrifying Bhairavas—all the Pramathas and the rest—became either tranquil or intoxicated with passion.
O Brahmins, thus was that most auspicious and beautiful wedding ceremony performed by Himādri with great elaboration at that time.
Four days have passed with a completely fulfilled mind; Himādri has performed worship of the trident-bearing God of gods. (48)
Then, having worshipped Mahādeva with garments, ornaments, jewelry, and various kinds of gems, he became intent upon the words of Viṣṇu.
Himavat worshipped Viṣṇu, who was accompanied by Lakṣmī, as well as Brahmā, with auspicious garments and ornaments.
Having likewise worshipped the omnipresent Indra together with his priest and Indrāṇī, as well as the guardians of the world individually, [he performed the rites].

In that very manner, Caṇḍī was worshipped by the Bhūtas, Pramathas, and Guhyakas with garments, ornaments, and various kinds of jewels; and all others who had arrived there were likewise fully honored.
Thus, at that time, all the gods, sages, yakṣas, gandharvas, vidyādharas, siddhas, and cāraṇas, as well as the hosts of mortals and apsarases, were duly honored.
Lomaśa said: In that same manner, all the mountains were honored by Viṣṇu—Sahyācala, Vindhya, Maināka, and Gandhamādana.
Then Mālyavat, Malaya, Mahendra, Mandara, and Meru were also worshipped with great effort by Viṣṇu.
Śveta was made Śvetagiri, and likewise Nīlādri; as well as Udayādri, Śṛṅga, and the great Astācalavara.
Likewise, Mount Mānasa, the mountain Kailāsa, the best of peaks, and the Lokāloka mountain were worshipped by the Supreme Lord.
In this way, all those foremost mountains were indeed honored by him, as were all the others who dwell upon the mountains.
Everything was performed appropriately by Viṣṇu together with Brahmā; and when the next day arrived, the procession for the bridegroom's choice (varayātrā) was likewise conducted.
Accompanied by Himādri and their kinsmen, all the hosts of gods as well as many of the Gaṇas went to Mount Gandhamādana.
Likewise, all the Pramathas, as well as the other fierce Gaṇas and many others who had come there from the Himālaya, [were present]. (8)
O Brahmins, having witnessed that couple at that time, the sages, who were themselves graced by Śiva, attained supreme joy upon seeing the marriage of Śiva.
Śambhu together with Pārvatī, and Pārvatī together with Śambhu, were in reality like fragrance and a flower, or like speech and its meaning. || 10 ||
Likewise, Prakṛti and Puruṣa were expressed as a single word and not otherwise; those two, husband and wife, mounted upon the elephant, shone with great splendor.
Then Brahmā stood upon his vehicle, Viṣṇu was upon Garuḍa, Indra was mounted on Airāvata, and Kubera was atop the Puṣpaka.
Varuṇa is mounted upon a crocodile, Yama likewise upon a buffalo; Nairṛta should be mounted upon a ghost, and the great Agni seated upon a goat.
Then Pavana was mounted upon a deer, and Īśa upon a bull; thus were the world-protectors, along with the planets and Parameṣṭhin.
Likewise, other Pramathas and others arrived with their respective forces, as did the great mountain Himādri, the Ṛṣabha, and Gandhamādana.
The Sahya mountain, Nīlagiri, Mandara, the Malaya mountain, Kailāsa of great splendor, and Maināka of great radiance; || 16 ||
These and other mountains are indeed full of grain and possess great splendor; they are all delightful, accompanied by their wives and their sons.
All the powerful, embodied mountains there, such as Meru and others, became intent on the worship of Śiva during the course of their excellent journey.

Indeed, Nandin seated those mountains, Meru and the others, there; and the bridegroom’s procession was conducted by Himādri as prescribed. Then, together with all those kinsmen, he returned once more.

Established in his own abode, that Himavat of great renown shone with a supreme splendor born indeed from his association with Śiva; for that great mountain was famous and celebrated throughout the three worlds. || 20 ||
Those for whom Śaṅkara is pleased by the great gift of a daughter are truly blessed, they are high-souled, and likewise they have accomplished all that was to be done.

Those on the tips of whose tongues the two-syllabled name always resides, and those by whom the two-syllabled name "Śiva" has indeed been uttered today from their hearts—they are Rudras themselves in human form; of this there is no doubt.
Mahādeva is constantly satisfied with even a small gift, and likewise with a mere leaf, or even with water alone.
Indeed, this Sadāśiva is always pleased with a leaf, a flower, or even water; therefore, Śiva should be worshipped by all here, for he bestows great good fortune upon men.

He is the one great light, the unborn, the Supreme Lord, the highest among the high and low, the Great Soul—without interval, changeless, without a superior lord, unassailable, free from conceptual construction, and effortless.

Stainless, eternal in form, cessation itself, eternal bliss, and eternally liberated—such is the God of gods, Bhava, who is known by all; he is worshipped by those gods and others, and when praised, meditated upon, honored, and contemplated, he is the omniscient one who bestows everything at all times.

Just as the Himavat is renowned as the most excellent by all virtues, so that great-souled one, possessing every virtue and worthy of worship by the Lord of the Universe, then became the Himalaya, the preeminent among mountains at that time. (27)
Then the righteous lord of mountains, having returned to his proper place together with Menā, dismissed all the other mountains.
When they had departed, Himavat, the preeminent king of mountains, by the grace of Mahādeva, was accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. || 29 ||
Then Maheśa, assuming his own form, set his mind upon sporting in a secluded place on Mount Gandhamādana together with Girijā.
Indeed, through great passion and ascetic fervor, when the two were united, that sexual union was initiated between the two, and it continued for both of them at that time.
When that great and terrible festival, which was like the dissolution of the world, arrived, they did not find even the slightest happiness.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were established in the determination of what ought and ought not to be done; yet by means of that seed, the entire world—both mobile and immobile—was destroyed.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the bestower of spiritual knowledge, remembered Agni; and as soon as he was remembered in their minds, Agni arrived with great haste.
Sent by those two, he beheld the beautiful temple of Śiva; and at the entrance, he saw Nandin standing there, possessing great splendor.
Then Agni, having become small in stature with a complexion like saffron, entered the inner apartments of Śambhu, which were filled with various wonders.
Having reached that courtyard, which was covered with many jewels and beautifully adorned with palaces, the bearer of oblations (Agni) sat down and said: || 37 ||
"O Mother, give alms from the inner apartments to me, who have a bowl for my hands. Having heard those words of his, the young girl [responded] to him whose bowl was his hands. (38)
Just as she began to give alms to him herself, Śiva, rising from that state of amorous union, became exceedingly enraged. (39)
Then Rudra, having raised his trident, became truly Bhairava; however, Śiva himself was restrained from that slaughter by Girijā. With her words, she gave alms to him, saying, "To Agni Jātavedas."
Then, having taken alms in his hand, Girijā was personally begged for alms by that fire; becoming enraged, she cursed him. || 41 ||
"O monk, by my curse you shall indeed quickly become an eater of all things; by this semen, you shall immediately experience suffering on all sides."
Having been addressed thus, the carrier of oblations (Agni) consumed the seed of the Lord, and went to where all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were stationed in every way.
Having arrived, he related everything regarding the consumption of that semen; indeed, all the hosts of deities, beginning with Indra, became pregnant.
Just as the oblation reaches all [deities] through Agni, so too those lords of the gods [were conceived] by means of the semen originating from the mouth of Agni. 45.
All of them, both those within and those outside, being greatly oppressed by anxiety, sought refuge with Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods of gods and the Sovereign.
The gods said: "You are the protector of all the gods and the very lord of the worlds; therefore, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge, protection must be granted."
We are all desirous of death, oppressed by this semen; we, all the inhabitants of heaven, are terrified of the Asuras.
Having sought refuge in Śaṅkara, we have undertaken this marriage so that he may protect us. For when he becomes the son of Rudra, then we shall all be happy and fearless in heaven.
As all of them were being thus paralyzed, fear came upon them: "O Viṣṇu, how is it possible to live with this semen? (50)
For indeed, the three aims of life, though well-prepared for men, inevitably turn into their opposite without the grace of the Divine; it cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, considering that indeed to be the strength of all embodied beings, we all agree regarding the determination of what ought and ought not to be done.
Having thus heard the lamentation of the gods, the Supreme Lord, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, spoke these words to the gods with a smile.
Indeed, let Mahādeva, the Great Lord, be praised because of the gravity of the task.
Saying "So be it," all those gods led by Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā and all the others, departed; and likewise, all the sages praised Hara.
Oṃ, salutations to the god Bharga, the blue-throated one, the bountiful giver; to the three-eyed one, the embodiment of the three Vedas, the sustainer of the three worlds. || 56 ||
To him who possesses three notes, three measures, the three Vedas, and the three forms; to him who is the three goals of life, the three abodes, the three steps, and the wielder of the trident.
Save me, save me, O Mahādeva, Lord of the world and of the seed! || 58 ||
As soon as he was praised by Brahmā, the bull-bannered god appeared right there for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. 59.

Then the sole kinsman of the world was seen by the great-souled ones and the best of gods, who honored him most highly while he was being praised with various words that were both novel in form and in accord with the Vedas.
And as the gods were offering praise, the Supreme Lord said: "Let none of you feel fear, though you are afflicted by this semen."
"O gods, you must indeed perform an emesis this very day! Thinking "So be it," all those hosts of deities, headed by Indra, then discharged that semen of Śaṅkara, O brahmins.
In a single moment, that semen became as large as a great mountain, resembling molten gold, and was most wonderful to behold. (63)
And all the hosts of deities, Indra and the others, became happy; indeed, even without Agni, they were all completely satisfied at that time.
And by that fire, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was addressed: "O Mahādeva, O best of deities, what should be done by me today? (65)
Therefore, O Lord, tell me today that by which I shall always be happy, and by which I may become the carrier of oblations for the gods. (66)
Then Śiva himself spoke while the gods were listening here: "Let the seed be discharged into the womb," and then Agni laughed aloud.
He said to the god Śaṅkara, "Your splendor is difficult to approach; how can this fierce and intense radiance be borne by ordinary beings? (68)
Then the Blessed Maheśvara spoke to Agni: "Let your splendor be released into the bodies of those who perform penance month after month."
Thinking "so be it" at those words, that Jātavedas of great splendor, blazing with supreme luster and possessing mighty power, sat down there during the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Then, having risen in the morning, those women, ever devoted to the truth and intent on their morning ablutions, went to the sacrificial fire of the sages.
Seeing that [fire] blazing there, all of them, afflicted by the cold, desired to warm themselves; however, they were all then restrained by Arundhatī. || 72 ||
Although they were forbidden by her, those Kṛttikās themselves discharged [their seed]; and as they all discharged it, the atoms of that semen quickly entered the pores of their skin right there.
Then, when the water was gone, the fire arose and rested by itself.
Then those wives of the sages indeed departed toward their own abodes; however, having been cursed by the sages, the Kṛttikās then became wanderers in the sky.
At that very moment, all of them, distressed by their infidelity, then discharged their semen upon the back of the Himalaya mountain.
In a single stream, that semen, possessing the luster of molten gold, was then swiftly cast into the Gaṅgā and surrounded by reeds.
Recognizing the child as having six faces, all the gods were filled with joy; at that moment, they were told by Garga, "Let him be taken away in peace."
By the grace of Śambhu, everyone becomes eternal; Kārttikeya, endowed with great strength, was born upon the banks of the Gaṅgā. || 79 ||
Then the son of Gaṅgā sat down, having fasted for a day and a night; he was Śākha, Viśākha, the exceedingly powerful Ṣaṇmukha, and the one of great strength.
When the six-faced son of Śaṅkara was born in the Gaṅgā, at that very moment Girijā’s breasts became full of milk.

Beholding Śiva, she said: "O Śambhu, O Mahādeva, a great flow has arisen within me; for what purpose has this occurred? Let it be examined. Then Mahādeva, though omniscient, spoke to her as if he were ignorant.
Nārada arrived there and spoke of that birth: "A beautiful son has indeed been born to Śiva and Śivā. (83)
Having heard those words, O Brahmins, all the Pramathas became filled with hearts overflowing with joy, while the Gandharvas became intent upon singing. (84)
With many banners, cloth-pendants, and archways, as well as numerous celestial chariots, the great mountain shone brilliantly, ablaze due to the birth of a son for the high-souled Śaṅkara.
Then all the hosts of gods, the sages, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas, as well as the Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas, attended by throngs of Apsarases, [gathered there]. || 86 ||
Then all of them together, in a single file, went with Śaṅkara to see Gāṅgeya, who was staying upon the riverbank.
Then, having mounted his bull, the Blessed One went forth together with Girijā, accompanied by the other gods, such as Indra and the rest.
Then conchs and kettledrums, as well as many kinds of musical instruments, resounded.
At that very moment, Vīrabhadra and all the other Gaṇas followed the Lord, eager for sport and playing various musical instruments—both stringed (tata) and percussion (vitata) instruments.
Some there were intent on dancing, others likewise were singers; some were panegyrists and others were being praised, and they all performed the chanting of his virtues.
Thus, those gods, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Pannagas, with hearts full of joy, went together with Śiva to see that bestower of boons, the son of Śaṅkara.
As soon as they beheld the son of Gaṅgā, who resembled Śaṅkara, they saw that his great splendor had pervaded the three worlds.
Then he saw that child, enveloped in splendor, with the luster of molten gold; fair-faced and endowed with great beauty, possessing a fine nose and eyes with lovely smiles.
Beholding that son of Gaṅgā, whose face was beautiful and serene, who was likewise lovely in every limb, and who was renowned for his great majesty, they were struck with great wonder.
Then all the Pramathas and Gaṇas, as well as Vīrabhadra and the others, paid homage to the youth, the prince who possessed the splendor of the sun.
They stood surrounding him on his left and right sides; likewise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra also stood there, surrounded by the gods.
The sages, yakṣas, and gandharvas, having surrounded the youth, fell prostrate on the ground like staffs, while some remained with their necks bowed low.

Others bowed their heads, recognizing him as the imperishable Lord; various musical instruments were sounded during that great festival. Thus, amidst that auspicious occasion, the sages recited propitiatory hymns.
In the meantime, Śaṅkara, the lord of Girijā, descended quickly from his bull along with Pārvatī, O you of excellent vows.

Then the sole kinsman of the world, filled with supreme joy along with Bhavānī, gazed upon his son; the Lord of All, accompanied by the coils of the serpent and surrounded by the Pramathas, was visibly full of affection and exultant. (101)
There, Pārvatī, overcome with agitation and overflowing with affection, embraced Guha and caused him to drink from her breast, which was flowing with milk. 102.
Then, having been honored with the lustration rite (nīrājita) by the gods together with their wives who were filled with joy, the vault of the sky was pervaded by a great sound of "Victory! (jaya).
The sages with the chanting of the Veda, the singers with song, and the instrumentalists with musical instruments attended upon the young prince.

Then, having placed that Kumāraka, who was of great splendor, upon his own lap, the Lord of the Mountains, the husband of Bhavānī, shone forth visibly endowed with glory—the most excellent among those possessed of sons. (105)
Then the couple rejoiced there in unison, while he was being consecrated, surrounded by the sages and the best of the gods.
The boy played upon the lap of Śaṅkara and squeezed Vāsuki, who was situated around his neck, with both his hands.
Pressing his face, he then counted his fingers in reverse order: one, three, ten, and eight.
Then the Blessed Lord Śambhu, having laughed, spoke to Girijā.
