Then the Blessed Maheśa, together with Girijā, attained supreme joy through her gentle smile; yet the sole kinsman of the world and the unique lord of the universe, his voice faltering with love, said nothing at all.
Lomaśa said: Having placed Kumāra upon his own lap, the powerful Bharga, Rudra, the Lord of the Universe, then spoke to the gods, including Indra.
"O gods, let it be told what task must now be performed for me by Kumāra. Then they all together spoke regarding the god Paśupati: || 2 ||
O All-pervading Lord, fear has arisen from Tāraka for all the worlds; you are the protector and the master of the worlds, therefore let protection be provided.
"O Lord, Tāraka shall be slain by the Kumāra this very day; therefore, we shall set out this very day, prepared to slay Tāraka."
Thinking "so be it," those gods then suddenly went forth, placing Kārttikeya—the very son of Śaṅkara—at their head.
Having heard of the exertion of the gods, all of them, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, suddenly assembled; and the exceedingly powerful Tāraka also [heard of it].
Accompanied by a vast army, he marched forth to fight against the gods; the great force of Tāraka was seen by the deities as it approached.
Then a voice from the sky spoke, consoling them: "Placing the son of Śaṅkara at your head, you have all been established."
Having conquered the Daityas in battle, you shall indeed be victorious.
Having heard the speech of the sky-farer, all the gods became eager; placing Kumāra at their head, they were all freed from fear.
As soon as the gods, desiring battle, had all assembled for the purpose of choosing the son of Mṛtyu, who was difficult to overcome, as their bridegroom— 11.
Formerly impelled by Brahmā, she resorted to supreme austerity; by virtue of that great penance, the daughter of Mṛtyu, named Senā, who was uniquely beautiful, then arrived before Kumāra.
Seeing her, they all spoke to the god Paśupati: "Indeed, this exceedingly beautiful woman has come for the sake of this youth. (13)
And at the word of Brahmā, Kumāra was then chosen; thus Kumāra, the son of Śaṅkara, became the commander-in-chief.
Then conchs, kettledrums, tabors, ānakas, and gomukhas, as well as dundubhis and mṛdaṅgas of great sound, resounded. || 15 ||
The vault of the sky was filled by that great sound; then Gaurī, Gaṅgā, and the Kṛttikā mothers spoke to one another, saying, "He is my son! He is mine! (16)
Thus, having fallen into dispute, all of them, Mātṛkā and the others, were restrained by Nārada with the words, "Do not act out of folly. (17)
Born from Śaṅkara upon Pārvatī for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, all the Kṛttikās then became silent along with the Mothers.
Then Guha said to all those wives of the sages and the Kṛttikās: "Taking refuge in the lunar mansions, you must remain here for a long time. (19)
Likewise, that host of Mothers was established in heaven by that Lord; and Kārttikeya, filled with haste, took the daughter of Mṛtyu.
The Blessed Lord Kumāra, the son of Śaṅkara, said to Indra: "Go to heaven together with the gods and rule the kingdom perpetually."
Indra said to Kumāra: "Indeed, we have all been tormented by Tāraka; driven from heaven, we have fled in the ten directions."

"Why do you ask us, O illustrious one, who have fallen from our station? When he was addressed thus by the wielder of the thunderbolt, the son of Śaṅkara then laughed and granted fearlessness to Indra, saying, "Do not fear."
While he was speaking thus, Rudra, the great-souled lord of Śaṅkara, departed for Kailāsa along with Pārvatī and his attendants.
The great Daitya arrived, surrounded by the Daitya armies; then the drums of war resounded, terrifying as the dissolution of the world.
Battle-hardened trumpets, wonderful ḍiṇḍimas, gomukhas, donkey-horns, and numerous kāhalas [resounded]. || 26 ||
Various musical instruments were sounded during that assembly of Daityas, while the heroes were roaring together with Tāraka.
Nārada spoke these words to Tāraka, the thorn of the gods.

Nārada said: "O best of Asuras, in former times an effort was made by the gods for the sake of your destruction; there is no doubt about this. And what has been spoken by me to you alone shall not be otherwise."
And this prince has been brought forth for the sake of Śarva and for your own sake; knowing this, O mighty-armed one, exert yourself with a concentrated mind. (30)
Then, having heard what was spoken by Nārada, the intelligent Tāraka, as if laughing, spoke these words: "Go you to Purandara. (31)
O great sage, speak my words quickly and exactly as they are: you desire to fight with me while placing the prince at the forefront. || 32 ||
Relying upon a state of delusion, you desire to act otherwise; you do so by taking recourse to a single man named Mucukunda alone. (33)
By the power of that [merit], you reside in Amarāvatī and not otherwise; relying upon the strength of Kaumāra, you stand before me.
"I shall surely slay you along with the dull-witted world-protectors; speak thus to the Lord of the Gods, O celestial sage, and do not say otherwise. (35)
Thinking "so be it," the blessed and wise Nārada went to the gods, headed by Śakra; he related everything that had been said by the lord of the Asuras, including the mockery, exactly as it was.
Nārada said: "O gods, listen to my words; let it not be otherwise. Pay heed to that which has been spoken by Tāraka along with his followers. (37)
Tāraka said: "O fool, I shall kill you; my word shall not be otherwise."
Having approached Mucukunda and being honored by the world-protectors, [Indra said: "I shall not fight with you, O timid one; having become a god, I have taken refuge among men. (39)
Having heard his words, all the gods, including Indra, placed the Kumāra and Nārada, the best of sages, at their head and spoke. (40)
O celestial sage, you surely know the strength and weakness of the prince; how is it that, being ignorant, you spoke such words in my presence? (41)
Laughing, Nārada spoke these words in his presence: "I too uttered a mocking word regarding Tāraka. (42)
"Know, O all you immortals, O gods, that Kumāra shall be victorious; my word in this matter shall come to pass—no hesitation should be entertained here. (43)
Having heard the words of Nārada, all the gods were filled with joy; they rose up simultaneously, desiring to fight Tāraka.
Having placed the prince upon an elephant, the Lord of the Gods indeed went at the head, surrounded by a great army of deities and the guardians of the world.
Then kettledrums resounded, along with many bherīs and tūryas; likewise, there were the sounds of lutes, flutes, and mṛdaṅgas, as well as the voices of the gandharvas.

Having given the elephant to Mahendra, the prince ascended a vehicle that was covered with many jewels, endowed with various wonders, variegated with diverse paintings, very large, and likewise filled with marvels.

Then, having ascended the celestial chariot, that illustrious son of Śaṅkara, accompanied by all his hosts and endowed with supreme splendor, shone forth as a great being while being fanned with lustrous yak-tail whisks.

Then he held over the head of the prince a parasol made of precious gems, possessing the luster of great jewels, adorned with many ornaments, and beautifully graced by rays like those of the moon. (49)
Then all the gods, led by Indra, having assembled and surrounded by their respective armies, were of great strength and desirous of fighting.
Yama was there with his own attendants and the Maruts; Varuṇa with the waters; Kubera with the Guhyakas; Īśa with the Pramathas; and Nairṛta with the diseases. || 51 ||

Thus, all eight of those world-protectors, desiring to fight, united together solely for the purpose of slaying Tāraka; they placed at their head the son of Śaṅkara, the commander-in-chief, who is honored by the universe and the most excellent among the knowers of the Self.
Thus, desiring to fight, they all descended to the earth and took their positions within the sacred enclosure (antarvedī), situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers.
And from the netherworld (pātāla) arrived the followers of Tāraka; endowed with great strength and forces, they moved about, desiring to slay the gods in battle.
For Tāraka arrived, resplendent in his celestial chariot, that being of great luster with a parasol held over his head.
Being fanned with chowries, the king of the Daityas himself shone resplendent.
Thus, at that time, the gods and the Daityas stood within the sacrificial enclosure (antarvedi), having each formed their respective battle arrays there with a great army.
Having placed the elephants on one side, as well as various horses, and diverse chariots endowed with many jewels; 58.
There were many foot-soldiers there, adorned with spears, tridents, and battle-axes, as well as swords, javelins, iron arrows, nooses, and mallets.
Those two armies of the gods and the Daityas shone against one another; desiring then to slay each other, they were indeed being praised by their kinsmen.

Lomaśa said: Then those two armies—the gods and the enemies of the immortals—filled with many wonders and endowed with the fourfold forces, shone as they roared at one another like clouds at the onset of the rainy season.
In the meantime, all the gods and asuras of great strength, leaping at one another, then engaged in combat.
Indeed, a most tumultuous battle took place, crowded with gods and daityas; in an instant, the entire field became marked with headless trunks and severed heads.
There, they fell upon the ground by the hundreds and thousands; the arms of some were severed by the most terrible blows of swords.
For Mucukunda is powerful in the three worlds, possessing immeasurable valor.
Then Tāraka was struck in the chest with all his might by the sword of the wise Mucukunda; and having endured that blow, he spoke these words while laughing.
"O fool, what have you done today by using force? Out of shame, I do not wish to fight with a mere mortal. (7)
Having heard the words of Tāraka, Mucukunda replied: "O Lord of Daityas, you have been slain by me; it cannot be otherwise."
"Having seen my sword-stroke, you do not remain before me; I shall slay you—behold my valor, O King of Daityas! Stand firm! (9)
Having spoken thus, the heroic and mighty Mucukunda struck him with his sword; at that moment, he was struck by a spear and the son of Māndhātṛ fell there upon the field of battle.
Having fallen, the slayer of enemy heroes rose up at that very moment.

Then that son of Māndhātṛ, the sole conqueror of the world and possessed of exceedingly great strength, having taken up his bow and raised the Brahmāstra, prepared to slay Tāraka, the lord of the Daityas. || 12 ||
Desirous of fighting Tāraka, that great and powerful son of Brahmā, Nārada, filled with rage and with eyes wide open, then spoke thus to Mucukunda, the hero among men.
Tāraka cannot be slain by a human; therefore, do not release this great weapon.
Having heard those words of the celestial sage Nārada, Mucukunda said this: "Who will be his slayer? (15)
Then the highly effulgent Nārada, possessed of divine vision, said: "The Kumāra shall indeed slay him; this Kumāra is the son of Śiva. (16)
Therefore, you all must stand firm with one accord against those who fight; and you, O high-minded Mucukunda, remain standing at the front.
Having heard those enchanting and auspicious words uttered by that one of great splendor, all the gods became intent on peace through that best of men, effortlessly.
Then the kettledrums resounded and the conchs were blown with firm resolve, accompanied by various musical instruments played by both gods and demons.
There, the asuras roared, making an effort against the gods; meanwhile, the heroic Vīrabhadra, born from the wrath of Śiva, was filled with fury.
Having approached the exceedingly powerful Tāraka with many hosts, and having likewise placed Mucukunda and the gods behind him, [he spoke].
Then all those Pramathas, led by Kumāraka, as well as the hosts headed by Vīrabhadra, fought there in that battle.
In that battle, during the conflict between the gods and the asuras, they struck one another with tridents, spears, nooses, swords, axes, and sharp-edged spears.
Struck violently by Vīrabhadra with his trident, Tāraka suddenly fell there, overwhelmed for a moment by unconsciousness.
And rising after a moment, Tāraka, the bull among the Daityas, having regained consciousness and filled with strength, struck Vīrabhadra.
Then that powerful Vīrabhadra, of great splendor and a follower of Śiva, struck Tāraka with his formidable trident.
Thus fighting, those two struck one another; a most tumultuous duel broke out between those two great-souled ones. (27)
Then, in that very battle, the gods became spectators; likewise, their kettledrums, clay drums, tabors, cymbals, and gomukhas [resounded]. (28)
Likewise, the three worlds were pervaded by the sound of the ḍamaru; by that great noise, the two of great strength continued to fight.
Exceedingly enraged and mangled by blows, the two shone as they attacked one another like the planets Mercury and Mars.
Then Nārada announced the slaying of Vīrabhadra; however, those words did not please Vīrabhadra at all.
Indeed, regarding the slaying of Tāraka, as was said by Nārada: "As is Rudra, so too is that mighty Vīrabhadra. (32)
Fighting in this manner, those two struck each other, vying with one another and roaring like two lions.
Thus, as those two were fighting on the earth at that time against the high-souled one, the best among the wise, Vīrabhadra was indeed restrained by Nārada with many words.
Having thus heard those words issuing from the mouth of Nārada, Vīrabhadra, overcome with rage, replied to Nārada.

"I shall slay Tāraka; behold my prowess today! Those heroes who bring their master into the assembly of battle are indeed sinful and most unrighteous when they reflect thus upon having entered the fray. (36)
They should be known as cowards and must never be spoken to; you do not understand, O celestial sage, the counter-measures of warriors.
Having cast death behind them, those who remain free from agony on the field of battle, their limbs pierced by weapons and missiles, are praised; of this there is no doubt. (38)
Having spoken thus, the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra addressed the gods: "May the gods, led by Indra, listen to my words. (39)
Today I shall make the earth starless; of this there is no doubt.
Then, taking up a trident, he fought with Tāraka and with many others mounted on bulls who bore excellent tridents.
Those hosts, with matted hair and marked by the bull, were fierce strikers; possessing the prowess of Vīrabhadra, they placed Vīrabhadra at their head.
All of them bear tridents; all are adorned with serpents as ornaments; all have the moon as their crest-jewel and are graced by masses of matted hair.
Blue-throated, ten-armed, possessing five faces and three eyes, they were all enveloped by umbrellas and chowries, and all had exceedingly fierce arms.
Placing Vīrabhadra at their head, all those who possessed the prowess of Hara then fought against the Daityas, who subsisted upon the life-force of the Tāka Asura.

Again and again, those asuras were defeated by those hosts and turned their backs in retreat; at that time, there occurred a most terrifying and intense battle between them and the foremost of the Daityas.
Unable to endure this, those hosts, skilled in supreme weapons, then became victorious. Defeated by the hosts, those asuras, being distressed, reported that defeat to Tāraka. || 47 ||
Having bent his bow, Tāraka, desiring to fight, entered the army; just as a great fish enters the ocean, so did that high-souled chief of the Daityas. 48.

Accompanied by his hosts, that exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra then fought against all the gods headed by Indra, as well as the Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Guhyakas; indeed, having entered a state of extreme fury, that mighty one crushed them all.
Then there occurred a great battle, crowded with gods and dānavas, causing a massive clash among the gods, dānavas, and yakṣas.
Likewise, trumpeting bulls struck down horses along with their riders; and elephants, together with their riders, struck down chariots along with their charioteers. || 51 ||
Mounted upon bulls and accompanied by their chariots, they all tore asunder and crushed those asuras. || 52 ||
At that time, many who were refined fell to the earth in destruction, and some were slain; indeed, some entered the subterranean realm (rasātala), and likewise many fled.
And some sought refuge with the servants who follow Rudra. Seeing his army thus destroyed, Tāraka, the protector of the Asuras, overcome with rage, advanced to slay the hosts of gods.
Having created ten thousand arms, Tāraka, the king of the Daityas, mounted a lion and suddenly struck them down in battle.
Some bulls were torn apart by the armored lion, and likewise, many of the Gaṇas were slain by Tāraka himself.
Thus was it accomplished then by that high-souled Tāraka; indeed, the great Tāraka was invincible to all the gods.
Then that mighty-armed one was born, the destroyer of the three worlds; the followers of Tāraka were invincible and exceedingly powerful.
Mounted on great [beasts], armored, and formidable, those strikers seized all the Gaṇas; even the lions and bulls were slain by them. || 59 ||
While their hosts were thus being struck down on the field of battle, Viṣṇu laughed and spoke to Kumāra, the beloved of Śiva.
Viṣṇu said: "O son of the Kṛttikās, there is no other slayer of this sinner except you; therefore, O mighty-armed one, you must indeed carry out my word."
O son of Śiva, you have been born for the sake of slaying Tāraka; therefore, the destruction of Tāraka must be accomplished by you alone.
Having heard that, the great Lord, the son of Pārvatī, became enraged and spoke these fitting words to Viṣṇu with a smile.
"I am observing the wonderful battle of these great-souled ones correctly; however, O Viṣṇu, I am ignorant in discerning what ought and ought not to be done."
"I do not know in any way who are ours and who are the others; for what purpose indeed are they fighting, intent on slaying one another? (65)
Having heard the words of the prince, Nārada spoke these words: || 66 ||
Nārada said: "O mighty-armed one, you are a youth born from a portion of Śaṅkara; you are the protector and lord of the worlds, and the supreme refuge of the gods. (67)
O hero, in former times Tāraka performed most terrible ascetic penance, by which he conquered the gods and likewise won over heaven.
By that fierce austerity, he attained invincibility; by this [austerity] alone, even Indra and the guardians of the world were conquered.
Indeed, the entire three worlds have been conquered by this very evil-souled one; therefore, you must slay Tāraka, that sinful man.
"O Lord, you must today indeed bring about the welfare of all. Having heard Nārada’s words, the Great Kumāra, smiling, descended from his celestial chariot and became a supreme pedestrian.
Then, as he was running about on his feet, this son of Śiva, in the form of a youth, seized by the hand that great and powerful spear, which was as radiant as a massive meteor.
Seeing him approaching—exceedingly fierce, of unmanifest form, and the foremost among the strong—the Daitya spoke to that best of gods: "This is Kumāra, the slayer of his enemies. (73)
Indeed, I alone, as a hero, shall fight with him; I alone shall fight all the heroes. I shall instantly strike down all the hosts, as well as the Maheśvaras and the world-protectors.
Having spoken thus, the exceedingly powerful one set out to fight, directing his course toward Kumāra; Tāraka seized a most wonderful spear and uttered these words. (75)
Tāraka said: "How is it that you have placed Kumāra before me today? You gods are truly shameless, you for whom Purandara is king!"
Whatever karma was performed by him in the past, all of that is indeed known; those who were asleep, those tormented in the womb, and those situated within the belly have been cast down.
By Kaśyapa’s own son, the asura Bahurūpa was slain; the heroic Namuci was slain, and likewise Vṛtra was slain. (78)
"This Lord Indra, the slayer of Bala, desires to kill the prince; O gods, this prince has been killed by me today, without a doubt. (79)
"O high-minded Vīrabhadra, O hero skilled in battle, many Brahmins were indeed slain by you previously at Dakṣa’s sacrifice; today, O hero, I shall show you the fruit of that deed in combat. (80)
Having spoken thus, that great-souled lord of the Daityas, Vīravara, he alone—Tāraka, the most eminent among those skilled in battle—then seized a most wonderful spear.
Thus overcome by supreme rage and surrounded by the lords of the asuras, the powerful Tāraka, victorious in battle, then set his mind upon slaying him in combat. (82)
Lomaśa said: As Tāraka was approaching, leaping with great vigor, Indra, the best among the wise, struck him with his thunderbolt.
By that blow of the thunderbolt, Tāraka was rendered unconscious; though he fell, he rose again and struck the elephant with a spear.
Indeed, you caused Purandara, who was mounted upon his elephant, to fall to the ground; and when Purandara had fallen, there was a great cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
O Lord, hear also what was done there by Tāraka: having seized the thunderbolt from his hand, he stepped upon the fallen [Indra] with his foot. || 4 ||
Beholding the Lord of the Gods struck down, Tāraka, the destroyer of enemies, struck Purandara with a mighty blow of his thunderbolt.
Then, raising his trident, the mighty Vīrabhadra, filled with rage, struck Tāraka—the Daitya who was protecting Purandara—with that trident of great luster.
Struck by the blow of the trident, he fell to the surface of the earth; yet even though fallen, the immensely powerful Tāraka rose up once more.
Then he struck Vīrabhadra in the chest with supreme power; indeed, Vīrabhadra fell from the blow of that power.
The gods along with their retinues, as well as the gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas, cried out again and again with a great wailing of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).

Then that mighty Vīrabhadra, the slayer of enemies, suddenly arose; raising his trident, which flashed like lightning and blazed incessantly with radiance, illuminating the canopy of the quarters with its own luster and possessing the splendor of the sun, the moon, fire, and the host of stars.
Then, as the one of great strength desired to destroy him with his trident, he was restrained by Kumāra: "Do not kill him, O high-minded one! (11)
And the immensely powerful Kārttikeya, possessed of great splendor, roared aloud.
Then, hailed with cries of "Victory! by the beings stationed in the sky, the hero, equipped with his supreme power, prepared to slay Tāraka.
There, a battle with Tāraka’s son Kumāra broke out; it was unbearable, most terrible, and struck fear into all living beings.
Those two heroes, with spears in their hands, fought each other; though their hands were pierced by the spears, they remained possessed of great courage.
Deceiving one another like two lions of great strength, they resorted to the gait of a bard as well as the movement of a bird in the sky.
Resorting to their respective systems of thought—the Pārvata and the Māta—they struck each other with their powers; by means of these doctrines, the two great heroes waged an excellent battle.
Acting as mutual supporters and possessing great strength and prowess, those two experts in combat struck each other with streams of spears in the battle.
On the head, the throat, as well as on the arms, the knees, the hips, the chest, the breast, and the back, they struck one another.
Then, as those two of great strength fought, desiring to slay one another, all the gods, Gandharvas, and Guhyakas became mere spectators.
They all said to one another, "Who will be victorious in this battle? Then a voice from the sky spoke, consoling them indeed: ||| 21 ||
"O gods, this Kumāra shall indeed slay Tāraka today; let no grief be felt by any of you, O gods, and remain happily in heaven."
Then, having heard that voice uttered in the sky, Kumāra, surrounded by the Pramathas, desired to slay Tāraka, the lord of the Daityas, who was of fierce form.
With that spear, the mighty-armed Kumāra, who was exceedingly powerful, struck Tāraka, the best of the asuras, in the middle of his chest.
Perceiving that blow as ineffective, Tāraka, the bull among the Daityas, became enraged and struck Kumāra with his own spear.
By that blow from the spear, the son of Śaṅkara fell unconscious; after a moment, he regained consciousness while being praised by the great sages.
Just like a lion intoxicated with pride and desiring to kill, so too did the powerful Kumāra strike the Daitya Tāraka.
Thus, the prince and Tāraka, both exceedingly enraged and intent on combat with spears, fought with one another.
Driven by a mutual desire for victory, those two ascetics, possessing wonderful forms, fought with each other until their practice reached its ultimate limit.
With torrents and with sharp edges, well-employed, they struck each other; all the gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras were intent on the sight. (30)
Struck by supreme amazement, they indeed said nothing to him; at that time, the wind did not blow, and the sun became lusterless.
Then the Himalaya, Meru, Śvetakūṭa, and Dardura; Malaya, the great mountain Mahāśaila, Maināka, and the Vindhya mountain. || 32 ||
The two great mountains Lokāloka, the Mānasottara mountain, Kailāsa, Mandara, Mālya, and Gandhamādana; || 33 ||
Mount Udaya, Mahendra, and likewise the great Mount Asta; || 34 ||
These and many other mountains of great splendor, afflicted by affection and desiring to protect Kumāra, then arrived. || 35 ||
Then, seeing all those mountains terrified with fear, the son of Śaṅkara, the offspring of the Mountain-Daughter, spoke to them in order to awaken their understanding.
The prince said: "Do not grieve, O illustrious ones; let no anxiety be felt, O mountains. Today I shall slay this most wicked one while everyone here looks on. (37)
Having thus comforted those mountains together with the hosts of gods, the wise Kumāra, beloved of Hari, bowed his mind to Śambhu and prostrated before his own mother.
Then Kārttikeya severed the head of his enemy with his spear; that head of Tāraka fell upon the earth at that very moment. Thus did the great lord Kārttikeya attain victory. (39)
The hosts of gods, the ṛṣis, the guhyakas, the birds, the kinnaras, the cāraṇas, the serpents, and likewise the throngs of apsarases beheld him.
Overcome with great joy, the Vidyādharīs praised that youth; then the dancers danced and the singers sang. (41)
Seeing him thus victorious, everyone was filled with joy; then, approaching out of delight, they placed their son upon their own laps.
Having embraced him firmly, Girijā was indeed delighted; she then placed the boy, who possessed the splendor of the sun, upon her own lap.
Then the slender-limbed Pārvatī, with her beautiful eyes, caressed him; Śambhu, honored by the sages, was then accompanied by Pārvatī.
Seated upon a noble throne, the virtuous and measured-speeched lady shone brightly while being praised by sages, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Pannagas.
Then Pārvatī was consecrated with the lustration rite (nīrājana) by the gods together with Śambhu; thereafter, the virtuous lady shone resplendent along with Kumāra.
Then the Himalaya, having arrived surrounded by his sons as well as by mountains such as Meru and others, became supreme while being praised. || 47 ||

Then all the hosts of gods, led by Indra and accompanied by the sages, rained down a great shower of flowers upon him of immeasurable splendor; placing Kumāra at their head, they became intent on performing the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
He was extensively praised with the sounds of song and instrumental music, and with the voice of the Veda by the best among those who know the Vedas through various hymns.
The divine life-story named Kumāravijaya is most wonderful; it removes all sins and bestows all desires upon men. || 50 ||

Those who, being pure and endowed with immeasurable fortune, recite this noble majesty of Kumāra’s prowess—which bestows bliss and accomplishes the goals of men—attain a state that is infinite in form, free from old age, and immortal. (51)
Whoever reads or even hears this life-story of the high-souled Kumāra, known as the Tāraka episode, is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Victory Festival of Svāmikārttikeya Following the Slaying of the Asura Tāraka," in the Śiva-śāstra of the Kedāra-khaṇḍa, within the first section, the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 30 ||
Śaunaka said: O Brahmin, after that great-souled Kumāra had slain Tāraka in battle, what did he do next? You ought to tell me all of that in full.
For this prince is indeed another Śambhu, by whom all this is pervaded; Śambhu, gratified by his ascetic penance, bestows the supreme state.

Indeed, the sight of the Kumāra is always fruitful for men immediately; for even those who are sinful, most unrighteous, or even outcaste dog-cookers (śvapacas), O Lomaśa, have their sins shaken off by the mere sight of him—of this there is no doubt.
Having heard the words of Śaunaka, the highly wise disciple of Vyāsa then related the life-story of the high-souled Kumāra.
Lomaśa said: O best of the twice-born, Kumāra then achieved victory over that Tāraka, who was invincible to the gods in battle and could not be slain by them.
For the greatness of the Kumāra is indeed proclaimed in all the scriptures—by the Vedas, by one's own Agamas, and likewise by the Purāṇas.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, this Kumāra, who is thus constituted by the Upaniṣads and the two Mīmāṃsās, is impossible to describe fully.
For the King of the Ancestors himself, having heard of the protector of this world—who purifies the entire universe by his mere sight—[approached him].

Placing Brahmā and Viṣṇu, along with Indra, at his head, he went with great haste to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world; having become purified, the Lord of the Southern Quarter himself offered praise.
Homage to the divine Bharga, the lord of the gods; homage to Rudra, the conqueror of death, the sovereign, the one with matted hair. 10.
Salutations indeed to the blue-throated Śarva, whose form consists of the parts of the sky; salutations to Time, the Lord of Time, who is the very embodiment of Time.
Being praised by Yama, the Lord, the Sovereign, said: "For what purpose have you come? Tell us all of that."
Yama said: "Listen, O Lord of the gods of gods, you who are skilled in speech; O Śaṅkara, you have attained satisfaction through this supreme austerity alone. (13)
By supreme action alone, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, attains satisfaction; of this there is no doubt, for he is always the lord of boons.
Likewise, the Lord Viṣṇu, the eternal one who is to be known through the Vedas, was indeed gratified by numerous sacrifices as well as by fasts and vows.
He bestows only that disposition by which all men may attain liberation; this is my teaching, for there is no other word than mine. (16)
When pleased, the Sun indeed bestows enjoyment as well as the riches of heaven and other realms; through salutation, he grants health in this world, and not otherwise. (17)

O Śambhu, Gaṇeśa, the Great God, will indeed ensure that there is no obstacle through the repetition of mantras and by means of water for honor, water for the feet, sandalwood paste, and so forth. (18)
Likewise, O Śaṅkara, all the other world-protectors bestow fruits according to their power when they are well-pleased by sacrifices, Vedic study, gifts, and other such acts. (19)
A great wonder has arisen here for all living beings; indeed, your son has opened the gate of heaven.
O Mahādeva, by the mere sight of the Kumāra, all men—even those who are sinners—become inhabitants of heaven; of this there is no doubt. (21)
"O Lord, what can be done by me regarding the determination of what ought and ought not to be done, for those who are truthful in character, peaceful, generous, and free from all constraints? (22)

They were masters of their senses, free from greed, and devoid of lust and passion; they were performers of sacrifices, devoted to righteousness, and had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
O Śambhu, whatever destination all those who have performed virtuous deeds attain, even the lowest of outcastes (śvapacas) shall reach that same destination merely by seeing [you].
And for the youth, O Lord of Gods, whose deeds are of great wonder, and for Śiva, on the full moon day of Kārttika when it is joined with the constellation Kṛttikā.
Upon seeing the son of Śiva, they indeed go to my own abode together with their many millions of kinsmen, having been completely liberated.
"By the mere sight of the Prince, even all outcastes (śvapacas) indeed attain a good state with great speed; what, then, can I do now? (27)
Having heard the words of Yama, Śaṅkara spoke these words: || 28 ||
Śaṅkara said: O Dharma, those people of meritorious deeds whose sins have come to an end—pure-mindedness dwells in their minds.
Indeed, for the sake of visiting the seven sacred fords and beholding the virtuous here, a great longing arises in them due to their past actions. (30)
O Yama, at the end of many births, a disposition toward me persists in living beings through the practice of their previous lives and by means of their entire being.
Therefore, all those whose disposition follows [the path] are doers of good deeds; one should not feel any astonishment toward those whose nature has persisted through birth after birth.

Even women, children, Śūdras, and the lowest outcasts such as Śvapacas—who, by the power of impressions from previous births, abide in sinful wombs—nevertheless become pure human beings through dharma. (33)

Likewise, all beings exist with a pure mind, and they become knowers of those [objects] in all their respective domains; all the gods, such as Indra and the world-protectors, exist by virtue of their past conduct and former deeds.
For all these hosts of beings have been born; indeed, these are the sages and these are the deities.
You should not feel any astonishment, nor indeed should the prince; O Dharmarāja, listen to me regarding the sight of the prince. (36)
Speech joined with action bestows fruit upon all; all sacred fords, sacrifices, and various kinds of gifts must be performed for the sake of purifying the mind—of this there is no doubt. (37)
For the Self is meditated upon by the mind, and by the self one meditates on the Self alone; indeed, the Self abides within all living beings as "I. (38)
"I am always endowed with being, established in the Self, and eternal; I tell you this truth regarding all things moving and unmoving. (39)

Transcending dualities, free from conceptual construction, truly established in his own nature, eternal, ever-united [with reality], and effortless; indeed, immovable amidst the proclamations of various mental constructs, he is beyond the reach of speech, the infinite one who is both consciousness and the object of consciousness. 40.
Having forgotten this very Self, which is characterized solely by pure consciousness, all the multitudes of living beings are seen as transmigrating souls.
I, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—these three are the performers of the qualities; we are the agents of creation, preservation, and destruction, and it cannot be otherwise. (42)
"Driven by action alone, which is veiled by the ego-sense, you all—gods, humans, birds, and so forth—have been brought into being. (43)
Cattle and other such beings, as well as these many others, are indeed distinct; they are individually appropriate and possessed of qualities within the cycle of worldly existence.
We have all fallen into a mirage and are ensnared by illusion; though we are wise and learned, we consider ourselves to be scholars. (45)
Mutually defaming one another, those wicked people are devoted to false speech.

They are possessed of the three qualities (guṇas), endowed with worldly existence, ignorant of reality, and full of passion; they are joined with desire, anger, fear, hatred, pride, and envy. || 47 ||
For those who revile one another are ignorant of reality and are outward-looking; therefore, having understood this, [know that] untruth arises from the differentiation of the qualities (guṇas).
And when the object is a reality beyond qualities, there is the vision of the single ultimate truth. || 49 ||
Listen to that supreme Vāma, wherein indeed duality becomes non-duality, wherein passion becomes dispassion, and wherein anger indeed turns into non-anger. (50)
Sound does not illuminate that [Brahman], because it is produced, just like a jar; for sound is a property (dharma) whose primary function is directed toward worldly activity. || 51 ||
Where both worldly engagement and withdrawal, as well as all dualities whatsoever, go to their dissolution—that alone is considered the eternal state.

It is continuous, devoid of qualities, pure consciousness alone, stainless, unmanifest, and effortless; it is mere existence, accessible through knowledge, self-established, self-luminous, brilliantly radiant, and attainable through awakening.

Those who know wisdom speak of this knowledge; they perceive it as the self of all. Having realized that which transcends all and is accessible through wisdom, they move about established in themselves with equanimity.

Having transcended saṃsāra—which is rooted in beginninglessness, composed of illusion, and difficult to discern through illusion—they abandon illusion; free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of passion, those leaders of the departed go to the state beyond conceptual construction.
Transmigration has its root in conceptual construction; indeed, conceptual construction is like nectar. Those by whom conceptual construction has been abandoned go to the supreme goal.
The cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the cognition of a rope in a snake, and the cognition of water in a mirage are false; they are indeed false and not otherwise.
Perfection is the state of acting according to one's own will, for dependence is indeed false. One who is bound is called dependent; one who is liberated possesses the realization of independence.
For when the one Self has been realized, one becomes free from the sense of "mine" and free from all constraints; how then can there be bondage for them? It is just like a flower in the sky.
This protection is indeed like the horn of a hare, and so too is this cycle of existence (saṃsāra). What is the use of much speech that is truly fruitless? 60.
Having cast off the sense of "mine-ness" and desiring to attain the supreme state, they are indeed the wise ones—possessing knowledge, free from passion, and having conquered their senses. (61)
Those by whom the sense of "mine" has been abandoned, and by whom greed and anger have been cast out—being free from desire and wrath—they go to the supreme abode.
As long as desire and greed persist, and as long as passion and hatred remain established, those who understand only the mere sound [of the teachings] do not attain that perfection.
Yama said: "From sound, sound proceeds, and knowledge itself is indeed soundless. O Lord, how then has the impermanence of sound been declared by you? (64)
The syllable is indeed the supreme Brahman, for sound is essentially composed of vowels; therefore, it has been heard in the Vedas that sound was proclaimed by you as the "Observer."
O Śambhu, tell me how everything that is to be established—regarding the determination of what ought and ought not to be done—can be expressed by anything at all without words. (66)
Śaṅkara said: Listen attentively to these words endowed with the highest truth, by the mere hearing of which nothing remains to be known.
All sages who proclaim knowledge are free from defilement; they abide in the practice of knowledge, for those who know knowledge understand what knowledge truly is.

Having known knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge, it is fully proclaimed: how is it to be known, by what means is it to be known, and what is intended to be said regarding it? (69)
I shall explain all this to you in brief; understand it from me: for that which is one is seen as manifold through the conception of difference.
O Yama, just as the earth appears to whirl to one who suffers from vertigo, so too does the Self appear manifold through the intellect's perception of duality.
Therefore, having reflected upon it, it should be known through hearing (śravaṇa) alone; it should be contemplated through proper application, especially by means of reflection (manana). || 72 ||
Having extracted the self from the self, one is happily liberated from bondage; all this world, including the moving and the unmoving, is but a net of illusion.
This great cycle of worldly existence is composed of illusion and characterized by the sense of "mine-ness"; by casting aside this sense of "mine-ness," one is happily liberated from bondage. (74)
Who am I? Who are you? And from where have others come, who rely upon the Great Illusion? This phenomenal world is as useless as the fleshy nipple on the neck of a goat.
"This is fruitless, devoid of appearance, and substanceless—a mere display of smoke. Therefore, O Yama, remember the Self with every effort! (76)
Lomaśa said: Thus urged by that Śambhu, Yama himself, the king of the departed, having become enlightened, then became manifest as the Self.
For he was the teacher of all beings according to their respective actions; he became the majestic lord of men and all creatures, remaining ever composed.
The sages said: "O sirs, after Tāraka had been slain in battle by the high-souled Kumāra, what great wonder was performed thereafter? Please tell us."
Sūta said: When the Daitya Tāraka had been slain, the mountains headed by Himavat approached Kārttikeya and praised him with beautiful words.

The mountains said: "Salutations to you whose form is auspicious; salutations to you, the source of universal welfare! O friend of the universe, let there be salutations to you; salutations to you, the creator of the universe! (81)
By the mere sight of you, even the lowest outcastes have been made most excellent; we bow to you, the kinsman of the world, for we have come to you for refuge. || 82 ||
Salutations to you, son of Pārvatī; salutations to you, son of Śaṅkara. Salutations to you, son of the Kṛttikās; salutations to you, O Agnibhūta.

Homage be to you, who are well-worshipped by the best of gods; homage be to you, the most excellent among those who possess knowledge. Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious, O refuge, you who are skilled in destroying all afflictions.
Thus praised by the mountains, Kārttikeya, the son of Umā, with a highly pleased soul, was eager to grant a boon to those mountains.
Kārttikeya said: "O you excellent mountains, listen now to my words; you shall be served by both those engaged in ritual action and those possessed of knowledge. (86)
For these stones, when attended with effort, abide in you alone; by my word, may they purify the universe—of this there is no doubt. (87)
The sacred sites shall belong to the mountains, and not otherwise; there shall be divine abodes of Śiva and divine sanctuaries.
O mountains, by my word, there will undoubtedly be various, beautiful, and great solstices (ayanas). || 89 ||
This Himavat, the best of mountains, who is my maternal grandfather, shall indeed become a highly blessed bestower of fruits upon ascetics today.
And this Meru, the king of mountains, shall indeed be the support; as well as Lokāloka, the best of mountains, and the highly renowned Udayādri.
For the Blessed One will indeed exist in the form of a *liṅga*, and not otherwise; for Śrīśaila, Maheṃdra, and likewise the Sahya mountain, [shall be so]. (92)
Mālyavat, Malaya, Vindhya, as well as that Gandhamādana; Śvetakūṭa, Trikūṭa, and likewise the mountain Dardura. || 93 ||
These and many other mountains shall take the form of lingas; by my word, they will indeed be the destroyers of sin.
Thus Śaṅkara’s son granted boons to those mountains; then Nandin spoke, honoring all the scriptures.
Nandi said: "O Lord, since these mountains have been fashioned by you in the very form of lingas as abodes of Śiva, how might they be worthy of worship by all the deities at all times? (96)
The youth said: "The Liṅga should be known as the abode of Śiva, the trident-bearing God of gods, by all men and deities, beginning with Brahmā, who are unwearied. (97)
Sapphire, pearl, coral, lapis lazuli, moonstone, agate, ruby, emerald, and likewise gold.
Lingas made of silver, copper, iron, and likewise those made of lead, as well as those consisting of precious gems and minerals, have thus been described to you. (99)
These sacred substances alone are worthy of worship and bestow all desires; yet among all of them, the saffron of Kāśmīra is indeed preeminent.
It bestows everything pertaining to this world and the next upon the one who performs the worship. || 101 ||
Nandi said: "O you of excellent vows, tell me all of this: how is it that even among all liṅgas, the Bāṇaliṅga has been described by you as the most supreme and worthy of worship?"
The youth said: "Those stones which are indeed seen in the midst of the waters of the Revā, by the grace of Śiva they shall take the form of liṅgas, and not otherwise. (103)
They should be made with smooth bases and placed upon the pedestal; indeed, they must be worshipped with great effort by one who possesses the Śiva-initiation.
One should worship Śiva with the *piṇḍī*, according to the scripture and the prescribed rite; for the Lord of the World is the bestower of boons upon the worshipper, and not otherwise. (105)

He in whose mouth the five-syllabled mantra always resides has the cessation of mental activity through constant contemplation of Śiva; he maintains equanimity toward all beings, remains mute regarding slander, and is as if impotent toward the wives of others.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of the Śiva-liṅgas Proclaimed by Kārttikeya," in the Śiva-śāstra of the Kedāra-khaṇḍa, within the first section, the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Lomaśa said: Thus, O twice-born ones, those Śiva-dharmas were indeed recounted by him in detail, including the specific Pāśupata teachings, through his grace.
Enveloped by numerous scriptures and set forth according to their true nature, the various divisions of the Kāpālikas have been described both in detail and in brief.
At that time, various kinds of teachings were indeed proclaimed to Nandin.
The sages said: "O highly fortunate one, we have heard the entirely auspicious life-story of the Kumāra; now we wish to ask you something. (4)
The life story of Śveta, that lion among kings, is most wonderful; by it, Rudra Śiva was gratified through his immeasurable devotion.
They are devotees, they are great-souled ones, they are possessors of knowledge, and they are performers of action—those who worship the god Mahāśambhu, completely enveloped by devotion.
Therefore, we all ask about the life of Śaṅkara; by the grace of Vyāsa, you know everything, and no one else.
Having heard the words of those sages, Lomaśa spoke.

Lomaśa said: Listen, O highly fortunate ones, to this most wonderful account. For as that king Śveta enjoyed royal pleasures in every respect, a firm resolve arose in the mind of that high-souled one.
He protected the earth, governing his subjects with righteousness; he was devoted to the Brahmanas, truthful in speech, heroic, and a constant devotee of Śiva.

Then that king ruled his kingdom according to his ability, and with devotion he always worshipped Śambhu—the Supreme Lord, the highest, higher than the high, the peaceful, the ancient one, whose form is the Supreme Self.
The life of that one who was worshipping the Supreme Lord has come to an end; now, O highly fortunate one, hear this account from me.
The speech of that king was joined with stories of Śiva and filled with supreme wonder; indeed, he had neither mental anxieties nor physical ailments. (13)
Neither afflictions nor these calamities troubled that king; indeed, the people were free from drought and entirely free from distress.
On the earth of that king, medicinal herbs grew without being cultivated; likewise, there were ascetic Brahmins and people belonging to the various castes and stages of life.
They never experience the suffering of a son's death, nor humiliation, nor Māras, nor poverty; indeed, they never encounter any of these things. (16)
O brahmins, thus a very long time passed fruitfully for that great-souled king who was indeed devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Once, while Śaṅkara, the bestower of the supreme goal, was being worshipped, Yama dispatched his messengers toward the king.
"Upon the word of Citragupta, 'Let Śveta be brought here,' those messengers, acknowledging 'So be it,' arrived at the abode of Śiva. (19)
Desirous of leading away the king, those terrifying messengers of Yama, with nooses in hand, arrived and quickly beheld the king.
At that time, the messengers did not carry out the command of Dharma; for Yama himself, having learned of everything, arrived there in person.
Having suddenly raised his staff, the mighty-armed one, desiring then to lead away the king, beheld him intent upon meditation on Śiva.
Even Yama, upon seeing the king—who was endowed with devotion to Śiva, tranquil, and possessed of pure knowledge—fell into a state of great agitation.
Indeed, the King of the Dead, who is eternally the form of Time and the destroyer of all creatures, became instantly overwhelmed with agitation as he stood before the painting. (24)
Filled with wrath toward the king, he arrived at that very moment, armed with a sharp-edged sword and an excellent shield.
Then he too saw him standing at the door, overcome with fear; for at that time, Kāla spoke to Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
"O King of Dharma, why have you not led away this great king? Accompanied by the messengers of Yama, you appear to me as if you were afraid. (27)
"O you of firm vows, let there be no delay because of my word. Thus addressed by Kāla, Dharma then spoke these relevant words: || 28 ||
"I shall carry out your command; there is no need for deliberation here. This Huratyaya is a constant devotee of Śiva. (29)
"We stand as if fixed in a painting out of fear of the trident-bearing God. Having heard Yama's words, Kāla, filled with rage, began to slay the king; he quickly took up his sword.

He entered the abode of Śiva, which resembled three times eight spokes [twenty-four pillars], while he was filled with great wrath; at that moment, he was seen by the wielder of the Pināka bow, who desired to kill his own excellent devotee, King Śveta.
And [he saw] himself established in meditation, with a purified mind by means of the lamp of pure knowledge, as the self itself, continuously and self-luminous, the supreme [Self] before him. (32)

Having thus observed that time being reflected upon with an unwavering mind—that state of Śiva which is the nature of the supreme reality and which, by its very essence, brings about liberation through union—(33)
That wicked Kāla, unrestrained and arrogant, was seen by Sadāśiva, the end-maker of Time, as he was entering into his very presence.
He remained standing in the midst of Nandikeśvara until he was seen by Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, that kinsman who is affectionate toward his devotees.
Gazed upon by the Supreme Lord with his third eye, while he was protecting his own devotee, [the enemy] was reduced to ashes in an instant.

He consumed that Time, which was multicolored, with its mouth wide open and its form terrifyingly fierce; it was being scorched by garlands of flames, exceedingly violent, and the sole devourer of the world.

The assembled hosts of gods were seen there, along with yakṣas, gandharvas, piśācas, and guhyakas; as well as siddhas, apsarases, all the birds, serpents, winged creatures, and likewise the guardians of the world.
Enveloped in garlands of flames, Kāla stood before the Lord; then the king regained consciousness, seeing that Kāla had come to slay him.
Then, seeing him being repeatedly consumed by fire, he, filled with agitation, prayed to Rudra, who resembled the fire of cosmic destruction.
The King said: Salutations to Rudra, the peaceful one; salutations to the self-piercer who is his own radiance; salutations to the continuous, the subtle, the lord of lights. || 41 ||

For you alone, O Lord of the World, are the protector, the father, the mother, the well-wisher, and the friend; you alone are the kinsman, the relative, the sovereign, and the supreme lord of all beings. 42.
"O Śambhu, what have you done? Who is this that has been burnt before me? I do not know what has happened, nor by whom this great deed was performed. (43)

Having heard his prayer and his lamentation, Śaṅkara spoke these words as if awakening that king: Thus he prayed, and having heard his lamentation, Śaṅkara spoke these words, as if enlightening the king. (44)
Rudra said: "Indeed, this Kāla has been burnt by me for your sake and in your presence; for you have seen him being consumed, great and wreathed in garlands of flames."
Thus addressed by Śambhu at that time, the best of kings, becoming humble, spoke these words in the presence of Śiva.
"O Śambhu, tell me truly what wrong has been done by him, that he has reached this state which threatens his very life? O Bhava! (47)
Thus addressed by him, the Supreme Lord said: "O Great King, this one here is a devourer of all living beings."
"O Lord, O Great King, this cruel one has now come into my presence for the purpose of devouring you; therefore, O Lord, he has been burnt by me. (49)
Seeking the welfare of many, I have especially endured this for your sake.

"Those who are indeed sinful, most unrighteous, and bringers of destruction to the world, who are joined with heretical doctrines—they must certainly be slain by me. Having heard these words of Rudra, Śveta spoke this speech: || 51 ||
For it is only in due time that this world constantly practices merit; yet some are devoted to righteousness, endowed with supreme devotion.
Some are devoted to worship, while others are indeed possessors of knowledge; some are united with the inner self, and others are liberated.

For Time is indeed the destroyer of all things moving and unmoving, and likewise he alone is their protector; he is truly the creator and the very life-force of living beings. Therefore, restore him to life once more immediately.
If you are intent on creation, revive Time quickly; if you are the agent of destruction for all living beings here. (55)
"In that case, O Śambhu, act thus regarding the Great Soul Kāla; for nothing whatsoever can come to pass without Kāla, O Śaṅkara. (56)
Thus addressed by that powerful king, Śambhu carried out his word and fulfilled what his devotee desired to do.
Then Maheśa, the wielder of the Pināka bow, laughed and restored him to life; he assumed his former appearance and was embraced by Śambhu in the midst of the messengers of Yama.
Then, having approached while feeling ashamed, he praised that bull-bannered god; bowing down and standing before the fire-like Kāla, he spoke these words with wonder: || 59 ||
Kāla said: O Lord who brings an end to Time, O Master of Tripura, O Destroyer of Tripura! Indeed, O God, Lord of the World, Madana has been rendered bodiless by you. (60)
Indeed, the most wonderful destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice was wrought by you; as was the great, unbearable Kālakūṭa poison, which brings about the ruin of all. (61)
O Śambhu, that which was difficult even for others to grasp has been swallowed by you; the three worlds were pervaded by your great form as the Liṅga. || 62 ||
It is called *liṅga* by all the gods and asuras because it is the place of dissolution (*layana*); even the gods, led by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, do not know its end.

The greatness of the supreme Liṅga, the God of gods; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord; salutations to you, the auspiciousness of the universe; salutations to you, the blue-throated one; salutations to that one with matted hair.

Salutations, salutations to You, the cause of all causes; salutations, salutations to You, whose nature is auspiciousness among all that is auspicious. You are the Self of knowledge for the wise who possess knowledge; You are the primordial God, the ancient Puruṣa. || 65 ||

O Friend of the gods, you alone are the entire universe; O Great-Souled One, you are the one to be known through the Vedānta. O Lord of the Universe, you alone are worthy of praise by the great-souled and honored by the whole world.
O Great Lord, you protect and you destroy the three worlds; you alone are the creator and the lord of all beings, and there is no other.
Thus praised by him at that time, Kāla, the Lord of the World, spoke to King Śveta as if awakening him.
Kāla said: "In the entire world of mortals, indeed there is no one other than you; for by you, even the God who is unconquerable in the three worlds has been defeated. (69)
By me this entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, has been slain; I am the conqueror of all the gods, and I am insurmountable by all.
"He has indeed become your follower, O Great King; grant me immunity from the fear of the Supreme Lord, the God of gods, who wields the trident. (71)
Thus addressed by him at that time, Śveta, together with Kāla, spoke with a laugh, his voice as deep as the roar of a thundercloud.
The king said: "You alone are the supreme form of Śiva; of this there is no doubt. You are Time itself for all beings, possessing the nature of both preservation and destruction. (73)

Therefore, you are the most worshipful of all and the controller of everyone; out of fear of you, all the perfected ones, intent on the true nature of the Self, go for refuge to the Supreme Lord with various dispositions.
Suta said: Protected in this manner by that most righteous king, Kāla regained his senses through the mere grace of Śiva. || 75 ||
Then, praised by Yama, Mṛtyu, and the messengers of Yama, and having bowed to and extolled Śiva as well as King Śveta, he went to his own abode, O Brahmins, and considered himself born again.
Reflecting again and again upon the great deeds of Śiva together with his wife Māyā, he attained a state of supreme wonder.
He himself spoke to all the messengers: "O messengers, listen quickly to my words! (78)
And this must be performed with diligent effort; otherwise, my word shall not be fulfilled. || 79 ||
Kāla said: "Those who wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), as well as those who wear matted hair (jaṭādhara), those who wear rudrākṣa beads, and likewise those who bear the names of Śiva. (80)
Indeed, even those men who, out of fear for the sake of livelihood, though sinful and of wicked conduct, wear the garb of Śiva—these are they. (81)
They must never be led by you to my world; for they are always to be avoided with effort, even if they are sinners.
What need is there to speak of others, even the messengers who worship Sadāśiva with supreme devotion? They are Rudras; of this there is no doubt. (83)

Those virtuous ones who wear a single rudrākṣa on their head as well as the tripuṇḍra in the middle of the forehead, and who mutter the five-syllabled mantra—they are to be honored by you, and never otherwise. (84)
In whatever kingdom, country, or even village a wise person devoted to Śiva is not seen, that is said to be no better than a cremation ground; this I tell you as the truth. (85)
In whatever village there are no people endowed with constant devotion to Śiva, all the inhabitants of that village must undoubtedly be disciplined. 86.
Thus Yama commanded his own servants; thinking "So be it," they all remained silent, greatly amazed.

Such is this Sadāśiva, the sole lord of the world and the unique teacher of the universe; he is the giver and the destroyer, endowed with his own innate nature, the eternal one, and the singular kinsman of the world. (88)
Having consumed Kāla, the all-pervading Mahādeva granted fearlessness to Śveta, the king of kings and the most excellent of protectors of the earth. 89.
Then the high-minded Śvetarāja, having attained fearlessness, became liberated through supreme devotion, having reached a firm resolve. || 90 ||
Then, being honored by the gods, the sages, and likewise by the serpents, that best of kings, Śveta, attained union with Śiva.
Thus, for those who are devoted to Maheśa, the teacher of the world, success rests in the palm of their hand; I tell you this as the truth.
Even an outcaste (śvapaca) may become most excellent through the grace of Śaṅkara; therefore, Śaṅkara should indeed be worshipped with every effort. 93.
In the end, devotion to Śiva arises within the minds of many people.
For the wise whose intellects are perfected, Śaṅkara is the end of birth after birth; what need is there for me to say more? Sadāśiva is to be worshipped. 95.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history concerning the most wonderful vow performed by a hunter, by which this entire world of moving and non-moving beings was delivered.
The sages said: O best of Brahmins, what was the name of that Kirāta, and what vow did he undertake? Tell us the truth, for our curiosity is great.

We wish to hear all of that; let it be told exactly as it is. For there is no one else in the world besides you who is a superior speaker; therefore, O Brahmin, speak everything to us who are eager to listen.
Thus addressed at that time by the high-souled Śaunaka, he related everything that had been done by the Puṣkasa.
Lomaśa said: In ancient times, there was a very fierce and evil-minded man named Caḍa; he was a companion of the cruel, merciless, and a bringer of fear to all living beings.
Indeed, that evil-minded one constantly kills fish with a net; he slays deer, wild beasts, black antelopes, and porcupines with arrows.
And seeing some with swords, that wicked-souled and sinful man, being enraged, slaughtered them; he did so especially toward the Brāhmaṇas.
For the hunter was a great sinner, wicked, and a favorite of evil folk; his wife was likewise like him, a Puṣkasa woman of great terror.
As he lived in this manner, a great deal of time passed; and after a long period had elapsed, he remained devoted to a flood of evil deeds.

Carrying water in his quiver and being severely afflicted by hunger and thirst, that wicked man once took his stand upon a banyan tree at night; with bow in hand, he remained wide awake, not even blinking, in order to kill a boar.
Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, he dropped bilva leaves in front [of the deity], desiring to behold the path of the deer.
There, although filled with rage, he cut down many leaves of the Śrīvṛkṣa tree; yet as he moved about at the foot of the Śrīvṛkṣa, he perceived the nature of the Liṅga situated above it.

The wicked-souled one happened to spit water, and by chance those drops fell upon Śiva; furthermore, by the turn of fate, leaves of the Bilva tree also fell, and thus all that became an act of worship to Śiva.
A great ablution was performed with that water from his mouth-rinse, and a great worship was performed with countless bilva leaves.
O Brahmins, even by that wicked-souled Puṣkasa through ignorance, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha at the rising of the moon, [this was performed].
Then that Puṣkasa of wicked conduct descended from the tree; having arrived at Jalasaṃkāśa, he set about killing fish. || 15 ||
A certain greedy man had a wife named Ghanodarī; she was wicked, devoted to sin, and a thief of others' property.
Having departed from her home in the evening, she stood outside the city gate, gazing toward the forest path in the hope of her husband's return.
When her husband had not returned for a long time, the female hunter began to worry: "Today, at the hour of evening, all the hunters have arrived. (18)
The four intermediate directions and the cardinal points were completely shrouded by a mass of darkness; two watches of the night had passed—could it be that Mataṅga has arrived? (19)
Or was he torn apart by a lion out of greed for his mane? Or was he afflicted by the venom of a snake after stealing the jewel from the hood of a serpent? (20)
Or did he meet his death by the blows from the tips of a boar's tusks? No, it was surely because of his greed for honey that he fell from the top of the tree to the ground.
"Where shall I search? Whom shall I ask? And where shall I go? Having lamented thus in many ways, she turned back toward her own home.
On that day, she ate neither food nor even a drop of water; thinking only of her husband, the huntress passed the night in this manner.
Then, at the clear dawn, the Puṣkasī woman went to the forest, quickly taking food for her meal.
Wandering through that forest, she saw a great river; seeing her husband seated upon its bank, she was filled with joy.
Having set that food on the bank, he proceeded to cross the river; then, observing the fish, he brought them along, impaled upon his net.
Then she said to that fierce one: "Come quickly and eat; food has been brought for your sake by me after fasting for the day. (27)
"What have you done today, O dull-witted one? And what was done yesterday when the day had passed? You did not eat, O fool, having fasted today like a sinner. (28)
When the husband and wife, both pure in their vows, had likewise bathed in the river, just as he was about to go to eat, a dog arrived there of its own accord.
He himself indeed devoured all of that food; then Caṇḍī became enraged and set about to kill the dog.
"Our food was eaten by this very sinner; moreover, O fool, what will you eat today, for you shall become hungry? (31)
Thus addressed by her, that fierce devotee of Śiva spoke to her: "I am fully satisfied by that food which was eaten by the dog. (32)
What is the use of this perishable body, whose life is spent? This body, so difficult to obtain in the world, is honored despite being fragile as a moment. (33)
Those who, being unassailable, nourish their own bodies with their whole being, should be known as fools and sinners, excluded from both worlds.
Therefore, having abandoned pride and the difficult-to-restrain anger, be composed; through reflection, remain steadfast with the realization of reality.
Then that fierce woman was thoroughly awakened by that Puṣkasa, and the Puṣkasa also reached the fourteenth day, beginning with the vigil (jāgara).
And that supreme knowledge which undoubtedly arises through the occasion of Śivarātri—that he has attained by virtue of the occasion of Śivarātri. (37)
Two watches of the night had passed during that new moon; indeed, many hosts impelled by Śiva arrived there.
Many celestial chariots arrived there in his presence; he beheld those very chariots as well as the hosts.
And the Puṣkasa also spoke to them with supreme devotion: "Why have you all come here, wearing rudrākṣa beads? (40)
Some were situated in celestial chariots and some were mounted upon bulls; all were as radiant as crystal, and all had the crescent moon as their crest-ornament.

O sirs, tell me truly what is appropriate for yourselves—those who wear matted hair and garments of skin, who have made necklaces and ornaments from the coils of serpents, who are endowed with splendor, and whose prowess is equal to that of Rudra. (42)
Then, questioned by Puṣkasa, all those lotus-eyed attendants, bowing low before Rudra, the God of gods, spoke.
The Gaṇas said: "O Caṇḍa, we have been sent by Śiva, the Supreme Lord. Come quickly, and having mounted your vehicle, go together with your wife."
Because you performed the worship of the Liṅga of Śiva during the night, by the ripening of that karma, you have attained the presence of Śiva.
Thus addressed by Vīrabhadra, even the Puṣkasa, as if smiling, spoke words appropriate to the occasion according to his own intellect.
The Puṣkasa said: "What has been done today by me, a sinner and a violent man, a wicked-souled Puṣkasa who delights only in hunting? (47)
"For I am always of evil conduct; how then shall I go to heaven? How was this worship of the Liṅga performed by me? Let that be told. (48)
Filled with great curiosity, I ask you for the truth as it is; O illustrious one, tell me everything exactly according to the rules.
As that Puṣkasa asked thus according to the prescribed manner, he, filled with joy, related all of that Śiva-dharma to him.
Vīrabhadra said: "O Caṇḍa, today the God of gods, Mahādeva, the Lord and Sovereign of the gods—that Maheśa, the Consort of Umā—is thoroughly pleased."

By the way, you performed the worship of the Liṅga during the month of Māgha; it has brought satisfaction to Śiva today, and you have been purified—of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, you performed worship on the occasion of Śivarātri as well.
"O Caṇḍa, while you were looking at the *kola* fruit, you indeed cut some *bilva* leaves; they fell right then upon the top of the Liṅga. Therefore, O Lord, you are a man of meritorious deeds. (53)
Then, a great vigil was certainly performed atop the tree; by that very vigil, the Lord of the World was gratified.
"O highly fortunate one, it was indeed through this trickery—the manifestation as a boar—that on the day of Śivarātri you had no dreams and no women [appeared to you]. (55)
Pleased indeed by that fast and vigil, this supreme deity, the great-souled one, for the sake of your favor, being of great majesty and a great granter of boons, bestows all things.
Thus addressed then by the wise Vīrabhadra, the Puṣkasa also ascended the foremost of celestial chariots while all were looking on.
Then, for all the hosts of deities and for all living beings as well, kettledrums resounded, along with many bherī drums and musical instruments.
Vīṇās, flutes, and mṛdaṅga drums were brought before him; the lords of the gandharvas sang and the hosts of apsaras danced.
All the hosts of Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas offered hymns of praise; being fanned with chowries and shaded by various umbrellas, he was brought to Gandhamādana with great festivity.
By that deed, this Caṇḍa attained proximity to Śiva; through fasting on Śivarātri, he reached the supreme abode.
Even a Puṣkasa attained [liberation] in this manner through incidental contact with Sadāśiva; how much more so those endowed with faith toward Śiva, the Supreme Self! 62.
Those in this world who offer flowers and the like, fruits, perfumes, betel, and excellent foodstuffs, are Rudras; of this there is no doubt. (63)
By Caṇḍa, the Puṣkasa, it indeed became fruitful for him; even though it was performed by that man of little intelligence merely as a matter of circumstance.
The sages said: What is its fruit, what is its purpose, and by whom was it first performed? From what did this vow originate, and by whom was it practiced in the past, O Lord? (65)
Lomaśa said: When the entire world was created by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, then the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra) arose in ancient times, accompanied by the zodiacal signs (rāśi).
Therein are the twelve zodiac signs as well as the twenty-seven principal lunar mansions for the sake of accomplishment. (67)
Through these and all the fierce lunar mansions and constellations, Time, joined with the wheel of time (Kālacakra), creates the world while sporting.
O twice-born ones, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, he creates, maintains, and destroys; all is bound by that very same single Time.
For time alone is powerful in the world, and there is no other; therefore, all this is of the nature of time—of this there is no doubt. (70)
In the beginning was Time; from the measuring of time came the Leader of the Leaders of the World. From that, indeed, the worlds were born, and immediately thereafter, creation.
Indeed, from the creation a lava was produced, and from the lava a kṣaṇa; and from the kṣaṇa a nimiṣa arose, occurring continuously for all living beings.
Sixty nimiṣas are indeed called a phala; fifteen days and nights are called a pakṣa.
From two fortnights comes a month; twelve months constitute a year. Those who desire to know that time must apply their discernment with wisdom. (74)
Starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight and ending with the full moon, the fortnight is indeed called "full" (pūrṇa), and for that reason it is designated as "Pūrṇimā. (75)
That day on which the moon is full is called Pūrṇā, beloved by the gods; that day on which the moon has disappeared is declared by the wise to be Amā.

It was exceedingly dear to the ancestors, such as the Agniṣvāttas and others. These thirty days are indeed endowed with merit; O best of the twice-born, listen to that which is the distinction among them. (77)
Among yogas, Vyatīpāta is likewise; among constellations, Śravaṇa is likewise; and among lunar days, both the new moon and the full moon are indeed such [auspicious times]. || 78 ||
Likewise, the transits [of the sun] should be known as pure for the act of giving; similarly, the eighth day is dear to Śambhu, and the fourth day to Gaṇeśa. (79)
The fifth is for the Naga King, the sixth for Kumara, the seventh is known as that of Bhanu, and the ninth is dear to Chandika.
The tenth is to be known as that of Brahmā, and likewise the eleventh as that of Rudra; the twelfth is dear to Viṣṇu, and the thirteenth belongs to Antaka.

Likewise, O Śambhu, the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) is dear to Him; of this there is no doubt. That fourteenth day of the dark fortnight which is joined with midnight is the most excellent lunar day to be observed as a fast, for it bestows union with Śiva.
The Śivarātri lunar day is renowned as the destroyer of all sins; in this very context, they cite this ancient historical narrative.
In former times, there was a certain Brāhmaṇī widow who was indeed fickle; out of lustful desire, she was devoted to a Caṇḍāla and was full of longing. (84)
To that wicked-caste Śvapaca was born a son, Duḥsaha by name, whose soul was evil and who was excluded from all dharma. || 85 ||
And due to the practice of great sins, he constantly undertakes evil deeds: he is a gambler, a drinker of liquor, a thief, and one who violates the teacher’s bed. (86)

That evil-minded hunter was indeed a *caṇḍāla* by his actions; for he was most unrighteous and of wicked conduct. Yet, once upon a time, he arrived at a temple of Śiva on the night of Śivarātri and stayed in the presence of Śiva.
When the hearing of the Śaiva scripture occurs by chance in the presence of a self-manifested (svayambhū) Liṅga-form of Śiva, at that time— || 88 ||
Having stayed in one place, that wicked man performed a vigil on Śivarātri; by the ripening of that karma, he obtained a meritorious birth. (89)
Having enjoyed the most meritorious worlds and having dwelt there for eternal years, he became the son of Citrāṅgada, possessing the characteristics of a sovereign lord of kings.
Known by the name Vicitravīrya, he was fortunate, well-disposed, and beloved; having obtained a vast kingdom, he became truly great and free from pride.

Practicing devotion to Śiva, he became intent on performing auspicious rites; placing the Śaiva scriptures at the forefront, he was devoted to the worship of Śiva and diligently performed the night vigil in the presence of Śiva.
Singing hymns to Śiva, he repeatedly shed tears of joy from his eyes, his body covered with horripilation.
And his lifespan came to an end while he was devoted to the meditation on Śiva; for Śiva is indeed easily attained in this world by both bound souls and those possessed of knowledge. 94.
Indeed, Sadāśiva alone is to be served for the attainment of happiness; by fasting on Śivarātri, he attained unsurpassed knowledge. (95)

Through knowledge, everything has been attained as a continuous state of equilibrium among the elements; having realized that which consists of all beings, which is absolute and eternally auspicious, there is no object whatsoever here or anywhere that exists apart from Śiva.
In this way, he attains that perfect, non-conceptual knowledge which is difficult to obtain; having attained that knowledge, the king then indeed became beloved of Śiva.
He attained liberation in the form of *sāyujya* through fasting on Śivarātri; by that, he obtained birth from Śiva, as was previously described by me. (98)

He who was born from the head of Śiva, the Supreme Soul, wearing the skin of Dakṣa’s daughter and with matted locks spread wide, became renowned as Vīrabhadra, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. || 99 ||
By the very vow of Śivarātri, many were delivered in former times; O Brahmins, embodied beings such as Bharata and others attained perfection in the past. (100)
Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāri, Hariścandra, and other kings indeed attained perfection through this supreme vow alone.

Then the Lord of the Mountains, accompanied by the Daughter of the Mountain, engaged in play upon the summit of the King of Mountains; that Supreme Lord, joined with Bhavānī, played a game of dice with great intensity.
Lomaśa said: The great Lord of the Universe ruled his kingdom on Mount Kailāsa, accompanied by many hosts and joined by Vīrabhadra.
Rudra, together with the sages, and Indra along with the other gods, as well as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, stand before him intent on his praise like servants.
Indra, together with the hosts of gods, became devoted to the duty of service; Candra was his umbrella-bearer, and Vāyu likewise held the chowries.
He was a constant and tireless preparer of soups and rice; the Gandharvas were his singers and the Pinākin (Śiva) was his panegyrist.
Many Vidyādharas as well as hosts of Apsarases danced before him on that Mount Kailāsa.
Together with his sons, Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and others, as well as with Girijā, he ruled the kingdom fearlessly through his majesty and his constant wandering.
By which [weapon] the great Daitya Andhaka, the great enemy of the gods, being wicked, was pierced with a trident and held fast in the sky for a long time.

Having slain Gajāsura, he indeed cut off his hide and made it a divine garment to wear for a long time; likewise, as Viṣṇu acting as the protector, he shone, beautiful in every limb, having set the three cities ablaze.
Desirous of seeing him, the blessed Nārada, possessed of divine vision, went to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, white as the moon.
Having seen that most wonderful being, possessed of great strength, white as camphor and served by supreme nectar, Nārada was filled with amazement and entered Gandhamādana.
It was endowed with many wonders, beautifully adorned by suns, filled with singing vidyādharīs, and possessed of great splendor.
And there were many wish-fulfilling trees entwined with creepers; in their thick shade stood especially the cows that grant all desires.
Many bees were greedy for the fragrance of the *pārijāta* groves, and many *kalahaṃsa* swans were sporting in the lake. (13)
There, all the birds, including the peacocks who utter their cries in the fifth note, filled with great joy and delight, raised a loud clamor of "ke-ka" sounds.
The majestic male elephants rejoiced together with their females, and likewise the roaring lions were joined by the tigers.
Bulls led by Nandin were bellowing incessantly, as were many celestial trees and sandalwood groves. || 16 ||
Nāgas, puṃnāgas, bakulas, campakas, and nāgakesaras, as well as wild rose-apples and golden ketakīs. || 17 ||
