There were many white water-lilies, oleanders, and night-blooming lotuses, as well as mandāra trees, jujube trees, areca palms, and trumpet-flowers.
Likewise, many other trees there, endowed with various trees and creepers, were seen all at once as they brought great satisfaction to Śambhu; indeed, many groves there became twice as vast.
Immediately, an exceedingly wonderful torrent of the Gaṅgā issued forth from the sky and fell upon the beautiful summit of that mountain.
Indeed, that well from which the purifier of waters does not flow for the world was also seen by the high-souled Nārada to be divided into two parts at that time.
O brahmins, at that time everything was seen by that great-souled Nārada to have become twofold, as he gazed upon it with supreme vision.
Beholding thus, the venerable sage Nārada proceeded with great haste, intent upon beholding Śiva.
While standing at the gate, he beheld a truly great marvel; then he saw two gatekeepers who had been fashioned by Viśvakarman.
Nārada was indeed deluded; he then questioned those two, saying: "I desire to enter, longing for the sight of Śiva. (25)
Therefore, permission should be granted for the sake of seeing Śiva. Hearing nothing at that time, Nārada was filled with wonder upon seeing them. (26)
Then, having observed them with the vision of knowledge, he became indifferent; for, knowing those two to be artificial, the high-minded one entered [the city]. (27)
Likewise, other beings of similar form were seen by that great-souled one; and the venerable sage Nārada was saluted by them. || 28 ||
He beheld many such wonders; then he clearly saw the three-eyed Lord accompanied by the Daughter of the Mountain.
The virtuous daughter of the King of Mountains sat upon half the seat of the high-souled Śaṅkara; by her, the three worlds were pervaded.
Gaurī, white-eyed, young, slender-limbed, and beautiful of eye—by her Śambhu was made embodied, and the Great One was made worthy of being attained.
Though himself free from change, he was rendered agitated by many transformations; by him, that goddess of Śiva was seen clinging to his half-body.
In that manner, Nārada beheld Śambhu, the Lord of the three worlds, who resembled pure gold and was being served by gods and asuras.
The lotus-feet were served by Śaṅkha, the best of serpents, as well as by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and especially by Takṣaka; likewise by Padma and especially by Mahāśeṣa.
Indeed, he is constantly served by other excellent nāgas; Vāsuki, possessing great luster, is fastened around his neck as a necklace.
Kambala and Aśvatara are eternally adorned with earrings, while these other excellent great serpents have their coils wound around the base of his matted locks.
Enveloped through many births, there were lotus-dwelling serpents of various colors: Takṣaka, Kulika, Śaṅkha, and the highly radiant Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Padma, Dambha, Sudambha, Karāla, and Bhīṣaṇa—these and many other such serpents were indeed venomous.
Indeed, some of the best of serpents, who serve as limbs of Hara—the one worthy of worship in the three worlds—shone forth with a single hood. (39)
For some there are two hoods, for others three of great luster; likewise four, five, six, seven, and eight.
The group of nine, the ten, and likewise the eleven; the twelve, the eighteen, and also the nineteen. || 41 ||
Some have forty hoods, some fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, and likewise ninety.
Likewise, there were hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of jewels, as well as those measured by the conch. || 43 ||
Then all those serpents, whose hoods were infinite and who served as the ornaments of Śiva, were beheld by the high-souled Nārada.
Though they were all possessed of knowledge, they were enjoyers of pleasures and beautifully adorned; they were like necklaces of ornaments, endowed with jewels and immeasurable luster.
His matted hair, marked by a half-moon, was exceedingly beautiful, and he shone with a third eye situated upon his forehead.
The great god Mahādeva has five faces and is endowed with ten arms; likewise, his neck is emerald-green and exceedingly beautiful.
The chest of Rudra was broad, as were his thighs and hips; and his two feet were most beautiful and exceedingly great. (48)

That incomparable, radiant, and beautiful lotus-foot of Śambhu was seen—auspicious with the glow of twilight, the supreme dispeller of suffering, a source of massed splendor, higher than the highest, the abode of the play of loveliness, the ultimate cause for the increase of happiness for all, and purifying. (49)

Having seen her in that very way—the supreme among the supreme, the ultimate reality, beautiful and lovely, shining with the great majesty of good fortune and charm—she was indeed exceedingly beautiful and auspicious.

Having seen that pure couple shining throughout the three worlds—those who were non-different yet had attained difference, and who were both devoid of qualities and possessed of qualities—(he was amazed).

Having forms and yet formless, fearless and bestowers of happiness, Nārada, the beloved of the Lord, joyfully saluted them both; rising again and again, he then offered praise to the two Lords of the universe.

Nārada said: I bow to you both, the best of gods, who are higher than the highest; nevertheless, I have beheld you as a radiant couple by your partial manifestation (kalā), you who are the seeds of all that is mobile and immobile.
"Today, by your grace, I have come to know the parents of the entire world in their true essence; of this there is no doubt. (54)
When he had thus offered praise at that time by the high-souled Nārada, the Blessed Lord Śambhu, together with Pārvatī, was then gratified.
Mahādeva said: "O Brahmin, do you dwell in happiness? What service may I perform for you? Having heard those words of Śambhu, Nārada spoke this speech: || 56 ||
"O Lord, my vision [of you] has been born this very day; therefore, I am gratified, O All-pervading One. Through this vision, O Śambhu, everything today belongs to me—of this there is no doubt. (57)
"O Blessed Lord, O Master, you have come here to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, for the sake of sport; for you always abide within the hearts of men. (58)
Nevertheless, the vision [of the deity] must be constantly cultivated by living beings here. (59)
Girijā said: "Tell me quickly before me, what sport indeed is to be performed by you? Having heard those words of hers, he spoke as if laughing: 60.
O Mahādeva, various forms of gambling are seen here; indeed, from the pleasure of gambling with two people, great happiness arises. (61)

Having spoken thus, the virtuous woman, being deeply provoked, addressed these words to the rishi in anger: "How do you know of gambling, which is well-known as the supreme ruin for high-minded men, and [how do you know of] the wicked Udaraka?"

You are the son of Brahmā, a sage, and indeed the teacher of the wise through your various well-known utterances; as you shall wander through the three worlds, there is truly no other person more resolute than you.
Thus addressed by the Goddess, Nārada, who has the vision of the gods, spoke these words with a smile to the Daughter of the Mountain in the presence of Śiva.

Nārada said: "I do not know gambling, nor do I resort to it; for I am an ascetic and a servant of Śiva. Why then do you ask me about it, O princess, who are the supreme purifier of the lords of yogis?"
Having heard those words, the virtuous Girijā then laughed and spoke these words to him: "O boy, you know everything today; behold my game of dice as I play it before you with Maheśa."

Having spoken thus, the daughter of the King of Mountains, the peerless beauty of the world, took up the dice; then, standing there together with Bhava, she engaged in play before the witness of the great sages.
Then the wise sage Nārada, seeing that couple engaged in their play, his mind blossoming with wonder as he gazed upon them, was exceedingly delighted.
Then, surrounded by her circle of female friends and intent on the game of dice, she met with Śiva and engaged him in a match of dice through deception.
Then, overcome by great deception, he made a wager; and Bhavānī was then defeated by Śiva, who seemed to laugh as he did so.
Then Nārada became a source of derision for her because of Śiva; having heard that the game of dice had been lost and having heard the mockery.
Greatly incensed by Nārada’s harsh words, Pārvatī quickly spoke, having delivered a half-moon (a slap) to him.
Furthermore, seeing her crest-jewel and her tremulous, captivating face—so beautiful even when she was angry—Hara played at dice with her again and again. (73)
Thus addressed by Girijā, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, replied: "I have been won by you; the wager has been paid, and it cannot be otherwise. (74)
"And what stake, O Śambhu, is being made by you? Let that indeed be told. Then the Three-eyed One, laughing, spoke to Pārvatī.
"I am making this wager: you shall have for yourself this great ornament—the crescent moon, the large necklace, and likewise the pair of lotus-earrings. (76)
"O slender one, let this very thing be taken by you as a prize after defeating me; then the game of dice was commenced with Śaṅkara himself. (77)
Thus sporting, those two who were experts in the science of dice—then Śaṅkara, adorned with many ornaments, was defeated by Bhavānī.
Laughing, the exceedingly beautiful Gaurī said to Śaṅkara: "O Śaṅkara, give me now this very day the stake that you have lost."
Then Maheśa, laughing, spoke these true words: "O slender-limbed one, I have not been conquered by you; let this be examined according to the truth."
"I am invincible to all living beings in every way; therefore, O virtuous lady, do not speak what you have said. Play at dice today as you wish, and I shall surely win again; behold! (81)

Then Ambikā said to her husband Maheśa, "You have been defeated by me today; there is no cause for wonder here. Having spoken thus to Śambhu, the fair-faced lady took him by the hand and said, "You have been defeated, there is no doubt; you do not realize it, O Śaṅkara. (82)

Having laughed thus, Girijā looked at Śambhu with playful words, and he was overcome by her; "O Lord of all auspiciousness, grant me that which was cherished and approved by the speech of the enemy of Smara. (83)
Śiva said: "O large-eyed one, I am invincible; there is no doubt about this for you. Let that which was spoken out of egoism be reflected upon according to its true nature."
Having heard those words of his, she laughed and said: "O Lord, Mahādeva is indeed invincible even to all. (85)
Indeed, you have been defeated by me alone through this pure game of dice; you do not understand at all what ought and ought not to be done, nor what is intended to be said.
While that supreme couple were thus disputing, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke these words with a smile.

Nārada said: Listen, O lady with eyes as wide as the ears, to these words which are the sole auspiciousness of the world. This man, the most excellent among the highly fortunate, has been conquered by you; why then do you speak falsely?
For Mahādeva is indeed Ajita, the supreme teacher of the gods; he is formless, yet he possesses beautiful form, and he is said to transcend all form. || 89 ||
There is but one supreme light, which is also the majesty of those [others]: Śaṅkara, the Lord of the three worlds, the Soul of the universe, the benefactor of the world. (90)
"How, O Goddess, have you conquered him who is indeed invincible in the three worlds? You do not recognize this Śiva because of your female nature, O fair-faced one. (91)
Thus addressed by Nārada, the virtuous Pārvatī became exceedingly angry; seized by resentment, she spoke these words of reproach.
Pārvatī said: "O son of Brahmā, salutations to you; one should not speak out of fickleness."
"I am afraid of you; may it be well with you, O divine sage, please observe silence. (93)
O divine sage, how is it that you have spoken so much about Śiva? For by my grace, he who is indeed recited as Īśvara has become Śiva. (94)
"He has become one who has attained a firm footing through me; of this there is no doubt. (95)
Having heard these various things, Nārada resorted to silence; seeing him standing there, Bhṛṅgī then spoke these words.
Bhṛṅgī said: "O beautiful woman, you should not speak further at all; for my lord, O slender-waisted one, is indeed invincible and free from change. (97)
O fair-faced one, you are possessed of womanhood; you do not know the God who is supreme among the supreme. Long ago, O Bhavānī, you approached the fierce Maheśa, placing desire at the forefront.

O fortunate one, tell us what was remembered by that wielder of the Pināka bow when he performed this in the past; for at that time, he rendered Ananga bodiless and burned the forest belonging to your father, that mountain.
Indeed, this Śiva, the supreme self of the highest beings, has been propitiated by you alone. || 100 ||
Having been addressed thus by Bhṛṅgin, she, being greatly provoked, spoke while Maheśa was listening; and having been questioned, she replied to Bhṛṅgin. || 101 ||
Pārvatī said: O Bhṛṅgin, because of your partiality, you have spoken such words to me; O dull-witted one, you are indeed a favorite of Śiva, and for that reason you possess a sense of duality.
O fool, I am of the nature of Śiva, and Śiva is eternally established in me; how then can you assert, by the mere power of your speech, a separation between us two? 103.
Then, having heard those auspicious words of Pārvatī, Bhṛṅgin spoke to Pārvatī in the presence of Śiva with indignation.
At the sacrifice of Dakṣa, you heard the censure of Śiva; because of hearing that which was unpleasant, you immediately cast off your body.
"O fair-limbed one, what indeed have you done this very moment? Out of confusion, do you not recognize that he is a reviler of Śiva? (106)
O woman of excellent complexion, how were you born from that best of mountains? And how, O slender-waisted one, have you performed such fierce austerities?
"O slender-limbed one, it has become clear that you possess no loving devotion for Śiva; you are merely dear to Śiva, and therefore I speak thus to you. (108)
There exists nothing higher than Śiva in the three worlds; O woman of excellent complexion, you should cultivate loving devotion toward Śiva.
"You are a devotee, O Great Goddess, the best among those possessed of great fortune; let this [fruit], acquired by you through austerity, be enjoyed with diligent effort. (110)
"Śiva is the most excellent, the Lord of all; you ought not to act otherwise. Having heard the words of Bhṛṅgin, Girijā spoke to him.
Girijā said: "O Bhṛṅgin, observe silence and remain steady, or else depart; you do not know what should or should not be spoken—why do you speak like a ghost?"
By what austerity was this Śiva brought here, and by whom? Who am I, and who is he, that you speak to me with a sense of duality?
"Who are you? By what are you possessed? And why do you speak so much? I shall cast a curse upon you; what can Śiva do now? (114)
Having been addressed thus by Bhṛṅgī, the virtuous lady then cast aside [his plea] and uttered a curse: "O dull-witted Bhṛṅgī, beloved of Śaṅkara, become devoid of luster, you fool! (115)
Having spoken thus, the goddess Pārvatī, beloved of Śaṅkara, was then filled with anger toward Śaṅkara.
Taking hold of the serpent Vāsuki with her hand, that slender-limbed woman likewise drew him from her throat, as well as many others.
Enraged, she quickly seized the ornaments of Śambhu; she took away his crescent moon and his unsurpassed elephant hide.
The two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara, who were adorned by Maheśa, were indeed carried off by that Great Goddess with a laugh and through deceitful words.
Laughing at her with deceptive words regarding the covering of her loincloth, the Gaṇas and her friends were then indeed tormented by shame.
And Bhṛṅgī, of great asceticism, became averse to others; likewise did Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, Mahāloma, and Mahodara. (121)
These and many other hosts became miserable; seeing them in such a state, Maheśa was filled with shame. || 122 ||
Enraged, Śaṅkara spoke these words directed toward Pārvatī.
Rudra said: "Indeed, all the sages, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and these others such as Indra, are laughing at me excessively. (124)
"O auspicious one, what have you done today that has made us all objects of ridicule? O slender-limbed lady, born as you are in a noble family, how could you act in such a manner? (125)

"O fair-browed one, if you truly know that I have indeed been defeated by you, then do this for me: give me the supreme covering of a loincloth. Give me only my loincloth; you ought not to act otherwise. (126)
Having been addressed thus by that yogi Śambhu at that time, Pārvatī, with her beautiful face, smiled and spoke these words.
"What need have you for a loincloth, you sage of purified soul? For it was by being clothed only in the directions that Dāruvana was thus established. (128)
Under the very pretext of wandering for alms, the wives of the sages were awakened; O Śambhu, go there, for a great worship was performed by them for you at that time.
"The loincloth fell there; it was not stated otherwise by the sages. Therefore, you must abandon it, for it has indeed been lost at gambling. (130)
Having heard that, the supreme lord Rudra became enraged; looking at Pārvatī with extreme fury, he gazed upon her with his very third eye.
Seeing Śaṅkara enraged, all the hosts of gods as well as the young attendants were then overcome with great fear.
There, they all spoke slowly to one another with apprehension: "Today, Rudra has become angry toward Girijā."
"Just as Madana was burnt, so it is with this; these words are not otherwise. Thus did those hosts and celestial sages deliberate at that time.
Having been gazed upon by that goddess with her seal of auspiciousness, Satī then spoke laughingly to that virtuous man.
"Having become intent on light with my supreme eye, I am indeed neither Time, nor am I Desire, nor am I the sacrifice of Dambha. (136)

"O Śambhu, neither Tripura nor Andhaka exists; O Bull-bannered One, what will come of that glance of yours today? You have become truly 'Virūpākṣa' (the deformed-eyed one) in my presence for nothing at all. (137)
The Supreme Goddess spoke these and many other such words; having heard her words, the Lord set his mind upon departing.
In the ultimate sense, even a solitary forest is better today; for one who is alone, with mind and self restrained, having renounced all possessions. (139)
He who is free from desire and passion is happy, he knows the ultimate truth; he is the wise one, he is the scholar. He who is liberated is truly happy.

Having reflected thus, the supremely compassionate Śrī Śaṅkara then abandoned Girijā; separated from his beloved, he went to the wonderful forest of Siddhāṭavī, which was likewise inhabited by Paramahaṃsas.
Seeing Śaṅkara departed, all the inhabitants of Kailāsa and all the Gaṇas, led by Vīrabhadra, followed after him.
Bhrṅgin, taking up the parasol, followed behind him, while two fly-whisks resembling the Gaṅgā and Yamunā were being waved.
Then the wise Nandin followed behind them, while the bull, adorned with the Puṣpaka chariot, went ahead.
Shining with all these most beautiful [ornaments], Mahādeva appeared resplendent; yet the goddess Pārvatī, remaining within the inner apartments, was indeed dejected in spirit.
There, well-surrounded by many female companions as well as others, Girijā meditated in her mind upon the Supreme Lord.
Then Śambhu, having dismissed Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, Vīrabhadra, and others, as well as his hosts (gaṇas), went a great distance away.
Bhṛṅgī, Nandin, Caṇḍa, and Somanandin—these and all the others who dwell in the city of Kailāsa.
And having dismissed them, Mahādeva, the great ascetic Śiva, went alone a long distance to the edge of the forest to Siddhavaṭa.

Variegated with Kāśmīra saffron, precious stones, perfected gems, and lapis lazuli, and adorned with white plaster, a divine seat was prepared for him by the Earth; there the Great Lord, the Master of Yoga, took his place. (150)
Seated upon the lotus posture, Maheśa, the supreme knower of yoga, closed his eyes and meditated solely on the Self by means of the self.
That Great God, the moon-crested one, shone in meditative absorption; he made the high-souled Śeṣa his yogic belt, and the great Vāsuki, king of serpents, was bound around his waist. 152.

He who is praised as the Self by the very nature of the Self, who is the one to be known through the Vedāntas, and who is not moved by the activities of the universe; who is indeed both one and many, whose further shore is difficult to reach, who is worthy of worship, and whose form is innate consciousness—the sole Lord of the worlds remained at that time, beholding the Supreme among the supreme.
Lomaśa said: When Mahādeva had gone to the forest, the slender-limbed Girijā, distressed by separation, found no happiness either in palaces or in her own chambers.
The slender and beautiful woman meditated upon Śiva with her whole being; perceiving that Śivā was thus reflecting, her friend Vijayā spoke to her.
Vijayā said: "O beautiful one, you have attained Śiva through great asceticism; that ascetic Śaṅkara has played at dice deceitfully."
O sinless one, have you not heard of the many evils inherent in gambling? O slender lady, O wise one, forgiveness is auspicious; therefore, be patient with haste.
"O Goddess of beautiful countenance, go, go together with us. || 5 ||
Before Śambhu comes from afar, go to him and ask Śaṅkara for forgiveness; otherwise, O timid one, if you do not seek Śiva’s pardon, suffering will surely befall you later.
Having heard the words spoken by Vijayā, she, smiling and with a steady mind, spoke these words—both marvelous and endowed with ultimate truth—to her friend Vijayā. (7)

"He was defeated by me and is now shameless; indeed, he was previously chosen with supreme splendor. I have no further task remaining, for he has immediately been rendered deformed and deprived by me. (8)
"I have personified the god Maheśa; speak not otherwise! Between me and him, neither separation nor union ever occurs. (9)
Indeed, Maheśa, who is both with form and without form, has been made manifest by me.

"I have created this entire universe in its completeness, including all moving and non-moving beings together with the best of gods; behold my victory as I sport for the sake of play, by means of these causes for the manifestation of this world. (11)
Having spoken thus, the goddess Girijā, the source of all auspiciousness, then assumed the form of a Śabarī woman, desiring to approach Maheśvara.

Dark-complexioned, slender, with teeth like mountain peaks, her lower lip like the bimba fruit, endowed with a beautiful neck, bent by the weight of her breasts, Girijā has glossy hair; she is thin at the waist, with broad hips, golden plantain-like thighs, and fair skin; she is adorned with a braid, excellent bracelets, and a crest of peacock feathers. (13)

Holding in her hand a bow resembling a lotus stalk, with a shining quiver of artificial ketaki arrows upon her back, that fair-faced woman, attended by many companions, gazed there at the Lord who was without a consort.
Making the three worlds resound with her great humming like a bee, Girijā brought Manmatha back to life again and again.
At that very moment, the royal swans became filled with desire; likewise, all the bees and peacocks were possessed by love. (3516)
There, Maheśvara was seen by that goddess standing alone and established in self-restraint (yama), having been deluded by the humming sound of the bhrṅgin insect.
For Mahādeva, having gazed upon Śabarī at that time, was bound [by her]; Maheśa, filled with passion, immediately rose from his meditative absorption.
As soon as he, having approached Girijā, was about to seize her by the hand, Satī suddenly vanished from before him.
Having seen that, at that very moment, Lord Śambhu, the destroyer of delusion, while wandering about, did not see the dark-eyed lady.
Then Śambhu, the enemy of Madana, who is the embodiment of knowledge, was constantly possessed by longing and filled with desire due to that separation.
Free from delusion though having fallen into delusion, he beheld Girijā again; he spoke these great words to Śabarī, appropriate to the occasion.

Śiva said: "Listen to my words, O slender-limbed one; having heard them, you ought to act accordingly. Who are you, whose are you, O slender-limbed one, and for what purpose do you wander in the forest? Let that be told in truth, O highly fortunate one of beautiful waist. (23)
Śiva said: "I shall seek a husband who is omniscient, the bestower of all objects, independent, changeless, and the supreme lord of the worlds."
Thus addressed, the bull-bannered god replied this to Girijā: "O auspicious one, O beautiful lady, I alone am a worthy husband for you; indeed, no other is."
"O lady of excellent hips, O fair-faced one, let this be reflected upon according to its true nature. Having heard these words of Rudra, she spoke with a smile:
"O illustrious one, you have been requested by me as my husband; do not speak otherwise. However, I shall say this—blessings be upon you—you are devoid of merit, O scorcher of foes."
Indeed, she by whom you were formerly chosen through supreme asceticism—that passionate lady was abandoned by you in the forest in a mere moment.
"You are always difficult to propitiate for all living beings; therefore, what you have spoken before me must certainly not be repeated. (29)

Having heard Śabarī’s words, the bull-bannered Lord replied: "Do not speak thus, O large-eyed one; that ascetic woman has not been abandoned by me. O slender one, if she had indeed been abandoned by me, what could possibly be said here?"
Knowing this, O large-eyed one, that he is miserable and fond of those who are miserable, you must therefore carry out my word, O slender-waisted lady. (31)
Thus entreated in many ways by the wielder of the trident, the Daughter of the Mountain laughed and spoke these words, full of derision.
O Lord of Yogis, you are a treasury of austerity; you are dispassionate and stainless. You indeed delight in the Self, free from dualities, by whom Madana was destroyed.

You, who are Virūpākṣa himself, have indeed been seen by me today in person. For you are impossible for me to attain, being insurmountable for all; therefore, you must not speak that which was previously said to me.
Having heard those words of hers, the Destroyer of Madana (Śiva) said: "Become my wife indeed; you ought not to act otherwise."
Having spoken thus, he, afflicted by passion, seized the Śabara woman by the hand; she, smiling, spoke to him respectfully, saying, "Release me! Release me! (36)
"O Blessed One, it is not fitting for you, an ascetic, to take this by force. Beg it from my father; otherwise, you shall not prevail. (37)
Mahādeva said: "O lady of auspicious countenance, tell me quickly where your father is staying; O large-eyed one, I shall see him preceded by prostrations. (38)
Having heard this spoken by him at that time, she of the dark eyes said: "Indeed, that slender woman has brought Vṛṣabhadhvaja here to her father. (39)
He saw Himavat, the best of mountains, situated on the peak of Kailāsa, surrounded by many serpents and possessing great luster.
She showed him, who was standing at the gate, to Śaṅkara, saying: "O God, ask my father without shame; he will give me to you, there is no doubt. O ascetic, do not delay! (41)
Thinking "so be it," he quickly bowed to Himālaya and spoke these words: "O best of mountain lords, O high-minded one, grant that auspicious maiden today to me, who am afflicted."
Having heard those piteous words, Himālaya rose up and, taking Maheśa with him, the King of Mountains himself spoke.
"What are you saying, O Lord? That is indeed improper at this time. You are the giver in the three worlds; you are the sovereign of the worlds, O All-pervading One. (44)

"This entire universe, this world of moving and non-moving beings, is pervaded by you. Thus did the great mountain Himālaya become intent on offering praise. Then Nārada arrived there, surrounded by sages.
Laughing, he spoke these words: "O Lord, salutations to you, O wielder of the trident! O Śambhu, listen to my supreme speech, which consists of the essence of reality. (46)

Association with women leads to the mockery of men; you are the Lord of the worlds, the Master, the highest of the high, and the Supreme beyond the supreme. O Lord of Gods, having reflected upon everything, you ought to speak accordingly.
Thus enlightened by that high-souled Nārada, Śambhu attained awakening and the Supreme Lord laughed.
Śiva said: "O Nārada, what you have spoken here is true and never otherwise; by the mere company of women, men surely fall. (49)
There will be no doubt; your word shall not be otherwise. Deluded by her today, I have been brought to Gandhamādana.
This most wonderful deed was performed like that of a Piśāca. || 51 ||
"Therefore, I shall not remain near the mountain; I shall go this very day once more to another forest. Having spoken thus, he set out upon a path difficult to traverse, inaccessible even to yogis.
Having realized that [the Lord] was without support, Nārada quickly spoke these words to Girijā, the Lord of Mountains, and his attendants.
He is worthy of salutation and praise; let him be forgiven in the ultimate sense. This is Maheśa, the Lord of the World, the enemy of Tripura, possessed of great glory. (54)
Having heard these words emerging from the mouth of Nārada, the mountains of great splendor placed Girijā before them.
All the Pramathas, Guhyakas, and others fell prostrate like staffs before Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, and, bowing down, they all offered praise.
For the Blessed One, being praised, arrived at Gandhamādana; indeed, the Lord of All was consecrated there by the high-souled Aṅgirases.
Then the kettledrums resounded and many musical instruments were played; all the gods, headed by Indra, rained down a shower of flowers.

Surrounded by many hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā, the Lord of Yogins, who is worshipped by the entire universe, sat together with Girijā upon a divine throne; requested by those most auspicious blessings, he shone with great majesty.
O Brahmins, such are the many deeds of the Great-Souled Maheśa, which remove the sins of those who hear them.
Whatever great deeds of Rudra there are here that have been heard as supreme, what more shall I tell you? (61)
The sages said: "O Sūta, this life-story of Śaṅkara has been told by you; we are undoubtedly fully satisfied by this very account. (62)

Sūta said: By the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard all this—the wondrous form of Śaṅkara that is pervasive, most extensive, containing the marvels of the Vedas, consisting of knowledge, and supreme. Thus has it been spoken.

Those who, endowed with supreme faith, cause this beloved of Śiva to be heard, and those who listen with devotion to the wonderful majesty of Śambhu—those who recite this scripture of Śiva with affection attain the state of the Immortal.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Coronation of Śiva’s Kingdom Performed by Bṛhaspati," following the account of how Pārvatī, in the form of a Śabarī, led Śiva to Mount Gandhamādana, within the Śiva-śāstra of the Kedāra-khaṇḍa, in the first Māheśvara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 35 || || cha ||
Thus ends the first section, the Kedārakhaṇḍa, in the first part, the Māheśvarakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 1 ||
The venerable sages said: O large-eyed one, tell us of those five sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist on the shores of the southern ocean; describe them, for they are highly praised.
We desire to hear the greatness of the deeds of those whom Nārada and others declare to possess the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).

Ugraśravas said: Listen to this wonderful, meritorious, and virtuous narrative concerning the great power of Kumāranātha, which Dvaipāyana formerly told me, his limbs covered with horripilation born of joy.
O best of sages, let the verses sung by Kumāra be heard here, which are honored by all the gods, sages, and ancestors.
That man who would constantly resort to that holy ford, Madhvācāra-tīrtha, his residence shall surely be in the world of Brahmā, just as mine.
From the world of Brahmā comes the world of Viṣṇu, and from that, the world of Śiva; yet because he is dearer than a son, the world of Guha is even greater than his.
O best of sages, I shall relate to you in detail that wonderful story of Phālguna which was previously told by Nārada.
Formerly, on a certain occasion, Karīṭī went from Maṇikūṭa to the southern ocean to bathe at the five sacred fords (tīrthas).
Those holy fords which ascetics always avoid out of fear—there, to the east of Kumāreśa, is a ford dear to the sage.
The second is Stambheśa, which is dear to the sage Saubhadra; another is Barkareśvara, the most excellent, which is dear to Paulomī.
The fourth is Mahākāla, beloved by King Karaṃdhama; and the fifth is indeed the Bharadvāja Tīrtha, known as Siddheśa.
The bull among the Kurus beheld these five sacred fords, which were highly meritorious yet devoid of ascetics.
Seeing the great sages belonging to Nārada by his side, he asked them about these delightful holy fords (tīrthas) which possess wonderful powers.
"For what reason are these always avoided by the exponents of the Veda? The ascetics replied: "Five crocodiles dwell within them and carry off those whose wealth is their penance. (14)
"Therefore, O joy of the Kurus, these sacred fords (tīrthas) are to be avoided. Having heard this, the mighty-armed one set his mind upon departing. || 15 ||
Then the ascetics said to him: "O Phālguna, you ought not to speak thus; many kings as well as sages have been devoured by crocodiles."
Even if one were to bathe in tens of millions of sacred fords for twelve years, what would be the use of these holy places? Do not become one who follows the vow of a moth [falling into fire].
Arjuna said: Let that essence which was spoken by those whose very core is compassion be stated here: a man who seeks dharma and artha should not be obstructed by high-souled beings. (18)
Indeed, the dull-witted person who obstructs a human being who desires the Dharma will be reduced to ashes by the sighs of the world that depends upon him. (19)
If this life, which is as fragile as a momentary flash of lightning, is spent for the sake of Dharma, let it go; indeed, what fault could there be? (20)
Those men on earth for whose sake life, wealth, wives, sons, fields, and houses are sacrificed for the sake of Dharma—they alone [truly live]. (21)
The ascetics said: "O Pārtha, as you speak thus, may your long life increase; may you always have delight in dharma. Go now and accomplish what you desire. (22)
Having been addressed thus, that best of the Bharatas bowed to them and, being honored with blessings, departed to visit those sacred fords.
Then, having reached the Saubhadra, the supreme tirtha of the great seer, the hero, the scorcher of foes, plunged in with speed and performed his ablutions.
Then, while he was within the water, a great crocodile dwelling in the depths seized that tiger among men, Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī.
Taking hold of that quivering aquatic creature, the mighty-armed son of Kuntī, the best among the strong, rose up by his own power.
And that crocodile, having been pulled out by the illustrious Arjuna, became a beautiful woman adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
The Brahmins, possessing divine forms and beautiful to behold, had flaming crests; seeing that great wonder, Dhananjaya, the son of Kunti, [was amazed]. (28)
Filled with supreme joy, he spoke these words to that woman: "Who indeed are you, O auspicious one, and from where have you come as a dweller of the waters? (29)
"And for what purpose have you committed this great sin? The woman replied: "O son of Kuntī, I am indeed an Apsaras who dwells in the forest of the gods. (30)
O mighty one, I am named Varcā, the constant beloved wife of Dhanapati; I have four other auspicious friends, all of whom can travel wherever they desire.
Accompanied by them, I set out from the abode of the king of the gods; then we all beheld a brahmin who was without a fixed dwelling.
O hero, that forest was indeed pervaded by the splendor of the ascetic power of that handsome man, who was studying alone and wandering in solitude.
Like the sun, he illuminated that entire region; having seen his asceticism of such a nature and its wondrous appearance, [the people were amazed]. (34)
I, Saurabheyī, Sāmeyī, and Budbudālatā have descended to that place with the desire to create obstacles to his ascetic penance.
O Bhārata, we approached that brahmin simultaneously, singing, sporting, and enticing that twice-born man.
That hero did not direct his mind toward us in any way; possessed of great splendor, he did not waver, remaining steadfast in his pure austerity.
Enraged at us, O bull among Kṣatriyas, that Brāhmaṇa cursed us: "You shall become crocodiles in the water for a hundred years. (38)
Then, O best of the Bharatas, we were all deeply distressed and approached that sinless Brahmin, whose wealth was his asceticism, for refuge. (39)
Proud indeed because of our beauty, our youth, and our passion, we have acted improperly; O twice-born one, you ought to forgive us.
O ascetic, this alone is sufficient punishment for us—that we have come to seduce you, whose soul is so highly praised. (41)
Those who contemplate dharma consider that women were created as beings not to be slain; therefore, O knower of dharma, this is the teaching of the wise regarding righteousness.
The virtuous provide protection to those who have sought refuge; we have come to you, the worthy refuge, as our protectors—therefore, you ought to forgive us. (43)
Thus addressed, that righteous-souled Brahmin, a performer of auspicious deeds, who possessed a splendor like that of the sun and moon, showed his favor to the hero.
The Brāhmaṇa said: I am bewildered in my mind by your conduct. Oh, what audacity! Oh, what delusion—that you should proceed toward such sin! (45)
If this person were to see death standing right upon his head, even food would not be pleasing to him, let alone the performance of improper deeds. (46)
Ah! Among all births, a human birth is the most difficult to obtain; yet it is treated like a blade of grass by certain foolish women who are difficult to restrain. (47)
We questioned them: "What is the cause of your birth? Or what is the gain [therein]? Having reflected upon this with the mind, let it be told. (48)
We do not revile these women from whom birth proceeds; we revile only those who are unrestrained toward them. (49)
Since this pair was created by the Lotus-born One for the increase of the universe, it must indeed be protected accordingly; there is no fault whatsoever in this. (50)
She who is given by her kinsmen in the presence of the sacred fire and the twice-born—blessed indeed is the maintenance of the householder's life with her, for it bestows all things.
Just as a union between a man and a woman, according to their innate natures, may lead to excellence even when pursued with effort, yet leads to failure if not so pursued. || 52 ||
Thus, one's own excellent state of household life, when accomplished with effort, shall lead to great merit; yet, if left unaccomplished, it leads even to demerit. (53)
Pure, stationed at the five gates, accompanied by eleven soldiers, together with his wife and many offspring—how could he be insentient? (54)

Alas! That union with women and the performance of the five great sacrifices and other rites, which were created for the benefit of the entire world, are instead pursued by fools in a contrary manner.
"Alas! Listen, unless a pure desire to hear us arises in you; nevertheless, we shall raise our arms and wail aloud—who will listen? (56)
Having abandoned that vigor which was the essence of the six elements and remained constant, Yama spoke this regarding its casting into a wretched womb: || 57 ||
First the betrayer of medicinal herbs, then the betrayer of himself, then the betrayer of his father, and finally the betrayer of the universe—he goes to the blinding darkness for eternal years.
The ancestors, the gods, the sages, as well as human beings and all living creatures, subsist upon him; therefore, one should remain self-restrained for their sake.
One who is self-controlled through speech, mind, tongue, hands, and ears is said to possess the true sacred ford; any other is merely a "crow-ford."
In that man who is like a crow, the people of darkness find delight; what purpose could there be for the gods in considering him to be a swan? (51)
For one who thus remembers in their heart the creation of the universe, how could the mind take pleasure even in committing a sin against the three worlds? (62)
"Alas, women! This very thing, seen in the scriptures regarding other mortals, has now been witnessed by me directly in the world of Yama; how can I not be bewildered? (63)
And what anger can there be toward you, for those things by which one is created perform their intended purpose—whether it be true or even false.
"Śata," "sahasra," and "viśva" are all synonyms for "all" and denote the inexhaustible; however, "parimāṇa" and "śata" alone do not denote the inexhaustible. || 65 ||
And when you have become crocodiles, seizing men in the water, some most excellent man shall pull you out from the water onto dry land. (66)

Then you shall all regain your own forms; never before have I spoken an untruth, even in jest. For just as the purification of a well-bonded auspicious thing is excellent, so too is this for you, O noble ladies.
The woman said: Then, having saluted that brahmin and performed a circumambulation of him, || 68 ||
Having departed from that place, deeply distressed, they reflected: "Where indeed might we all find that man in a short time? (69)
"O Bhārata, having reflected here for a mere moment on who among us might restore our own forms, we [reappeared]. (70)
Then they all beheld the illustrious celestial sage Nārada; having seen that celestial sage of immeasurable splendor, they all thought, "We have truly seen him."
Having saluted him, O Pārtha, we stood there with distressed faces; he questioned us regarding the root of our sorrow, and we spoke it to him.
Having heard that according to the truth, he spoke these words: "In the marshy region of the southern ocean, there are indeed five sacred fords (tīrthas)."
Go to those meritorious and delightful places without delay; staying there, Dhananjaya, that tiger among men, the Pandava, will protect you.
That pure-souled one will liberate us from this suffering; of this there is no doubt. O hero, having heard his words, we have all come here.
O Pāṇḍava, you ought to make this word of truth; for the birth of virtuous men such as yourself is for the sake of assisting the distressed. (76)
Having heard her words, that son of Pāṇḍu bathed in the sacred fords in succession and rescued those who had become crocodiles, restoring them to their former states.
Then, having bowed to that hero while pronouncing blessings of victory, and being desirous of departing, Pārtha Dhananjaya spoke:
This very firm doubt revolves within my heart: why did the sage Nārada permit you two to go into exile? (79)

How is it that Nārada, though he is anyone at all and even extremely lowly, has proclaimed his residence in the sacred fords of his own worshipful deity, thereby accomplishing the purpose of that worshipful one? (80)
Likewise, while Navadurgās and Atibalā are present, as well as Siddheśa and Siddhagaṇapa, how can your residence be here? (81)
For each one of them individually was indeed capable of warding off even the gods; how then did she not ward off all those who were obstructing the sacred ford? 82.
As I reflect thus, my mind wavers greatly; great curiosity has arisen within me, so you ought to tell me whether this is true. (83)
The Apsarases said: "O son of Kuntī, you ask what is fitting; look again toward the northern direction."
Sūta said: Then that Pāṇḍava, having approached Nārada—who was surrounded by twice-born brahmins and honored by the gods—paid homage to him and all of them.
Then Nārada said to him: "O Dhanañjaya, conqueror of enemies, your intellect is fixed upon dharma, upon the gods, and upon the Brahmins."
O Hero, while performing this great twelve-year journey, are you not thus wearied, nor do you feel any resentment? (3)
O Pāṇḍava, even the minds of sages are distressed and agitated during pilgrimages because of the root cause of obstacles to their spiritual welfare.
O Pāṇḍava, I hope you have not been seized by this fault; for in this regard, we have heard this verse sung by Aṅgiras: || 5 ||
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained, and all whose actions are free from agitation, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
This you must bear in your heart; or what do you think, dear brother, of him whose friend is Yudhiṣṭhira and whose companion is Keśava? (7)
Furthermore, it is fitting that the instruction of men should be given by Brahmins; for we have been established as teachers of Dharma by that Viṣṇu.
And here we hear a verse sung by Viṣṇu concerning the twice-born.

I am that very person, O Vikuṇṭha, whose immersion in the hearing of your stainless nectar-like fame instantly purifies the world from the outcaste onwards; I, whose renown as a holy place has been attained by you, who would even cut off my own arm if it were acting in opposition.
And we speak what is pleasing to you, O Pārtha, for we desire your welfare; all those Yādavas and likewise the Pāṇḍavas are well.
Now, by the command of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, King Vīravarman—the oppressor of the Kurus—has been slain by Bhīmasena. 12.
For he was indeed invincible among kings, just as the powerful Bali was in former times; Dhṛtarāṣṭra conquered him, as one thorn might overcome another thorn.
Having heard these words spoken by Nārada, Phālguna was exceedingly delighted and said, "How could there be any misfortune for them? (14)
Those who always follow the opinion of the Brahmins, those who worship the Brahmins, and I myself, being constantly restrained by my own power, wander through the sacred fords.
Having come to this sacred ford, there is indeed exceeding joy in my heart; the sight of sacred fords is blessed, and immersion therein is even more so. (16)
"Therefore, even the sage Aurva spoke of listening to its greatness; O Sage, I wish to hear those virtues of this sacred ford."
O Sage, that which you have accepted must indeed be proclaimed by this very means; for as you wander through the three worlds, you know the essential nature of everything.
I consider this, which has been taken away by you, to be superior to all other sacred fords.

Nārada said: O Pārtha, it is fitting for you, who possess virtues, that you inquire about virtues; for it is only those endowed with virtues who are worthy of hearing the qualities born of righteousness. Through daily listening to the dharma and the recitation of the praises of the virtuous, one progresses day by day.
Just as the lives of the wicked pass away day by day through improper speech, so shall I proclaim the many virtues of this sacred ford.
"O Pārtha, as you have heard and understood, this was indeed accepted by me; formerly, while wandering through the three worlds following Kapila, I [spoke thus]. (22)
I went to the world of Brahmā, and there I beheld the Grandfather; he was indeed surrounded by royal sages and celestial sages, both embodied and unembodied.
The stainless Brahmā shone like the moon among the stars; having prostrated before him, I was then welcomed by his gaze.
Seated there with Kapila, he was filled with joy; meanwhile, messengers arrived at that place.
For they were constantly being dispelled by Brahmā as he beheld the world; then, once they had offered their salutations and were seated, the Grandfather [spoke].
As if flooding them with eyes that were like nectar, he said: "Where have you searched? Have you seen anything, or even heard anything? (27)
"Tell me some wonderful thing, by hearing which merit may be gained. When the Blessed One had spoken thus, he who was considered the most eminent among them [replied]:
Having prostrated before the Brahmin named Suśravas, he spoke these words: "Before the Lord, this is my petition; it is like a lamp compared to the sun. (29)
Nevertheless, urged by you for the sake of others, I must indeed speak; having heard many further teachings on the Dharma from the sage named Kātyāyana. (30)
Desiring to know its essence, he stood on one big toe for a hundred years; then a divine voice spoke to him: "O Kātyāyana, listen! (31)
On the holy bank of the Sarasvatī, inquire of the sage Sārasvata; he, who knows the dharma, will declare to you the essence that is to be accomplished through dharma.
Having heard this, the excellent sage approached that best of sages, prostrated with his head upon the ground, and asked this which was dwelling in his heart.
Some praise truth, while others likewise praise austerity and purity; some praise Sāṃkhya, and others declare Yoga to be supreme.
Some praise forgiveness, and likewise others highly extol straightforwardness; some praise silence, while others say that sacred learning is supreme. (35)
Some praise right knowledge as supreme, others regard dispassion as the highest; likewise, some consider rituals such as the Agniṣṭoma and others to be the ultimate.

Some consider self-knowledge to be supreme, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal; such being the state of the world, people remain uncertain regarding what ought and ought not to be done.
They fall into utter delusion, asking "What is the highest good?", yet that which is the supreme duty among these must be performed by the high-souled ones. (38)
O knower of dharma, you should tell me that which accomplishes all my goals.

Sārasvata said: Listen to that essence which Sarasvatī spoke to me: this entire world is a mere semblance of shadow, subject to the laws of birth and destruction; it is as transitory as the flickering of a courtesan’s eye.

Having thoroughly reflected with his intellect upon wealth, life, youth, and enjoyments—which are as unstable as the moon reflected in water—one should take refuge in the gift of a pillar (sthāṇudāna). || 41 ||
"A man who gives gifts is not capable of committing sin"—such is the Vedic revelation; likewise, "one devoted to Sthāṇu does not undergo birth and death"—such is the Vedic revelation. (42)
And two verses were recited by Sāvarṇi; hear them as they were formerly told: "The Blessed One is indeed Dharma, the Bull, whose vehicle is the bull. (43)
He is worshipped as Mahādeva; he is said to be the supreme Dharma, within the terrible whirlpool of suffering, where the waters are both merit and demerit.
In the mire of anger, where pride is the crocodile and greed the treacherous bubble, with the profound abyss of arrogance and adorned by the vehicle of sentient beings; || 45 ||
Hara alone rescues one who is drowning from the ocean of worldly existence; likewise, he saves one's charity, conduct, vows, speech, fame, merit, and lifespan.
One should extract the essence from this essenceless body by means of helping others: passion for the Dharma, reflection upon the scriptures, and an excellence of devotion toward giving. (47)
Having attained a human birth in this land of Bhārata—a birth that is transient—the fruit of one's existence is the attainment of detachment from the objects of the senses. (48)
One should not act so as to deceive oneself for a long time; for among all the gods and asuras, the human state is exceedingly difficult to attain. (49)
Having attained that [human birth], one should act in such a way that one does not go to hell; for human birth is the root of everything and the means for accomplishing all goals. (50)
If you have no concern for gain, then protect the root with great effort; for with the precious price of merit, this boat of a body has been purchased by you.
Cross over to the further shore of the ocean of suffering while this immutable state of the body has not yet been shattered; for once it is destroyed, that state is indeed difficult to attain again.

That lowest of men, who destroys himself, does not escape from saṃsāra. Here ascetics perform austerities, and here sacrificers offer oblations; and here gifts are bestowed with devotion for the sake of the next world. (53)
Kātyāyana said: "O Blessed One, what is difficult to perform—either giving or austerity? Or what yields great fruit after death? O Sārasvata, tell me that. (54)
Sārasvata said: "O Sage, there is nothing on earth more difficult than giving; this is directly perceived and witnessed by the world. (55)
Indeed, for the sake of wealth, out of great greed they abandon their dear lives and enter the ocean, the forest, and the mountains, despite the great danger.
Others resort to service, which is remembered as the "dog's livelihood," while still others take up agriculture, which is full of violence and involves much suffering. (57)
The renunciation of that wealth, acquired here through hardship, more precious than life itself, and obtained through hundreds of labors, is exceedingly difficult to accomplish. (58)
Whatever one gives and whatever one eats—that alone is the wealth of the wealthy; others play with the wife and the riches of the deceased. (59)
Day after day, I consider one who begs of me to be like a teacher, for he performs for me a daily polishing, as it were, of a mirror.
For that which is being given does not diminish; rather, it increases all the more. Just as a well, when being drawn from, becomes pure and filled with abundant water. || 61 ||
For the sake of happiness in a single birth, a wise person may squander thousands [of lives]; yet in a single birth, he accumulates [merit] for thousands of births. 62.
For the fool does not give away wealth in this world out of fear of poverty; but the wise man bestows wealth here out of fear of it in the next world. (63)
What will embodied beings, whose refuge is fragile, do with wealth? That very body for the sake of which they desire wealth is impermanent. (64)
Those two syllables—"na asti," "na asti"—which were practiced in the past, have now appeared in their reverse form as "dehi," "dehi. (55)
And as many people as there are who piteously say "Give," they awaken [the donor]; such is the state resulting from not giving—may you never become like that.
The seeker says "Give to me" for the benefit of the giver alone; for by this, the giver goes upward while the receiver remains below. (67)
Those who fail to give gifts are born poor, diseased, and foolish, always performing service for others; indeed, they become vessels of suffering alone. (68)
A wealthy man who is uncharitable and a poor man who lacks austerity—both should be cast into the water with a great stone tied around their necks.
A hero is born among hundreds, and a scholar among thousands; an eloquent speaker among hundreds of thousands, but a donor may or may not even be born at all.
The earth is sustained by these seven: by cows, by learned brahmins, by the Vedas, by virtuous women, by speakers of truth, by those free from greed, and by those whose nature is generosity. (71)
Śibi, the son of Uśīnara, having offered his own limbs and his beloved biological son for the sake of a Brahmin, departed from here to the heights of heaven.
Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī, having given his own eyes to a Brāhmaṇa, enjoys incomparable fame both in this world and in the next.
Nimi gave his kingdom to the Vaidehas, Jamadagnya gave the earth to the Brahmins, and Gaya likewise gave the earth with its cities to the Brahmins.
And when the rain-cloud did not pour forth, Vasiṣṭha, who provides a dwelling for all beings, sustained them like Prajāpati sustaining his subjects.
And King Brahmadatta, the ruler of Pañcāla and the best among the wise, having given the treasure Śaṅkha to the foremost of the twice-born, attained heaven. (76)
The royal sage Sahasrajit, of great renown, having renounced his own dear life for the sake of a Brahmin, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
These and many others, peaceful in soul and having conquered their senses, went eternally to the world of Rudra through their devotion and gifts to Śiva. (78)
"The fame of these shall remain established as long as the earth endures. Thinking thus, you who seek the essential truth, become intent upon the gift of a *sthāṇu* (an immovable pillar). 79.
Having likewise abandoned delusion, he became like Kātyāyana. || 80 ||
Nārada said: Having heard this story thus narrated by Suśravas, the Lotus-born One (Brahmā), filled with tears of joy, praised it again and again.
"Well spoken by you, my child; it is exactly so and not otherwise. Sarasvata spoke the truth, and the Veda likewise declares this to be true. (82)

"Charity is the protection of sacrifices; in this world, all beings depend upon the giver. By means of charity they drive away enemies; by means of charity those who hate become friends. Everything is established in charity; therefore, they say that charity is supreme. || 83 ||
In the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, crowded with the waves of merit and demerit, one should practice generosity there; for it is fashioned like a ship. (84)
Having reflected thus, I established the twice-born in Puṣkara; and the twice-born were settled in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa) between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers. || 85 ||
The most eminent knowers of the Vedas were established by Śrī and Hari; the Nāgaras by Rudra; and those born in Śaktipur by Pārvatī. (86)
And likewise in Śrīmāla, by Lakṣmī and other such foremost gods, various agrahāras were bestowed with the desire for the upliftment of the world. (87)
Indeed, O best of gods, there is no desire whatsoever for the fruit of giving; for it is proclaimed that our giving is solely for the sake of protecting the virtuous. (88)
And the Brāhmaṇas, having established themselves through various instructions on Dharma, uplift the other three castes; therefore, the twice-born are most worthy of worship. (89)
Giving is fourfold: giving, renunciation, as well as that which is prepared, and that which is promised; these various types are proclaimed in their respective order. (90)
The dedication of step-wells, wells, and tanks; of trees, learning, and temples; and of monasteries, water-stations, houses, and fields—this is known as *utsarga*.
And whatever other person lives by these [gifts] and performs meritorious deeds, he obtains a sixth part of the merit, provided that the twice-born man who gave them releases them [for his use]. (92)
Therefore, the supreme establishment of all these very [beings], as well as the establishment of the gods, is dharma, since it is rooted in that alone. (93)
As far as a temple of the gods extends, and as far as a brahmin’s house extends, so far does a share of merit accrue to the deceased ancestors of the donor. (94)
Indeed, this trade is very small, yet it yields abundant fruit; and in the case of restoring what is decayed, this very same activity is proclaimed to yield double that result. (95)
Therefore, O best of gods, I too say this: there is nothing equal to giving; thus Sārasvata sang the truth.
Nārada said: Thus, when these words were spoken by Sarasvatī and likewise uttered by the Lotus-born Brahmā, the gods and I, greatly amazed, rejoiced, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (97).
Then, at the conclusion of the assembly's dismissal, sitting upon the surface of a rock on the most beautiful summit of Mount Meru, I reflected as follows: (98)
Virañci has spoken the truth; but for what purpose does he live, since not even one of those deeds has been performed by him through which one attains fulfillment?
Therefore, how indeed shall I clearly perform the merit of giving? Possessing only a loincloth, a staff, and my own self as my wealth, I have truly no small amount of riches. (100)

That which one gives to the undeserving, and likewise does not give to the deserving—because of this failure to discern the worthy from the unworthy, the dharma of giving is indeed difficult to perform. (101)
He who gives at the proper place and time, to a worthy recipient, with a pure mind, and that which has been acquired through righteous means, enjoys the fruit of that gift in his youth. (102)
But he who, enveloped by darkness, gives out of anger likewise, indeed enjoys the fruit of that gift while remaining in the womb; of this there is no doubt. (103)
Even in his childhood, he consumes that which was given for the sake of hypocrisy, as well as wealth acquired through unjust means for the sake of material gain.

For in old age, a man indeed consumes [the fruits of his deeds]; this shall not be otherwise. Therefore, at the proper place and time, and toward a worthy recipient, a person should employ what has been righteously earned with faith and free from deceit, according to the prescribed rule. (105)
"And how indeed will this come to pass, given our poverty? Truly, the pure ancient sages spoke these words long ago: || 106 ||
For one who is destitute, neither this world nor the next exists in any way; people look with contempt upon a poor man standing even at their side. (107)
In this world, poverty is a sin; who could possibly praise it? One who has fallen is mourned by all, and one who is destitute is likewise mourned. (108)
He who has meager horses, meager wealth, meager servants, and meager guests—he indeed is called "meager" (kṛśa), not he whose body is meager. || 109 ||
Even a man born of a low family is most worthy of honor in the world if he possesses wealth; whereas one who is destitute is despised, even if his lineage is equal to that of the moon. (110)

Those who are advanced in knowledge, those who are advanced in austerity, and those who are advanced in great learning—all of them stand at the door of one who is advanced in wealth like servants. (111)
Although this object in the three worlds is not dear to us as anything else, nevertheless, when requested by another, it alone becomes the bestower of its fruit. (112)
"Or rather, I shall first consider all of this very clearly; for now, let me look for some suitable location. (113)
Having reflected thus in many ways upon countries, villages, cities, and hermitages, I wandered extensively and indeed found a suitable place where I might establish the Brahmins.
Sūta said: O best of heroes, Nārada, thus wandering here and there upon this earth, beheld whatever holy places existed here on the ground.
Wandering over the entire earth, I arrived at the hermitage of Bhṛgu, where the excellent and holy river Revā flows, which preserves the memory of seven kalpas.
Greatly meritorious, pure, consisting of all sacred fords, and auspicious, she purifies by mere mention and especially by sight.
O Pārtha, by immersing oneself there, a living being is liberated from sin, just as that piṅgalā channel is situated within the center of the body.
This is proclaimed to be in the place of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍapiṇḍa); there, on the Revā river, lies the sin-destroying site known as Śuklatīrtha.
O Pārtha, in its very vicinity, on the northern bank of the Revā, even the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa is destroyed by merely bathing there.
It was crowded with various kinds of trees, adorned with creepers and shrubs, endowed with diverse flowers and fruits, and decorated with groves of plantain trees.
It was filled with many beasts of prey, made resonant by birds, richly adorned with the beauty of fragrant flowers, and made to ring out with the cries of peacocks.
Just as bees abandon everything and settle down together with their humming, so too does a devotee abandon the cycle of worldly existence and settle at the feet of Hara.
The cuckoos cause the sages to resound with their sweet notes, just as the Brahmins [console] those who fear worldly existence with the nectar-like narrations of sacred stories.
There, the trees gladden with their fruits, flowers, and leaves, as well as with their shade and wood, just as those who observe the vow of Hara gladden the worlds.
Where birds fond of their young cry out "Son! Son!", just as devotees of Śiva, who are dear to Śiva, constantly call out "Śiva! Śiva! || 12 ||
Such was the hermitage precinct of that sage Bhṛgu, adorned on all sides by Brahmins well-versed in the three Vedas.
The quarters of the sky were filled with the resonant sounds of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, just as the three worlds are pervaded by a steadfast devotee of Rudra.
There, O Pārtha, I arrived where that best of sages resided—Bhṛgu, whose soul is supremely righteous and whose radiance is illumined by asceticism. || 15 ||
But seeing me approaching, both dejected and yet joyful, all the brahmins, led by Bhrigu, rose from their seats to greet me.
Having offered a warm welcome and presented the guest-offering (arghya) and other honors along with Bhṛgu, I had those lords of sages seated upon their thrones.
Then, perceiving that I was rested, Bhṛgu spoke to me as well: "O best of sages, where are you to go, and for what reason have you come here? (18)
"Explain clearly the entire reason for your arrival. Then, overcome with anxiety, O son of Pṛthā, I spoke to Bhṛgu. (19)
Listen, for I shall declare the purpose for which I have come here. I have traversed the entire earth, bounded by the oceans.
Seeking at every step land for the purpose of gifting it to the twice-born—land that was faultless, pure, and even endowed with sacred bathing places (tīrthas).
"I do not see any beautiful or pleasing land anywhere. Bhṛgu said: "In the past, while I was wandering about for the purpose of establishing brahmins," (22)
O sinless one, the entire earth as far as the ocean was then seen; there was a holy river named Mahī, auspicious and consisting of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Divine, delightful, gentle, and the destroyer of great sins—that very Earth exists there in the form of a river; of this there is no doubt. (24)
O Nārada, whatever holy places exist on earth, whether seen or unseen, they all reside right there in that great water.
That great river of holy waters reached the ocean; there, O celestial sage, the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean was formed.
There is a sacred site there known as Stambha, renowned throughout the three worlds; those wise men who perform their ablutions there—
"Those who are completely liberated from all sins do not indeed approach Yama; for a wonder was seen by me there in the past when I had gone to bathe."
Therefore, O Sage, listen as I recount this great wonder: how far I went to bathe at this confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. (29)
I beheld the Lord of Sages standing on the bank, resembling a blazing fire—tall, aged, reduced to mere skin and bone, yet adorned with the splendor of his asceticism.
Then, raising my arms and weeping again and again, I became sorrowful upon seeing him so distressed.
"For this indeed is the characteristic of the virtuous: that upon seeing a person in distress, one should feel it as if it were one's own; thus did I lament. (32)
"Non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing are difficult to find even when one possesses human birth; therefore, having approached him at that time, I questioned him. (33)
"O sage, for what reason do you weep? What is the cause of your grief? Even if it be a great secret, tell me; for my desire to know is very great. (34)
Then the sage said to me, "O Bhṛgu, I am unfortunate; that is why I weep. Do not ask me, for who would speak of their own misfortune? (35)
Overcome with wonder, I spoke this once again to him: "Birth in Bhārata is difficult to obtain, and even there, human status is rare. (36)

Within the human state, the status of a Brahmin is difficult to attain, and within that, the state of a sage; even there, the perfection of asceticism is rare—having attained these five supreme conditions, [one should strive for liberation].
"For what reason do you weep, O sage? This is a source of great wonder to me. Even as he was questioning me in this manner, at that very moment—
A sage named Subhadra arrived there; for he had abandoned Mount Meru, having recognized the essential excellence of that sacred ford.
Having established his hermitage, the sage constantly worshipped Stambheśvara; he too, thus questioning me, asked the sage the cause of his weeping.
Then, having sipped water, that sage said: "O sages, listen to the cause; for I am a sage named Devaśarman, with speech and mind restrained. (41)
I dwell, having established my abode, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean; there I always offer libations and gratify the ancestors.
At the conclusion of the śrāddha, they appeared before my very eyes and pronounced blessings upon me. Then, on one occasion, the ancestors, being greatly delighted, spoke to me: ||| 43 ||
"We always come here into the presence of Devaśarman; why is it, O son, that you never come to our place? (44)
Desiring to see that place, yet unable to restrain myself, I then said, "It is supreme," and departed along with my ancestors.
The meritorious abode of the ancestors is situated on the earth; and wherever I was stationed there, I saw those who were difficult to behold due to their circles of radiant splendor.

Seeing those richly adorned ones before me, I asked my own ancestors: "Who indeed are these who approach, so thoroughly satisfied and so highly honored? They are exceedingly joyful, not at all like you. (47)
The ancestors said: "Blessings upon you! We, the meritorious ancestors of the great sage Subhadra, have been gratified by that sage at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. (48)
At that place where the earth, containing all sacred fords, is submerged in the ocean, the auspicious son Subhadra gratifies those ancestors during the new moon.
Having heard their words, I was then deeply ashamed and filled with wonder; bowing down to these ancestors, I returned to my own abode. (50)
Whatever I have thought in this manner, there I shall certainly go—to that famous and meritorious confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
Having established my hermitage right there, I shall offer libations to my own ancestors on every new-moon day, just as this auspicious one of praiseworthy name does.
Of what use is that sinful wretch, a disgrace to his lineage, who, while he lives, even his own parents must harbor longings for another? (53)
Having reflected thus, he spoke joyfully to his wife Ruci: "O Ruci, joined by you, [let us go] to the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. (54)

"Having gone there, I shall remain right there; you must quickly appear before me. O illustrious lady, you are devoted to your husband, pure, and of noble birth; therefore, O auspicious one, you ought to fulfill this wish of mine. (55)
Ruci said: "O wicked one, how was his birth not destroyed by that evil-souled man?"
"O pillar of the cremation ground, since I have been given to you for your service, what need is there that is not fulfilled here by subsisting on roots and fruits? (57)
If you wish to take me to that place where there is always salt water, then you yourself go there; let your ancestors rejoice!
"Go, or stay, O old man, or live as long as a crow; while she was speaking thus, I covered my ears. (59)
Having dispatched my many disciples, I came here alone to my home; there, devoted to faith, I bathed and offered libations to the ancestors.
He fell into a state of immense anxiety, like a wrongdoer in hell, thinking: "If I remain right here with only half my body remaining... (61)
For a man deprived of his wife is considered to be only half a body; just as without the self, no function whatsoever can be accomplished by the body. (62)
For the fruit of these two is to be grasped; there is no essence whatsoever here [in the body]. And a human being who possesses only half a body is considered untouchable by the virtuous. (63)
For the fruit of these two alone is to be grasped; there is no essence whatsoever here [elsewhere]. And a man who possesses only half a body is considered untouchable by the virtuous. (64)
Indeed, Auttānapādi has been made untouchable by the gods; if I were to go there, then Mahīsāgara would not exist.
Or rather, how is it that my feet move at all? My mind is pierced and distressed within this crisis of ignorance.
"Therefore, I am utterly bewildered; I grieve intensely and weep. Having heard these words of his, [the sage] was filled with a great thrill of horripilation.
Then Subhadra also said to him, "Excellent! Excellent! and likewise prostrated himself like a staff before the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
And both of us reflected in our minds upon a remedy for the sage, for he, having attained this human state which is as fragile as a bubble on the water— (69)
"This man exists for the sake of others; others are merely like excrement. Having reflected thus, Subhadra spoke these words to the best of sages: || 70 ||
"Do not weary yourself, O Sage Devaśarman; be steadfast. I shall destroy your sorrow, just as the sun destroys the darkness. (71)
"I shall go to the hermitage, and you will not be abandoned even here; hear the reason for that, for I shall offer libations to the ancestors on your behalf. (72)
Devasharman said: "Since you desire to perform such a great and impossible task for my sake, may your life last for a hundred years as you speak thus. (73)
And yet, even at a time for joy, despondency again afflicts me; listen, O Sage! Even virtuous people do not accept auspicious words in vain. (74)
"O you who speak in vain, how can I cause such a great task to be performed? I shall tell you something more so that there may be atonement for me. (75)
"You are bound by me under oath; do exactly as I say. I shall always perform the rites for the ancestors on the new moon day. (76)

"Perform here a śrāddha for my ancestors at the ocean of the Gaṅgā; and I too shall grant you a fourth part of the merit accumulated through my asceticism over this lifetime—perform it exactly thus. (77)
Subhadra said: "If this is your satisfaction, O Lord of Sages, let it be so; for one who understands, an action should be performed in such a way that it brings joy to the virtuous."
Bhṛgu said: Then Devaśarman, being delighted, gave the merit of the three-fold recitation and went to his own abode, which is a fourth part [of the merit]; Subhadra also remained there.
O Nārada, such is that confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, remembering which even now my hair stands on end. (80)
Nārada said: Having heard this, O Phālguna, with a voice faltering with joy, I spoke like one returned from death, saying "Excellent! Excellent! to that Bhṛgu.
"You and we shall go to the most beautiful riverbank; the two of us will behold that entire, unsurpassed place. (82)
Having heard these words of mine, Bhṛgu went with me to the entire, highly meritorious bank of the Mahī, which had been surveyed.
Seeing that, I was exceedingly delighted, my body covered in horripilation; O tiger among sages, I spoke to him with a voice faltering with joy. (84)
"By your grace, O Bhṛgu, I shall establish an unsurpassed station; please go to your own abode, O Brahmin, so that I may deliberate upon what must be done next. (85)

Having thus dismissed Bhṛgu on that shore, which was filled with the clamor of surging waves, I then sat down and reflected upon what ought to be done, like a solitary yogi contemplating his own self.
Nārada said: Then I reflected, "How might this place come under my control? For this earth is always subject to the will of kings."
If I were to go to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and beg for the earth, they would surely grant it to me when requested; but not so another. (2)
For thus it has been declared by the sages: substance is of three excellent kinds; the white is called middling, and the variegated is said to be the lowest.

That which is obtained from a pupil through the teaching of the Vedas, that which is received from a daughter-in-law as a white gift, as well as what is gained through usury, trade, agriculture, and begging; || 4 ||

That which is acquired through gambling, theft, acts of violence, or by means of deceit is called *śabala* (variegated) by the virtuous; that which is obtained through fraud is declared to be *kṛṣṇa* (black).
He who, endowed with faith, performs a righteous act with white wealth, having encountered a worthy recipient at a sacred site, attains that same state in the realm of the gods.
One should give gifts to supplicants with a passionate disposition and with variegated wealth; one experiences the fruits of that in the human state.
But that lowest of men who, enveloped by darkness, gives with black wealth, reaps the fruit of that action after death while in the state of an animal.
That wealth obtained by begging would clearly be of a rajasic nature for me; therefore, I shall ask the king for a gift while maintaining my status as a brahmin. (9)
Even that, alas, I consider to be an exceedingly painful cause for me; this terrible acceptance of gifts is like the taste of honey that is comparable to poison. (10)
For through the acceptance of gifts, disease enters a twice-born man; therefore, I have desisted from this sinful act of accepting gifts.
"Therefore, by some means or other, let us make one of the two positions our own; this I have reflected upon again and again. (12)
Just as a man with a wicked wife does not reach the end of his anxieties, even so, though I reflect upon it, I do not find even a slight end to my concerns.
In the meantime, O Pārtha, many sages gathered there at the meritorious confluence of the Mahī and the ocean to bathe.
I said to them all, "From where have you come? Having bowed down to me, O Sage, they replied, "In the region of Saurāṣṭra... (15)
The king who was the sovereign of this land, named Dharmavarman, sought the true essence of charity and performed austerities for many series of years.
Then a voice in the sky spoke to him: "O King, listen to this one verse: It has two causes, six substrata, six limbs, and is endowed with two results. (17)
"Generosity is said to be of four kinds, three types, and three ways of destruction. Having spoken this single verse, the voice in the sky fell silent.
O Nārada, even though he was questioned, he did not explain the meaning of the verse; thereupon King Dharmavarman caused it to be proclaimed by means of a drum.
But to him who provides a correct exposition of this very verse obtained by me through ascetic penance, I shall grant this as well. (20)
I shall grant seven hundred thousand cows and an equal amount of gold, as well as seven villages, to whoever provides a commentary on this verse.
O Sage, having heard these great words of the king through the sounding of drums, millions of Brahmins from many lands arrived.
Furthermore, O Sage, that verse with its difficult arrangement cannot be explained by those eminent brahmins, just as a ball of molasses cannot be described by the mute.
O Nārada, we went there out of greed for wealth; however, because it was difficult to understand, we paid our respects and returned here with this verse. (24)
This verse is difficult to explain: "Wealth is not to be obtained by us, nor indeed is it [already] ours; 'How shall I go on pilgrimage?'—thinking thus, we have come here. (25)
O Phālguna, having thus heard the words of those great-souled ones, I was exceedingly delighted; and after dismissing them, I thought as follows: || 26 ||
