"Aha! A means for me to attain a position has been found; of this there is no doubt. By explaining a verse to the king, I shall obtain both a position and wealth. (27)
"Nor should such acceptance be requested for the price of knowledge; the ancient seer Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, has truly said this. (28)
He who has faith in the Dharma shall find it never fails to be fulfilled; he who has faith in evil shall likewise find that it never fails to be fulfilled. (29)
Having reflected thus, the wise act according to their inclination; for this word of the Lord is true, even as it was difficult for me to obtain.
This desire has clearly become fruitful and has sprouted; and I know this verse, which is difficult to understand, with perfect clarity. (31)
"Indeed, this was previously proclaimed to me long ago by the formless ancestors. O Pārtha, having reflected thus repeatedly with a heart full of joy, I then spoke.
Having prostrated before the holy ford, I set out for the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; then, assuming the form of an elderly Brahmin, I went to the king.
"I have spoken this; O King, listen to the explanation of the verse. Prepare that gift of yours which is renowned throughout the land by the sound of the drum. (34)
When this was said, the king spoke: "Indeed, millions of the best of the twice-born have spoken thus; however, it is possible to state the meaning [of the word] *nasyam* once again. (35)
What are the two causes? What are the six declared bases? What indeed are the six limbs? And what are the two maturations as they are traditionally taught? (36)
O twice-born one, what are the four types [of gifts], and what indeed are those three? What are said to be the "destructions of milk"? Explain this clearly regarding giving. (37)
"O Brāhmaṇa, if you can answer these seven clear questions, then [I shall give] seven hundred thousand cows and an equal amount of gold."
"Otherwise, you shall go to your own home; I will give you seven villages," O Pārtha, having spoken these words to the king, the lord of Saurāṣṭra.
"Let it be so for Dharmavarman; listen as I speak. I shall explain the verses clearly; hear also those two reasons for giving. (40)
Whether small or great, a gift brings about prosperity; yet it is faith and the capacity [of the donor] that cause gifts to increase and become inexhaustible. (41)
In this regard, there are verses concerning the object of faith: "Neither by many bodily afflictions nor by heaps of unfulfilled desires... (42)
The subtle Dharma is attained through faith; faith is Dharma, and faith is wondrous austerity. Faith is heaven and liberation; faith is this entire world.
If one were to give away all one's possessions and even one's very life without faith, one would not obtain any fruit at all; therefore, one should be full of faith.
Dharma is accomplished through faith, not by vast hoards of wealth; for the sages, though possessing nothing, have gone to heaven by means of their faith.
The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds; it is born of their own nature. Listen to that: it is sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. (46)
Those of sattvic nature worship the gods; those of rajasic nature worship the yakṣas and rakṣasas; and those of tamasic nature worship the pretas, bhūtas, and piśācas.
Therefore, whatever has been earned by righteous means and given to a worthy recipient by one possessed of faith—even if it be very little—by that alone the Blessed Lord Rudra is satisfied. (48)

And there are verses regarding the scope of one's capacity: "That which remains in excess of what is required for the clothing and food of one's family should be given; otherwise, the donor's merit becomes like poison following a taste of honey. (49)
One who gives to strangers when he has the means, while his own kin live in misery, is like one who drinks honey only to find it turns to poison; such a person is a mere counterfeit of the righteous.
Whatever one performs for the sake of the afterlife by oppressing one’s dependents results in unhappiness for that person, both while living and after death. || 51 ||

A common property, a requested loan, a deposit, a pledge, one's wife, a viewing [of goods], a secondary deposit, a formal entrustment, and one's entire estate—these may not be taken when there is a male descendant. (52)
Even in times of distress, the wise should not give away these nine things; the man who gives them is a fool of soul and must undergo penance.
Thus, O King, these two causes have been declared to you; now hear from me further. I shall describe the six substrates; listen to them as well. (54)
Dharma, wealth, and pleasure, as well as modesty, joy, and fear—these six are declared to be the foundations of gifts. (55)
That which is given constantly to worthy recipients without regard for any ulterior motive, solely with the thought of performing a duty, is called the gift of dharma (dharmadāna).

One should induce a wealthy person to give by tempting them with greed for wealth and then take the object; this they call "giving for the sake of that [wealth]. Now hear about "giving according to desire. (57)
That which is given out of attachment to unworthy recipients, motivated solely by a specific purpose or as a consequence of some other matter, is called the gift of desire (kāmadāna). || 58 ||
When one gives to supplicants in an assembly out of shame, or when a gift is given back after having been received, that is known as the "gift of shame" (vrīḍādāna). || 59 ||
That which is given with joy upon seeing or hearing pleasant things is called "the gift of joy" by those who contemplate the Dharma. (60)
That which is given to those who do not return the favor, for the sake of countering abuse, misfortune, and violence, is called the gift of fear. (61)
The six bases have been declared; now hear also the six ancillaries: the giver, the recipient, purity, the gift, and that which is joined with dharma. (62)

The wise know these six to be the constituent factors of gifts: the place, the time, and [the recipient], as well as one who is free from disease, righteous in soul, desirous of giving, free from vices, and pure. (63)

One whose livelihood and actions are beyond reproach is praised as a donor when endowed with these six qualities; whereas one who is crooked, lacking faith, unpeaceful in soul, audacious, or timid [is not].

This lowest of men, characterized by darkness (tāmasa), is untruthful in his word, prone to sleep, and a miserly giver; yet he is pure in three respects, possesses a meager livelihood, is compassionate, and has all his senses intact. (65)

One who is liberated from the defects of birth is called a Brahmin and a worthy recipient. Always showing a cheerful countenance and manifesting great joy upon seeing those in need, as well as offering hospitality and being free from envy—that is traditionally known as purity.
Wealth acquired by one's own effort, without harming others or causing distress—whether it be small or vast—is said to be "what ought to be given. (67)

It is said that even by means of that dharma, something should be given with a specific recipient in mind; for that is considered the pair of dharmas, whereas in the case of an empty [recipient], the fruit is held to be empty.
Wealth that is difficult to obtain even at a particular place or time is rare; yet, those two—place and time—are excellent for giving only when they are appropriate, and not otherwise. (69)

These are called the "sixfold groups," and now hear about the two types of ripening (pāka). They say there are two kinds of ripening born of giving: that which occurs in the next world and that which is said to occur in this one.
Whatever is given to the virtuous stands by one in the next world; whatever is given to the wicked, that gift is enjoyed here in this world.
Two types of cooking have been specified; now hear the four varieties in their proper order: the obligatory (dhruva), the triad (trika), the optional (kāmya), and the occasional (naimittika). (72)
This Vedic path of giving is described by the twice-born as being fourfold; it certainly yields the fruit of all desires, such as water-stations, gardens, and tanks.
Regarding this, they say: "They call it *trikā* (the threefold gift) that which is given day after day; it is bestowed for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, women, and children. (74)

And that gift which is established in desire is designated as "kāmya" (motivated by desire); it is recorded in the Smṛti as being dependent on time, dependent on ritual action, and dependent on qualities.
The occasional [vow] is said to be of three kinds, always excluding the fire-oblation (homa). Thus the types have been declared; now their threefold classification is being described.
Eight are the best, four are middling according to the rule, and the remaining ones are the smallest; they know this to be the threefold classification.
A house, a palace, knowledge, land, cattle, a well, life, and gold—these are the supreme gifts, because they consist of the giving of supreme substances. (78)
Food, gardens, garments, and vehicles such as horses—these are called "middling gifts" because they consist of middling substances. (79)
Shoes, an umbrella, a vessel, curd, honey, and a seat; || 80 ||
Lamps, wood, stones, and so forth, as well as that which lasts for many years—these are called "inferior" gifts; now hear of the three types of lost gifts. (81)
That which, having given, one later regrets is considered an Asuric gift and is in vain; that which one gives without faith is Rākṣasa and is likewise useless.
O dear one, that which one gives after reviling, or having given, reviles the twice-born—that gift is of the Piśāca type; these three are the destructions of a gift.
Thus, O King, the supreme greatness of giving, bound together in these seven verses, has been recounted by me according to my ability; say whether it is well done or not.
Dharmavarman said: "Today my birth has become fruitful; today my asceticism has become fruitful. Today I have accomplished my purpose, O best among the wise. (85)
Just as one who remains a celibate student throughout his entire life does so in vain, so too is she a vain wife, obtained through great hardship, who speaks only unpleasant words.
Just as one might laboriously dig a well that contains only brackish water in vain, so too is a life spent amidst many afflictions in vain, devoid of Dharma. (87)
Thus, that which was born as my name "Vṛthā" (in vain) has been made fruitful by you; therefore, salutations to you, and repeated salutations to the twice-born.
In former times, Viṣṇu spoke the truth to the Kumāras in the abode of Viṣṇu.

I do not consume with such satisfaction the sacrificial oblation, dripping with ghee and poured into the fire by the officiant, as I do when eating the remnants of the food from the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa who is contented and whose own karmic fruits have been directed toward me.
Whatever unpleasant thing has been done by me, even through distress, toward the Brahmins—since Brahmins are the lords of all, may they forgive that; I seek their favor.
"And who are you? You are no ordinary person; bowing down, I seek your favor. Reveal yourself, O Sage. Thus addressed, he then spoke.
Nārada said: "O best of kings, I am Nārada, who has come seeking a place to stay. It was said [by you], 'Give me wealth and land for the sake of a dwelling. (93)
Although this land belongs to the gods and the wealth is the king's, nevertheless, it is certain that at whatever time a particular king is to be petitioned, he is the one to be approached.

He is an incarnation of the Lord of Lakshmi, a husband, and a giver of fearlessness; likewise, I entreat you with the desire to obtain pure wealth—being intent on my prayer for the sake of what must be given—first grant me a dwelling.
The king said: "O Brahmin Nārada, if you are [the master], let the entire kingdom be yours; for I shall undoubtedly perform service to you, as I do for the Brahmins. (96)
Nārada said: "If you are devoted to us, then this task must be performed by you at our word. (97)

"Give me all that wealth which was mentioned, and seven gavyūtis of land; let the protection of this [wealth] be from you as well. He agreed, saying, 'I too shall think of the remainder of the matter.'"
Nārada said: Then, having spoken to Dharmavarman—saying, "The wealth shall remain with you; I will take it at the time of need"—I went to the Raivata mountain.
And I was filled with joy as I beheld that best of mountains, which, like the upraised arm of the earth, seemed to be calling out to virtuous men. || 2 ||
In which various kinds of trees shine forth on all sides, just as sons, wives, and others do upon reaching a virtuous householder.
Where the cuckoos and other birds warble with full satisfaction, just as the hosts of disciples on earth who are endowed with knowledge [rejoice] under a true guru. || 4 ||
Where mortals, having performed austerities, obtain their desires just as they wish, even as a devotee attains his heart's desire upon reaching the illustrious Mahādeva.
O Pārtha, having reached a great rock on that mountain, we were refreshed by the gentle, cool fragrance, and I reflected thus in my heart: || 6 ||
I have attained a station that is exceedingly difficult to reach; now, for the sake of the Brahmins, I shall undertake this endeavor.
And those Brāhmaṇas whom I consider to be the most worthy recipients—I have indeed heard such words regarding them from the exponents of the Vedas. (8)
Just as a boat devoid of a helmsman is incapable of crossing the waters, so too a Brahmin, though most excellent, is unable to deliver others if he lacks proper conduct.
For a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas is extinguished like a fire of straw; one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes. || 10 ||
Whatever is given to an unworthy recipient by bypassing a worthy recipient of gifts is like giving a cow’s daily fodder to a donkey after passing over a cow.
A seed sown in salt-waste, a cowherd’s vessel broken, or an oblation poured into ashes—such is the impermanent gift given to a fool.
If one gives a gift to an unworthy recipient or in a manner devoid of ritual injunctions, not only does that gift go to waste, but one's remaining merit is utterly destroyed. (13)
The earth is obtained, as well as cattle, enjoyments, gold, and the body itself; likewise the horse, the eye, clothing, clarified butter, splendor, sesame seeds, and progeny. (14)
Therefore, they destroy [the merit of] the ignorant; thus, one should fear accepting gifts from them. Even by a very small amount, the ignorant man sinks like a cow in the mud. (15)
Therefore, that which is given to those who have secret austerities, who practice secret Vedic study, who are devoted to their own wives, and who are peaceful, is always inexhaustible.
Whatever substance, endowed with faith, is given to a worthy recipient at the proper place and time through the right means—all that is characterized as dharma. || 17 ||
Neither by knowledge alone nor even by austerity is one a worthy recipient; that in whom both of these, as well as right conduct, reside—that indeed they declare to be a worthy recipient.
Among those three, knowledge is the primary great virtue; for without knowledge, O Brahmins, they are considered blind, whereas with it, they are truly possessed of sight.
Therefore, let the wise one with sight examine every region; those who will answer my questions, to them I shall give [the reward] from that. (20)
Having reflected thus in my mind, I rose up from that place; O Phālguna, I am now wandering through the hermitages of the great sages.
Listen to these verses in the form of questions as they are being sung: "Who understands the Mātṛkā? In how many ways does it exist, and what is its nature of syllables? (22)
"O twice-born one, who indeed understands that house of five times five wonders? And who is able to make a woman of many forms into one of a single form? (23)
Who, dwelling within the realm of worldly existence, understands the composition of this wondrous narrative? Or who, devoted to sacred knowledge, understands this great crocodile of the ocean? (24)
Who, then, is the best of Brahmins who knows the eightfold nature of Brahminhood? Or who can declare the root days of the four ages? (25)
Who knows the root-day of the fourteen Manus, or on which very day the Sun first obtained his chariot? (26)
Who knows who can terrify living beings like a black serpent? Or who could be the most skillful in this terrible cycle of existence? (27)
"Two paths—does some Brāhmaṇa know them and speak of them? These are my twelve questions; other excellent Brāhmaṇas know them. (28)
"They are most worthy of my worship, and I am their great devotee for a long time"—singing thus indeed, I wandered over the entire earth. (29)
And they said, "We pay homage to those who are known as givers of suffering; these are the questions we shall address. Thus, having searched the entire earth, I failed to find a Brāhmaṇa.
Seated upon a peak of the Himalaya mountains, he again fell into reflection: "All the Brahmins have been examined; what should I do next? (31)
Then, as I was reflecting, this thought arose within me once more: "Even now, I have not gone to the excellent village of Kalāpa."
In that place dwell eighty-four thousand Brahmins, who are distinguished by their learning and study of the Vedas, appearing like the very personifications of ascetic penances.
Having said, "I shall go to that place," I then set out; moving through the air, I traversed the Himavat and reached the further shore.
I beheld a great jewel of a village situated on a ground of merit, extending for a hundred yojanas and filled with various kinds of trees.
There, hundreds of excellent hermitages belonging to the meritorious exist; there, among all living beings, there is no mutual malice.
That which always brings benefit to the sages who partake in the sacrifice is such that the benefit to those virtuous and righteous ones never ceases.
Wherein there is the supreme abode of the sages, which is imperishable; where the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭ, and Hantakāra never perish.
In that place, O son of Pṛthā, the seeds for the sake of the Kṛta Yuga shall remain—those of the Solar dynasty, the Lunar dynasty, and likewise of the Brāhmaṇas. (39)
Having reached that place, I entered the hermitages of the twice-born; there, those best of the twice-born were debating various arguments.
Meditating upon one another like the Vedas personified, some among them there were wise men who [perceived] the meaning fulfilled by others.
The great-souled ones scattered [the food] like a piece of meat in the sky; thereupon, raising my hand, I said, "O twice-born ones, let it be filled! (42)
What is the use of these cawings of yours, if you possess the state of being wise? Then explain my many questions, which are difficult to withstand. (43)
The Brahmins said: "Speak, O Brahmin; having heard your questions, we shall attend to them. For it is a supreme gain for us that you ask us questions. (44)
They indeed obstructed one another by taking precedence, saying, "I first! I first! just as heroes do on a battlefield.
Then I asked them those twelve questions from before; having heard them, those lords of sages replied to me while playing.
"O twice-born one, what is the use of these childish questions of yours, however small they may be? Let him who considers our conduct to be inferior speak to them. (47)
Then, filled with great wonder and considering myself to have achieved my purpose, yet reflecting upon their lowliness, I said: "Let him speak. (48)
Then that boy, named Sutanu, who was no mere child, spoke to me: "O twice-born one, my voice falters at your many questions; nevertheless, I shall speak because you consider me to be lowly. (49)
Sutanu said: "The syllables of the Mātṛkā are proclaimed to be the devourers of the elephant. (50)
The syllable *oṃ* is the first therein, followed by the fourteen vowels, the thirty-three consonants (*sparśas*), and likewise the anusvāra. (51)
The visarjanīya, the jihvāmūlīya, and also the upadhmānīya—these are remembered as the fifty-two [consonants]. || 52 ||
Thus, O twice-born one, the enumeration has been told to you; now hear their meaning. In this regard, I shall relate to you the ancient legend.
In the city of Mithilā, in the past, there lived a Brāhmaṇa named Kauthuma in the house of another Brāhmaṇa. (54)
O twice-born one, he who has diligently studied the sciences that exist on earth for thirty-one thousand years shall be honored.
Having studied without interruption for even a moment, he became a householder. Then, after some time, there was a son born to Kauthuma.
Behaving like one who is dull-witted, he mastered the alphabet; yet after reading the alphabet, he could not learn anything else by any means. (57)
Then his father, appearing dejected, addressed that dull-witted boy: "Study, my son, study! I will give you sweetmeats."
"Otherwise, I shall give them to another; I will tear out your ears! || 59 ||
The son said: "Father, why is study pursued for the sake of sweetmeats or out of greed? For that which is called 'study' by men is indeed remembered as the supreme goal. (60)
Kauthuma said: "May your life be as long as that of Brahmā for speaking thus; may this virtuous intellect remain yours—why do you not study further?"
The son said: "O father, since all that is to be known is indeed contained within this very knowledge, tell me, why do you undergo such parching of the throat beyond this?"
The father said: "O child, you speak wonderfully; what meaning have you understood here? Speak, speak again, my dear son; I wish to hear your words. (63)
The son said: "O father, although you have studied thirty-one thousand various systems of logic, only delusion has been established within your own mind. (64)
Regarding those phenomena that arise in vision as "this" and "that," your mind behaves like the wind toward them; therefore, I shall destroy that for you.
You merely recite the instruction, yet you do not truly know its meaning; for those Brahmins who are mere reciters are indeed two-legged beasts.
I shall tell you those words, which are a wondrous sun that dispels delusion.
The letter A is said to be Brahmā; the letter U is called Viṣṇu; and the letter M is remembered as Rudra—these three are known as the qualities (guṇas). || 68 ||
And that half-mora at the summit is the supreme Sadāśiva; such is the greatness of the syllable Om, according to this eternal Śruti.
The greatness of the syllable Oṃ cannot be described in its true essence even in ten thousand years or by means of ten million books.
Furthermore, listen to that supreme essence which has been proclaimed: those fourteen mantras begin with the letter 'a' and end with the syllable 'aḥ'. (71)
Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Auttama, Raivata, Tāmasa, Cākṣuṣa as the sixth, and now Vaivasvata.
Sāvarṇi, Brahmasāvarṇi, Rudrasāvarṇi, Dakṣasāvarṇi, and Dharmasāvarṇi as well. (73)
Raucya and Bhautya—these are the fourteen Manus. Śveta, Pāṇḍu, Rakta, Tāmra, Pīta, and Kāpila; || 74 ||
Kṛṣṇa, Śyāma, Dhūmra, Supiśaṅga, Piśaṅgaka, Trivarṇa, Śabala, and Karkaṃdhura by color—in this sequence. (75)
O dear one, Vaivasvata and the letter *kṣa* are seen as Kṛṣṇa; from the letter *ka* to the letter *ha*, there are thirty-three deities.
The twelve Ādityas are recorded as beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ṭha*: Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Śakra, Varuṇa, and Aṃśu; || 77 ||
Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Savitṛ as the tenth; likewise Tvaṣṭṛ as the eleventh, and Viṣṇu is called the twelfth. (78)
He was the youngest of all the Ādityas, yet superior to them in qualities; and there were exactly eleven Rudras, beginning with the letter 'ḍa' and ending with the letter 'ba'.
Kapālī, Piṅgala, Bhīma, Virūpākṣa, Vilohita, Ajaka, Śāsana, Śāstṛ, Śambhu, Caṇḍa, and likewise Bhava. (80)
Indeed, the eight Vasus are considered to begin with the letter *bha* and end with the letter *ṣa*: Dhruva, Ghora, Soma, Āpa, Nala, and Anila. (81)
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa—these are remembered as the eight Vasus; and Sauha and [Sahasa] are known as the two Aśvins; these are remembered as the thirty-three [deities]. || 82 ||
The anusvāra, the visarga, the jihvāmūlīya, and the upadhmānīya—these are the viviparous and the egg-born. (83)

Thus, living beings are proclaimed to be of two kinds: those born from sweat and those born from sprouts. This has been stated as the meaning of the categories; now hear the true nature of reality (tattvārtha).
Those men who, devoted to ritual action, take refuge in these deities, indeed become absorbed in that eternal state which consists of the half-measure.
One is liberated from the four wombs of living beings at that very moment when one has worshipped the gods through mind, speech, and action.
That scripture in which these gods are not honored by the sinful should not be accepted as authoritative, even if Brahmā himself were to speak it. (87)
And these gods are established everywhere upon the path of the Śruti; they are forbidden everywhere in the heretical scriptures by those of sinful deeds.
Transgressing those [prescribed duties], these evil-minded ones perform asceticism, charity, and recitation; even the wind trembles on their path.
Oh, behold the greatness of delusion among those who have not conquered themselves! These sinners recite the Mātṛkā, yet they do not acknowledge the gods here.
Sutanu said: Having heard these words of his, the father became exceedingly amazed; he asked many questions, and he (the son) answered them accordingly.
I too have explained this excellent question regarding the Mātṛkā to you; now hear the second question concerning the house of five times five wonders.
The five elements, the five organs of action and the five organs of knowledge, the five objects of the senses, as well as mind, intellect, and the ego—these alone [are my manifestation]. (93)
Prakṛti and Puruṣa, along with Sadāśiva as the twenty-fifth—by these five sets of five, this is said to be the completed house.
He who knows this body as it truly is goes to Śiva; the exponents of Vedānta call the intellect "the woman of many forms. (95)
For she, by resorting to various objects, assumes various forms; yet, through her union with a single dharma, though manifold, she remains truly one.
He who knows the true meaning of this in such a way shall not fall into hell; nor shall he go to hell who does not believe in those things that have not been proclaimed by the sages or by the gods.
The wise declare that speech which is full of varied tales to be bondage; now hear also about the fifth type, which is speech accompanied by desire.
Greed alone is the great predator; from greed evil proceeds. From greed anger arises, and from greed desire comes forth. (99)
Delusion, deceit, pride, arrogance, malice toward others, ignorance, and lack of wisdom—all these proceed from greed. (100)
The seizing of others' wealth, the violation of others' wives, and likewise the performance of all acts of violence and forbidden deeds; || 101 ||
That greed, along with delusion, must be conquered by one who has mastered the self; as well as hypocrisy, malice, slander, backbiting, and envy. (102)
All these qualities belong to those who are greedy and of undisciplined self; even though they may possess great weapons and be highly learned, [they remain as such]. (103)
Those who dispel doubts but are seized by greed go to the lower realms; likewise, those who are addicted to greed and anger are excluded from the conduct of the virtuous.

Those who, endowed with the power of sophistry, create various paths—whose speech is as sweet as honey but whose inner core is like a razor, and who are like wells covered over with grass—[are to be avoided]. (105)
Out of greed, these cruel men destroy every path among the various births; these base individuals, who wear the crest-jewel of dharma and carry its banner, plunder the world.
These should be known as exceedingly sinful, always possessed by greed: Janaka, Yuvanāśva, Vṛṣādarbhi, and Prasenajit. (107)
Other lords of men likewise have attained heaven through the destruction of greed; therefore, those who abandon greed cross over the ocean.
Therefore, those who follow the wrong path are undoubtedly seized by the crocodile known as saṃsāra. Now, O Brahmin, listen attentively to the eight divisions of Brahmins.
Furthermore, there are the Mātra, the Brāhmaṇa, and the Śrotriya; beyond that, the Anūcāna, the Bhrūṇa, the Ṛṣikalpa, the Ṛṣi, and the Muni. || 110 ||
For these eight types of Brāhmaṇas are first designated in the Śruti; among them, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding by virtue of the distinction of their knowledge and conduct. (111)
When one is born into a family of Brāhmaṇas but possesses nothing more than birth, being uninitiated and devoid of sacred rites, he is designated as a Mātra. || 112 ||
Having transcended the single object of desire, being learned in the Veda, upright in conduct, restrained, truthful in speech, and compassionate—he is called a Brāhmaṇa. (113)
Having studied one branch of the Veda together with its ritual manuals and the six ancillary sciences, a Brahmin devoted to the six duties is called a Śrotriya, a knower of Dharma. (114)
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, whose soul is pure, who is free from sin, who is preeminent, learned in the scriptures, and wise—he is remembered as an *anūcāna*.

One who is endowed with the qualities of a learned Vedic scholar, restrained by sacrifice and self-study, who eats only the remnants of the meal and has conquered his senses, is called a *bhrūṇa* by the wise. (116)
He who, having attained all knowledge—both Vedic and worldly—remains constantly self-controlled while established in his stage of life (āśrama), is remembered as being equal to a Ṛṣi. || 117 ||
One whose vital energy is drawn upward becomes foremost, one whose diet is restrained, and free from doubt; capable of both cursing and blessing, such a sage becomes true to his word. (118)

Withdrawn from worldly life, knowing all principles, free from desire and anger, established in meditation, inactive, self-controlled, and regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal—such is the sage.
Thus, those eminent Brahmins known as Triśuklas, who are exalted by their lineage, sacred knowledge, and conduct, are honored at the Soma sacrifices and other rites.
Thus has the nature of the Vipra been described; now hear of the beginnings of the Yugas: the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika is proclaimed as the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga.
The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is called the beginning of the Tretā age; the fifteenth day of Māgha is recorded by the wise as the beginning of the Dvāpara age.

The thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhasya is indeed remembered as the beginning of the Kali Yuga; these are known as the Yugādis, which cause whatever is given on them to become inexhaustible.

One should know that these four lunar days, the beginnings of the Yugas, render whatever is given or offered as a sacrifice immediately inexhaustible. A gift bestowed over a hundred years during each Yuga yields the same fruit as one bestowed on a single day at the time of a Yuga-beginning.

These have indeed been declared as the beginnings of the Yugas; now hear of the beginnings of the Manvantaras: the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, and likewise the twelfth day of Kārttika.
The third day of the month of Caitra, as well as that of Bhādrapada; the new moon day of Phālguna, and likewise the eleventh day of Pauṣa. (126)
The tenth day of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of the month of Māgha, the eighth dark lunar day of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
The fifteenth day of the bright fortnight in the months of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha—these are the beginnings of Manvantaras, which cause what is given to be inexhaustible.
The lunar day on which the divine Sun-god first reached his chariot in the month of Māgha is called Rathasaptamī by the learned brahmins. (129) || 4 || Dra || 4 ||

Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or performed as ritual action upon that [day] is considered entirely inexhaustible; it is regarded as the pacifier of all poverty and as a means for pleasing the Sun. 130.
Listen to the truth concerning that which the wise call "constantly agitating": he who is a constant beggar is not a fit vessel for heaven. (131)
He terrifies living beings just like thieves; that evil-souled one, who causes constant anxiety, goes to hell. (132)

"By what karma was my birth here [attained], and where must I go from here? Having reflected thus, he acted as a remedy; O twice-born one, he is called by the wise "Dvija Dakṣadakṣa" (the most skillful among the twice-born).
With eight months, a day, and the first half of his life and lifespan, a person should perform that action by which he prospers in happiness at the end.
The exponents of Vedānta say that there are two paths: light and smoke. By means of light one attains liberation, and by means of smoke one returns again. (135)
By sacrifices, smoke is reached; by the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya), the flame is attained. The other path between these two is proclaimed as the heretical way (pākhaṇḍa).
He who thinks neither of the gods nor of the duties taught by Manu does not travel upon these two paths; this is the reality as it has been determined. (137)
Thus have these questions been recounted by me according to my ability, O best of Brahmins. Speak whether they are good or bad, and reveal yourself as well. (138)
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard this, O Phālguna, my hair stood on end with thrill; manifesting my true form, I spoke these words to the brāhmaṇas. || 1 ||
"Oh, blessed is our father, whose created beings have protectors such as you, O best of Brahmins! Hari spoke the truth long ago."
Even for me, there is nothing whatsoever beyond the Infinite One, the Supreme Lord of all beings; what then could be gained by others for those lords of the twice-born who proclaim my path? (3)
Therefore, in every respect, I am blessed today; I have attained the fruit of my birth, since I have beheld you all, who are free from the afflictions of sin.
Then those twice-born ones, led by Śātātapa, rose up suddenly and honored me with hospitable offerings such as water for the hands and feet.
And they spoke these words, appropriate for virtuous people, to me, O Pārtha: "We are indeed blessed, O celestial sage, since you have come here to us."
"O best of sages, from where have you come, or where are you to go now? Please tell me the purpose of your arrival here."
O Pāṇḍava, having heard these pleasing words of the twice-born, I replied to those lords of sages: "Listen, O best of the twice-born! (8)
Indeed, at the command of Brahmā, I desire to grant a auspicious abode for the Brahmins at the great tirtha, the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
"Having examined the Brahmins here, I have arrived; you have been tested. O twice-born ones, I shall remain with you, so grant me your permission. (10)
Thus addressed, Śātātapa looked at the twice-born and said: "O Nārada, the Bhārata is truly difficult to attain even for the gods. (11)
Furthermore, right there is the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, where one who has bathed obtains the entire fruit of all great sacred fords.
Furthermore, there is one great danger because of which we are exceedingly afraid: there are very many thieves who are merciless and fond of violence. (13)
"Among our own kin, they do not accept even the sixteenth or the twenty-first part of our wealth. For us who are deprived of that wealth, what kind of life shall we have? (14)
"It would be better to live in hunger than for us to fall into the hands of thieves. Arjuna said: "O Brahmin, you describe something wonderful; who indeed are proclaimed to be thieves? (15)
"What wealth do these robbers carry away from whom the Brahmins are afraid? Nārada said: "Lust, anger, and the like are the thieves; asceticism alone is their wealth. (16)
Fearing the loss of their water, those brahmins said this to me; I then replied to them, "O best of the twice-born, discern this for yourselves. (17)
What indeed can wicked thieves do to men who remain awake? He who is terrified by fear, lazy, and likewise impure—[is he not their prey]? (18)
What indeed can he accomplish by that? The earth swallows such a man. (19)
Śātātapa said: "We are terrified by the fear of thieves; they carry away great wealth. How, then, can it be possible to perform that [vow], as well as the night vigil for the limbs? (20)
The wicked thieves have gone somewhere; therefore, having bowed down, we have returned. O Sage, we are terrified by fear and shall abandon everything.
"Indeed, the acceptance of gifts is terrible and yields only a sixth part of its fruit. While he was speaking thus, one named Hārīta said:
For what person of deluded intellect would indeed abandon the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, where both liberation and heaven are as if held in the palm of one's hand? (23)
What wise person would dwell in villages such as Kalāpa and others, if even for half a moment one can obtain residence at Stambhatīrtha? (24)
And what will all fear arising from thieves do there for those who firmly hold the Lord Kumāra in their minds as their protector? (25)
"Without daring, prosperity is never attained in any way; therefore, O Nārada, I shall go there at your word."
Twenty-six thousand Brāhmaṇas were in my service; they were pure, devoted to the six duties, and free from greed and deceit. (27)
"I shall come along with them; this is my supreme resolve. When these words were spoken, I placed them at the tip of my staff.
Suddenly turning back, O Pārtha, that sky-traveler was filled with great joy; having traversed a snowy path measuring a hundred yojanas, he departed.
Having arrived at Kedāra accompanied by those best of the twice-born, that region was easily accessible through the sky or else by way of a subterranean passage.
It cannot be transcended otherwise than through the grace of Skanda. || 31 ||
Arjuna said: "Where is Kalāpagrāma, and how can it be reached by way of a subterranean passage? How may the grace of Skanda be obtained? Tell me this, O Nārada. (32)
Nārada said: One hundred yojanas from Kedāra is remembered as Himasaṃyukta; at its end lies Kalāpaka, extending for a hundred yojanas.
At its end, the Vāsukārṇava extends for a hundred yojanas; that region, measuring one hundred yojanas, is known as Bhūmisvarga.
Listen now to how it is possible to go there by way of the subterranean passage: one should propitiate the god Guha while remaining without food and without water.
Then, O Bhārata, when he considers himself free from sin in the southern direction, Guha approaches him in a dream and says, "Go."
From there, to the west of the cave, there is a much larger opening; having entered there, one must proceed for seven hundred steps.
Therein stands a linga made of emerald, possessing a luster equal to the sun; before it lies clay that is golden-colored and perfectly pure. (38)
Having paid homage to that liṅga and taken that clay, you should return to Stambhatīrtha after having propitiated Kumāraka.
At midnight on the Bhūta day, one should take a kola-fruit from a well; with that water and earth, one should prepare an ointment for both eyes. (40)
And at times, while massaging his body at the sixty-third step, he beheld a beautiful cave by the power of the eye-salve.
Then, by the power of his bodily rubbing, he passes through the midst of them; indeed, he is not devoured by the extremely fierce insects known as Kārīṣas.
And beholding within the center of Bilama those perfected ones who resemble the sun, he proceeds, O Pārtha; thus he goes to the excellent village of Kalāpa.
There, a lifespan of four thousand years is proclaimed; one shall subsist on fruits, yet one shall not acquire further merit.
Thus has this been told to you; now listen further to that which followed: by the power of his asceticism, he placed those subtle beings at the tip of his staff.
"O twice-born ones, I have arrived at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean."
Then, having disembarked them, I released them onto the bank of that sacred pool; thereafter, I performed my ablutions together with those best of the twice-born.
At the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, which is like a forest fire for all defects without exception, he performed the hospitable rites of libation for the ancestors and the deities.
Performing the supreme recitation, we were seated at the confluence, gazing at the sun while meditating on Hari within our hearts.
And in that very interval, O Pārtha, the gods led by Śakra, all the planets beginning with Āditya, and the guardians of the worlds assembled together.
For there were eight wombs of the gods, as well as hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases; then, during that great festival, there was the finest singing and instrumental music.
I was prepared to wash the feet of the Brahmins when, at that moment, I heard the words of the guest.
Accompanied by the sound of the *sāman* chants and resonating with the third musical note, it was exceedingly delightful to the mind, like the supreme devotion to Śiva.
Having risen, he was questioned by the brahmins: "Who are you, O brahmin, and from where have you come? What do you seek? Speak what is pleasing to your mind. (54)
The Brahmin said: "I am the sage named Kapila; let it be announced to Nārada that I have come for the very purpose of making a request. Having heard that, I then spoke.
I am blessed that you have come here, O Kapila, great sage! There is nothing that we cannot give to you, for there is no recipient more worthy than you.
Kapilā said: "O son of Brahmā, if you must give something to me, then listen to this from me, O Nārada: grant me eight thousand Brahmins. (57)
"I shall bestow a gift of land upon these Brahmins residing in the village of Kalāpa; therefore, let this be carried out, O Lord. (58)
"Therefore, O Great Sage, I have indeed made this vow: you too must establish a sacred site for Kapila, the most excellent of Kapilas. (59)
Whether at a śrāddha ceremony or when the proper time has arrived, if a guest should turn away from one whose hermitage he has approached, all of that indeed becomes fruitless.
He who does not honor a guest shall go to the Raurava worlds; he by whom the guest is honored is honored even by the gods.
Through gifts and sacrifices, the sage Kapila was thus gratified; thereafter, the illustrious great sage Hārīta was invited.
In that assembly of Siddhas and gods, for the purpose of washing his feet, Hārīta then stood with his left foot placed forward.
Then a great laugh arose from the Siddhas, Apsaras, and gods; having reflected in many ways upon the earth, they cried, "Well done! Well done! O twice-born ones. (64)
Then a great surge of sorrow arose in my mind as well; and I considered that very verse, uttered by former Buddhas, to be indeed true. (65)
In all undertakings, the word "hail" (heti) is censured; for those performing excessive deeds, a fall like a stone is certain.
Then I said to the brahmins: "You shall become fools, possessed of little wealth and grain, and shrouded in the thick mire of poverty. (67)
When this was said, Hārīta laughed and spoke these words: "O sage, this is indeed your own loss, that you revile us. (68)
"What curse is being given to you? This very thing is itself a curse for you. Then, having reflected further, I said: "O twice-born one, what is it that I [have done]? (69)
By the gift of your left foot to one such as you. || 70 ||
Hārīta said: Listen, O wise one, to the cause from which my state of emptiness arises. (71)
As he thought thus in his mind: "Alas, this acceptance of gifts is painful; for by accepting gifts, the Vedic luster of Brahmins is extinguished. (72)
For when a brahmin accepts a great gift, he indeed takes away whatever merit the donor possesses; and the giver, in turn, bestows his own demerit upon the recipient. (73)
Both the giver and the receiver indeed regard each other's words with contempt; he who acts thus is of small intellect and is ruined. (74)
O Nārada, as I was reflecting thus, emptiness (śūnyatā) arose within me; I was afflicted by sleep, afflicted by fear, afflicted by desire, and tormented by grief.
Those whose wealth has been taken away and those whose minds are elsewhere—these indeed become empty [of purpose]. Therefore, O wise one, you should not feel anger toward them. (76)
"O Sage, because you became angry, this loss has come upon you alone. Then, filled with remorse, I spoke again to those Brahmins: (77)
"Fie on me, the evil-minded one who acts without deliberating on the matter! For those who act without reflection, what is there that cannot happen? (78)
One should not perform an action impulsively; this is the path of great calamities. All prosperity chooses the wise man who acts with deliberation. (79)
The highly intelligent Cirakārin spoke the truth indeed; for in former times, there was a certain renowned Brāhmaṇa born in the lineage of the Aṅgirases. (80)
Gautama had a son named Cirakārin, who was possessed of great wisdom; he would undertake all actions only after reflecting upon them for a long time. 81.
Because he accomplishes his tasks after a long time, he is called "Slow-acting"; likewise, because he is dull-witted, he is seized by the label of being "lazy. (82)
By what person of shallow intellect and short-sighted vision could he be transgressed, bypassing his other sons through such infidelity? (83)
Then, addressed angrily by his father, "Kill this mother," he replied after a long time, "So be it," for by his very nature he was one who acted with deliberation.
Reflecting with his characteristic deliberation, he pondered for a long time: "How can I carry out my father's command, yet how can I avoid killing my mother? (85)
"How might I sink into this [sin] like a wicked man under the pretext of dharma? For the command of a father is the highest dharma, yet the protection of one's mother is adharma. (86)
Moreover, sonship is not independent; yet let it not cause me distress here. For who, having killed a woman—and a mother at that—could ever be happy? (87)
Who, having shown contempt for his father, could attain a firm standing? It is proper not to despise one's father, and it is likewise proper to protect one's mother.
How indeed could he not forgive these two who are worthy of it? For the father places himself within the wife, thinking, "I have been born [again] through her. (89)
For the sake of upholding the lineage of my family’s conduct and character, I, that very self, have been personally fashioned by my father into the state of a son. (90)
Whatever was said by the father at the birth-ceremony and at the initiation-ceremony—that is sufficient confirmation for one who desires to honor his father. (91)

The body and other such things are to be given away, yet it is the father alone who bestows them; therefore, the word of the father must be carried out and should not be questioned in any way whatsoever.
Even sins are crushed for one who carries out the word of his father; the father is heaven, the father is dharma, and the father is the supreme austerity.
When the father is pleased, all the deities are pleased; they bestow upon that man those very blessings which the father pronounces.
When the father expresses his approval, it is the atonement for all sins; one is released from bondage, just as a flower is released from its stalk upon bearing fruit.
Even when his son is suffering, a father does not abandon his affection; reflect upon this, first of all, as the filial reverence due to a father.
I shall not think of my father as a lesser station, nor of my mother; for this aggregate composed of the five elements which exists in me in the state of mortality [is due to them]. (97)
My mother is the cause of my birth, just as the fire-drill is the cause of fire; the mother is the fire-drill for a man’s body and the fulfillment of every purpose.
Upon gaining a mother one has a protector; in the opposite case, one is without protection. Such a person does not grieve, nor does even the rigidity of worldly existence drag him down.
Even one who is destitute of fortune, if he addresses his mother as "O Mother" within the home, and having obtained sons and grandsons, remains supported by her; || 100 ||
Even at the end of a hundred years, he should behave like a two-year-old calf—whether [the cow] is capable or incapable, emaciated or likewise not emaciated.
A mother alone protects her son, for no one else has the duty to nourish him; when he becomes old, then she becomes sorrowful. (102)
Then the world is empty for him when he is separated from his mother; there is no shadow equal to a mother, and there is no refuge equal to a mother. || 103 ||
There is no protection equal to a mother; there is no refreshment equal to a mother. She is the nurse because she sustains one in her womb, and likewise the progenitor because she gives birth. (104)

She is called Ambā because she nourishes the limbs; she is Vīrasū because she gives birth to heroes; she is Śvaśrū because she cares for her infant; and likewise, she is Mātā because she is worthy of honor.
They know that the gathering together of deities constitutes a single father; yet the assembly of mortals and deities does not surpass the mother. 106.
Teachers who have fallen [from their status] should be abandoned, but a mother never; because she bears and nourishes [the child], the mother is therefore more venerable.
Thus, on the bank of the Kauśikī, he was destined by fate to kill his own mother—who had long been accustomed to the behavior of a woman—as she gazed upon King Bali.
Having reflected for a long time, he indeed could not reach the end of his deliberation; in the meantime, Śakra assumed a physical form.
Having approached Gāyangākhā near his father’s hermitage, he reflected: "For the author of the Sūtras has declared that all women are indeed free from debt. (110)
"Therefore, a wise person should accept the fruit from them and not look for faults. Having heard this, the noble-minded Medhātithi honored him.
Afflicted and reflecting, he arrived there shedding profuse tears: "Alas! I have been cast down by envy; I am submerged in an ocean of misery. (112)
"Having killed both a woman and a virtuous wife, who indeed will deliver me? Indeed, the noble-minded Cirakārin was commanded by me with great haste. (113)
"If this one were to act with long deliberation, he might save me from sin. O Cirakārika, may it be well with you; may it be well with you, O Cirakārika. (114)
Since today you have acted with such delay, you are indeed "Cirakārika" (the slow-acting one); save me, and my mother, as well as the ascetic merit I have earned.
"O you who are called auspicious, O Cirakārika! I am plunged into sin. Thus did the distressed Gautama reflect when he had arrived there. (116)
Then he saw his son Cirakārika near his mother; but Cirakāri, seeing his father, was deeply distressed.
Having cast aside his weapon, he stood with his head bowed and proceeded to seek grace; Medhātithi, seeing his son prostrate on the ground with his head to the earth, [acted accordingly].
And seeing his wife still alive, he experienced supreme joy; she did not even realize that her son stood there with a weapon in hand, ready to kill him.
Upon seeing his son prostrating at his father's feet, the thought occurred to him: "Out of fear, he is concealing his impulsive desire to take up weapons. (120)
Then, after his father had remembered him for a long time, smelled the crown of his head for a long time, and embraced him with both arms for a long time, he was addressed: "Live long! (121)
Then Medhātithi, filled with joy for a long time, said to his son: "O Cirakārika, may it be well with you; may you be a 'long-doer' for a long time. (122)
"O gentle one, because of what was done long ago, Gautama, the wise and best of sages, has remained sorrowful in this state for a long time; he has even uttered these verses. (123)
One should form an alliance with a mantra slowly, and one should abandon what has been done slowly; a friendship that has been broken slowly deserves to be maintained for a long time. (124)
In matters of disease, pride, arrogance, malice, sinful action, and indeed in doing what is unpleasant, one who acts slowly is praised. (125)
Regarding relatives, friends, servants, and women, one who acts with deliberation is praised when offenses are unmanifested.

One should practice the Dharma for a long time, and one should pursue its investigation for a long time; having attended upon the learned for a long time, and having served those who are dear for a long time. (127)
Having long disciplined himself, he long remains free from contempt, even when hearing the words of another that are connected with the Dharma. (128)
One should inquire for a long time and listen for a long time; one is not disregarded when dharma, an enemy with a weapon in hand, or a worthy recipient is standing nearby. (129)
"In times of danger or in the worship of the virtuous, one who acts with delay is not praised. Having spoken thus, he reached his hermitage together with his son and wife.
Then, after attending upon him for a long time, the sage departed for heaven; yet we, though speaking thus, have been deceived by delusion in this manner. (131)
And in the Kali age, O Brahmins, my curse shall fall upon you; yet some Brahmins will always remain endowed with all virtues.

In former times, there was a king on earth renowned as Indradyumna; he was generous, a knower of all dharmas, honorable, one who honored others, and a sovereign lord.

On the night of the tenth day, that king gave gifts to thousands of those seeking wealth; meanwhile, Dundubhi was upon the back of an elephant.

Having reached the abode of Prajāpati by means of a celestial chariot, O best of the Kurus, he then enjoyed pleasures that are difficult even for the immortals to attain.
