Brahmā said: O Indradyumna, best of kings, go quickly to the surface of the earth; you must not remain even for a moment today in my world.
Indradyumna said: "O Brahmin, why do you now send me from here back to the earth? Since my merit is still abundant, tell me the reason. (14)
Brahmā said: "O King, merit alone is not the secret means for attaining heaven, without a stainless fame spread throughout the three worlds. (15)
The destruction of your fame upon the surface of the earth has now occurred after a long time; go and make it new again. (16)
Or if you have a desire, O protector of the earth, to remain in my abode.
Indradyumna said: "O Brahman, how might my merit remain upon the earth? What must I do? This does not rest within my mind. (18)
Brahmā said: "O protector of the earth, this Time (Kāla) is powerful; it impels all things by its own power."
Even the cosmic eggs and myself are but a mere count; what need is there to mention those like you? Therefore, O King, I consider this alone to be your [true] state at present.
"Having brought your own fame to manifestation, return once more to heaven. Having heard these words of Brahmā, that lord of the earth [acted accordingly].
He beheld himself thus descended to the surface of the earth; once again in the city of Kāmpilya, he questioned himself by means of his own mind.
Then, filled with wonder, he asked the people of that country about the city. The people said: "We do not know King Indradyumna, nor do we know that city. (23)
"What you ask, O good sir—'Ask someone who is long-lived'—Indradyumna said: 'Who at present on the face of the earth is renowned among people as being long-lived? (24)
"O King Pṛthivījaya, speak in this assembly without delay! The people said: "It is heard that in the Naimiṣa forest there is a sage who remembers seven kalpas. (25)
"Go and ask him, who is known as Mārkaṇḍeya, about your doubt. Having been thus instructed by them, he went there to that bull among sages.
Having heard this and prostrated, the king spoke what was in his heart. Indradyumna said: "The Blessed One is long-lived and is now renowned throughout the earth. (27)
"I ask you: do you know King Indradyumna or not?"
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O King, within the interval of seven kalpas, there has been no one named Indradyumna. What else shall I tell you? Ask me about any other doubt. (29)
Having heard those words, the king then became despondent regarding the accomplishment of the fire-rite; seeing him thus, the sage then spoke to him.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O gentle one, do not commit this rash act; listen to my words. Joy comes even to a man who has lived for a hundred years. (31)
"I shall provide that remedy for the pacification of your suffering; listen, my good friend, for I have here an old friend, a crane. (32)
"He is known as Nāḍījaṅgha; he will undoubtedly recognize you. Therefore, come quickly so that we two may go there together. (33)
For the life of the great-souled ones has as its sole fruit the benefit of others; if he knows Indradyumna for certain, he will speak of him.
Then those two, the eminent lord of brahmins and the preeminent king, set out joyfully toward Himācala and toward the abode of Nāḍījaṅgha.
Then, seeing his own friend Mārkaṇḍeya returned after a long time, Baka went out to meet him with great affection and longing, accompanied by the twice-born brahmins.
Having first established a rapport with him through kind greetings and the like, he then asked about his business and the reason for his arrival.
Then Mārkaṇḍeya spoke to that crane regarding the matter at hand: "Do you know King Indradyumna on this earth? (38)
For this reason, my friend will not give up his life by entering the fire before he has been recognized by him. (39)
Speak for the sake of protecting his life, if you know the king.
Naḍījaṅgha said: "O best of brahmins, I currently remember fourteen kalpas; as for that [encounter], let it be—neither its sight nor even its report do I remember. (41)
"There was no king named Indradyumna on the surface of the earth; I know only this much, O bull among the twice-born. (42)

Nārada said: Then, filled with wonder upon hearing that this was his lifespan, the king asked, "What is the cause—whether it be charity or asceticism—by which such a long life has been attained? Thus he spoke, amazed. (43)
Nāḍījaṅgha said: "O Brahmin, by the power of the *ghṛtakaṃbala* of my trident-bearing Lord, I have attained this long life; now hear how I came to possess the body of a crane due to a curse."
Formerly, in a previous birth, I was a young boy on earth belonging to a Brahmin of the Pārāśarya gotra, the virtuous sage Viśvarūpa.
The boy was known as Baka; he was exceedingly dear to his father. Though very fickle in childhood, he was by nature exceptionally virtuous.
Then, having taken away my father's emerald linga from the place where the deity was installed, I hid it out of fickleness and childishness. (47)

During the transit of the sun into Capricorn at the commencement of the northern solstice, while a jar of clarified butter was being prepared, my father remained awake throughout the night until morning had passed.
He cleared away the withered flower offerings until the temple of Śiva became empty; hearing this, he became terrified and questioned me in a sweet voice. (49)
"My child, tell me where you have surely hidden the linga; I shall give you whatever you desire, or any other food you wish for. (50)
Then, out of childishness and greedy for food, I drew it from within my father's jar of ghee and offered it as a *bhadra-liṅga*.
Then, when the time had arrived, I died in the king's palace and was born as the son of the lord of Ānarta, endowed with the memory of my former birth.
Due to the greatness of the Ghṛtakambala rite when the sun was situated in Capricorn, even because of his childhood ignorance and the contact between the ghee and the liṅga, [the fruit was attained].
Then, remembering my previous birth, I installed that Liṅga; from that time forward, I have been covering the Liṅgas with ghee.
Having obtained the kingdom inherited from my father and grandfather according to my capacity, the blessed Lord, the husband of Pārvatī, being pleased, then spoke to me: || 55 ||
"In a previous birth, I was pleased by your worship with a blanket of ghee; I grant you this kingdom now, so choose what you desire. (56)
Then Śiva, being well-pleased, granted me the leadership of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya) which I had desired; and on Kailāsa, he spoke thus to me constantly: || 57 ||
With that very body, bowing down and standing before me, from this day forward, whoever else [performs this] during the transit of the sun into Capricorn— || 58 ||
"O auspicious one, he who shall perform worship with clarified butter will clearly become my attendant (gaṇa)"; having said this to me, Śiva made me the lord of ten million attendants.
The teaching of Śiva is established under the name *Pratīpapālaka*; from that, by means of the six steps beginning with *kāma*, it consists of the nature of movement.
Having obtained that fortune, which is as naturally fickle as a female bee, I was utterly unable to sustain it due to the turn of fate. (61)
Then I wandered about like an intoxicated elephant, utterly devoid of any consideration for what ought or ought not to be done, and exceedingly arrogant. (62)
Just as a low-born man, having acquired knowledge, noble lineage, and wealth, becomes a vessel for calamities like the ocean is for rivers, so it is with such a person. (63)
Then, after some time had passed, wandering at will, I went to a mountain whose caves were blocked by masses of snow.
There the sage Gālava was performing austerities together with his wife; he was always emaciated by intense penance, his body covered with a network of veins.
For this body of a Brahmin is not fond of worldly fruits; it is intended for the practice of austerities in this life and for infinite happiness after death.
His wife, Viśvavarṇinī, surpassed all women in beauty; she was slender, youthful, with eyes like a deer's, and possessed full, elevated breasts. (67)
Her speech was as soft as the cry of a swan, her gait like that of an elephant in rut; she possessed broad hips, a slender waist, and long hair. (68)
The Creator, desiring to behold her, fashioned this woman with a deep navel; she stands like beauty itself, as if gathered together and concentrated into a single vessel.

Then, O Bhadra, having seen that beloved of Gālava, I, the undisciplined one, was struck by the showers of arrows from the flower-bowed god; for even sages who possess discernment remain discerning only so long as they have not encountered such a sight.
As long as I had not been gazed upon by the corners of the eyes of those fawn-eyed women, at that time I resolved in my mind, desiring to carry her away.
"I shall take her away by force, protected as she is by the ascetic power of the sage; for if the sage should curse me on her account, there would be defeat. (72)
"She may become my wife, or perhaps she will be my death; therefore, I shall become the disciple of this sage, devoted to his service. (73)
"I shall seize her once I have gained access; this woman is not fit for him. Having thus resolved, he assumed the form of a student seeking knowledge and approached Gālava. (74)
Having paid homage, I spoke these words, impelled by the destiny yet to come: "Such shall be the intellect of men, such their friends, and such their resolve. (75)
That which was performed by men in the past must necessarily come to pass; O Blessed One, I have approached you endowed with discernment and dispassion. (76)
"I am your disciple; you must instruct me in the Great Sage who is the helmsman, Viṣṇu, who has reached the further shore of the boundless ocean and has assumed the form of a Brahmin. (77)
I pay homage to the conscious Brahman, who is directly perceived under the name Gālava; he was bitten by the black serpent of ignorance and afflicted by its venom. (78)
O Jāṅgulika, revive me with the great mantras of instruction! The great tree of delusion has arisen, planted within my heart. (79)
Irrigated by association with the foolish and pervading the path to liberation, it shall go to destruction by the sharp-edged axe of your words. (80)
"Let it now be severed by the master of the thread with the axe of knowledge; I am your disciple, and I shall long practice worship of you. (81)
"I shall fetch kindled darbha grass, roots, fruits, firewood, and water; please favor me, who have approached you in humility. (82)
Thus, in the past, when I was known as Baka and had adopted the conduct of a crane, the sage, his mind set on rectitude, showed me favor.
Then, becoming exceedingly humble, I daily gratified him along with his wife in order to inspire firm confidence. (84)
And that sage, though knowing [the truth], did not trust his wife who was a worthy recipient; having made her an expert in the conduct of women, the twice-born one went to sleep. (85)
Then, on another day, that ascetic Brahmin woman became menstruating; out of trust in me, she slept far from me during the night. (86)
Thinking "this is the opportunity," I was filled with joy; assuming the form of a thief, I then carried her off at midnight.
Then, as she was being carried away by me, the young woman cried out loudly; recognizing me by her voice, she spoke to the sage, saying, "Not so! Not so! (88)
"This wicked man, following the conduct of a crane, has donned the cloak of dharma; he is seizing me by his evil behavior. Therefore, O Gālava, protect me! (89)
Having formerly been your disciple, this thief now disguised as a mendicant desires to seize me; therefore, O protector, protect me and be my refuge. (90)
Simultaneously with those words, the sage Gālava woke up; saying to me, "Wait, wait," he brought about a paralysis of my movement.
Then, with my form rendered variegated, I was paralyzed by the sage; as if out of shame, I seemed to shrink into my own limbs.
Then, becoming enraged, Gālava approached me and spoke those words as unbearable as a thunderbolt, by which I became a crane.
Gālava said: "Since I have been deceived by you by resorting to the conduct of a crane (bakavṛtti), therefore, O lowest of men, you shall become a crane for a long time."
Thus was I cursed by the sage for resorting to unrighteousness; having pursued another's wife, I have come to this calamity. (95)
Indeed, there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man’s pursuit of another's wife in this world. (96)
Then that ascetic woman Satī, her body defiled by my touch, was released by me; having bathed, she likewise cursed me.
Thus cursed by them both, trembling with fear like a leaf of the holy fig tree, I bowed down to that couple and spoke.
"I am indeed a most ill-behaved member of the Lord's own assembly; O Blessed Ones, grant me favor by thus restraining me. (99)
In speech they are like razors, yet their hearts are like clarified butter; for the twice-born, when provoked, may become enraged, but when appeased, they may become gracious in even a moment.
For one who has gone astray regarding you, you alone are my refuge; for those whose feet have stumbled upon the ground, the ground itself is their support. 101.
Even this leadership of my own group has become a source of contempt; for the riches of one who is ill-mannered result only in poison-like fangs. (102)
Others who possess discernment perceive danger from others through the intellect that anticipates the future; but the base, lacking personal experience, understand neither. (103)
One who is ill-behaved, having attained prosperity, knowledge, or even sovereignty, does not remain long in his position, just as I, arrogant with pride, [did not]. (104)

Pride of learning, pride of wealth, and thirdly, pride of noble birth—these are the intoxications of those blinded by intoxication; yet these very same things are the means of self-restraint for the virtuous. (105)
Those who have not conquered themselves possess an intellect devoid of foresight; by such people as I, the fickle goddesses of fortune are led to be spoken of [with contempt]. (106)
Therefore, be gracious, O best of sages, and grant me an end to this curse now; for the virtuous are always characterized by forgiveness, even toward those who are ill-behaved. (107)
When these words had been thus spoken by me, even though I was disciplined, he became inclined toward grace and then brought about the end of my curse.
Gālava said: "You shall become the helper in the restoration of the obscured fame [of Indradyumna]; when that is accomplished for King Indradyumna, then you will attain liberation. (109)
Thus, due to the sage’s curse, from that time forward I have lived on the Himalaya mountain, having become a crane of the lineage of Kaśyapa.

"Kingdom, long life—these were my [desires]; and Ghr̥takambala’s memory of his former births persists even now through its influence. Due to a curse, Gālava became a crane; thus, O gentle one, everything you asked has been explained today. (111)
Nārada said: Having heard the words spoken by Nāḍījaṅgha and Baka, the king, together with Mārkaṇḍeya, became exceedingly distressed. || 1 ||
Having observed that the king was distressed with tearful eyes, the sage, sharing in his sorrow, spoke again for his sake to the crane.
"O illustrious one, O twice-born, having formed this hope, we two have come into your presence; we are the long-lived ones who know Indradyumna as a partial incarnation [of Viṣṇu]. (3)
His purpose for that was already accomplished; he did not wish to preserve his life-breaths, having attained supreme detachment through entering the fire.
He has come to me, and I have come to you; his desire remains unfulfilled. Therefore, I swear by you that I shall follow him in death.
Virtuous people are unable to look upon one who has come seeking refuge only to be left without hope; therefore, for them, death is better than life.
That which was desired by him remained in his heart, and I promised it to him, keeping you, O long-lived friend, in my heart for the sake of recognizing that [truth]. (7)
It would not be right for me to fail to fulfill my promise regarding my lifespan, while this distressed seeker remains with his hopes unfulfilled and his heart clouded by sorrow.

One’s promise fulfilled is praiseworthy even as servitude in the quarters of outcasts; for men, however, being true to one's word is not praiseworthy [if it leads to such a state], as was the case with Hariścandra.
Friendship is a synonym for affection, and that is said to be formed by walking seven steps together. What kind of affection is there toward a friend who is not seen when one is suffering? (10)
Therefore, O friend, I shall now certainly perform the means of entering the fire together with her for the sake of my body of fame; this is the truth. (11)
"Grant me permission for this final audience with you, O illustrious Nāḍījaṅgha, best of the twice-born. (12)
Nārada said: Having heard those words uttered by Mārkaṇḍeya, which were as difficult to endure as a thunderbolt, he reflected for a moment and, being convinced, spoke to both of them.
Nāḍījaṅgha said: "If this is so, O best of sages, then restrain this friend of mine from entering the fire now; he is longer-lived than I."
This owl named Prākārakarṇa, on Śivaparvata, will undoubtedly know King Indradyumna. (15)
Therefore, I shall go with you and him to that mountain, the abode of Śiva, for the successful accomplishment of my friend’s purpose.
Having spoken thus, those three best of the twice-born departed; they beheld Kailāsa there and saw that owl in his own nest.
Having made an agreement with him, that crane, honored with a welcome, was questioned by both of them and spoke all that they desired.
"You are long-lived; if you know King Indradyumna, then tell us of him through that knowledge, for we live by it. (19)
Thus questioned, Kauśika, dejected because he had not accomplished the task for his friend, said: "I do not know King Indradyumna. (20)
Twenty-eight kalpas have passed since my birth upon this earth; yet neither seen nor heard of before was this King Indradyumna on the face of the world.
Having heard that, the king was struck with wonder; though distressed by her exceedingly long life, he then asked for the cause of that longevity.
Tell me this: how did you obtain such a lifespan, and how did you come to have this owl-form which is so exceedingly loathsome? (23)
Prākārakarṇa said: Listen, my good friend, how through the worship of Śiva I obtained long life, and how, by the curse of a great sage, I attained this loathsome state of an owl.
"In former times, I was a twice-born man born into the lineage of Vasiṣṭha; well-known by the name Ghaṇṭa, I was devoted to Śiva in Vārāṇasī. (25)
O Lord, having personally heard [the teachings] from the assembly of the virtuous while being devoted to listening to the Dharma, I worship the Lord with unbroken bilva leaves.
Neither the *mālatī*, nor the *mandāra*, nor the *śatapatra*, nor the *mallikā* is as dear to the Enemy of Madana as the *śrīvṛkṣa*. (27)
By placing even a single unbroken bilva leaf upon the head of Śiva, men obtain the merit born of offering a hundred thousand flowers.
Having performed the worship of the Liṅga with unbroken bilva leaves personally gathered with faith, one shall dwell in heaven for a hundred thousand years.
Having heard this from the true scriptures, I worship the Lord with three leaves each of the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, thrice a day, with faith.
Then, at the end of a hundred years, the moon-crested Lord was pleased; appearing before me, he spoke to me with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: || 31 ||
Īśvara said: O best of Brahmins, I am pleased with you because of your worship with unbroken bilva leaves. Choose whatever you desire; I shall grant it to you, even if it be difficult to attain.
Great satisfaction arises from even a single unbroken bilva leaf; for me, it is not so even with ten million of other [offerings]. (33)
Thus addressed by the Blessed Lord Śambhu, I chose the boon that resided in my own mind: "O God, make me free from old age and death. (34)
Then Līlāvilāsa, having said "So be it," vanished from sight without hesitation; and I too attained great joy.
At that time, I perceived myself on earth as one who had accomplished all that was to be done; and at that very moment, there appeared a twice-born man born of the lineage of Bhṛgu.
He had a virtuous wife, renowned as Sudarśanā, who was born from three pure wombs, who understood the meaning of the syllables of the Vedas, and who was beloved by him.
Beholding her husband’s face, she was exceedingly joyful from the sight of him; this daughter of Devala is peerless on earth in her beauty. (38)
From her, by him, was born a daughter who was indistinguishable from his own sister; having passed beyond childhood, she became a maiden on the verge of youth.
Her father was not able to give that virtuous daughter to anyone; and she was seen by me at the transition of her youth.
Entering with states of the fullness of youth, she is exceedingly enchanting; yet, as other [states] are being cast out, her form becomes like sesame seeds interspersed with rice grains.
O Brahmin, as I gazed upon that slender-waisted woman who was playing with her companions like an embodiment of beauty itself, I began to reflect.
"By that rite through which he was fashioned with a form unlike any other, I have, at that very moment, come within the range of those sattvic states. (43)
Having been struck effortlessly with arrows by the flower-bowed god, she was then brought [to me]; then I asked her friend, whose daughter was she, as her hair fell in disarray? (44)
He said: "This is the daughter of one born of the Bhrigu lineage; she has not yet been married by anyone and has come here to play. (45)
Then, severely struck by the multitude of arrows of the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāma), he went before his father and, bowing down, entreated that descendant of Bhṛgu for her hand.
And he, perceiving me to be his equal in virtue and lineage, and seeing me to be exceedingly eager for wealth, first gave me his word and then [the gift] in due order.
Then his daughter heard this from the descendant of Bhṛgu as he was speaking: "I have been given to that brahmin Virūpa. (48)
Wailing loudly, she said to her mother: "Behold what has been done; the father-in-law has acted most improperly by bestowing such a bridegroom. (49)
I would rather stir up poison and drink it, or enter the fire, than ever become the wife of an ugly husband.
Then, having awakened his mother, he said to that descendant of Bhṛgu: "The maiden must not be given by you to this deformed man, despite his persistence."
Having heard the words of his beloved and having consulted the treatises on dharma, he may take back even a previously given bride if a more excellent suitor arrives.
"The completion shall occur before she steps upon a stone, at the seventh step"—having thus resolved, the twice-born man gave his daughter to another.
When the wedding was to take place on the following day, I heard all of that; consequently, I was then extremely embarrassed in the presence of my companions.
O auspicious one, he was unable to show his own face; thus, afflicted by desire, he carried her away that very night while she was fast asleep.
Having led her to a secluded place, most difficult of access, I performed the marriage rite; then, by the Gāndharva form of marriage, I accomplished my heart's desire.
Then, while the young girl was unwilling, her father arrived immediately after me that very morning and forcibly compelled her to engage in sexual union.
O Brahmins, sighing and restraining himself upon seeing his daughter married off, that descendant of Bhṛgu then became enraged and cursed me, O gentle one. (58)
Bhārgava said: "Since you have married my daughter according to the custom of a night-stalker (niśācara), therefore, O sinful one, become a night-stalker yourself without delay. (59)
Thus cursed, he bowed down to him, clasping his feet, crying out "Alas! Alas! with eyes full of tears and a voice choked with emotion.
Then I said: "Why do you curse me, who am without fault? Previously, your daughter was given by you to me through a formal verbal agreement. (61)
"A maiden has been married by me; 'the gift is given once' is the traditional law. Kings speak but once; scholars speak but once. (62)
Daughters are given away but once; these three things happen only once each. Furthermore, the fulfillment of what has been promised is the vow of the virtuous.
For virtuous men such as you, the abandonment of a virtuous person is censurable; moreover, this was obtained by me from you at that time after it had been promised.
Furthermore, I am not now a fit recipient for a curse; consider this, for you are cursing me in vain. (65)
It is determined in the treatises on Dharma that the evil-minded man who, having verbally given away his daughter, later takes her back, goes to hell. (66)
Having heard that and determined in his heart that my words were true, the sage, filled with remorse, then spoke to me as follows: (67)
My word could not be otherwise; you shall become an owl. For even an owl is called a "night-walker" (niśācara), O best of the twice-born. (68)
"O Brahmin, when you become a companion to Indradyumna in his realization, then you shall attain your true nature"—thus did he speak to me.
And at the very moment of those words, this state of being a kauśika was mine; for these many days it has been so—the twenty-eighth day of Brahmā.

"In former times, it is said that through the worship of Śaśiśekhara with bilva leaves, my lifespan became exceedingly long; yet here on the slopes of Kailāsa, due to his curse, this loathsome form of a night-stalker arose. (71)
Ulūka said: Thus has been told to me everything arising from my previous birth—both my true nature and the cause of my long life and of this state of being an owl.
When he who bears the name Puruhūta had ceased speaking thus, the crane Nāḍījaṅgha, being distressed, spoke these words to his friend: || 2 ||
Nāḍījaṅgha said: "O high-minded one, that purpose for which we have come has not been accomplished; surely death has now arrived for all three of us. (3)
If Indradyumna is not recognized, this Bhadraka will die; his friend is Mārkaṇḍeya, and it is clear that he follows him even now.
He who looks on while his friend is dying once the friend's business has been accomplished—fie on that unaffectionate and evil-minded person for whom the friend's life is of no concern!
Therefore, O twice-born one, I shall follow you as you die; I take my leave of you, for this is my final salutation, embrace, and farewell.
Having promised and yet failing to fulfill it for a friend who has arrived as a guest, how is it that those wretched ones, though desiring life, feel no shame? (7)
Therefore, I shall undoubtedly enter the fire along with these two; having been asked now out of affection, give me a handful of water.
When the owl had spoken thus, Nāḍījaṅgha, steadying himself with a faltering voice and tearful eyes, spoke words that were like nectar.
Ulūka said: "While I, your friend, am still alive, you have met with death; from this day forward, who then shall receive my heart?"
There is a great means in this matter on Mount Gandhamādana: there is a vulture named Cirāyus, my friend, who is as dear to me as my own life. (11)
"He will recognize your desired lord of the earth, Indradyumna"; having said this, the owl stood before him, as did that king.
Mārkaṇḍeya and Baka then proceeded to Gandhamādana; and seeing their friend approaching and standing before them, [they were filled with joy]. || 13 ||
Joyful, that vulture came forward from his own nest; he had previously made an agreement with him regarding welcome, a seat, and food.
The king of vultures likewise questioned the owl regarding that matter, and he replied: "This crane is my friend; indeed, this sage is his. (15)
This third friend of even the Sage is wealth, which is now exerted; it lives on its own for the sake of identifying Indradyumna, and not otherwise.
"He will clearly enter the fire, and immediately after him, we shall do so as well; for he has been dissuaded by me, having recognized you within himself as the eternal one. (17)
If you know that, tell it; grant life to these four. Attain fame through truth and bring about the destruction of all your sins.
The vulture said: "Fifty-six kalpas have passed since I was born, O Kauśika; yet neither seen nor heard of by us is this King Indradyumna. (19)
Having heard that, Indradyumna was filled with wonder and, being distressed, questioned the bird about the cause for such extraordinary life.
The vulture said: "Listen, O blessed lady; formerly I was born as a restless monkey. Once, in the course of time, the season of spring arrived."
There, in front of the God of gods, in the midst of the forest within the abode of Śiva, before Bhavodbhava, who is named Jagadyogeśvara.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, under the asterism of Hasta, during the yoga named Harṣaṇa, the Damanaka festival took place.
There, when the Liṅga had been placed upon a golden swing by the people, I climbed onto that swing at night and set it swinging.
Due to his innate and natural fickleness, after a long time and repeatedly, the people arrived at dawn once more to worship the monkey.
Seeing me mounted upon a swing, they struck me with clubs; yet while still seated on the swing, I passed away in the abode of Śiva.
By means of their many very firm blows, which were as difficult to endure as thunderbolts, I was born in the king’s palace through the greatness of the swinging of Śiva.
I am the renowned Kuśadhvaja, the son of the Lord of Kāśī; remembering my past births, I subsequently attained sovereign power over the kingdom.
I shall cause the Damanaka festival to be celebrated on the surface of the earth in the month of Caitra, so that people may swing Śiva as he stands upon the swing.
In that very way, his impurity departs and auspicious merit arrives; having received the initiation of Śiva, he becomes refined by all the purificatory rites.

Through those scriptures, I was liberated from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu-pāśa) by the Śiva-ācāryas, having fully received all the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) up to the final initiation (nirvāha-dīkṣā).
I propitiate the Lord of Gods, the Lord of Umā, whose mind is turned inward, the Teacher of the worlds, and the cause of the severance of all afflictions.
By means of the yoga of practice and dispassion, through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, he should chant the Udgītha while contemplating its meaning—the eighth flavor.
Then, having recognized that I was unassailable by obstacles due to my firm ground of resolve and practice, Hara, being pleased, said to me: (34)
Īśvara said: "O Kuśadhvaja, I am pleased today; choose a desired boon. Indeed, no one else on the surface of the earth possesses such a performance of penance."
Having heard what was said by me, Śambhu replied, "I shall indeed become your Gaṇa with this very body"; "So be it," the Lord said to the Earth.
Then, having brought me to Kailāsa, he assigned to me a celestial chariot made of all kinds of jewels, divine, and filled with wonderful marvels.
I wandered about with confidence, having ascended that mountain by chance; then, after some time had passed on this very mountain— || 38 ||
Standing at the window during the spring, while the southern wind was blowing, I beheld the daughter of a sage, set ablaze by the fire of passion.
O auspicious one, [he saw] the daughter of Agniveśya, naked and standing in the midst of the water, in the full bloom of youth, dark-complexioned, slender-waisted, and with eyes like those of a doe.
With her expansive hips, thighs like plantain stalks, and closely set breasts, she was like beauty itself having sprouted forth at the very sight of the water-sprinkling. || 41 ||

She whose face was like a blossoming lotus and whose form was most worthy of description—though she was being described by those possessing wisdom according to the true nature of their own understanding.
With the discharge of her rising side-glances, as if with volleys of arrows, Smara himself, having taken possession of her body, struck me most severely. (43)
While she was thus playing with her companions in private, I, overcome by passion, descended from my celestial chariot and carried her away by chance.
As she was being seized by me while letting out a long, loud cry, she stood in her celestial chariot and wept most piteously, "O Father! O auspicious one.
Then those companions, distressed, ran toward the sage and said: "Your daughter is being carried away by some celestial being."
"O Blessed One, protect this woman who is weeping; arise!"—hearing those words from all sides, the sage Bhadra, a treasure-house of penance, [arose].
Agniveśya quickly approached her in the sky; saying "Stay! Stay! to me, he arrested my movement through his ascetic power.
Then, becoming enraged, Agniveśya spoke these most unbearable words to the sage: "Since my daughter has been snatched away by you like a piece of flesh... (49)
Therefore, become a vulture immediately, like a vulture now in the sky; for this young daughter of mine is a poor, wretched girl who does not desire [this]. (50)
"O evil-minded one, now reap this fruit of that which was stolen by you! Having heard this, the king was overcome with fear and stood with his face cast down in shame before the sage. (51)
Then, grasping his feet, I fell down weeping most bitterly: "This was not taken by me after I recognized her; even now she has not been violated. (52)
"Be gracious and turn back your curse, O treasure of asceticism! For those who are humble, the masters of penance are by their very nature endowed with forgiveness. (53)
"O holy one, may I not become like that vulture; be gracious to me. Thus did I, having sought refuge, bow down to that great sage.
Being pleased, he said: "My word can never be false; however, [I shall provide] assistance in the matter of identifying King Indradyumna. (55)
When you go [there], then you shall obtain release from the curse. || 56 ||
Having spoken thus, that sage departed for his own abode taking his daughter of unimpaired character; at that time, I became a vulture.

Thus, at that time, during the festival of Damana, my descent occurred in the royal palace through the agitation of the Lord. Likewise, Śambhu attained the status of a Gaṇa; and by the curse of Agniveśya, you became a vulture here, O Bhadra—this has been told to you.
Nārada said: Having heard these words of the vulture, Indradyumna, filled with both grief and wonder, questioned him and prepared for death.
Then, observing him thus desirous of death and reflecting upon his own long life joined with that of Kauśika and the others, he spoke.
"Do not act thus; listen to my words, O auspicious one, for you are ancient. There is indeed someone even more capable than I who will clearly understand what you desire. (3)
"In Lake Mānasa there is a tortoise well known by the name Maṃtharaka; nothing is unknown to him, so come, let us go there."
Then, being satisfied, the king, the sage, the vulture, and the crane, together with the owl, all went forth, desiring to see the tortoise.
Standing on the bank of the lake, the tortoise, seeing them at a distance, became terrified and then quickly entered the water.
Then Kauśika himself, laughing, spoke these words to him: "O tortoise, why have you now vanished and turned away, even though we have arrived? (7)

Fire is the preceptor of the twice-born, and the Brahmin is the preceptor of the social orders; the husband is the preceptor of women; the teacher and the father are the preceptors of sons; and the guest is the preceptor of everyone.
Having abandoned this Dharma and being averse to hospitality, how can you take upon yourself the sin of all? O Tortoise, speak your answer now! (9)
The tortoise said: "I am indeed ancient and know how to perform the hospitable rites of hospitality; the honoring of those who have arrived is firmly established in the treatises on dharma."
Listen also to the very great reason for this which I shall tell you: I have not turned my face away for all these days.
He is devoted to the noble vow of offering every form of hospitality to whoever arrives; however, this fifth one among you who is seen here has a straightforward (or simple) appearance.
I, King Indradyumna, am exceedingly afraid of him; formerly, in the city named Raucaka, he was a sacrificer.
"The back of my body, though burnt by the sacrificial fire, is not yet free of scars; therefore, fear has arisen within me once more—will he [the fire] consume me again? (14)
"Having bestowed his power upon the earth, he shall now consume [all things]," O best of the Kurus, at the conclusion of these words of the Tortoise. (15)
A rain of flowers fell from the sky, released by hosts of apsarases; and divine musical instruments resounded upon the restoration of the king’s fame.
Filled with wonder, they then beheld a celestial chariot standing before them, which had been stationed there by a divine messenger for the sake of Indradyumna.
The gods and the twice-born bestowed upon him blessings that were never stale; there was a great cry of "Well done! in heaven for that lord of the earth.
Then, taking hold of the celestial chariot, the divine messenger spoke these words loudly to Indradyumna in the hearing of the inhabitants of heaven: ||| 19 ||
The divine messenger said: "O King, your stainless fame has now been renewed even throughout the three worlds; therefore, ascend this celestial chariot immediately. (20)
"Go to the world of Brahmā, which has been earned through asceticism for an entire kalpa; I have been sent by him himself for the purpose of bringing you back."
For as long as a person's fame remains celebrated upon the earth, for that long shall he dwell in heaven, provided his merit is indeed infinite.
The construction of temples, lakes, ponds, wells, gardens, and so forth, is indeed determined in the treatises on Dharma as the practice known as *pūrta* for this very purpose. (23)
Indradyumna said: "These—Mārkaṇḍeya, the crane, the owl, the vulture, and the tortoise—are indeed my friends; this is their power, which serves for my own advancement. (24)
If they indeed go with me to the world of Brahmā, I shall come there standing before them; I shall go to the world of Brahmā, and not otherwise.
He who acts solely for the benefit of others, without even expecting a return for what has been done, is called a true friend by the wise. (26)

Even those whose minds are intent on their own welfare are truly named [as such] only so long as they possess life; for when death is the natural state and life itself is a mere anomaly, [what purpose is there in self-interest]? (27)

The supreme gain for living beings is solely friendship toward all creatures; those who are impoverished, full of passion, false to their promises, and treacherous to their teachers [possess nothing]. (28)
Those who dwell with friends are wicked and are generally the ornaments of hell; those ruined by the interests of others—these five are now truly virtuous.
This is the power of these great-souled ones, which rescues my reputation; if they go to heaven along with me, then I too shall go, O messengers of the gods, and not otherwise. (30)
The divine messenger said: "All these attendants of Hara have fallen to the earth, deprived by a curse."
"At the end of the curse, O lord of the earth, they shall go to the side of Hara; therefore, O King, leave these behind and come with me. (32)
"And heaven does not please them, having abandoned the god Maheśvara. Indradyumna said: "If this is so, go then, O messenger; I shall not come to Triviṣṭapa."
In such and such a manner I shall strive so that this community, which is censured for the defects of impurity, decay, and excess, may become pure.

Heaven is always characterized by what is heard [in scripture]; therefore, I do not desire it. For one staying there, there is the fear of falling again; thus, fear does not depart from the mind. (35)
Furthermore, since it leads to a man's downfall, I do not desire heaven; for even when merit exists, one is cast down from one's own world by that very merit itself. (36)
"I have become embarrassed before the Four-faced One; how can I go to him? Having said this to the messenger, he spoke while that very person was listening in astonishment.
Then the king questioned the tortoise regarding the cause of his longevity: "O tortoise, how has this exceedingly long life of yours come to be? (38)
"You are my friend, my ally, and my teacher, by whom my fame has been restored. (39)
The tortoise said: "Listen, O King, to this divine story which destroys sin upon hearing; listen to this most sweet narrative endowed with the majesty of Śiva. (40)

O King, even by hearing this story with great faith, a person becomes liberated from the body of sin; having attained the grace of Śambhu, just as [the sage] lived his life, so too was this state of being a tortoise granted to me through His grace. (41)
The tortoise said: O King, in former times I was a brahmin renowned as Śāṇḍilya. While playing in my childhood, O monarch, I constructed [this].
Formerly, during the rainy season, there stood an elevated temple of Śiva, consisting mostly of sand moistened by water, and adorned with a lofty rampart.
O King, it was more enchanting with the arrangement of the five shrines, embodying the forms of Vināyaka, Śiva, Sūrya, and Madhusūdana.
It had golden jars with yellow clay, was adorned with garlands of banners, featured wooden archways set upon it, and was further embellished by a swing.
It was resplendent with rows of stairs rising high and firm, divine, and full of every wonder; and I was surrounded by my companions.
There, having taken that *jāgeśvara* linga which had been placed there since childhood in the form of a stone, it was purified by the waters of the rainy season.
Likewise, with *bakapuṣpa* flowers and others gathered from the fields, and with other tender blossoms produced upon the boundary hedges and creepers; || 7 ||
With kūṣmāṇḍa fruits and other varieties, including those with unmatta flowers, with mandāra blossoms, bilva leaves, dūrvā grass, and fresh sprouts; || 8 ||
"O King, after I had thus performed this beautiful worship of Śambhu, I then began the tāṇḍava dance, regardless of the formal ritual."
In my childhood, surrounded by a group of children, I once sang before Śiva, though my singing was devoid of proper musical notes due to my youth. (10)
Then, O King, having died, I was born as a Brahmin endowed with the memory of my former birth; in the city of Vaidiśa, I performed the worship of Śiva with particular devotion.
Having received the Śiva-initiation and being graced by the Śiva-scriptures, he installed a Liṅga in the temple of Śiva, endowed with faith.
He who constructs a temple of Śiva shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas, O King, for as many atoms as there are within that abode of Śiva.
Remembering the words of the Purāṇas, "The thunderbolt remains for so many years in the abode of Śiva," he [beheld] the mountain as the dwelling place of Śiva.
"I have constructed this beautiful [shrine] according to the rules of Viśvakarman, whether it be made of clay, fashioned from wood, of baked brick, or even of stone. (15)

One who has established a sanctuary shall receive fruit tenfold at each successive stage; likewise for one who sleeps on ashes, performs the three daily ablutions, and subsists on food obtained by begging. || 16 ||
"O King, while I was thus wearing matted hair, performing austerities, and intent on the worship of Śiva, my execution occurred once again."
Having been born there with the memory of my previous lives, I acted as a sovereign ruler of the earth in that third interval of existence, in the excellent city of Pratiṣṭhāna.
Known as Jayadatta, he was born of the Solar dynasty; thereafter, O King, various kinds of palaces were caused to be built by me.
In that other existence, by him who was intent on the propitiation of Śambhu, Bakapuṣpa and others were then appointed as his attendants.
O King, O best of monarchs, with flowers made of gold, silver, and jewels, I likewise perform the giving of food and other offerings in such a manner. (21)
"I performed worship of the Śiva-liṅgas with flowers alone; thereupon the Lord Śambhu was pleased and granted me a boon. (22)
O King, he was enveloped in that very body with the state of being free from old age and death; then, having obtained such a boon as was unique and shared by no other.
Abandoning devotion to Śiva, I, a king afflicted by passion, now wander this earth like an elephant blinded by rut. (24)
He began to violate women who were the wives of others, [thereby destroying] his lifespan, austerity, fame, splendor, glory, and prosperity. (25)
The primary cause of destruction is the violation of another’s wife; though possessing ears, he is deaf to the scriptures; though seeing, he is blind; and though speaking, he is dull-witted. (26)
O King, at that moment, a person clearly becomes insentient or sentient, a fool or even a scholar, all in a mere instant. (27)
The very moment he comes within the range of the eyes of those fawn-eyed women, for one who is dead there is residence in hell, and for one who is living there is fear of the Lord.
Thus, the violation of another's wife destroys both worlds; yet I remained fixed in the conviction, "I am free from old age and death. (29)
O King, having abandoned all fear of this world and the next, he thereafter began to violate the wives of others.
Then, having fully recognized me as one devoid of moral restraint, Yama approached the presence of the Lord due to the granting of a boon; he reported my transgression of dharma to Śambhu.
Yama said: "I shall not carry out the execution of this man who is protected by your power."
"O God, I am unable [to do this] for a sinner; by my command, appoint another. For you, O Lord, have declared that devoted wives are the very support of the world. (33)
"O Lord, among cows, Brahmins, those who frequent assemblies, the non-greedy, and those whose nature is generosity—those who are established in truth are the most excellent among them. (34)
"Having been violated by him while he was intoxicated by the granting of the boon, they have subverted my decree of dharma, treating me with utter contempt. (35)

O Lord of Gods, having heard these words of Dharma from Jayadatta, the resident of Pratiṣṭhāna, the Blessed One became enraged; he summoned me as I stood trembling with palms joined in reverence and cursed me. (36)
Īśvara said: "O you of wicked conduct, because those devoted wives were insulted by you," (37)
"Afflicted by desire, I cursed you; therefore, become a tortoise in an instant. Then, having prostrated, I entreated him to remove the torment of that curse.
"Sixty kalpas hence, this host shall become my own Gaṇa," Śiva declared, and having said this, he vanished from sight.
At that time, I was born as a tortoise ten yojanas in extent; I was brought by you into the waters of the ocean for the accomplishment of the sacrifice.
Remembering that which was done by the sacrificer before me, I am afraid of you; I have been burnt by you here on my back—look at these wounds of mine. (41)
O Indradyumna, at that time many sacrificial altars were constructed by you upon the back [of the tortoise] according to the prescriptions of the Kalpasūtras.
O lord of the earth, the earth, further tormented by sacrifices, flowed forth the essence of all sacred fords; she became the river Mahī. (43)
And by merely bathing in it, one is liberated from all sins; thereafter, some occasional dissolution (pralaya) occurred. || 44 ||
O King, this Lake Mānasa, measuring one hundred yojanas, has been floating for fifty-six kalpas according to my calculation, O monarch. (45)
Four [ages] have passed here; liberation remains thereafter. Thus is this long life, and thus has the state of a tortoise come about due to a curse.
"O King, it occurred to me that you are indeed a lord who violates the dharma of virtuous women. Tell me, what should be done to you, even though you are an enemy who has come to my home? (47)
O King, in the past my back was long ago scorched by you with fire; even today I see it as if it were still burning from that sacrificial rite.
"Why have you rejected this celestial chariot that has arrived, accompanied by a messenger of the gods? Enjoy the pleasures you yourself have earned! (49)
Indradyumna said: "I have been personally banished from heaven by that four-faced one; ashamed and defiled by the excessive sin of killing a bird, I shall not go there."
Therefore, having attained discernment, I shall embrace detachment—which destroys ignorance and sin—and strive for the sake of liberation.
Since you have become my host today while I was in my home, therefore command me as some teacher who leads one to the further shore of that which has no shore.
The tortoise said: "O King, there is a great sage named Lomaśa who is longer-lived than even I; he was previously seen by me once in the village of Kalāpa."
Indradyumna said: "Therefore, come; let us go together to him alone. The wise say that association with the virtuous is more purifying even than a sacred pilgrimage site. (54)

Having thus heard the words of the king at that time, all those six, placing that chief of sages in their hearts, departed joyfully toward the lord of brahmins, desiring to know the cause of his long life.
Nārada said: Then, O Pārtha, they beheld the great sage established in self-restraint. This is the eleventh chapter, named "The Narrative of the Tortoise."
Then he saw the one named Lomaśa, bearing matted locks tawny from bathing three times a day, like a fire sprinkled with clarified butter.
In his left hand he held a bundle of grass for the sake of shade, O best of Brahmins; in his right, he carried a rosary of beads, following the path of Maitra.
He who attains perfection through the recitation of mantras while not harming living beings that move upon the earth with harsh words and the like, is called a benevolent sage (muni).
Having beheld that ancient treasure of asceticism in the village of Kalāpa, the crane, the serpent-king, the twice-born, the owl, the vulture, and the tortoise bowed down to him. || 5 ||
Highly honored by this welcome, seating, and hospitality, they were pleased and spoke to him of the matter residing in their hearts as was appropriate.
The tortoise said: "This King Indradyumna, the foremost of those who perform sacrificial sessions, has been cast down from the vault of heaven by the Creator due to the loss of his fame."
O best of men, having attained the restoration of his fame through Mārkaṇḍeya and others, he no longer desires heaven, which is terrifying due to the fear of falling back from it again.

"Having been favored by you, this king desires great prosperity here; therefore, O Blessed One, he must be dismissed. He is your disciple and has been brought here by me to your presence; tell him what he wishes for."
Indeed, assisting others is the vow undertaken by the virtuous, especially those who have been dismissed [from their duties] and have entered the conduct of disciples.
When wicked deeds are not repelled, what has been well-spoken becomes undoubtedly harmful; it engenders either hatred or even death for one of the two parties.
"Being vigilant regarding those things to be cast off, this Sage bestows that very [state]; since you yourself understand the Dharma in this way, how could we [know it]? (12)
Lomaśa said: "O Kūrma, all that has been spoken by you today to us is fitting; we have been reminded of that ancient teaching which is set forth in the Dharmaśāstras."
"Speak with full confidence, O King, regarding the doubt residing in your heart. Who said what to you? Whatever remains, I shall tell you; of this there is no doubt. (14)
Indradyumna said: O Blessed One, let my first question be answered: why is it that your hermitage is not [visible] even during the summer season when the sun is at the meridian?
Even a mere hut provides shade when grass is placed upon the head and held in the hands. (16)
Lomaśa said: Death is inevitable, and this body will surely fall; for whose sake is a house built by those dwelling in the midst of impermanent existence?
For one whose friend is Death, or who has drunk the supreme nectar of immortality, it is appropriate for him to say: "This shall be mine tomorrow. (18)
This day, which was to occur after thousands of yugas, has now arrived as if it were today; what then can be said of the limit of death? (19)
This body, which is an effect following its cause, has arisen from semen; tell me, how can it attain purity, like charcoal that has been washed? (20)
O best of kings, how is it that those conquered by the six internal enemies do not feel shame when they commit sin for his sake? (21)
Having been born here from that Brahman, produced from two grains of sand, how shall he live while reciting and hearing what is declared in the Vedas? (22)
Nevertheless, the illusory power of Viṣṇu deludes the undiscerning; for even those with a lifespan of a hundred years do not perceive Death residing within their own hearts.
O King, teeth are fickle, fortune is fickle, youth is fickle, and life is fickle; even more so than these, the giving and the home of men are utterly unstable.
Having thus understood that the essence of saṃsāra is both moving and unsteady, for whose sake, O King, is this attachment to houses and other such things maintained? (25)
Indradyumna said: "The Blessed One alone is heard of as long-lived throughout the three worlds; for that reason I have come here, so why do you speak thus?"
Lomaśa said: "In every kalpa, a single hair from my body perishes; and when all [the hairs] are destroyed, my own death shall come to pass."
Behold my knee region, two finger-breadths wide and devoid of hair; such a body has been born, and since death is certain, what is the use of a home? (28)
Nārada said: Having heard those words, the king, laughing and greatly amazed, asked him the reason for such a long lifespan.
Indradyumna said: "O Brahmin, I ask you this: since your life is so long as this, is it due to the power of your charity or your austerity? (30)
Lomaśa said: Listen, O King, I shall relate this meritorious story arising from a previous birth, endowed with the dharma of Śiva, which destroys all sins.
Formerly, I was a Śūdra, extremely poor upon this earth; indeed, I wandered over the surface of the world, greatly oppressed by hunger. (32)
Then, at midday, I saw that great liṅga situated within a lattice-work, and its reservoir of water was seen not far from it.
Then, having entered that water, drunk it, and bathed, he bathed that Śambhu-liṅga and performed worship with auspicious lotuses.
Then, O best of kings, with my throat parched by hunger, I bowed to that Śrīkaṇṭha and set out on the path once more; however, I perished along the way.
Then, due to bathing the Śiva-liṅga and once worshipping it with a lotus, I was born as a son in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, endowed with the memory of my former birth.
Reflecting that this world is a false play of appearance, having the semblance of reality though consisting of ignorance—having realized this, he remained silent. (37)
By that brahmin, having propitiated Maheśvara in his old age, the name "I am attained" was given to me, and the name "Īśāna" was established.
Then, out of affection, that brahmin gave me very many medicines, being determined that "I shall remove your muteness."
He employed many mantra-recitations, physicians, and other various means, as did his parents, whose minds were deeply attached to Mahāmāyā.
Beholding that foolishness, there was laughter in my mind at that time; for, having reached such youth, he had abandoned his own home in the night.
Having worshipped Śambhu with lotuses, I then retired to my bed; thereafter, when my father had passed away, I was abandoned as a fool.
Then, recognized by his kinsmen, he remained subsisting on fruit; thus recognized, he worshipped the Lord with many kinds of lotuses.
Then, at the end of a hundred years, the moon-crested Lord, the bestower of boons, appeared before his eyes; he was entreated: "Grant me the destruction of old age and death."
Īśvara said: "Since there is no such thing as freedom from old age and death for one who bears a name and form, even for me the fall of the body must occur; therefore, set a limit to my life."
Having heard these words of Śambhu, I then made this resolve: "Let there be the shedding of hair at the end of a kalpa; let death occur during the universal dissolution. (46)
"Therefore, may you become my attendant; this is the boon I desire. Having said, "So be it," the Blessed Lord Hara vanished from sight.
From that time forth, I became devoted to asceticism; moreover, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin through the worship of Śiva. 48.
Whether with *bradhnābja* flowers or other lotuses, there is no doubt in this matter; act thus, O Great King, and you too shall attain your desire. (49)
For a person devoted to Hara, there is nothing difficult to attain within the three worlds; having withdrawn external activity, as well as the organs of knowledge and action, [he attains all]. 50.
This dissolution in Sadāśiva is always called the internal yoga; because it is difficult to perform, Śiva himself proclaimed it as external yoga. (51)
Worship performed with the five elements certainly bestows distinguished fruits; it is moreover free from the latent tendencies such as afflictions, karma, and its maturation.
By worshipping Īśāna and chanting the Praṇava, one shall attain liberation; when all sins have been destroyed, devotion to Śiva arises.
For those whose intellects are struck down by evil, even mention of Śiva is difficult to obtain; birth in Bhārata is difficult to attain, and the worship of Śiva is difficult to achieve. (54)

Bathing in the Jāhnavī is difficult to attain; devotion to Śiva is very difficult to attain; giving gifts to a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain; and the worship of the Fire is difficult to attain. (55)
And the worship of the Supreme Person is difficult to attain for those with little merit. (56)
The confluence of the Lakṣa and Dhanuṣā is at that [distance]; half of that is the Hutāśana; Pātra is at one hundred thousand [yojanas], as are Revā and Rudra at sixty thousand.
Thus, O lord of the earth, I have related all this to you—how his life became long by propitiating Maheśvara.
For those great-souled men who have performed devotion to Śiva, nothing in the three worlds is difficult to obtain, difficult to reach, or impossible to accomplish; this is certain. (59)
O King, having observed the attainment of perfection by Nandīśvara through the worship of Śiva with that very body, who would not bow down to Śaṅkara?
Even Time met its end for King Śveta as he was bowing to Śrīkaṇṭha; who would not worship that Lord? (61)
Who would not go for refuge to Him, by whose will this universe is born, maintained, and likewise dissolved at the end? (62)

This is the secret; this alone is the primary duty for men, O King: the worship of Śiva. Those people who enter upon the path of obstacles [are quickly overcome]; a man devoted to Śiva truly attains Śiva himself. 63.
Nārada said: Having heard these words of that lord of sages, the king said, "I shall not go anywhere, leaving you, O man. (1)
Today I shall worship the Liṅga, which bestows all perfections upon men; favored by you today, let everyone depart as they came.
Having heard those words of the king, the crane, the vulture, the tortoise, and likewise the owl, bowed down and spoke to the sage Lomaśa.
And that friend of all, saying "So be it" to them at that time, favored all those who had approached him with prostrations, as if they were his disciples.

Intent on bestowing grace upon them, the sage, who was compassionate toward the distressed, instructed them in the worship of the Liṅga according to the ritual of Śiva-initiation. For the virtuous, the company of the good in a sacred place is superior even to a holy pilgrimage site. (5)

It is like the rising of the thousand-rayed sun of a noble assembly—an unprecedented occurrence that immediately dispels the impurities of the end of the age, just as the ripened fruit removes long-standing stains.
Those waves of the nectar-like essence of happiness arising from the assembly of the virtuous completely and utterly dispel the darkness within.
All excellent things—ambrosia, sugar, honey, and the six flavors—then attained the state of being associated with the virtuous through the teaching of Śiva.

Mārkaṇḍa, the king, and the others began the practice of Kriyā-yoga. While they were thus engaged in penance, one day there arrived [a sage] who was eager for a vision of Lomaśa in the course of his pilgrimage.
"O King, the primary purpose of a journey is indeed the journey of life; a region of the earth is so described by the virtuous when it is resorted to as a secondary consequence of a pilgrimage. (10)
O Phālguna, after I had performed the rites of hospitality and honored them, and once I was rested, they, led by Nāḍījaṅgha, bowed down to me and then questioned me.
They said: "O Brahmin, all four of us have fallen due to a curse as a result of our own actions; therefore, please point out some place for the purpose of attaining liberation from it. (12)
For this land is fruitless, O Sage; it is a mere wasteland, though belonging to Bhārata. (13)
"Even there, tell us of some single place where the fruit of all holy fords (tīrthas) may be obtained. Thus questioned by them, I then spoke this to them: || 14 ||
"Ask Saṃvarta; he will tell you in truth about that region of the earth which brings about the attainment of the fruits of all sacred fords. (15)
They said: "Where is that yogin? We did not know him; yet, by the mere sight of Saṃvarta, our liberation has been achieved—this is his grace toward us. (16)
"If you know him, tell me; for association with a friend is never fruitless. Then, after reflecting upon this again and again, I spoke to them: || 17 ||
In Vārāṇasī, this Saṃvarta dwells, bearing his secret signs; smeared with dirt, naked, subsisting on alms, and following the Kutapa [time].
Taking his food from the hollow of his hands, entirely free from possessions, he meditated upon the Supreme Brahman, the Lord known as the Praṇava.
Having eaten, he departs for the forest in the evening without being noticed by people; he is a lord of yogis, while others who bear his outward marks exist as well.
I shall describe his characteristics so that you may recognize that sage: at night on the royal highway by the city gate, a corpse was seen on the ground by people. (21)
That which is not understood should be set aside; one should remain near it. He who, having approached that ground, suddenly turns back [is to be known]. (22)
That Saṃvarta will undoubtedly not step upon this thorn; he should be questioned about what is desired, having approached him with humility.
If he asks, "By whom was I told this?", then you should inform him of me and say: "Having informed you, he entered the fire. (24)
Having heard that, they all acted according to my word; reaching Vārāṇasī and seeing Saṃvarta, they did exactly as instructed.
Upon seeing the corpse placed there by them, Saṃvarta indeed turned back; yet, though overcome by hunger, they recognized him and followed after him with great speed.
