Whoever shall recite this Śatarudrīya every morning, the god Śiva, being pleased, will grant him all boons.
There is nothing more meritorious than this, nor anything that yields greater fruit; and this secret of all the Vedas was told to me by the Sun. (199)
Whatever sin has been committed by speech or even acquired by the mind, that sin goes to destruction when the Śatarudriya is recited. (200)
He who recites the Śatarudriya shall be freed from disease if afflicted by disease, released from bondage if bound, and liberated from fear if afraid. (201)
He who worships the Lord with a hundred names, with as many jars and flowers, and even with a hundred prostrations, is liberated from all sins.
There are one hundred lingas and likewise one hundred worshippers; their names are remembered as the destroyers of all defects.
Whoever shall recite [this] regarding these five specific marks is completely liberated from the defects arising from the five sense objects. || 204 ||

Nārada said: Having heard this, they remained in Guptakṣetra filled with joy; even while being entreated [by others], they continued to worship the five liṅgas, intent on meditation upon Śiva. || 205 ||
Then, after a long period of time, the god Śaṅkara, appearing before them in person out of his particular devotion to them, spoke joyfully.
Śiva said: "O Baka, Ulūka, Gṛdhra, Kūrma, and King Indradyumna, you have attained liberation in the form of the deity (sārūpya-mukti); you shall dwell in my world."
"Lomaśa and Mārkaṇḍeya shall also become liberated while still alive," said the God of gods; having been told this, the king installed the Liṅga. (208)
Having learned of the virtues of that sacred ford, the king, desiring eternal fame, [worshipped] the one named Indradyumneśvara, also known as Mahākāla. (209)
Having installed this incomparably beautiful triple-liṅga, he spoke as follows: "As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth remains... (210)
"May the Indradyumneśvara Liṅga rejoice for eternal years! Then the Blessed Lord Śiva, having said "So be it," spoke again:
Whoever here constantly worships the Liṅga Aindryadumna shall certainly become a Gaṇa and will dwell in my world. || 212 ||
Having spoken thus, the moon-crested god went to the world of Rudra together with those five; they, too, were born again as Gaṇas.
Such was the power of King Indradyumna, the lord of the earth; by that hero, while performing sacrifice, this river Mahī was created.
Such is this meritorious confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; therefore, O Pārtha, it has been described to you in brief. (215)
That man who, having bathed here at the confluence, worships Indradyumneśvara, shall have his residence wherever the Lord, the husband of Pārvatī, resides.
This Liṅga removes all bonds and bestows the status of a Gaṇapati; for it was installed by him after casting off all fetters, O Phālguna. (217)

Thus has this majesty of the supreme Saṅgama been told to you, O performer of merit; and the majesty of Indradyumneśvara, which possesses most wonderful merit, has also been told, O performer of merit.
Arjuna said: O great sage, I desire to hear in detail that majesty of Kumāranātha which was mentioned by you in the course of another narrative.
Nārada said: O Phālguna, having slain Tāraka, the son of Vajrāṅga, the Lord Guha installed this very Liṅga.
O Pārtha, through seeing, hearing, meditating upon, worshipping, and through scriptural study and salutations, Kumāreśa removes all sins; of this there is no doubt.
Arjuna said: "O Nārada, this story is full of great wonder, delightful, and destructive of sins; tell it to me in detail and according to the truth."
Is that Daitya Vajrāṅga invincible, and what is the power of Tāraka? How was he slain, and how was Guha born?
How was the Liṅga named Kumāreśvara established? What is the fruit of this Liṅga? Tell me that in detail.
Nārada said: Having prostrated before Kumāra, the commander of the army, and the Lord, listen with a single-minded focus, O Pārtha, to the great life-story of Kumāra.
O Phālguna, the mind-born son of Brahmā, the Prajāpati named Dakṣa, begot sixty daughters upon his wife named Vīriṇī.
He gave ten to Dharmā, thirteen to Kaśyapa, twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
The lord gave two daughters each to Bhūta, Aṅgiras, and Kṛśāśva; hear from me the names of these wives.
From whose births the three worlds were filled: Bhānu, Lambā, Kakud, Bhūmi, Viśvā, Sādhyā, and Marutvatī. || 11 ||
Listen to [the account of] Vasu’s sons, the auspicious muhūrtas, his lawful wives, and his sons; O bull among gods, Bhānu had a son. (12)
From Lambā came Vidyota, and from him the Stanayitnus; Kakud was the son of Śakaṭa, and from him came the son Kīkaṭa.
Bhuva, Durga, and Svarga were born, and from him Nanda was also born; the Viśvedevas were born of Viśvā, and they are declared to be childless.
Sādhyā had twelve sons, and Arthasiddhi was her son. From Marutvatī were born Marutvān and Sujayanta. (15)
Those whom people who know the truth call Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and from Vasu came the eight Vasus, and from Muhūrtā the Muhūrtakas.
Those indeed who bestow upon living beings their respective fruits arising from their own time are Saṃkalpa, and Āśā is the wife of Saṃkalpa; Kāma is the son born of Saṃkalpa.
Surūpā gave birth to eleven sons who were indeed Rudras: Kapālī, Piṅgala, Bhīma, Virūpākṣa, and Vilohita. || 18 ||
Ajaka, Śāsana, Śāstṛ, Śambhu, Antya, and Bhava—these others are known as the attendants of Rudra and the sons of Virūpā.
Svadhā was the wife of Prajāpati Aṅgiras; she gave birth to the Pitṛs, as well as to her son, the lord Atharvāṅgiras.
Kṛśāśva had two wives, Arci and Diṣaṇā; their son is celebrated as the collection of missiles (astragāma) together with the means of its withdrawal.
Pataṅgī, Yāminī, Tāmrā, and Timi were the daughters of Ariṣṭanemi; Pataṅgī gave birth to birds, and Yāminī to locusts.
From Tāmrā were born the hawks, vultures, and other birds; likewise from Timi were born the hosts of aquatic creatures. Now, this entire world is the progeny of Kaśyapa’s wives.
Listen to the names of the mothers of the worlds, which bring about welfare: Aditi, Diti, Danu, Siṃhī, Danāyu, and likewise Surabhi. (24)
Ariṣṭā, Vinatā, Grāvā, Dayā, Krodhavaśā, Irā, Kadrū, and Muni—these two pairs are proclaimed as the mothers. (25)
The Ādityas are the sons of Aditi; the Daityas are proclaimed as the sons of Diti; the Dānavas are said to be the sons of Danu; and Rāhu is the planet who is the son of Siṃhī.
From Danāyu was likewise born the powerful host of Danāyus; and from Surabhi were born the cows, as well as the sons of Ariṣṭā, the Yugaṃdharas.
Vinatā gave birth to Aruṇa and the mighty Garuḍa; Grāvā’s sons were the beasts of prey, as well as the host known as Krodhavaśa.
The trees are known as born from Krodhavaśā and Irā; the Nāgas are known as the sons of Kadrū, and the hosts of Apsarases are said to be from Muni. (29)
Therein, the two sons of Diti who were slain by Viṣṇu were the hero Hiraṇyakaśipu and the other, Hiraṇyākṣa.
Then, her sons having been slain, that goddess Diti propitiated Kaśyapa and requested a boon for another son of great strength.
The Lord gave her that slayer of Śakra in battle, and he said: "Furthermore, abide in this vow for a thousand years."

Having been addressed thus, she, remaining at Puṣkara, performed accordingly with a concentrated mind; while she was engaged in that religious observance, the thousand-eyed Indra remained intent upon her.
She practiced service toward him with devotion, and Diti likewise gave her consent; at that time, ten years remained of the thousand-year period.
Greatly pleased and gratified by Śakra’s devotion, Diti spoke to Śakra: "O best of gods, know that I have nearly completed my vow here. (35)
A brother shall be born to you; with him, you shall enjoy this sovereignty, just as he has enjoyed these three worlds with its thorns removed.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Diti, impelled by the power of destiny, fell asleep during the day with her hair trodden upon by her feet.
Having observed that very opening, he who was embodied as Yoga entered it; with his thunderbolt, he divided Diti’s embryo situated within her womb into seven parts.
Then Maghavan further divided each fragment into seven parts, seven by seven, out of anger; and then Diti woke up.
"Let him not be killed! Let him not be killed! she said to Śakra, as he was cutting them with his thunderbolt, both by her speech and by her weeping.
Then Śakra said to them variously, "Do not weep," and having emerged from that belly, he stood before them with palms joined in reverence.
And, undaunted, he spoke these words to his mother, who was filled with distress: "O Mother, you have slept during the day, while your hair was being trampled by feet. (42)
"O Vāta, your fetus was held by me for a very long time while you were asleep; your sons have been divided into forty-nine portions by means of the thunderbolt. (43)
"Let your word come true; I shall enjoy prosperity together with them. I will grant them places in heaven for as long as I exist, O Diti. (44)
"Do not weep," they said to me, "for you shall be known as the Maruts. Having been addressed thus, Diti became ashamed and remained speechless.
Accompanied by them, Indra went to the ends of the quarters, where he is known as the winds; then Diti, distressed, spoke again to her husband.
"O Blessed One, grant me a powerful son who shall be a slayer of Śakra, one who cannot be killed by the missiles or weapons of the inhabitants of the three heavens. (47)
"Know that you are as good as dead if you do not give me an answer, O Prajāpati! Thus addressed, he then spoke to his deeply distressed wife.
For ten thousand years you shall practice asceticism with steadfast devotion, your limbs being as firm as adamant, unbreakable, and as solid as iron.
"A son named Vajrāṅga, who is devoted to the Dharma, shall be born to you. Having obtained this boon, the goddess went to the forest for ascetic penance.
For ten thousand years he performed severe penance; at the conclusion of his penance, the Blessed Lady gave birth to Durjaya.

He had a son who was beyond ritual decoration, invincible, and difficult even for the thunderbolt to pierce; as soon as he was born, he became one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures.
With devotion he said to his mother, "O Mother, what shall I do? Then Diti, delighted, spoke to her son, the lord of the Daityas.
"O dear son, many of my sons have been slain by the thousand-eyed one; I desire to perform their requital by slaying Śakra. (54)
Having replied, "So be it," the powerful one departed for heaven; and with his arms as weapons, he defeated Śakra along with his army in battle.
Having dragged Indra of the gods by his foot like a lion drags a small animal, he approached his mother while [Indra] was pleading for mercy, overcome with fear. || 56 ||
In the meantime, Brahmā and Kaśyapa of great asceticism arrived there in great alarm; then Brahmā spoke to him.
"Release, release this suppliant, my son; what need is there for him? For one honored as a hero, humiliation is said to be equivalent to death. (58)
He who is released by my word is indeed dead even while living; those who merely kill an enemy in battle are not proclaimed as heroes.
Those who, having endured the exhaustion of pride, are able to abandon it are indeed excellent; for you, considering it the most insignificant thing, have carried out your mother's word.
"Likewise, the word of your father must be carried out; release this Vāsava, my son. Having heard this, Vajrāṅga bowed and spoke these words: || 61 ||
"I have no further business with him; I have fulfilled my mother’s command. You are indeed the lord of gods and asuras, and my great-grandfather."
"O God, I shall carry out your word; here is Śatakratu released. Yet, I do not desire this sovereignty over the three worlds enjoyed by Śakra."
Like a woman enjoyed by another, or like a garland already worn by another—tell me what essence exists within the three worlds that is not so. (64)
Brahmā said: There is nothing superior to austerity; indeed, austerity is the wealth of the great. Everything is attained through austerity; you are fit for austerity, my son. (65)
Vajrāṅga said: "O Lord, my delight is in asceticism; may there be no obstacle for me therein through your grace, O Blessed One. Having spoken thus, he became silent.
Brahmā said: "O son, if you desire to perform penance after abandoning this cruel disposition, then by means of this state of mind and intellect, you have attained the fruit of your birth."
Having spoken thus, the lotus-born god created a large-eyed maiden and gave her to him as a wife.
And the Grandfather gave her the name Varāṅgī; then Brahmā departed for heaven together with Kaśyapa.
Vajrāṅga also went to the forest for penance along with her; that lord of the Daityas stood there with his arms raised for a thousand years.
The lotus-petal-eyed one, pure in intellect and great in austerity, spent that much time with his face turned downwards, and for that long he practiced the penance of the five fires.
Subsisting on no food, performing terrible austerities, he became a mass of penance; then, remaining within the water, he spent a thousand years.
While he had entered into the water, his wife, who was devoted to great vows and dedicated to him, remained on the bank of that very lake, observing silence.
Perceiving her husband to be without food, the devoted wife performed penance; while she was engaged in that austerity, Indra created a terrifying apparition for her.
Having assumed the form of a monkey, he approached her vicinity; casting his gaze upon her, he discharged urine and excrement.
Desiring to cause an obstacle to her asceticism, he made her garments disheveled, her face disordered, and her hair disarrayed.
Then he caused her distress in the form of a ram; thereafter, in the form of a serpent, he bound her by both her feet.
Thus, that servant of the gods drew him far away; moreover, because of his youth resulting from asceticism, she did not become subject to slaughter by him.
And by means of her forbearance, O fortunate one, she did not harbor even the slightest anger; consequently, he defiled that hermitage in the form of a jackal.

In the form of fire, he burned her great hermitage; and in the form of a most fierce wind, he dragged that auspicious woman away. Thus, by means of repeated terrors such as lions, wolves, and other beasts, [he pursued her].
When Vajrāṅga’s queen did not cease at all, she then perceived the wickedness of the mountain and resolved to utter a curse.
Seeing her intent on pronouncing a curse, the mountain, assuming a human form, then spoke in haste to that beautiful-eyed woman of noble hips.
Śaila said: "O observer of great vows, I am not wicked; I am to be resorted to by all embodied beings. However, this slayer of Vṛtra causes me excessive distress, and for that reason he is angry."
In the meantime, a period of a thousand years elapsed; when that time had passed, the Blessed One, born from the lotus, [arose].
Being pleased, he approached Vajrāṅga at the reservoir and spoke to him.

Brahmā said: "I grant you all your desires; arise, O son of Diti! Thus addressed, the lord of the Daityas, a treasury of asceticism, then rose and spoke these words with palms joined in reverence to the Grandfather of all the worlds.
Vajrāṅga said: "O Grandfather, let there be no asura-nature for me, nor any delight in the kingdom of Śakra; let there be a delight in austerity and dharma—this is what I choose. (87)
"So be it," Brahmā said to him with a mind filled with wonder; and he overlooked Śakra, for who can overstep what is destined to be?
Even the sages, humans, gods, and those headed by Śiva and Brahmā, do not transcend the destined future, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore.
Having thought thus, Viriñca also vanished right there; and Vajrāṅga too, having completed his penance with steadfast self-restraint, [departed].
Desiring food, he did not see his own wife in his hermitage; thinking to himself, "I am fruitless because I am without a wife," he wandered here and there. (91)
Looking at his own wife while desiring to perform his daily rites, he then beheld her as one who brings companionship both in this world and the next.
Then, seeing his own beloved weeping in distress with her face hidden by a tree, the Daitya spoke to her, consoling her.

Vajrāṅga said: "O timid one, who has done you wrong while you were engaged in your own ascetic penance? Why do you weep, O young girl, while I, your husband, am still alive? Or what desire shall I grant you? Speak quickly, O beautiful lady. (94)

He who does not cherish his auspicious mistress of the household, adorned with excellent virtues and united with her husband like the union of the lame and the blind, and who does not fulfill her desires—is he a man? In my opinion, he is no man at all.
Varāṅgī said: "I have been destroyed, cast aside, terrified, and tormented many times by the fierce Lord of Gods, whose own protector has perished. (1)
Seeing no end to her suffering, she resolved to give up her life, saying: "If you have compassion, grant me a son who may deliver me from this terrible misery. (2)
Thus addressed, the lord of the Daityas, though distressed, reflected in his heart: "Even regarding the dispositions of the Asuras, I have no desire."
Nevertheless, I believe that because you consider your wife worthy of compassion, you have taken up all the stages of life (āśramas) and, as one with a wife, abide by your own stage of life.

Relying upon her, one crosses the ocean of calamities as if crossing the sea by means of water-vessels; she overcomes the enemies that are the senses, which are otherwise invincible to other supports.
Like a lord of a fortress easily defeating his enemies, she conquered householders with ease; nor were there any capable of emulating that mistress of the home.
Furthermore, she from whom one desires to give the entirety of one's life-span and the Dharma, and in whom one finds one’s very self—she is therefore called "jāyā" (wife).

Because she is indeed to be supported, she is traditionally called "bhāryā" (the one to be supported); she alone is called the "house" (gṛha), and therefore she is traditionally known as "gṛhiṇī" (the mistress of the house). || 8 ||
She is called "wife" because she protects one from the defilements of saṃsāra; who indeed would not feel compassion for a beloved such as this? (9)
"Three are the lights of a man," so indeed Devala said: "Wife, work, and learning—these three must be accomplished with diligent effort. (10)
Therefore, if I, having become her husband, do not protect her while she is thus afflicted, then according to the declarations of the scriptures, I shall undoubtedly go to the very depths of hell.
"Indeed, I am capable of conquering this Indra so that he becomes free from his debt; furthermore, I shall fulfill her desire and grant her a son of great strength. (12)
Having reflected thus, Vajrāṅga, his eyes agitated with anger, resolved once more to perform austerities in order to take revenge upon Mahendra.
But having understood his even more cruel resolve, Brahmā again came with haste to where that son of Diti was.
The Blessed Lord, the Master, spoke to him with a sweet voice.
Brahmā said: "O Daitya of great vows, why do you again desire such a cruel restraint? Tell me that, O you who are intent on food. (16)
The fruit that is obtained by one who remains without food for a thousand years has been attained by you in a mere moment through the renunciation of food.

"O lotus-eyed one, the renunciation of unattained desires is not considered as weighty as the renunciation of a desire already attained. Having heard these words of Brahmā, the Daitya spoke with palms joined in reverence: (18)
The Daitya said: "O Grandfather, for the sake of a wife I shall perform severe penance; and I am intent on obtaining a son who will be the destroyer of the pride of the gods. (19)
Having heard these words, the four-faced god born from the interior of a lotus then spoke to the king of the Daityas with a gracious countenance.
Brahmā said: "Enough of your penance, my child; do not enter into further extensive hardship. A son named Tāraka shall be born to you, possessed of great strength. (21)
"Having loosened the beautiful braided hair of the celestial women,"—having been addressed thus, the king of the Daityas bowed down to the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā).
Having dismissed her and gone to the queen, he gladdened her with joy; then that couple, having achieved their purpose, departed for the hermitage.
Then Varāṅgī, of excellent complexion, bore that conceived embryo within her very womb for a full thousand years.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Varāṅgī gave birth; indeed, as that lord of the Daityas, who was terrifying to the world, was being born.
The entire earth trembled, the great oceans were violently agitated, the mountains shook, and terrifying winds blew. || 26 ||
The best of sages, like deer pierced by a hunter, lost their luster as they muttered prayers; even the sun and other luminaries faded, while mists shrouded the directions.
When that great asura was born, all the great asuras as well as the asura women arrived there, filled with joy.
Overcome with joy, the wives of the asuras sang and danced; then, O son of Pṛthā, a great festival arose among the dānavas.
Then the gods, including Indra, became despondent in mind; for as soon as he was born, Tāraka, the lord of the Daityas, possessed fierce prowess.
The Asura was consecrated by the Daityas, including the Kuraṅga, Mahiṣa, and others, as the great sovereign of all the Asuras, joined by all the mighty Asuras.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, having attained the great sovereignty, that Tāraka spoke these words, full of reason, to the foremost of the Dānavas: || 32 ||
Listen, all you mighty asuras, to my words; having heard them, let your intellects become more steadfast and act according to my speech.
"An inexhaustible enmity has grown between us by the very nature of our birth; I shall therefore carry out that enmity for the sake of victory over them. (34)
However, O sons of Danu, I consider union with the gods to be achievable through austerity; therefore, I shall first perform severe penance.
"Then we shall conquer the gods and enjoy the three worlds; for a man who employs the proper means becomes one whose prosperity is indeed stable. (36)
"Unrestrained and fickle, he is incapable of protecting even what he has obtained. Having heard those words of that asura, all the Dānavas [spoke].
Then, filled with wonder, they spoke these words to him: "Excellent! Excellent! He then went to an excellent cave of Mount Pāriyātra.
It was strewn with flowers of every season and illuminated by various medicinal herbs; it contained diverse dwellings, variegated by the flow of juices from many mineral ores.
Abounding in many diverse forms, crowded with various factions and families, endowed with manifold springs, and possessing various kinds of reservoirs of water. || 40 ||
Having reached that cave, the Daitya performed extensive penance; observing the Pāśupata initiation, he chanted the five mantras.
It is said that for ten thousand years he remained without food, performing the penance of the five fires; then, day by day, he cut off pieces of his own flesh, each weighing one karṣa.
He offered his flesh as an oblation into the fire, and thereby he became devoid of flesh; thus, with his body stripped of flesh, he became a mass of ascetic austerity.
All beings blazed on every side with his splendor; and all the gods were agitated, terrified by his ascetic power.
In the meantime, Brahmā, having attained supreme satisfaction, went to the peak of the mountain to grant a boon to Tāraka.
Having reached that king of mountains and mounted his swan-vehicle, the Lord then spoke to Tāraka with a sweet voice.
Brahmā said: "Arise, my son! For you now, nothing is unattainable through your asceticism. Choose a boon that is desired, whatever dwells in your mind. (47)
Thus addressed, the Daitya Tāraka, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to that Lord.
Tāraka said: "O Lord, we are bound by our birthright and have long harbored enmity toward the gods; yet those cruel and pitiless ones have utterly exterminated the Daityas."
"It is my resolve that I shall be their deliverer; he is invulnerable to all beings and to weapons of great power. (50)
"May I possess chowries; this is the boon residing in my heart. Grant this to me, O Lord of Gods; indeed, I desire no other boon. (51)

Then Virañci, the leader of the immortals, spoke to that Daitya: "The maintenance of a body by an embodied being is not possible without death; for one who is born, death is certain—this truth has been proclaimed by the Vedas. (52)
Having reflected thus, choose a boon from whom you have no apprehension; then, having reflected, the lord of the Daityas [chose] from one seven days old since birth.
Tāraka said: "Except for children among the seven classes of beings, may I be unslayable even by the gods; thus was I entreated. (54)
Deluded by pride, the great asura chose death from Brahmā; then, at the word of Hara, Brahmā said to him, "So be it."
The god went to heaven and the Daitya also to his own abode; then the lords of the Daityas [honored] that Daitya who had emerged from his ascetic penance.
They surrounded him, just as birds surround a tree laden with fruit, while that great Tāraka, the son of Diti, remained established in his sovereignty.
O Pārtha, at that place directed by Brahmā on the northern shore of the great ocean, auspicious trees of all seasons grew there.
Beauty, splendor, fortitude, intelligence, and unbroken prosperity—all these qualities indeed surrounded the Dānava, who was filled with virtues and entirely free from flaws.
His limbs were smeared with black agallochum, he was adorned with a great crown, equipped with beautiful armlets, and seated upon a magnificent lion-throne.

The most excellent Apsarases dance and the Gandharvas sing; the moon and sun serve as lamps on his path, and the wind acts as his fan; the planets go before him, proclaiming his life-span and destiny.

Thus, having obtained the kingdom through the strength of his own arms and rejoicing, that Daitya, arrogant with the power of his entire body which had been uplifted, once addressed his ministers and spoke: (62)
Tāraka said: Deluded by a kingdom that resembles a bubble, by women, dice, and intoxicating drinks, a man here squanders his human birth and his manly prowess.
His entire birth is in vain until the end of the kalpa; of this there is no doubt. || 2 ||
That man who does not fulfill the desires of his parents, nor brings joy to his kinsmen, nor acquires fame or honor, is as good as dead in this world even though he has been born.

Therefore, for the sake of victory over the leaders of the immortals and for the swift seizure of the Fortune of the three worlds, let my eight-wheeled chariot be yoked, and let my army—the circle of Daityas difficult to conquer—be assembled for me.
My banner shall have its golden bands fastened, and my parasol shall be adorned with nets of pearls; today I shall arrange the unfastened hair-ornaments of these celestial nymphs.
Just as formerly I was a monkey to that mother, by that truth may I become a savior.
Nārada said: Having heard the words of Tāraka, the Dānava named Grasana, who was the commander-in-chief of the Daitya king, acted accordingly without delay.
Having struck the deep-sounding drum and swiftly summoned the Daityas, the Daitya prepared the chariot of the wise king of the Daityas.
Accompanied by a thousand Garuḍas whose splendor was like that of Garuḍa himself, those sons of Suparṇa were stationed in a cave of Mount Meru.
Having been conquered by the king of the Daityas, they were appointed as his mounts; his chariot had sixty-four wheels and was four yojanas in width.
Endowed with various pleasure-houses and enchanting with song and instrumental music, it appeared joined together like a city of the Gandharvas. || 11 ||
Then ten Daityas of fierce prowess arrived there, accompanied by retinues of millions upon millions, as did many others for the battle.
Jambha was their leader, followed by Kujambha; then Mahiṣa, Kuñjara, Meṣa, Kālanemi, and Nimī.
Mathana, Jambhaka, and Śumbha—these ten are the leaders of the Daityas; these lords of the Daityas possess bodies as massive as mountains and are endowed with fierce prowess.
Wielding various weapons and masters of diverse missiles and arms, Tāraka’s banner appeared in many forms and was a source of great terror.
In some places it was a terrible Rākṣasa, and in others a Piśāca, a crow, or a vulture; thus did that banner appear in many different forms.
The commander Grasana shone with a banner in the form of a crocodile; for there, Jambha’s mouth was of the Piśāca type and made of iron.
A donkey with its tail lashing was on Kujambha’s banner; and on Mahiṣa’s, a beautiful golden jackal shone forth.
The vulture was indeed the [son] of Kuñjara, and the Rākṣasa was that of Meṣa; Mahākāla was the son of Kālanemi, and Mahātimi was the son of Nimi. || 19 ||
The banner of Mathana was a rākṣasī, and that of Jambhaka was a crow; Mahāvṛka was the banner of Śumbha—such were their banners.
And there were other banners arranged in various forms, [including] a hundred tigers of swift speed adorned with golden garlands.
Grasana’s chariot, yoked and sounding like a great cloud, shone forth; and Jambha’s chariot was likewise harnessed with a hundred lions.
The chariot of Kujaṃbha was yoked with donkeys having the faces of Piśācas; it was likewise equipped with as many buffaloes, camels, elephants, and horses.
Having ascended Mount Meṣa, which was firmly held by elephants and supported by the formidable leopards of Kālanemi, he remained there.
Upon a black horse, a hundred cubits long, adorned with golden ornaments, which had four tusks, was fragrant, neighed, and resembled a cloud; || 25 ||
Adorned with a network of white chowries and flower garlands, the lord of the Daityas named Mathana shone forth, holding a noose in his hand.
Jambhaka mounted a camel adorned with a garland of small bells, while the Dānava Śumbha mounted the great cloud Kālamuñca.
And other heroic Dānavas, possessing various mounts and weapons, wearing fierce and variegated armor, were adorned with earrings and turbans. || 28 ||
Wearing various kinds of upper garments, adorned with diverse garlands and ornaments, enriched with the fragrance of various sweet scents, they were praised by hundreds of various bards. (29)
In that army, there were great chariot-warriors preceded by the flow of various musical instruments, who were devoted to recounting tales of diverse heroic deeds.
The army of that lion among the Daityas appeared fearsome in form, with its horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers covered by the dust of the earth.
And that lord of the Daityas, mounted upon his great chariot, shone with ten Daityas like the ten-armed Lord [Rāvaṇa] when enraged; intent on destroying the world, he set out against the gods.
In the meantime, Vāyu, the messenger of the gods, having seen that army of the Dānavas, went to the abode of the gods to inform Indra.
Having gone to the divine assembly hall of the high-souled Mahendra, he announced this imminent matter in the midst of the gods.
Having heard that, the high-minded king of the gods, with his eyes closed, spoke these words to Bṛhaspati at the proper time.
Indra said: "This great conflict between the gods and the dānavas has arrived. Tell me what must be done here, fortified by the means of political wisdom."
Having heard these words of Mahendra, the highly fortunate Bṛhaspati, the lord of speech and possessor of noble intellect, replied.
Bṛhaspati said: O best of gods, for those desiring victory over a fourfold army, policy is traditionally held to begin with conciliation; this is the eternal rule. (38)
Conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and fourthly, punishment—these should be employed in due order according to statecraft, depending on the specific requirements of place and time. (39)

In this regard, conciliation should be employed toward the noble and the virtuous; bribery toward the greedy; sowing dissension toward those who are suspicious; and from this, the conclusion [is reached]. (40)
Punishment must also be applied at all times toward those of evil nature; for there is no conciliation to be used against Daityas who are of evil nature due to their lack of virtue.
And what use is prosperity to them, even though they are so affluent? For they are considered by the Creator himself to be indivisible from the very nature of their caste. (42)
If it pleases you, punishment is indeed the only means here; for a wicked person can never be transformed into a virtuous one.
Whether cherished or even protected, one does not abandon their own inherent nature; such is my conviction—may you decide what is to be done.
Thus addressed, the thousand-eyed one replied, "So be it," and having reflected upon what must be done, he spoke in the assembly of the immortals.
O inhabitants of heaven, listen to my words with great respect.
Sirs, you are the enjoyers of sacrifice, beloved by the virtuous, and characterized by goodness; you remain eternally established in your respective positions, devoted to the protection of the world.
On account of you, the lords of the Dānavas are causing oppression; they have no regard for authority—let punishment indeed be ordained against them.
"Let your mind be set on battle; let the army be marshaled; let the weapons be sounded, and let the deities of the weapons be worshipped. (49)
Thus addressed, those who were the foremost among the gods equipped themselves for battle with ten thousand horses adorned with golden bands.
"O immortals, harness my vehicles and celestial chariots; having made Yama your general, O gods, set forth quickly! (51)
Endowed with various wonderful qualities and invincible even by gods and dānavas, Mahendra’s chariot, yoked by Mātali, also came into view.
Yama, mounted upon a buffalo, stood at the head of the army, surrounded on all sides by a multitude of fierce tinkling bells.
The Fire-god, filling the expanse of the sky with flames blazing for the duration of a kalpa, stood mounted upon a ram, holding a spear in his hand.
Then Pavana, with a goad in his hand and having unleashed his great speed, was seen at the head of the army mounted upon a great bear. || 55 ||
The Lord himself, the Master of Waters, mounted upon the king of serpents and, as a hero bearing a great noose, took his place within the army.
In a divine chariot yoked with men, the Lord of Wealth moved about; in the battle, he stood firm with a mace in hand, emitting the roar of a great lion.
Then Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, appeared on his chariot drawn by horse-faced demons; armed with a bow and surrounded by hosts of Rākṣasas, he was seen making a great roar.
The Moon and the Sun, the two Aśvins, the Vasus, the Sādhyadevas, the Viśvedevas, and the Rudras stood ready for battle, clad in armor. (59)
The Gandharvas were seen with Viśvāvasu at their head, wearing golden seats and upper garments, and bearing variegated armor, weapons, and banners. 60.
Likewise, Rākṣasas were seen wearing red upper garments, adorned with stainless iron ornaments, bearing vulture banners, and having blood-red hair.
Likewise, millions of Yakṣas led by Maṇibhadra were seen there—great chariot-warriors clad in black garments who wielded terrible thunderbolts.
The fierce Piśācas there, bearing copper-colored owl banners and clad in leopard skins, shone forth, preceded by those of great speed. (63)
In that very manner, the Kiṃnaras stood in the battle, dressed in white garments, bearing white silk banners, and mostly mounted upon elephants in rut. 64.
Adorned with a network of pearls, resembling a swan and possessing a luster like a necklace, the banner of the Lord of the Ocean shone with a gentle form. (65)
And the banner of the Giver of Wealth, adorned with the five-colored great jewels, rose up and shone as if desiring to go into the sky.
Yama’s great banner was a crow made of black iron; the face of the lord of the Rākṣasas shone as the banner of the Preta.
The two gods [Nāsatya and Dasra] possess the splendor of the moon and sun, with golden lions upon their banners; the banner of the two Aśvins was marked by a variegated-colored pitcher. (68)
The banner of Śatakratu was an elephant made of gold, adorned with various jewels, and set upon white chowries.
And there in that battle, the banners of others appeared in various forms, belonging to the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Mahoragas, and Niśācaras.
That army of the king of the gods appeared invincible, consisting of thirty-three crores of various classes of deities. (71)

With white chowries like the Himalayas, with a beautiful garland of pure golden lotuses, with lovely and radiant saffron sprouts applied [to her], and with playful sounds released from her cheeks; || 72 ||

Mounted upon that elephant named Airāvaṇa, he was possessed of great strength, his garments were adorned with various patterns, he was decorated by a vast canopy of diamond-studded limbs, and the circles of his forearms were graced with scattered armlets.
The thousand-eyed subduer of Pāka shone in Triviṣṭapa, praised by thousands of bards.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Commencement of the Battle between Tārakāsura and the Lord of the Devas," in the Kaumārīkā-khaṇḍa of the first section (Māheśvara-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Then the encounter of those two armies took place, like that of two agitated oceans when the end of a Yuga has arrived.
In that most terrible clash between the gods and the asuras, a great and tumultuous conflict ensued between both armies.
With the roar of shouting gods and demons, the sound of conchs and kettledrums, the blare of trumpets, and the trumpeting of elephants; || 3 ||
With the neighing of the herds of horses, the sound of chariot wheels, and the resonance of musical instruments, it was as if the end of the age had arrived.
With their limbs distorted by rage and their minds intent on abandoning life, they became excessively bloodied as they clashed with one another in succession.
Chariots were engaged with chariots, and elephants with great elephants; foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers, and horses with great horses.
Then, with spears, thunderbolts, clubs, javelins, axes, pikes, sharp-edged spears, tridents, mallets, iron-tipped arrows, and balls of stone; || 7 ||
With discuses, spears, javelins, and even goads; with barbed arrows, reed-shafts, iron arrows, calf-tooth-headed shafts, and crescent-shaped arrows.
With bhallas, vetasapattras, and stainless śukatuṇḍas, as well as with showers of wondrous form, the sky became filled.
Having completely shrouded all directions, it became as if composed of darkness; in that tumultuous gloom, they could not recognize one another.
Becoming invisible in the darkness, they slaughtered one another; then [the ground was covered] with arms, banners, umbrellas, and heads adorned with earrings.

The earth was strewn with elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers—both those falling and those already fallen—who, having descended from the heights of the sky, resembled lotuses dropped from the heavens. 12.
With broken tusks, shattered temples, and severed long trunks, elephants resembling mountains fell upon the earth, streaming with blood.
Chariots with broken shafts fell, shattered with their axles broken; foot soldiers fell by the millions, and horses by the thousands.
Then, rivers of blood, bringing joy to flesh-eaters and delight to the *vaitālas*, suddenly burst forth in great numbers. (15)
In that kind of battle, the commander Grasana, the slayer of enemies, caused the army of the gods to tremble with a great shower of arrows.
Then, beholding Grasana, Yama, overwhelmed with rage, rained down a shower of arrows, especially those possessing the brilliance of fire.
Pierced by many arrows, that exceedingly valiant Grasana, desiring to retaliate for what had been done to him, bent his formidable bow.
He struck him with thousands and even five hundred thousand arrows; and he, having warded off those arrows released by Grasana, [proceeded].
With fierce showers of arrows, Yama tormented Grasana; but Grasana, the lord of the Dānavas, cut down the advancing volleys of Kṛtānta’s arrows with his own rain of shafts.
Beholding that succession of his own arrows to be fruitless, Yama [reflected].
He hurled a blazing mallet toward Grasana’s chariot; leaping up from his excellent chariot, Grasana [seized] that approaching mallet.
Then, the enemy-slayer Grasana playfully seized that very mallet with his left hand and, in a fit of rage, struck Yama’s buffalo with it.
He struck him with great force, and he fell upon the surface of the earth; then Yama leaped up from that buffalo just as it was about to fall.
He struck Grasana firmly in the mouth with a javelin; struck by that blow, he fell to the ground unconscious.
Seeing Grasana fallen, Jambha of terrible prowess struck Yama in the heart with a bhindipāla weapon.
From that blow, blood flowed from Yama's mouth; afflicted by the exceedingly severe strike, the Ender (Kṛtānta) fell unconscious.
Seeing Kṛtānta oppressed, the Lord of Wealth, mace in hand and surrounded by hosts of tens of thousands of Yakṣas, rushed toward Jambha in a rage.
Jambha, surrounded by a host of Dānavas, angrily seized those words which the king had spoken with affection as he approached.
Then Grasana, having regained consciousness, hurled at Yama a heavy noose adorned with jewels and gold, which was capable of crushing even iron bars.
Beholding that mace as it came rushing toward him, he whose vehicle is the buffalo [Mahiṣa] hurled a weapon, terrifying like the blazing fire of the world, in order to counteract the mace.
In his rage, he released a staff wreathed in garlands of flames; having reached the sky with its mace, it roared like a surging cloud.
The clash between those two was as unbearable as that of two mountains; the quarters of the sky were numbed by the roar produced by their collision.
The world fell into a state of agitation from the fear of the arrival of universal dissolution; yet in an instant, its roar was stilled as it became strewn with blazing meteors.
A terrifying crushing of those two took place within the range of the mountain; then, having struck down the mace, Daṇḍa [struck] upon the head of Grasana.
Having struck down his manly prowess, he fell like destiny that had been previously earned; and by that blow, he saw the quarters of the sky shrouded in darkness.
He fell unconscious upon the ground, adorned by the dust of the earth; then a terrible cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from both armies.
Then, after only a moment, Grasana regained consciousness and saw his own body ruined, with its ornaments and garments disarrayed.
And he too reflected upon the act of returning a favor: "Fie upon my manliness! How can I stand before my master? (39)
The armies are dependent upon me, and when I am conquered, they too are conquered; for a virtuous person, whose true nature is inconceivable, rejoices in happiness.
"If he is honored though he is incapable, neither this world nor the next will belong to him. Having reflected thus, the one of great strength rose up with speed.
Grasping a mallet that resembled the staff of Death and was like a mountain, Grasana, with his fierce resolve, bit down upon the corners of his lips.
Hurrying by chariot, he went and encountered Antaka in battle; having reached Yama in the fight, Grasana whirled his mallet.
With great force, he hurled the terrible mallet at the head of Yama; beholding that blazing mallet, Yama’s eyes became bewildered with fear.
The one of great strength evaded that invincible mallet; and when it had retreated far away, [he confronted] those of fierce deeds who were terrible.
He crushed ten thousand of Yama’s servants; then, seeing those ten thousand slain, the army of the servants [fled].
Ten billion enraged [beings] rushed toward Grasana; but Grasana, having beheld that auspicious army composed of servants, [remained unshaken]. (47)
For she possessed such form and strength that she was thought to be thousands of Yamas; having plunged into the devouring army, she rained down showers of arrows.
That great battle became as terrible as the end of an eon; some pierced [the enemy] with a mountain, while others did so with straight-flying arrows.
Some crushed him with maces, some with showers of mallets, and others, acting with arrogance, struck him with blows from spears. || 50 ||
Other servants of his clung to the circle of his arms; others struck him with rocks, and still others with very tall trees.
Others bit his limbs with their teeth, and other servants struck his back with their fists. || 52 ||
Thus assailed by them, Grasana, frantic with rage, thrashed his body upon the surface of the earth and crushed it a thousand times.
Rising up, he struck some of the *kiṃkara*s with his fists in battle; others he crushed by running and striking them with his feet.
In a single moment, O descendant of Bharata, he led them to the realm of Yama; and he grew in size through his battle with the servants, like a fire fed by fuel.
Beholding him unwearied, those who were weary, and his own slain followers, Yama, whose vehicle is a buffalo, approached raising his staff.
But Grasana struck him with a mace on the chest as he was approaching; yet Antaka, the slayer of enemies, disregarded that deed of Grasana.
He struck the tigers with his staff, and they fell from their chariots to the ground; then, rising in an instant, he became arrogant, reflecting upon himself.
With the speed of the wind, he suddenly went toward the chariot of Yama; on foot, he then ascended that chariot and approached Yama.
The best among the strong drew [him] with his two arms and fought; Yama too, casting aside his weapons, engaged in a hand-to-hand struggle.
Seizing Yama by his loincloth, he who was preeminent in strength whirled him around with great force, while Yama’s mind was filled with agitation.
Then Yama, having released him from his hardship, seized the Asura by the neck and whirled him around with both arms; yet he too freed himself.
Then those two, mercilessly striking one another with their fists, fought on; yet, due to the extreme prowess of the lord of the Daityas, Yama became more exhausted.
Having placed the face of the Daitya upon his shoulder, he desired rest; then, observing that the Daitya was exhausted, he uprooted him by his own power.
He crushed him upon the surface of the earth, striking him with his heels and hands; then, from the mouth of Yama, much blood flowed forth.
Seeing him as lifeless, the Dānava then abandoned him; having achieved victory, he let out a haughty roar and terrified the gods.
Having reached his own army, he stood firm and immovable like a mountain.
By the roar of that devourer in battle, and with all their limbs afflicted by great weapons, those gods—fleeing in all directions as the sun set and the earth grew lusterless—trembled.
Nārada said: By Jambha, the enraged lord of wealth, the quarters were obstructed with arrows that pierce the vital organs, and his army was violently oppressed.
Having witnessed that deed of the Daitya, the powerful Lord of Wealth drew his bow back to his ear and [assailed] the mighty Jambha in battle.
He pierced him in the heart with a thousand arrows possessing the brilliance of fire; then that hero, laughing, [discharged] thirty thousand arrows.
In an instant, he hurled a hundred thousand, ten million, and a hundred billion [arrows]. Seeing that lightness of hand, the enraged [opponent] seized a great mace.
The treasurer, desiring heaven, cast away his wealth as if it were his own property; when she was released, a roar arose like that at the time of universal dissolution.
The cries of living beings arose in many ways in the sky, inspiring great fear; and a mighty wind arose, filling the atmosphere with a mass of clouds.
For that mace of Vaiśravaṇa stands there, worshipped by the three worlds; beholding it approaching, as difficult to look upon as a mass of lightning flashes— || 7 ||
The Daitya, for the purpose of warding off the blows of the mace, released a shower of weapons: discuses, clubs, spears, śataghnīs, and likewise paṭṭiśas.
That mace, by means of its incomparable prowess, rendered useless all those weapons—iron clubs, pestles, trees, and mountains.
Just as the sun at the end of an aeon might fall upon the chest of a Daitya, so he, deeply pierced by her, vomited blood mixed with foam.
Jambha fell from his chariot to the earth, deprived of consciousness; seeing Jambha fallen, Kujambha, firm in his terrible resolve, [advanced].
Enraged at the Lord of Wealth, filling the quarters with his roar, he created a net of arrows like a cage for a bird.
Having cut through that fierce web of arrows as if it were a web of illusion, the powerful lord of the yakṣas discharged other arrows at him.
And the Daitya effortlessly cut those [arrows] down as if they were well-spoken words; then, seeing those arrows rendered fruitless, the Lord of Wealth became enraged. (14)
He seized an invincible spear that resounded with the great noise of a hundred bells; once hurled, that spear then tore open his heart.
Just as suffering born of cyclic existence afflicts a man of little understanding, so too did it pierce his heart and descend to the surface of the earth. (16)
In the blink of an eye, that demon of fierce appearance, having completely paralyzed him, seized his spear (paṭṭiśa), which could even split mountains.
With that sword in battle, he struck the chest of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) with words of sharp form that pierced his vital organs.
Just as a wicked person pierces the heart of a noble man, so too was the Lord of Wealth (Dhaneśa) rendered unconscious by that blow from the *paṭṭiśa* weapon. || 19 ||
He sat down on the seat of the chariot like a good man [afflicted] by harsh words; indeed, seeing the Tathāgata there as if he were dead, the Lord of Wealth [fell]. (20)
The Rākṣasa Nirṛti, the god followed by the hosts of night-stalkers, rushed with speed toward Kujaṃbha, who possessed terrible prowess.
Then, seeing the exceedingly invincible lord of the Rākṣasas, Kujaṃbha urged the Daityas toward the chariot of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Seeing that formidable and terrifying army urged forward with powerful weapons, Nirṛti leaped down from his chariot with speed toward the lord of the Rākṣasas.
With sword of sharp edge in hand and shield in grasp, he rushed forward, entering the army of the Dānavas like an elephant entering a lotus pond.
Having cut them down by the thousands in many ways, he churned them about; with his excellent sword, he cut some into hundreds of pieces and pierced others.
With their mouths biting their lips, he covered the earth with those Daityas; then, seeing his own army almost entirely destroyed, [he was struck with grief].
Leaving the Lord of Wealth, the Daitya Kujambha went to Nirṛti; meanwhile, Jambha, having regained consciousness, [attacked] the followers of the Lord of Riches.
He seized him alive, binding him with thousands of nooses, as well as the personified jewels and the treasures such as Padma and the others.
And having regained his senses, Dhaneśa beheld all those divine mounts and celestial chariots in that state. (29)
Sighing long and hot breaths, his eyes copper-red with rage, he meditated upon the divine Gāruḍa weapon and fixed an arrow to his bow.
He released that enemy-piercing arrow against the host of Dānavas; first, his bow was seen blazing with the flames of fire.
Then millions of sparks issued forth from the bow, and he discharged that weapon on all sides, filling the sky with flames.
Then, suddenly beholding that weapon, Jambha of terrible prowess released the Saṃvarta [weapon], by which the Gāruḍa was then pacified.
Then, seeing Kubera, that Dānava, overwhelmed with rage, rushed impetuously on foot toward the Giver of Wealth, shouting aloud.
Then, seeing the Daitya approaching toward him, the Lord of Wealth became overcome with agitation and intent on flight. || 35 ||
Then, as he was fleeing, his crown adorned with jewels fell upon the earth, blazing like the solar disc falling from the sky.
The battle of the noble yakṣas broke off from the field; for them, dying at the head of the fray was fitting and served as their ornament. (37)
Having thus resolved, those invincible yakṣas, with various weapons and missiles in their hands and eager for battle, surrounded Mukuṭa.
Seeing those heroes, whose wealth was their pride, following after riches, the Dānava of fierce prowess looked upon them with indignation.
Then, seizing a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon of terrifying form and mountain-like weight, he crushed the night-stalkers who were guarding the crown.
Then, having crushed those [guards] and seized a million [attendants], the enemy of the gods, having conquered the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) in battle, placed that crown upon his own chariot.
Having seized wealth and treasures, surrounded by his own army, he put all the gods to flight on every side with a great roar.
Dhanada too, having had all his wealth seized and his hair shorn, stood there like a wretched man, terrified and alone on foot. || 43 ||
Then the son of the night-stalker, the lord of the Rākṣasas, became engaged with Kujambha, having resorted to an unerring, dark illusion.
The lord of the Daityas caused delusion by enveloping the world in darkness; consequently, the eyes of the Dānava forces became useless.
At that time, they were unable to move even a single step from their place; then, by means of a rain of various weapons, the great army of the Dānavas [was overwhelmed].
The god Nirṛti struck them violently with darkness while the Daityas were being slain, as Kujaṃbha remained bewildered in mind. || 47 ||
Then Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas, who resembled the clouds at the end of a kalpa, discharged the Sāvitra weapon, which was adorned with a multitude of meteors.
Then, as the supreme weapon of Savitṛ blazed forth, the intense, terrible, and all-pervading darkness was utterly destroyed.
Then, from that [darkness] marked by sparks of missiles, a white light was born, like a pure lake in autumn filled with a multitude of fully blossomed red lotuses.
Then, when the darkness had subsided and the lords of the Daityas regained their sight, they employed a cruel darkness against the most wonderful army of the gods.
Then, taking up a terrible bow and an arrow resembling a venomous serpent, Kujambha quickly rushed toward the army of the gods and the Rākṣasas.
Seeing him approaching in that manner, the lord of the Rākṣasas, followed by his attendants, pierced him with sharp arrows whose sound was like the thunderbolt of Time.
Neither his taking up of the bow, nor its joining, nor even its release could be perceived; with fierce volleys of arrows, he cut down those very shafts through extreme dexterity.
With a sharp arrow he cut down the banner of the enemy of the gods, and with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla) he struck his charioteer away from the seat of the chariot.
And with an arrow resembling Death itself, he struck him in the chest; by that blow, he trembled, being severely afflicted.
The lord of the Daityas, like a mountain at the trembling of the earth when struck by the lord of the Rākṣasas, recovered his breath after a moment and considered him invincible in battle.
Having reached the chariot on foot, the Rākṣasa seized Nirṛti by the hair with his left hand and stood there, having pressed him down with his knee. || 58 ||
Then, filled with indignation, he desired to sever his head with a sword; thereupon a great clamor arose among the gods, seeing Nirṛti fallen under the power of Kujaṃbha in the battle.
In the meantime, the god Varuṇa, bearing his noose, swiftly bound both arms of the lord of the Dānavas with that noose.
Then the wielder of the noose, casting aside all mercy, struck with his mace the Daitya whose arms were bound and whose manly prowess had been rendered fruitless.
From that blow, with blood flowing from his orifices, he bore the appearance of a dark cloud charged with streaks of lightning.
Seeing Kujaṃbha reduced to that state, Mahiṣāsura, with a roar from his turned face, desired to devour both the gods.
With his face fierce with sharp fangs, he [approached] Nirṛti and Varuṇa; having observed their corrupted intention, that of the Daitya.
Abandoning both their chariots, terrified, they fled swiftly on foot; fearing Mahiṣa, they went for refuge to Pākaśāsana (Indra).
Then the Daitya Mahiṣa, enraged, rushed toward Varuṇa; seeing him as near as the mouth of Death, the Moon (Himadīdhiti) [intervened].
Indeed, Candra discharged the weapon Vāyavya, which was incomparable and like a formidable mass of snow, as a second missile.
By that fierce wind, by the parching frost, by the falling of great masses of snow, and by weapons impelled by the moon; || 68 ||
The limbs of the asura armies were being scorched on all sides; all the Dānavas were distressed, their prowess shrouded by the cold.
There they were unable to move, nor even to take up their weapons; Mahiṣa became motionless, his face trembling from the cold.
Embracing his shoulder with both hands, he sat down with his face cast downwards; all those Daityas were defeated by Candramas and rendered incapable of resistance.
Abandoning their desire for battle from afar, they stood there seeking only to preserve their lives. Then Kālanemi, inflamed with rage, spoke to the Daityas: ||| 72 ||
"O you ornaments of beauty, cruel ones, who have mastered all weapons and missiles! Even each one of you is capable of lifting the entire world with your arms. (73)
Even each one of them is capable of devouring the entire world, including all things moving and stationary; even all the gods together are not a match for each one of them individually.
"Why are you with such terrified eyes, as if utterly defeated in battle? This is not fitting for heroes, especially for those born of the Daitya race. (75)
And what face will you show to King Tāraka? Enraged, he will take away the lives of those who have desisted from battle.
Thus addressed, those great asuras said nothing at all; their hearing was lost by the cold, and they were likewise deprived of speech.
Thus the Daityas became mute and like unto the dead in that great battle; seeing those Daityas deprived of their senses and afflicted by the cold, [he acted]. (78)
Considering his task to be one that required time, the great asura Kālanemi resorted to human illusion and expanded his massive body.
That lord of the Dānavas filled the sky and the intermediate directions as well; he manifested ten thousand suns from his own body.
He filled the cardinal and intermediate directions with fires; then, in an instant, the entire triple world became filled with flames. 81.
By that mass of flames, the moon quickly fled; thereafter, the cold, gloomy weather gradually vanished and shone forth.

That was the power of the lords of the Dānavas through the illusion of Kālanemi. Seeing that army of Dānavas restored to consciousness, the Sun-god, his eyes extremely red with anger at the corners, spoke to Aruṇa.
Divākara said: "O Aruṇa, drive the chariot quickly to where the chariot of Kālanemi is."
In that terrible conflict, there will be a destruction of living beings; for this Moon has been conquered by the very power upon which we rely. (85)
Thus addressed, the elder brother of Garuḍa urged on the chariot, which was drawn by those horses adorned with white chowries, even though he himself was already seated upon the chariot.
