At Kāmarūpa, where the great intoxicating waters flow, Śatakratu stood upon a peak of the Himavat mountain like the radiant sun; Māruta of immeasurable prowess guarded his left flank.
And Agni, filling the quarters of the sky with his flames, protected him from behind; Viṣṇu became the rear-guard of Śatakratu, the lord of battle.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Viśvedevas, and Maruts, as well as the two Aśvins; the Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, along with the Kiṃnaras and Mahoragas. || 25 ||
Taking them by the millions and in vast throngs distinguished by their emblems, they proclaimed their own glory while accompanied by groups of bards leading the way.
Arrogant in the slaughter of the Daitya Celu, they possessed various colors, weapons, and banners.

Protected by the hosts of immortals under Śatakratu, resounding with the noise of vehicles, and adorned with the tips of white, lofty banners and cloths, that army—which increased the joy of the sons of Diti—became formidable.
Then, beholding that celestial army approaching, Gajāsura—great in form as an elephant and possessing the prowess of the ocean of destruction—advanced.
Armed with a battle-axe, the Daitya, his teeth pressed against his lips, trampled some gods with his feet and hurled others away with his hand.
The lord of the Daityas, possessed of fierce prowess, struck down his enemies with an axe; as he was thus slaughtering them, the gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras became enraged.
All of them together released a multitude of various weapons and missiles: battle-axes, discuses, slings, and mallets.
The Daitya leader devoured all those spears, javelins, sharp arrows, and unbearable mallets, just as one might swallow mouthfuls of food.
Then that Dānava, with the tips of his fangs quivering in rage, making the earth resound with the slapping of his hands, and slaughtering the gods in battle, became difficult to behold.
Upon whichever group of gods the elephant-demon Gajāsura fell, in each of those places a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Then, beholding that army fleeing in every direction, the Rudras, whose flames of energy arose from their own ego, spoke to one another.
"O, O you of great strength! Seize the lord of the Daityas! Pierce him! Drag him away! Transfix him with sharp spears! Indeed, crush him in his vital organs!"
Having heard the words, Kapālī wiped the spear, bright as snow, upon his mouth with his left hand, his eyes wide open in fury.
Then, like a mass of fully blossomed red and blue lotuses, he came from all directions toward the lord of the Daityas in battle, his face contorted with a frown.
Grasping the trident with a firm grip, the stainless Kapālī struck the Dānava Kumbha in the region of his frontal globe.
Then all ten of those Rudras, with stainless iron spears, struck the lord of the Daityas—who possessed a body as massive as a mountain—in the battle during the fray.
Thereafter, blood flowed from all the channels of that elephant-demon; with that blood and the pain, the Dānava shone like Rudra himself. || 42 ||
Like a stainless lake in autumn filled with fully blossomed, pure blue lotuses, it was covered by Rudras whose bodies were as white as ash, resembling swans. (43)
The demon Jaga, his ear-lobes quivering, bit the enraged Kapālin Bhava with his teeth in the region of the navel.
Seeing that he was devoted to the two Rudras, the nine Rudras then swiftly pierced the body of the enemy of the gods with arrows and spears.

Then, abandoning both Kapālin and Bhava, the enraged Daitya, that bull among Asuras, rushed with speed toward the nine Rudras; he crushed them with blows from his feet, with his teeth, and with his trunk.
Then, when he had become exhausted by the combat with the trident, Kapālī seized the hand of that enemy of the gods.
And she whirled the elephant-demon with extreme velocity, seeing the Daitya distressed and his life-force slightly departing.
Lacking enthusiasm for that battle, he became one who had lost all joy in fighting; then, while he was still wandering about, they cut off his head from his body with a terrible roar. 49.
He made his own garment a flood of blood flowing from all his limbs; then the gods praised him in many ways with numerous hymns.
And they said to him: "Whoever should strike you would die from that; for he beheld the form of Kapālin, clothed in an elephant hide. (51)
They fled, they struck, and they fell by the thousands; thus was that mighty lord of the Dānavas thrown into utter confusion.
Then, mounting an elephant resounding with a hundred drums, Nimi rushed swiftly toward the divine armies, agitating them.
Whichever direction the elephant Nimi went, toward that very direction the gods, along with their mounts, fled; trembling repeatedly with fear, they cried out.
At the scent of his elephant, the gods' elephants fled; and when the armies of the gods had retreated, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, [acted].
He stood together with the eight guardians of the quarters and Keśava; meanwhile, his elephant approached the elephant of Śakra.
Then Śakra’s elephant, terrified, let out a most dreadful roar; though held fast with great effort, it stood there like a cakora bird.
As that elephant fled, Indra, mounted upon it, engaged in a head-on battle with the lord of the Dānavas. || 58 ||
Śatakratu, however, struck Nimi in the chest with his trident, and violently struck that elephant on the region of its cheek with his mace.
Reflecting upon that blow, Nimi, whose prowess was fearless, struck Airāvata on the region of its waist with a mallet.
Then, struck by the mace in battle, Śakra’s elephant, who was as massive as a mountain, fell to the earth upon its hind legs.
Then, rising quickly due to his agility, that great celestial elephant, terrified by Nimi’s elephant, retreated from the battlefield.

Then a harsh wind blew, filled with much gravel and dust; facing him was Nimi-mātaṅga, the unshakable one who makes even mountains tremble. With blood flowing, that mountain shone like a mountain of thick mineral ores with its springs running.
Dhaneśa also hurled a heavy mace at that Dānava-elephant with great force; that mace fell upon its head.
Stunned by that blow from the mace, the elephant, resembling a mountain, broke the earth with its tusks and fell down with great force.
And when that elephant had fallen, a great lion-roar arose from all sides among the divine armies, augmented by the trumpeting of elephants.
Upon seeing that elephant slain and Nimi also turning his back in retreat, there arose the neighing of horses and the slapping of arms by the archers.
And hearing the lion’s roar of the gods, which resounded throughout the quarters of the sky, Jambha blazed with anger like a kindled fire.
Then, his eyes red with anger, he fixed an arrow upon his bow and said loudly, "Stay! and thus gladdened his charioteer.
Beholding him approaching with an arrow fixed upon his bow, Śatakratu, undaunted in spirit, firmly grasped his own bow.
And an arrow with a straight flight, its tip cleansed with oil, shaped like a half-moon.
With that [arrow], the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra cut his bow along with the shaft; having cast aside that severed bow, Jambha, the joy of the Dānavas, [acted].
Taking up another bow, powerful and capable of bearing a great strain, as well as arrows shaped like venomous serpents, cleansed with oil, and straight-flying; (73)
He pierced Śakra with ten feathered arrows in the region of the collarbone, with three in the heart, and with two in each of the two shoulders.

Śakra also discharged a net of arrows at the lord of the Dānavas; however, the lord of the Dānavas [intercepted] those arrows before they had reached him, as they were launched from the hand of Śakra.
Then, with arrows resembling flames of fire, Devendra cut the lord of the Dānavas into a hundred pieces in the sky by means of a net of shafts.
"Cover him with effort, as clouds cover the sky during the rains! Even the Daitya pierced him with a net of arrows, with sharp shafts.
Just as the wind cannot be restrained when it gathers into dense masses at the face of the quarters, so too Śakra could not prevail through his violent outburst of anger.
Then he discharged the most wonderful Gandharva weapon at the lord of the Dānavas; thereupon, the entire range of vision became pervaded by its splendor.
And with cities of the Gandharvas, featuring various ramparts and gateways, emitting a rain of weapons of wondrous form from every side.
O descendant of Bharata, that great army of the Daityas, being struck by that rain of weapons, sought refuge with Jambha, crying out, "Save us! Save us! (81)
Then Jambha, of great prowess, roaring and laughing repeatedly, and mindful of the noble conduct of the Daityas, granted them freedom from fear.
Then he released the weapon named Mauśala, which inspires great terror; thereupon, the entire world became filled with fierce clubs.
And by them all the cities of the Gandharvas were shattered; then, with a single fierce blow, [he struck] the chariot, the horse, the elephant, and the god.
He quickly pulverized it into hundreds and thousands of pieces; then Sakra, the lord of the gods, discharged the Tvaṣṭra weapon.
Then, as the weapon was being joined together, flames of fire issued forth; thereafter, thousands of mechanical sciences manifested themselves.
With those machines, the battle took place in the sky until the stars were no longer visible; by those machines, the mace-array was shattered, and the asuras were then slain.
Jambha discharged the mountain-weapon, which pulverized masses of machines; from that, a rain of stones measuring a fathom in size began to fall.
O Bhārata, those mechanical weapons which had been swiftly fashioned by the son of Tvaṣṭṛ were then reduced to pieces as small as sesame seeds by that falling rock.
Then, stones of great velocity fell upon the heads of the gods, tearing asunder the earth and that fourfold army.
Then, with eyes wide open, Purandara discharged the Vajra weapon; the great shower of rocks was shattered on all sides.
Then Jambha, who resembled a mountain, having neutralized the peaceful mountain-weapons, being his prowess unimpaired, discharged the Aiṣīka weapon.

By means of the Aiṣīka weapon, he brought to ruin the Vajra missile that shatters mountains; then, while the exceedingly terrible and supreme Aiṣīka weapon was expanding its power, [the enemy's weapons failed].
The divine armies, together with their chariots and elephants, blazed up as the troops were consumed on all sides by the splendor of the weapon.
The subduer of Pāka, the destroyer of Bala, then discharged the Āgneya weapon; by that weapon, the Aiṣīka was then brought to destruction.
When that weapon was neutralized, the fire-weapon (pāvakāstra) manifested; the army of Jambha, as well as his chariot and charioteer, blazed up.
Then that powerful lord of the Daityas, his weapons having been repelled, discharged the Vāruṇa weapon, which extinguishes the flames of fire.
Then the sky was filled with clouds thick with flickering streaks of lightning, and the earth was drenched by deep, continuous downpours.
Seeing the world filled with streams resembling the trunks of lordly elephants and the fire-weapon (āgneya-astra) pacified, Indra indeed acted.
By that incomparable Vāyavya weapon, the clouds went to their destruction; then, the circle of clouds was blown away by the power of the Vāyavya weapon.
The sky became cloudless, possessing the luster of blue lotus petals, and the Dānavas were shaken by a wind of extraordinary form.
Even those who were powerful were unable to remain there in that battle; then Śālva became as large as ten yojanas in extent.
To obstruct the path of the Maruts, the lord of the Danavas [constructed] a mountain endowed with various wonders and covered with diverse trees and creepers. (103)
Then, once the wind-giant who was shaped like a mountain had been pacified, Śatakratu swiftly released a great thunderbolt made of diamond.
By that fallen thunderbolt, the caves and the waterfalls of the Daitya, who was in the form of a mountain, were shattered on all sides. || 105 ||
Then that mountain-illusion of the lord of the Dānavas ceased; having withdrawn his mountain-illusion, the lord of the Dānavas became intoxicated with pride.
There was a terrifying elephant with the form of a great mountain; it crushed the army of the gods and struck the gods with its tusks.
The Dānava tore some apart from behind, dragging them with his trunk; then, as he was thus destroying the divine armies, the slayer of Vṛtra [attacked him].
He released the Narasiṃha weapon, which is invincible in the three worlds; then, by the power of the mantra, thousands of lions issued forth.
With their bristling tusks, loud "aṭṭahāsa" laughter, and claws resembling saws, they tore apart his body; thus he cast off the illusory form of the elephant.
Thereupon, he became a terrible venomous serpent, crowded with hoods, whose poisonous breath consumed the great chariots of the celestial army. || 111 ||
Then Śakra, striking in the battle, invoked the Gāruḍa weapon; from it, thousands of Garuḍas emerged.
Having encountered Jambha, who had assumed the form of a serpent, those Garuḍas tore the Daitya to pieces, and his illusion was destroyed.
And when that illusion had vanished, the great asura Jambha then assumed an incomparable form that followed the path of the moon and the sun.
With his eyes rolling, he desired to devour the foremost of the gods; then, along with great chariots and elephants, they entered his mouth.
The army became terrifying as its palates were raised high like the underworld, while the troops were being devoured by the powerful Dānava.
Śakra, having fallen into a state of dejection with his vehicle and its mount exhausted, could not determine what ought to be done; he spoke thus to Janārdana: || 117 ||
"What specifically must be done by us immediately next? Command that, and we shall strive against this Dānava who desires to fight. (118)
Then Hari, the noble-minded one, spoke thus to the wielder of the thunderbolt: "It is not right to abandon this battle, which is terrifying to those who are cowardly toward their enemies."
"Do not fall into delusion; do not fall into delusion! Quickly remember your weapon, O Lord! Having heard this, he, being self-restrained, released the Nārāyaṇa weapon.
In the meantime, the Daitya, with his mouth wide open, instantly devoured three hundred thousand each of Kinnaras, Uragas, and Rakshasas.
Then the Nārāyaṇa weapon fell upon his chest; with his heart pierced by that great weapon, he bled profusely.
Then, by his own splendor, the form of that Daitya was destroyed; thereupon the Daitya vanished after letting out a most boisterous laugh.
Stationed in the sky, that lord of the Daityas, possessing weapons like thunderbolts beyond the senses, released a supreme, all-destroying [missile] upon the divine armies.
Likewise, [they hurled] battle-axes, discuses, thunderbolts, arrows, along with mallets, spears, swords, slings, and iron-tipped clubs.
Out of rage, the Dānava rained down weapons that were both indestructible and inexhaustible; by those terrifying missiles released by the Dānava, the divine armies were struck.
The earth was covered with arms, with heads adorned with earrings, with thighs resembling the trunks of elephants, and with lordly elephants like unto mountains.
With these chariots—their poles, shafts, wheels, and axles broken—the earth became impassable, mired in mud of flesh and blood.
With whirlpools in its pools of flowing blood, with the bodies of elephants as its massive boulders, abounding in the dancing of headless trunks, it was a great river carrying away the gods.
Causing supreme delight to jackals, vultures, and crows, she drank the flesh along with the blood, while being thronged by various classes of piśācas.
Accompanied by her unflurried wives who were dancing exultantly, one wife became enraged with pearls from the interior of an elephant's frontal globes.
Where a piśāca gathered the hooves of horses together, others rejoiced in their ear-ornaments while looking on with wrath. (132)
Those experts in the welfare of Mahākarṇa propitiated him in many ways; some said, "O gods, O Daityas, we make this request. (133)
"We must fight thus until the end of the kalpa for our own satisfaction. Some said, "This one is a Daitya; this one is a Deva; this one is exceedingly stout. (134)
If he dies in battle, his relics (dhātu) should be requested from the giver; while some heroes are fighting, they lick the corners of their mouths.
By this milk we know who is a wicked person and who is a virtuous one; for some, possessing a mind fixed on religious faith, dwell upon the banks of rivers of blood. (136)
They gratify the ancestors and the gods with blood and auspicious meats; some, standing amidst heaps of meat, see the meat on another's hand. (137)
Just as miserly people cry out "Give! Give! to the wealthy, so too are some who, though fully satiated themselves, see others eating. (138)
Some, their lips quivering with rage, looked on with extreme indignation; others, filled with anger, reviled and struck their own bellies. (139)
Desiring to consume everything and satiated with the wealth of others, some say that today alone is the praiseworthy creation of the Creator.
"What a beautiful dawn! What an auspicious star!"—thus did various conversations arise among the flesh-eaters here and there. (141)
Remaining invisible in battle, Jambha pulverized the gods with his weapons; then Śakra, Dhaneśa, Varuṇa, Pavana, and Anala [attacked him]. || 142 ||
Then Yama and Nirṛti, as well as all the other mighty ones, aimed at the Dānava and released celestial weapons into the sky.
The weapons of the gods became useless against the Dānava, just as even hundreds of noble deeds become futile toward those whose hearts are exceedingly cruel. 144.
Neither the Daityas nor the deities could discern their course; they were exhausted, with all their limbs pierced by the weapons of the Daityas, like cows afflicted by the cold.
Crying out "Alas! Alas! What will happen?", they collapsed into one another; seeing that state, Hari spoke to the gods and Śakra.

O King of Gods, remember the non-terrible mantra, for it is a weapon possessing the power of the Pāśupata; it was granted to you by the gratified Rudra, unimpeded and capable of slaying even the best of heroes.

Thus, having been awakened by Hari, Śakra then bowed to the Lord, the bull-bannered Īśvara, and took up his crescent-shaped arrow, the destroyer of enemies, which had been worshipped for the divine battle.
Having fixed his mind upon that invincible bow, the wise one then applied the Aghora mantra to it.

Then, for the sake of slaying him, he quickly drew back his arrow of unobstructed luster to the tip of his ear and released it; thereupon, the Asura, beholding that great weapon approaching, suddenly abandoned his illusory power and stood firm.

With a trembling face and unsteady limbs, he was overwhelmed by agitation; then, in that great battle, a crescent-headed arrow consecrated with the supreme weapon-mantra was forcibly discharged at him.
Released from the bow of Purandara, it mimicked the orb of the midday sun with its form.

He struck down the head of Jambha, complete with its earrings, its hair resembling the glow of rising smoke, scented with various fragrant flowers, and crowded with the radiance shimmering from the peak of his crown.
When Jambha had been slain by Indra, the gods praised him greatly; the blessed Lord Vāsudeva also said, "Excellent! Excellent! (154).
Then, seeing Jambha slain, all those lords of the Dānavas turned their backs; with their resolutions shattered, they all fled toward Tāraka.
Beholding them terrified and hearing that four had been slain, he urged his charioteer, saying, "Go quickly against Indra in battle. (156)
Having said "So be it," he departed as Tāraka mounted his chariot—with arrogance, anger, pride, and valor.
The lord of the Dānavas departed with open defiance and contempt, mounting his well-equipped chariot drawn by a thousand Garuḍas.
Equipped with all weapons and implements, protected by all missiles, endowed with the supernatural power of the three worlds, and resounding like the Destroyer at the end of an eon. || 159 ||
Accompanied by a vast army and making the intermediate and cardinal directions resound, the Thousand-eyed One (Indra), upon seeing him, abandoned his mount, the elephant.
The chariot, yoked by Mātali, was adorned with refined gold; it was four yojanas in width and attended by hosts of Siddhas. || 161 ||
It was filled with the songs of Gandharvas and Kinnaras, and crowded with the dances of Apsarases.
Surrounding that chariot on all sides, they took their positions upon it, which was equipped with every kind of weapon, capable of warding off great calamities, and adorned with many great jewels.
The world-protectors, clad in armor and accompanied by Garuḍa-bannered Viṣṇu, stood ready; then the earth trembled and a harsh wind blew along with the hosts of Maruts.
The seven oceans receded and the radiance of the sun vanished; then the weapons blazed forth and the mounts trembled.
Then, as everything rose up together, Tāraka came into view; on one side was the Daitya Tāraka, and on the other side were the hosts of gods.
On one hand was the destruction of the world, and on the other, the uplifting of the world; all beings, both moving and unmoving, were filled with fear and wonder.
Then, at that assembly, the gods praised Pārtha.

O dear one, the missiles, splendors, wealth, warriors, fame, strength, heroic prowess, and the vital energies of these gods and asuras all arose from their asceticism; however, for us, asceticism alone is supreme.
Then, as he was approaching them face-to-face, the gods pierced Tāraka with arrows that had points like fire, using bows bent low. || 170 ||
Disregarding those arrows that had pierced his heart, the lord of the Daityas, the Dānava, filled the sky, the quarters, and the earth with his own shafts. || 171 ||
One should worship Nārāyaṇa with seventy [strokes], Hutāśana (Fire) with ninety, Māruta (Wind) on the head with ten, and Yama likewise with ten.
The Daitya struck Dhanada with seven arrows, Varuṇa with eight, Nirṛti with twenty, and again with eight more.
He pierced each one of them again with ten arrows that pierce the vital organs; likewise, the Daitya struck Mātali with three swift shafts.
He struck Garuḍa with ten arrows and likewise Mahiṣa with nine; then the Daitya [struck] the gods, limb by limb, with his smooth-jointed shafts.
He created networks of armor and cut down their bows; consequently, the gods were deprived of their armor and bows, and were greatly afflicted.
While they were grasping other bows and discharging arrows, he fixed an arrow upon his bow that was as radiant as the fire of cosmic destruction.
He struck Śakra in the heart, and he too released [an arrow]; then, looking into the sky, he saw [forms] having the appearance of a hundred suns.
Tārkṣya and Viṣṇu struck him with two arrows, and those two were bewildered by the sharp arrows of the Lord of the Dead (Yama), Agni, and Varuṇa.
He performed the work of Nirṛti, terrifying and utterly bewildering him; having restrained his breath, he rendered the wind motionless with his arrows.
Then, having regained consciousness and encouraged the lords of the quarters, Hari severed from the body of his charioteer the head adorned with earrings by means of an arrow.
Enraged, Vāsava cut down the blazing crest of Dhūmaketu and struck him down; thereafter, he also severed the crown of the king of the Daityas.
And the enraged Dhaneśa shattered the bow into many pieces with his arrows; Vāyu, moreover, reduced the chariot—along with its horses and pole—to the size of sesame seeds.
Then, in that battle, Nirṛti cut his body into pieces as small as sesame seeds with his arrows; having performed this incomparable feat, they cried out, "Stay! Stay! (184).
Then, licking the corners of their mouths, the gods, headed by Vāsudeva, watched that deed of the gods; Tāraka, possessed of incomparable prowess, [beheld it].
He hurled a terrible mallet at the Thousand-eyed One in the battle; seeing that mallet approaching on the field of combat, it was impossible to ward off.
Leaping from the chariot, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) descended to the earth; the mallet too fell upon the seat of the chariot with a harsh sound. || 187 ||
He crushed the chariot, yet Mātali did not die; seizing a sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa), the Daitya struck Keśava in the chest.
He too, rendered unconscious, sat upon the shoulder of Garuḍa; and having pierced the lord of the Rākṣasas with his sword, he cast him down to the ground. || 189 ||
And he struck Yama down to the ground, having hit him in the face; and having struck Vahni with a bhindipāla, he rendered him unconscious. || 190 ||
Then, kicking Vāyu with his foot, he cast him down to the ground; the enraged one struck Dhaneśa with the tip of his bow.
Then, in a mere instant, he struck each of those classes of gods with his weapons, just as a teacher strikes his young pupils.
Then Viṣṇu, having regained consciousness, seized his irresistible discus, which was stained with the fat, marrow, and blood of the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Keśava released [the discus] firmly upon the chest of the lord of the Dānavas; the discus, possessing the brilliance of the sun, fell upon the Daitya.
Then it shattered against his body like a blue lotus against a stone; thereafter, even Mahendra released the thunderbolt, which had been worshipped for a long time.
In that battle, Śakra’s hope for victory rested upon the body of the heroic Tāraka, the lord of the Dānavas.
It shattered and its flames were scattered, reduced to a hundred fragments; then the Wind, undaunted in spirit, roared with great force.
He indeed released a goad that shone like a blazing fire; seeing it shattered against his body, Vāyu became greatly enraged.
Then, having uprooted the king of mountains, with its flowering trees and caves, he hurled it, ten yojanas in width, at the lord of the Dānavas.
As that mountain approached with a smile, the bull among the Daityas caught him with his left hand, as easily as a child plays with a ball.
Then, having struck him with that very [weapon], he caused Antaka to fall; thereafter, Kṛtānta, overwhelmed with rage, raised his staff.
Having whirled the invincible [missile] with great speed, he hurled it at the head of the lord of the Daityas; it fell upon the asura’s head, but the Daitya seized it, smiling.
The fire that blazes with wrath, a conflagration that burns the world at the end of an eon, hurled an irresistible spear at the lord of the Dānavas in the battle.
Then she shone upon his chest like a garland of śirīṣa flowers; then he drew from its scabbard a sword as stainless as the sky.
Nirṛti, the guardian of the world, who illuminates the three worlds with his splendor, hurled [his weapon] at the lord of the Dānavas; it fell indeed upon his head.
And that sword, having fallen, was quickly shattered into a hundred pieces. Thereupon, Varuṇa became enraged and [assumed] a form as terrifying as Mahābhairava.
Desiring to bind the arms of the lord of the Daityas, he released the noose; yet upon reaching the Daitya’s arm, that noose was instantly destroyed.
The Lord of Serpents, his rows of teeth cruel as saws, was split apart; then the two Aśvins, along with the Moon and the Sun, the Sādhyas, and those who are the Vasus [emerged].
The Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gaṇas, Gandharvas, and serpents—all those of great strength—again struck the lord of the Daityas with various kinds of weapons. (209)
And weapons did not adhere to his body, which was like a mountain of adamant; then Tāraka, the lord of the foremost Dānavas, leaping up from the sky, [attacked].
Enraged, he struck them by the millions with his fists and heels; and beholding such prowess on his part, the Blessed Lord Hari—
"Fly away, O gods!"—saying this, he vanished. Thereupon, Śakra and the other gods became intent on flight. (212)
Surrounded by the Daityas led by Kālanemi, who were intoxicated with pride, they joyfully seized her by the hair and struck her with their fists and kicks.
The Lokapālas were made to cross dry rivers and divine paths while clad in armor; furthermore, they were dragged about in many ways by the great Asuras.
Then, O Bhārata, a roar arose from those powerful Daityas, making the earth, the heavens, and the netherworlds tremble.
Then the Daityas, filled with joy, praised Tāraka, crying "Victory!", and they blew their conchs which possessed a luster like that of jasmine and the moon.
The Daityas, filled with intense joy, made fierce sounds from their bows and arrows and struck their palms; they shouted repeatedly and danced again and again.
Then, placing the gods at his front like a herdsman with his cattle, the lord of the Daityas mounted his chariot and departed accompanied by the asuras.
That powerful Tāraka had a city situated on the shore of the Mahī and the ocean, twelve yojanas in length and adorned with copper ramparts.
The city was filled with many palaces, adorned with divine wonders, wherein three sounds never ceased to resound incessantly.
Amidst the sound of singing and the roar of drums, with cries of "Enjoy the objects of the senses!", the king entered the city and went to his own palace.
Accompanied by a great festival and greeted by his sons and wife, the king reached that divine assembly hall there and took his seat upon the throne.
Being praised by the sons of Diti and entertained by the Apsarases, the Lord was surrounded by the lords of the Daityas seated upon divine thrones, like a lion surrounded by lions.
In the meantime, a certain celestial woman appeared in that city; surrounded by those Daityas, she spoke these words as if smiling, while they looked on in amazement.
O Pārtha, incomparable in beauty and adorned with various ornaments, King Tāraka was truly struck with great wonder upon seeing her. (225)
"Tell me, O goddess, who are you? O beautiful one, we have never before seen a woman equal to you in beauty. (226)
The woman said: "O best of Daityas, know me to be the Fortune (Lakṣmī) of the three worlds; O Lord, I have been acquired by you through your asceticism or your prowess. (227)
I serve with propriety that man who is energetic, untiring, ascetic, undaunted, both a giver and an enjoyer. (228)
O son of Diti, I immediately abandon that man who is cowardly, excessively despondent, a tormentor of virtuous women, and one who suspects everyone. (229)
When your mother was insulted by Mahendra, he was already as good as abandoned; now he is truly under your control.
Then Tāraka spoke to her again, saying, "And [I am] supreme. Thereupon, the goddess Ramā, who is worshipped by the three worlds, entered into him.
Then the adorned women of the Dānavas, taking up heroic brass vessels, joyfully celebrated the lord of the Daityas.
And the gods stood at the gate, bound by the Daityas and deeply distressed, being mocked by women, by the Daityas, and by other citizens.

In the meantime, Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a Daitya and standing in the midst of the jesters, the intelligent one spoke two verses: The intelligent one, having assumed the form of a Daitya and standing in the midst of the jesters, spoke two verses.
What appears to be a minor matter in their case—what indeed will the king not do when he recalls his mother's wrath? (235)
Having encountered one who is more powerful, he who does not bow down does not exist; O gods, remain steadfast by employing the stratagems of Śvetabākin, like the monkey Marka.
Having heard these instructions from the mouth of Hari under the guise of a joke, the gods then assumed the forms of monkeys.
Dancing in many ways, those Daityas and the wives of the Asuras urged them on greatly and joyfully gave them food.
Then the wise Viṣṇu spoke to the doorkeeper of the Daityas: "For the amusement of the great king, describe these monkeys."
Then the gatekeeper, filled with joy, entered the midst of the assembly; having knelt upon the ground and joined his palms in reverence, he spoke. (240)
He spoke words that were unclouded, concise, and perfectly clear: "O Lord, leader of the Daityas, hosts of Maruts are standing at your gate. (241)
"If you have a desire to see that which provides such great diversion, you ought to look. Having heard that, the king said: "Why do you delay? (242)
Having heard these words, the steward then said to Kālanemi: "The great king wishes to see these monkeys immediately. (243)
"O Rakṣapāla, together with these [monkeys], you must win over the king; then, taking Kālanemi and the other monkeys, go to the king. || 244 ||
In the midst of the solar orb, Viṣṇu, having abandoned his demonic form, went forth; then they danced vigorously before the Daitya Tāraka.
Then, delighted by the monkeys who were entertained by the sounds of joy produced with clapping hands like those of the Daityas, the king spoke to them as they danced. (246)
"O Markadevas, may you have no fear; being pleased, I grant this to you. You must simply remain in my house, and let no fear dwell in your hearts. (247)
Having heard this, Viṣṇumarka, dancing, spoke as follows: "O King, we wish to know the extent of your domain. (248)
When this was said, Tāraka, the best of the Daityas, laughed and said: "Indeed, these three worlds are my own three-storied house. (249)
Then Harimarka said: "If it is so, remember your own word: O King, let these monkeys wander through the three worlds entirely free from fear. (250)
O King, truth excels even a hundred horse-sacrifices; remembering this dharma, O Lord of Daityas, make your word true. (251)
Then the Daitya, greatly astonished, spoke these words: "O monkey, you have indeed awakened; tell me truly, who are you? (252)
The Blessed Lord said: "I am named Nārāyaṇa, who has come to your ears; for the sake of protecting the gods, I have assumed the form of a monkey. (253)
If that is your chosen dharma, then preserve your own word; let these gods roam about your home.
Furthermore, O Indra among kings, you must not harbor in your heart the thought "I am a hero," while observing the power born of Time. (255)
For those who are being struck by various means, no striker exists; it is merely delusion that one thinks, "I am the hater" and "I am the doer. (256)

To whom do calamities not come in due time—be they sages, gods, great asuras, those aged in the three Vedas, or forest-dwelling munis? This is the power of Time (Kāla), and not the power of the agent.
Neither by the power of mantras, nor by prowess, nor by wisdom, nor by human effort is that which is unobtainable obtained; yet in due time, even while sleeping, one finds it.
Neither service to mother and father, nor worship of the deities, nor any other virtuous conduct brings happiness to a man. 259.
Neither knowledge, nor austerity, nor charity, nor friends, nor kinsmen are able to protect a man who is afflicted by Time. (260)
For indeed, even by means of hundreds of obstacles, men are unable to turn back one who is intent on not returning, except through the power of Time. (261)
Like a body, meritorious deeds are performed; like a living soul, time is said to exist. O Daitya, it is held that the accomplishment of all tasks occurs through the union of these two.
O Daitya, alas! In former times, crores of Daityas superior even to you were cast like cotton from a silk-cotton tree by the wind of Time into a miserable state. (263)
Having obtained this position, you consider yourself highly esteemed, like the eternal god Brahmā, the source of all beings. || 264 ||
This state is neither immovable nor infinite for anyone; yet you, with a foolish intellect, think, "This is mine. (265)
You place your trust in what is untrustworthy and consider the impermanent to be permanent; out of delusion, you desire the splendor of the three worlds, thinking, "This is mine. (266)
This [intellect] is considered to belong neither to you, nor to us, nor to others; it is stable. Having passed over many [others], it has remained with you for this long. (267)
O Tāraka, having remained with you for some time, this fickle woman, as excessively unsteady as a harlot, will go to another once again. || 268 ||
I no longer see those [gods] by whom the three worlds—endowed with precious gems and medicinal herbs, along with their rivers, mountains, and mines—were once enjoyed.
The hero Hiraṇyakaśipu, the invincible Hiraṇyākṣa, Prahrāda, the hero Namuci, Vipracitti, and Virocana; || 270 ||
Kīrti, Śūra, Vīra, Vātāpi, Ilvala, Aśvagrīva, Śambara, Puloman, Madhu, and Kaiṭabha. || 271 ||
And other mighty lords of the Dānavas, headed by Viśvajit, were all slain by Time; for Time is indeed more powerful. (272)
All of you performed austerities for ten thousand years, yet you alone are a great ascetic; all of you were devoted to the vow of truth, and all of you were deeply learned in the scriptures.
All were givers according to their worth, all were sons of Dākṣāyaṇī; blazing and victorious, they were eventually withdrawn by Time.
Relinquish your desire for sensual enjoyments, and abandon this intoxication born of prosperity; for when this sovereignty perishes, sorrow will overwhelm you.
Do not grieve in times of sorrow, and do not rejoice in times of joy; for you are bound by the present, while the past has passed and the future has not yet come.
If the time has come for Indra, who is ever-yoked and unwearied, then forgive him; O Daitya, it will not be long before he too shall approach you.
"For who in this world would be able to stand before me when I am enraged in battle? But Time has arrived with its power; it is for that reason, O Tāraka, that I remain."
O Daitya, you alone know who I am and what kind of prowess I possess; in kalpa after kalpa, great Daityas have been slain by the millions and the hundreds of millions.
O Savior, you are not even equal to a ten-millionth part of those for whom I create this entire world, beginning with Brahmā, in kalpa after kalpa.
If you desire it, I shall restore this [life]; if you do not desire it, I shall destroy it in an instant. Indeed, I am not unable to slay you, together with all the Daityas.
O Lord of Daityas, do not again destroy dharma with the tip of your finger; for if I, having become supreme, [uphold] dharma which consists of the boon of Brahmā... (282)
Whom then shall I cause to perish, and to whom shall this Dharma go for refuge? Do not think "I am the doer," for the one who is always the Lord is the true doer. (283)
This very Time ripens the universe like fruit that has come upon a tree; by those very same actions one experiences happiness, and by those very same actions, suffering. (284)
A person attains [this], O Daitya; behold the wondrous nature of Time! Everything is subject to Time alone; this must be understood by men endowed with wisdom. (285)
The wise know that the ripening of one's own karma indeed yields its fruit; therefore, auspicious action should be performed—action that is meritorious and of a virtuous nature. (286)

"Happiness there comes from merit, while suffering certainly results from sin; reflecting thus, O Lord of Daityas, uphold your own word. If you deem it right to forgive everything I have said here," (287)
Tāraka said: "Seeing me stationed here, accompanied by Kālanemi and the others," (288)
Whose mind here would not tremble, even that of one wishing to live, at the sight of death? Yet this intellect of yours does not tremble; it is immovable and perceives reality as it is.
Whatever word you speak, it is exactly so, there is no doubt; for what embodied being can have confidence in objects or in the body? (290)
Seeing that the world is setting out [on its journey], one is emboldened to act in this world; I too know this world to be exactly thus, impermanent. (291)
Cast into the terrible and secret fire of Time, which is ever-moving, those who say, "I will do this today," or "I shall do it tomorrow," [perish]. (292)
Time carries away those who have arrived before it, like the current of a river sweeps away those facing it; yet, he was seen by me just now and has not been forgotten.
The lamentation of men being carried away by Time is heard amidst envy, pride, greed, desire, anger, and fear. (294)
O Keśava, the world, attached to longing, delusion, and excessive speech, does not perceive whether something is heavy or light, nor what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
I know you, O Viṣṇu, to be the Lord, the foremost among all beings; yet, due to our own powerful nature, we do not recognize you. 296.
Some worship you with devotion, others with enmity or even with indifference; all of them are worthy of your compassion, for you are the inner self of all embodied beings.
"Let all the inhabitants of heaven, relying upon me and released by me, go forth; for this is the ancient, eternal Dharma, equal toward all living beings. (298)
Furthermore, you must wander through the three worlds in the form of a monkey; not even a desire for sacrificial portions should be entertained—this is your vow. (299)
When Tāraka had spoken thus, the gods were filled with joy: "Even though its wool has been plucked out, the ram is released; indeed, this is a gain from the butcher. (300)

The Blessed Lord said: "O Lord of Daityas, become a knower of reality, endowed with learning, wisdom, and austerity; you shall perceive time as clearly as an amalaka fruit in the palm of your hand. (301)
O knower of the truth of the movements of time, devotee of Śiva, great-minded one! O son of Vajrāṅga, you are blessed; you are an object of envy for the wise. (302)
"As great as is the power of your asceticism, so much of the three worlds shall you enjoy; by this agreement, these gods shall move through the world."
Having spoken thus, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, surrounded by the troop of monkeys, departed from this place and then proceeded toward Mount Meru.
Then, having reached Mount Meru, Hari spoke these words: "Go to Brahmā; he shall provide for your welfare."
"One must always remain vigilant, and likewise, the sacred pledge (samaya) must be observed. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished right there.
Having bowed down and offered praise, the gods went to Brahmā.

There, praised by those who had arrived from the highest celestial realms, the hero Vajrāṅgaputra, whose splendor blazed throughout the three worlds, rejoiced, having attained great supernatural power through the grace of Śiva. (308)
Svayamindra, Nimi, Vahni, Kālanemi, and Yama; Stambha in the place of Nirṛti, as well as Mahiṣa and Varuṇa. || 309 ||
Meṣa became the superintendent of the wind, while Kujaṃbha became the giver of wealth; Tāraka assigned other offices to the remaining Daityas. || 310 ||
Nārada said: Thus insulted, the gods, together with Mahendra, then went to the abode of Svāyambhuva Manu, having assumed the form of monkeys.
Then, filled with wonder, Brahmā said to those foremost of gods: "Remain here in your own forms; you have no fear here from Tāraka."
Then all the gods, established in their own forms with lotus-faces withered, bowed down and offered praise like sons to a father.
Salutations to You, the source of the world; salutations to You as its cause, its protector, and its destroyer. O Lord, these three states are Yours alone.
Having first created the waters, you deposited your seed within them; that became a golden egg, wherein were the worlds, both moving and unmoving.
In the Vedas, they declare you, who are of such a single form, to be Virāṭ; the netherworld (Pātāla) is the soles of your feet, and Rasātala is your heels and feet.
Mahātala is his two ankles, and Talātala is his two shanks; Sutala is his two knees, and Vitala and Atala are his two thighs.
The surface of the earth is his hips, and the vault of the sky is his navel; the region of light is his chest, and the heavenly world is said to be his arms.
The neck is proclaimed as Maharloka, the face as Janaloka; the forehead is Tapoloka, and the head is declared to be Satyaloka.
The proponents of the Vedas declare that the moon and sun are your eyes, the quarters of space your ears, the Aśvins your nose, and that you are the Self abiding in the aperture of Brahmā.
Thus, those who worship while constantly remembering Your form as Virāṭ, being liberated from the bondage of birth, go unto You, the supreme state.

Thus they praise You as the gross, as that which dwells within living beings, and as the subtle, meditated upon in every state of being; therefore the Vedas declare You to be present everywhere—to You, O Lotus-footed One, we pay homage. 12.
Thus praised, Virañci, overflowing with compassion, spoke even though he already knew [the truth], for the sake of giving them consolation.
All of you are afflicted by suffering, with lotus-faces withered; your weapons have suddenly fallen away, as have your ornaments and garments.
O gods, this mockery of yours is actually my own creation, in that you are designated as my arms within my Virāṭ body. (15)
Whatever being is possessed of majesty, righteous, powerful, and great—in that, my arm was present; and you were my arm in its proper place.
Surely my two arms have been broken by that evil-minded one, by whom the gods were carried away; it behooves you to tell me who he is.
The gods said: "O Lord, that son of Vajrāṅga to whom you granted a boon has greatly oppressed us; you know this in its true essence."
O Lord, having overrun that shore of the great ocean known as Śārvika-tīrtha, he made it equal to a desert land.
The supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) of all the gods were seized by him from every side; he alone, in the form of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), is the Lord of the World.
Having set aside the moon, the sun, the planets, the stars, and whatever else belongs to the side of the gods, he established the faction of the Daityas.
We were held captive by him and likewise subjected to much mockery; yet, through his grace, we have somehow been released from that hardship. (22)
"Afflicted and tormented by hunger and thirst, we have come to you for refuge; considering that you are the protectors of Dharma, it behooves you to save us. (23)
Thus addressed by the gods regarding the activities of the Daityas, the blessed Lord, who is his own self-born source, reflected upon the matter according to its true nature and spoke to the gods.
The Daitya Tāraka was unslayable by all the gods and asuras alike; yet that Blessed One, who was to be his slayer, has now been born once again.
And I, having enticed him with the granting of a boon, dissuaded him. || 26 ||

By means of his ascetic penance, he indeed became radiant, possessing the nature of a conflagration that could burn the three worlds; and that Daitya chose his death at the hands of a child only seven days old.
And that boy, seven days old, shall become Śaṅkara and others; he shall be the slayer of the heroic Tāraka.
But that goddess named Satī, who was destroyed by Dakṣa’s negligence, shall become the auspicious one born from the body of Himācala.
An effort must be made for the union of Śaṅkara and her; I too shall undoubtedly complete the remainder of this task.
Having been addressed thus by that manifest source of all arts (Kalayoni), the thirty gods bowed to the Lord and departed for Mount Meru, disguised in the form of monkeys.
Then, after the gods had departed, the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, called to mind his own body that had been produced in the beginning.
Then the blessed Night presented herself before the Grandfather; beholding her in that secluded place, he spoke thus to the Goddess of Twilight.
O Vibhāvarī, a great task has presented itself for the gods; it must be performed by you, O Goddess—listen to the determination of this task. (34)
There is a lord of the Daityas named Tāraka, who has not been conquered by the banner of the gods; for his destruction, the Blessed Śiva will beget one.
He shall be born as his son and will be the one who brings about Tāraka’s end. When I was first born, I saw him standing before me.
Having seen that god Ardhanārīśvara, who stands pervading the entire universe, I spoke to him with devotion: "Worship him. (37)
From that [union], the woman was born separately and the man likewise separately; and all women in the three worlds are remembered as being born from her portions. || 38 ||
The eleven Rudras were born from portions of that Puruṣa; then, beholding that great woman, I spoke to her son, Dakṣa.
Accept my daughter; she belongs to both me and you. This daughter of yours is destined to be a protector who saves one from the fear of the suffering of men. (40)
Thus addressed by me, Dakṣa, having given her the name Satī, devotedly bestowed her upon Rudra as his adopted daughter.
Then, at a certain time, that evil-minded and wicked soul, a stain upon his lineage, who was intent on sin and desirous of death, insulted her. (42)
Those who do not even acknowledge Rudra are clearly the soot of their own lineage; those evil-minded ones become Piśācas and Brahmarākṣasas.
How the Goddess abandoned her body due to his insult, and how that sacrifice was destroyed by Bhava—all this is indeed known to you. (44)
Now she shall become the daughter of the Himālaya mountain, and she will certainly obtain Maheśvara as her husband once again. (45)
And this must be done by you: having entered the womb of Menā, make her complexion dark so that she may become Kālī.
When she, having been mocked by Rudra, performs great penance, and when the goddess has completed her observances and becomes fierce; || 47 ||
When she herself regains her naturally fair complexion, Hara will consider the three worlds empty due to her absence.
In a cave of that very snowy mountain, frequented by perfected beings (siddhas), he will perform severe penance while awaiting that goddess.
The great son who shall be born from those two who have performed intense austerities will be the destroyer of the Daitya Tāraka.
For without austerity, O beautiful one, there is no success anywhere; indeed, austerity is said to be the root of all successful undertakings. (51)
O Goddess, you too, having then emerged from my body, must slay the Dānavas who are invincible to the world, headed by Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
And because you, O Goddess, shall slay Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, you shall therefore become renowned in the world as Cāmuṇḍā.
"Therefore, O bestower of boons, the world shall worship you, the goddess who pervades all and who accomplishes all desires, through various kinds of manifestations. (54)
The best of the twice-born worship you, Gāyatrī, whose mouth is the syllable Oṃ; kings of great strength, O sinful one, worship you as the exalted giver of power. (55)
The Vaiśyas likewise seek prosperity, and the Śūdras seek auspiciousness, O blessed lady; for the sages, forbearance is unshakeable, and compassion belongs even to those who observe vows.

You are the treasury of great expedients, the policy for those who expand through statesmanship; you are the foundation of all purposes, and oh, you are considered the very life-force of living beings. 57.
You are the reasoning of all beings; you are the refuge of all embodied souls. You are the delight of those whose minds seek pleasure; you are the joy of those who behold the heart.

You are the splendor of those with auspicious forms; you are the peace of those who perform virtuous deeds; you are the delusion of those with deluded minds; you are the fruit for those who sacrifice in rituals.
You are the great tide of the oceans, and you are the playful sport of the amorous; you are the origin of all things, and you are the stability that protects the worlds.
You are the Night of Doom, the destroyer of the entire succession of worlds; you are the dark night that bestows the bliss of embracing the neck of your beloved. 61.
Be gracious; look upon us who are prostrate before you with a gentle gaze.
O auspicious Goddess, those who worship you while praising you thus shall surely attain all their desires; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having been addressed thus, Queen Niśā said, "So be it," and with palms joined in reverence, she went quickly to the great abode of Himavat that was located to the east.
There, seated in a great palace resting against walls of jewels, he beheld Menā, whose lotus-face was pale in complexion.
With her face slightly darkened and her lofty breasts bent forward, she was attended by the king of mantras bound with a multitude of great medicinal herbs.
Then, as soon as Menā’s two lotus-eyes were slightly closed, Night entered her mouth at the command of Brahmā.
In due course, the night delighted the complexion within the womb of the Mother of the World, the mother of Guha, who had granted him birth.
Then, at the auspicious hour of Brahma-muhurta, Menā, the beloved wife of Himavat, gave birth to a daughter of beautiful countenance who was the life-giver of the world. (69)
When she was being born, all living beings—both stationary and moving—who dwell in all the worlds, became happy.
The minds of cruel beings became peaceful, as did those of embodied beings; even the brilliance of the luminaries became exceedingly great at that time.
The medicinal herbs dwelling in the forests bore sweet fruits, the flower garlands were fragrant, and the sky became stainless.
The breeze was pleasant to the touch, the quarters were most enchanting, and the sacred scriptures, having been forgotten, reappeared. (73)
At that time, the power of the foremost sacred fords became most meritorious in regard to truth, righteousness, study, sacrifice, charity, and austerity as well.
At the time of Guhāraṇi’s birth, faith arose in everyone; even the gods in the intermediate space had their eyes wide open with great joy.
Led by Hari, Brahmā, Mahendra, Arka, Vāyu, and Agni, they released a rain of flowers upon that auspicious house of Menā.
And the great mountains, Meru and others, having taken embodied form, arrived at that great festival, adorned with heroic bronze vessels.
The oceans and the rivers likewise all assembled from every direction. || 78 ||
O Bhārata, at that time the Himālaya mountain became worthy of being served, approached, and worshipped by all beings, both mobile and immobile, in the world.
Having experienced the festival, they then departed for their own abodes.

Nārada said: Then the fortunate goddess, the daughter of the mountain, played there with the daughters of the gods and Gandharvas born of the mountains and Kinnaras, as well as with those who were the daughters of the sages—she, the beautiful one.
Then once, O son of Pāṇḍu, Vāsava, while staying on Mount Meru, remembered me; and being thus remembered, I then went to Vāsava.
Upon seeing me, the thousand-eyed one rose up with great joy and honored me; having accepted that worship, I spoke.
O Great Asura, O Kālānala of great intoxication, O Lord of Heaven! Is all well with you, and do you rejoice?
Thus questioned by me, Śakra smiled and spoke these words: "The sprout of virtue has indeed now emerged in the three worlds. (5)
O Sage, you have been remembered by me for the attainment of the arising of that fruit; indeed, you know every doctrine, yet you are one who prompts [others] toward it.
Having communicated his purpose to his friends, he attains supreme peace.
Therefore, you should honor the goddess Śailajā, the lord of mountains, and the beloved of the mountain—Hara—who is the bestower of boons, for there is no other whom they find pleasing.
Then, having heard those words, I went to that best of mountains, the abode of medicinal herbs, which was like the Lord of Heaven himself in person.
There, upon a magnificent golden throne personally offered by him with great devotion, I sat down in great bliss, having been duly honored.
Then, having accepted the guest-offering (arghya), the Mountain, his lotus-like face slowly blossoming, questioned me in gentle words regarding the well-being of my ascetic penance.
Having said that to him, I replied to the Lord of the Mountains: "O Lord of Mountains, you [should protect] both the eastern and likewise the western direction."
"Having plunged in and remained there, you perform the protection of living beings; oh, you are blessed, O best of Brahmins, by your assistance, O Mountain! (13)
Some strive for the supreme self through austerities, recitations, vows, and ritual baths; others by means of the implements of sacrifice, and some by the offering of roots, fruits, and the like.
You uplift the brahmins; what more can be said of you? O Upholder of the Earth, other living beings as well depend upon you in many ways.
Joyfully they turn back toward the household life, like living beings enduring cold, heat, rain, and various kinds of afflictions.
"You bring benefit to living beings; for such indeed are the virtuous. What more can be said to you? You are blessed, O supporter of the earth! (17)
"And the cave which Maheśvara himself inhabits"—when these words, which were true to the facts, had been spoken by me to Phālguna, O Arjuna.
Menā, the queen of the snowy mountain, arrived with a desire to see [him], followed by her daughter and a few female attendants. (19)
With all her limbs bowed down in modesty, she entered the great assembly hall; then that queen of the mountain, having prostrated herself, paid homage to me.
With her face veiled by her garment and her lotus-like hands joined in *añjali*, I honored her with blessings that were true in form.
O auspicious one, be a devoted wife of virtuous conduct, a beautiful woman who gives birth to heroes; may you always be blessed with heroic sons and grant the exaltation of your lineage. (22)
Then, with gentle words, I spoke to the daughter of the Himavat mountain, whose eyes were wide with wonder: "Come, O child, into my presence."
Then the Goddess, the Mother of the World, displaying her own childhood state to me, took her father by the neck and entered his lap.
She spoke these words softly: "O daughter, pay homage to the sage; by the grace of the sage, you will certainly obtain a husband who is worthy of your esteem."
Having been addressed thus, that young woman then lowered her face within the fold of her garment; uttering a slight, trembling sound of "hum," she said nothing further.
Then, with a mind filled with wonder, I, the best among those skilled in formal etiquette, replied to the goddess once more: "Come, O auspicious one; I shall grant you [your wish]."
"This delightful jewel-toy has been cherished by me for a very long time. Having said this, she then rose up quickly from her father's lap. (28)
As she was bowing at my feet, I drew her close to my own body; consider her worthy of worship by the whole world, for I have said, "O girl, this is what is fitting for you."
"I do not see anything that I could give you; what blessing would be appropriate for you? When this was said, the queen of the lord of mountains, out of maternal affection, then [replied]: (30)
Then, fearing for my life, she did not urge me on; "O Blessed One, O Lord, you know everything—past and future. (31)
"Therefore, I wish to know what kind of husband she will have. Hearing this, he whose face was smiling, being fond of jesting, replied: ||| 32 ||

"O blessed lady, her husband has not yet been born; moreover, he will possess inauspicious family marks. He will be naked, utterly destitute, prone to anger, and always surrounded by cruel people. (33)
Having heard this, the great mountain Himācala, overcome with agitation and his vigor destroyed, then replied to me with a voice choked with tears: 34.
Oh, how wondrous is this saṃsāra, difficult to comprehend even for the great! For even one who is preeminent among men in power does not show compassion. (35)
With great effort and through manifold meritorious deeds, people achieve for themselves this human state, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (36)
That which is unstable is somehow imagined to possess stability; even in that case, a wife who observes the same vows is difficult to find. (37)
A virtuous wife, born of a noble family and devoted to her husband, should be sought; yet even among such, it is rare indeed that she should be one who practices righteousness.

Together with that which is declared in the Vedas and Purāṇas, which brings benefit to the three worlds, and whatever else is exceedingly difficult to obtain, all that is produced within her alone. (39)
O Nārada, it is said that in this cycle of existence, a meritorious person may indeed obtain something for the sake of offspring from among these things which are so difficult to attain. (40)
Whether such a person attains all of this or not, the world indeed makes every man deficient in something by means of someone else. (41)
Moreover, O Nārada, the Vedas all praise the householder’s life, wherein the consequences of one's own actions within the cycle of existence are experienced.
