Uttering a terrifying roar that struck fear into the world of the Asuras, the Rākṣasa then [seized] the peak of Mount Śveta, which was covered by ten padmas.
With great force, he pierced with a spear that mountain which extended for a hundred yojanas; by that single blow, it fell to the earth in fragments. (155)
Those Rākṣasas, who were constant enemies of Dharma, were ground to powder; consequently, the earth was distressed and shattered on all sides. || 156 ||
All the mountains, terrified as if at the dissolution of the world, cried out; and the living beings there wailed most piteously, "Save us! Save us! (157)
Having heard this, the gods then spoke to Vāsava: "By whom, with a single blow, the three worlds have been thrown into turmoil. (158)
O Vāsava, once enraged, he will destroy the universe in an instant; and we have been created by the divine Creator for the purpose of protection.
And that protection must always be maintained, even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat; for while we are looking on, the world is thus being thrown into turmoil. (160)
"Fie on that birth of heroes; for death in an instant is indeed praiseworthy. Therefore, O Vāsava, you ought to endure this along with us. (161)
Thus addressed, having replied "So be it," Śakra then went toward him together with the gods, desiring very swiftly to test his prowess.
Beholding that fierce and highly impetuous army of the gods, difficult to approach and roaring aloud, Guha bellowed like the ocean.
By that great roar, the army of the gods, resembling the surging ocean, wandered here and there, deprived of its senses.
Seeing the gods who had arrived seeking to slay him, that son of Agni emitted from his mouth there great, blazing flames of fire.
He consumed the divine armies as they strove upon the earth; their heads and bodies were set ablaze, as were their weapons and vehicles.
Suddenly fallen from heaven like clusters of stars, they appeared as if being consumed by fire; thus they sought refuge with the son of Agni.
The gods said to the wielder of the thunderbolt, "O Śatakratu, cast aside the vajra! Thus addressed by the gods, Śakra then discharged the vajra at Skanda.
That which was discharged by him quickly struck the right side of Skanda and pierced that high-souled one, O best of the Kurus. (169)
From the blow of the thunderbolt upon Skanda, another man was born—young, wearing golden armor, holding a spear, and adorned with divine earrings. || 170 ||
He who was renowned as Śākha also let out a wondrous roar; thereupon Indra, becoming enraged once more, tore at Skanda’s heart.
There too, one such as that was born, known by the name Naigameya; then, having roared, Skanda and the other four approached him.
Then Indra, having cast down his thunderbolt, went for refuge with palms joined in reverence; Skanda, the most excellent of beings, granted safety to him and his army.
Then the gods, greatly delighted, sounded their musical instruments; and from the stroke of the thunderbolt, daughters of great strength were born to him.
The cruel ones who seize children—both those already born and those still in the womb—are Kākī, Hilimā, Rudrā, and likewise Vṛṣabhā. (175)
Āyā, Palālā, and Mitrā—these seven are the mothers of Śiśu. Endowed with their combined power, Śiśu became exceedingly terrible.
The son born from the grace of Skanda is Lohitākṣa, the terrifying one. This is declared to be the Vīrāṣṭaka, the wonderful host of Skanda’s mothers. 177.
Always to be worshipped with devotion, he grants peace from all forms of epilepsy; thereafter, he approached Skanda, who was adorned with golden armor and garlands.
Having bowed to him, who was clothed in red garments, possessed a splendor surpassing even that of the three worlds, and was in the prime of youth, Śrī herself, embodied, took her place beside him.
And all the gods, having indeed bowed down to him who was graced with glory, said: "O golden-hued one, may it be well with you; become the bringer of welfare to the worlds. (180)
O Lord, may you become the Indra of existence for us, truly for the welfare of the three worlds.
Skanda said: O best of gods, what does Indra do here for all the worlds? And how does the lord of the gods constantly protect the hosts of deities? (182)
The gods said: "Indra, the lord of the gods, bestows upon living beings strength, splendor, progeny, and happiness; likewise, he grants wisdom as well as all inheritances. (183)
He takes away from those of evil conduct and bestows it upon those established in right conduct; being most powerful, he instructs all beings in their duties.
He becomes the sun where there is no sun, and likewise the moon where there is no moon; he becomes fire and wind, and is the cause of life within the earth. (185)
"This must be performed by Indra, for Indra possesses vast power; O hero, become our Indra, slay Tāraka, and homage be unto you! (186)
Indra said: "O mighty-armed Skanda, you shall become Indra, bringing happiness to us all. Bowing down, I entreat you: slay Tāraka and protect us. (187)
Skanda said: "You yourself rule the three worlds; may you be Indra forever. I shall perform the duties of Indra, for the position of Indra is not what I desire."
"You alone are the king—blessings upon you—of the three worlds and of me as well. What command of Śakra shall I carry out for you? Tell it to me. (189)

Indra said: "If this speech has been spoken by you with certainty and truth, O one of great strength, then be consecrated in the generalship of the gods. I shall become Indra at your word; let there be glory unto you. (190)
Skanda said: "For the destruction of the Dānavas, for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods, and for the sake of cows and Brahmins—let your word be so! (191)
When this was said, a great roar arose from the gods and from all living beings, crying out for the protection of the three worlds.
They praised him, crying "Victory!", and sounded musical instruments; they danced, offered hymns of praise, and clapped their hands.
Amazed by that great sound, the daughter of the mountain spoke to Śaṅkara: "O Lord, what is this sound that resounds so excessively?"
Rudra said: "O Goddess, today the various voices of the gods, who are surely overjoyed, are being heard, saying that a son has been born to you. (195)
Your son, though he himself possesses merit, shall wipe away the tears of cows, brahmins, virtuous women, and the inhabitants of heaven. (196)
As that goddess spoke thus, she became eager to see him; for Śaṅkara, possessed of great splendor, was exceedingly full of affection for his son.
Then, having mounted his bull along with the Goddess, Bhava, eager and longing to see his son, arrived there accompanied by his attendants.
Then Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, spoke thus to Mahāsena: "O Lord, go to your father Mahādeva and your mother. (199)
"Your first birth shall indeed come from the union of the virility of these two. Having said, "So be it," Mahāsena addressed Maheśvara. (200)
The immeasurable-souled one honored his father and that mother; then, having embraced his son and bestowed upon him long-lasting blessings, he [departed].
Both Pārvatī and Parameśvara rejoiced for a long time; and Śaṅkara, being pleased with him, bestowed upon him the essential truth of the Siddhasāra.
And the Goddess, delighted and overflowing with joy, [attained] liberation into her own nature; at that very moment, the six goddesses arrived there.
Abandoned by the sages, they then cried out, "He is our son! Thereupon Pārvatī said, "This is not your son; he is mine. (204)
Svāhā said, "He is mine," and Pāvaka also said, "He is mine. Rudra said, "He is mine," and the celestial river said, "He is mine. (205)
They engaged in a terrible quarrel, disputing with one another; for O Pārtha, the affection for a son is powerful—what indeed will it not cause one to do? || 206 ||
Then, laughing, he said to them: "A dispute is not appropriate; Guha is the son of you all, so let a boon indeed be chosen from me."
Then the six goddesses said, "May heaven indeed become inexhaustible for us. "So be it," Śakra replied to them from his abode; in the meantime, he spoke there.
And Rohiṇī’s younger sister, the wicked Abhijit, emulating Skanda, was devoted to asceticism, desiring seniority and a separate status for herself. (209)
"From that time forth I have been bewildered; therefore, O Lord, establish me in that very place. Then, when it was said, "So be it," those Kṛttikās departed for heaven.

The constellation resembling seven heads shines there, having Agni as its presiding deity. Then Svāhā said to him: "I am not dear to this one of great radiance; therefore, grant me to Agni as his beloved, and grant me eternal residence with him. (211)
Skanda said: Whatever oblation for the gods (havya) or oblation for the ancestors (kavya) the twice-born shall offer into the fire, [that shall belong to me]. || 212 ||
They shall grant you a garment by that name, which shall belong to you along with [the other]. Pāvaka then requested shares in the sacrifice and sons once again.
And he too said, "From this day forward, may you receive shares in the sacrifices. The others requested, "May you become our famous son. (214)

"It is even so," Skanda said to them, "for that is indeed very difficult to attain. Thereupon, all the yogins, Sanaka and the others, having assembled together, consecrated him on that mountain as the sovereign lord of the yogins.
Therefore, the yogis called him the Lord of Yogins; the deities also rejoiced and played various musical instruments.
With him consecrated, that White Mountain shone like the beautiful Mountain of Sunrise with the radiant sun.
Then the gods along with the gandharvas danced, as did the apsarases; a great roar was heard from all the delighted beings.
Thus, beholding Skanda seated upon the White Mountain, the entire world together with Indra was filled with joy and could not satiate itself from the sight of him.
Nārada said: Then Skanda, together with the gods, descended from the summit of Mount Śveta and went toward the southern direction to slay Tāraka.
Then, O Nārada, whatever beings there were on the banks of the Sarasvatī—the planets and secondary planets, as well as the vetālas and the hosts of śākinīs—[all gathered].
Those who are possessed by madness, those who suffer from epilepsy, the flesh-eaters, and the Piśācas—over them as their sovereign, that son of Agni was consecrated by the gods.
Just as those of evil intent do not abandon their limits, therefore one who is assailed by these should seek refuge with the son of Agni, the protector.
The malevolent spirits and other such beings avoid one whose senses are not distracted, who is self-controlled, pure, ever-vigilant, a believer, and a devotee of Skanda.
Those who are devotees of Maheśvara and those who are devotees of Nārāyaṇa—by the mere sight of them, [the obstacles] perish from afar.
Then Guha went to the shore of the earth together with all the gods; there, the supreme majesty of the earth was proclaimed by the deities.
Hearing this, Skanda was filled with wonder and bowed down to that river; then he took his stand, having reached the southern bank of the earth.
Having prostrated before Guha, those led by Śakra spoke these words: "O Skanda, without having consecrated a sinless general, [you have departed]."
The army finds no peace; therefore, you must perform the consecration with the auspicious and meritorious waters produced at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. 10.
And we shall consecrate you there; it behoves you to witness that, just as the inclusion of all footprints within the footprint of an elephant is recognized.
Just as Tryambaka is proclaimed to consist of all beings, so too does he abide within all sacred fords, the ocean, and the waters of the earth.
Likewise, the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean embodies all sacred fords; it is like the form of Rudra as Ardhanārīśvara, which bestows all things.
Likewise, bathing in Mahīsamudra bestows all fruits, by which the ancestors are gratified here through a spirit of devotion, O Skanda. (14)
By that, one has undoubtedly offered libations at all sacred fords (tīrthas); yet, this should not be thought in the heart, "For this water is indeed salty. (15)
Just as pungent, bitter, and other such substances, when consumed by a cow, yield milk; even so, this water provides satisfaction to the ancestors.
While the gods were speaking thus, the sage Kapila also declared: "O son of Umā, this is true; the earth consists of all sacred fords. (17)
I, Kardama, having likewise recognized the great virtues of this sacred ford, have abandoned the entire earth and established my hermitage here.
Then Maheśvara said, "This which has been spoken by the gods is true. Brahmā and the others spoke likewise to him; then, once more, the Guru [spoke].
"O hero, we shall perform the consecration for you here; give us your command. Then, greatly amazed, the high-minded Skanda bathed there.
"May the gods consecrate me," he spoke these words to them; then, having gathered all the requisites for the consecration according to the scriptures, || 21 ||
The four chief officiating priests—Brahmā, Kapila, Jīva, and Viśvāmitra as the fourth—offered oblations into the fire purified by mantras.
And there were hundreds of other sages there who had mastered the Vedas; O Bhārata, Mahādeva manifested a marvel there.
Since I was seen in the form of a linga situated in the midst of the fire-pit, I myself, standing in the middle of the fire, constantly receive the oblation.
For the purpose of manifesting this, the omnipresent Lord assumed the form of a Liṅga; the gods, filled with joy, bowed down to that incomparable Liṅga.
O Pārtha, it removes all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires; and there, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the auspicious [vessel] was given by Himavat.
Skanda sat upon a supreme throne adorned with divine jewels, amidst an abundance of all auspicious things, preceded by ritual procedures and mantras.
Then, O Phālguna, the gods—Indra, Viṣṇu of great prowess, Brahmā, and Rudra—consecrated Kumāra, the son of Śaṅkara.
All the planets beginning with Āditya, as well as both Vāyu and Agni; the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and both Aśvins. (29)
The Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Gandharvas and Apsarases, as well as the divine Brahman-sages, the Vālakhilyas, and the Marīcipās. || 30 ||
The Vidyādharas, the Yogasiddhas, Pulastya, Pulaha, and others; the Pitṛs, Kaśyapa, Atri, Marīci, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras. (31)
Then Dakṣa, the Manus, the luminaries, and likewise the seasons; as well as the rivers in embodied form, the Earth, and others. || 32 ||
The oceans beginning with the salt sea, the sacred fords beginning with Prabhāsa, the earth, the sky, the quarters, as well as the trees and the mountains; || 33 ||
The Ādityas and other mothers performed the auspicious rite for Guha; likewise did the Nāgas headed by Vāsuki, as well as both Garuḍa and Aruṇa.
Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Yama along with his followers, as well as Nirṛti the Rākṣasa and the flesh-eating spirits (bhūtas). || 35 ||
Dharma, Bṛhaspati, Kapila, and the son of Gādhi; and because of their great number, the various hosts of deities who have not been mentioned.
And all of them joyfully consecrated Guha upon the bank of the earth; then [they sounded] a loud, fierce sound that humbles the pride of gods, Daityas, and others.
Paśupati gave him a great army consisting of all types of beings, and Viṣṇu gave him the Vaijayantī garland which increases strength.
Umā gave him two dustless garments with the splendor of the sun; Gaṅgā gave him a divine water-pot, excellent and born of nectar.
The Earth, along with the great rivers and the oceans, joyfully gave a rosary to that Kumāra, and Bṛhaspati likewise gave him a staff.
Garuḍa gave his beloved son, the peacock with its variegated plumage; and Aruṇa gave the red-crested cock, whose weapon is its feet.
And King Varuṇa gave a goat endowed with strength and vigor, while Brahmā gave a black antelope skin and victory to the one devoted to Brahman.
And he [appointed] four attendants of great heroism and exceeding strength—Nandisena, Lohitākṣa, Ghaṇṭākarṇa, and Mānasa.
And the fourth, known as Atibala, was Kusumamālin; then the god Sthāṇu gave Kratu as a great attendant.
For in the war between the gods and the asuras, he, being enraged, slew fourteen million Daityas of terrible deeds with his two arms.
Then Yama gave him two attendants, Unmātha and Pramātha, who were like Yama and Kāla themselves, possessed of great heroism and great splendor.
O Pārtha, Sūrya, filled with joy, gave those two who were always the radiant followers of Bhāskara himself to Kārttikeya.
Soma also gave two attendants who resembled the peaks of Mount Kailāsa and were adorned with white garlands and unguents, as well as Maṇi and Sumaṇi.
Agni gave two very powerful sons, Jvālajihva and Jyotiṣa; as well as Parigha, Bala, Bhīma, and Sumahābala.
Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one, gave three attendants to Skanda: Utkrośa, Pañcaja, and both Vajra and Daṇḍadhara.
Vāsava, the slayer of enemy heroes, gave them to the son of Maheśa; for those two slew many of Mahendra’s enemies in battle.
O bull of the Bharata lineage, the two Aśvins, experts in Āyurveda, being well-pleased, bestowed both Vardhana and Bandhana upon Skanda.
Vāyu gave to Kārttikeya both his two attendants, Bala and Atibala, who had large faces and great strength.
The lord Varuṇa gave to the two heroes Ghasa and Atighasa, as well as Suvarcas and the high-souled Ativarcas.
O Pārtha, Himavat indeed gave [the chariot] to his own grandson; and Meru gave the one called Meghamālī, made of gold. || 55 ||
And being pleased, that Vindhya gave two auspicious attendants, Ucchrita and Atiśṛṅga, who fought with great boulders, to Svāheya.
Accompanied by Mahīnadī, the ocean also gave two heroic attendants, Saṃgraha and Vigraha, as well as Gadādhara. || 57 ||
The auspicious-looking Pārvatī likewise gave Unmāda, Puṣpadanta, and Śaṅkukarṇa to the son of Agni.
The two Nāgas, Jaya and Mahājaya—the best among the powerful—both became the attendants of Suparṇa for the son of Agni.
Thus the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Vasus, and the Pitṛs—as well as all those who are preeminent in the world—gave attendants to Skanda.
O Phalguna, because they possess diverse powers and great prowess, and are adorned with various weapons, they cannot be counted due to their vast number.
And then, O Lord, the Mothers gave him the hosts of Mothers, by whom—the auspicious ones—these three worlds, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, are pervaded.
Prabhāvatī, Viśālākṣī, Gopālā, and likewise Gonasā; Apsujātā, Bṛhaddaṇḍī, Kālikā, and Bahuputrakā. (63)
Bhayakarī, Cakrāṅgī, Tīrthanemi, Mādhavī, Gītapriyā, Alātākṣī, Caṭulā, and Śalabhāmukhī. (64)
Vidyujjihvā, Rudrakālī, she whose girdle consists of a hundred mortars, she who possesses a hundred bells and tinkling ornaments, Cakrākṣī, and she whose abode is the crossroads.
Pūtanā, Rodanā, Tvamā, Koṭarā, Meghavāhinī, Ūrdhvaveṇīdharā, Jarāyu, and Jarjarānanā. || 66 ||
Khaṭakheṭī, Dahadahā, as well as Dhamadhamā and Jayā; she has many braids, many heads, many feet, and many breasts.

She has the face of a hundred owls, she is black, and likewise her ears serve as a covering; she dwells in empty houses and resides in granaries; she is always the giver of cattle and the giver of grain. 68.
O bull among the Bharatas, there are these and many other mothers; because of their great number, I do not venture here to enumerate them.
They dwell in trees and at crossroads, reside at junctions of four paths, live in caves and cremation grounds, and have their abodes in mountains and springs.
Adorned with various ornaments and attire, assuming diverse forms, and bearing various languages and weapons, they then surrounded Guha.
Then that glorious Guha shone like another Guha, having been consecrated in the command of the army by the gods and various lords of sages.
Then, having bowed down to all of them one by one, the son of Agni said to those led by Bhava and Brahmā, "Choose a boon."
Nārada said: Having honored Guha with blessings, they requested a boon from him: "This itself is our boon—that you slay the sinful Tāraka."
Having said "So be it" to them, and uttering "Yoga, yoga," the one of great splendor, the enemy of Tāraka, mounted his peacock.
Then Guha, with a spear in hand, having roared, spoke to the gods: "O best of gods, if I do not slay the wicked Tāraka today... (3)
"Therefore, I shall clearly go to the destination of those who insult cows and Brahmins. When he had thus made his vow, a very great sound arose.
"Yoga, yoga," they cried out at the command of the one born in the reeds; for the son of Pārvatī was wearing two red garments free from dust.
Then, standing at the forefront of all the gods, the hero went forth with joy; his banner shone brilliantly, adorned with the weapon of a claw.
He who is capable of splitting mountains with his two feet in battle; he who possesses the activity, splendor, tranquility, and strength of all living beings. (7)
Therefore, that power of Guha shone intensely in my hand; likewise, my armor was composed of that very firmness which exists throughout all the worlds.
As the hero was about to fight, Dharma, truth, freedom from delusion, splendor, beauty, and invincibility manifested themselves within his body.
Strength, vigor, and compassion likewise stood bound at his hands; they remained before that great-souled one, ready to carry out his commands.
And as he was proceeding ahead, the Lord Hara, accompanied by Pārvatī, followed behind him in a chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
By the Lord Hara himself, through his own playful power, a thousand lions were yoked to that most excellent chariot by the one who was himself created.
O tiger among men, Brahmā himself took hold of the reins; they seemed to drink up the sky, terrifying all that is mobile and immobile.
Lions with beautiful manes, roaring as they go, draw the chariot; upon that chariot, Paśupati shines resplendent together with Umā.
The sun was flanked by lightning, like it were accompanied by Indra’s bow and clouds; and in front of him was the Lord Dhaneśa, together with the Guhyakas.
Mounting the beautiful Puṣpaka, the one whose vehicle is man (Kubera) departs; and Śakra too, having mounted Airāvaṇa, goes along with the gods.
He followed from behind as the boon-granting Lord whose banner bears the bull was proceeding; to his right were the gods and the Maruts, who fight with diverse weapons.
They go together with the Vasus and are joined by the Rudras; and Yama goes with Mṛtyu, surrounded on all sides.
Accompanied by hundreds of terrible diseases, he proceeds on the left side when provoked; and behind Yama follows a white, three-peaked, and formidable [mountain].
The trident named Vijaya, fashioned by Rudra himself, was seized by the Lord Varuṇa, the master of the waters, who wields a fierce noose. || 20 ||
Surrounded by hundreds of various aquatic monsters, Rudra’s spear (paṭṭiśa) follows behind Vijaya as it moves along.
Surrounded by excellent weapons such as maces, clubs, and spears, O Pārtha, the great Paśupata weapon followed behind the paṭṭiśa.
It has many heads, is most terrible, possesses one foot and many bellies; and behind it is a water-pot, served by hosts of great sages. || 23 ||
To his right shines the Staff, proceeding, enveloped in splendor, accompanied by the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, and honored even by the gods. (24)
Rākṣasas and other gods, Gandharvas and likewise serpents, rivers, streams, oceans, sages, and hosts of Apsarases; || 25 ||
The constellations and the planets, as well as all things mobile and immobile, and the Mothers, followed Mahādeva, overcome by hunger.
And behind them all was the wise Hari, mounted upon Tārkṣya, protecting the entire army while surrounded by his own retinue.
Thus, accompanied by his army, the son of Tryambaka reached the northern bank and stood there, taking refuge behind a copper wall.
Beholding the unsurpassed prosperity of Tārakapura as well, Mahāsena was filled with wonder and praised his ascetic power.
Standing there, Guha shone as he looked on, seated upon his peacock, with a parasol being held over him that possessed a luster equal to the moon itself.
Fanned by two chowries that were like wind and fire, the one of great splendor was surrounded by his mothers, by the gods, and by his own attendants.
Then, having bowed to him, Śakra spoke these words in the midst of the gods: "Behold, behold, O Mahāsena, the strength of the Daityas who are powerful! (32)
But those mortals who do not know you as Time, being as if attached to their homes—for them, let this messenger announce you, the Deliverer (Tāraka). || 33 ||
"O Dhanañjaya, this is indeed appropriate for heroes and brings glory among great men; therefore, with my permission, [give] this devotee of Skanda. 34.
Having instructed me, he dispatched me as a messenger fit for the lord of the Asuras; I myself was desirous of going, and I have also been sent by Śakra. (35)
In the midst of thousands of women in the palace, I spoke: "O lowest of Asuras, you of evil intellect, Śakra speaks to you; listen to that! (36)
O Dānava, whatever sin has been acquired by you through the crushing of the world, I shall be the destroyer of that today, provided you become a man. (37)
"Depart quickly, O most wicked one! If you do not depart, I shall in an instant cast your city into the ocean for the sake of its purification. (38)
Having heard these harsh words, he became enraged; surrounded by a group of women, he raised his fist and rushed at me, and I, being terrified, fled. || 39 ||
Agitated, I reported the events there to the prince; and when I had arrived, the Daitya reflected thus in his mind: (40)
Śakra, having found no refuge, does not deign to speak thus here; moreover, these terrible omens produce terror within me.
Having reflected thus, he rose and ascended to the window situated on the pinnacle of his thousand-storied residence.
He beheld the army of the gods covering both heaven and earth; the ten directions were also made to resound by chariots, elephants, and horses.
With celestial chariots of wondrous form resounding with the songs of kinnaras, and filled with the sounds of drums, cow-horns, cymbals, and conch shells; || 44 ||
Seeing that army as if it were Akṣobhya himself, he then reflected: "These have been conquered by me before; why have they returned once more? (45)
While the Daitya was thus lost in thought, he heard the harsh words, terrible and heart-piercing, uttered by the bards of the gods.

Victory to you, O Lord Kumāra, who illuminates the divine army with your arm whose orb is reddened by the golden glow of the light of your spear; O moon that causes the forest of night-lotuses in the city of Tripura to bloom! Victory to you, O Mahāsena, who are the submarine fire to the great ocean of Diti’s lineage; O Mahāsena, whose sprout-like toenails have crushed the peaks of the crowns of the asuras, and whose sweet voice is like the cry of the peacock! Victory to you, O Skanda, the forest fire to the dry grass of the Tāraka dynasty; O Lord of Yogins, whose lotus feet are adorned by a multitude of claws that dispel the dense darkness of the continuous stream of anxieties spread across the sky of the hearts of yogis! Victory to you, O Child of seven days, who burns away the grief of the succession of worlds!

Homage, homage be to you, the enchanting one; homage be to you, the remover of the fear of the virtuous. Homage be to you, who are immovable even by children; homage again and again—O God, destroy the enemies! 48.
Nārada said: Having heard this hymn of praise resounded by the celestial bards, the Daitya remembered the words of Brahmā regarding the imminent slaughter at the hands of a child. || 1 ||
Having heard this, the king, with his entire body drenched, spoke these words to the doorkeeper: "I wish to see my ministers; bring them here quickly, do not delay."
Then, at the king's command, they approached Kālanemi; the Daitya Tāraka said to them, "What is this deed you have undertaken?"

"Since no news whatsoever arising from the enemy has reached Your Majesty, it is not fitting for you—who are intoxicated by wine and lust—to act as ministers. One is called a minister because he counsels what is beneficial to the king. (4)
