Some perform his propitiation by way of the path of yoga; for that is difficult to accomplish for those who constantly worship the void. (26)
Therefore, he who desires worldly enjoyment and liberation should worship his *liṅga*; at the beginning of creation, he existed in the form of a *liṅga* during my dispute with Brahmā.
We were unable to fully comprehend that [Brahman], within which the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is eternally dissolved. (28)
Therefore, it is proclaimed as the *liṅga* of the wise Rudra by the gods. Whoever bathes the *liṅga* with pure water and with faith, [attains the highest state]. (29)
By him this entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, has been gratified; and the wise man who bathes that Liṅga with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) [attains the same].
By him the entire universe is gratified with nectar, equal to the ancestors; he who worships the Liṅga with flowers produced according to the season [attains this].
By him the entire universe has been fully worshipped; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, the wise man who offers an oblation (naivedya) there before the Liṅga— [attains the same merit]. || 32 ||
By him the entire universe is fed; such is the great fruit of the liṅga. What is the use of much speaking here, whether it be very little or even much? (33)
Whatever is performed for the sake of the Liṅga bestows delight upon the entire universe; and whoever installs that Liṅga in a pure place with true devotion, [attains the highest goal]. || 34 ||
Freed from all sins, he rejoices in the world of Rudra; that which the wise declare to be the fruit of one who constantly performs sacrifices. || 35 ||
And for one who installs that linga of Śiva, it is a mark of auspicious characteristics; just as, O Skanda, fire is proclaimed to be the mouth of all the gods. (36)
In the same way, the Liṅga is undoubtedly the face of all the worlds; by its commencement alone, one is liberated from sins committed even throughout all previous births. (37)
One shall cause a hundred generations of one's family, both past and future, to cross over [to liberation], whether the image be made of clay, fashioned from wood, baked brick, or even stone. (38)
One should give a constructed sanctuary; the fruit increases hundredfold in successive stages. Having placed a water-pot there, one is joined with twenty-one generations of one's lineage. || 39 ||
Until the end of the kalpa, he rejoices in the world of Rudra, happy like Rudra himself; such is the fruit of this kind of linga, and there is nothing superior to it.
Therefore, O Mahāsena, you ought to install a *liṅga* here; for whatever has been spoken here that may be considered indecorous, let it be so. (41)
"O Mahāsena, let Maheśvara himself, who is the witness, speak this. When Govinda spoke thus, a great cry of "Well said! arose.
Then Mahādeva, having embraced Skanda, spoke these words: "Since you are bestowing supreme grace upon my devotees. (43)
Because of that, the highest joy has arisen in me toward you; however, as for what the Blessed One Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, has said: (44)
Indeed, nothing has been spoken here by Viṣṇu that is otherwise than the truth; for he who is "I" should be known as Hari, and he who is Hari is "I. (45)
O observer of noble vows, there is no difference between us two, like that between two lamps; whoever hates him hates me, and whoever follows him follows me. (46)
Thus Skanda understands; he is my devotee, for it is not otherwise.
Skanda said: "O Śaṅkara, it is exactly so; I know both you and Viṣṇu."
And that which Hari, who is fond of dharma, told me regarding the establishment of his linga, the voice in the sky spoke to me exactly the same way long ago concerning the slaying of Tāraka.
"Therefore, I shall install a Liṅga that removes all sins, wherein I have made a single vow for his slaughter. (50)
The second is where an asura, abandoned by living beings and truth, became powerful; the third is where he was slain, which grants the pacification of the sin of killing.
Having spoken thus, the son of Agni summoned Viśvakarman and said: "You ought to fashion three pure lingas quickly."
At the command of Bāhuleya, the divine architect fashioned three pure liṅgas and presented them to him.
Then, together with Brahmā and the others, as well as Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, he first established [the image] not far to the west.
This most beautiful linga is indeed known as Pratijñeśvara; having bathed and fasted here on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra, [one attains the fruit].
"By performing worship and keeping a vigil, one shall be liberated from the sin of harsh speech; thus spoke Maheśvara himself there for the sake of pleasing Skanda. (56)
Then he likewise installed a second liṅga situated in the south-eastern corner, where the Śakti emerged from the lake.
Having praised that Śakti, he installed there the auspicious Linga named Kapāleśvara, which destroys all sins. || 58 ||
In the vicinity of Kapāleśvara is the goddess Kāpālikeśvarī; and there, in the northern direction, they speak of Śakticchidra.
Where the auspicious Pātālagaṅgā, the remover of all sins, is located, there Skanda, overflowing with compassion, bathed and gave [the gift].
Then, accompanied by Tāraka and all the gods, he [approached] the water.
"May this water, accompanied by sesame seeds, be inexhaustible for the great-souled son of Vajrāṅga, a follower of Kāśyapa and a devotee of Rudra. || 62 ||

Then Maheśvara, being pleased, spoke while Skanda listened: "And whatever man here, having bathed and fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Madhu, worships Kapāleśvara and the Goddess," (63)
He is liberated from the sin arising from the destruction of [another's] splendor. || 64 ||

On this very lunar day, when there is the conjunction of Soma, Śiva, and Taitila—the sixfold yoga known as Śakticchidra—one who recites the Rudra mantra at night and bathes here will indeed go to the world of Rudra with his physical body.
In the presence of Kapāleśa, indeed, the Śakticchidra is celebrated; there is no other holy site on earth equal to it.
Having heard these words of Rudra, Skanda became exceedingly pleased; and all the gods were delighted and cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (67).
Nārada said: Then, desiring to perform the installation of the third Liṅga, Brahmā spoke to Guha for his pleasure: "We ourselves shall fashion another."
Although this auspicious linga is free from all defects, nevertheless, I shall create another which is indeed the most excellent of all.
Then Brahmā himself fashioned [the Linga], which was free from all defects, pleasing to the eye, pleasing to the mind, pleasing in its fruit, and possessed of excellent marks.
There, for the sake of Skanda’s delight, all the gods created a most beautiful lake, and they likewise established sacred bathing places (tīrthas) there.
"Those holy fords such as the Gaṅgā and others which the inhabitants of heaven have proclaimed—let everyone dwell here in this lake until that time."

"So be it," they said for the sake of pleasing the one born in the reeds (Kārttikeya). Then Brahmā himself, accompanied by the sons of Gādhi and other Brahmins, gratified the sacrificial fire there with Rudra-mantras.
Then, on the auspicious fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, the twice-born brahmins, having been long liberated from their vows, performed the consecration of the Liṅga.
The lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced; then Skanda, filled with joy, bathed in the beautiful lake.
Having bathed that liṅga with the waters of all the sacred fords, he, filled with devotion, worshipped it with various flowers and the five mantras.
At the time of worship, Hara himself remained there within the center of the liṅga; together with all moving and non-moving beings, he personally accepted the worship.
Then Skanda, overflowing with devotion, honored him and said: "By which offering, and by what gift given to you, what fruit is obtained?"
Śrī Mahādeva said: "He who installs my liṅga and causes a beautiful temple to be built shall dwell in my world for as long as the moon and sun endure. (12)
For as many times as one whitens my abode with lime, for that many births he shall shine with glory. (13)
By giving a banner one becomes like a banner; by means of a pennant, one becomes free from sin; and by arranging a variegated display, one rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
Having performed the purification of the *rajas*, a person is liberated from diseases; and by anointing the temple of the gods, he attains a heart-pleasing body. (15)
Having offered arghya upon the head of Śambhu with flowers, milk, and other substances, along with sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and darbha grass, one shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand years.
By bathing the Liṅga with ghee, one becomes cleansed of sin; by honey, one becomes fortunate; and by curd and milk, one is born free from disease. (17)

By bathing [the image] with water, curd, milk, and so forth, in sequence, one obtains tenfold fruit; having bathed it with devotion for a month, one should then dry it with flour and other such substances.
Having bathed me with the five products of a tawny cow or with the water of the celestial river, and having worshipped me, one attains my world.

Fragrant water is superior to water with kusa grass; from that, water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) is better; and from all sacred fords, the water produced at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean on the new moon day is the best.

The fruit that one obtains by giving a tawny cow is obtained separately in the case of a water-pot; moreover, the fruit increases tenfold respectively when the pot is made of clay, copper, silver, or gold.
Sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, and camphor—each succeeding one being superior to the preceding—having anointed me and himself with these, one shall become illustrious, fortunate, and happy. (22)
Guggulu incense is highly praised, and therefore candana and agaru are excellent; by offering these incenses, a person shall attain happiness and heaven.
The giver of a lamp attains fame as well as supreme vision; by the offering of food, a man becomes an eater of delicacies.
By wearing a double-strand garland of *puṣpa* flowers on the ear, a person obtains twice the fruit [of the pilgrimage] and becomes true to his word. (25)
By filling the Liṅga with unbroken bilva leaves or even with various kinds of flowers, one shall dwell in heaven for a hundred thousand years.
But the man who, with a pure intention, constructs a house of flowers, shall sport for a long time in heaven upon a celestial chariot made of flowers.
By the gift of ornaments and garments, a man becomes a partaker of enjoyments; by the gift of a fine fly-whisk, a man is born as a king. (28)
He who gives a beautiful canopy is not overcome by enemies; having provided song, instrumental music, and dance, he shall go to me purified. (29)
By the gift of a conch and a bell, one becomes learned and possessed of renown; and by performing a chariot procession, one is liberated from sorrows for a long time. (30)
Having performed salutation and prostration, one shall be born into a great family; and by reciting my scripture before me, one becomes a man of wisdom. || 31 ||
By praising me with devotion, a person is liberated from the delusions of the mind; and by removing my floral offerings (nirmālya), one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow.
By waving the ārārtika lamp, one becomes free from distress; by performing the śītalikā rite, one is liberated from the afflictions born of the bodily humors.
Having bowed and given a gift according to one's capacity in the presence of the Liṅga, one obtains a hundredfold fruit and rejoices both in this world and the next.
I forgive fifteen offenses through prostration, twenty through bathing, and a hundred through worship according to the prescribed rite. (35)
O Kumāra, all this that has been described shall come to pass here for those who worship me while I am established as Kumāreśvara. (36)
Just as I, O child, am established as Viśvanātha in Vārāṇasī. || 37 ||
Likewise, I shall remain in the Guptakṣetra, situated in the midst of Kumāreśvara. || 38 ||
Having heard these words from Rudra while the gods were listening, Guha was struck with wonder; he prostrated before him and praised the Lord of Girijā.

Salutations to Śiva, who is free from all affliction; salutations to Śiva, who consists of the mind; salutations to Śiva, who is worshipped by the gods; to you, who are eternally intent on showing compassion to your devotees. || 40 ||

Salutations to you who exist as the source of worldly existence; salutations to you who have destroyed the power of the mind-born god of love. Salutations to you whose great vows are hidden; salutations to you who take refuge in the dense thicket of illusion. || 41 ||
Homage be to Śarva, homage to Śiva; homage be to the Siddha, the Ancient One. Homage be to Kāla, homage to Kalā; homage be to you who transcend both time and its parts.

Homage to you whose body is composed of innate, elemental power; homage to you of immeasurable and great supernatural might! Homage to the one worthy of refuge; homage to the one beyond attributes; homage be to you who follows after formidable virtues! 43.

Salutations to the sovereign of various worlds; salutations to the bestower of the desires of devotees; salutations to the creator who brings forth the fruits of karma; O Blessed One, salutations ever to you, the maker of bliss. 44.

Salutations to you who are of infinite forms, always; salutations to you whose anger is ever irresistible. Homage be to you who are immeasurable; homage be to you whose vehicle is the lord of bulls. || 45 ||

Salutations to the renowned Great Medicine; salutations be to you, the remover of the multitude of diseases. Salutations to the Lord of the moving and the unmoving, the bestower of discernment, to the Youthful Lord, to Śiva. (46)

O Lord of me, Lord of beings, Great Lord, you are the Lord of desire, Lord of speech, Lord of strength, and Lord of intellect; O Lord of anger, Lord of delusion, Lord of the high and the low, salutations to you, the Lord of liberation and the Lord who lies within the cave of the heart.
Having thus praised the boon-granting Lord of Umā, who holds the trident in his hand, the son of Umā prostrated himself and said, "Salutations, salutations! (48).
Having thus long rejoiced in this hymn, which was characterized by devotion and prowess and was worthy of himself, Śiva spoke these words: ||| 49 ||
"You should not contemplate the suffering caused by the killing of my devotee; by this deed, my son, you are praiseworthy even among the sages. (50)
And those who, with supreme devotion, shall praise me with this hymn composed by you in the evening and likewise at dawn—listen to the fruit that belongs to them. (51)
Free from disease, free from poverty, and free from separation from those they love, and having enjoyed pleasures difficult to attain, they shall go to my abode.
Likewise, O dear son, being exceedingly pleased by your devotion, I shall grant you other boons as well, which are most difficult to obtain, for the sake of your satisfaction.
But for those in the Mahīṣāgaraka lineage who shall praise and worship me with offerings on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, all their gifts and acts of worship shall be inexhaustible.
And those men who shall perform their ablutions here in this lake on the full moon day of Vaiśākha will obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 55 ||
Having bathed at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, one should always worship me as Kumāreśa with devotion; for such a person, the recollection of past lives shall arise.

"O son, this is the recollection of past births; in whichever birth one is born, one remembers what ought to be done in this state, which is of the nature of the highest good and very difficult to attain. (57)
O son of Kṛttikā, at whatever time a drought occurs, one should bathe me according to the prescribed rites with various auspicious jars.
For one night, three nights, five nights, or seven, one should bathe [the image] with fragrant water and smear it with saffron.
One should worship with *karavīra* flowers, red blossoms, and likewise with *japā* flowers, adorning [the deity] with garlands of flowers after having put on two crimson garments.
One should feed Brahmins as well as ascetics who observe auspicious vows; one should perform the Lakṣahoma, the Śivahoma, and the rites for the planets and so forth.
Then one should perform the gift of land, and after that, give daily fodder to cows; one should proclaim auspicious peace and indeed cause the recitation of the Rudra-mantra to be performed.
When this very rite is performed by the best of the twice-born, the clouds, having become pregnant, will then rain; of this there is no doubt.
The earth shall be filled with various kinds of grain and lush green pastures; indeed, there shall be health among the people as well as within the community of cowherds.

A king who is endowed with righteousness shall not be oppressed by the armies of enemies; and whatever man here bathes me with ghee during the transit of the sun [into Capricorn], [he shall likewise be protected].

The fruit of giving a daughter in marriage belongs to him; there is no need for deliberation on this point. He who bathes the Lord with milk, as well as with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), [attains that same fruit]. || 66 ||
Indeed, he who gives up his life at the Kumāreśvara Tīrtha obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
One shall dwell in the world of Rudra until the dissolution of all beings—at the solstices, at the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.

On the full moon day, on the new moon day, at the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), and likewise during the Vaidhṛti yoga, a man who bathes at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean [attains great merit]. 69.
Listen to the meritorious fruit for one who worships me with devotion: it shall be the great fruit that comes from bathing at all the sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the surface of the earth. (70)
Whatever fruit may be obtained from all those lingas that have been worshipped, that includes health, the birth of a son, the acquisition of wealth, happiness, and excellent offspring. (71)
A mortal certainly attains his goal by serving Kumāreśvara; for that ascetic who remains here, having become pure and observant of celibacy, [attains success]. (72)
Having attained the supreme Pāśupata yoga, one goes to dissolution in me; and for mortals of sinful nature, I am the immediate bestower of the fruits [of their actions]. (73)
In this place, there is a common treasury of eight divine kinds; and having bathed the exceedingly radiant Liṅga with the five mantras beginning with Aghora, [one should worship]. (74)
One should offer that water to the divine [deity] with the Aghora mantra alone; and having uttered "Drink this," one should drink three handfuls (prasṛti) of it.
If Dharma, Truth, and the Lord exist here in these three worlds, then I shall immediately behold the fruit—whether auspicious or inauspicious—of this ordeal by sacred libation.

If one thinks "I shall go," it destroys the family; if one goes, it destroys the household; if one looks [at her], there is auspiciousness; but if one drinks [the water] with a false intent, it destroys the body. (77)
Within three days, three fortnights, three months, or three years, one experiences the fruit of extremely intense merits and sins according to their measure.
"These boons have been granted here to the Liṅga installed by you; for the sake of increasing your satisfaction, speak further, O son of Umā. (79)
Skanda said: O Maheśvara, I have accomplished my purpose through these boons granted by you; salutations, salutations, salutations to you! O All-pervading Lord, you must not abandon me here.
Having thus prostrated before the God, he bowed to his mother and said: "O Mother, out of a desire for my welfare, you too must not abandon me here. (81)
I shall establish you here as well; O Parvatī, be the bestower of boons.
The illustrious Goddess said: "O son, wherever Śarva dwells by his very nature, there I abide."
"Especially through your devotion, I shall remain here as the bestower of boons upon women; I shall [witness] your deeds in battles and show my grace toward those devoted to Rudra."
The foremost among those with sons behold you, for you have been greatly gratified by them; I consider that only then does the suffering of pregnancy attain fulfillment for a woman. (85)
"O Six-faced One, when your son is proclaimed by the virtuous as a devotee of Rudra with joy, then, for the sake of his pleasure, I shall remain here. (86)
Worshiped by women, she grants good fortune, an excellent husband, and sons; and having bathed in cold water on the third day of the month of Caitra, [one obtains these same rewards].
And those women who, being intent on devotion, shall worship me with flowers, incense, and ointments—to them I shall grant the eightfold prosperity.
Parents, parents-in-law, sons, and a husband [are attained]; as are the wealth of good fortune, saffron, flowers, sandalwood, betel, collyrium, and sugarcane. (89)
The seventh is said to be salt, and the eighth is black cumin; one should weigh them on a scale so that they are measured with a quarter-part added.
If she eats salt after first consuming good ghee, fragrant substances, and auspicious fruits, she shall certainly not become a widow. (91)
Having bathed either in the month of Māgha, Kārttika, or Caitra, she who worships me shall not come into contact with misfortune, sorrow, or poverty.
Having heard these words of Girijā, the son of Pārvatī was filled with joy; he then established the daughter of the mountain and spoke to Kapardin.
O Lord, having first worshipped you with flowers, incense, and sweetmeats, those who worship Kumāreśa—be the remover of their obstacles.
Kapardinī said: "O brother, since this Liṅga has been installed by you, for those men who are devoted to it, there shall be no obstacles from me; my word follows after them. (95)
When this was said, the King of Obstacles (Vighnarāja) understood and established him; therefore, he should always be worshipped, especially on the fourth lunar day.
Having thus established Kumāreśa and having obtained these boons from Śiva, the Six-faced One considered himself to have accomplished all his purposes in his mind.
He remained right there, in part, in the presence of Kumāreśvara. Those who, while on pilgrimage to the Lord, behold Kumāra stationed here— || 98 ||
O Bhārata, their pilgrimage to the Lord becomes fruitful; especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should worship Kārttikeya.
O Pārtha, one shall obtain that same fruit which is gained from a pilgrimage to one's own lord at this confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, which is of such a nature.

Having taken oneself as the object of focus, one who is afflicted by diseases or overcome by ailments should worship the Linga for the sake of well-being, reciting the names one hundred and eight times.
Having recited [this] while pure and observing celibacy for a month, one is liberated from sin; by worshipping this in ancient times, Raji, Rāma, and others were born.
They enjoyed a kingdom with the strength of a hundred [armies] and the world of Rudra; and the son of Jamadagni, having propitiated this Liṅga for ten thousand years, [attained the same].
He obtained the axe with which he uprooted Arjuna’s arms in battle; having recognized the great virtues of that sacred ford, he stood before the God of gods.
The supreme Liṅga known as Rāmeśvara has been established; whoever worships it with devotion goes to the world of Rudra. || 105 ||
Rāma and Kumāreśa will be pleased with him, O Phālguna. Thus, the description of Kumāreśa has been told in brief. (106)
Whoever proclaims the majesty of Kumāreśa in his presence, and those who listen to it daily, shall dwell in the world of Rudra.
Whoever recites this greatness of the Liṅga at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, it becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors; of this there is no doubt. || 108 ||
If one causes a pregnant woman to hear the majesty of this Liṅga, she will give birth to a virtuous son, or else a daughter who is devoted to her husband.
This [narrative] is meritorious, destructive of sin, righteous, and joy-inducing; it bestows the fruit of all desired objects upon those who recite it. (110)
Nārada said: Then Kumāreśa was installed here by Kumāra; thereafter, the gods, having bowed down with their palms joined in reverence, spoke to Guha. || 1 ||
We shall inform you of something; listen to it according to the truth. This is declared to be the ancient, well-established practice of the victorious ones.
Those who conquer their enemies in battle must establish a pillar as a sign; therefore, for the purpose of manifesting your victory, this excellent pillar [is erected].
"We shall not cast it away as long as you deign to permit us; for there is also that third, most excellent *liṅga* fashioned by Viśvakarman. (4)
"O son of Śiva, establish him at the top of that pillar. When the gods had spoken thus, the high-minded Skanda said, "So be it."
Then the hosts of gods, led by Śakra, being delighted, cast down that excellent, brilliant pillar made of Jāmbūnada gold upon the field of battle.
All around that sacrificial ground, in every direction, were those made of all kinds of jewels; there, ten groups of beautiful Apsarases danced joyfully.
The delighted Mothers sang auspicious songs for Skanda; Indra and the other gods danced there, while Viṣṇu himself was the musician.
Showers of flowers fell from the sky and celestial instruments resounded; thus, having erected the pillar named Jaya, he who delights the universe [performed the rite].
Then the god Stambheśvara was installed by the son of the Three-eyed One (Skanda), together with the gods headed by Viriñci (Brahmā), who were filled with joy at that time.
By those [gods] beginning with Hari, Hara, and Āditya, as well as by the hosts of sages including Indra, [the ground] was pierced by the tip of the spear of that Great-Souled One in its western part.
A well was constructed there by Guha, from the bottom of which the Gaṅgā emerges; on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, one should perform the libation for the ancestors.
O son of Pāṇḍu, a man who performs a bath in the well with devotion clearly obtains that same fruit which is the merit of a Śrāddha performed at Gayā. || 13 ||
Then one should worship the god Stambheśvara with fragrances and flowers; having obtained the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice, he rejoices in the abodes of Rudra.
On the full moon or the new moon day, at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, he who is free from sin should perform a śrāddha ceremony and worship Staṃbheśvara.
His ancestors are satisfied, and being satisfied, they bestow their blessings; having shattered all his sins, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lord Rudra in ancient times for the pleasure of Skanda; in this very manner, the fourth and most excellent Liṅga was established. || 17 ||
All the deities prostrated and cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! || 18 ||
Nārada said: Having thus seen those lingas upon the earth by the son of Hara, the gods, headed by Hari, Brahmā, and Indra, spoke to one another.
Oh, how blessed is this prince at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, by whom these four lingas have been established in this most difficult place to attain! (2)
We too, for the sake of purification, for the gratification of Skanda and Rudra, and for the sake of spiritual practice and the attainment of the Self, shall establish a succession of lingas here.
Or else, even if millions of gods and sages, beyond all counting, were to establish lingas here on this shore of the earth; || 4 ||
The worship of these [deities] is prescribed here because of their great number; yet, in whose kingdom Rudra’s liṅga is not worshipped according to one's ability, [that kingdom suffers].
His kingdom will perish through famine, disease, and thieves; therefore, we shall unite and establish a single auspicious Liṅga.
Having thus formed this resolution and obtained permission from Maheśvara, all the gods, headed by Hari and Brahmā, were filled with great joy and affection.
Then, having observed an auspicious spot in a secluded place, they themselves installed an excellent linga fashioned by Brahmā himself.
Because it was consecrated by the Siddhas and by the gods themselves, beginning with Brahmā, Guha indeed gave the name "Siddheśvara" to that Liṅga.
There, an excellent lake was excavated by all the gods at that linga, and it was filled with the pure waters of all sacred fords by those high-souled ones.
In the meantime, O Pārtha, the son of Śeṣa named Kumuda arrived from Pātāla and spoke to the serpents and nāgas of Śeṣa’s lineage.
In this battle with Tāraka, however, a sinful Dānava named Pralamba fled out of fear of Skanda and entered the netherworld (Pātāla).
"O lords of the nāgas, he destroys your wealth, sons, wives, daughters, and homes; run, run quickly! (13)
Having heard those words of Kumada, the son of Śeṣa, the lords of the nāgas became filled with eagerness, saying, "Let us go, let us go! (14)
Having warded them off, Skanda then became enraged and took up his spear; he then discharged it toward Pātāla, saying, "Let the Daitya be slain! (15)
Then the spear, released from Skanda’s arm, suddenly pierced the earth with great force and entered it, just as destiny strikes down a man.
Having slain that Pralamba and his ten billion followers, she gladdened the Nāgas and departed, preceded by the sound of water-drops.
O Pārtha, the cavity that was created in the earth by her as she departed with all her power has been filled by the waters of the Pātālagaṅgā, which destroy all sins.
Skanda gave him a name, which is remembered as Siddhakūpa; on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days of the dark fortnight, a man himself should observe a fast.
Having bathed in the well, one who worships Lord Siddheśvara with undivided mind—his sins accumulated through abundant worldly existence are dissolved.
And the wise man who, having bathed in Siddhakuṇḍa, performs the Śrāddha rite, becomes liberated from all taints and fit for devotion in birth after birth.
Even as he was cutting it down, Rudra, being pleased with him, granted a boon: "O Prayāga, this [tree] is equal to the Vaṭa; this is the truth, there is no doubt. (22)
Having come here, O illustrious one, one should perform the śrāddha with great devotion; that offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for all the ancestors shall be inexhaustible.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā and accompanied by Skanda, prayed to the sovereign Mahāśakti, the perfected Ambikā.
For it was Janārdana, the Blessed One in the form of a fish, possessed by you, who performed many deeds for the sake of rescuing the world. || 25 ||
Thus they entreated her: "O auspicious one, you must not abandon this place; all these mighty guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas) are stationed here."
O auspicious one, those who worship you with offerings and flowers on the eighth or the fourteenth day shall always be protected by you in all calamities.
Thus addressed, Siddhamātā agreed, saying "So be it. Then they established her to the north of the Liṅga.
Then the gods, the lords of the fields, themselves installed the sixty-four Maheśvaras for the protection of the sacred field, under the name Siddheya.
And those who shall always worship you at the commencement of their undertakings, especially every year with an offering of rājamāṣa beans; || 30 ||
Being pleased, he protects them just as a father protects his own children; the gods who grant success are there, along with Siddhivināyaka.
Having entreated the son of Kapardin, they joyfully installed him; and those who always worship him here at the commencement of their undertakings [attain success].
This powerful Bhavodbhava, the Lord of Obstacles, grants them success if anyone here constantly worships the group of seven Siddhas.

Whether one beholds or even remembers them, one is liberated from all defects. Siddheśvara, Siddhavaṭa, the manifest Siddhāmbikā, Siddhavināyaka, Siddheya Kṣetrādhipati, Siddhasaras, and Siddhakūpa—these are the seven.
Being pleased here at Siddhakūpaka on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, Rudra granted boons difficult even for the gods to obtain.

Having bathed and offered rice-balls at the banyan tree, one who worships me becomes a possessor of perfection; likewise, he who always honors me while remaining a celibate student with his senses subdued [attains the same].
The eight desired accomplishments shall always be his; for that man who performs the recitation of mantras, the offering of oblations, and the fire-sacrifice here [in this place]. (37)
Becoming pure and single-minded, he shall attain his desired perfection; furthermore, he whose mind is composed and who beholds the Lord of Siddhis [shall likewise succeed]. (38)
Success will surely come to him unless he is struck down by obstacles, for the great goddess Siddhāmbikā is indeed present here.
Those who recite this great vidyā—which bestows success upon the foremost of practitioners—should do so for those who are steadfast, celibate, and possessed of truthful minds. (40)
Through the recitation of mantras, she bestows all desired perfections (siddhis). And this great cavern of Pātāla was created by the power of Guha.
By the grace of Siddhāmbikā, there shall be the direct manifestation of both Vighneśvara and Kṣetrapāla before me, where many various wonders will abound.
O gods, here millions of men shall attain perfection—attaining the state of Vidyādharas, the state of deities, the state of Gandharvas, and the state of Nāgas. (43)
And here, by the power of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) known as Vijaya, practitioners shall attain the state of yakṣas and the state of immortals. 44.

Having propitiated Siddhāmbikā, one shall attain a success that is difficult to obtain. Whoever shall behold me stationed here, or whoever shall worship me—even by the mere mention of my name—there shall be the acquisition of merit. (45)
Nārada said: O best of gods, even though the boons had been granted in this manner by Tryambaka, [the gods remained concerned].
They became overjoyed and then sang this verse: "We have been gratified by him through sacrifices, recitations, hymns of praise, and austerities. (47)
"Whatever man shall worship the Siddhi-liṅga, all his desires shall be fulfilled"—thus spoke Śaṅkara. (48)
Having spoken thus, those gods, together with Skanda, attained victory; and they caused beautiful palaces to be constructed, adorned with lovely things produced from the Tāraka.
Having bestowed the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life upon that sacred field, they departed; some praising Skanda, others the Tīrtha, and others Hari. (50)
Some went to heaven even with their five limbs, while others went after the battle; then, having embraced Mahāsena in the intermediate space, Hara spoke.
O dear son, he shall always reside in the seventh wind-sphere; indeed, O son, you must always consult me regarding all matters to be done.
"By beholding me and through devotion, you shall attain the highest welfare; I shall dwell at Stambhatīrtha and shall never depart from it. (53)
Having spoken thus, Maheśvara embraced him and dismissed him; he was likewise honored with devotion by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others.
Having been dismissed, the gods went to their respective abodes; Śarva went to Kailāsa, and Guha indeed to the seventh world, Skaṃdha.
Thus, O Pārtha, has this account of the origin of the five Liṅgas been told; the high-minded mortal who recites this story connected with Skanda [attains the highest goal]. (56)
Whether he hears it or causes others to hear it, that man shall be renowned; he shall be long-lived, fortunate, prosperous, radiant, and of auspicious appearance. (57)
Fearless toward all living beings and free from all suffering, that man who has become pure in the presence of Kumāreśvara—58.
One who hears the life-story of Skanda shall become a great lord of wealth; [this applies especially to] children afflicted by disease and those who serve at the gates of kings. (59)
This is that supreme, most auspicious [teaching], which always removes all defects; upon the dissolution of the body, a person shall attain union with the Six-faced One.
Then the gods gave this boon to Skanda and departed for heaven.
The venerable Nārada said: Now, O Arjuna, I shall describe to you the majesty of the Barbarī Tīrtha, and how the princess Śataśṛṅgā became Barbarikā.
Renowned as Kumārikā, this section called the Kaumārikākhaṇḍa is proclaimed by her name; it bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
By her the arrangement of various villages and other settlements was made upon the earth, and by her this land of Bharata was properly fashioned.
Dhanañjaya said: "O Sage, this is a great wonder to me and most excellent to hear; tell me the entire life-story of the maiden in full detail. (4)
How was this entire universe born, fashioned by karma and the various classes of beings? And how is the land of Bhārata? I wish to hear this always.
Nārada said: In this unmanifest and lightless realm, both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, unborn and united as one, we hear of them as being absolute.
Then, impelled by both its own nature and time through their respective forms, the principle of Mahat was born from Prakṛti by the mere act of her looking.
From the principle of Mahat, undergoing transformation, the principle of Ahaṃkāra was born; that is declared by the sages to be threefold: Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa.

The wise know that from the *tāmasa* [aspect] the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are born; and from the subtle elements, the five specific gross elements (*bhūtas*), which arise from them, are produced.
From the *sāttvika* ego, they know the ten organs of action and the mind as the eleventh to arise; and they consider both [the group of senses and the mind] to be *rājasa*.
The wise of old understood that twenty-four principles (tattvas) had come into being; indeed, O Bhārata, they were perceived by Sadāśiva and by the Puruṣa.
They attained the form of bubbles, and from that, the auspicious cosmic egg (aṇḍa) was born; this is called the Brahmāṇḍa, measuring a hundred koṭis [in extent].
Brahmā was declared to be his self; he divided this [universe] into three parts: the gods are situated there above, and humans in the middle. (13)
The Nāgas and Daityas are in Pātāla; this [region] is conceived as threefold, and each one of these is further divided sevenfold by him.
There are seven netherworlds, seven islands, and seven heavenly realms. I shall describe the seven islands; listen to their arrangement. (15)
Jambūdvīpa is proclaimed to have an extent of one hundred thousand yojanas; it is shaped like the orb of the sun and is surrounded by the salt ocean of equal size.
Beyond that is Śākadvīpa, twice the size of Jambūdvīpa, surrounded by an ocean of milk of the same extent. || 17 ||
Indeed, the ocean of wine, which causes delusion for the Daityas, surrounds the continent of Puṣkara, which is twice as large as that [preceding one]. || 18 ||
Beyond that, Kuśadvīpa is known to be twice its size; it is surrounded on all sides by an ocean of curd-water of equal extent. (19)
Beyond that is the island named Krauñca, which is indeed twice the size of the ocean of ghee; beyond that is Śālmalidvīpa, which is twice as large as that very [island].
Surrounded by an ocean consisting of the essence of sugarcane juice, Gomeda [is situated]; it is twice as large as that [ocean] and is encircled by it.
Surrounded on all sides by the ocean of delightful sweet water, O Pārtha, it measures thus: two crores and fifty-three lakhs.
And fifty thousand [yojanas] are the seven continents together with the oceans; and there are exactly five hundred and ten finger-breadths [of the earth's thickness]. || 23 ||
The increase and decrease of the waters is observed during the bright and dark fortnights; beyond that, O best of the Kurus, is the golden land extending for one hundred million [yojanas].
Beyond that is Lokāloka, the sporting place of the gods; it is a mountain in the shape of a ring, ten thousand yojanas in extent.
Outside of this is a terrible darkness, difficult to behold and devoid of living beings; it is recorded as being thirty-five crores and nineteen lakhs [in extent]. (26)
O Phālguna, it measures forty thousand yojanas; immediately beyond that is the Garbhoda ocean, equal in extent to the seven oceans.
The shell is established with an extent of ten million yojanas; the egg of Brahmā is joined with that shell at the center of Mount Meru.
Fifty crores [of yojanas] are to be known as extending everywhere in the ten directions; in the center of Jambūdvīpa, however, there is a mountain named Meru. (29)
It should be known as being one hundred thousand *yojanas* in measurement from bottom to top; it is situated at a depth of sixteen thousand *yojanas*.
Its height is eighty-four [yojanas], and it is thirty-two [yojanas] wide at the summit; it is endowed with three peaks and has a top shaped like a shallow bowl. || 31 ||
In the middle peak is the abode of Brahmā, and in the northeast that of Tryambaka; in the southwest is the abode of Vāsudeva, and the golden peak belongs to Brahmā.
The mountain of Śaṅkara is made of jewels, and that of Keśava is made of silver; these are known as the supporting mountains (viṣkaṃbha) situated in the four directions of Meru.
To the east is Mandara by name, to the south is Gandhamādana; Vipula is to be known as being in the west, and Supārśva likewise in the north.
The Kadamba is to be known on Mandara, the Jambu on Gandhamādana; the Aśvattha is on Vipula, and the Vaṭa is considered to be on Supārśva.
There are four mountains with peaks like banners, each measuring eleven hundred [yojanas]; upon their victorious summits are four forests. (36)
To the east is the grove named Caitraratha, to the south Gandhamādana, Vaibhrāja is to be known in the west, and Citraratha forest is in the north.
Now learn from me concerning the four lakes situated in the four directions: the one named Aruṇoda is in the east, while Lake Mānasa is in the south. (38)
Pratyakśīta and Udakanāman are the names of the great lakes in the north; these supporting mountains are indeed twenty-five yojanas in height. (39)
It is recorded that its mass measures one thousand thousand yojanas; furthermore, there are indeed many other Kesara mountains there as well.
And to the south of Meru, there are three boundary mountains; those three are Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat.
Each is one hundred thousand yojanas in length and two thousand in width; and to the north of Meru are three mountains: Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān.
Mālyavat is to the east of Meru, and likewise Gandhamādana is to the west; thus these mountains are said to surround Jambudvīpa on all sides.
The fruits of the Jambū tree, which stands on Mount Gandhamādana and is as large as a great elephant, are known by its name as Jambūdvīpa.
There was a first Prajāpati named Manu Svāyambhuva; there was a woman named Śatarūpā whom that Prajāpati married. He had two sons, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda.
And Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, who was supremely righteous, having propitiated Viṣṇu through devotion, attained an imperishable station.
Ten sons were born to the royal sage Priyavrata; among them, three renounced the world and took refuge in the Supreme Brahman.
Seven sons were established by him in the seven islands; the eldest, the lord of Jambūdvīpa, was renowned as Āgnīdhra. (48)
O Pārtha, he had nine sons who are remembered as the lords of the nine regions (Varṣas); even today, those regions remain marked by their names. || 49 ||
Each of the fourteen regions of Meru, situated between the two mountains Gandhamādana and Mālyavān, is recorded as being nine thousand yojanas in extent.
In the interior, that which stands upon the golden land is here called Ilāvṛta; that which extends from Mālyavat to the ocean is called Bhadrāśva.
That which extends as far as the ocean of Gandhavat is known as Ketumāla.
Within the ocean of Śṛṅgavat lies the region known as Kurukhaṇḍa; and between Śṛṅgavat and Śveta, the region is declared to be Hiraṇmaya.
Between Sunīla and Śveta, they call the region Ramyaka; and between Niṣadha and Hemakūṭa lies the region of Hari.
The region between the Himavat and the Himakūṭa mountains is known as Kimpuruṣa; the region between the Himādri and the ocean is known as Nābhi-khaṇḍa.
The region of Nābhikhaṇḍa and the two Kurus are bow-shaped; the Himavat and Śṛṅgin mountains are proclaimed to be in the position of the bowstring.
The son of Nābhi was Ṛṣabha, and from Ṛṣabha, Bharata was born; after his name, this region is celebrated as Bhārata. (57)
Here, O descendant of Kuru, one may acquire dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; elsewhere, there is only the land of worldly enjoyment, yet [these goals] exist everywhere.
In Śākadvīpa there is a Śāka tree measuring one thousand yojanas; after its name, that region is known as Śākadvīpa.
And his sovereign was Priyavrata himself, known by the name Medhātithi. || 60 ||
Its seven regions are named after his sons: Purojava, Manojava, Vepamāna, Dhūmrānīka, Citrarepha, Bahurūpa, and Viśvacāra. || 61 ||
And in Śākadvīpa, those named Ṛtavrata, Satyavrata, and Anuvrata perform the worship of the Blessed One according to the Vāyavya ritual and recite his name.
May the Inner Controller, the Lord, under whose power the universe stands, who having entered within divides all beings by means of his own manifestations, directly protect us. 63.
Thus ends the recitation. In Kuśadvīpa there is a clump of Kuśa grass a thousand yojanas in extent; because it is marked by that as its sign, it is therefore known as Kuśadvīpa. (64)

And the lord of that island is Hiraṇyaroman, the son of Praiyavrata; its seven regions are named after his sons—Vasu, Vasudāna, Dṛḍha, Kavi, Nābhigupta, Satyavrata, and Vāmadeva. And the castes, known as Kuliśa, Kovidābhiyukta, and Kulaka, praise the blessed Jātavedas.
O Jātavedas, you are the direct bearer of oblations to the Supreme Brahman; through sacrifice, worship the Puruṣa who is the limbs of the gods and of the Puruṣa himself.
Thus ends the praise. In Krauñcadvīpa there is a mountain named Krauñca, extending for many yojanas; that very mountain which was pierced by Guha is the defining mark of Krauñcadvīpa.
And there, the son of Priyavrata named Ghṛtapṛṣṭha [ruled] over seven regions marked by the names of his seven sons: Amadurūha, Meghapṛṣṭha, Svadāman, Ṛtāśva, Lohitārṇava, and Vanaspati. || 68 ||
And the [four] castes are known by the names Guru, Ṛṣabha, Draviṇa, and Devaka. || 69 ||
They praise the Blessed One as consisting of water. || 70 ||

The waters, possessing the potency of Puruṣa, and the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—purifying, may they, together with those [worlds] that destroy disease, touch me, the earth, with their own selves.
Thus ends the recitation. There, the dwelling of the tree named Śālmali extends for a thousand yojanas; that sign is called the Śālmali-dvīpa.
Its sovereign was Praiyavrata Yajñabāhu; his sons—named Surocana, Saumanasya, Ramaṇaka, Devabarhiṣ, Pāribhadra, Āpyāyana, and Abhijñāna—inhabited the seven regions [of that continent].
And the castes named Śrutadhara, Vīryavasuṃdhara, and Eṣaṃdhara worship the Blessed One Soma. || 74 ||
May Soma, who distributes his own essence to the ancestors and the gods during the bright and dark fortnights, be our king over all subjects below. 75.
Thus is the recitation. There is a beautiful Plakṣa tree named Gomeda; because joy increased through its shade due to greed, it is called the island of Gomeda. (76)
There, the son of Priyavrata was Idhmajihva; his sons were named Śiva, Suramya, Subhadra, Śānti, Aśapta, Mṛta, and Abhaya, and these were the names of the seven regions. || 77 ||
And the four castes, known as Haṃsa, Pataṅga, Urdhvāñcana, and Satyāṅga, worship the Blessed Sun.
Having offered salutations to that form of Viṣṇu which arises from Brahmā and the immortal, we meditate upon the Sun as our own Self, who is also death. 79.
Thus ends the recitation. A hundred million golden leaves extend for a thousand yojanas; the lotus shines brilliantly, and that is the sign of the island of Puṣkara.
Its sovereign was named Vītahotra, a descendant of Priyavrata; his two sons were Ramaṇaka and Ghātaka.
That [text] consists of two sections marked by their respective names. || 82 ||
Between those two is the mountain named Mānasācala, which is circular in shape, upon which the blessed Sun-god revolves. || 83 ||
There, no castes exist; they are all equal and meditate upon Brahman. || 84 ||
Salutations to that Blessed One, who is non-dual and absolute, yet whom people worship as the Brahman-liṅga through various ritual forms consisting of action, perceiving Him as distinct.

Thus is the recitation. Among these, there is neither anger nor envy, nor is there the accumulation of merit or sin; their lifespan is proclaimed to be ten thousand and twenty thousand years respectively. (86)
Chanting prayers and accompanied by their beloveds, they sport like the immortals. Now, I shall describe to you the arrangement of the higher worlds.
Nārada said: O descendant of Kuru, the solar disc is one hundred thousand yojanas from the earth; the chariot of the sun consists of nine thousand yojanas.
The pole of his chariot is proclaimed to be twice that length; for Vivasvat, it is one and a half crores and seven hundred thousand [yojanas].
Its axle measures a yojana, and upon it the wheel is established; that wheel is proclaimed to have three naves, five spokes, and six rims.
O Pāṇḍava, the second axle of the chariot was also forty-five thousand [yojanas] in width.
The axle is the measure for both; it is equal to half the length of that yoke. The short axle and half of that yoke indeed constitute the support of the chariot's pole.
Likewise, the second axle is on the left, and that wheel is situated in his mind; the seven horses are the Vedic meters—listen to their names from me.
The Gāyatrī, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇih, Jagatī, Triṣṭubh, Anuṣṭubh, and Paṅkti—these are said to be the meters (chandas) that serve as the bay horses of the Sun.
There is neither setting nor rising for the sun, which exists at all times; for what are called "rising" and "setting" are merely the visibility and invisibility of the sun.
Abiding in the city of Śakra and others, he touches the three cities; thus, being scattered and situated in Vikarṇa, he likewise resides in the half-city of Trikoṇa.
At the beginning of the northern solstice, the Sun enters Capricorn; from there he proceeds to Aquarius and Pisces, moving thus from one zodiac sign to another.
Then, when these three have been traversed, the sun proceeds toward the equinoctial course (vaiṣuvatī gati), making day and night equal.
Then the night comes to an end and the day increases day by day; thereafter, at the conclusion of the sign of Gemini, it reaches its ultimate limit.
Upon reaching the zodiac sign of Cancer, it begins its southern course; just as the rim of a potter's wheel turns rapidly, so does it move swiftly.
In its southward course, the sun likewise returns quickly, moving with extreme velocity through time by the power of the path of the wind.
Therefore, he traverses the highest stage in a short time, just as one situated in the middle of a potter's wheel moves slowly when it has slowed down. || 15 ||
Likewise, during the northern course, the sun moves with slow velocity; therefore, it traverses the earth over a long period of time. || 16 ||
And at the time of twilight, O Phālguna, the Mandeha demons desire to devour the sun; such is the curse imposed upon those Rākṣasas by Prajāpati.
The bodies [of the demons] became indestructible, yet they died day after day; consequently, a most terrible battle ensued between them and the Sun.
Then, O twice-born ones, those sins are always consumed by that water which the twice-born sprinkle, purified by the Gāyatrī, through the performance of the Sandhyā worship.
Those ungrateful ones who do not even perform the twilight worship go to the Raurava hell; every month, the Sun is separately [attacked] by sages, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas.
Then he proceeds with seven Apsarases, Grāmaṇīs, and Serpents; namely Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Vivasvat, and Indra.
Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Bhaga, and Tvaṣṭṛ are also proclaimed; Viṣṇu and the others are remembered as the twelve Ādityas in the months beginning with Caitra. || 22 ||
From the position of Divākara (the Sun), the mandala of Śaśin (the Moon) is situated at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas]; its chariot is also said to have three wheels.
And ten horses, white as kunda flowers, are yoked to the left and right; and it is at a full hundred thousand yojanas from the moon.
The entire circle of constellations shines above, as do fourteen arbudas and eighty [yojanas] of the lord of rivers.
Twenty crores of constellations are likewise proclaimed; and two hundred thousand [yojanas] beyond that constellation-mandala is the position of Mercury.
And the chariot of the son of the Moon (Budha) was composed of the substances wind and fire, drawn by eight tawny horses possessing the speed of the wind.
Two hundred thousand yojanas further from that Budha, Uśanas is said to reside; the chariot of Śukra was likewise equipped with eight horses born of supernatural origin.
The priest of the gods is remembered as being two hundred thousand [yojanas] from the earth; his golden chariot is yoked with eight pale-white horses.
Situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] above Bṛhaspati is the chariot of Sauri (Saturn), which is drawn by eight dappled horses born of the ether.
The eight horses of Svarbhānu, which have the luster of bees, carry his grey chariot; yoked once, they likewise remain positioned below the Sun.
One hundred thousand [yojanas] above that is said to be the constellation of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣimaṇḍala), and one hundred thousand yojanas further above the sages, Dhruva is situated.
Dhruva is indeed the central pivot of the entire circle of luminaries; Dhruva, in turn, is situated upon the support of the tail of the Śiṃśumāra.
O Phālguna, that which they call the imperishable self, the form of Vāsudeva, is all this bound by the ropes of wind within the eternal.
The orb of the sun is known to be nine thousand yojanas; the orb of the moon is known to be twice the extent of the sun.
But Rahu, becoming equal to those two, moves below them, having raised up the shadow of the earth in the form of a spotless orb.
The son of Bhṛgu (Venus) is ordained as being one-sixteenth part of the Moon; and Jupiter is to be known as being one-quarter less than the son of Bhṛgu.
Venus and Saturn have feet less than Bṛhaspati; likewise Mercury has five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, two hundred, and one hundred yojanas [respectively]. (38)
The stars have a measurement of half a *yojana*, and none are smaller than that. The terrestrial world (*bhūloka*) is proclaimed to be accessible on foot. (39)
The space between the earth and the sun is proclaimed as Bhuvarloka; the distance between the Pole Star (Dhruva) and the sun is fourteen hundred thousand [yojanas].
That too is declared by those who contemplate the structure of the worlds to be Svarloka; likewise, Maharloka is proclaimed to be Koṭacir, situated above Dhruva.
Two crores of people who possess the four types of sustenance dwell there; beyond that, Tapoloka is said to consist of four crores.
Where those gods, free from burning heat, abide as the Vairājas; the Satyaloka shines forth, sixfold in extent beyond the Tapoloka.
Where there is no returning again, that indeed is remembered as the Brahma-world; it consists of eighteen crores, and eighty-five lakhs [of yojanas]. (44)
Above that, a beautiful and incomparable realm shines forth; this triad of worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar is indeed created. (45)
Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—these three are known as the uncreated; between the created and the uncreated is what is remembered as Maharloka. (46)
It becomes empty at the end of the kalpa, yet it does not utterly perish; these seven worlds are thus described as acquired through meritorious deeds.

Through sacrifices, gifts, recitations, burnt offerings, pilgrimages, and the performance of various vows—as well as other means proclaimed in the Vedas and elsewhere—they know these worlds to be attainable. (48)
Then, from the head of Aṇḍa, a auspicious stream of water flowed forth; having inundated all the worlds, it reached Mount Meru as the Gaṅgā.
Then she entered the entire surface of the earth and the netherworld; the Goddess, who dwells eternally at the gate, remained stationed upon the summit of the cosmic egg.
Surrounded by tens of millions upon tens of millions of goddesses and by Piṅgala, that auspicious one, stationed there, always provides protection for the cosmic egg.
Possessing great strength and prowess, he destroys the hosts of the wicked, just as one might hear the seven layers of the wind-elements even as they remain present.
Having traversed the earth, he stands established in the circle of clouds; he is the exceedingly powerful one named Pravaha, who causes the clouds to flow.
O descendant of Bharata, clouds born of smoke, fire, and heat, as well as those filled by the ocean, become dark-bodied and most abundant with water.
The second is named Āvaha, which is fixed to the solar disc; bound by that [pole star] Dhruva, this solar disc is made to revolve.
The third is named Udvaha, situated upon the shoulder of Candra; by it, this lunar orb is bound to Dhruva and made to revolve.
The fourth, named Saṃvaha, situated within the circle of the constellations, is bound by the rays of wind and revolves together with Dhruva.
Among the planets, that fifth wind is named Vivaha; by it this wheel of planets, fixed to Dhruva, is caused to revolve.
The sixth wind, named Parivaha, is situated within the circle of the Seven Sages; it is by means of this that the Seven Sages revolve in the sky, bound to Dhruva.
And the seventh wind, named Parāvaha, is fixed to the Dhruva; by it, O Bhārata, the Dhruva-wheel and the other [wheels] are established.
Having encountered him with great speed, the ten thousand sons of the progenitor Dakṣa reached the ends of the quarters.
Thus these sons of Diti, established in groups of seven, wander about without resting; they go everywhere and sustain all things.
Above Dhruva is that which is without sun, without lunar mansions, and without stars; for those [beings] are eternally presided over by their own splendor and their own power.
Thus the regions above have been fully described to you; now hear from me concerning the netherworlds (pātālas).
Nārada said: At a height of seventy thousand [yojanas], there are the Pātālas situated one above the other: Aṭala, Vitala, Nitala, and Rasātala.
Talātala, Sutala, and Pātāla as the seventh; they are black, white, reddish, yellow, sandy, rocky, and golden respectively.
O Kauravya, those grounds were adorned with excellent palaces; there, thousands of Dānavas, Daityas, and Nāgas resided.
I have seen many places even more delightful than the world of the gods, where various jewels provide delight to the serpents.
In Pātāla, who would not feel delight—even one who is liberated—amidst the daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas, who possess such magnificent forms? || 5 ||
Where there is neither heat nor cold, neither rain nor even suffering, and where the time for great enjoyment of various foods and edibles arises; (6)
O Pārtha, in the seventh netherworld (Pātāla) there is the Śrī Hāṭakeśvara Liṅga, established by Brahmā and rising a thousand yojanas high.
The temple of the Liṅga made of gold is ten thousand yojanas in extent; it is divine, composed of all kinds of jewels, and adorned with various wonders.
That is the noble sign, O best of various lords of serpents; beneath that is abundant water, and below that, the hells are said to be located.
O high-minded one, hear now of those places where sinners are cast down: fifty-five crores and twenty-one kings.
Raurava, Śūkara, Rodha, Tāla, as well as Viśasana, Mahājvāla, Taptakumbha, Lavaṇa, and Vimohaka. || 11 ||
Rudhirāndha, Vaitaraṇī, Kṛmiśa, Kṛmibhojana, Asipatravana, Kṛṣṇa, Lālābhakṣya, and Dāruma.
Likewise, there are Pūyavaha, the sinful Vahnijvāla, Adhaḥśiras, Sandaṃśa, Kṛṣṇasūtra, Tamas, and Avīci.
The one who feeds dogs goes to Viśūci, and another to Avīci; the false witness goes to Raurava, and the one who obstructs cows or Brahmins goes to Rodha.

The drinker of spirituous liquor goes to the Sūkara hell; the liar and the murderer of a human being go to the Tāla hell; the violator of the Guru’s bed goes to the Taptakumbha hell; and the stealer of food goes to the Taptaloha hell.
One who insults his gurus is cast into Mahājvāla; one who destroys the scriptures is cast into Lavaṇa; and one who is lawless and deludes others is cast into Vimohaka.
In Kṛmibhakṣya one becomes a hater of the gods; in Kṛmiśa, one performs ill-sacrifices; and in Lālābhakṣya, one eats before offering to the ancestors and gods, and there he goes.

One who opposes right livelihood is reborn in Viśasana; one who manufactures false weapons is reborn in Adhomukha; one who holds wrong views is reborn in Asadgrāhin; and one who eats alone is reborn in Pūyavāhaka. (18)
One who rears cats, cocks, dogs, and birds, and one who sets fire to the ears of the deaf, the eyes of the blind, houses, fields, grass, grain, and so forth, goes [to hell]. (19)
The man who lives by the stars and the stage goes to the Vaitaraṇī river; he who, intoxicated by wealth and youth, seizes the property of others, goes to Kṛṣṇa.
The one who cuts down trees goes to the Forest of Sword-leaves for no purpose; all those who live by deceit fall into the Blazing Fire.
One who approaches another's wife or another's food falls into the *saṃdaṃśa* hell; so too do those who are intent on sleeping by day and those who are intent on violating their vows.
Those intoxicated by pride in their bodies go to the state of being food for dogs; those who do not regard Śiva and Hari as one go only to the Avīci hell.
Through such sins as these, by following a flood of unscriptural practices, they fall indeed by the thousands into most terrible hells. (24)
Therefore, the wise man who desires liberation from these [sins] should worship both gods, Hari and Hara, by way of the path of sacred revelation (śruti). 25.
Situated below the hells is the one known as Kālāgni; below that is Haṭṭaka, and below that Ananta is traditionally taught to reside.
He for whom this entire universe appears like a mustard seed upon the tip of his head is celebrated as Ananta because of his infinite power. || 27 ||
The elephants of the quarters there are Padma, Kumuda, Añjana, and Vāmana; beneath that is the shell of the cosmic egg (aṇḍakaṭāha), and Ekavīrā is also located there.
Four hundred and ninety thousand; by this very measure, the water is likewise recorded. (29)
Below that are ten million hells, and below that, twenty million, is the great fire; forty thousand yojanas beneath that is said to be darkness.
There were forty-four crores, and beyond that, eighty-nine lakhs and eighty thousand. (31)
Below that is another eggshell measuring ten million [yojanas], and there too is the goddess Kapālīśā, joined with him who holds a staff in his hand.
There, the Protectress is surrounded by tens of millions upon tens of millions of goddesses; she is the consuming fire impelled by the breath of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
It is indeed Kālāgni who impels [all] so that at the end of the kalpa the world is consumed; such is the lower thread (adhassūtra) fashioned here, O Bhārata.
Listen to me regarding those guardians of the central meridian and the basin: Vasudhāmā is stationed in the east, and Śaṅkhapāla in the south.
Takṣakeśa is situated in the west, and Ketumān in the north; Harasiddhi, Suparṇākṣī, Bhāskarā, and Yoganaṃdinī [are also there].
A goddess joined with ten million times ten million goddesses protects this; thus was this great wonder, the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), established by them.
I constantly bow to those—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; the world of Viṣṇu and the world of Rudra are proclaimed to be outside of this.
Even Brahmā is not able to describe it, much less those such as ourselves; it is there that those who have attained liberation and those devoted to Hari and Hara go eternally. (39)
Indeed, this Brahmāṇḍa is enclosed on all sides by a shell, just as the seed of a wood-apple fruit is well-enclosed by its rind.
That [egg] was surrounded by water ten times its own size, and that water by fire; the fire by air, and the air by space, and that space by the ego-principle (ahaṃtā).

And ego (ahaṃkāra) [arises] from the Great One (mahat), and that too from the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti); they say all these six [evolutes] increase tenfold each, and that [nature] is the seventh.
O Pārtha, that Prākṛta-caraṇa is proclaimed to be infinite; it consists of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of cosmic eggs.
And likewise, there are hundreds of millions upon millions of such [beings] here; all are exactly like this, just as has been described.
O Pārtha, I bow always to that Sadāśiva whose majesty is such; alas, he is dull-witted and sinful-souled—who indeed could be more senseless than him? (45)
He who would not worship Śiva, the deliverer from such delusion as this—now I shall proclaim the measurement of time for him; understand that.
They say fifteen *nimeṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*, and one should count thirty *kāṣṭhās* as a *kalā*. Thirty *kalās* make a *muhūrta*, and thirty of those make both night and day.
There are five periods of time during the day, each consisting of three muhūrtas; listen to them: morning (prātaḥ), then forenoon (saṅgava), midday (madhyāhna), and afternoon (aparāhṇaka).
The fifth [muhūrta] is Sāyāhna; fifteen muhūrtas, both [day and night], are designated as a pakṣa (fortnight). || 49 ||
A month is said to consist of two fortnights; two solar months constitute a season (ṛtu). Three seasons make an ayana, and two ayanas are called a year.
They say that a month has four divisions and a year has five; the first is the *saṃvatsara*, and the second is the *parivatsara*.
This third is Idvatsara, the fourth is Anuvatsara, and the fifth is named Yuga; such indeed is the determination of the calculation.
A month of humans is a day and night of the ancestors; the dark fortnight is said to be their day, and the bright fortnight their night.
A human year is recorded as one day of the gods; among them, the northern course [of the sun] is the day, and the southern course is the night.
A year of the gods is considered a single day for the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), and a year of the Seven Sages is recorded as a single day for Dhruva.
The Kṛta age, followed by the Tretā age, consists of seventeen hundred thousand and twenty-eight thousand years of human beings. (56)
The Parā age consists of twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand years; the Dvāpara age consists of eight hundred and sixty-four thousand years. (57)
The Kali age is recorded as four hundred and thirty-two thousand [years]; these four [ages] together are designated as a Yuga of the gods.
The lifespan of Manu and the yugas together amounts to seventy-one [units]; by this time, fourteen Manus constitute one day of Brahmā. (59)
And a thousand yugas constitute one kalpa; listen to them: Bhavodbhava, Tapobhavya, Ṛtu, Vahni, and Varāhaka.
Sāvitra, Āsika, Gāndhāra, Kuśika, as well as Ṛṣabha, Khaḍga, and Madhyama belonging to Gāndhārī; || 61 ||
Vairāja, Niṣāda, Meghavāhana, Pañcama, Citraka, Jñāna, Ākūti, Mona, Daṃśa, and Bṛṃhaka. || 62 ||
Śveta, Lohita, Rakta, Pītavāsas, and Śiva the Lord; this month consists of all these forms, and thus it lasts for a hundred years.
This measurement of Brahmā, consisting of both the first and the second halves, is traditionally known; I am not capable of describing that of Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara as well.
Where am I, O Pārtha, of such meager intellect, and where are the other two, Hara and Tryambaka? Even in the netherworlds, one is reckoned only by the measure of divinity.
Thus it has been indicated to you by my intellect; now hear again that which pertains to primordial nature (prakṛti).

Such is the ordinance of the Creator. Śrī Nārada said: O Pārtha, in the Kali age there will arise various fabrications of heretical doctrines under the name of Ṛṣabha, which are intended to delude the people.
His son was Bharata, and Śataśṛṅga was his son; to him were born eight sons as well as one daughter.
Indradvīpa, Kaseru, Tāmradvīpa, Gabhastimān, Nāga, Saumya, Gāndharva, Varuṇa, and Kumārikā. (69)

Extending as far as the Mahī and the ocean, adorned with rows of trees, and filled with thickets, shrubs, and creepers, it was in the vicinity of Stambhatīrtha.
From among the goats and rams, a certain she-goat, having become bewildered, arrived at that difficult region. (72)
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, that auspicious woman wandered here and there throughout the midst of the thicket, yet she was utterly unable to escape.
Having become entangled within the thicket, she then met her death; after some time, [the cord] broke from his head and fell down.
And on the day of Saturn's appearance, he fell at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean—a place consisting of all holy fords, which grants liberation from all sins.
Indeed, her entire head remained in that very state, fixed there; though entangled in the thickets and shrubs, it did not fall into the water at all.
O best of the Kurus, by the power of that sacred ford at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, Barkarī attained [liberation] through the falling of the remainder of her body.
To King Śakaśṛṅga, there was indeed a daughter born among the Siṃhalas; her face clearly appeared to be like that of a monkey. 78.
A divine woman of auspicious form shone beautifully upon his entire body; though he was previously childless, she appeared to that king like a hundred sons.
A daughter was born, increasing the joy of her kinsmen with great delight; then, having beheld her face, which had the form of a young goat, [he spoke]. (80)
All those royal officers were struck with amazement, while the king, together with his harem, then fell into a state of extreme despondency.
All the subjects were distressed by the sight of such a form; therefore, the citizens, greatly amazed, asked, "What is this wonder? (82)
Then, having reached youth, she who resembled the daughter of a god in person looked at her own face in a mirror and remembered her former existence.
"O father, by the power of that sacred ford, it has been revealed regarding my mother and father; you must certainly not feel any grief on my account. (84)
"Do not grieve for me, O mother; this is the fruit earned in a previous birth. Having said this, that young girl then related her own history from before.
She informed her parents of her intention to go to that place where her body had fallen, arising from her previous birth.
"O father, I shall go to the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; O King, act in such a way that I may reach it. (87)
Then her father, Śataśṛṅga, promised that it would be so; the king had her massaged with boats filled with jewels.
Then, having reached Stambhatīrtha together with Potārī, she also gave abundant gifts, including the gift of all her possessions.
Having searched within the thicket of creepers, he then beheld his own head, which remained as nothing but bone and skin; taking it up with great effort, he departed.
Having cremated [the body], his bones were cast into the confluence at the site of the union; then, by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), his face became as radiant as the moon.
Neither among the daughters of the gods, nor among the wives of the nāgas, nor among mortal women was there a face such as her face. (92)
All the gods, asuras, and humans were infatuated by her beauty; they entreated her in many ways, yet she did not desire a husband.
With joy, she began that difficult penance there; then, when a year was complete, Maheśvara, the God of gods, [appeared].
Having become visible to her, he said, "I am the granter of boons. Then, having worshipped him, the young girl spoke these words. || 95 ||
If you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, and if a boon is to be granted to me, then let your presence be established here at all times, O Śaṅkara. (96)
When Śarva had said, "So be it," the maiden was delighted; O best of the Kurus, that is where the head of that she-goat was burnt. (97)
At that time, Śiva, known as Barkareśa, was established there by her; and having heard this great marvel from my mouth, she [attained it] from the Talātala realm.
The lord of the nāgas named Svastika came to see Kumārī; as he moved along with his head raised, the earth was tossed up by him. (99)
To the northeast of Barkareśa, there was a well named Svastika; it was filled by the Gaṅgā and bestows the fruit of all holy places, O Pārtha.
And having seen the installed linga, Śiva was pleased and granted a boon: "For those whose dead bodies are cremated here," || 101 ||
Their bones are cast into the ocean, and thus their destiny shall be inexhaustible; having dwelt in heaven for a very long time, they have now returned here.
Those men who worship Barkareśa with devotion become kings, endowed with all prosperity and possessed of majesty. || 103 ||

Having bathed in the waters of the ocean or on land, whatever is desired by his mind shall be attained; provided he is endowed with faith on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
Having bathed in the well and offered libations to his own ancestors, the man who worships Barkareśa is liberated from all sins. (105)
Having thus obtained all the boons, she returned once more to Siṃhala and reported her own account to her father, Śataśṛṅga.
Having heard that, O Phālguna, the king was amazed and all the people praised the sacred ford on earth, and they came there with great reverence. || 107 ||
Having bathed and given various gifts, they then departed once more for Siṃhala, thrilled by the majesty of the sacred ford.
O King, listen to what that monarch joyfully gave—both the bridegroom and wealth—to the maiden who did not desire them, as well as other things he bestowed out of affection. || 109 ||
Having divided this land of Bhārata into nine parts, he gave eight to his sons and the ninth to his daughter.
I shall describe their divisions, adorned by mountains; hear from me the names of the sons [who rule] the regions and the mountains. (111)
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, Ṛkṣaparvata, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra—these are the seven principal mountain ranges here. || 112 ||
Beyond Mahendra is indeed called Indradvīpa; and the region on this side of Pāriyātra is known as Kaumārika. (113)
One thousand and one of each of these various regions, as well as the origin of the rivers—listen to this in brief, O Phālguna.
The rivers headed by the Vedas and the Smṛtis are considered to originate from the Pāriyātra mountain; while the rivers such as the Narmadā and Sarasvatī have emerged from the Vindhya range. (115)
The Śatadrū, Candrabhāgā, and others arise from the Ṛkṣa mountains; the Ṛṣikulyā, Kumārī, and others arise from the foothills of the Śuktimat mountain.
The Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Kāverī, and the river Mahī, as well as the Kṛṣṇā, Veṇī, and Bhīmarathī, are known as those originating from the foothills of the Sahya mountains.
The rivers headed by the Kṛtamālā and Tāmraparṇī are known to originate from the Malaya mountains; those headed by the Trisāmā and Ṛṣyakulyā are recorded as originating from the Mahendra mountain.
Having thus divided [the kingdom] among his sons and his daughter, the lord of the earth went to Mount Śataśṛṅga in the north and performed austerities.
Having performed severe austerities there on Śataśṛṅga, the best of mountains, that best of kings, Śataśṛṅga, went to the world of Brahmā.
O son of Kuntī, you were born there along with your brothers Pāṇḍu and the illustrious maiden Satī, who remained at Stambhatīrtha.
With wealth produced from sugar-candy, she performed austerities while bestowing gifts; then, after some time had passed, [she gave] to her eight brothers.
Nine new sons were born, endowed with great heroism, strength, and energy; having come together and assembled, they then spoke to the maiden.
"You are our family deity; O auspicious one, show us favor! Divide our eight regions yourself and grant them to us, so that there may be no dissension among the seventy-two of us."
Thus addressed by Brahmā, she who knows all dharmas and is equal to Viṣṇu in wisdom divided the land into nine regions consisting of seventy-two divisions.
O Phālguna, I shall tell you truly their names, as well as their villages, towns, and coastal ports, along with their numbers.
In that mandala, there was a district consisting of four crores of villages; with two and a half crores of villages, it is called the Bālāka country.
They know there are one hundred and twenty-five million villages in Purasāhaṇaka; likewise, four hundred thousand villages are recorded for Andhaka.
One hundred thousand villages are proclaimed to be in Nepāla; however, the measure of thirty-six hundred thousand is proclaimed for Kānyakubja. (129)
Seventy-two hundred thousand villages are recorded as being in Gajaṇaka; likewise, eighteen hundred thousand villages are in the Gauḍa country. (130)
In Kāmarūpa, nine hundred thousand villages are proclaimed; and in Ḍāhala, known as Veda, there are nine hundred thousand villages. (131)
Nine hundred thousand villages are proclaimed to be in Kāntipura; likewise, nine hundred thousand are proclaimed to be in Mācipura. (132)
In the land of Oḍḍiyāṇa, nine hundred thousand [mantras] are proclaimed; likewise, in the land of Jālandhara, nine hundred thousand are proclaimed. || 133 ||
Likewise, in the region of Lohapūra, nine hundred thousand villages are said to exist; and seven hundred thousand are proclaimed to be in Pāmbīpura. (134)
Seven hundred thousand villages are proclaimed to be in Raṭarāja, and in Harīāla, the number of villages is measured at five hundred thousand. (135)
Three hundred and fifty thousand are said to be in the region of Draḍa, and likewise three hundred and fifty thousand are said to be in Avaṃbhaṇavāhaka.
O Pārtha, there are twenty-one thousand villages in Nīlapūraka, and likewise one hundred thousand villages in the territory of Āmala.
In the country named Nareṃdu, there are one hundred and twenty-five thousand; and in the country of Atilāṅgala, one hundred and twenty-five thousand are said to exist.
In Mālava there are one hundred and eighteen thousand and ninety-two; likewise, in the land of Sāyaṃbhara, one hundred and twenty-five thousand are said to exist. (139)
And likewise in Mevāḍa, one hundred and twenty-five thousand (lakṣa) are declared; and eighty thousand are proclaimed as Vāguri. (140)
The region of Gurjarātra is proclaimed to have seventy thousand villages, and likewise, the territory of Pāṇḍu has seventy thousand.
Just as there are forty-two thousand oblations, so too the Kāśmīra maṇḍala is said to consist of sixty-eight thousand [squares]. 142.
They know there to be sixty-three thousand villages in Kauṅkaṇa; Laghu-Kauṅkaṇa consists of one thousand four hundred and twenty [villages]. (143)
