Sindhu is proclaimed to consist of ten thousand villages. || 144 ||
The district of Kaccha consists of one thousand four hundred and twenty [villages], while Saurāṣṭra is said to have fifty-five thousand villages. || 145 ||

The Lāḍa country is proclaimed to have twenty-one thousand [villages]; beyond the Sindhu, ten thousand villages are said to exist; likewise, O Pārtha, Aśvamukha is said to have ten thousand [villages]. (146)
And Ekapāda is also proclaimed to have ten thousand [years]. || 147 ||
In the same way, the region known as Sūryamukha is recorded as ten thousand [yojanas]; likewise, the region Ekabāhu is said to be ten thousand [yojanas].
The teacher Saṃjāyu is said to have ten thousand [disciples]; likewise, the region named Śiva is recorded as having ten thousand; and similarly, Kālahayañjaya is renowned for having ten thousand.
Likewise, there is the region Liṅgodbhava, consisting of ten thousand [yojanas]; Bhadra and Devabhadra are each recorded as having ten [thousand]. (150)
The two, Caṭa and Virāṭaka, are recorded as thirty-six thousand; and Yamakoṭi is proclaimed to be thirty-six thousand. (151)
Likewise, eighteen crores are said to be the region of Rāmaka; Tomara, Karṇāṭa, and Yugala—these three [make up the remainder]. 152.
It is proclaimed that there were one hundred and twenty-five thousand villages [per division], and the kingdom of women is proclaimed to consist of five hundred thousand villages. (153)
The territory of Pulastya is said to consist of ten lakhs; likewise, the two countries of Kāmboja and Kosala each consist of ten lakhs.
Four hundred thousand villages are proclaimed to belong to Bāhlīka, and thirty-six thousand are celebrated as the region of Laṅkā. || 155 ||
The land of Kuru is proclaimed to consist of sixty-four thousand [yojanas], and Kirātavijaya is likewise said to be one hundred and fifty thousand [yojanas]. 156.
They say there are five hundred thousand villages in Vidarbha, and Vardhamāna is proclaimed to have fourteen thousand.
Ten thousand is said to be Siṃhaladvīpa, and the Pāṇḍu country consists of thirty-six thousand villages. (158)
One hundred thousand villages are said to constitute the terrifying Bhayāṇaka; and sixty-six thousand [villages] are called the Māgadha country. (159)
Likewise, Pāṅgu-deśaka has sixty thousand villages, and Vareṃduka is said to have thirty thousand villages. (160)
The primary seat is proclaimed to consist of twenty-five thousand [units], while the territory of Yavana is recorded as comprising forty thousand villages.
The extent of its wings and arms is declared to be exactly four thousand [yojanas]; these seventy-two regions are proclaimed to be the number of villages. (162)
Thus, in this Bharata-khaṇḍa, ninety-six crores and seventy-two lakhs of cities are proclaimed. (163)
And thirty-six thousand coastal regions, O Bhārata; having thus divided the territories, he gave nine to his nephews.
Moreover, that queen was her own [sister] even though they were unwilling; for brothers become enraged at a sister whom they ought to respect. || 165 ||
Having deliberated with her brothers, the auspicious sister gave [the gift]; having done that and honored them, she arrived at Stambhatīrtha.
Then, among those regions, the means for accomplishing the four aims of life (caturvarga) was declared to be the most excellent of all, namely Kumārīśvara itself. || 167 ||
There too, that maiden knows the secret field (guptakṣetra); in the secret field, those of great vows worship Kumāreśa.
She remained bathing at the confluence of the six rivers, and subsequently, after a long period of time, in the temple constructed by Skanda.
When that [old temple] had decayed, she also caused a new golden palace to be built; thereupon Mahādeva, being exceedingly pleased by her devotion, was highly gratified.
Rising from the form of a youth, he appeared before her and said: "O blessed lady, I am pleased with both your devotion and your wisdom."
"O Kumārikā, this temple, having fallen into ruin, has been restored by him; he has been gratified, and I shall become renowned by your name. (172)
"The creator and likewise the deliverer—these two are indeed remembered as having equal merit. Therefore, they shall call me Kumāreśa and Kumārīśa. (173)
O lady of excellent complexion, those boons that were always granted to Barkareśa have indeed been given; and now, O fair one, the time has arrived even for you.
For a woman who has no husband, there is neither heaven nor even liberation, just as in the case of the old maiden on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī. (175)
Therefore, O blessed one of excellent complexion, choose him who is known here at this sacred ford as Mahākāla and has attained perfection, to be your husband.
Then, by the word of Rudra, she chose him as her husband; accompanied by Mahākāla, she went to the world of Rudra.
There, Pārvatī, filled with great joy, embraced her and said: "O auspicious one, since the earth has been depicted by you as if in a painting," (178)
"Therefore, become my friend by the name Citralekhā. From that, that auspicious lady became her friend Citralekhā.
She by whom Aniruddha was described as the supreme husband of Uṣā; she who is the most excellent among yoginīs and the beloved of Mahākāla. (180)
She drank a drop of water from the rainy season every hundred years while performing penance; therefore, she is called an Apsaras in heaven.
O Phālguna, this maiden of such a kind established this Liṅga, which bestows auspiciousness and is known by the name Barkareśvara. || 182 ||
Therefore, O Bhārata, the cremation of men here and the casting of their bones are declared to be superior even to Prayāga, according to the word of Maheśvara.
Arjuna said: Who is this Mahākāla, and how did he attain perfection at this sacred site, O best of sages? This is a great wonder to me.
Explain all of this to me, who am full of faith and inquiring.
Nārada said: Having paid homage to Mahākāla, the granter of boons, the imperishable Sthāṇu, I shall describe his life and conduct according to my ability, O scion of the Pāṇḍu lineage.

In the city of Vārāṇasī, in ancient times, there lived a most excellent among those who recite prayers, a highly fortunate and greatly renowned man named Māṃṭi, who was a constant reciter of the Rudra-hymns.
While that sonless man was indeed muttering the Rudra-mantras for the sake of a son, a hundred years passed; then Śaṅkara, being pleased, spoke to him.
Therefore, your wise son, possessing my power and prowess, shall be the restorer of your entire lineage.
Having heard these words of Rudra, Māṇṭi attained supreme joy. Then, after some time had passed, the wife of the high-souled Māṇṭi—
The sparrow bore the embryo, as if she were the very embodiment of asceticism; indeed, four years passed for that embryo.
But he did not emerge from outside after leaving his mother’s womb; then Māṇḍitri, having approached him, addressed him with conciliatory words.
"My child, even an ordinary son always brings happiness to his parents; you are born of me, a pure mother—why do you trouble me so excessively? (10)
My child, why do you have no longing for dwelling among humans, where there is the continuous attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and even liberation?
"When shall we be born as humans, where worship yields great fruit, and where indeed there are various duties toward the ancestors and the gods? (12)

Thus do beings grieve, even those born into various wombs. Tell me, how can you remain thus within your very belly, disregarding that incomparable human state which is envied even by the dwellers of heaven? (13)
The Embryo said: "O Father, I know all this, which is exceedingly difficult to attain; nevertheless, I am perpetually and excessively afraid of the path of Time."
Indeed, two paths are proclaimed in the Vedas: Kāla and Arcis. By means of Arcis they attain liberation; by the path of Kāla they enter into ritual action.
Whether in heaven or even in hell, this one who has entered the path of time finds no peace anywhere, like a deer pierced by a hunter.
For that very reason, the wise person, being composed, should strive so as not to experience suffering when confronted by time in its terrible and profound form. (17)
If, O father, my mind is not deluded by various defects, then may I quickly attain this rare human birth once again. (18)
Then, O Pārtha, his father, fleeing in all directions, went for refuge to the god Maheśvara, crying out: "Save me, save me, O Maheśvara! (19)
"O Lord, who else besides you is the granter of my son's desires? You alone have granted him [this boon]; therefore, you yourself must cause my son to attain this birth. (20)
Then, being highly pleased by her extreme devotion, Maheśvara spoke to her regarding his own manifestations, as well as dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
"And let Māṇḍitīputra be quickly awakened from his error. Then those radiant splendors spoke to the womb.
O Mahāmati Māṇḍīputra, you should not harbor fear in your heart; for the four qualities, beginning with Dharma, shall never abandon you. 23.
Then others, beginning with Adharma, said: "We shall certainly not become like that; we will remain as mind for you, and you shall have no fear of us. (24)
When this was said, that boy, having suddenly manifested his supernatural powers, emerged outside; once born, he trembled and wept.
Then the supernatural powers said: "O Māṇḍī, that son of yours even now trembles and weeps, terrified of the path of Time."
"Therefore, he shall become known as Kālabhīti. Having granted this boon, they departed to the presence of Mahādeva.
That boy also grew like the moon in the bright fortnight; and he, wise and devoted to the vow of Paśupati, was refined by the purificatory rites.
Purified by the recitation of the five mantras, he became devoted to pilgrimage; O descendant of Bharata, he bathed in the sacred sites of Rudra while chanting those mantras.

Having heard of the qualities of the Kṣetra protected from fear by Time, he approached it; then, having bathed in the waters of the Mahī and having recited mantras tens of millions of times, [he remained there].
Having turned back, he saw a bilva tree not far away; having seen it, he recited one hundred thousand [mantras] beneath it.
As that Brahmin was chanting, his senses dissolved; in an instant, he became the very embodiment of absolute supreme bliss.
Nowhere can there be a comparison for that bliss with heaven and the like; it is like the measurement of the water of the Gaṅgā—it is only that, and nothing else.
There he remained absorbed for a moment, and then he became as he was before; thereupon, O Pārtha, Kālabhīti was struck with wonder and said: (34)
This great joy of mine is not at Vārāṇasī, nor at Namiṣa; it is not at Prabhāsa, nor at Kedāra, nor even at Amarakaṇṭaka. (35)
On Śrīparvata and nowhere else does such a discourse proceed; my words are free from modification and as clear as the waters of the Gaṅgā. (36)
Supreme joy toward all beings shines forth clearly throughout the three worlds; my mind also understands that Dharma alone is supreme for me. (37)
Oh, how manifest is this power of the place! It is clearly proclaimed here as a site that is faultless, pure, and free from all calamities. (38)
For one established therein, the meaning of the Dharma becomes manifold, like a thousandfold [expansion]. Indeed, by virtue of this power, I know it within my own mind. (39)
This sacred site is indeed superior even to the foremost holy places such as Kāśī; therefore, remaining right here, I shall perform abundant penance.
He who, always thirsting, wanders about thinking, "This is a sacred ford" and "That is a sacred ford," does not attain perfection; he dies only in suffering. (41)
Having reflected thus, he stationed himself beneath a bilva tree and, standing upon his big toe, recited the mantras of Rudra.
Having undertaken the vow of consuming only a drop of water, which [burns] like fire for a hundred years, O Bhārata, when those hundred years had passed while he was engaged in silent recitation; 43.
A certain man, carrying a jar filled with water, approached; having bowed down to him, he spoke these words out of great joy, fearing for his time. (44)
"O high-minded one, today your vow is fulfilled; accept this water from me, which shall bring fruit, for you ought to undertake this labor here. (45)
Kālabhīti said: "Who are you? Tell me truly according to your appearance and what your conduct is. Having learned of your birth and conduct, I shall accept you; otherwise, certainly not. (46)
Nara said: "I do not know my own parents, nor whether they have perished; indeed, in every way, I always perceive them as being exactly like this."
"Neither by conduct nor by religious duties is there anything at all to be done by me; therefore, I shall not speak of this, nor shall I practice it. (48)
Kālabhīti said: "If it is so, I shall never accept water from you. Listen here to these words of mine, spoken by my preceptor as they were heard from the Vedas. (49)
Since the lineage of one who lacks purity of seed is not known, a virtuous person perishes at that very moment by eating or even drinking from him. (50)
Whoever does not know Rudra and whoever is not a devotee of Rudra—if one eats his food or water, one becomes a sinner; of this there is no doubt.
He who eats without knowing Śiva is called a slayer of a Brahmin in this world; moreover, the slayer of a Brahmin wipes away the merit from the food-eater—therefore, one should not eat his food.

Just as a jar of Gaṅgā water becomes [polluted] by even a single drop of liquor within it, so too does one who eats [the food of] a knower of Śiva become like that very person if he is ignorant of Śiva. (53)
Even one who is of low caste, if he is a devotee of Śiva, is not [unworthy]; therefore, two qualities should be observed when accepting a gift. || 54 ||
Nara said: "By these words of yours, laughter arises within me. Oh, you are deluded; you are false, epileptic, and even dull-witted. (55)
Śiva dwells eternally and constantly within all beings; therefore, whether a word be good or bad, it is never a censure of Śiva.
For him who acts as an adversary toward both himself and another—him whose vision is divided, death ordains a most intense fear.
Or rather, tell me, what impurity could there be in water? This vessel is born of clay and has been heated by fire as well. (58)
And since it is full of water, why is there impurity among these [beings], and from where does it arise? (59)
If, moreover, impurity is measured by contact with me, then tell me: while I am situated within this earth, how can you claim "I-ness" [in relation to it]? (60)
"From where do you move upon the earth? Or do you not move at all in the sky? When examined in this way, your speech would seem like that of a fool. (61)
Kālabhīti said: "If it is thus declared that Śiva alone exists within all beings, then why, O Nabhasyaka, do atheists eat clay?"
For the sake of purifying the universe, he established the cosmic order; it has been maintained by him through its fruit and not otherwise—listen to that.
In the beginning, the Creator projected this world consisting of forms; and that [world] is bound by the expansion of names, just as a cow is bound by a rope. (64)
That conceptual proliferation of names (nāmaprapañca) is indeed divided into four types; its four bases are sound (dhvani), phonemes (varṇa), words (pada), and sentences (vākya).
In that regard, resonance consists of sound, and the phonemes begin with the letter 'A'. A word is said to be "śā vam," and one should worship Śiva as the sentence.
And that speech, according to the view of the Śruti, is also of three kinds: one approved by a master, and likewise one approved by a friend. (67)
For they know that even speech agreeable to one's beloved is of three kinds; just as a lord or master commands a servant, saying, "Perform this. (68)
Likewise, both Śruti and Smṛti declare that which is approved by the Master; the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth are said to be approved by the Friend. (69)
Having awakened him like a friend, he leads him toward reality; and whatever poetic discourse and the like is spoken that is agreeable to his beloved [is also employed]. (70)
One who desires heaven should maintain purity both internally and externally, remembering the words of the Lord as well as the words of a friend, and thus observe the practice of purification.
This very thing must be protected by those born of the earth; so says the Śruti. If you, however, speak this with words of atheism, [then the world will perish]. (72)
By this, what need is there to mention the Vedas, the Śāstras, and the Purāṇas? Formerly, those Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas who were preceded by the Seven Sages [became so]. (73)
All those who followed the Veda became deluded, for they were indeed clever; likewise, those established in goodness who follow the words of Vedānta are those who ascend upwards.

Those characterized by passion (rājasa) remain in the middle, while those characterized by darkness (tāmasa) go below; by consuming pure food and through virtuous conduct, one then becomes a traveler to heaven.
Nor do we begrudge this, for Śiva is indeed not absent from all beings; listen here to an illustration of this as well. (76)
Just as there are many ornaments produced from gold, some of which have an excellent form while others have an inferior form. (77)
Gold exists indeed within all [alloys], and likewise is that Sadāśiva; when the base form is purified, it attains purity, yet not oneness [with the alloy]. (78)
Likewise, this purified body, being cleansed, will clearly ascend to heaven; therefore, alas, nothing inferior should be accepted by a wise person with his whole being. (79)
If one should purify this body, nothing at all should be grasped from any side; for he who grasps everything on all sides does not distinguish between excrement and food.
It would become pure in just a few days; that stone would clearly become so. Therefore, with my whole soul, I shall certainly not take up water here. (81)
"Whether it be good or even bad, for us the supreme authority is the Veda. When this was said, that man laughed and [struck] with his right [hand].
Scratching the ground with his thumb, he made a most excellent pit; he poured that water there, and by it the pit was filled.
The water overflowed, and as he scraped it away with his foot, he created a lake filled with that surplus water.
Having seen that great marvel, the brahmin was not at all astonished, for such manifold wonders might occur among those who worship spirits and the like. (85)
And one should not abandon that eternal path of the Vedas, even for the sake of a painting. || 86 ||

Nara said: "You are exceedingly foolish, O Brahmin, yet you speak words of wisdom! Have you not heard the verse uttered by those who know the past? 'The well belongs to one, the jar to another, and the rope to yet another, O Bhārata. (87)
Some are giving it away and others are drinking; all of them share equally in that water. Why, then, you who know the dharma, do you not drink this water of mine?
Nārada said: Then he reflected upon the verse in many ways; because of uncertainty, he deliberated upon this equality of shares through examples such as jars and the like.
Just as there is an equal distribution of all the goods and vessels among many [traders], so too shall the performer [of the rite] repeatedly share equally in all the fruits.
For one who is pure and meditates on Śiva while constructing a temple or a well, the fruit is equal to that of one drinking water, even in the absence of accepting water as a gift.
Having thus resolved, Kālabhīti spoke to that man: "This is true; however, regarding the filling of the pit with the water from a jar—" (92)
"Tell me, O sir, how can one like me drink [this] having seen it with his own eyes? Whether it be good or bad, I would not drink it under any circumstances. (93)
O descendant of Kuru, having seen this firm resolve, that man laughed and then vanished from that spot in an instant. (94)
Terrified by the time and overcome with great wonder, he reflected deeply: "What kind of event is this? (95)
Then, as he was reflecting, beneath the bilva tree, there appeared a most beautiful, lofty, and great liṅga that illuminated the quarters of the earth.
Then, O descendant of Bharata, upon the manifestation of that great Liṅga, a multitude of Apsarases danced in the sky and the Gandharvas sang charmingly.
Indra released a rain of flowers made of *pārijāta* blossoms; the gods and sages praised him with various hymns, crying out, "Victory! (98).
While that great festival was taking place, O Kauravya, Kālabhīti, being overjoyed, offered salutations and uttered a hymn of praise. (99)

I take refuge in the god Mahākāla, the destroyer of sin, the destroyer of the mire of worldly existence, the destroyer of every fraction of time, and the ender of the path of time—the glorious Kālakaṇṭha, whose form is the very death of worldly existence. 100.
I bow down to you, the face of Īśāna; the Veda praises you: "You are the Lord of all sciences, you are the Lord of beings, you are the Great-Grandfather; salutations to that Maheśvara. (101)
I take refuge in that second form known as Tatpuruṣa, whom the Veda praises; we know You—grant that to us, O Śrī Rudra, Lord of Gods; salutations, salutations to You! 102.
I take refuge in the triad of faces beginning with Aghora; I always bow to your forms favored by the Atharva Veda—those that are non-terrible, terrible, and most terrifying—to you, O Being! (103)

I always take refuge in your fourth face; salutations, salutations to you, Sadyojāta! O Śiva, in every birth, become my primordial source; arise as the origin of existence for me in each and every state.

Salutations to you, Vāmadeva, the Eldest Rudra, Time itself, the transformer of all parts; to the one who bestows strength and yet shatters strength, the slayer of beings, and the one who transcends the mind. 105.
We worship you, O Tryambaka, who increase the prosperity of Śiva with most holy fragrances; like a ripe cucumber from its stem, O Tryambaka, protect me from the path of death.
O Lord, those sages free from passion who chant this supreme six-syllabled mantra of yours—be gracious toward them; we too chant it, preceded by the syllable Oṃ: "Namaḥ Śivāya. (107)
O descendant of Bharata, having been thus praised, Mahādeva emerged from the liṅga and, illuminating the three worlds with his splendor, appeared visibly before the twice-born man and spoke.

"O twice-born one, because you have propitiated me most intensely here at this great sacred ford, I am exceedingly pleased with you, my child; therefore, Time shall not be the master over you in any way whatsoever. (109)
And I, appearing in human form, having seen your steadfastness in the Dharma, [declare]: "Blessed is this path of Dharma, since it is protected by those such as you. (110)
My lake has been filled with the waters of all sacred fords; this highly meritorious water has been gathered by me for your sake. (111)
And this secret of the seven mantras, which is my hymn of praise that has been composed—by its recitation, the fruit of the seven mantras shall be attained.
Choose from me a desired boon that is cherished by your heart; for I have been so thoroughly gratified by you that there is nothing that cannot be granted to you.

Kālabhīti said: "I am blessed, I am graced, O Śaṅkara, since you are pleased with me; through your satisfaction, all religious duties become fruitful, whereas otherwise they are considered to be mere labor. (114)
If you are pleased, may your presence be established here in this liṅga forever; and may whatever is performed here in this liṅga become inexhaustible.
May that fruit which arises from ten thousand recitations of the five mantras of the gods be produced for people by the sight of this Liṅga. (116)
"O Maheśvara, since I have been liberated from the path of Time (Kāla), let this Linga therefore be known as Mahākāla."
And whatever mortal bathes in this well and offers libations to the ancestors, may he obtain the fruit of all sacred fords, and may there be an inexhaustible state for the ancestors. || 118 ||
Having heard these words of his, Śaṅkara, being pleased, said to him: "I dwell eternally where the Svāyambhuva Liṅga is located."
A liṅga made of self-manifested stone, bāṇa-stone, precious gems, minerals, rocks, or metals yields fruit progressively, each preceding one being ten times superior to the one following it.
The Tārakāliṅga is in the sky, Hāṭakeśvara is in the netherworld (pātāla), and the Svāyaṃbhuva is upon the surface of the earth; this triad is equal [in power].
And whatever is requested with special distinction shall come to pass; herein lie the flower, the fruit, the worship, the food offering, and the act of hymn-singing.
O son, whatever gift or other act is performed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha during the Śiva-yoga, that shall become inexhaustible.
Whoever bathes in the well to the east of the Liṅga and offers libations to the ancestors attains the fruit of all sacred fords, and the ancestors achieve an inexhaustible state.
During that night, one should worship Mahākāla in every watch; he who makes offerings at all the lingas shall obtain the fruit of keeping vigil.
O best of the twice-born, for him who always worships me here with his senses conquered, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are never far away.
Having bathed in the lake on the fourteenth or eighth day of the month of Māgha, or on a Monday or a festival day, and having worshipped this Liṅga, one shall go to Śiva.
Charity, austerity, and the recitation of the Rudra-mantra—all these shall indeed be inexhaustible; and you, Nandin, shall be my second doorkeeper.
"O child, because he has conquered Time and the Path, the royal sage Karandhama, known by the name Mahākāla, will soon arrive here."
"Having declared the dharmas to him, you may then return to my world. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Rudra dissolved into the midst of the liṅga.
Mahākāla, also being delighted, performed great penance there. || 131 ||

Thus ends the manifestation of Mahākāla. Nārada said: Then, after some time had passed, O Pārtha, King Karaṃdhama, desiring excellence in his religious duties, heard of the great virtues of sacred fords (tīrthas).
And there he arrived at the Mahākālacaritra; having bathed in the waters of the Mahīsāgara, he then worshipped the lingas.
Having reached Mahākāla, he attained supreme joy; beholding that great liṅga, the lord of people could not look enough.
Just as a poor and wretched man, having discovered a jar of treasure, considers his life to have borne fruit upon beholding Mahākāla. (135)
The fruit of reciting fifty thousand mantras is obtained here by the mere sight of him; therefore, having worshipped him with great reverence and having prostrated before him, [one should proceed].
Having heard this, he approached Mahākāla, the most excellent of Liṅgas; then Mahākāla, remembering the words of Rudra, spoke as if smiling.
Having gone out to meet the king, he offered him worship and the guest-offering (arghya). Then, after the king had made inquiries regarding his welfare and so forth, his face became serene.
Having addressed Mahākāla, he spoke these words at the conclusion of their conversation: "O Blessed One, this doubt always revolves within me. (139)
When this rite called *tarpaṇa* is performed for the ancestors by men, the water merely goes into the water; how then are the forefathers satisfied? (140)
In this way, the worship with the ritual ball (piṇḍa) and so forth—all of it is seen right here. How then can we think that it is consumed by the ancestors and others? (141)
And this is not the case, that nothing at all remains for them; for those beggars appear to them just as they do when, in a dream, one pursues a person who is seen there. || 142 ||
The direct perceptions of even the gods are always visible; how then can they accept [this]? My mind is utterly bewildered in this matter.
Mahākāla said: Such is the origin of those ancestors and the dwellers of heaven; for them, there is distant speech, distant worship, and likewise distant praise.
They know and traverse all that is past, present, and future; they consist of the five subtle elements (tanmātras), as well as mind, intellect, ego, and the insentient.
The body consists of nine principles, and the tenth is considered the Person (Puruṣa); therefore, they are satisfied by scent, and likewise by the principle of taste.
They are satisfied by the essence of sound and they grasp the essence of touch; seeing what is pure, they are satisfied—O King, there can be no falsehood in this. (147)
Just as grass is said to be food for cattle and grain for men, so too is the essence of food the nourishment for those born of divine origin. 148.
The powers of all entities are inconceivable and within the domain of knowledge; therefore, they grasp the true essence, while the remainder is seen right here.
Karaṃdhama said: "The Śrāddha is offered to the ancestors, yet they are subject to the power of their own karma; whether they reside in heaven or in hell, how is it that they enjoy it? (150)
Furthermore, those who abide in heaven or in hell, being constrained by their karma, how can they be considered lords if they are unable to grant these boons? (151)
May the ancestors, being pleased, bestow upon men long life, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and other auspicious things, as well as sovereignty. (152)
Mahākāla said: "O best of kings, it is true that the ancestors abide in their own respective karmas; however, those of the gods, asuras, yakṣas, and others are formless. (153)
The personified ancestors of the four castes are remembered as being sevenfold; for they all bestow everything that is desired upon the giver.
O King, this Śrāddha has been performed for those ancestors who possess thirty-one powerful groups; may it satisfy those supreme ancestors. (155)
Satisfied themselves, they satisfy his ancestors who are established there; thus the śrāddha reaches one's own kin, and they grant boons.
The king said: O Brahmin, just as offerings are given by specifying the names of beings and others, why indeed are they not given in brief for the gods and the rest? (157)
"This [is for] the ancestors, the gods, the twice-born, and the purifier (fire). Why, then, should there be such elaborate rituals that cause suffering to the mind, body, and so forth? (158)
Mahākāla said: "Proper conduct must always be observed toward all; indeed, people will not accept even appropriate conduct from you if it is lacking. (159)
Just as a dog standing at the door of a house takes the sacrificial offering, O King, does the chief minister take it in the same way, like a dog? (160)
Thus those gods, like elemental spirits, never accept [an offering]; they do not enjoy a pure desire nor the oblation from one who lacks faith.
O King, those stainless ones do not accept that which is given without mantras; regarding this matter of mantras, even the Śruti declares as follows: || 162 ||

The mantras are the deities; whatever a learned man does with mantras, he does that with the deities themselves. When he gives, he gives with the deities themselves; when he receives, he receives with the deities themselves. Therefore, one should not receive anything without mantras, nor should one undertake anything without mantras. || 163 ||
Therefore, it should always be given with mantras, both from the Purāṇas and the Vedas; otherwise, they do not accept it, and it remains among the spirits (bhūtas).
The King said: "Why is a gift given consisting of these—darbha grass, sesame seeds, unbroken grains, and water—well combined together? I wish to know the reason for this. (165)
Mahākāla said: "In former times, indeed, many gifts of land were given; yet the Daityas, having entered by force, seized them. (166)
Then the gods and the ancestors replied to the Lotus-born One: || 167 ||
"O Lord, while we are looking on, everything is being seized by the Daityas; provide protection for them so that we do not perish. (168)
Then, having reflected, the performer of rites performed the protection of the Rākṣasa with sesame seeds for the ancestors and with unbroken grains (akṣata) for the gods. || 169 ||
Water and darbha grass are required everywhere; thus the asuras do not accept them. Whatever fruit is offered by the Daityas without these is seized [by the gods]. (170)
Sighing, the ancestors and gods depart, for they do not receive the fruit from the giver; therefore, in all the ages, the gift itself is bestowed.
Karaṃdhama said: "I desire to hear, in accordance with the truth, the arrangement of the four yugas; this great curiosity has always been present within me. (172)
Mahākāla said: Know that the first is the Kṛta Yuga; after that, the Tretā Yuga is remembered; and Dvāpara and Kali—these are the four [ages] in brief. (173)

Sattva is established in the Kṛta age, Rajas in the Tretā, and both Rajas and Tamas in the Dvāpara; Tamas alone is to be known as the Kali age—such is the conduct of the ages throughout the Yugas. (174)
In the Kṛta age, meditation is supreme; in the Tretā age, sacrifice is said to be so; in the Dvāpara age, conduct; and in the Kali age, truthfulness and charity alone. (175)

But in the Kṛta age, creation was mental; its function was the direct manifestation of aesthetic essence (rasa). The subjects were composed of light, ever-satisfied, eternally blissful, and enjoyers of delights. || 176 ||
Among them, there was neither inferior nor superior; those auspicious beings were without distinction. In that Kṛta Yuga, their lifespan, happiness, and form were equal.
They experience neither displeasure nor duality, neither hatred nor even exhaustion; for those who dwell upon mountains and in the ocean are lovers of compassion.
At that time, there was indeed no confusion regarding the system of castes and stages of life; they meditated always upon the one, supreme Śiva, and never upon anything else. 179.
Then, upon the fourth step, she became radiant with aesthetic flavor (rasa) as it was lost; thereupon, trees known as "horses" and "houses" appeared before them. (180)
From them are produced garments, fruits, and ornaments; within those very fruits, their [fruits'] scent, color, and taste arise.
At the end of the Kṛta age, those creatures then subsisted on honey from large-bee hives, which was highly potent and contained honey in every individual cell.
Thus the subjects were indeed joyful, well-nourished, aged, and free from affliction; then, after some time, their sense-faculties became matured.
Likewise, due to the nature of the age (yuga) and because Śiva’s meditation had become somewhat diminished, they forcibly seized those trees and the honey produced by bees.
Due to that conduct of theirs, brought about by the fault of greed, the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) perished here and there along with the honey.
And when that [period] was also nearly exhausted, pairs of opposites indeed arose; through cold and heat, and through mental sufferings, they were then exceedingly distressed.
For they established shrines here and there for the purpose of protection; thereafter, their spiritual perfection (siddhi) manifested once again during the Tretā Yuga.
Through the rain, fourteen kinds of medicinal herbs—both cultivated and wild—came into being; they ripened without being ploughed and grew without being sown, due to the union of water and earth.
Trees and shrubs grew with seasonal flowers and fruits; by means of those grains, flowers, and fruits, they sustained their livelihood. (189)
Then, once again, passion and greed arose among them on all sides; or rather, they seized the rivers, fields, and mountains by the power of Time.
Trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs were forcibly consumed quickly according to their strength; and conversely, fourteen types of medicinal herbs perished.
Having bowed down, those plants entered the earth when the subjects were oppressed; then Pṛthu, the son of Vena, milked the Earth for the welfare of all living beings.
From that time forward, the medicinal herbs were ploughed with the share, and the subjects thereafter sustained themselves through agriculture while being protected by the Kṣatriyas.

The establishment of the castes and stages of life, as well as the threefold sacrifice, is proclaimed [as the means]; yet, being devoid of consciousness, they abandon liberation which consists of meditation upon Sadāśiva. (194)
Relying on flowery speech and out of passion, they failed to achieve heaven; and in the Dvāpara age, divergences of intellect arise among men.

Whether through mind, deed, or speech, one's livelihood is accomplished only with great difficulty; likewise, greed, lack of fortitude, the abandonment of auspiciousness, and the confusion of duties arise. (196)
In the Dvāpara age, the destruction of the castes and stages of life proceeds; then, from that Dvāpara onwards, the [Veda] is divided into four parts by the Vyāsas.
The single Veda is divided into four parts for the sake of the twice-born; the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are differentiated out of regard for the world.
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Śaiva, as well as the Bhāgavata, and likewise the Nāradīya, and the Mārkaṇḍeya as the seventh. (199)
The eighth is declared to be Āgneya, the ninth is remembered as Bhaviṣya, the tenth is Brahmavaivarta, and likewise the eleventh is Laiṅga.
The twelfth is indeed the Vārāha, and the thirteenth is the Skānda; the fourteenth is the Vāmana, and the fifteenth is remembered as the Kaurma.
The Mātsya is declared to be the sixteenth, and after that the Gāruḍa; beyond this is the Brahmāṇḍa—thus indeed are there eighteen [Purāṇas].
And in this Vārāha-kalpa, hear from me concerning the Vyāsas: Ṛtu, Satya, Bhārgava, Aṅgiras, and likewise Savitṛ. (203)
Mṛtyu, Śatakratu, the wise Vasiṣṭha, Sārasvata, Tridhāman, and the sage Vedavid Trivṛta shall now be [the seven sages]. || 204 ||
Śatatejas was Viṣṇu himself, known as Nārāyaṇa; Karaka, the wise Āruṇi, and likewise the divine Ṛtañjaya. || 205 ||
Kṛtañjaya, Bharadvāja, Gautama, the best of poets, Vājaśravas, the sage, and likewise the sage Yuṣmāyaṇa. (206)
Tṛṇabindu, as well as Ṛkṣa, Śakti, Pārāśara, Jātūkarṇya, Viṣṇu, and the sage Dvaipāyana himself. (207)
And these future ones, headed by Aśvatthāman, have been indicated to you; furthermore, in the Dvāpara age, the treatises on dharma will also be divided for the sake of the world.
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati. (209)
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras. || 210 ||
Then, at the twilight of the Dvāpara age, as the Kali Yuga begins and Śaiva yoga is perishing, those who delight in yoga are born.
In the first [kalpa], Śvetakalaurudra, Sutāra, Tāraṇa, Suhotra, Kaṅkaṇa, and the great sage known as Lokākhyamuni [were the seven ṛṣis]. || 212 ||
Jaigīṣavya, Bhāvya, the venerable Dadhivāhana, the sage Ṛṣabha, Dharmaugra, and Atri with Bālaka. (213)
Gautama, Vedaśīrṇa, Gokarṇa, Śikhaṇḍibhṛt, Gṛhāvāsī, Jaṭāmālī, and the terrible Aṭṭahāsa.
Lāṅgalin, Saṃyamin, Śūlin, Ḍiṇḍi, Juṇḍīśvara himself, Sahiṣṇu, Somaśarman, and Lakulīśa, O King. (215)
Kāyāvarohaṇa, Bhāvin, and the others, these lords of yoga (yogeśvaras), will in due order briefly proclaim the Śiva-dharma in the Kali age. (216)
Thus, O King, the summary of the scriptures for the Kali age is declared; now hear of the onset of the Tiṣya age, which indeed causes both joy and agitation.
During the Tiṣya age, men whose senses are agitated by darkness practice deceit, malice, and even the slaughter of ascetics. (218)
In the Kali age, there will be constant, tormenting passion, perpetual fears of hunger, terrible fear of drought, and the ruin of countries.

There is no authority for men derived from the Śruti, because of their practice of unrighteousness; for they are unrighteous, lacking in proper conduct, highly irascible, and possessed of little spiritual luster.
Greedy people speak untruths, and those of wicked progeny are mostly women; they do so through ill-performed sacrifices, poorly studied texts, bad conduct, and false scriptures.
Through the ritual faults of the Brahmins, the destruction of the subjects occurs; the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas perish, while those who are Śūdras and Brahmins flourish.
Śūdras sit together with Brahmins on the same beds, seats, and at meals; Śūdras adopt the conduct of Brahmins, and Brahmins adopt the conduct of Śūdras. (223)
Thieves will abide by the conduct of kings, and kings will adopt the behavior of thieves; women faithful to a single husband will not remain, while women who go to meet their lovers will flourish.
For at that time, the land yields little fruit, though in some places it may yield much; kings, fearless of sin, do not protect but rather plunder.
Kings who were not Kṣatriyas, Brahmins who lived like Śūdras, and all Śūdras who were litigants were honored by the Brāhmaṇas. || 226 ||
Seeing the twice-born seated, those of very small intellect move about; O twice-born ones, Śūdras place their hands upon the mouths and ears of the twice-born.
At that time, they will speak with humility even to a low-born person, and will address Śūdras seated on high thrones even while Brahmins look on.
Having understood this, the king does not cause harm; behold the power of Time, O King! [The twice-born] [worship him] with pure white flowers and other such ornaments. (229)
Endowed with little learning, meager fortune, and weak strength, they honor Śūdras; and Brāhmaṇas accept improper gifts from heretics.
By this [sin], those lowest of the twice-born go to the Raurava hell, which is so difficult to cross; likewise, those twice-born who are sellers of the fruits of austerity and sacrifice.
In the Kali age, there will be many ascetics by the tens of millions; men will be few while women are many, and the birth of offspring among men will be rare.
In the Kali age, they revile the words of the Vedas and the meanings of the Vedas; whatever scripture is composed by Śūdras themselves, that alone is considered authoritative.
There is an increase in wild beasts and a decline in cattle; furthermore, there is no purity in any religious practice, such as giving and so forth. (234)

There will be many destructions of the virtuous and kings who fail to protect; the countryside will be plagued by extortion, and the crossroads will be dominated by those devoted to the god Śiva. (235)
In the Kali age, women will have disheveled hair; households will be dominated by women, and those women will be poorly dressed and harsh.
Furthermore, all people become like *kṛtyā* spirits, greedily smeared with much food; all merchants likewise [suffer], and Indra pours down rain in a strange manner. (237)
Enveloped by those of immoral conduct, heretics, and false appearances, the world will become one of mutual begging. 238.
At that time, the world will become fearless regarding sins; there will be those who steal the jewels of others and those who violate the wives of others. (239)
At the end of the Yuga, children are born when women are less than sixteen years of age; likewise, at that time, women give birth when they are twelve years old.
There are thieves who steal from a thief, and yet another who steals from that stealer; when knowledge and action have ceased and the world has reached a state of inactivity. (241)
Insects, mice, and snakes will harass human beings, as will other heretics who oppose the system of castes and stages of life.

O King, they will then come into being, and their growth will be characterized by suffering regarding sons, wives, and so forth, as well as the wasting away of the body and the state of being afflicted by disease.
Because of the adherence to unrighteousness, darkness arises in the Kali age; yet, listen now to this great virtue of the Kali age, that very treasury of faults. (244)
"In that [age], human beings do not attain perfection in even a short time; those who practice dharma are blessed," so say the followers of the three ages (Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali). || 245 ||

In the Kali age, those devoted to faith perform that which is declared in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas; the dharma that lasts for a year is prescribed for the Tretā age, while that lasting for a month is remembered for the Dvāpara age.
O King, that which a wise man attains by practicing with effort during this Kali age in a single day, others attain as their spiritual perfection over the course of three ages.
Learn from me that which will come to pass in the twenty-eighth Kali age, regarding as many as shall attain perfection through the vows of Hari and Hara during the Kali age. (248)
O King, when three thousand years of the Kali age have passed, and three hundred less ten remain, he will appear upon this earth.
There, Śūdraka, the lord of heroes and the remover of the earth's burden, shall attain perfection after propitiating her while she is being worshipped. || 250 ||
Then, after three thousand three hundred and ten years, Cāṇakya will cause the kingdom of Nanda to be destroyed.
He who desires liberation from all sins at Śuklatīrtha [shall attain it] after three thousand and twenty more [years].
Then he shall obtain the future kingdom of Vikramāditya; for by the grace of the Lord of Siddhas, he will indeed deliver the distressed from their fortresses.
Then, after one hundred and ten thousand more [years], there will be one named Śaka, who shall remove extreme poverty.
Then, after three thousand six hundred and sixty years, he will be born in Añjanī at Māgadha from Hemasadanā.
An incarnation of Viṣṇu and the protector of dharma, Budha is himself a manifest lord; the deeds of that great-souled one shall be manifold. (256)
He will slay tens of millions of those favored by Jyotirvidumukha and others; having enjoyed the seven continents for sixty-four years, he [will rule]. || 257 ||
Having bestowed his own glory upon his devotees, he will afterwards go to heaven, since he is superior in qualities to all other incarnations. (258)
Then, with devotion, they shall speak of that wise one who removes all sins, during four thousand and four hundred [years]. (259)
In the Sādhika lineages, the great king Pramiti will arise; and among the lineages of the Moon, there will be a powerful general of vast armies.
Having slain millions of Mlecchas and all heretics everywhere, he shall establish the pure, singular Dharma of the Vedas.
The king will meet his end between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā; thereafter, the subjects will be severely oppressed by some means at the hands of Time.
Resorting either to terrible dharma or to deceit, they become unrestrained; indeed, possessed by greed, they act in groups.
Agitated and oppressed by exhaustion, they will harm one another; when both the Śrauta and Smārta traditions have perished, they will then strike each other down.
Without restraint, devoid of compassion, lacking affection, and shameless—these twenty-five short-lived ones have abandoned their homes and wives. (265)
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", they will wander with their senses overwhelmed by despair; struck by drought and abandoned by their livelihoods, they will be filled with suffering.
Abandoning their own countries, they resort to those borderlands; likewise, they frequent the banks of rivers and oceans as well as mountains.
Extremely distressed, they subsist on meat, roots, and fruits; wearing rags, leaves, and skins, they are inactive and possess nothing.
The barbarian Śālva, a doer of terrible deeds, will destroy even the mere vestige of Dharma, utterly eradicating all distinctions of superior, inferior, and middling.
Then, O best of kings, for the sake of his destruction, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe in person, became the son of Viṣṇuyaśas in Śambhala.
Surrounded by the best of the twice-born, he will destroy that Śālva, having slain the wicked by the millions, the billions, and the trillions.
He shall protect that Dharma which is preceded by the sacred revelation.
Having constructed a boat in the form of the Dharma and having performed manifold deeds, the Supreme Lord will go to the higher world for the sake of the virtuous. (273)
Then, O King, the Kṛta Yuga shall begin once more; this first Kṛta Yuga is distinct from and superior to all others.
And the remaining twenty-eight *kalis* will proceed from another source; thereafter, in the *Kṛta* age, the Solar dynasty (*Sūryavaṃśa*) shall flourish.

From Marurāja and Devāpi the Brahmins [received it], and from Śrutadeva as well; thus, O King, this arrangement pertaining to the four ages revolves. And in the four ages, those are blessed who worship Hara and Acyuta. (276)
Karadhama said: Some, having taken refuge in Śiva, Viṣṇu, or Brahmā, describe liberation; but why do you, however, hold such a view? (1)
Mahākāla said: "O bull among men, even these three gods possess boundless majesty; even the minds of the lords of yogis are bewildered by this—how much more so mine?"
In ancient times, it is said, the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, being in doubt as to who was the most excellent, went to the world of Brahmā.
At that moment, Viriñca too, bowing low, spoke this verse: "Salutations to that Ananta, whose end is not perceived."
"May Maheśa and Bhakta always show compassion toward me. Then, considering him to be the most excellent, the sages went to Kṣīroda.
There, the Lord of Yoga, awakening, spoke this verse to Brahmā, who is the supreme form of Brahman among all beings.
"I also salute Sadāśiva; may those two bring auspiciousness to me. Then those Brahmins, filled with wonder, withdrew and departed once more.
On Mount Kailāsa, they beheld Sthāṇu speaking to Girijā: "I shall dance during the vigil on the eleventh day in the abode of Viṣṇu."
"I always practice austerities for the sake of pleasing Hari and Brahmā. Having heard this, those sages withdrew and, being distressed, said: ||| 9 ||
Or rather, since even the gods do not reach the further shore of those who are mutually created by one another’s creations, what count can there be for those such as ourselves?
Those sinful speakers of untruth who describe these [beings] as superior, inferior, or middling, certainly go to hell.
Thus did those ascetics of Naimiṣa resolve; "This is the truth, O Indra among kings, and this is clearly my opinion as well. (12)
Thousands of reciters of prayers—both Vaiṣṇavas as well as Śaivas—abandoned their respective rules regarding Viṣṇu and Sthāṇu.
Therefore, whichever deity a person’s devotion is clearly directed toward, let him worship that one; he shall become free from sin—this is my supreme opinion. (14)
Karaṃdhama said: O best of Brahmins, what are those sins by which the minds of the deluded do not find delight in the Vedas nor in the duties of righteousness? (15)

Mahākāla said: "The varieties of unrighteousness (adharma) are to be understood through the distinctions of the modifications of the mind; they are gross, subtle, and non-subtle, with many millions of different divisions. (16)

In this regard, those accumulations of sin which are gross and cause rebirth in hell—those accomplished by means of mind, speech, and body—are here described in brief. (Mahābhārata, Anuśāsana Parva 2)
The mental action is fourfold: the intent toward another's wife or property, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind, and the inclination toward what ought not to be done. (18)
Idle chatter, falsehood, that which is unpleasant, slandering others, and backbiting—these are the fourfold actions of speech. (19)
Eating what is unfit to be eaten, violence, the pursuit of falsehood, and the appropriation of others' property—this fourfold action is physical. (20)
Thus, this twelvefold action arising from the three sources has been declared. I shall further describe its divisions, the fruits of which are infinite.
Those who hate Mahādeva, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra, being possessed of very great sins, go into the fires of hell.
They say there are six great sins that yield continuous fruit: those who do not rejoice upon seeing Śaṅkara, and those who do not praise him. (23)
Free from hesitation, they remain and take delight in the presence of Śiva and their Guru, acting as they please and liberated from formal ritual observances. 24.

They do not respect the conduct of Śiva and they hate the devotees of Śiva; these are the six [faults]. Likewise, [they abandon] a guru who is afflicted, incapacitated, or has departed for a foreign land. || 25 ||
He who abandons one who has been humiliated by enemies is a doer of evil, as is he who shows contempt for that person’s wife, son, or friends. (26)
This great sin should be known as equal to the censure of one's guru; [namely,] the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the teacher’s bed. (27)
These are indeed great sinners, and the fifth is he who associates with them; those who speak ill of a Brāhmaṇa out of anger, hatred, fear, or greed [are likewise]. (28)
He who, having summoned a Brahmin who is destitute and begging, [refuses him], is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmaghna), a great sinner who reaches the very vital point [of sin]. || 29 ||
He who says that [the self] does not exist hereafter is indeed remembered as a slayer of a Brahmin; and he who, out of pride in his learning, humiliates a virtuous twice-born man.
Remaining indifferent in the midst of the assembly, he is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin; for by force, through false qualities, he leads himself to a state of superiority.

He who acts in opposition to his elders is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin; so too is he who refuses food to twice-born men whose bodies are tormented by hunger and thirst and who desire to eat. (32)
They call him a slayer of a Brahmin who creates obstacles; he is a slanderer of all people, intent on searching for their faults. (33)
He who causes agitation and is cruel is indeed remembered as a slayer of a Brahmin; [so too is he who obstructs] cows overcome by thirst as they approach for water. || 34 ||
They call him a slayer of Brahman who creates obstacles for one who is practicing [virtue], and he who, having learned of another's fault, whispers it into the ear of the king. (35)
They call that man a slayer of Brahmins who is wicked, malicious, and cruel, as well as one who seizes the wealth lawfully acquired by Brahmins. (36)
Whether through deceit or even by force, that which is considered equal to the killing of a Brahmin is when a person of deluded intellect, having studied the scriptures, abandons them. (37)

One should know that [the omission of these] is equal to drinking liquor; or one might recite [the scriptures] merely for the sake of a livelihood. The abandonment of the *agnihotra* and the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) [is likewise a grave fault]. || 38 ||
Abandoning one's mother and father, giving false testimony, killing a friend, eating what is unfit to be eaten, and the intentional slaughter of wild animals. (39)
One who, out of anger, sets fire to a village, a forest, or a cow-pen—these are terrible sins equal to the drinking of liquor. (40)
The seizure of all the possessions of the destitute, as well as the taking of men, women, elephants, horses, cattle, land, jewels, gold, medicinal herbs, and liquids; 41.
The theft of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, or fine garments by means of placing one's hand upon them is recorded as being equal to the theft of gold.
Not giving daughters who are marriageable to a suitable bridegroom, and having sexual relations with one's own sons, friends, wives, or sisters. (43)

The violent killing of a maiden, the consorting with women of the lowest castes, and sexual intercourse with a woman of one's own caste are recorded in tradition as equal to violating the teacher’s bed.
Furthermore, he who, having promised wealth to a twice-born man, neither gives it nor reminds the brahmin of the promise, incurs a sin equal to that minor offense (upapātaka). || 45 ||
Arrogance, excessive anger, hypocrisy, ingratitude, extreme attachment to sense objects, miserliness, deceit, and envy; 46.
The abandonment of servants, as well as of virtuous kinsmen, ascetics, cows, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and Śūdras; and the beating of them. (47)
The destruction of flowering groves and trees belonging to the hermitages of Śiva, performing sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, and begging from those who should not be begged from; || 48 ||
The sale of sacrifices, pleasure gardens, ponds, and so forth; the sale of one's wife and children; and the sale of pilgrimages, fasts, vows, temples, and ritual acts—[these are forbidden]. (49)
They subsist on the wealth of women, being utterly conquered by them; they fail to protect their wives and consort with women who drink liquor. (50)
The non-payment of debts, living by means of false interest, taking wealth from those who are censured, and defiling a virtuous maiden with words—these [are sins]. (51)

The employment of lethal and poisonous mechanical devices, rites of root-eradication (mūlakarman), acts of expulsion and malevolent sorcery, as well as the practices of inciting passion and hatred; || 52 ||
He whose undertaking of his own duties is for the sake of enjoying the pleasures of the tongue, who teaches for a fee, and those who study for a fee; (53)
The state of being a *vrātya* consists of the abandonment of vows, the consumption of all kinds of food, the study of false scriptures, and the reliance on dry logic. || 54 ||
Censuring the gods, the sacred fire, teachers, and virtuous people, as well as cows and Brahmins—whether done openly or in secret—and likewise censuring kings and provincial governors; 55.
Those who have abandoned the worship of ancestors and gods, who have forsaken their own duties, who are ill-behaved, atheistic, sinful, and never speakers of truth; (56)
He who practices sexual intercourse on a sacred festival day, during the daytime, in water, in non-vaginal openings, in animal wombs, or with women who are menstruating or not his own wife; || 57 ||
Those who shatter the hopes of wives, sons, friends, and well-wishers; those who speak unpleasantly to people; those who are cruel and break their agreements. || 58 ||
He who breaks tanks, wells, bridges, or irrigation channels, and he who causes a breach in the cooking of those who sit in a single row; || 59 ||
By these aforementioned sins, men are known as "minor offenders" (upapātakin); now learn from me of those sinners who are joined with even lesser sins than those. || 60 ||
Those men who interfere in the affairs of cows, Brahmins, maidens, their masters, friends, or ascetics, are considered sinners. (61)

Those who, being base, burn with envy at the prosperity of others, those who shed tears over women, and those who do not perform acts such as giving gifts and sacrifices for the sake of the assembly (of the virtuous). || 62 ||
Those who void excrement and other waste in cow-pens, near fire, in water, on roads, in the shade of trees, on mountains, in gardens, and in temples; || 63 ||

Constantly devoted to song and instrumental music, they were intoxicated and intent on making joyful clamors; their dress, actions, and conduct were fraudulent, and they engaged in deceitful dealings.
Those who forge false edicts, those who engage in treacherous warfare, he who is exceedingly merciless toward his servants, and he who is a tamer of animals; || 65 ||
He who listens slowly to words while feigning false devotion—he who is fickle, deceitful, treacherous, and falsely humble—[is such a person]. (66)
He who eats while leaving his wife, sons, friends, children, the elderly, the emaciated, the sick, servants, guests, and kinsmen hungry; || 67 ||
He who eats fine food himself while giving something else to a Brahmin should be known as one who cooks in vain; he is censured by those who speak the truth of Brahman.
Those who, having themselves taken up the religious observances, abandon them because their senses are unsubdued; those who constantly beat cows and yoke them again and again; (69)
They do not nourish the weak; when their wealth is lost, they even hate them; they afflict them with malevolent magic and cause those who are wounded to be carried away.
They do not give them even water, nor do they treat the sick; [so too are] those who keep goats and sheep, those who keep buffaloes, those who live by the sea, and the husband of a low-caste woman.
A physician who is of low caste and base character, one who makes a false display of righteousness, and one who, transgressing the scriptures, collects taxes according to his own will; || 72 ||
He who always delights in punishment, or even he who does not delight in punishment, is oppressed by bribe-takers, officials, and thieves. (73)
That king in whose kingdom the subjects suffer in hell shall see one who is not a thief as if he were a thief, and a thief as if he were not a thief.
A king overcome by laziness and addicted to vices goes to hell; those who know the past have spoken of these and other such evils. (75)
Whether it be this or that, even if it is another's property as small as a mustard seed, a man who steals it becomes a sinner and goes to hell; of this there is no doubt. (76)
Immediately after such sins as these have departed, a person obtains a body of the same form as before for the purpose of undergoing torment. (77)
Therefore, one should avoid all three of these hellish states; instead, endowed with true faith, one should always go for refuge to Sadāśiva.
Whether it be prostration, praise, worship, or likewise the chanting of his name—whether performed through association, curiosity, or greed—it shall never be fruitless for him. (79)
Karaṃdhama said: You should explain the procedure for the worship of Śiva in brief, by performing which a person may obtain the fruit of worshipping Śiva. (80)
Mahākāla said: One should always worship Śaṅkara in the morning, at midday, and in the evening; by seeing him or touching him, a mortal will clearly attain fulfillment.
First, one should perform a bath, or else a bath with ashes; if fallen into distress, a bath up to the neck, or else a bath with mantras. (82)
One should wear a woolen garment, or else a white one, or one dyed with mineral pigments; it should be new, not soiled, and not patched. (83)
One should also put on the upper garment; without it, the worship is fruitless. And one should wear the triple mark of ashes on the forehead, the heart, and the two shoulders. (84)
He who worships Mahādeva with devotion beholds him repeatedly; having cast all defects outside, he should enter the abode of Śiva. 85.
Having entered and prostrated before the Lord, one should then enter the inner sanctum; having washed one's hands and being focused on Him, one should remove the floral offerings.
Because he acts with devotion as if he were Rudra and performs the rite of purification (mārjana), therefore Sthāṇu purifies him; thus this mutual interaction occurs between them. 87.
Through devotion to Rudra, one should remain steadfast; then one shall wipe away all impurity. For one who constantly wipes away impurity, devotion to the God shall endure.
Thereafter, one should fill the jars with pure water; all the jars should be equal in size, and all should be of auspicious appearance.
All of them were free from cracks, possessed a pleasing appearance, and were filled with water; they were full of water purified by cloth and perfumed with fragrant incense. || 90 ||
Having washed and filled them, one should perform the recitation of the six-syllable mantra over a hundred or twenty-eight water-pots (gaḍukas).
There should be eighteen [pots], or one may not make fewer than four; likewise, milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugarcane juice [should be provided]. (92)
Thus, one should deposit all that substance from the left side of Bhava; then, having gone outside, one should worship the gatekeepers.
From here on, the mantras that express all of these shall be stated in their proper sequence.

Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Oṃ Kṣāṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla. Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to the Gurus. Thus [one offers salutations] in the sky. Oṃ Kauṃ, salutation to the Family Deity (Kuladevī). Oṃ, salutation to Nandin. Oṃ, salutation to Mahākāla. Oṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ. Then, having entered, being pure and standing slightly to the south of the Liṅga, facing north, one should meditate for a moment while remaining seated with the body held straight. (95)

One should meditate upon the circle of fire, surrounded by darbha grass and other materials, situated within the solar orb at the center of a lotus, and itself residing in the middle of the lunar orb.
In the center of that [is] Viśvarūpa, who possesses the eight śaktis beginning with Vāmā, has five faces, ten arms, three eyes, and is adorned by the moon. (97)

One should meditate upon the Lord, who has the Daughter of the Mountain on his left lap and is repeatedly praised by the Siddhas; then, O King, one should first offer water for the feet and the arghya-oblation to Śambhu.
Water, unbroken grains, darbha grass, fragrance, flowers, ghee, milk, curd, honey, and the juice of punarnavā are proclaimed to constitute the arghya offering.
Then, with a heart moistened by faith, one should perform the bathing of the Liṅga; first, taking a water-pot, one should perform the cleansing bath.
First, one should bathe [the image] with half [of the water] and perform the rubbing away of impurities; afterwards, one should bathe it with the whole [amount] and then worship it after bathing.
Then, having bowed with devotion, one should bathe [the deity] with the root mantra: "Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to Śiva, whose form is the universe. This is the twelve-syllable root mantra. || 102 ||
One should bathe [the deity] with water, milk, curd, honey, ghee, and sugarcane juice, using the root mantra for each separately, followed by water, incense, and worship.
One should bathe [the image] with all the medicinal pastes (gaḍukas) and, once bathed, rub it dry with fragrant unguents.
Then, having bathed the [image] that has been dried, one should smear it with sandalwood paste; one should worship it with various flowers—listen to the procedure by which this is done. || 105 ||

In the southeast quarter: *Oṃ dharmāya namaḥ*. In the southwest: *Oṃ jñānāya namaḥ*. In the northwest: *Oṃ vairāgyāya namaḥ*. In the northeast quarter: *Oṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*. In the eastern quarter: *Oṃ adharmāya namaḥ*. In the south: *Oṃ ajñānāya namaḥ*. In the west: *Oṃ avairāgyāya namaḥ*. In the north: *Oṃ anaiśvaryāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ anantāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ padmāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ arkamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ somamaṇḍalāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ vahnimaṇḍalāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ vāmājyeṣṭhādipaṃcamantraśaktibhyo namaḥ*. *Oṃ paramaprakṛtyai devyai namaḥ*. *Oṃ* to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who possesses the five faces of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta; who is the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) of Rudra, the Sādhyas, the Vasus, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, and other deities; whose forms consist of the born-from-egg, born-from-sweat, born-from-germ, and born-from-the-womb, as well as the stationary and moving beings; *Oṃ hūṃ*, salutation to Śiva, the embodiment of the universe (*viśvamūrti*). Salutation to the trident, bow, sword, skull-bowl, staff, and axe. (106)
Then, at the mouth of the water reservoir, one should say, "Salutation to Caṇḍīśvara. Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should then present the *argha* offering.
O Mahādeva, accept this *arghya*—consisting of water, unbroken grains, flowers, and the finest fruits—for the sake of completing the worship. (108)
After the offering of *arghya*, the capable practitioner should worship with the worship of the Vasus; thereafter, he should successively present incense, a lamp, and food offerings.
One should ring the bell there, and then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana); one should cause it to be whirled before the God of gods amidst the sounds of conchs and musical instruments.
Whoever beholds the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) of the trident-bearing God of gods shall be liberated from all sins; how much more so for one who actually performs it?
Even if one should perform dance, song, and instrumental music falsely, the Infinite One (Ananta) will indeed be pleased with him, because the fruit of song and instrumental music is infinite.
Then, having praised him with hymns, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff; and one should ask forgiveness from the Lord of Gods, saying, "Forgive my good deeds and my misdeeds."
Whoever worships Rudra in this very liṅga, especially [worships] his father, grandfather, and likewise his great-grandfather.
Having been delivered from all sins, he shall dwell for a long time in the world of Rudra; thus, having become a devotee of Maheśvara, he remains established in the vow of right conduct. || 115 ||

If one worships with a mind focused on that for the sake of liberating the bound soul (paśu) from its fetters (pāśa), then whoever thus sacrifices to Rudra has thereby gratified this entire world. || 116 ||
But this is fruitful, O King: one should not transgress established conduct. For from conduct dharma arises, and through conduct one enjoys heaven. (117)
For through right conduct one gains long life, and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks; yet in this world, sacrifices, gifts, and penances do not lead to a man's ultimate welfare.
O King, listen as I describe briefly the conduct of one who proceeds by transgressing the rules of right behavior. 119.
A householder must exert effort in accomplishing the three aims of life; for upon their complete fulfillment, the householder achieves success both in this world and the next.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha; then, having risen and sipped water (*ācamana*), one should first perform the cleansing of the teeth.

A wise man, being tranquil, self-restrained, and pure, should perform the twilight devotions: the morning twilight while the stars are still visible, and the evening twilight while the sun is still present. (122)
One should attend upon her according to the rule and not abandon her except in times of distress; likewise, one should avoid falsehood, frivolous chatter, and harsh speech. (123)
O King, avoiding the company of the wicked, false speech, and wicked scriptures, one should perform the looking into a mirror, the cleaning of the teeth, and the dressing of the hair. (124)

The great sages have declared that the worship of the gods should be performed in the forenoon; one should avoid using a seat made of Palāśa wood, as well as sandals and a tooth-stick. A wise man should not drag a seat along with his foot.
A wise man should not simultaneously pour water and fire together.
One should never stretch out one's feet toward a teacher, a deity, fire, a crossroads, a sacred tree, a temple, or an ascetic.
One should circumambulate these three times: a teacher who is superior in knowledge, an elder, and an aged person.

One who knows the Dharma should practice the proper conduct regarding food, excretion, and movement with great restraint; likewise, one's speech, intellect, vigor, austerity, livelihood, and lifespan, as well as one's most secret affairs, must be guarded.
One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day, and facing south at night; by doing so, one's lifespan is not diminished. (130)
The wisdom of one who urinates facing the fire, facing the sun, facing a cow, facing one observing a vow, facing Soma, facing water, or facing the twilight is destroyed. (131)
After eating, lying down, standing, voiding excrement or urine, and walking upon a road, one should always perform the fivefold sipping of water (ācamana) while still wet.
One should not urinate in a river, nor in a cremation ground, nor on ashes; nor on cow dung, nor in a ploughed field, nor on uncut grass, nor on a verdant lawn. (133)
A wise person should perform purification with water that has been drawn up, and not from within a body of water, nor from a temple, nor from an anthill, nor from a place frequented by mice. (134)
A wise person should avoid five kinds of earth that are discarded or impure; rather, he should perform purification by removing both odor and residue.
One should not strike oneself, nor should one inflict suffering upon oneself; furthermore, one should not scratch one's own head with both hands. (136)
A wise man should protect his wife and abandon groundless jealousy toward her; likewise, he should never perform any ritual action without the setting of the sun.
One should acquire wealth through non-injury to living beings, or at least with minimal injury; one whose mind is fixed on Śiva should not be excessively miserly.
One should not be envious, nor ungrateful, nor intent on deeds of malice toward others; one should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes, nor crooked.
One should not be fickle with speech or limbs, nor should one enter the sphere of the uncivilized; one should not engage in idle talk, nor likewise in groundless enmity. (140)

One should accomplish one's goals through skillful means; the rod of punishment is a resort only when there is no other way. One should avoid eating with those who are alienated, sleeping with them, and using vessels shared with them.
O best of kings, one should not pass between two burning fires, nor between two Brahmins, nor between a husband and wife.
One should not create a distinction between the sun and the sky, nor between Śiva and his bull; for by doing so, one incurs sin.
A wise man should not eat while wearing only a single garment, nor should he perform a fire-oblation (homa), nor worship the twice-born, nor indeed perform the worship of the gods. 144.
Breaking, grinding, rubbing, as well as purifying with water, cooking, eating, sleeping, rising, walking, and sneezing—145.

Having uttered words concerning the commencement or completion of a task, as well as pleasant speech; while drinking, smelling, touching, hearing, or desiring to speak; and likewise during sexual intercourse. (146)
He who maintains purity, performs recitation, and likewise worships Sthāṇu twenty times should be known as a Māheśvara; any other is merely one who bears the name.
Having indeed become one with Rudra, he shall thereafter go to Śiva at the end; likewise, he should not address another's wife, yet if he should speak to her, [he must do so in this manner].

A wise man should address his mother as "Mother," his paternal aunt as "Sister," and his daughter as "Noble Lady" (Āryā). One who is impure from eating should not partake of anything, nor should he look at the sun. 149.
One should not look at the moon, nor the stars, nor touch one’s own head; one should not sit in a secluded place with a sister, a daughter, or a mother.
The group of senses is indeed difficult to conquer; even a wise man becomes deluded [by them]. When a teacher has arrived at one's home, one should rise up from one's seat with effort. (151)
One should prepare a seat for him and perform a prostration at his feet; a wise man should never sleep with his head toward the north, nor with his head toward the west.
Having placed Agastya upon his head and likewise Purandara, he should avoid seeing or touching a woman in her courses, as well as conversing with her.
One should not discharge urine, feces, or engage in sexual intercourse in water; having performed the worship of gods, humans, and sages according to one's means. (154)

Then, having offered the remainder to the ancestors, one who is devoted to Maheśvara, restrained in speech, pure, and having sipped water (ācamana), is worthy to eat while facing either the east or the north. (155)
With his hands between his knees and his mind focused on that, he should eat the food without disparaging it; the wise man should not speak of its defects unless there is a reason for doing so.
One should not bathe naked, nor should one sleep or walk about [naked]. One should not speak of the teacher's misdeeds, and if he is angry, one should appease him. 157.
One should not listen to the slander of others even when they are speaking it; rather, one should always listen to the Dharma, even at the cost of abandoning hundreds of other tasks. 158.
For he should constantly polish [his body] as one does a house or a mirror; and on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, he should always eat only at night. 159.
If one is unable [to observe the vow] for three nights, he may still become a devotee of Maheśvara in this way: he should not provide himself with *saṃyāva*, *kṛsara*, or meat. (160)
One should eat in the evening and in the morning only after having fed the guests; furthermore, one should avoid sleeping, studying, and eating during the two twilights.
Eating during the two twilights out of delusion, one becomes the abode of asuras; having bathed, one should not shake one's hair, nor should one do so upon sneezing or spitting on a path.
He should touch his right ear and ask forgiveness from all beings; furthermore, he should not wear blue garments, nor should he wear clothes that are disarrayed.
One should avoid soiled clothing that is devoid of its fringes; having washed one's face, hands, and feet, one should then sit down. (164)
Placing his hands between his knees, he should sip water three times and wipe his mouth twice; he should then touch the sense-entrances with water, as well as his own head.
Having sipped water and sipped again, one should perform all ritual acts; likewise after sneezing, spitting, and when something has become stuck between the teeth. (166)

Upon conversing with those who have fallen [from their caste], one should perform the act of sipping water (ācamana); the triple Veda (trayī) must be studied constantly, and one should become a man of wisdom.

Having acquired wealth in accordance with the Dharma, one should perform sacrifices with diligence. One should never address even those who are lowly with the term "thou," for addressing elders as "thou" is equivalent to killing them; indeed, addressing elders as "thou" and killing them are both the same.

Truth must always be spoken; one should be constantly friendly; that which causes constant weariness should be abandoned. Just as it is in this world, so too in the next—those who are profound should strive for the yoga of the Self during every day. (169)

The self, which is stained by impurities, must be constantly purified through bathing at sacred fords, fasting, vows, gifts to worthy recipients, burnt offerings, recitations, sacrifices, worship of Śiva, and special rites of adoration to the gods. (170)
O King, even in that which one performs where one’s own self does not feel revulsion, it must be done with equanimity, provided that it is not something to be concealed from great men.
Thus, this brief summary has indeed been proclaimed to you; the remainder must certainly be heard by you from the Smṛtis and Purāṇas. (172)

For one who practices the Dharma in this manner while residing in the house of Maheśa, there is excellence both in this world and the next through the attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure. || 173 ||
O Phālguna, as Mahākāla was thus speaking of various kinds of dharmas, a very great sound arose in the sky.
Listen to those who gathered there and beheld it: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra himself, the goddess, and likewise the hosts of Rudras. (175)
