Likewise, Indra and the other gods, Vasiṣṭha and the other lords of sages, as well as the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases headed by Tumburu; (176)
The high-minded Mahākāla, overflowing with an excess of devotion, worshipped all of them, headed by Maheśa, in many ways. || 177 ||
Then, having been seated upon an excellent jewel-encrusted throne by the gods headed by Brahmā, he was consecrated at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
Then, O Pārtha, the goddess joyfully embraced the high-minded Mahākāla, took him onto her own lap, and adopted him as her son.
And it has been said: "O observer of the Śiva-vow, as long as this universe exists, so long may you remain in the abode of Śiva, like Śiva himself, through devotion to Śiva. (180)
And a boon was granted by the God: "Whoever shall worship your liṅga, having become self-controlled and pure, shall go upward to my world. (181)
Beholding, praising, worshipping, and bowing down, as well as the recitation of mantras and the giving of gifts performed here at my Liṅga, are the causes of my supreme satisfaction. || 182 ||
When this was said, the gods were struck with wonder and cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others likewise offered high praise to Mahākāla.
Then he was praised by the gods, honored by the Cāraṇas, while the Apsarases danced and auspicious Gandharvas sang.
He was surrounded on all sides by hosts numbering in the tens of millions who were offering praise. || 185 ||
Mahākāla went to the abode of Rudra, preceded by Bhava. Thus, O descendant of Kuru, was this great liṅga produced. 186.
There is also a well and a meritorious lake that grants success at Mahākāla; O Pārtha, those men who here are devoted to the worship of the Liṅga [attain their goals]. || 187 ||
Mahākāla, having embraced her, should offer her to Śiva; this most wonderful Liṅga is renowned throughout the three worlds. (188)
Having been seen, touched, and worshipped, they have gone to that abode of existence; thus, O Phālguna, these seven lingas were produced.
Those who hear and recite this—they too are blessed, the best among men. || 190 ||
Nārada said: Then, after I had established that place, at a later time, I again reflected in my heart with the desire to show favor to the twice-born.
Indeed, this sacred ford does not please me when devoid of Vāsudeva; for it is like a world without the sun, O ornament of ornaments. || 2 ||
Where Hari is not the master—whether at a sacred ford, in the home, in the mind, or in the scripture—all that is non-existent; it is a swan-like holy place, not a crow-like one.
Therefore, having propitiated Puruṣottama, the giver of boons, at this sacred ford, I shall bring him here in person with a portion of his being, out of a desire to bestow grace upon the universe.
Having reflected thus, O descendant of Kuru, I remained there; for a hundred years, I gratified that lord of yogis through the yoga of knowledge.
Reciting the eight-syllable mantra and restraining his senses, he became absorbed in Vāsudeva and devoted to compassion for all living beings.
Thus being propitiated by me, Hari, mounted upon Garuḍa and surrounded by ten million attendants, became manifest before my eyes.
Having offered arghya to Hari according to the prescribed rites with palms joined in reverence, I then bowed down and replied to him with my hands folded in supplication.
O Lord Viṣṇu, in former times on Śvetadvīpa, I beheld Your form—unborn, eternal, and consisting of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
"O Janārdana, establish here a single portion of that form; O Viṣṇu, if you are pleased with me, let this be done by you. (10)
Thus entreated by me, he whose banner is Garuḍa then spoke: "So be it, O son of Brahmā, regarding that which you have desired in your heart. (11)
"Everything situated here shall indeed always remain exactly so. Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu departed, O Lord, after having established his own portion there.
Viṣṇu was established by me out of a desire to bestow grace upon the worlds, because Hari himself, the resident of Śvetadvīpa, remains here.
The ancient one, known as Viśva, is therefore remembered as Vāsudeva. Then there is the auspicious Ekādaśī that occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
Having performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rite at waterfalls and other such places, he should worship Acyuta with devotion through the fivefold ritual service.
Having observed the fast, one should keep a vigil before Hari with song and instrumental music, or one should engage in the recitation of Vaiṣṇava stories, free from hypocrisy and anger.
Restrained and with a joyful mind, one should give gifts according to one's ability, [thereby purifying oneself] from all the impurities accumulated throughout many births. (17)
He is liberated without a doubt, even if he were a slayer of a Brahmin; by means of a Garuḍa chariot, he shall attain the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
O Pārtha, such a man shall deliver one hundred and one generations of his family—provided he is endowed with faith, filled with joy, possessed of enthusiasm, and likewise full of longing. (19)
And [this rite] is devoid of egoism, consisting of bathing, incense, and offerings, joined with flowers and food oblations, and accompanied by the presentation of the *arghya* water.
In every watch of the night, with great devotion, accompanied by the performance of the ārārtika rite, joined with the joy of waving chowries, and preceded by the sound of kettledrums—21.
O Bhārata, it was enriched by the hearing of the Purāṇas, accompanied by devotional dancing, free from sleep, and devoid of desire for food, thirst, or taste.
Accompanied by the smelling of the fragrance of his feet, beloved by Viṣṇu, joined with song and the performance of worship, it was attended by the journey to that sacred field.
It was endowed with the restraint of the anus, possessed of celibacy, accompanied by the recitation of hymns of praise, and adorned with water for washing the feet. || 24 ||

The man who performs the vigil on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), endowed with truth, joined with the practice of truth, accompanied by meritorious discourse, and possessed of the twenty-five qualities, is not born again upon this earth. (25)
In this excellent sacred place (tīrtha), the illustrious twice-born Aitareya formerly attained perfection through the grace of Vāsudeva.
Arjuna said: O sage, whose son was Aitareya, and where did he dwell? How did that wise man attain perfection through the grace of Vāsudeva? (27)
Nārada said: "In this very place of mine, there was one born in the lineage of Hārīta. (28)
Māṇḍūki was the foremost of brahmins, one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
He had another wife named Itarā, who was endowed with the virtues of a virtuous woman; from her was born a son known as Aitareya.
And from his very childhood, he incessantly recited the mantra known as the twelve-syllabled one, which he had practiced in a previous birth.
He neither heard nor spoke anything at all, even mentally; such was the power he possessed as the son of a Brahmin in his childhood.
Then, when he did not set his mind upon worldly affairs despite being awakened by his father through various means with the words, "This boy is mute," [the father continued].
Then, having determined in his mind, O Bhārata, that "this man is dull-witted," he married another wife and likewise begot sons.
And his wife was named Piṅgā, and from her were born four sons who were skilled in ritual action and learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (35)
They were worshipped everywhere by the twice-born in sacrifices and peace-offerings; and Aitareya also constantly [worshipped him] three times a day in the temple of Hari.
He recited the supreme mantra to be recited and exerted no effort elsewhere; then his mother, having observed her co-wives' sons in that same manner, [became distressed].
With a heart being torn asunder, he spoke these words to his son: "You have been born only for my suffering; fie upon my birth and my life! (38)
In this world of men, it is clear that no woman is more unfortunate than she who is disregarded by her husband; from such a woman, a son endowed with virtues shall not be born. (39)
Truly fortunate is this Piṅgā, whose sons possess great virtues; they are knowers of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and are honored everywhere for their qualities. (40)

Therefore, O son, unfortunate as I am, I shall immerse myself at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; death is better for me—what fruit is there in my life? You too, remaining thus in great silence, rejoice as a long-time devotee of Hari.
Nārada said: Having heard these words of his mother, the son of Itarā laughed.
Having meditated for a moment, the knower of Dharma bowed to his mother and said: "O Mother, you have been overcome by delusion; though possessed of knowledge, you are as if ignorant. (43)

O auspicious lady, you grieve for that which is not to be grieved for, and you do not grieve at all for that which truly deserves grief; for the sake of this body, why do you delude yourself in this false cycle of existence? 44.
"This is indeed the conduct of fools; it is certainly not fit for my mother. The essence of worldly existence is one thing, yet those who are deluded consider another to be the essence. (45)
Just as people at night perceive a firefly as if it were a lamp, so too you consider this [world] to be essential; hear now its lack of essence. (46)
For such is this human body, O Mānuṣī, which brings suffering from the very moment of conception; it is like a pillar made of a framework of bones, held together by the binding of tendons. (47)
It is smeared with blood, flesh, and fat; it is a vessel for the substances of feces and urine; it is covered with hair, body hair, and grass; and its appearance as gold is utterly deceptive. (48)
In the great single door of the face, adorned with six windows [the eyes], with the two lips as its lintel and likewise provided with the bolt of the teeth; || 49 ||
O beautiful one, when the flow of the channels is like a stream of sweat and the fire of the mouth of Time is present, in such a house there exists a living being named "the Householder. (50)
His wife there was Prakṛti, composed of the three qualities (guṇas); and therein were also awakening, egoism, desire, anger, greed, and the like.
"Alas, what misery! His offspring—thus the fool proceeds. Listen now to the truth regarding his various delusions, exactly as they are. (52)
For the sake of this body, from which streams of phlegm, urine, and other fluids constantly flow like those from a mountain, one becomes deluded. (53)
In this body, which is a repository of all impurities, not even a single spot is pure, just as there is no clean place in a leather bag filled with feces and urine. (54)
Even after touching the channels of one's own body and cleansing the hand with earth and water, why does a man not feel revulsion toward that vessel of impurity? (55)
Even when carefully refined with fragrant waters and other means, the body does not abandon its own inherent nature, just like a dog's tail that cannot be bent.
If a man is not repelled by the foul odor of his own body's impurities, what other cause for detachment could possibly be taught to him? (57)
Purification of the body is prescribed for the purpose of removing odors and stains; after the removal of both, one becomes pure through the purification of the internal state. (58)
Even if one performs purification until death with all the water of the Gaṅgā and with loads of earth as large as mountains, one whose inner disposition is corrupt is not purified. (59)
A person of wicked soul is never purified by bathing at sacred fords or by austerities; does a piece of leather attain purity merely by being steamed and washed at a holy site? (60)
For one whose internal disposition is corrupted, even if they enter the sacrificial fire, there is neither heaven nor liberation; rather, there is only the complete burning away of the body.
Purity of intention is the supreme cleanliness in all actions; otherwise, a beloved wife is embraced with one feeling, while a daughter with another.
A son thinks of the breast in one way, while a husband thinks of it in another; therefore, one should purify the mind—what is the use of other external purifications? (63)

One whose self is completely purified through right disposition attains heaven and liberation; furthermore, by means of the stainless water of knowledge and the clay of true detachment, a person [achieves this]. (64)
It cleanses the stains and odors of ignorance, passion, feces, and urine; for thus do the wise know this body to be impure by its very nature. (65)
Having realized that this body is as worthless as its mere skin, resembling the pithless core of a plantain tree, the wise man who perceives it thus becomes detached from its defects.
He departs from cyclic existence, yet he remains firmly grasped; thus is this great misery, birth, proclaimed to be suffering. (67)
Due to faults unknown to men and by the power of various karmas, one remains in suffering, like someone oppressed by a great mountain.
Just as an embodied being remains in suffering, enveloped by the fetal membrane, so too does one remain agitated in suffering when fallen into the ocean. || 69 ||
With his limbs drenched by the amniotic fluid, the man remains thus distressed, like someone cast into an iron cauldron being cooked by fire.
Likewise, cast into the vessel of the womb, he is cooked by the digestive fire; being pierced incessantly by needles the color of fire.
Whatever suffering arises for a living being, that very suffering becomes eightfold within the womb; indeed, this is what is proclaimed as the suffering of the womb for all creatures. (72)
For all those who are firm in their practice, there shall arise a recollection of all their births, both those residing therein and those conforming to the womb of the Self.
I have died and been born again, and having been born, I have died again; thousands of various wombs have been seen by me in many ways. (74)
Now that I have just been born and have already received the sacraments, I shall therefore perform what is beneficial so that a future conception may not occur.
"I shall request the knowledge of Hari, which brings about the cessation of saṃsāra. Thinking thus, he remained reflecting upon the means to liberation. (76)
For one being born, suffering arises ten million times greater than that experienced while in the womb; the memory that existed during the stay in the womb perishes once he is born. (77)
Upon being touched by the external wind, stupor occurs; for one who is stupefied, a loss of memory arises again very quickly. (78)
Then, due to the loss of mindfulness and by the power of his previous karma, attachment quickly arises for that living being in that very birth. (79)
This world, being passionate and deluded, engages in what ought not to be done; therein it knows neither itself, nor another, nor the divine. (80)
He does not hear what is most beneficial, nor does he see with his eyes; though walking on a level path with even steps, he seems to stumble at every step. (81)
Even when the intellect is present, one does not know, even when being awakened by the wise; therefore, following the sway of passion and delusion, one suffers in saṃsāra. (82)
Due to the absence of memory of the womb, the great sages have declared that the scripture, which accomplishes heaven and liberation, is intended for the purpose of describing that suffering. (83)
That those who, despite possessing this knowledge of the scriptures which accomplishes the purpose of all actions, do not perform what is for their own welfare—this is truly most wonderful.
Furthermore, in childhood there is great suffering because the functions of the senses are unmanifest; even though he desires to do so, he is unable to say or do anything at all. (85)
There is great suffering during the eruption of teeth, as well as from hereditary diseases, various ailments of childhood, and even afflictions by childhood-demons. (86)
With his body overwhelmed by thirst and hunger, he remains in some place crying out loudly; and out of delusion, like a child, he might even consume excrement, urine, and other such things. (87)
In childhood, there is suffering from the piercing of the ears, from being beaten by one's mother and father, from the study of the alphabet and so forth, and from the discipline of the teacher. (88)

And because one is oppressed by desire and passion through the activities of the heedless senses, how indeed can there be happiness for one whose mind is constantly agitated by passion during youth? (89)
From envy, great suffering arises for one who is deluded and attached; like that of one who is intoxicated or provoked, passion leads only to harm. (90)
Tormented by the fire of desire, he finds no sleep at night; for even during the day, how can there be any happiness when one is consumed by the anxiety of acquiring wealth? (91)
Regarding women, who are the abode of all defects and have already been experienced, the pleasure born of sexual union is said to be like the relief of voiding excrement and urine. (92)
Honor is met with dishonor, union with loved ones by separation, and youth is swallowed by old age; where, then, is there any happiness free from affliction?
With a body marked by wrinkles and grey hair, his frame rendered flaccid, he was incapable of all activities, worn out and shattered by old age. (94)
That youth and beauty of man and woman which formerly depended upon one another, once seized by old age in this manner, is no longer pleasing to either.
A man overcome by old age is treated with contempt by his wife, sons, and other kinsmen, as well as by ill-behaved servants, because of his incapacity.
Since one who is not afflicted by disease is able to accomplish dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, therefore a young man should practice dharma.
The imbalance of wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth is called disease; and this body is proclaimed to be a collection of wind and the other humors. (98)
Therefore, this body of the self should be known as consisting of disease; through various kinds of ailments, manifold sufferings arise within the body. (99)
These are not known by their own nature; what else shall I tell you? One hundred and one deaths are established within this body.
Among these, one is associated with time (the constitutional), while the rest are known as adventitious. Those which are declared here to be adventitious are pacified by medicines.
Neither recitation, fire-offerings, nor gifts can pacify untimely death; likewise, various diseases, as well as serpents and other such creatures, are formidable. (102)
Poisons, malevolent spells, and the gates of death for embodied beings—even those afflicted by snakes, diseases, and the like—[are overcome] by Dhanvantari himself. (103)
Neither asceticism, nor mantras, nor friends, nor kinsmen can restore to health a living being whose time has come; such was the case with the King of Niṣadha. (104)
Even great-souled ones perfected in yoga through elixirs, austerities, and recitations are unable to protect a man afflicted by Time.
Even timely death cannot be avoided by the wise, nor by those who are united [in strength]. There is no suffering equal to death; there is no fear equal to death. (106)
For all embodied beings, there is no fear equal to death; [it seizes away] one's virtuous wife, sons, friends, as well as kingdom, sovereignty, and pleasures. (107)
Death severs all those who are bound by the snares of affection; do you not see it, O Mother, even in the midst of a thousand? (108)
People are said to have a lifespan of a hundred years, yet they either do or do not reach it; some men perish at eighty, while others perish at seventy.
The maximum lifespan is established as sixty [thousand years], yet even that is not fixed; for a living being, it lasts only as long as the life-span ordained by their prior karmas. (110)
Half of that lifespan is taken away by night in the form of death; likewise, it is lost through childhood, delusion, old age, and decay.
Twenty years pass for men, devoid of dharma, desire, and wealth, through various adventitious existences consisting of diseases and sorrows. (112)
For even there, half is taken away; what remains is indeed life. At the end of that life, one encounters death, which is most terrible.
Having died, one is born again among millions of wombs by the power of karma; that which is the separation of men from their bodies occurs according to the number of their karmas. (114)
That which is designated as death is not, in the ultimate sense, a destruction; it is merely for one who has entered into great darkness while his vital organs are being severed. (115)
There is no comparison anywhere for the suffering that death brings to a living being; "O father! O mother! O beloved!"—thus one cries out, utterly distressed. (116)
Like a frog swallowed by a serpent, a person is devoured by death, utterly abandoned by kinsmen and surrounded by those once dear to him.
Sighing long and hot with a parched mouth, he turned repeatedly upon the four corners of his bed.
Utterly deluded, he throws his hands and feet about in every direction; from the bed he seeks the ground, and from the ground he seeks the bed again, and then the ground once more. (119)
Naked, stripped of shame, and smeared with excrement, he begs for water with his throat, lips, and palate parched. (120)
Drawn by the noose of Time, he dug five pits while reflecting on his own riches, wondering, "To whom will these belong when I am dead? (121)
While others are looking on, the life-force dies, making a gurgling sound in the throat; like a leech from a blade of grass, it enters body after body in succession.
Having attained the higher [state] in part, he abandons his former body; for the suffering of longing after death is indeed greater for the man of discernment.

The suffering at the moment of death is momentary, whereas that caused by longing is infinite; this has now been understood by me, that when the Guru dies, [the disciple] becomes dead [to his purpose]. (124)
One should not further crave another's wealth, for craving is the cause of lightness; it is suffering in the beginning, likewise in the middle, and indeed terrible suffering in the end.
"The succession of sufferings for all beings is natural; and among all diseases, hunger is considered the most severe. (126)
And that [pain] is pacified for a mere moment by the application of food and medicine; yet the intense agony of the disease of hunger cuts away one's strength entirely. (127)
Overcome by it, a man dies just as he would from other diseases; for in my house, there exists only the pride of a king. (128)
Every ornament is a burden; every ointment is for me [a source of distress]; every song is mere idle chatter, and all my conduct is that of one perpetually intoxicated. (129)
Thus, when one reflects upon them, what happiness can there be in the enjoyments of sovereignty for kings whose minds are distracted by their mutual desire for victory? (130)
Generally, because of the intoxication of wealth, great kings such as Nahuṣa and others fell even after reaching heaven; who finds happiness in prosperity? (131)
Situated higher and higher above the gods in a state of mutual excellence, the fruit of merit is enjoyed by men in heaven through the total exhaustion of its root. (132)
And no other action is performed; that is the most terrible fault here, just as a tree with its roots severed falls helplessly to the earth. (133)
In the same way, when their roots of merit are exhausted, the dwellers of heaven cause them to fall; thus, upon reflection, there is no happiness even for the gods in heaven. (134)
Likewise, the suffering of hell-beings is already well known; what more need be described? Even among immobile beings there are sufferings, such as forest fires, frost, and withering. (135)
There was the intense lopping of bark with axes, the carving of it, and the felling of leaves, branches, and fruits by fierce winds.
There is constant trampling by wild elephants and embodied beings, as well as thirst and hunger for serpents, along with their fury and terrible suffering. (137)
O Mother, the slaying of the wicked in this world, their binding with nooses, and likewise the suffering of reptiles occurs again and again. (138)
The birth and death of insects and the like occur thus unexpectedly; the suffering of beasts and birds from rain, cold, and heat is extremely painful. (139)
Deer are also constantly terrified by the great affliction of hunger and thirst; now hear what the sufferings are for the various classes of beasts and serpents.
The subduing of hunger, thirst, cold, and so forth; killing, binding, and beating; piercing the nose; causing terror; and striking with a goad or a hook. (141)
The punishment of canes, spears, and so forth; fetters, mallets, and goads; the affliction of carrying heavy loads; and the torment of training and warfare. (142)
Separation from one's own herd, being led away into the forest, famine, misfortune, folly, and poverty. (143)
There is the state of high and low, death, and the turmoil of the kingdom; there is suffering from mutual subjugation, and again, from mutual rivalry. (144)
Since the world of the moving and the stationary is pervaded by such sufferings as the impermanence of powers and the downfall of those who have attained eminence, [it is not to be desired]. (145)
Therefore, the wise person should renounce everything from the hells up to the human realm; one merely shifts the burden from one shoulder to the other, yet mistakenly considers it to be rest.
In the same way, all this suffering in the world is pacified by suffering; thus, this entire world is characterized by mutual rivalry and striving for superiority. (147)
Having recognized that [the world] is agitated by sufferings, one should attain supreme detachment; from detachment arises dispassion, and from dispassion comes the birth of knowledge. || 148 ||
Having known that supreme Viṣṇu through knowledge, one may attain liberation; O Mother, I would never take delight in such a world as this.
Just as a pure royal swan reveals the impurity of crows, listen, O Mother, to where I may dwell free from affliction and find delight. (150)
It has ignorance as its fierce current, various karmas as its many branches, volitions as its gadflies and crocodiles, and grief and joy as its frost and heat. (151)
[He taught] the darkness of the gloom of delusion, the predatory beasts and reptiles of greed, the false path of the sense-objects, and the liberation from desire and anger.
Having passed beyond that great fortress, I have entered the vast forest; having entered it, those who know that [reality] neither grieve nor become corrupted. (153)
He does not fear anyone, nor do any fear him.

In that forest, there are seven great trees, seven rivers, and seven fruits; there are seven hermitages, seven meditative absorptions (samādhis), and seven initiations—such is the nature of this wilderness.
There were divine flowers and fruits of five colors, some of four colors, and others of three, two, or even a single color. (156)
Producing [fruits and flowers], the trees stand there pervading that forest.
Seven true women dwell there, who, with faces turned downwards, draw up the essences from the people of the sun; let anyone speak truly of all of them as they really are.
There are exactly seven mountains here, by which the three worlds are supported; and there are seven rivers, streams that always carry the waters of Brahma.
Vigor, the granting of fearlessness, non-malice, as well as skill, steadiness, freedom from anger, and pleasant speech as the seventh; || 160 ||
Thus these mountains situated in that Forest of Knowledge are to be known: Dṛḍhaniścaya (Firm Resolve), Bhāsā (Radiance), Samatā (Equanimity), Nigraha (Restraint), and Guṇa (Virtue). || 161 ||
Freedom from possessiveness and austerity are here, and contentment is the seventh lake; from the realization of the Lord’s qualities, devotion becomes the first river. (162)
The second is worship with flowers and other offerings; the third is circumambulation; the fourth consists of words of praise; and the fifth is dedication to the Lord. (163)
The sixth is declared to be oneness with Brahman, and the seventh is indeed perfection; these seven rivers have been described here by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
Brahmā, Dharma, Yama, Agni, Indra, and Varuṇa as well. || 165 ||
These people worship the seven [groups] beginning with Dhruva and Dhanada; there, in the vicinity of Vaikuṇṭha, is the confluence of rivers.
Satisfied in the Self, peaceful and self-controlled, they go from the highest to the Supreme; some are like trees, some are women, and others are knowers of reality.
Some who are most proficient in knowledge say that there are exactly seven rivers; here, with the desire for unswerving vows, I practice celibacy.
In this state, Brahman alone is the fuel, Brahman is the fire, and Brahman is the sacrificial grass; water is Brahman, the teacher is Brahman, and this vow of celibacy is Brahman for me.
The wise know this very thing to be such subtle celibacy (brahmacarya). And hear from me, O mother, about the guru who was the bestower of knowledge upon me. (170)

There is one Teacher, there is no second Teacher; dwelling within the heart itself, he instructs the person. Directed by him as water is drawn up by the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), I act exactly as I am enjoined.
O King, I declare that there is no second Guru residing in the heart like Him; for it was by disregarding Mukunda as their Guru that all the Dānavas were utterly defeated.

There is but one kinsman, no second exists; him who dwells within the heart, I speak of as my kin. Guided by him, the Seven Sages became possessed of true kinship and shine with splendor in the seven heavens.
The life of celibacy (brahmacarya) should be practiced; now hear what the state of a householder (gārhasthya) is like: my wife is the form of Prakṛti, and my mind is never fixed upon her.
O Mother, she who always dwells within my mind is the accomplisher of all my goals; she is the nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, and the ear as the fifth. || 175 ||
Mind and intellect—these seven are my blazing fires; smell, taste, form, sound, and touch as the fifth. || 176 ||
That which is to be reflected upon and that which is to be understood—these seven are my sacrificial fuels; Nārāyaṇa himself partakes of the oblation offered through meditation on Nārāyaṇa.
With such a sacrifice as this, I worship that Lord. For one who desires nothing, all desires shall be fulfilled; and for one who harbors no hatred, all faults shall cease.

No taints cling to my essential nature, just as a drop of water does not adhere to lotus leaves; for me, who am eternal, the impermanent states do not exist at all as I perceive them through their manifold nature.
The web of enjoyments does not cling to his actions, just as the web of rays does not cling to the sun in the sky.
O mother, do not be sorrowful because of such a son; I shall lead you to that state which cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices.
Having heard these words of her son, she was struck with wonder and reflected: "If this is truly so, then my son is certainly wise. (182)
"While I am thinking such things as, 'I shall attain renown in the worlds, and from that I shall have supreme fame,' the Blessed Lord Hari [appeared] during the night. (183)
Delighted by those words and filled with wonder, he appeared before him; having emerged in person from his own form, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Illuminating the world with his radiance, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, he then emerged from the earth with his hair standing on end and his voice choked with tears.
Then the wise Aitareya, with his hands joined in reverence upon his head, offered praise.
We meditate upon you, the Blessed One Vāsudeva; salutations to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Homage to him who is consciousness alone, whose form is supreme bliss, who delights in the Self, who is peaceful, and for whom the perception of duality has ceased.
Salutations to the one who is followed by the bliss of the Self, to the one whose form is perfect renunciation; salutations to the great Hṛṣīkeśa, to you of infinite power.
May He who is to be attained when speech has ceased along with the mind, who is nameless, formless, pure consciousness alone, and who transcends both being and non-being—may He protect us. 190.
Salutation to You, that Brahman, in whom this world exists, from whom it departs, and from whom it is born—just as the nature of clay persists in all things made of clay. 191.
I bow down to that which neither the mind, the intellect, nor the vital breaths of the senses touch or know, which is spread within and without like the sky.

These—the body, senses, vital breath, mind, and intellect—function in their respective activities because they are supported by a portion of Him; otherwise, they would not exist, just as iron does not burn unless heated, for these have been placed in their positions by His glance.
I bow fourfold, threefold, twofold, and in a single manner to him, the Teacher, the Supreme Lord, throughout the preceding, subsequent, and future ages. (194)
Having abandoned the various states of existence, those desiring liberation worship you who consist of ten aspects; we, therefore, pay homage to you, the supreme, stainless Truth. (195)

Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Great Being, the one of great majesty, the Lord of manifestations; O Supreme Most High, whose pair of lotus-feet are cherished by the lotus-buds in the hands of the entire assembly of lords of the Sātvatas—salutations to You! 196.

O Blessed One, salutations to You! Fire is Your mouth, the earth Your pair of feet, the sky Your head, and the moon and sun Your eyes; all the worlds are Your belly, and the four directions are Your arms. 197.
O God, even if one were to compress all births throughout all time, they would not equal the number of living beings that have been swallowed by me here in this terrible great ocean of saṃsāra. (198)
O Lord, although I have assumed many bodies upon mountains such as Himavat, Mahendra, Kailāsa, and Meru, I have never attained such great prosperity as I have now.

O King, there are no regions on earth where I was not born, nor where I have not perished; nor are there any places where living beings did not come into existence, nor where I was not devoured by hosts of creatures. (200)

O Lord, throughout my various births, the quantity of tears that have fallen from me overcome by grief is such that even the clouds could not release that much water, even in hundreds of thousands of divine years. (201)
O God of gods, I believe that the number of atoms in the earth might reach my count of parents, but I am not able to count my friends, enemies, dependents, and kinsmen. 202.

"O Lord, though my mind has been offered to you again and again, that most difficult enemy, Kāma, forcibly seizes it along with his allies such as wrath and the rest; what am I to do about this, O Blessed One? (203)

Thus, O Viṣṇu, I am deeply afflicted, while you are the mine of compassion; for one who has fallen into the pit of saṃsāra, having sought refuge in the Great-Souled One, does not perish, even if he is utterly destitute. (204)

For the sick, the physician is indeed the ultimate refuge; for a man submerged in the great ocean, it is the boat; for a child, it is the mother and father; and for one distressed by this most terrible saṃsāra, O Hari, you alone are such a refuge.
Be gracious, O Lord of All, Soul of All Beings, Cause of All, Essence of the Ultimate Truth! Lift me up from this pit of saṃsāra, from this mass of manifold sufferings, by taking me as your own.

O Urukrama, O Acyuta, as I sit here, I behold this world being repeatedly tormented by hunger, thirst, and the three qualities of nature; by cold, heat, wind, and water, both individually and in combination; and by the fire of desire and by unbearable anger.
May all things be auspicious and may every fault perish for the entire world, now that I have praised with devotion today the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign, the Sustainer of the Universe, Vāsudeva.

May those beings who are on the earth, in heaven, in the intermediate space, or in the netherworld—whatever multitudes of living creatures there may be—be endowed with success today, now that Vāsudeva, the sustainer of the world, has been praised by me.

May those who are ignorant become knowers of wisdom, and may those whose minds are constantly fierce partake in tranquility, once Vāsudeva—the sustainer of the universe, the infinite, and the creator of the world—has been praised by me.
May those who hear me as I praise [the Lord], and likewise others who see me uttering this, including gods, asuras, humans, and animals—may they all become partakers of the yoga of Acyuta. || 211 ||

And even those who are mute due to impaired senses, who neither recite nor behold [the scriptures], and even animals such as insects and ants—may they too become partakers of the yoga of Acyuta. (212)

May sufferings perish from the world; may the host of defects, beginning with greed, depart from living beings. May a person’s disposition toward other people be exactly as it is toward oneself, a brother, or a son. (213)

May the bonds of worldly existence become loosened for all people when Viṣṇu—the physician of saṃsāra, skilled in the removal of all defects, and the cause of ultimate bliss—abides within their hearts. (214)

May my evil be utterly destroyed—whatever I have done with my mind, whatever I have uttered with my speech, and whatever has been performed by my body—when Vāsudeva, the sustainer of the world, is remembered. (215)
Just as when "Vāsudeva" is uttered, or during the chanting of a devotee of Viṣṇu, or even when Hari is remembered, my sin departs; by that truth, let my sin be destroyed. (216)

"This man is deluded, of small intellect, and of little exertion; even my afflicted mind is not attached to sense-objects regarding You. O Lord of All, show such mercy to me who am prostrate before You; for even the Lotus-born Brahmā, O God, is not able to praise You.

Therefore, be gracious, O Blessed One; O Viṣṇu, show compassion toward me who am without a protector, for you are indeed the supremely merciful one. O Hari, you ought to lift up this wretched soul submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra; O Ananta, you are the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
O Bhārata, having been praised in this manner by Aitareya, the Lord Vāsudeva, whose self is vast, spoke these words to him with joy.
"O child Aitareya, I am pleased with this hymn of yours and with your devotion; choose from me whatever boon you desire, even if it be difficult to obtain."
Aitareya said: "O Hari, this alone is the boon I have eternally desired as my protector: become the helmsman for me as I sink in the terrible cycle of worldly existence."

The Blessed One said: You are indeed already liberated from saṃsāra, you whose devotion is such as this. Bound by the planets and the great planets, the thirteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] does not exist for you at all.
And whoever shall constantly praise me, Vāsudeva, who is desired in the Guptakṣetra with this hymn, he shall attain the destruction of his sins.
Since evil shall reach destruction by means of this hymn, it shall therefore attain renown as "Aghanāśana" (the Destroyer of Evil). || 224 ||
Whoever, having fasted on the eleventh day, shall recite this hymn before me, that person of purified soul will attain my world. || 225 ||
Just as the Guptakṣetra is dear among all sacred fields, so too is this hymn most dear to me among all hymns of praise. (226)
And those beings for whose sake this is recited by the great-souled ones shall, through my grace, attain peace, fortune, and wisdom. (227)
And you, my child, should practice the Vedic duties correctly with faith; by performing them without desire for reward and having surrendered them to me, you shall not incur bondage.
Perform sacrifices with offerings and, having obtained a wife, gladden your mother; by means of intense meditation upon me, you will undoubtedly attain me.
The intellect, the mind, the elements, and the organs of perception and action—those which consist of thirteen planets are the thirteen great planets. (230)
That which is to be awakened to, that which is to be reflected upon, the sense of "I," and sound; touch, taste, form, and smell; as well as speech and grasping. (231)
Vihṛti, utsarga, and ānanda—these are the thirteen great grahas (planets). O son, these great grahas are purified by their own respective pure grahas.
"Accept this through the yoga of meditation; in this way, you shall attain liberation from me. Thus, O hero, through actions you will attain freedom from action. (233)

Just as a skillful person obtains gold from lead when it has been pierced by mercury, so too [does one obtain Me] through one who follows the conduct of their caste and stage of life and has surrendered all actions unto Me. (234)
For one joined with meditation upon me, liberation is not difficult to attain here; therefore, O Nanda, remaining thus, be devoted to your vows. (235)
Having rescued seven generations of your lineage, you shall attain me; furthermore, the Vedas shall now manifest to you even though they have not been studied.
Therefore, go to Koṭitīrtha at the sacrifice of Harimedhas; there, everything that your mother desires shall be fulfilled for you.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu entered into the midst of the forms, being gazed upon for a mere moment by Mātṛ and Suta.
Then, having prostrated before the image of Vāsudeva, the astonished Aitareya, filled with joy, spoke these words to his own mother: || 239 ||
In the past, I was a Śūdra, terrified by the defects of saṃsāra; I went for refuge to a Brāhmaṇa who had attained the ultimate Dharma. || 240 ||
That compassionate one told me the twelve-syllable mantra; having said, "Chant this always," I have chanted it constantly.
By the power of that recitation, my birth from your womb occurred; having regained my memory, I possess devotion to Viṣṇu and shall remain here forever.
And now I am departing for that sacrifice of Harimedhas; having bowed to you in your form for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, I seek your favor. (243)
Then he approached him as he was performing sacrifice, surrounded by millions of Brahmins, at the site of Koṭitīrtha in the city named Mahīnagara.
Having informed his mother that he was going home, that twice-born man declared at the sacrifice: "Salutations to that Blessed Viṣṇu of unimpeded intellect. (245)
"Deceived by Māyā, we wander in the ocean of karma"—this verse of great significance was [spoken] by those twice-born ones, headed by Harimedhas. (246)
Having heard him, they honored that noble one with offerings of seats and worship; then those twice-born ones were gratified by him through his mastery of the meaning of the Vedas.
Harimedhas gave away all his sacrificial fees, including his daughter; having taken the wealth and the maiden, he returned to his own home.
Having paid homage to his mother and fathered stainless sons, Aitareya, devoted to the vow of the twelfth day, performed sacrifices with various rites.
"Through meditation upon Vāsudeva, he subsequently attained liberation; such is Vāsudeva himself who is present here, O Bhārata. (250)
Whatever one offers, worships, or praises, all that is known to be inexhaustible for him; as for the fruit previously declared by me to you in the Śivadharmas, [it shall be so]. || 251 ||
Such a state does a mortal obtain through the grace of Vāsudeva. || 252 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Then, O Pārtha, desiring once again to show favor to the people, I wished to bring the Sun-god Mārtaṇḍa, who is perceptible to the senses, to this place.
Because the Lord Sun is the boat for all living beings, O son of Kuntī, the Sun is considered the sustainer of the universe both in this world and the next.
Those men who remember the Sun with devotion, those who glorify him, and those who worship him constantly—they have achieved their life's purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Those who are devoted to the Sun, whose minds are constantly fixed upon Him, and who always remember the Sun—they do not become partakers of suffering.
Charming mansions, women adorned with various ornaments, and wealth whose limit is unseen—these are the fruits of the ritual of worshipping the Sun. || 5 ||

Devotion to the Sun is difficult to attain, and his worship is likewise difficult to achieve; giving gifts to him is difficult, and therefore, the performance of fire-offerings for him is also difficult.
The life of that person whose tongue-tip bears the two syllables "ra-vi" joined with "namaskāra" and so forth is truly fruitful.
Thus, O Pārtha, reflecting in my heart upon the great majesty of the Sun-born, I propitiated the Sun with devotion for a full hundred years.
By means of very pure recitation and by subsisting on air alone, the omnipresent Lord then fashioned a second form from space through the power of yoga.
Resplendent with brilliance, he became visible to the eye like the shining sun.
Having joined my palms in reverence and bowed down to that Lord Ravi, I fully gratified the divine Sovereign with various Sāman hymns.
Pleased, the giver of boons said to me, "O celestial sage, I have been propitiated by you through penance for a very long time; choose a boon as you desire. (12)
Thus addressed, I, with palms joined in reverence, praised the Lord of the World with these words: "If you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me—" (13)
Then, O Lord, that portion which functions in Kāmarūpa was formerly propitiated by King Rājavardhana and by the people.
"And with that digit of yours, O Bhānu, you ought to remain here forever. Then, O Bhārata, the gratified god replied, "So be it. (15)
I installed the Sun-god under the name Bhaṭṭāditya; because he was installed by me as a Bhaṭṭa, the Sun proclaimed [him thus] throughout the world.
Then, having worshipped that Sun-god who had been made to enter [me] with flowers, my limbs overflowing with an excess of devotion, I then performed this hymn of praise.

He who possesses the secrets of all the Vedas, who is known by one hundred and eight names, who is the seven-horsed Sun, whose nature is inconceivable, and who is the supreme among the most compassionate; (18)
The reviver, victory, life, the lord of life, the master of the world; the refuge of time, the creator of time, the great yogi, the one of great intelligence. || 19 ||
The God who brings an end to all beings, the delighter of Kamalānanda, the thousand-footed, the bestower of boons, adorned with divine earrings.
He who loves dharma, whose nature is appropriate, the progenitor, he whose vehicle is the wind; Āditya, the one free from anger, Sūrya, the one garlanded with rays, the possessor of light. || 21 ||

The maker of day, the stealer of days, the silent one, the one with a beautiful chariot, the best among charioteers, the husband of the queen, he whose seed is gold, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the maker of light.
The ornament of the sky, the sustainer, the distributor, the captivating one; the wise one, the lord of creatures, the fortunate one, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Śrī, the best of physicians. (23)
The Lord of the World, who creates light, is honored by the guardians of the world; he knows the intentions [of beings], is well-guided, great-souled, and compassionate toward his devotees. (24)
He who makes fame renowned, the eternal, the radiant, the remover of impurity; he who has conquered joy, the one of great heroism, the swan, the agent of dissolution. || 25 ||

One who has accomplished all that was to be done, who possesses excellent associations, who is widely learned, and a master of speech; one who is worshiped by the universe, who removes death, who is compassionate, and the cause of righteousness. (26)

He who removes the suffering of those who bow before him, who is free from disease, who bestows long life, who grants happiness, who is himself blissful; he who is auspiciousness itself, whose eyes are like lotuses, who observes vows, and who grants the fruit of vows. (27)

He is pure, full, the giver of the path to liberation, the enjoyer, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), Dhanvantari, the speaker of pleasant words, the knower of the science of archery (Dhanurveda), and the sole sovereign.

He is the father of the world, the smoke-bannered one, the dispeller of darkness, the teacher who has shaken off all impurity; he is the lord of rays, the guest of honor, possessed of auspicious conduct, and fond of purity.

He who is fond of conciliation, the kinsman of the world, manifold in form, the creator of the ages and the rest; the bridge of dharma, the witness of the world, the rider of the celestial chariot, the bestower of all, and the Lord. (30)
Thus praised by me with these eight hundred names, may the Lord, who is dear to all the worlds, be pleased for the sake of all the worlds. (31)
Pleased by this praise, Bhāskara said to me: "O divine sage, desiring to do what is pleasing to you, I shall always remain here with a portion of myself."
Whoever worships me here as Bhaṭṭāditya with great devotion obtains that same fruit as if they had worshipped me thousands of times in the form of Kāmarūpa.
And whatever a Brahmin shall give here, whether it be very little or much, intended for me, that shall become inexhaustible and I shall accept it as if it were produced from my own hand.
On a Sunday, a person [should offer] three hundred great lotuses consisting of red utpalas, kahlāras, kesaras, and karavīrakas. (35)
Furthermore, those who shall worship me here on the seventh or the sixth lunar day will certainly attain whatever desires they may pray for.
Through seeing me and through devotion, there is the destruction of disease and poverty; by prostrating, one attains heaven, and by hearing [of me] constantly, one attains liberation.
And whoever shows me lack of devotion shall undoubtedly go to destruction; as for those one hundred and eight names that were recited by you before me—
For one who recites or listens [to this] three times a day or at a single time, the fruit is as follows: he becomes famous, fortunate, learned, very happy, and pleasing to behold. (39)
He who, being self-restrained and pure, should constantly hear or recite this, shall live for a hundred years, free from all diseases. (40)
Even a very small amount of food prepared for him shall become inexhaustible; he shall be eternally victorious, and likewise, he shall remember his past lives.
Therefore, you should recite this supreme and great benediction; likewise, prepare an excellent sacrificial pit before me for the purpose of bathing.
"Wherever there is a portion of Kāmarūpa, there a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made in the forest. Having thus granted these boons, the Sun vanished right there.
Then, at the word of Bhāskara and to the left of Siddheśa, I drew a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the middle of the forest with a blade of darbha grass.
O Bhārata, that the Kunda tree and those other trees had become the existence of the desire-realm and the form-realm—this great wonder arose in my mind.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, whether a woman or a man, having performed an auspicious bath in the pool, beholds Bhaṭṭāditya.
The merit of one who worships that chariot shall be infinite; and on whichever path he performs the chariot procession, [therein his merit is likewise boundless]. (47)
And those people who behold it are all fortunate, without a doubt; they shall be endowed with sons, grain, and wealth, free from disease, and possessed of splendor.

Those men who cause the chariot festival to be performed will become such; they shall obtain that fruit which has been proclaimed by the wise as residing in all sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others. (49)

And that same fruit is obtained on the seventh day at the pool of Bhaṭṭāditya. Whoever bathes in that pool and offers an oblation (arghya) to the Sun, enjoys the fruit of having given a hundred tawny cows.
Arjuna said: "O great sage, Vāsudeva and all the others speak in this very way. (51)
"Without the offering (arghya) to the Sun, all that is performed becomes fruitless. O best among those who know the rules, I wish to hear the procedure for that. (52)
Nārada said: Listen to that ritual which destroys all sins—the manner in which Brahmā and the other gods offer arghya to the Great-Souled Bhāskara.

First, at dawn when the sun has risen, having become pure, one should prepare a small mandala with red sandalwood paste upon a larger circle made of cow dung. Then, having filled a copper vessel with water mixed with red sandalwood, white sandalwood, and other such substances, one should place within it gold, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), *dūrvā* grass, curd, and clarified butter, and set it down. || 54 ||

One should touch one's own body with this mantra: *oṃ khakholkāya namaḥ*. Having recited it seven times, one should remain standing; thereby purification arises and the body becomes fit for worship. Afterwards, having meditated upon the god Savitṛ seated upon his throne in the center of the maṇḍala as the twelve-fold [sun] being worshipped by the gods and others, and having placed the previously mentioned arghya vessel upon the head, kneeling on the ground and facing the sun, one should recite the arghya-mantra with the mind fixed upon him. That is said to have "issued forth from the mouth of the Sun. || 55 ||
By the sound of whose recitation the Sun-god halts his chariot, accepts the water-offering (arghya), and bestows whatever desired boon is sought. || 56 ||
Oṃ! To him they say the seven meters stand upon his chariot as his steeds; he whose charioteer is Aruṇa stands at the front, driving the chariot.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayaṃtī, and Pāpanāśanī, as well as Iḍā and Piṅgalā—these horse-faced ones likewise carry [the waters]. || 58 ||
And Ḍiṇḍi, Śeṣanāga, and likewise Gaṇādhyakṣa; Skanda, Revanta, Tārkṣya, and likewise the two birds Kalmāṣa and Pakṣin. || 59 ||
And Queen Nikṣubhā, the goddess Lalitā, and Saṃjñikā, as well as the gods who partake in the sacrifice and others who have been proclaimed. || 60 ||
Surrounded by these who dwell both below and above, I invoke that creator of the world, the dispeller of darkness.
O Blessed One, the Sun, as you set this sacrifice in motion, please accept this water for honor and this water for the feet; salutations, salutations!
Invocation: "O thousand-rayed one, granter of boons, embodiment of life, salutations to you. Thus is the rite for effecting presence (*sāṃnidhyakaraṇa*).

Having uttered "Oṃ vaṣaṭ" and looking at the two feet of the Sun, one should set down the vessel upon the ground with both feet; that is called the *pādya* (water for the feet). Having thus offered the *pādya*, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should say: "A most welcome [welcome], O Blessed One! Come, having bestowed your grace upon me, please be seated. Accept this worship here and grant your favor in your mind. Remain right here while I perform the worship. (63)

One should thus offer the request with this mantra to the Lotus-Seated One (*kamalāsana*). Then that Lotus-Seated One, the Delighter of Kamalā, takes his seat. Once he is seated upon the throne, one should perform the remaining worship according to this procedure: *Oṃ somamūrtaye kṣīrodapataye namaḥ.* (This is the bathing with milk and other substances. *Oṃ bhāskarāya nīra-vāsine namaḥ.* (This is the bathing with water.)

Then one should give a pair of white garments with this mantra: "O Sūrya, please accept out of compassion this pair of garments for me; one is a waist-ornament for you, and the second is a covering for your body. (64)
Then one should offer the sacred thread with this mantra: "O Lord of Gods, please accept this pure and supreme sacred thread, consisting of threads of [cotton] fiber; salutations be unto you. (65)

Then, according to one's capacity, one should offer ornaments such as a white crown and a ring with this mantra: "This crown bound with jewels, this ring, and these ornaments—accept this decoration offered by me with devotion. (66)
Having thus presented the ornaments, one should afterwards offer an unguent mixed with saffron filaments, saffron, camphor, and red sandalwood. || 67 ||
Obeisance! O Lord of fierce rays, this essence of trees is most dear to you; it is worthy of you alone, O Master, so please accept it from me out of compassion. (68)
Then one should perform worship with *campaka*, *japā*, *karavīra*, *karṇaka*, *kesara*, *kokanada*, and other such flowers. || 69 ||
Oṃ! This divine incense, the essence of the forest trees, rich in fragrance, the most excellent scent, and the food of all the gods—may it be accepted. (70)

The mantra for the incense of *śallakī*: Then, one should present the food offering (*naivedya*) prepared from milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other ingredients with this mantra: "This food offering is nectar for all beings, increasing their vital breaths. It is given by me in a full vessel; accept it and be gracious unto me. (71)

Then, having offered water for purification, betel, a lamp, the *ārārtika* ceremony, cooling refreshments, and a renewed worship (*punar-pūjā*), and having praised [the deity] according to one's ability, one should say, "Forgive my good deeds or my evil deeds," and dismiss [the deity]. Then, bowing once more and offering gold, garments, a sacred thread, and ornaments to a Brāhmaṇa, one should collect the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) and cast them into the water. || 72 ||
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the *arghya*.
Whoever should thus daily present the arghya offering to Bhāskara, whether in an image or even in a mandala, at dawn, shall become as dear to the Sun as his own self.
By this rite, Karṇa offers the arghya to the Sun; thereafter, O son of Pṛthā, he is considered by Sūrya to be as dear to him as his own self.

If one is unable [to perform the full ritual], one should daily offer a single arghya to the Maker of Day (the Sun). Then, on this Rathasaptamī day, it should be offered with diligence into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having obtained the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), one shall attain the world of the Sun; therefore, O Bhārata, the arghya offering should be given here with every effort.
Such is this Lord Bhaṭṭāditya who resides here; he is far greater than that, for he is manifoldly the destroyer of sins and the increaser of dharma.
And here, O Pārtha, is the eightfold divine [vision] which produces immediate conviction; for it is like the halāhala poison that has already been consumed by those who have committed sins. (78)
Arjuna said: O Lord of Sages, I desire to hear about the divine wall; how and what things should be done here, by which [actions] merit and demerit become clearly manifest? (1)
Nārada said: The ordeal of the oath, the balance, the pot, poison, fire, the heated gold coin, the fruit, and the rice—these eight, the wise know, are the divine ordeals.

And in matters where there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another; likewise in cases of treason against the king, in accusations of defamation, and in cases of violence. (3)
One who does not know the truth in its essence should swear an oath; for even the great seers and the gods have taken oaths for the sake of truth.
O descendant of Bharata, King Javana, being weakened, was said to have taken a false oath in the presence of Vasiṣṭha, along with his lineage, within the course of a year.
The blind man who would go to the house of an enemy by performing false oaths is a fool who opens for himself the very door to the Raurava hell.
"Evil-doers indeed think, 'No one sees us'; yet the gods see them, as do their own inner selves."
The sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire; heaven, earth, the waters, and Yama; day and night, and both twilights—Dharma indeed knows the conduct of a man.
Thus, having understood this, one should employ oaths for the sake of truth; for by making vain oaths, one perishes both in this world and after death.
"Speaking thus, 'I speak this truth,' the witness shall become [pure]; then, having bestowed the fruit of his good and evil deeds, he, being pure, shall touch the feet of the Sun. (10)
Then, even a Brāhmaṇa touching a weapon, a Kṣatriya touching me, a Vaiśya touching me, and a Śūdra touching his own guru likewise [become impure]. || 11 ||
One should touch one's venerable mother and father; this is indeed common to all. O son of Pāṇḍu, the nature of the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa) has already been explained to you.

The king should likewise cause the hair of those in the stages of life (varṇins) to be shaved, with the exception of the brahmins; whichever man is devoted to whichever deity, he should have that man drink [the water] dedicated to that deity.
One should cause an equal portion to be offered to the gods and specifically to Āditya; and for all the fierce deities, one should bathe their weapons and missiles.

Alternatively, having taken the bath-water or the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should cause the person to drink fresh [water]; within three weeks, one should declare the result regarding the treasure-trove.
Henceforth, hear the procedure for the great ordeal (*mahādivya*), which cuts through the doubts of all and is indeed a divine test of one's courage. (16)
"In the past, Brahmā declared that [the gift] should be given with the head; however, for those who are exceedingly fierce, it may clearly be given even without the head. (17)
A king should not cause the heads of virtuous ascetics to be shaved; nor should he provide a water-pot during a strong wind, nor a fire during the heat of the season.
Likewise, for those of the [four] castes, [one should give] time, and for those with diseases of the mouth, rice.
And for those Brahmins afflicted by leprosy or bile, poison is not [the appropriate punishment]; rather, they all deserve the heated gold coin (*taptamāṣaka*), which is righteous and free from harm.
In a region afflicted by disease or pestilence, some here paralyze oaths, the treasury, and even divine ordeals by means of demonic mantras.
The lord of the earth, having recognized those who obstruct divine beings as constant evildoers, should employ those who are devoted to the Dharma against them to dispel their hostility. (22)
The king should banish them from his own kingdom, for they are thorns to the world; he should constantly exert effort in their pursuit.
For they are of evil conduct and are thieves even among thieves; therefore, one should employ those whose faults have been previously observed in minor ordeals.
Even regarding great matters, those who know the Dharma and are devoted to righteousness do not utter false speech, which has never been found in them since their very birth.
O King, descendant of Bharata, a wise monarch, having recognized the righteousness of a man, should place his trust in their words. || 26 ||

One who causes [an ordeal] to be performed out of anger or greed becomes defiled himself; therefore, the divine test should be administered against sinners, and among those, the balance (dhaṭa) is first described.
On level ground in the south-eastern direction, two "shaven-headed" (muṇḍaka) vessels should be placed beneath a sacrificial tree.
The measurement of the pillar is proclaimed to be seven cubits; one should bury two cubits of the wood so that five cubits remain visible. (29)
The distance between the two should be four cubits; furthermore, the wise man should construct a firm wooden beam over the top of the pillar.
One should have a weighing beam made four cubits long, free of blemishes, and stable; it should be made from the wood of the Khadira, Arjuna, Śiṃśapā, or Śāla trees.
The beam of the balance must be made, as well as two loops for the strings; likewise, the scale (dhaṭa) should be placed in a clean place, facing east, and kept steady.
A balance-beam should likewise be made from stone or from pillars; it may be crafted by a skilled merchant, a goldsmith, or a worker in bell-metal.
The holder of the balance should be one who is impartial toward both enemy and friend; the wise presiding judge (Prāḍvivāka) should also cause such a person to hold the balance.
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin and for the killer of women and children, those same worlds belong to Tulādhāra who holds the scales falsely.
On one scale, the wise man should weigh a well-fed man whose identity is known; on the second, he should weigh pure, white clay. (36)
One should avoid bricks, ashes, stones, potsherds, and bones; having weighed [the body] first, one should then lower it from that [balance].
Then, having placed a leaf upon the head, one should cause the person whose leaf has been placed to sit down; this mantra, which was previously spoken by Svayambhū, should be written upon the leaf.
O Goddess, you are the daughter of Brahmā and are called by the name Tulā; the syllable *tu* signifies eternal dignity, while the syllable *la* is remembered as meaning lightness. (39)
Because of your union of weight and lightness, you are called the "Balance" (Tulā); therefore, O auspicious one, release this man who has been falsely accused from his doubt.
One should then place that man back upon it together with the leaf; if, when weighed, he increases in weight, he is pure according to the law. || 41 ||
Those who know the Dharma understand that one who loses weight would not be pure; if the suspension cord breaks or the balance beam snaps, one should weigh the man again.
Thus, this knowledge is beyond doubt; and whatever is improper, one should not let it lapse. All of this should be performed on a Sunday after having worshipped the Sun.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ordeal of poison; listen to me.
And that is said to be of two kinds: namely, the poison of a jar-serpent, or that of the horned vatsanābha variety originating from the snowy mountains.
Seven barley grains, or alternatively six soaked in ghee, should be offered; one should likewise place them upon the leaf that has been laid on the head.
O Poison, you are the son of Brahmā, established in truth and righteousness; protect this man from evil, and by his truthfulness, let there be nectar for him. (47)
Those who know the Dharma understand that one should recognize as pure that [emetic] which has been digested without violent urges and is free from vomiting and fainting. (48)
Having declared, as before, "I am hungry; [here is] a hungry snake in a jar," he should strike seven claps of the hands; he shall not be bitten and is thus purified. (49)
Listen to me as I relate what Virañci has declared regarding the fire-ordeal: one should likewise prepare seven circles before the deity, the Sun.
It is the settled rule that one should proceed from mandala to mandala toward the east; the distance from one mandala to the next should be sixteen finger-breadths.
Having summoned one who is wearing wet clothes and likewise one who has fasted, he should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the gods and Brahmins.
He should cause a divine ordeal to be performed for the king or his appointed official, as well as for learned Brāhmaṇas and the subjects. 53.
In the afternoon, indeed, being pure, facing the east with palms joined in reverence, and having formed a square mandala, one should place both hands level with each other.
They should observe the marks on his hands, such as the signs of the Kṛta age and others; then they should bind seven leaves of the holy fig tree (aśvattha) upon his two hands.
Having made it firm with a new cotton thread, one should then make it perfectly level and eight finger-breadths long.
Having first performed worship to the Sun, one should then perform worship to the Fire; [the ordeal consists of] a firm ball of iron weighing fifty palas, heated in the fire.
With red sandalwood and incense, and likewise with red flowers, one should also bind a leaf upon the head of the accused.
Accompanied by this mantra uttered by the Brahmins: "O Agni, you are the four Vedas, and you are offered as oblation in the sacrifices. (59)
Because you indeed purify evil, you are called Pāvaka; you are the mouth of all the gods, and you are the mouth of those who discourse on Brahman.
"Since you reside within the bellies of all beings, you therefore know their good and evil; O Purifier, reveal yourself among the wicked and become blazing with flames!"
Alternatively, O Śītabhava, you who possess great power, if [the practitioner] is pure in disposition, then being consecrated, he should slowly circumambulate the mandalas.
Having walked around slowly, he should then drop the iron ball upon the ground; thereafter, he should have him perform the trampling of grain while holding a leaf in his hand.

Seeing that the two hands are free from alteration, one becomes pure according to the nature of reality (dharmatā). However, if one should drop [the object] out of fear, or if it is perceived as falling below, [it is not pure].
One should cause the metal to be brought back again; this is the procedure proclaimed. Now, therefore, I shall explain the rite of the heated gold-piece (taptamāṣa); listen.
One should have a vessel made of iron or copper measuring sixteen finger-breadths [in height], with a cavity four finger-breadths deep; or one may likewise have it made of clay.
Then, one should fill it with twenty palas of ghee and oil; once it is well-heated, one should cast into it a māṣaka of gold.
One should place the mantra associated with fire upon the head of the accused; then, by joining the thumb and the fingers, one should extract the heated gold coin.
The object of knowledge is pure, free from doubt, and devoid of eruptions and the like; I shall now declare the purification of the ploughshare—listen to it, O Dhanañjaya. (69)
A plowshare made of iron weighing twelve palas is prescribed; it should be eight aṅgulas in length and four aṅgulas in width.
One should place the mantra joined with the fire-seed (RAṂ) upon the head of the accused; then, licking the tongue, one should rotate it three times at a distance of six finger-breadths from him.
Cow’s milk should be administered as the supreme purifier of the tongue; one should perform an examination of the tongue, for if it is burnt, the patient is not released [from the disease].
One should know that [the seed] is pure if it is born from a pure [mother]; now I shall declare the eternal rule for the ritual of the rice grain.
In the case of theft, however, rice grains should be offered, and never otherwise. Having sprinkled the rice grains with water, one should leave them right there during the night. (74)
At dawn, it should undoubtedly be given to the performer to eat; then, facing eastward, he should spit upon the leaf three times.
These should be made from either Pippala or Bhūrja wood, but by no means from any other; and one should likewise have pure rice grains produced from the Śāli variety.
Having placed them in an earthen vessel and standing before the Sun, one should consecrate pure rice grains with this mantra according to the Dharma: || 77 ||

O rice grain, you are bestowed by those who know the true nature of Dharma as a means of purification for human beings; being thus praised, it is right for you to protect me according to truth and Dharma.
If, while standing before the sun, one spits and blood is seen upon it, one should declare that person to be impure. (79)
Thus, O descendant of Kuru, this eightfold divine [vision] arises before Bhaṭṭāditya, which cuts through sin and doubt.

Those who know the ancient lore have declared that the divine rite involving water is of two kinds: one is known as *jalahasta* (water in the hand), and the other they understand to be *majjana* (immersion).
As far as the discharge and retrieval of an arrow is performed by one possessed of vigor, so long shall he sink [in the water] and live; thus one should declare his purification.
O descendant of Bharata, this place belonging to Bhaṭṭāditya has come into existence on the surface of the earth in such a manner solely through my grace and that of the Sun.
Nārada said: Likewise, hear the wonderful account concerning the place Bahūdaka, which exists in Kāmarūpa as Bahūdaka. || 1 ||
That [merit] has been transferred here; therefore, it is called Bahūdaka. And having performed austerities here for very many years, Kapila [attained liberation]. || 2 ||
An auspicious Liṅga named Kapileśvara was installed; and that Liṅga, O Pārtha, is always known as Nandabhadra. || 3 ||
The merchant, who was an expert in all the specific rules of conduct, honored him with great respect three times a day, as if he were another Dharma incarnate.
There was nothing among the dharmas proclaimed that he did not know; he was always a friend to all and devoted to the welfare of all.
Having resorted to this dharma through action, mind, and speech, there has never been such a dharma, nor will there ever be; indeed, no such dharma exists at all.
For he who is faultless in all respects and remains thus firmly resolved—of this ocean of Dharma, which has increased on every side— (7)
Listen to how it was acquired by Nandabhadra after he had churned [the sea]: at that time, he remained established in the belief that trade is the best means for one's livelihood.
With well-measured wood and grass, he had a shelter constructed; it was free from intoxicants, free from divisiveness, free from deceit, and likewise level.
He conducted trade among all beings with little profit; having received merchandise from others without deceit, he dealt with them.
His noble vow is that he sells his goods to living beings with absolute sincerity alone; while some praise sacrifice, Nandabhadra does not approve of it.
Having ascertained this fault, O son of Pāṇḍu, listen to it: he is greedy, untruthful, hypocritical, and devoted to praising himself. (12)
By performing sacrifices with improper rites, one would indeed destroy the world and lead oneself into blinding darkness; for an oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun. (13)

From the sun rain is born; from rain comes food, and from that, living beings. Whatever [is required] for the sacrificer, the officiating priests, and the sacrificial materials—at whatever time—[these arise]. 14.
Indeed, the birth of a person who is like a thief arises from impurity, as does that of one for whom a sacrifice is performed without sacrificial fees or contrary to the prescribed rules. (15)

If the sacrificial animals were struck with sticks while dead, they would strike the sacrificer; therefore, it is traditionally taught that a sacrificer becomes auspicious through pure barley-offerings.
Having thus reflected upon sacrifice, he established himself in the essence of sacrifice: that which consists of worship of the gods with faith, prostration, and auspicious praise. (17)
The offering of food and the sacrificial oblation—this indeed is the sacrifice free from blemish; for that alone is declared to be a true sacrifice by which the deities are satisfied. (18)
Some praise renunciation, but Nandabhadra does not approve; for he who, having renounced sense objects, is again grasped by them through the mind. (19)
He has indeed fallen from both; the ground is split and perishes. Yet, that which is the essence of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) remains here, unsurpassed and concealed by him.
He neither curses nor praises the actions of anyone; like the moon, he remains indifferent toward people situated on various paths as he dwells upon the earth. (21)
He neither hates nor desires; he is neither antagonistic nor attached. The wise man regards a stone and gold as equal, and views blame and self-praise with equanimity.
Fearless toward all beings, appearing like one who is blind and deaf, and having no desire for the fruits of actions—this indeed is the worship of Śiva. (23)
Seeking dharma for its sake, and practicing without greed for it. || 24 ||
Having discerned this, Nandabhadra grasped its essence regarding liberations; while some praise agriculture, Nandabhadra does not approve of it.
In which they cut the noses of bulls, make them pull heavy loads, bind them, and subdue them. (26)
They lead draft animals through regions full of gadflies and much mud; oppressed by their burdens, others perish due to improper treatment.
They consider even the killing of a fetus to be no more significant than this act; since "aghnyā" (the inviolable) is the name for cows in the Veda, how could one harm them? (28)

Just as a wooden arrow with an iron tip destroys both the earth and those who dwell upon it, so too does [the weapon of knowledge] strike down all that exists within the five senses; for in all living beings, every deity resides.
What need is there for deliberation regarding that utterly deluded man who sells the sun, the moon, the wind, and even the source of power itself?
The unborn Agni, Varuṇa as a ram, Sūrya, the Earth, Virāj, the cow, and the calf—Soma indeed; by selling these one does not succeed. || 31 ||
Agriculture is always beset by thousands of such defects; indeed, a plough should be drawn by eight oxen, and one should relinquish a thirtieth part of the harvest from the cultivation.
"One should give old cattle for the sake of Dharma; whence can there be agriculture from the Puṣya asterism? This is the essence of agriculture, and it was observed by that Nandabhadra. (33)
One should always eat only after having prepared food offerings for the gods, the ancestors, humans, the twice-born, and all living beings according to one's own ability. (34)
Some praise sovereign power, but Nandabhadra does not approve; humans merely enjoy other humans in a state of servitude.
They torment this body day and night with beatings and bonds; is this the property of the elements, or of the mother, or of the father? (36)
Reflecting thus—that [the child] belonged to the mother, or to the father, or to the powerful buyer, or even to the fire, or to the dog—the lords acted like the immortals.
The intoxication of power is more evil than the intoxication of great liquor and the like; for one intoxicated by the pride of power, having fallen, indeed becomes utterly drunk.
He regards all his servants as himself and does not become intoxicated by his royal splendor. || 39 ||
Where indeed is there a embodied being who possesses self-reliance like this Lord? Behold how he has seized even the very essence of sovereignty. (40)
Because he does not turn his back on any living being according to his own capacity, Nandabhadra does not approve of those who praise pilgrimage sites alone.
Through exertion, through impurity, or through heat, cold, wind, hunger, thirst, or anger, he shall not suffer the destruction of his house of Dharma. || 42 ||

Whether through happiness, or even through faith in wealth, one who possesses even a small amount becomes wealthy; for how could one who is capable of attaining great merit not be capable [of this]? (43)
One who is always pure and worships the gods finds the essence of sacred fords in every home; neither waters, nor mountains, nor great hermitages can purify sins.
The self purifies its sins if it turns away from evil; such indeed is the conduct that has manifested here and there. (45)
