Having unified [all things], the wise Nandabhadra remained ever established [in that state]; even the gods longed for that virtuous man as he lived in such a manner.
All of them, headed by Vāsava, were filled with supreme wonder; and at that very spot, there lived a Śūdra who was his neighbor.
That atheist of wicked conduct, known as Satyavrata, repeatedly reviled the most righteous Nandabhadra. (48)
He was constantly watching for an opportunity against Nandabhadra, thinking: "If I see a flaw in him, then I shall cause him to turn away from dharma."
The very nature of these cruel, atheistic, and evil-minded people is such that they cause their own downfall as well as that of others.
Then, as that wise Nandabhadra lived in this manner, he had one son; but in his old age, that son also perished through hardship.
Considering that to be the work of fate, the high-minded one did not grieve; for who, whether god or man, is ever released from destiny? (52)
Then his beloved wife, endowed with all the virtues of a virtuous woman, was like Arundhatī herself—the very embodiment of the duties of a householder.
O Pārtha, she who was known by the name Kanakā has met her destruction; consequently, even though he had restrained his senses, he has fallen through the ruin of his domestic dharma.
He lamented repeatedly, "Alas, what misery! I am a sinner! But seeing his inner state, Avrata rejoiced after a long time.
Approaching and crying out "Alas, what misery!", he reached Nandabhadra and spoke to him, just as Dadhikarṇa had done.
"Alas, Nandabhadra! If such is the fruit even for you, then I consider that even this dharma in the mind is indeed in vain. (57)
Having spoken these and many other such words here and there, Satyavrata, filled with compassion, then addressed Nandabhadra.
O Nandabhadra, I have always desired to say something to you; however, due to the absence of any occasion, I have never spoken it. (59)
Even Bṛhaspati, if he were to speak words out of place, would certainly incur contempt for his intellect and be treated with disdain like an inferior.
Nandabhadra said: Speak, speak! There is nothing at all that should be kept secret from me, my most beloved friend; by the words of those of pure being, even liberation itself cannot be compared.
Satyavrata said: "Free from the nine defects of speech and the nine defects of intellect, I shall speak words that are free from fault. (62)
Subtlety, enumeration, sequence, determination, and purpose—where these five categories of meaning are present, that is called a "sentence" (vākya). || 63 ||
That which is spoken with reference to dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is declared as the "purpose" (prayojana); this is stated to be the first characteristic of a sentence.
Having made a specific promise regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, that which is stated at the conclusion of the statement as "this is that" is called a *vinirṇaya* (final decision). || 65 ||

"That which must be stated first and that which must be stated afterwards according to their sequence—those wise ones who know the true nature of speech call this the 'application of sequence' (kramayoga). (66)
Having examined both the faults and the virtues according to their respective proportions and for the sake of both [the self and others], let that be understood as "number" (saṃkhyā). 67.
Where non-difference is perceived among things that are distinct and known through speech, one should designate that as "subtlety" (saukṣmya), which serves as the cause of excellence. 68.

Thus [have been described] the qualities of speech; now hear the twenty-two defects of speech: that which is devoid of meaning, that which has no distinct meaning, that which is inverted, and likewise that which is redundant. (69)
That which is harsh, ambiguous, has a heavy syllable at the end of a word, is turned away from the face, is false, or is unrefined; || 70 ||
That which is contradictory to the three aims of life (trivarga), deficient, excessively harsh in sound, presented in a disordered sequence, incomplete, and devoid of reason; || 71 ||
And hear from me those faults of speech arising from the intellect which are causeless, as well as those born of desire, anger, fear, greed, wretchedness, and ignobility. (72)
Out of compassion for the lowly and out of pride, I shall not say anything; for it is only when the speaker, the listener, and the speech itself are all complete that [truth is realized]. (73)
When there is the intention to speak with impartiality, then that meaning is revealed; but when the speaker, while speaking, disregards the listener, [the meaning is obscured]. (74)
Furthermore, the listener does not accept that speech from the speaker; nor does one who speaks what is pleasing to himself, while disregarding what is true for the listener. (75)
Suspicion arises regarding that [speaker], and thus even those words are faulty. Therefore, one who abandons what is dear to himself and speaks instead what is pleasing to the listener— || 76 ||
Only he is a speaker on this earth, and no other, who speaks only the truth, having abandoned false doctrines arising from the web of scriptures. (77)
Since truth alone is my vow, I am therefore Satyavrata; I shall speak the truth to you, and you should consider it as such.
O dear one, ever since you became devoted to the worship of stone, I have not seen anything auspicious whatsoever from that time forward. (79)
That one son of mine has perished, and even my noble wife has passed away; O virtuous one, such is the fruit of deceitful deeds. (80)
"Where are the gods? This is false; even if they were seen, it would still be so. This entire conceptualization is merely for the sake of wealth by deceitful Brahmins. (81)
When they offer [food] intended for the ancestors, laughter arises within me; for what indeed could one who is dead eat, given that food is subject to decay? (82)
However, as for this entire creation of the universe which the lowest of the twice-born, being deluded, describe in many ways—even so, listen to it according to the truth. (83)
Both the arising and the destruction of the universe—this pair—is false; for in this very way, this entire world exists as the Real. (84)

Indeed, this entire universe functions by its own inherent nature; these [planets] beginning with the sun revolve by their own inherent nature; the winds blow eternally by their own inherent nature, and this cloud rains by its own inherent nature. (85)
The various kinds of grain grow by their own nature; rain, cold, and heat exist by their own nature; the earth remains stable by its own nature; and the rivers flow by their own nature. (86)

By their very nature mountains appear eternally; by their very nature this ocean remains established; by its very nature a pregnant woman gives birth; and by their very nature these many living beings exist. (87)

Just as thorns on the jujube trees are crooked by their very nature due to the inherent character of the season, so indeed does all this manifest by its own nature; no creator whatsoever is perceived. (88)
While the world is situated thus, the fool becomes deluded like one intoxicated; listen now to this which even rogues declare to be the highest state—human birth. (89)
There is nothing more painful than being human; for that state becomes an enemy to us. For a human being, there are thousands of occasions for grief at every single moment. (90)
For one who possesses good fortune is liberated from this human state—which is characterized by constant mindfulness—just as beasts, birds, insects, and worms live according to their own pleasure.
These beings move about unbound; their state of birth is very difficult to attain. Indeed, these stationary ones are free from anxiety, and their happiness on earth is great.

What is the use of much talk? Every being born of another womb is more fortunate than humans; know that this is simply their inherent nature, while the conceptualization of merit, demerit, and so forth is merely a mental construction.

"Since some beings are stationary, while others are insects, moths, humans, and so forth, therefore, O Nandabhadra, abandoning falsehood, drink as you please along with your playthings; this is the truth on earth. (94)
Nārada said: "By these and other such words—unfitting and inconsistent—" (95)
Nandabhadra, the high-minded son of Satyavrata, who was as unshakeable as the ocean, spoke to him as if smiling, like one who cannot be disturbed.
As for what you said—that those who are most righteous always partake in suffering—that is false; for we see nets of suffering even among the sinful. (97)
Killing, imprisonment, afflictions, and even the death of sons, wives, and others are seen even among sinners; therefore, Dharma is considered the highest authority.
"Oh, what a saintly man! Alas, what suffering! Even great people say this of this saintly man; yet such words are difficult even for sinners to obtain. (99)
When a sinner enters the house out of greed for wealth such as a wife, you too fear him; yet it is in vain that you hate him and become angry.
That you say there is no Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the cause of this world is the talk of a child; for how could there be subjects without a king? (101)
And as for what you say—that you worship a stone linga in vain—you do not know the majesty of the linga, just as a blind man does not know the sun.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as kings of great supernatural power, human beings, and sages—all indeed worship the Liṅga. || 103 ||
They possess lingas that bear their own names as marks; however, these have become fools, whereas you are truly devoted to your vows and wise.
In ancient times, having installed Nīlalohita at Puṣkara, Brahmā attained supreme perfection and, as the Lord, created these progeny.
Even Viṣṇu, having slain Rāvaṇa in battle, established the Rāmeśvara Liṅga on the shore of the ocean; so why do you act in vain? (106)
In ancient times, having slain Vṛtra and established Śaṅkara on Mount Mahendra, Śakra was freed from sin and rejoices even now in the third heaven.
Having established Śiva at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Sūrya became free from disease; and Soma, at Prabhāsa on the western ocean, likewise attained freedom from ailment. || 108 ||
In Kāśī, Yama and Dhanada; on the Sahya mountain, Garuḍa and Kaśyapa; and in Naimiṣa, Vāyu and Varuṇa—having installed the Liṅgas, they were filled with joy.
In this very Stambhatīrtha, the omnipresent Lord Guha, Kumāra, installed a Liṅga; does it not indeed remove all sins? (110)
Likewise, I am not able to enumerate those lingas that have been propitiated by other gods, kings, and sages.
All those who dwell on earth, those who dwell in heaven, and those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) become satisfied through the worship of the Liṅga. || 112 ||
And as for what you say—that the gods do not exist, or if they do exist, why are they not seen anywhere?—because of this, my astonishment is great. (113)
"O highly wise one, why do those gods beg you like a pauper or like a lentil? For he whom you desire is indeed your master, as you are his practitioner. (114)
If, in your view, all things are not established by their own inherent nature, tell me: how could eating and such be accomplished without an agent? (115)
Indeed, thorns are seen even apart from the jujube tree; therefore, who has the power of creation? For whatever exists in a certain way, it remains exactly so.
And as for what you say—that these animals and others are happy and fortunate—this has never been said by anyone else, nor has it ever even been heard. (117)

Those who are tamasic and impaired—how lamentable is their state! Yet even they possess some degree of praiseworthiness; for how could human beings not be blessed, being endowed with all the senses and being the most excellent? (118)
I consider your vow to be true, yet you have chosen hell for yourself; you should not fear this great misfortune, for this desire shall be fulfilled before long.
"In the beginning, my ignorance was indeed proclaimed through mere ostentation; thus, the lack of substance is evident from that initial display. (120)
For the speech of deceivers, when they speak, is shrouded in deception like counterfeit coin; therefore, one must always examine the words of the virtuous.
Those whose speech is faultless in the beginning, middle, and end—like gold that is auspicious even when cut by scratching, burning, and heating—their words are auspiciously auspicious.
"You have made one promise and spoken otherwise once again; this is not our fault, for we are merely those who hear your words. (123)
This is the quality of atheists, of serpents, and of poison: that they delude others; yet this fault does not belong to the other.
Just as water, cloth, sesame seeds, oil, or even a scent [is transformed] by the perfuming of flowers, so too are qualities born of association. (125)
The source of the net of delusion is association with the foolish in this world; the source of dharma, day after day, is association with the virtuous. || 126 ||
Therefore, association should be maintained with those who are wise, aged, pure in disposition, ascetic, virtuous, and devoted to tranquility.
One should not [study] with those who are low-born, nor with the ignorant, and especially not with those who do not know the Self—those whose three [factors] are pure: birth, learning, and conduct.
One should especially associate with those who possess the sacred scriptures; for by the sight, touch, conversation, sitting together, and eating with the wicked, [one is defiled]. (129)
Through association with the base, men fall away from the practice of dharma, they do not achieve success, and their intellect declines. (130)

"By those who are middling one attains middleness, and by those who are supreme one attains supremacy. Remembering this principle of dharma, I do not seek union with you again—those twice-born ones whom you revile, by whom the ocean was made undrinkable. (131)

The Vedas are authoritative; the Smṛtis are authoritative; words endowed with righteousness and purpose are authoritative. For one for whom these three are not authoritative, who would consider his word to be authoritative? (132)
Having spoken these words, the high-souled Nandabhadra immediately departed from his home at that very moment and went to the meritorious Bahūdaka-kuṇḍa of Bhaṭṭāraveḥ.
Nārada said: Then the wise Nandabhadra, having worshipped the excellent Liṅga Kapileśvara situated on the bank of the Bahūdaka Kuṇḍa, [proceeded further]. || 1 ||
Having prostrated, he stood before him with his palms joined in reverence; somewhat distressed by the experiences of worldly existence, he sang this verse: || 2 ||
If I were to behold Sadāśiva, the creator of this world, I would then cause that Lord to feel ashamed with various questions. (3)
O desireless one, what need have you for creating the world if it is not already being replenished? For this world has been created by you in manifold ways, just like that of Bhārgava.
Since he is conscious, pure, and free from passion and other such defects, why then has he not created or fashioned something insentient that is similar to himself? (5)
Why indeed does the world, from Brahmā down to a mere insect, suffer, when it is equal in its lack of enmity and in its arising and passing away of pleasure and pain? (6)
O Sadāśiva, what fruit do you obtain by casting some into heaven and others into hell? Tell me, why do you act in this way?
O Lord, these men, separated from their beloved sons and others, are indeed weeping; O essence of compassion, would you have no pity? (8)
O Lord, all of this is utterly improper in every respect, that your devotees should sink together with sinners into the ocean of misery.
Deluded by such conduct within saṃsāra, I shall not go to another place; I will eat and I will drink no water.
"I shall go only unto death; I will remain here reflecting upon this. While thus deliberating, Nandabhadra himself stood still.
Then, on the fourth day, at the auspicious Bahūkataṭa, a certain boy of seven years, afflicted by pain, arrived.
Extremely emaciated, suffering from oozing leprosy, and fainting at every step, the boy steadied himself with great difficulty and spoke these words to Nandabhadra: || 13 ||
"O you whose every limb is so beautiful, why are you also sorrowful? Then Nandabhadra explained the entire reason for it to him.

Having heard the entire reason for that, the boy, with a dejected mind, said: "Alas! Oh, what a terrible and most intense calamity it is that even the wise should possess such lack of understanding! (15)
It is in vain that those with fully intact senses and limbs desire to die; for in this very place, Khaṭvāṅga attained the path of liberation within a mere moment.
On that day, who indeed would abandon the land of Bhārata while Satyāyu was still alive? I alone consider myself firm, even though I have been forsaken by my parents. (17)
I am unable even to move, nor do I wish to die; indeed, the Vedic scripture is true when it says that all gains are accompanied by their opposites. 18.
Contentment is indeed appropriate for you, whose body is so firm; yet, if my own body were somehow to become free from disease— || 19 ||
One should perform that [practice] moment by moment, even if it is experienced only age after age; for he whose senses are under control shall possess a firm body. (20)
If he desires something else, who is more insentient than him? There are thousands of occasions for sorrow and hundreds of occasions for joy. (21)
Day after day, fools are brought under control, but not the wise; for they do not engage in actions that are contrary to knowledge and fraught with many dangers.
Wise men such as yourself apply themselves even against those who strike at the very root; for they say that eightfold intelligence is that which destroys all that is inauspicious. (23)
That stainless intellect of yours, which is not in conflict with the Śruti and Smṛti, exists [even] amidst hardships, difficulties, and calamities concerning your own kin.
Those such as you do not despond because of physical or mental sufferings; they do not long for what cannot be attained, nor do they wish to grieve over what has been lost. (25)
Men of wise intellect do not lose their composure even in calamities; for the entire world is afflicted by the two kinds of suffering arising from the mind and the body. (26)

Listen to this means for their pacification, both in detail and in brief: [it arises] from the contact with the undesirable caused by disease, and from the exhaustion resulting from the abandonment of the desirable. (27)
Suffering, whether physical or mental, arises from four causes: mental suffering consists of union with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant. (28)
This great suffering of two kinds has been described for these two; indeed, by mental anguish the body is tormented. (29)
Like water contained in a jar [is cooled] by a heated iron ball, [the mind is purified] through immediate counteraction and through constant avoidance. (30)

The pacification of both disease and its cause is achieved through the two types of yoga; therefore, one should pacify the mental [affliction] with knowledge, just as one extinguishes fire with water. (31)
For when his mind is tranquil, his bodily suffering comes to rest; yet it is perceived that attachment is the root of the mind's suffering. (32)
Moreover, through affection, a virtuous being constantly encounters suffering; for sufferings have their root in affection, and fears are born of affection. (33)
Sorrow, joy, and likewise exertion—all these proceed from affection.

From affection (sneha), both the passion for the instruments [of action] and the passion for sense objects arise; both of these lead to what is not conducive to welfare, yet among them, the former is considered the more serious. || 35 ||
Therefore, the renouncer shall not suffer, being free from enmity and unrestrained; whereas the non-renouncer attains birth and death here again and again.
Therefore, one should not desire affection from friends for the sake of accumulating wealth; rather, one should eliminate that which arises from one's own body through knowledge.
Affection does not cling to those perfected ones who are endowed with knowledge, who understand the scriptures, and who have mastered themselves, just as water does not cling to lotus leaves. (38)
A person overcome by passion is dragged away by desire; longing arises within him, and from that, craving increases. (39)
For craving is considered the most wicked of all things; it is thought to cause constant agitation, to abound in unrighteousness, and to be followed by terrible consequences. (40)
Happiness belongs to one who abandons that craving which is so difficult for the foolish to give up, which does not grow old with them, and which is a disease that ends only with life. (41)
That craving of men, which is without beginning or end and resides within the body, destroys them once it has arisen, just as rust destroys iron.
Just as fuel meets its destruction by the fire arising from itself, so does one of undisciplined soul perish through greed born within himself. 43.
Therefore, one should not harbor greed for the body, for oneself, or for kinsmen; one should not rejoice when they are obtained, nor should one grieve at their loss.
Nandabhadra said: "O child, you are not a child in my estimation; I bow to you. I am exceedingly satisfied by your words, yet I shall ask you something."
O men, they constantly revile desire, anger, ego, and the senses; it is because of that that this desire to speak arises within me. (46)
"I am this," "this is mine," "I am such-and-such"—the self-knowledge expressed in such ways is known as egoism (ahaṃkāra). || 47 ||
If that [mind] is abandoned and, being free from madness, is scattered [into tranquility], then desire is said to be "longing"; if that is avoided by a man, [he attains peace]. (48)
How can heaven or the desire for liberation be achieved by means of a stone? And if anger must be abandoned, how then can enemies be destroyed? (49)
Whether they be external or internal, they know them to be like blades of grass without him; having restrained the senses, one should indeed subdue those that are wicked.
"How might there be the hearing of the Dharma, or how might my life be sustained? My mind is pierced by this and suffers in the crisis of ignorance. (51)
Likewise, why has this inert universe been created by the conscious Self? Thus, alas, from where does this manifold suffering arise that afflicts one so? (52)
The boy said: "This which you have asked is exactly so—a matter in which living beings are deluded. Listen with a one-pointed mind; it has been understood by me from Dvaipāyana. (53)
We have heard from of old that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are beginningless; prior to creation, they exist in a state of similarity, being free from old age and death.
Then, impelled by both time and its own inherent nature, primordial matter (prakṛti) formerly desired union with the Spirit (puṃs); due to the absence of that [union], she became agitated.
Then, beheld by the God with ease, that [nature] consisting of darkness became rajasic; being purified, it became sattvic. || 56 ||

Thus, having attained the state of the three qualities through the vision of the Divine, that primordial nature (prakṛti) became established therein, and from it the Supreme Being arose as the Threefold Form (Trimūrti).
And then, having set out for the purpose of uttering her, he brought forth from his own portion the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) consisting of the three qualities; that is what the wise know.
From that, ego (ahaṃkāra) was born, characterized by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; having attained rajas, tamas leads rajas toward the quality of sattva.

Therefore, the wise declare that liberation belongs to the pure being (sattva); for that reason, one must strive for complete purification from both darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas) in every respect.
The Supreme Lord divided his own portions, known as individual souls (jīvātman); for indeed, there are as many knowers of the field (kṣetrajña) as there are bodies.
Just as sparks issue forth from a heated iron linga, so too does this creation of the subtle elements and the gross elements proceed from the tamasic ego.
From the sattvic nature of the senses, those [objects] also possess the three qualities; through these, by means of the perfected instrument, there arises the vision of Saccidānanda.
Rajas and tamas are purified by sattva alone by those seeking liberation; therefore, [one should restrain] desire, anger, and the agitation of the senses.

By cultivating ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), one attains the perfection belonging to the quality of goodness (sāttvikī siddhi); these desires and other traits belonging to the qualities of passion (rājasa) and ignorance (tāmasa) must be abandoned. 65.
Those characterized by sattva should always be served by those who desire to conquer the cycle of worldly existence. I shall now describe to you, in brief, the characteristics of the three qualities.

The study of the scriptures, knowledge derived therefrom, purity, restraint of the senses, performance of righteous deeds, and contemplation of the Self—these are the characteristics of the quality of sattva.
Taking wealth by unjust means, sloth, atheism, cruelty, and [being a] beggar and so forth—these are the characteristics of the quality of tamas.

Therefore, those who are wise, self-controlled, and characterized by sattva should worship the deity; through rajasic qualities one attains the state of humanity, and through tamasic qualities, birth as an immobile being.
Liberation occurs through these very things, such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth; and by these same things, one undergoes torment.
Indeed, in the absence of these [means], nothing at all is possible; for just as a goldsmith purifies gold by means of other metallic alloys (kalāda). || 71 ||
In the same way, rajas and tamas are to be purified by means of the sattvic qualities; this is precisely because of the beginningless conjunction of these qualities.

The Lord [perceives] living beings who are happy and those who are suffering according to the teachings of the scriptures; and for each single quality, there are twenty-eight lakhs [of variations]. (73)
He divided those eighty-four hundred thousand classes of living beings into four; for they indeed originate from the mind, even as they do from the Self.
And all those who are portions of the Lord are deluded by the material qualities; they surely encounter afflictions, just like the appointed officials of the Sovereign.
For the welfare of grains, of waters, and of living beings, those who know the truth say that human birth is the best when it is permeated by the nature of Śiva.
Nandabhadra said: "It is so; however, O high-minded one, I shall ask this further: who are those by whom the lords, the givers of all, and the deities are worshipped? (77)
Why do those gods not protect their own devotees from sufferings? Indeed, some who are devoted to the gods are seen to be especially submerged in misery. (78)
Thus my intellect is bewildered; or do you think, O fool, that it is yours? (79)
The boy said: "A devotee of the God is remembered as being of two kinds: the impure and the pure. One who is devoted to Him in action, mind, and speech is called a devotee. (80)
When a man worships deities while being impure, then malevolent spirits enter him and he becomes deluded at that very moment.

Being deluded, he indulges in various improper actions and consequently perishes quickly; therefore, one who is impure should not worship [him], nor should one who is pure worship him, even if such a person were to meet with misfortune.

The manifest result of his previously performed actions is said to be ten million-fold; it was there, in that place, that Maheśvara fled hither and thither out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Why did he bathe in sacred fords, and how was the other released? [Tell me] how, after abducting the daughter of Ambarīṣa from Parvata through Nārada... (84)
Rāma underwent the abduction of Sītā; how could another be released? Even Brahmā, having desired his own daughter, suffered the severing of his head. (85)
Even Indra, Candra, Ravi, Viṣṇu, and the foremost of the gods would obtain the merit of the Kṛta age; therefore, men must always certainly eat what has been prepared.
"No one is ever liberated from their own actions; such is the conclusion of the Vedas. However, by means of divine grace, that which is unattainable through the vows of the gods may be obtained. (87)
That which would have been enjoyed over many lifetimes may be enjoyed in a single lifetime; and having experienced that, one's purpose will be fulfilled—this is the certain conclusion. (88)
Those who, having been purified of sins, perform austerities, being pure and devoted to the vows of the deities, rejoice here with their sons and grandsons, and in the hereafter as well.
Therefore, the gods should always be worshipped by those who are pure and endowed with faith; and one's own nature should be purified through the duties prescribed for one's own caste.
"Even a dharma well-performed may lead only to suffering for one who is perishing; even a god [cannot save] one of evil conduct—so has the Lord Hara declared. (91)
Therefore, one must enjoy the fruits of one's own actions; Sadāśiva is to be worshipped always. Through right conduct, passion and hatred—these two supreme obstacles—must be abandoned.
Nandabhadra said: O one of pure wisdom, why is it that even sinful men are seen rejoicing with their wives and their wealth? (93)
The boy said: "Clearly, in their previous births, they gave gifts characterized by tamas; Śambhu was worshipped with rajas, and thus they have obtained the fruit of their own deeds. (94)
However, O best of the learned, because of the power of that karma performed through darkness (tamas), may they have no delight in dharma. 95.
Having enjoyed the fruit of merit, he goes to hell; of this there is no doubt. Regarding this doubt, it is heard that Mārkaṇḍeya spoke thus: || 96 ||

For one person it is here and not in the next world; for another, it is in the next world and not here; for one person it is both here and in the next world; and for another, it is neither in the next world nor here. 97.

Merit previously acquired may exist, yet they do not even earn its enjoyment; that which is experienced here [in this world] is indeed called the "enjoyment" of one who is unfortunate and of small intelligence.

For that wise person who possesses no enjoyment acquired in a previous life and does not acquire any through ascetic practices, it is clear that his enjoyment in the next world will result from his actions.
He who possesses no merit acquired in the past and does not acquire any here in this life—alas, O friend, fie upon that lowest of men, whether he be in this world or the next! 100.
Knowing this, O illustrious one, abandon all thorns entirely; worship Rudra, observe the dharma of your own caste, for there is nothing higher than this.
He who grieves for beloved things that have perished, or even when they have been obtained, or who would be satisfied [with them], is certainly bound to another birth. (102)
Nandabhadra said: Salutations to you, who are not a child, yet possess the form of a child, and are wise. Who are you? I wish to know you in truth, O one of pure smiles. (103)
Many elders have been seen and constantly served by me; yet such an intellect as this has never been seen nor heard of by me among them.
"Since my doubts regarding [my] birth have been destroyed by you with ease, it is my firm conviction that you are not an ordinary being. (105)
The boy said: "This which is to be told is great; listen with one-pointed mind according to the truth. In my seventh birth, indeed seven births beyond this one, I [was... (106)

In the city of Vaidiśa, there was a brahmin named Dharmajālika, who was well-versed in the principles of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and was an eminent scholar of the meaning of the Smṛti scriptures.
I am an expounder of the treatises on Dharma like Bṛhaspati himself; however, I shall describe to you the various duties of the worlds in great detail. 108.
He himself was exceedingly wicked in conduct, a king of sinners among even the sinful; he was a meat-eater, a consumer of liquor, and always devoted to the wives of others.
A speaker of untruth, deceitful, always bearing the banner of righteousness, wicked, greedy, and evil-minded—such a preacher is never at any time or place a doer of what he preaches. (110)
Because I cast the net of the world like a fisherman’s net upon the worlds, those who know the truth call me Dharmajālika (the Fisherman of Dharma). || 111 ||
Thus, when my end arrived due to those many sins committed by me, I died, went to the abode of Yama, and was cast down upon the Kūṭaśālmalī tree.
Then, dragged by the messengers of Yama and made to remember my own deeds, being hacked with swords, I live and I die.
Reproaching myself in many ways, I have dwelt for eternal years in hell; may such a state of mind as that arise toward dharma in one who oppresses it.
If even for a mere moment it were to exist, then that person would be blessed; salutations again and again to the Land of Action, where both merit and demerit prevail! (115)
In which [state] one is not destroyed even in a mere moment, let alone by ages; from that hell, the wise Janaka then liberated him.
Having been released from them, I somehow escaped with difficulty; yet, having experienced the state of a pillar and encountered manifold afflictions, I remained there. (117)
Later, I became an insect on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī; there, by chance, I fell asleep comfortably upon the path.
I heard the loud sound of this approaching chariot; hearing that roar like the thundering of clouds, I was suddenly terrified and fled with speed. (119)
Having abandoned the path and fled far away, in that interval Vyāsa arrived there by chance.
The sage beheld me and, filled with compassion, [spoke] to me who was terrified: "Various dharmas have been proclaimed by me for all the worlds. (121)
Due to the power of that very birth as a Brahmin, he met Vyāsa; thereafter, having become a knower of all sounds, the venerable one spoke to me in the language of insects.
"Why do you perish thus, O worm, and why do you fear death? Oh, how appropriate is such fear for a human; whence could it come to you? (123)
Thus addressed, the wise man, due to his past merit, then spoke to Vyāsa: "O one revered by the world, I have no fear whatsoever of death from this."
O venerable one, this itself is my fear: that I might go to a low rebirth; for even from this wretched womb, there are millions of other even lower ones. (125)
I am terrified and trembling because of the afflictions beginning with conception within them; it is not otherwise.
Vyāsa said: "Do not fear any of the wombs for long; I shall certainly liberate you and cause you to attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa."
Having been addressed thus by Kāliya, I bowed to that Teacher of the World; then, having come to my path, I was struck by his discus and met my death.
Then, whenever I was born in the wombs of crows, jackals, and other such creatures, Vyāsa would come to me and remind me of that [past].
Having wandered through many kinds of wombs, I was worn out; then I was born in the house of a Brahmin, in this womb, exceedingly miserable. (130)
Since birth, I have been abandoned by my parents; I am a leper with oozing sores, and I endure this great suffering. (131)
Then, in my fifth year, Vyāsa came and whispered the Sārasvata mantra into my ear; by that means, I remember it.

"The scriptures, the Vedas, and the dharmas have all been studied in their entirety; this has also been told to me by Vyāsa: 'Go to the field of Guha, and there you must console the high-minded Nandabhadra. (133)
Having abandoned that [body] in Bahūdaka and cast his bones into the waters of the earth, you shall then become the excellent sage Maitreya.
"Vyāsa told me, 'From there you shall attain liberation'; and so I have come here from the Vāhīkas after enduring extreme hardship. (135)
Thus I have related to you my entire life story; O Nandabhadra, always abandon such grievous sin.
Nandabhadra said: "Oh, how truly wonderful is your life-story, by which my heart has become a hundred times more firmly established in dharma!"
However, I desire to perform an atonement for the deed you have described; therefore, remember the law and instruct me decisively regarding something [to be done]. (138)
The boy said: "I shall remain at this sacred ford for seven days without food; I will mutter the mantras of the Sun and thereafter I shall give up my life."
"Therefore, I am to be cremated by you on the bank at the Barkarikā-tīrtha, and my bones must indeed be cast here into the ocean."
If you possess toward me a mind that is excessively concealing, then I shall command you for the sake of a weighty task; listen to that.
In this Bahūdaka Tīrtha, where I shall give up my life-breaths, there you must install the omnipresent Lord Bhāskara, marked with my name.
"The Lord Bhāskara, when pleased, bestows health, wealth, grain, and the prosperity of sons, wives, and so forth; such is the word of the Śruti. (143)
Savitṛ is the supreme deity, or rather, he is everything belonging to the twice-born; he is extolled in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas—you too should always worship him. (144)
This pool, Bahūdaka, should always be resorted to by you; O Vyāsa, I shall describe its majesty as it was indicated in brief.
The man who bathes according to the prescribed rites in the excellent Bahūdaka Kuṇḍa shall possess health, wealth, grain, and other blessings throughout all his births.
And he who, having bathed in Bahūdaka on the seventh day of the month of Māgha, offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the ancestors, they shall obtain everlasting satisfaction. || 147 ||
For one who, being pure, performs a sacrifice on the bank of the Bahūdaka, the fruit is that of a hundred sacrifices; of this there is no doubt. || 148 ||
The man who gives up his life here on the bank of Bahūdaka rejoices in the world of the Sun and shall become the son of the righteous. || 149 ||

And whoever performs the practice of recitation on the bank of the Bahūdaka river, it is declared that all—the recitation, the fire-oblation, and the worship—is multiplied a hundred thousandfold. 150.
And on the bank of the Bahūdaka, one should feed a single twice-born man with sweet food; for him, it is as if ten million Brahmins have been fed. || 151 ||
If a woman offers food to auspicious young girls on the banks of the Bahūdaka river, Umā shall indeed offer her a most gracious welcome.
And whoever performs the practice of yoga on the bank of the Bahūdaka [river], success will be attained by him within six months; of this there is no doubt. || 153 ||
Whatever is given on the bank of the Bahūdaka river, dedicated to the deceased, reaches them inexhaustibly; it cannot be otherwise.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors—when performed on the banks of the Bahūdaka, all these yield exceedingly great fruit. (155)
O high-minded Nandabhadra, you should keep in your heart this fruit which has been indicated by Vyāsa regarding the Bahūdaka Kuṇḍa.
Having spoken thus, he became silent; then, having bathed in the pool and become pure, he sat upon a stone on the bank and himself recited the mantras.
Śrī Nārada said: Then, at the end of seven nights, that boy gave up his life-breaths; and he was consecrated with the funeral rites by Nandabhadra and the Brahmins according to the prescribed rules.
Where that child, devoted to the recitation of prayers, gave up his life, there he installed the Lord known as Bālāditya.
Whoever bathes in Bahūdaka and worships Bālāditya, Bhāskara shall be pleased with him, and he finds the means to liberation.
Then the wise Nandabhadra, devoted to Śiva and Sūrya, begot other sons equal to himself upon another wife. (161)
O Pārtha, he went to the body of Rudra, from which a return is difficult to obtain. Thus is this great pool known as Bahūdaka. || 162 ||
On its bank, the Lord of the Vallīs will behold his own portion, he who will indeed be the incarnation of the yogi Dattātreya.
And by worshipping that god, one attains perfection in yoga; for that Lord is the refuge of cattle and bestows prosperity upon them.
Likewise, in the west, that king Budhasuta established the field of Bhārata, known as Purūravāditya. || 165 ||
And that sun-like lord is the granter of all desires, equal to Bhaṭṭaditya; and his sacred field, O Bhārata, is equal to the Bahūdaka field.
The greatness of this sacred site (tīrtha) should be whispered into the ear of one's son or disciple; it must never be told to an atheist.
The Sun is pleased with him who listens to this with faith; holding it in his heart, he attains liberation and is released from the ocean of worldly existence.
Nārada said: O Jaya, listen then to how I propitiated the goddesses and established them for the protection of this sacred ford. || 1 ||
Just as the Supreme Lord, the Self, is all-pervading within all beings, so too is Prakṛti, the Supreme Goddess, eternal and all-pervading. (2)
Through the grace of Śakti, one obtains valor and all forms of prosperity; she is the sovereign lady within all beings, O Pārtha, and she is thus established.
Intellect, modesty, nourishment, shame, contentment, tranquility, forgiveness, longing, faith, consciousness, and power—these arise from Mantra, Utsāha, and Prabhava.
This alone leads to bondage and this alone leads to liberation at all times; by propitiating her, Indra and the other gods attained sovereign power.
And those base ones who do not acknowledge power and instead treat it with contempt—even if they are lords among yogis—they clearly fall, just like those born in Kāśī.
It is said that in ancient times, even masters of yoga who had attained perfection in Vārāṇasī fell back into ruin once again by disregarding Śakti.
Therefore, this power belonging to the embodied soul must always and eternally be worshipped; when pleased, she grants all desires, but when enraged, she destroys them in an instant.
That supreme primordial nature (prakṛti) is established in many divisions; among them, the great goddesses are indeed established here—listen.
There are four great Śaktis stationed in the four directions; Siddhāmbikā was established in the east by Guha.
She is proclaimed as having been produced from the primordial *mūlaprakṛti* at the beginning of the world; and because she was propitiated by the Siddhas, she is also known as Siddhāmbikā.
Likewise, Tārā was established by me in the southern direction; she was stationed there for the sake of delivering the gods, since she rests upon a tortoise.
"Empowered by her, the Tortoise, the teacher of the world, upheld the Vedas; and with his body possessed by her, the wise one shall destroy the followers of Buddha."
"Having propitiated her, I have brought here this daughter of the Mountain, who has destroyed millions of evildoers who were destroyers of the path of the Vedas."
Surrounded by millions of most formidable goddesses, she stands stationed in the southern direction out of respect for me.
Likewise, in the west, the auspicious goddess Bhāskarā is stationed; pervaded by her, the luminaries headed by the sun shine forth.
The forms of all the stars go forth and return swiftly; this, O joy of the Kurus, is that radiant Śakti of great power.
Having propitiated her, I brought her here from Kaṭāha, and she now resides here; surrounded by millions upon millions, she eternally protects the western direction. (18)
Likewise, in the north resides the goddess Yoganandinī, who emerged in the past from the body of the Supreme Prakṛti.
Beheld with their stainless vision, the four Sanas attained union (yoga); and that Goddess, the Mistress of Yogis, was highly pleased by Sanaka and the others.
That very [goddess], having been propitiated by me from the cosmic egg (aṇḍakaṭāha), has been brought here and remains stationed in the northern direction, surrounded by yoginīs.
Thus these four great powers are eternally established; when worshipped, they constantly grant desires, and when enraged, they are capable of destruction.
And so, nine fortresses have been brought by me; listen to them. || 23 ||
The supreme goddess named Tripurā is she by whom, in ancient times, Sthāṇu—the Lord of the World—was possessed and led the three cities to ashes.
Then the Blessed Lord Hara addressed her as "Tripurā," and he himself praised her; therefore, she is worthy of worship even by the worlds.
Having propitiated her, she was brought by me from the mountain of Amareśvara; she resides near Bhaṭṭāditya, granting the desires of her devotees.
And there is also another, the eternal Mahāśakti Kolaṃbā, possessed by whom Keśava raised up the earth in the form of a boar.
Therefore, she was addressed by Viṣṇu as "Kolaṃbā," and having been praised and worshipped, that goddess, O Pārtha, was gratified by me through the yoga of devotion.
Established on Vārāhagiri and brought here, she said to me: "O Nārada, it is there that I always remain out of compassion for those who seek my grace. (29)
In that regard, I must indeed remain with the well where Rudrāṇī resides; for without that well, no pleasure whatsoever arises for me. (30)
"Therefore, O twice-born one, you yourself dig an excellent well here. When this was said by the Goddess, O Pārtha, I then [dug it] with the root of a darbha grass.
A well was dug where Rudrāṇī herself appeared in the well; there, having bathed, recited prayers, and offered libations, the gods were gratified by me.
Then the divine Kolaṃbā, the sovereign of the world, was worshipped; being thoroughly pleased, the goddess then spoke to me as I bowed before her. (33)
"I shall always remain here, for I have been moved to grace by you; and those who bathe here in this well, especially on the eighth day of the month of Māgha," (34)
I shall sever the evil deeds of those mortals who worship me; for I am composed of all sacred fords and abide within groves of every season.
And this very well of Rudrāṇī is right near Meru.
O Nārada, I have proclaimed that bathing in this well is even more meritorious than at Prayāga, and especially so than at the Gaṅgā and Gayā. (37)
Therefore, O ascetic, abiding here at your word, I shall protect this sacred lake with Guha, remaining unwearied.
Having worshipped Kumāreśa, those who shall worship me, accompanied by sixty crores of goddesses, to them I shall grant their desires.
Nārada said: O Pārtha, having been addressed thus by the Goddess who was then well-pleased, I, being greatly delighted, replied to Kolambā, the Mother of the Universe.
"O Goddess, you are the mother of this hidden sacred field (guptakṣetra); the pilgrimage of those who do not worship you here is in vain. (41)
And this meritorious lake shall attain fame by your name; you are the mistress of this lake and likewise the mistress of this sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having performed such long penance, this auspicious Mahādurgā was established by me; therefore, she should always be worshipped by wise men. (43)
And she was established and installed by me in that third direction; and the power of this Kapāleśī has been described previously by Guha.
Blessed are those best of men who behold her constantly, having worshipped Kapāleśvara, for she is the power of the universe.
Thus, these three fortresses are situated in the eastern direction; now I shall describe the three most excellent fortresses in the western direction.
The goddess Suvarṇākṣī, who protects the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), has been worshipped by me here and established as a deity at this sacred ford (tīrtha). || 47 ||
And those who shall bow down to her and worship her with devotion, they too shall be honored by thirty-three crores of goddesses.
And another, Mahādurgā, who was smeared with [ashes], remained there; she was brought from the depths of the netherworld by me with great devotion. (49)
She is to be worshipped and meditated upon by those desiring to attain heroism; she bestowed heroic power upon many gods and daityas.
This very Mahādurgā shall, in the Kali age, by her prowess liberate Śūdraka—the best among heroes—who has been bound by thieves before her eyes.
Then, having propitiated her, he will attain the status of a lord of heroes and, having assailed them, he will slay his enemies headed by Kālasena.
Therefore, this Mahādurgā, who resides in the western direction and is praised by those desiring heroic power, should always be propitiated by men who possess vigor. (53)

Likewise, Trailokyavijayā resides in the third direction; having propitiated her, the Lord of Rohiṇī (the Moon) attained victory over the three worlds. Brought by me from the world of Soma, she is always worshipped as the bestower of victory. 54.
Thus these [goddesses] are in the west; now hear about those in the north: three goddesses stand in the north, facing Ekavīrā. (55)
"O Ekavīrā! That goddess who is directly worshipped by Śiva—possessed by her, this Lord of Beings destroys the entire world. (56)
Having reduced the worlds to ashes through the power of Vīryā, the foremost of heroes, he became bewildered in those ashes when eleven yugas had come to their full completion.
Such is this eternal Śakti, the sole heroine; when worshipped and propitiated, she grants all desired objects to men. (58)

O descendant of Bharata, she who is worthy of worship has been brought here by me from the world of Brahmā; they know that even the chanting of her name brings about the destruction of the wicked. (59)
The second goddess, named Harasiddhi, is the mighty Durgā; O Pāṇḍava, she was brought here by me after being propitiated at Śīkottara.
When Rudra, who was staying on Śīkottara and was entreated by Pārvatī, spoke the mantra of the Ḍākinīs out of compassion for the Goddess. (61)
Then, deluded by the power of the mantra, the virtuous Girijā stepped upon him and drank his flesh and blood.
Then, from the body of Rudra, there emerged Harasiddhi, the destroyer of suffering, the great Durgā, who is highly proficient in the great mantras.
That goddess of a thousand arms, having stepped upon him and pressed him down, liberated Giriśa and likewise released her from the curse.
From that time forward, she is celebrated in the world as Harasiddhi; surrounded by sixty crores of goddesses, she is worshipped by the gods.
Having propitiated this destroyer of faults, those led by Sugrīva became possessed of great heroism and destroyers of the hosts of ḍākinīs. (66)
Therefore, one should worship her through the actions of mind, speech, and body; then the ḍākinīs and others will not approach, immediately after the attainment of Hara-siddhi.
Caṇḍikā, the ninth, is situated in the northeast corner of the third [enclosure]; even Vāgīśa cannot reach the end of her description.
She who formerly emerged from the body of Pārvatī and, having slain the two great asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, devoured them out of wrath; (69)
Even a hundred akṣauhiṇīs and both Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa were not enough for even a single mouthful of hers; what indeed could be seen of her as she devoured them?
This very [goddess], thirsty for blood, drank it again from the Andhakas; then the Blessed Lord Bhava subdued Andhaka.
And having drunk the blood-born liquor of the Raktabījas, she offered that blood, which had been drunk by Cāmuṇḍā, to the Goddess.
O Bhārata, she is satisfied even by the prostration of devotees, as well as by hundreds of millions of crores of sinful Daityas. (73)
And for this goddess, I have prepared a meritorious and auspicious pool, by the mere touch of which one shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 74 ||

O Bhārata, various attainments—such as the attainment of power (Hara-siddhi), the attainment of divinity (Devatā-siddhi), and the attainment of dharma—are obtained at this sacred ford by those devoted to Caṇḍikā. (75)
And whoever worships the Goddess, whether with little or much, Kātyāyanī—surrounded by hundreds of millions [of attendants]—bestows prosperity upon him. (76)

Thus, these nine great goddesses of difficult access are established here at the sacred ford; likewise, the four deities of the directions are to be constantly worshipped by those desiring auspiciousness.
Especially during the Navarātra of the month of Āśvina, one should worship these goddesses after fasting or by eating only a single meal a day.

With offerings of bali, cakes, and food-oblations, as well as libations, incense, and perfumes, these [goddesses] provide protection for him in the streets, at the triple-junctions, and in the squares.
Spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and the like can neither help nor cause him affliction; calamities quickly flee from him, and the yoginīs bring him joy.
One desiring a son shall obtain sons; one desiring wealth shall attain wealth; one afflicted by disease shall be freed from disease; and one who is bound shall be released from bondage. 81.
Any man or woman who, with faith, offers devotion to these [deities], shall attain all desires whatsoever that they contemplate in their minds.

These goddesses are like wish-fulfilling cows (kāmagavya) and likewise resemble wish-granting gems (cintāmaṇi); furthermore, they are like the wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpavallī) for devotees—indeed, there are nine such forms here. (83)
Likewise, Bhūtamātā is located here to the south of Harasiddhi; I shall describe her incomparable majesty to you in brief.
It is said that formerly the wise Guha was consecrated on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī as the supreme sovereign over the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
And out of compassion, the Lord Guha established all beings within their proper bounds by providing this very food. 86.

Whatever has been offered without mantras, whatever has been performed outside the Vedic tradition, and whatever has been done without faith or with anger—that shall serve for the satisfaction of the spirits (Vastu).
Then, by means of that enjoyment, they all rejoice completely; subsequently, after some time, [the fruit of] what was performed with faith or without faith [is experienced].
Those very beings, having overcome the deities, swallowed their merit; thereafter, those gods, afflicted by hunger, reported this to Guha. (89)
Having heard that, Guha indeed became enraged like Time (Kāla) itself; from the middle of his angry brow-lotus, a certain [power] emerged.

A woman garlanded with flames, exceedingly difficult to behold and possessing twelve eyes, bowed to him and said: "O Lord, I am your Śakti; quickly command me as to what task I should perform for you that you desire. (91)
Skanda said: "By these sinful hosts of spirits, having transgressed my command," (92)
Everything given by humans is consumed at will by the base; therefore, you must quickly bring these things back within the bounds of propriety.
"O auspicious one, these hundreds of millions of goddesses shall follow you. Then she said, "So be it," and was surrounded by those goddesses.
Having approached the peacock, Guha’s power arrived; reaching a lotus grove, she beheld hosts of spirits.
And having approached him, the Goddess struck him with various kinds of weapons; then, in that great battle, the pretas, piśācas, and others were being slaughtered.
Some propitiated that goddess with various guises and in a very humble manner; others did so in the guise of Brahmins, using the words of ascetics. || 97 ||
"O lotus-eyed goddess, dance! Be gracious! they cried again and again. Then that goddess, being pleased, said to them, "Choose whatever you desire."
They said to her: "Protect us! O Sovereign Goddess, be the mother of all beings; we shall never abandon the boundaries established by Skanda. (99)
And to those who thus please you, always grant boons.

The Illustrious Goddess said: Those who thus propitiate me on the new-moon day of Vaiśākha with offerings of unblemished ornaments, flowers, curd-rice, and worship—for them, all calamities will clearly go to destruction. (101)
Having thus granted the boon, the goddess, surrounded by spirits, rejoiced. Such is the power of that goddess, O Bhārata, who was brought here by me.
The mortal who bows down to her is liberated from all calamities. || 103 ||

Thus have I proclaimed, in brief, the powers of these goddesses here at this most excellent sacred site; they are fourteen in number, O Arjuna, and are worshipped by the foremost of men at fourteen preeminent locations. (104)

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of the Illustrious Goddess," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 47.
Nārada said: Now, therefore, I shall clearly proclaim the greatness of Somanātha; by hearing it and by reciting it, one shall obtain liberation from sin. 1.
Long ago in the Tretā Yuga, O Pārtha, there were two brahmins of great luster born in the country of Cauḍa, named Ūrjayanta and Prāleya.
Once upon a time, they both saw a single verse concerning the meaning of the Purāṇas; having seen it, those two, who were knowers of all scriptures, had their hair stand on end with joy.
The Lotus-born Lord spoke of Prabhāsa and other sacred fords to Pulastya: "If one has not bathed in them, what purpose has been served by worshipping those sacred fords?"
Having recited this verse and praised him again and again, those two excellent ones then departed for Prabhāsa to bathe.
Gradually crossing through forests and rivers, they both reached the auspicious Narmadā, which was crowded with hosts of great sages.
Having heard the greatness of the Guptakṣetra and the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, they bathed there and set out for Prabhāsa by way of its center.
Then, because the path was empty, the two brahmins, severely afflicted by thirst and hunger, remained unconscious near the *siddha-liṅga*.
Having paid homage to Siddhanātha, they set forth with great fortitude; yet, tormented by the midday sun, they were overcome by the intense force of hunger and thirst.
The two pillar-feet suddenly fell to the ground, unconscious; then, after a moment, Prāleya spoke to Ūrjayanta.
O friend, have you not heard from some reliable source and with steadfastness how one’s limbs become pale through the performance of a pilgrimage? (11)
In that very manner, Hara, the Lord of Soma, became impoverished by his gifts; and even as this was being spoken and heard, those two continued to plunder in such a way.
While he was still stumbling along, at a short distance away, a Liṅga suddenly rose up, piercing the earth, and it was very difficult to behold.

Then a voice arose there, preceded by a rain of flowers: "O Prāleya, for your sake, a fruit equal to Somanātha has arisen as a Liṅga on the shore of the ocean; remain here, O observer of noble vows. (14)
Prāleya said: "If this is indeed true, nevertheless, the self has been postulated. (15)
"When it was clear that I must go to Prabhāsa before death, then Urjayanta also fell forward in a swoon. (16)
He saw the Liṅga arisen and understood it thus; then Bhava, having become manifest, made [the two of them] firm.
Then, having become attenuated by that vision, they both went to Prabhāsa and Śivasadma; these two are the two Somanāthas located near Siddheśvara. || 18 ||
In the west is Ūrjayanta, and another is Prāleyeśvara; having slowly bathed in the waters of Somakuṇḍa, one should bathe in the waters of the ocean and the earth.
One who beholds the two Somanāthas is liberated from the sins of birth; for Brahmā, having established here [the shrine] known as Hāṭakeśvara, [established these]. (20)
In the city of Mahī, he devoutly praised the most enchanting Liṅga that had emerged from Pātāla; O Pāṇḍava, listen to that hymn of praise.
Salutations to you, O Blessed Rudra, the sun of immeasurable splendor; salutations to Bhava, to Rudra, to Rasa, and to you who consist of water.
Salutations always to Śarva, who has the form of the earth and is ever-fragrant; salutations again and again to you, Īśa, the wind, the very essence of touch. || 23 ||
Salutations also to the Lord of creatures, to the Purifier of exceeding brilliance, to the Terrifying One, whose form is space, and who consists of the subtle element of sound. || 24 ||
Salutations be to you, Mahādeva, Soma, the Immortal; salutations to you, the Fierce One, the Sacrificer, the practitioner of the yoga of action. || 25 ||
Thus has this hymn been uttered with divine names; whoever should recite or even hear this hymn composed by the Grandfather (Brahmā), [he shall attain his desires]. || 26 ||
A man who is constantly self-restrained and worships the Hāṭakeśvara Liṅga attains union with the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti); of this there is no doubt.
O Jaya, even he who, being self-restrained, remembers the Hāṭakeśvara Liṅga, to him Brahmā shall be a granter of boons; it was for this reason that it was installed by him.
There are many such meritorious holy places at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; I have described them to you in brief. (29)

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Account of Somanātha," in the Stambhatīrtha-māhātmya, within the Kaumārikā-khaṇḍa of the first Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, in the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Arjuna said: O great sage, having heard from the lotus of your mouth about these most wonderful sacred fords (tīrthas) and lingas, my mind rejoices exceedingly.
O Sage, O Lord, please describe to me those principal sacred sites (tīrthas) that were established by you even in Mahīnagaraka. || 2 ||
Nārada said: O Phālguna, I shall describe those holy places (tīrthas) that exist in the illustrious Mahīnagaraka, where the Lord Sun, Jayāditya, resides.
The man who here proclaims the name of Jayāditya shall be liberated from all diseases and obtain whatever he desires in his heart.
O Pārtha, by the mere sight of him, a man endowed with faith is filled with auspicious things and is liberated from inauspicious ones.
O Pārtha, listen as I tell you of that god’s origin; by hearing it or even by reciting it, one shall obtain grace from the Sun-god.
Having established this foundation, after some time, I departed for the world of the Sun by chance, desiring a vision of him.
As I sat bowed before him, the divine Bhāskara honored me with the arghya offering and, as if smiling, spoke these words to me in a sweet voice.
O Brahmin, from where have you come, and where are you going? And where, O Sage Nārada, did you spend this time of yours?

Nārada said: Thus addressed by Bhāskara, I then spoke these words to him: "O Lord Bhāskara, having wandered through the Bhārata-khaṇḍa even beyond Mahīnagaraka, I have come here for the sake of beholding you."
Ravi said: "Tell me of the qualities of those Brāhmaṇas who reside in the place established by you; indeed, what are the virtues of those twice-born ones?"
Nārada said: Thus questioned by the Blessed One, I spoke these words once again.
If I praise them, it will be said that I am praising my own kin; if I censure those who do not deserve it, why should I? Alas, it is distressing in either case. (13)
Alternatively, since those great-souled ones possess supreme majesty, were I to provide only a brief description, it would indeed result in a great fault on my part. (14)
O Sun, if there should be a desire to hear from those eminent brahmins honored by me, then you should go and see them yourself; this is my opinion. (15)
Having heard these words of mine, Ravi was greatly amazed; the Lord of Day spoke again and again, saying, "I shall see it myself."
Then, having assumed the form of a Brahmin and dismissed me, the Sun-god, shining in the sky through his yogic power, departed for the shore of the ocean.
Then, wearing matted locks tawny from bathing three times a day, a highly effulgent elderly brahmin was seen by my brahmins.
Then those twice-born ones, headed by Hārīta, their eyes blossoming with great joy, rose from the Brahma-hall and rushed toward the twice-born one.
Having paid homage to that foremost of the twice-born, they spoke this out of great joy.
"O best of Brahmins, today our day has become sacred and this place has become most excellent, because you yourself have come here. (21)
O best of the twice-born, there is no doubt that by the very grace of a fortunate householder, they come in the guise of guests for the sake of his purification.
O Tattva, purify our houses by walking upon them with your feet, and by your sight, your food, and your presence, sanctify us together.
The guest said: "O Brahmins, food is of two kinds: the ordinary and the supreme. I desire that the supreme food be properly given to me. (24)
Having heard this from the guest, Hārīta said to his son: "O son, do you know what the twice-born Kamaṭha, who is eight years old, has said? (25)
Kamaṭha said: "Father, having prostrated before you, I shall describe such a supreme meal; and I shall satisfy the twice-born by giving him that supreme meal. (26)
"It is said that by the birth of a son, a father becomes free from his debt; I shall make those words true by fully satisfying this most excellent guest. (27)
Food is of two kinds, and this is their distinction: the first is called ordinary food, while the other is the supreme food. (28)
In that regard, that which is the "Prākṛta" name belongs to the group headed by Prakṛti; indeed, it is said to be the libation for the assembly of the twenty-four principles.
They say that food consists of six tastes and is further divided into five types; by eating which the field, characterized as the body, becomes satisfied.
Just as that which is beyond the highest is called the "Supreme," so too the Self is declared to be supreme; that [Supreme] shall be its food. (31)
Now, that which is the hearing of the Dharma in its various forms is indeed called the food; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the eater, and the ears are the mouth. (32)
"I shall give that to the foremost of the twice-born; ask, O Brahmin, whatever you desire. According to my ability, I shall satisfy you in this assembly of Brahmins. (33)
Nārada said: Having heard these significant words of the tortoise, that guest praised him within his mind and then addressed him with this question: ||| 34 ||
How is a living being born, and how does it perish? Having reached the state of ashes, where does this [being] go? (35)
Kamaṭha said: "O twice-born one, having first offered salutations to my guru and thereafter to Dharma, I shall explain this question sung in the Chāndogya according to my ability."
It is said that at birth, three kinds of karma serve as the cause for a living being: merit, demerit, and their mixture, corresponding to the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. (37)
Among these, he who is called *sāttvika* attains heaven; having descended from heaven when his time is up, he becomes wealthy, righteous, and happy. (38)
Likewise, he who falls into the hell named Tāmasa, having endured many tortures, attains the state of an immobile being. (39)

Through the sight and touch of the great, through their enjoyments and shared seats, and by the conjunction with the great over a long period of time, a human being, as he transmigrates, may become [great]. (40)
He too, surrounded by suffering, poverty, and the like, with impaired senses, is visible to all people; for this indeed is the characteristic of sin.
Now, he who possesses mixed karma may attain the state of an animal; yet, through association with the great, he may become a human being while wandering in saṃsāra.
He whose merit is vast and whose sin is indeed small shall first experience suffering and afterwards be endowed with happiness. (43)
He for whom evil is more extensive and merit is less will first be happy and then miserable; this indeed is the characteristic of one whose actions are mixed. 44.
In that regard, hear now what the human birth is like when it occurs through the union of the semen and blood of a man and a woman. (45)
The individual soul (jīva), clearly liberated from all defects, transmigrates, endowed with the qualities of mind and intellect, and accompanied by both auspicious and inauspicious [karmas]. || 46 ||
The living soul, having entered the womb, takes its stand in the *kalala*; being in a state of delusion, it remains there for exactly one month.
In the second month, however, it remains in a solidified state; in the third month, the formation of its limbs occurs. (48)
Likewise, the bones are formed in the fourth month; the skin is produced in the fifth month, and the growth of body hair occurs in the sixth.
And likewise, in the seventh month, awakening occurs for it; and in the seventh month, it partakes of what the mother eats and drinks.
In the eighth or ninth month, he then becomes greatly distressed; his limbs are enveloped by the placenta, and his fingers are clenched at his mouth.
The neuter stands in the middle, the female on the left, and likewise the male on the right; indeed, he stands with his face toward the fire at the region of the belly and the back.
In whichever womb he resides, he knows it without a doubt; he remembers the entire history of even many previous births.

In blinding darkness, what can be seen? One may experience intense delusion from [perceiving] scents. When cold water is drunk during the cold season, it feels cool; likewise, it feels hot during the heat.
Through strenuous exertion, one incurs the suffering of the mother and the pain of disease; moreover, other diseases arise that cannot be traced to either father or mother. (55)
Due to his extreme delicacy, those [instruments] cause him intense pain, and even that brief period of time he perceives as being like a hundred years.
It suffers intensely within the womb due to its past actions, and it repeatedly forms desires for the sake of performing virtuous deeds.
If I should obtain birth in the human state as well as life there, then I shall perform that by which liberation will clearly be attained.
As he was reflecting thus, two months passed while he remained afflicted by the form of the Triple-Aged One (Viṣṇu) following the Sīmantonnayana rite.
Then, when its time is fully completed, the creature, impelled by the winds of labor, becomes head-downwards, experiencing extreme pain.
Facing downwards, he emerges through the narrow passage of the birth canal, suffering from a pain comparable to having one's skin flayed.
Having been deluded for only a month, this newborn infant perceives the touch of his hands and other such sensations as being like the touch of a saw. (62)
Under the sway of past karma, his knowledge of the womb perishes; thereafter, he performs actions that are white, red, and black.

It is supported by pillars of bone-boards and scales, bound together with cords of sinew; it is plastered with the mud of blood and flesh, and serves as a vessel for the substances of feces and urine. (64)
It was well-constructed with seven walls, covered even with hair and grass, having the mouth as its single great door and adorned with eight windows.
It has the two lips as its door-panels, sealed by the bolt of the teeth; it possesses a flow of sweat from the channels and is drenched with phlegm and bile.
It is overwhelmed by old age and sorrow, situated within the fire of the mouth of Time, destroyed by passion, hatred, and the like, and born from the six sheaths.
In this way, O twice-born one, this body-house of a person is produced, wherein dwells the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), with the intellect as his housewife.
He remains even while fully accomplishing liberation, heaven, and hell.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Body of the Jīva," in the Kaumārikā-khaṇḍa of the first section (Māheśvara-khaṇḍa) of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, within the dialogue between Kamaṭha and Sūrya. || 49 ||
The guest said: "O child of unchildlike intellect, O tortoise, what you have said is excellent. However, I wish to hear again the characteristics of the body; please speak of that. (1)
Kamaṭha said: Listen now to how this universe and the body correspond: the soles of the feet are Pātāla, and the foreparts of the feet are Rasātala. || 2 ||
Talātala is his two ankles, Mahātala his two shanks, Sutala his two knees, Vitala his two thighs, and Atala his hips.
They say his navel is the surface of the earth; his abdomen is the Bhuvarloka; his chest is the Svarloka; and his neck and mouth are the Maharloka.
They say that the eyes are the world of austerity (tapas) and the region of the head is the world of truth (satyaloka); likewise, they speak of the seven continents situated upon the earth. || 5 ||
Likewise, understand from me these seven constituents (dhātus) here by their names: skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents.
There are three hundred and sixty bones here, and three million channels have been described.
Fifty-six thousand and nine others indeed carry the essence within the body, just as rivers on earth carry water.
The body is covered on all sides by three and a half crores of pores; these are indeed known to be both gross and subtle, visible and invisible.
Listen as I describe the six primary limbs: the two arms, the two thighs, the head, and the belly. (10)
The brahmins learned in the Vedas say that the intestines here are likewise three and a half vyāmas long, while those of women are three vyāmas long.
The lotus in the heart is proclaimed to have its stalk pointing upward and its face turned downward. To the left of the heart-lotus is the spleen, and likewise, the liver is on the right.
O twice-born one, [it arises] from marrow, from fat, and likewise from muscle-fat; and also from urine, bile, phlegm, and feces. (13)
In this case, for the final stage of blood, two handfuls (dvyañjali) are prescribed; these, when flowing, are said to sustain the body.
Likewise, O twice-born one, seven and five [veins] are situated upon the head; one has gone to the penis, and another has gone to the tongue.
All the channels proceed here from the navel-lotus; among them, the most excellent are those that go to the head: Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā.
Having reached the gateway of the nose, when the vital breaths are established within the body, there are fivefold divisions each for the wind, the fire, and the moon.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna are known as the five divisions of the vital air (vāyu); they also describe their respective functions. || 18 ||
Inhalation, exhalation, and the entry of food and drink—extending from the throat up to the head—this is proclaimed as the function of the vital breath (prāṇa). 19.
The evacuation of feces, urine, and semen, as well as the discharge of the fetus, is designated as the function of the *apāna*; its location is above the anus.
The *samāna* wind sustains the food and also separates it; tasting it, it moves unimpeded through all the channels. || 21 ||
The location of udāna is proclaimed to be from the throat up to the head, exerting effort during the initiation of speech and all physical actions. (22)

Vyāna is eternally situated in the heart as well as moving throughout the body; it provides the nourishment for the bodily constituents and performs perspiration, salivation, and the opening and closing of the eyes.
The digestive fire, the coloring fire, the accomplishing fire, the illuminating fire, and likewise the radiant fire—thus the fire exists in the body in five ways. (24)

The digestive fire (pācaka), situated in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), constantly cooks the food; the coloring fire (rañjaka), though situated in the receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya), transforms the nutrient essence (rasa) into blood.
The agent (sādhaka) resides in the heart and is the cause of the exertion of the intellect and other faculties; the observer (ālocaka) resides in the eye and effects the power of perceiving form.
The bhrājaka, residing in the skin, makes the body radiant when it has been purified; likewise, there are the kledaka, the bodhaka, and the tarpaṇa of the phlegm.
Likewise, the *ālaṃbaka* is said to be fivefold in the body; the *kledaka*, situated in the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), constantly moistens the food. (28)
Situated in the tongue, it is the awakener and the perceiver of tastes; situated in the head, it is known as the "satisfier" because it provides nourishment to the eyes and other senses. (29)
It is present in all the joints, as well as in phlegm and that which produces phlegm; residing in the chest, it indeed stays pervading all the limbs, for it is the "Alambaka" (the clinging one).
In this way, that body is sustained by air, fire, and the moon; likewise, the channels born of space as well as the distinctiveness of the internal cavities [are maintained].
Know that here the earth elements are the sense of smell, the hair, and the nails; the bones, fortitude, gravity, the skin, the flesh, the heart, and the anus. (32)
The navel, fat, liver, marrow, intestines, the stomach, the veins, the sinews, and the large intestine—these, the twice-born who know the Vedas declare [to be the constituents of the body]. (33)
The white circle of the eyes arises from phlegm and is paternal; the black circle arises from wind and is likewise maternal. (34)
The first is the circle of eyelashes, the second is the circle of the skin; the third is said to be white, and the fourth is the black circle. || 35 ||
The fifth is the circle of vision (dṛṅmaṇḍala); the eye consists of five circles. On the other part of the eye are the two [parts]: the inner corner (upāṅga) and the outer corner (apāṅga).
The upāṅgas are said to extend from the eyes to the base of the nose; likewise, the testicles are declared to consist of fat, blood, phlegm, and flesh.
The tongue of all embodied beings consists of blood and flesh; furthermore, there are six kūrcakas in the two hands, the two lips, the penis, and the neck. (38)
This being the case, while the individual soul (jīva) resides within this body composed of seven layers, it pervades the body as the twenty-fifth principle; its dwelling place is in the head.
They say that skin, blood, and flesh—this triad—is derived from the mother; while fat, marrow, and bone are declared to be born of the father; thus, O Kauśika, there are six constituents.
I shall describe to you how this body, composed of the elements, attains growth through foods produced from the five elements. (41)
When that food is consumed by embodied beings in the form of morsels and mouthfuls, the vital breath (prāṇa) first divides it into two parts within the thick receptacle (the stomach).
Having entered into the midst of the food, with the rice and water kept separate, one should place the water above the fire and that food upon that water.
The vital breath (prāṇa), situated below the water, gently fans the fire; the fire, being fanned by the wind, makes the water exceedingly hot.
That food is then cooked on all sides by hot water; once cooked, it becomes twofold: the waste matter separately and the nutrient essence separately.
Through the twelve impurities, the waste matter is separated from the body and goes outside: [the secretions of] the ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, and nails. (46)
