And there are the hair-pores; these twelve are the seats of impurity. Furthermore, all the channels are connected on every side to the heart-lotus.
Vyāna places that subtle essence within their mouths; then Samāna fills those channels again with that essence.
Then those [channels], being completely filled, spread throughout the body from all sides; thereafter, that nutrient essence situated within the channels is heated by the coloring heat.
As it is being cooked, it again attains the state of blood; from that arise the skin, body hair, head hair, flesh, sinews, vessels, and bones.
Nails, marrow, phlegm, impurities, and the increase of semen occur in succession; thus is the twelvefold transformation of food proclaimed. (51)
Thus, this body has been brought forth for the sake of merit, just as a bright chariot is intended for the carrying of a burden.
If it is not protected through many efforts such as anointing with oil and the like, what purpose is served by it if it indeed cannot bear a burden? (53)
Thus, what is the purpose of nourishing this body with the finest foods, if one does not perform meritorious deeds and acts like a mere beast? (54)
And there are verses on this point: "In whatever time, in whatever place, and at whatever age a good or evil deed was performed, it is experienced by that very person in that same manner. (55)
Therefore, those who desire uninterrupted happiness should always perform virtuous deeds; otherwise, enjoyments are severed like small streams in the summer heat.
Since through sin there arise many intense sufferings, therefore one must not commit sin; for it causes torment to oneself.
Thus, O virtuous one, this question of yours has been described by me according to my ability; now hear how a living being is born and how it perishes.
When the lifespan and the karma of men have been exhausted and death has arrived, the embodied soul, subject to the power of its own actions, is dragged away by the servants of Yama.
Accompanied by the five subtle elements (tanmātras), along with the mind, intellect, and ego, the individual soul (jīva), bound by the fetters consisting of merit and demerit, abandons the body.
For those of meritorious deeds, [the breath] exits through the seven apertures of the head; for sinners it goes downward; and for yogins, it departs from the *brahmarandhra*.
At that very moment, he then assumes a subtle body (ativāhika), the size of a thumb's joint, which is fashioned by his own vital breaths alone.
Then, the messengers of Yama bind the individual soul residing in that body and lead it along the southern path with all their might.
It was like a heated frying pan, like a glowing iron ball, like scorching sand, and like a vessel of molten copper.
Dragged from the surface of the earth by the soldiers of Yama, the evildoer is led eighty-six thousand yojanas toward the city of Yama. (65)
In some places there was cold, a great and impassable darkness; in other places, there were crows, ravens, and jackals whose mouths felt like the touch of fire.
He is bitten by flies, gadflies, mosquitoes, snakes, and scorpions; though being devoured by them, the creature cries out but does not die. (617)
In some places he is devoured by terrible rākṣasas, dragged, and cast away; being scorched by the most dreadful sand, he is led along.
In ten muhūrtas he traverses that exceedingly difficult path; yet a person perceives that time as being equal to a full year. (69)
And he is made to cross the terrible river Vaitaraṇī by name, which flows with pus and blood, with hair for its moss and grassy weeds.
Then he is placed before Yama by the servants of Yama; the sinner beholds a great terror, surrounded by those with faces like the God of Death at the end of time.
It is said that at that time, those of meritorious deeds go to Dharmarāja, who possesses a gentle form; others, however, go to the world of Yama as mere mortals.
Immediately after death, those beings fill their respective wombs; for it is heard that pretas become humans, but not other types of creatures. (73)
There, the righteous man is honored, while the sinner shall have a noose around his neck. Listen as I tell you how the righteous man travels that path. (74)
Just as those who give garden trees travel happily along a path provided with fruits, flowers, and shade, so too do those men who give parasols.

Those who give sandals travel by vehicles; those who perform acts of public utility travel free from thirst; those who give gifts of vehicles go by celestial chariots, as do those who provide beds and seats. (76)
Satiated with various kinds of foods and edibles, those who give food go [to that river]; those who give lamps go by means of light, and those who give cows cross that river with ease. (77)
Those who are devoted from birth to Śrī Sūrya, Śrī Mahādeva, and Puruṣottama, go [to their respective abodes] being honored by the followers of Yama.
By giving land, a cow, gold, iron, sesame seeds, cotton, salt, and the seven types of grain, a man goes to happiness.
Then, once those sinners and those who performed meritorious deeds have arrived there, Citragupta indeed reports their cases to the Lord of the Dead (Pretapa).
That man dwells in the world of the hungry ghosts for one year; and by the end of that year, his body is reborn.
Whatever food and water with a jar is offered by his kinsmen day after day, he consumes that and thereby attains growth. (82)
Furthermore, one obtains for oneself the food and other provisions previously given by others; yet, for that which has not been given by oneself, no giver exists. (83)
Moreover, that giver of water is not excessively afflicted by hunger and thirst; the water offered by his kinsmen approaches him, having become a river. (84)
And that monthly śrāddha, preceded by the sixteen śrāddhas, which is not performed for someone here—he is not released from the state of being a preta. (85)
A day in the world of the departed (preta) is considered to be equal to a human day; therefore, food should be given to the departed day after day for a year.
And there, the terrifying Yama-hosts known as the Śmāśānikas guard that sinner against cold, wind, and heat.

Just as someone here in this world of bondage might be watched over by treacherous men, so too, if the sixteen funeral rice-balls (piṇḍas) preceded by the śrāddha rites are not offered, [the deceased remains bound].

For whomever [this occurs], there is no liberation from the state of a preta even in the course of ages; therefore, when the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is properly performed by kinsmen, the man [is released]. (89)
When a full year has passed, he regains his body; the evil-minded one obtains one of terrible form, while the righteous one obtains a divine and most excellent one.
Thereupon, he goes to hell or to heaven according to his own karma; and the hells, beginning with Raurava, are situated in the depths of Pātāla. (91)

Beginning with the world of the gods (Sura) and ending with the world of truth (Satya), these are situated above the heavenly realm (Svarloka); this is what has been heard in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Vedas, and Smṛtis.
Through that merit, heaven shall come to be; from its opposite, hell. Even there, one dwells for a duration of time according to the nature of one's karmas.
Even for one whose *piṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before a year or after a year, it is declared that his state as a *preta* certainly lasts for a full year.
Those by whom the triad of gods has been worshipped or honored with three types of offerings do not go to the world of the departed, nor do those who have been slain in battle.

Through pure merit one goes to a pure heaven, and through pure evil likewise to the blinding darkness; through mixed karma one goes to both heaven and hell, and his body likewise becomes of such a nature.
These three questions—namely, birth, death, and dwelling in the next world—have been set forth by you. Just as my teacher explained them, so shall I speak; what more do you wish to hear? || 97 ||

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Soul’s Journey to the Other World and Other Matters," in the dialogue between Āditya and Kamaṭha, within the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 50 ||
The guest said: "That which you have described as the nature of the other world is exactly so, based upon scripture; of this there is no doubt. (1)
However, here the wicked nihilists of small intellect harbor doubts; therefore, speak that which is the fruit of action, so as to bring them certainty. || 2 ||
If you have it, please tell me: by the power of what specific kind of evil deed would one become such a tortoise as this? (3)
Kamaṭha said: "I shall explain all of this; remain steady and listen to it, just as my guru spoke it and as it is established in my mind. (4)

The killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; the drinker of spirituous liquor shall have blackened teeth; the thief of gold shall have deformed nails; and the violator of the Guru’s bed shall have a skin disease.
One who associates with these five types of sinners shall suffer from every disease; by hearing the censure of the virtuous, one becomes deaf.
Furthermore, he who proclaims [the teacher's faults] himself becomes a mute sinner; and a man who violates the commands of his teachers will become epileptic.
One who treats them with contempt is reborn as a mere worm; and for one who neglects the service due to those worthy of honor, a state of impaired intelligence arises.
For as many steps as that lowest of men takes toward stealing the property of a virtuous person, for that many years he shall suffer from lameness.
Having given something and then taking it back again, one is born as a lizard; by failing to appease those worthy of honor when they are angry, one will suffer from diseases of the head.
One who approaches a woman during her menses is born as a Caṇḍāla; a stealer of clothes becomes a Citrin, and likewise, one who sets fire [to a house] becomes afflicted with black leprosy.
One who steals silver becomes a frog; a false witness suffers from diseases of the mouth; and one who lustfully looks upon another’s wife shall suffer from eye disease. (12)
For the man who, having made a promise, does not fulfill it, is born short-lived; he who steals away what has been offered becomes one who suffers from indigestion, always the lowest of men. (13)

By abandoning the lifelong vow of celibacy, one becomes perpetually afflicted by disease; however, if there are many wives, the emission of semen upon only one of them leads to the wasting away of vital energy.
That fool who, though joined with righteousness by his master, should act unjustly or consume wealth himself, shall suffer from dropsy.
He who, being powerful, neglects one who is weak and oppressed, shall become deficient in limbs and shall suffer from hunger for food. || 16 ||
A man who is partial in legal disputes will suffer from diseases of the tongue; by obstructing the practice of dharma, he causes separation from his wife and other loved ones.
He who eats the first-fruits of his own cooking shall suffer from throat disease; he who eats without having performed the five great sacrifices is a village pig.
A man who engages in sexual intercourse before his wife’s period, who abandons his own wife, and who is infatuated with prostitutes and the like, becomes a bald-headed fool. (19)
Having disregarded his exhausted friends, kinsmen, master, and beloved followers, he should always remain self-restrained and maintain a disciplined livelihood. (20)
But he who treats his parents, his master, or his teachers with deceit shall suffer the loss of whatever wealth he has acquired through great hardship. || 21 ||
But he who steals from one who trusts him shall become a vessel for sufferings; that man who acts with meanness toward a righteous person shall become a dwarf.
And he who drives weak oxen shall suffer from a creeping eruption on his waist.

Furthermore, one who is blind from birth, a killer of cows, devoid of sight, a causer of suffering to cattle, merciless toward cows through acts such as striking them, and one who always wanders in distress upon difficult mountain paths; || 24 ||
He who is spiritless in the assembly is born with a goiter; he who is constantly angry becomes a Caṇḍāla, and the informer has a putrid mouth.

One who sells goats becomes a hunter; one who eats from a vessel belonging to another becomes a servant; an atheist becomes a grinder of sesame seeds; and one devoid of faith becomes a professional singer.
One who eats forbidden food becomes afflicted with goiter; one who consumes women becomes childless; and a person who acquires knowledge through unjust means becomes a fool. (27)
A thief of the scriptures, one with squinting eyes, and he who hates meritorious stories—that person of wicked intellect shall become worm-faced and fall from hell.
One who seizes the livelihood of gods, brahmins, or cows becomes a consumer of vomit; one who destroys tanks or groves becomes one with deformed hands.
In legal disputes, such a man becomes a seeker of fallacious arguments and is beset by servants; a man devoted to another's wife will always suffer from diseases of the male organ.

One who violates the preceptor’s bed shall suffer from skin diseases; one who has intercourse with a donkey shall be afflicted with diabetes; and one who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the same lineage shall be childless. (31)
One who approaches his sister, mother, or daughter-in-law, being seedless and ungrateful, encounters the failure of all his undertakings.
Thus has this brief description of the characteristics of sinners been proclaimed; even Citragupta would be bewildered by a full recounting of them all.
Having fallen from hell and passed through thousands of wombs, these men are born marked with such signs as these. (34)
For those who do not honor the Dharma, as well as those overcome by calamities, must be understood through inference to be among those whose sins remain.
Those whose evil has come to an end, or those who have arrived from heaven—freed from all calamities, they devote themselves solely to Dharma.
And there are verses on this subject: "From dharma comes happiness unsurpassed; from adharma arises suffering. Therefore, for the sake of happiness, one should practice dharma and avoid evil. (37)
Since it is said that whatever happiness exists in both worlds arises from dharma, one should therefore practice dharma alone for the sake of accomplishing all goals and purposes. (38)
A man may live for even a single moment by means of pure action; he should not live even for an eon by means of an action that opposes both worlds.
"O Brahmin, thus have I answered what you asked according to my ability; whether it was ill-spoken or well-spoken, it must be forgiven—what more shall I say? (40)
Nārada said: Having heard these words of the eight-year-old tortoise, the Lord Bhāskara became exceedingly pleased and filled with great wonder.
And then he praised those Brahmins, headed by Hārīta, saying: "O, blessed is this earth with such supreme twice-born ones as these! (42)
Now, Prajāpati is blessed that his boundaries are thus protected; and by these excellent Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas are likewise blessed at this time. (43)
Among those such as Hārīta and others, what indeed will their understanding be, when even this childish intellect of mine is so clearly manifest? || 44 ||
Without doubt, there is nothing situated within the three worlds that remains unknown to them; for this reason, Nārada spoke of them again and again in great detail.
Having thus praised those brahmins, the delighted Ravi said: "O foremost of brahmins, I am Sūrya; I have been made manifest to you because of your sight. (46)
Having come from the world of the Sun, I have obtained the fruit of my eyes through conversing and sitting together with eminent Brahmins such as yourself.
Even those born of the lowest castes are purified, how much more so twice-born men like me! In every respect, Nārada is blessed, for he is the knower of the truth of the three worlds.

I bow to all of you with my mind, intellect, and concentration—you who have shaken off all impurities and for whom the highest good is being cultivated by you; for it is from you that austerity, knowledge, and virtuous conduct derive their cause for maturity.
"Choose from me a boon, whatever you desire in your hearts, even if it be difficult to obtain; for you yourselves are givers of boons, and let my association with you not be in vain. (50)
For the company of deities never arises without fruit; therefore, choose some boon from me, and I shall grant it to you.
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard these words of Sūrya, those best of the twice-born were filled with joy.

Having worshipped him with supreme devotion through offerings of water for the feet, arghya, hymns of praise, and salutations, they addressed the Sun while reciting great mantras and prayers such as the Maṇḍala-stotra.
Victory to you, Jayāditya! Victory, O Lord! Victory, O Bhānu! Victory, O Immaculate One! Victory, O Lord of the Vedas! O Lord of Light, may you forever deliver us. 54.
You are the supreme deity of the brahmins, and even the creation of the brahmins is composed of you; O Lord, this place of ours has become utterly purified by being beheld by you.
Today our Vedas have become fruitful; today our ritual acts have become fruitful; today our home has become fruitful, O Lord of Rays, by being united with you.
"If you are to grant a boon, we choose this: this place of ours must never be abandoned under any circumstances. (57)
The illustrious Sūrya said: "Since you have previously addressed me as 'Jayāditya,' I shall therefore remain here forever, renowned by the name Jayāditya."
"As long as the earth, the oceans, the mountains, and the cities endure, O brahmins, I shall never abandon this place. (59)
Established here, I shall destroy poverty, the multitude of diseases, ringworm, circular skin eruptions, leprosy, and other ailments for those who resort to me.
Whosoever, being a human being, shall worship me even while I am stationed here, I shall come as if to the world of the Sun and partake of his worship.
Śrī Nārada said: When this had been spoken by the Blessed One, Hārīta and the other best of the twice-born installed the image according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas.
Then the twice-born said this to Kamaṭha: "Because of you, the Sun-god has stationed himself here as our lord; therefore, you should first praise the Sun."
Thus addressed by all the brahmins, Kamaṭha, the best among eloquent speakers, prostrated before Jayāditya and recited this great hymn of praise.

"You were not created [by anyone], yet you are merely one who has heard; thus the Primordial God speaks in the Yajurveda. The fourfold speech extends far and wide; I, bold and desiring my own ends, offer praise—forgive this. (65)
Mārtaṇḍa, Sūrya, Aṃśu, Arka, as well as Indra, Bhānu, Bhaga, Aryaman, and Svarṇaretas; || 66 ||

O God, you are indeed celebrated as Divākara, Mitraviṣṇu, and the twelvefold soul; salutations to you! The three worlds are your inner sanctum, and you are proclaimed to be the reservoir of waters and the entirety of space.
Salutations to you, the celestial Liṅga, who are garlanded with stars and adorned with a wreath of flowers. 68.

You are the God of gods, you are the protector of the helpless, you are the guardian of those who have found refuge, and you are compassionate toward the wretched. You are the eye of eyes, the intellect of intellects, the sky of skies; victory to you, the life of all living beings! 69.

O Treasure of treasures, you who remove poverty from poverty; O Source of blessings, you who dispel all inauspiciousness; O You who are renowned on earth as the conqueror of diseases and ailments—victory to you, O Āditya, victory to you, O Immeasurable One!

Seized by disease, overcome by leprosy, with life-breath failing, body shattered, and unconscious—your mother, father, and kinsmen all abandon you; who else but you is there to protect one forsaken by everyone? (71)

You are my father, you are my mother, you alone; you are my guru and you alone are my kinsmen. You are my dharma and you are my path to liberation. I am your servant; O Lord, abandon me or protect me.

I am sinful, I am deluded, my deeds are most fierce, I am cruel, and I am not a repository of good conduct; nevertheless, having prostrated at your feet, O Śrī Jayārka, bestow victory upon your devotees. 73.
Nārada said: Thus praised by the high-souled Kamaṭha, Jayāditya spoke to him in a smooth and deep voice, as if smiling.
"O Jayāditya, for whoever on earth shall praise me with this eightfold hymn which has been proclaimed by you, nothing shall be difficult to attain. (75)
Whoever recites this after especially worshipping me on Sunday, their diseases shall not remain, nor will poverty; of this there is no doubt.
And being pleased by you, my child, I grant this boon to you: having become omniscient on earth, you shall thereafter attain liberation.
Your father shall become an author of a Smṛti, honored by the twice-born; and there shall never be the destruction of this sacred place.
"O child, I shall never abandon this place. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One was honored and praised by the brahmins. (79)
Having taken leave of those best of the twice-born, the Lord vanished right there; thus, O Pārtha, Jayāditya was manifested here upon the surface of the earth.
O observer of noble vows, when the month of Āśvina has arrived and it is a Sunday, whoever worships Jayāditya on a Sunday in the month of Āśvina— || 81 ||
Having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, a man dispels the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa by worshipping [there] with red garlands, red sandalwood, and saffron.

Through anointing with perfumes, incense, and the like, and by offerings of food consisting of ghee and milk-rice, even a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, and one who violates the teacher's bed [are purified]. (83)
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of the Sun, having obtained sons, wives, wealth, long life, and worldly happiness.
Endowed with his desired objects of enjoyment, he shall dwell for a long time in the world of the Sun.
On every Sunday, beholding Jayāditya, or even praising or remembering him, grants the pacification of all diseases. (86)
Those who are devoted to the God who is without beginning or end, unmanifest, and the treasury of splendors, they dissolve into the stainless abode of the Sun.
O Pārtha, when a solar eclipse has occurred, one who is composed should perform a bath at Ravikūpa and diligently offer oblations.
O Jaya, listen with a focused mind to the majesty of that merit, as one who stands before Jayāditya performs a gift according to his ability. 89.

Whatever merit is found in Kurukṣetra, in Prabhāsa, and in Puṣkara; whatever merit is found in Vārāṇasī, in Prayāga, or even in Naimiṣa—that merit a mortal obtains through the grace of Jayāditya. (90)

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Jayāditya," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses. || 51 ||
Arjuna said: O Sage, how did Koṭitīrtha come to be, and by whom was it created? Or why, O Sage, is the fruit of ten million tīrthas said to be obtained here?
Nārada said: When my abode had been established, I propitiated the Lord, and Brahmā, the Grandfather, was personally brought here from the world of Brahmā.
Then, at the time of midday, the Blessed Lord Vidhi remembered ten million sacred bathing-places (*tīrtha*s), and they, being remembered, arrived there.
Three million from heaven, seventy thousand from the surface of the earth, and two million from the netherworld (pātāla) are recorded as having arrived.
O best of the Kurus, by this classification, even the lingas have arrived so that the Grandfather may perform worship according to their respective order.
Then, having performed his ablutions and worshipped the Liṅgas, the Lotus-born One completed his midday rites and, out of love for me, granted him a boon.
Then, a lake was created here by the Blessed One through his mind; having been honored by the holy fords, the Blessed Lord Prajāpati spoke this: || 7 ||
"What shall we do, O Blessed One? O Creator, O Lord, give us your command. Having heard those words of theirs, Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, spoke.
In this lake, one should remain along with all the sacred fords (tīrthas), and likewise, by worshipping me through a single linga, one performs the worship of all lingas.
If my words are true, then the fruit obtained here from bathing, worshipping, and giving gifts at ten million sacred fords and lingas [is attained by this alone]. 10.

Whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony here and offers the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) according to the prescribed rite, an inexhaustible satisfaction arises for the ancestors; of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
He who, with undivided mind, bathes and worships the deity Koṭīśvara, clearly attains the fruit of worshipping ten million liṅgas.
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist in the three worlds, as well as rivers such as the Gaṅgā—he obtains the fruit of them all by bathing at Koṭitīrtha.
Having thus granted the boon, the Lord Brahmā departed for the world of Brahmā; and from that time forward, Koṭitīrtha became renowned.
O Pārtha, in former times on its bank, the foremost of gods, beginning with Brahmā, performed various kinds of sacrifices and thereby attained supreme perfection. (15)
O sinless one, in former times, Vasiṣṭha and other eminent sages performed penance; other ascetics, whose wealth was their austerity, attained the desires cherished by their minds.
O Pārtha, in ancient times, penance was performed here at this sacred ford by Atri; to the south of Koṭitīrtha, an excellent Liṅga was installed.
Having installed that supreme liṅga known as Atrīśvara, which removes great sins, he then created a lake in front of it.
Having bathed there, the mortal who diligently performs a śrāddha ceremony and worships Atrīśvara shall dwell in the world of Rudra for a long time.
O mighty-armed one, it is said that the sage Bharadvāja performed austerities and conducted sacrifices at the lake of Koṭitīrtha.
Having established the most beautiful Bharadvājeśvara Liṅga there and having created a lovely lake, he attained supreme joy.
Having bathed there with devotion, a person should perform the śrāddha rite according to the prescribed rules; by worshipping Bharadvājeśvara, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
And then, at this Koṭitīrtha, the venerable sage Gautama performed severe penance with the hope of being reunited with Ahalyā.
Having attained that desire, the wise one experienced supreme joy; this union with Ahalyā occurred through the power of that sacred ford.
In this field, on the bank of the Ahalyā lake, the Blessed One established a great liṅga known as Gautameśvara.
Arjuna said: O Brahmin, when was this great lake excavated by Ahalyā? Tell me the entire reason for the existence of that Ahalyā lake.
Nārada said: O Phālguna, it is said that in former times Ahalyā incurred a curse from Gautama; upon her union with Indra, she experienced supreme misery. (27)
Then, afflicted by grief, that sage performed penance at Koṭitīrtha; by that very penance, O Pārthas, he was united with Ahalyā.
Then that virtuous woman, greatly delighted, created in this sacred field a very large and meritorious lake filled with the waters of holy pilgrimage sites.
One should perform a bath in the Ahalyā lake and offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas); by worshipping Gautameśa, one goes to the world of Brahmā.
O best of men, at Koṭitīrtha, many stainless sages, having performed most severe penance, attained supreme perfection.
In former times, many kings performed penance, practiced charity, and likewise conducted sacrifices at this sacred site; having done so well, they attained supreme perfection.
Whoever, on its bank, should satisfy even a single twice-born man with pure foods, by that act, accompanied by faith, it becomes as if ten million have been satisfied.
On its bank, O Pārtha, there are various jewels, cattle, land, sesame seeds, grain, and diverse garments.

O Pārtha, he who bestows [gifts] upon the twice-born with supreme faith gains merit a hundred-fold increased by ten million times due to the power of Koṭitīrtha; however, he who promises to the twice-born at Koṭitīrtha but does not give, [incurs great sin]. (35)
Having caused one hundred and one generations of his family to fall into hell, he shall afterwards cause himself to fall into the great and terrible Raurava.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, at the pure time of dawn while the sun is in Capricorn, listen to me regarding the merit of him who bathes. (37)
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, and whatever is gained through all gifts and vows—that is attained day by day at Koṭitīrtha.
A mortal obtains that merit; there is no need for deliberation on this point—namely, the man who performs a śrāddha when the sun has entered Virgo (Kanyā). || 39 ||
His ancestors are not as pleased by hundreds of śrāddhas performed at Gayā as they are when he performs ritual bathing and other rites once the month of Kārttika has arrived. (40)
All that has inexhaustible fruit, according to the word of Brahmā; by performing even a single sacrifice here, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
By giving a maiden in marriage according to the Brāhma rite, one obtains a fruit ten million times greater; for at Koṭitīrtha, every gift becomes ten million-fold.
O Pārtha, he who gives up his life at Koṭitīrtha while holding Mādhava in his heart shall indeed have an eternal and imperishable state in heaven for a long time.
Whoever casts off their body at Koṭitīrtha, the best of holy places, the hosts of deities led by Brahmā perform his worship.
On whosever bank the cremation of the body occurs, or whoever performs the casting of bones at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; || 45 ||
O Pārtha, even the Lord of Speech is not capable of describing its fruit; knowing this supreme [merit], O Pārtha, one should resort to Koṭitīrtha. (46)
Day after day, its fruit is equal to a thousand Kapila cows; therefore, this is very difficult to attain in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Koṭitīrtha," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 52 ||
Nārada said: Now I shall further proclaim another supreme greatness of the Śālā; formerly, when the sacred site had been established, I was addressed by the best of the twice-born.
"O you of noble vows, devise a means for the protection of this place. Thereupon, I promised: "I shall effect the protection of the place. (2)
Subsequently, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were propitiated by me with one-pointed mind; thereupon, those three supreme gods were pleased.
Then, having approached me, they said, "O Nārada, let a boon be chosen. After honoring them, I said to them, "Let the protection of this place be ensured."
This alone should be granted as my boon by the well-pleased gods: that there be no loss of my station, and that my fame endure. (5)
"O Sage, the lords of the gods then promised, 'So be it! We shall provide protection for you and the twice-born by means of our own portions.'"
Having spoken thus, Kalā was released by the gods themselves, the Lords of the Three Puruṣas; thereafter, all those most excellent of deities vanished from sight.
Then, together with the twice-born, I established the protection of the site at the front of the hall, and installed the three gods who are the lords of the three worlds separately.
Whenever the Brahmins are indeed oppressed by anyone, they should recite the Ṛgveda in the forenoon and the Yajus-mantras at midday.
And having recited the Sāman hymns in a loud voice during the third watch of the night, those who are intensely enraged shall utter a curse upon him at the front of the hall.
If the protection of this place was promised by you in the presence of Nārada, then within seven days, or within a year, or within three years, it shall be reduced to ashes. (11)
"By that truth, may our enemy be reduced to ashes in an instant! By this mantra of cursing, he shall certainly be turned to ashes. (12)
He who day by day beholds that hall extending for three generations, worships it, and gratifies it, is glorified in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the majesty of the Tripuruṣa hall. Nārada said: Now I shall further describe another great [site] of my own lake.
O Pārtha, its majesty is incomparable and difficult even for the gods to attain; formerly, I dug this lake with a blade of Darbha grass.
Then, having taken the finest water from all the sacred fords (tīrthas), he himself cast the clay into a copper vessel outside.
That [object] was thrown into that lake by him, and the lake was filled; when the month of Āśvina arrived, on a Sunday, a pure man [performed the rite]. || 17 ||
Whoever performs a śrāddha there after bathing, especially by giving gifts, his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
For this lake of Nārada is indeed renowned upon the surface of the earth; it is attained even by the gods only through the conjunction of great merit. (19)
Whatever gift is given here and whatever is offered into the fire, one should know that all of it becomes inexhaustible through the practice of recitation and fasting.
Having bathed in the excellent lake of Nārada, the mortal who worships Lord Nāradeśvara with faith is liberated from all sins. || 21 ||
O Pārtha, in ancient times all the nāgas performed penance at this sacred site for the sake of liberation from Kadrū’s curse and out of a desire for their own welfare.
Then, having attained supreme perfection through the power of this very purpose, they installed the powerful Liṅga known as Nāgeśvara.
To the north of Nārada, all the Nāgas are greatly delighted; whoever bathes in that excellent lake of Nārada and worships Hara [shall attain his goal].
For those who worship Nāgeśvara with great devotion, their merit is infinite; according to the word of the Nāgas, they have no fear of serpents. (25)
Thus ends the majesty of the Nāradīya-saras. Nārada said: O Pāṇḍava, there is also a goddess here named Aparadvārakā.
And she has her abode eternally established at the gateway of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), protected by twenty-four crores of goddesses.
Then, having performed long austerities, I brought her here and gratified her; thereafter, the Supreme Goddess was stationed at the western gate.
Dvāravāsinī is established at the eastern city gate; she is the one who occurs on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra.

Having bathed in the pool, a man should worship that goddess with offerings of bali and vākula flowers, with food offerings (naivedya), and with the worship of perfumes, incense, and other such items.
The sin committed over seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment; whatever desires a person prays for, he attains them all. (31)
Indeed, even a barren woman obtains a son merely by bathing there on the ninth day of the month of Caitra, through worship with flowers, incense, and water offerings.
The Goddess shall destroy all obstacles and bestow every accomplishment upon her devotees at that very moment; this is the truth, there is no doubt about it. || 33 ||
And having likewise worshipped the Northern Gate according to the prescribed rite, that best of men shall obtain this very same fruit. (34)
Indeed, by merely worshipping the goddess Dvāravāsinī who resides at the eastern gate, one shall obtain the desired fruit. (35)
When the month of Āśvina has arrived, especially during the nine nights, one should fast for those nine nights and, being composed, bathe in the pool.
One should worship the deity with devotion through offerings of flowers, incense, food, and libations; thus, one without a son obtains sons, and one without wealth obtains wealth. (37)
A barren woman gives birth, O Pārtha; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 38 ||

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Koṭitīrtha and Other Sites," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 53. 5.
Nārada said: "O Pārtha, I too have a form there out of a desire for the welfare of brahmins; O dear one, I do not abandon it there, which is adorned with an umbrella and a staff."
On that auspicious eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, by performing my worship, one is liberated from the defects of the Kali age.
Arjuna said: "O Brahmin, this doubt has resided in my heart since childhood; as I ask you about it, you should not be angry with me. (3)
You have always attained the highest perfection in the dharmas of liberation; you are impartial toward all beings, self-controlled, and free from passion and hatred.
O Sage Nārada, you are proclaimed to be one who has abandoned praise and blame, silent, and established in liberation; yet in the worlds, O sage, you are as fickle as the wind.
Wandering like a flash of lightning, you appear esteemed by the wise; yet you are always a source of strife in the world, merciless toward all living beings.
Indeed, many thousands of gods, Gandharvas, Rakshasas, kings, lords of sages, and Daityas have perished during the Kali age; they were no more.
O twice-born one, why do you have this behavior? Dispel my doubt; for due to doubt, one does not sleep in peace, like a deer pierced by an arrow.
Sūta said: Having heard these words from Phālguna, the sage Nārada, as if smiling, looked toward the face of Bābhravya.
And that Brāhmaṇa named Bābhravya, born in the lineage of Hārīta, always remained in the presence of the sage Nārada.
And he, the one of great intelligence, having understood Nārada’s intention, spoke to Phālguna with affectionate words as if smiling.
Bābhravya said: "O Pāṇḍava, what you have said regarding Nārada is true; indeed, every human being here falls into doubt concerning this matter."
I shall relate that to you exactly as I heard it from Kṛṣṇa; previously, after a short interval of time, the delighter of the Yādavas [spoke] everything.
During the pilgrimage to Mahī and the ocean, the Lord Kṛṣṇa arrived there together with Ugrasena, Vasudeva, and Babhru.
Then, by Rāma, the son of Rukmiṇī, Yuyudhāna, and the others, he was recognized as being like a kinsman at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
Having performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other rites, having given abundant gifts, and having diligently worshipped the Liṅgas such as Guheśvara; || 16 ||
Having bathed at Koṭitīrtha and worshipped Jayāditya, the high-minded Kṛṣṇa, being self-composed, honored the sage Nārada.
In the presence of many eminent brāhmaṇas, including Mada and others, and while his elder brother King Jaṭāyu was listening, the great king Ugrasena spoke to Kṛṣṇa in the assembly hall.
Ugrasena said: O Kṛṣṇa, I shall ask you one question; tell me the answer to it.
This Nārada, who is indeed of great intelligence and honored by the entire universe—why is he so extremely fickle and wanders through the world like the wind? (20)
And why is he fond of the Kali age, and for what reason does he have such great affection for you?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O King, what you have asked is true; I shall tell you all of this. In ancient times, the best of sages, Nārada, was cursed by Dakṣa. (21)
"Having observed those [beings] who have been set in motion by Nārada along the path of creation, they shall have no fixed abode in the worlds as they wander. (22)
And because he was a speaker of slander, as well as from causing the second [group] to waver—thus, having incurred these two curses due to the wavering of his two kinds of sons. (23)
Although the sage was capable of refuting it, he accepted it exactly as it was; for such is the praise of the virtuous, that they themselves practice forbearance.
Since he observes the time of destruction and thereby increases the Kali age, yet speaks the truth, he is not tainted by sin. (25)

Furthermore, because his mind is never separate from the object of meditation even while wandering everywhere, he is not subject to the defect of delusion; and as for his supreme love for me, listen to that as well.
Indeed, I always praise Nārada, who has the vision of the gods; listen to that hymn, O King, as it was spoken by Mahendra himself. (27)
I bow to that Nārada, in whom no sense of "I" has arisen regarding learning and conduct, and whose learning and conduct are unrestrained. (28)
I bow to that Nārada, who is free from discontent, anger, and fickleness, who knows no fear, and who is neither procrastinating nor lacking in steadfastness. (29)
I bow to that Nārada, who never speaks otherwise than the truth, whether out of desire or greed, and who is to be honored by all living beings.
I bow to that Nārada, who knows the truth regarding the internal course of existence, who is patient, capable, and has conquered his senses; who is upright and speaks according to reality.
I bow to that Nārada, who is advanced in spiritual luster, fame, wisdom, statesmanship, humility, birth, and asceticism. 32.
I bow down to that Nārada, who possesses a pleasant character, a pleasant appearance, excellent food, and auspicious conduct; who has beautiful eyes and eloquent speech. || 33 ||
I bow to that Nārada who performs great good, in whom no evil exists, and who takes no pleasure in the misfortune of others. 34.
I bow down to that Nārada, who is eternally established in the dharma declared in the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, and who is liberated from both the pleasant and the unpleasant. || 35 ||
I bow down to Nārada—the wise twice-born one who is unstained by food and other worldly things, who is free from indolence, highly learned, and a master of diverse discourses. 36.
Never before has there been any delusion in him regarding wealth, anger, or desire; I bow to that Nārada by whom these defects were destroyed. (37)
I bow down to that Nārada, who is free from the fault of delusion, who possesses firm devotion to the highest good, and who is both skillful in counsel and possessed of modesty.
I bow to that Nārada who, though unattached to all attachments, appears as one whose soul is attached; who is free from long-standing doubts and is eloquent in speech. (39)
I bow to that Nārada, who does not abandon the traditional scriptures, who does not live off his asceticism, and whose soul makes every moment fruitful. 40.
I bow to that Nārada, who has exerted effort and perfected his wisdom, yet remains insatiable regarding meditative concentration, and who is ever vigilant through constant application. (41)
I bow to that Nārada, whose intellect is steady and whose self is unattached, who does not rejoice at the gain of wealth nor feel distressed by its lack.
I go for refuge to Nārada, who is endowed with all virtues, skillful, pure, and undaunted; he who knows the proper time and is conversant in policy.
O King, I recite this hymn of Nārada daily; by that, the best of sages grants me supreme delight. (44)
Furthermore, whoever, having become pure, should daily recite this hymn of praise, the divine sage will soon bestow upon him his supreme grace. (45)
O King, having heard these qualities of Nārada, recite daily this meritorious hymn; the sage will become pleased with you. (46)
Bābhravya said: Having heard these qualities of Nārada from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa, the king became exceedingly pleased and acted accordingly upon those words. || 47 ||
Then, having given abundant gifts, he honored Nārada, saying, "May Nārada be pleased with these foremost of the twice-born who belong to the lineage of Nārada. (48)
Having performed this pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, went to Dvāravatī together with his brothers, kinsmen, and relatives. 49.
In the same way, O Kauravya, having heard these virtues of Nārada and becoming full of faith, listen now to what must be done in this matter.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, known as Prabodhinī, that sage always awakens from his meditation and absorption in Viṣṇu.
On that very day, having bathed with diligence in this very well constructed by Nārada, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony with a concentrated mind.
In this well, austerity, charity, and the recitation of mantras become inexhaustible. || 53 ||
Then, O Pāṇḍava, one should awaken Viṣṇu with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," and afterwards awaken the sage Nārada with this mantra.
O best of sages, just as Hari abandoned his yogic sleep, so too should you relinquish it for the benefit of the world. 55.
Having thus awakened Nārada with this mantra, one should worship him with the hymn proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa, with the sounding of cymbals, and with auspicious offerings.
According to one's capacity, one should give to the twice-born an umbrella, a pair of sandals, and a water-pot; having bowed to the Brahmins with devotion, one should say, "May Nārada be pleased."
When this is done, by the grace of the sage he is liberated from sin; for him, no strife arises, nor shall there be any unhappiness here in this world. (58)

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Nārada," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 54 ||
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Bābhravya, the joy of the Kurus, filled with wonder and his hair standing on end, bowed to Nārada with devotion.
And having praised him for a long time, he spoke again to Nārada.
O Sage, hearing the majesty of Guptakṣetra from your own lips, I do not attain satiety; you should speak of it further.
Nārada said: O best of the Kurus, I shall describe the greatness of the Great Liṅga; listen attentively to that concerning the Gautameśvara Liṅga.
The great yogi Akṣapāda became the sage known as Gautama; he was the lord who brought back the Godāvarī river and the husband of Ahalyā. || 5 ||
Having understood the exceedingly sublime majesty of Guptakṣetra, he performed great penance here while practicing the means of attaining yoga.
Then, having attained perfection in yoga, the high-souled Gautama installed a linga here under the name Gautameśvara.

Having bathed this great liṅga and anointed it with sandalwood paste, and having worshipped it with various flowers, one should burn guggulu incense before it; thus liberated from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Arjuna said: O Nārada, I wish to hear the true nature of Yoga according to reality, since everyone praises Yoga as the most excellent of all things. (9)
Nārada said: O best of the Kurus, I shall describe to you in brief the essence of yoga, by the mere hearing of which purity arises; what need is there to mention [the result] from its practice?
The true essence of yoga is proclaimed to be the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind; yogins accomplish this here by means of its eightfold method. (11)
Yama and niyama, and prāṇāyāma as the third; pratyāhāra and dhāraṇā, the object of meditation (dhyeya), and dhyāna as the seventh. || 12 ||
And what is called "samādhi" is proclaimed to be the eightfold yoga; O Pāṇḍava, hear the individual definition of each of those eight.
In due order, a person attains yoga through their practice: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness. (14)
These five restraints (yamas) have been declared; now hear their characteristics as well: he who acts for the welfare of all beings as he does for himself [is established in restraint]. (15)
This is declared to be non-violence, which is ordained by the Vedas; it consists of seeing, hearing, inferring, and experiencing according to reality.

Speaking the truth is said to be [right speech], provided it is free from causing harm to others; and the non-taking of another's property in any way whatsoever, even in times of distress, [is right conduct]. (17)

That which is practiced through mind, action, and speech is proclaimed as non-stealing; and for ascetics, celibacy consists of abstaining from sexual intercourse through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (18)
For householders, approaching their own wives during the fertile period constitutes celibacy; for ascetics, it is the renunciation of everything through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (19)
And for householders, this non-possessiveness is prescribed as a mental resolve. These five restraints (yamas) have been declared to you; now hear the five observances (niyamas). || 20 ||
Purity, contentment, austerity, recitation, and likewise devotion to the guru—listen now to the specific characteristics of each of these five. (21)
Purity is said to be of two kinds: external and internal. External purity is declared to consist of earth and water, while internal purity is a pure mind. (22)
That constant contentment which one possesses through a livelihood acquired by righteous means, whether by begging or by trade, is called *tuṣṭi*.
Furthermore, penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa have been prescribed; one who is intent on minimizing food intake should perform that, for it is called "penance. (24)
Self-study (svādhyāya) is declared to be the recitation (japa) of the Praṇava and other such practices; devotion to Śiva, to knowledge, and to the guru is remembered as guru-bhakti. || 25 ||
Having thus accomplished the observances (niyamas) and restraints (saṃyamas), the wise practitioner of yoga should apply himself to breath control (prāṇāyāma); not otherwise.
Since a great disturbance of the bodily wind (vāyu) occurs due to the impure body, one suffers from leprosy and conditions such as numbness resulting from that disturbance of the wind. || 27 ||
Therefore, a wise person, having purified the body, should strive for the supreme goal. O son of Pāṇḍu, listen as I describe the characteristics of prāṇāyāma. 28.
The restraint of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is proclaimed as prāṇāyāma; it is declared by the wise to be threefold, known as the minor, the middling, and the superior. || 29 ||
The light [recitation] consists of twelve mātrās; a mātrā is the duration of a blink of an eye. The medium is said to be double that, and the superior is traditionally held to be triple.
By the first [stage] one should conquer perspiration; by the middle, trembling; and by the third, dejection—one should thus conquer the defects in their proper sequence.
Having assumed the posture called Padmāsana and sitting comfortably, one should practice the threefold prāṇāyāma consisting of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka).
Prāṇāyāma is traditionally defined as the restraint of the vital breaths; just as the impurities of mountain ores are consumed when they are smelted. (33)
In the same way, the defect covered by the senses is burned away by breath control (prāṇāyāma); it yields the same fruit as that obtained by giving a hundred tawny cows.

Therefore, the knower of yoga should always restrain the breath through *prāṇāyāma*; by means of *prāṇāyāma*, the divine states such as tranquility (*śānti*) and the rest are gradually accomplished. (35)
Peace, tranquility, radiance, and clarity arise respectively for those who possess innate or adventitious desires, and for those in whom evils are active. (36)
The first quality arises, known as the "pacification of latent impressions" (vāsanāśānti), having completely cast off all defects consisting of greed and delusion. (37)
And when there is the attainment of austerities, that is called peace; as well as the clarity of all the senses, of the intellect, and even of the vital airs. (38)
This is declared to be "serenity" (prasāda); thus, this fourfold [result] is to be attained. A yogi should always practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) which has such a fruit. (39)
Just as lions, tigers, and elephants become gentle when served, so too does the vital breath (prāṇa) become submissive when mastered.
This is declared to be prāṇāyāma; now hear about pratyāhāra: it is the withdrawal of the mind that has been engaged with sense objects. (41)
The restraint of that [mind] which has been pointed out as withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is indeed what is called withdrawal; now hear the definition of concentration (dhāraṇā). 42.
Just as those seeking water might drink it slowly through tubes made of leaves and the like, so too does the yogi draw in the mastered breath.
The wind [is located] from the navel up to the heart; then at the palate, between the eyebrows, in the four-petalled, six-petalled, ten-petalled, twelve-petalled, and sixteen-petalled [lotuses]. (44)
Having slowly raised the breath to the head by means of contraction alone, the adept should fix that vital air (prāṇa) in the head at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are proclaimed to be equivalent to one concentration (dhāraṇā). By establishing these ten concentrations, one attains identity with the Imperishable.
Listen to the characteristics of that which is to be meditated upon by one established in dhāraṇā; O Pārtha, the object of meditation is manifold, its end cannot be found. (47)
Some meditate on Śiva, some on Hari, others on Sūrya, and still others on Brahmā; some meditate on the Great Being, the Goddess, while yet others meditate on her.
In that regard, whatever one meditates upon and whoever that may be, both dissolve therein; therefore, one should always remember the god Śiva, Hara, who has five faces.
Seated in the lotus posture, he was fair-complexioned, holding a citron fruit in his hand; he had ten arms, a most serene countenance, and was absorbed in meditation. || 50 ||
This object of meditation has been declared to you; therefore, one should practice meditation. And this is the clear definition of meditation: even for half a moment.
He who is firmly established in *dhāraṇā* is not born separately from the object of meditation; thus, the knower of yoga, having ascended this difficult-to-climb stage, [proceeds further]. (52)
One should not think of anything thereafter; this is proclaimed as "samādhi. Listen to me as I correctly describe the characteristics of samādhi. (53)
One who has attained the Supreme Person, which is devoid of sound, touch, and taste, and free from smell and form, is proclaimed as being established in samādhi.
Having attained that, a person shall never be overcome by obstacles; and established in samādhi, he cannot be moved even by great suffering. (55)
Even if hundreds of conchs and other instruments are sounded at his ears, or if kettledrums are beaten, he does not perceive any external sound. (56)
Struck by lashes of a whip and with his body scorched by fire, he stands as if overwhelmed by intense cold; in that terrible state, he does not perceive any external touch.
What need is there to speak of such a person regarding external forms, scents, or tastes—he who, having seen the Self by means of the self, attains samādhi once again? (58)
Neither thirst nor hunger ever afflicts him. (59)
Neither in heaven, nor in the netherworld, nor anywhere among humans is that happiness found which a person attains upon reaching unwavering meditative absorption (samādhi).
O descendant of Kuru, even for one who has thus ascended to yoga, five bitter obstacles arise; listen as to how they do so.
The Prātibha, Śrāvaṇa, Daiva, Bhramāvarta, and Bhīṣaṇa; the Prātibha is the intuitive flash regarding all scriptures, and it is of the nature of sattva.
Therefore, that yogi who would quickly take up intoxication of the mind [from afar]—he who hears from thousands of yojanas away is indeed a Śrāvaṇa.
This second [type], the *sāttvika*, perishes from me; he perceives the eight wombs of the gods, and thus he is called *daiva*. (64)
And this sattvic defect perishes through this very intoxication, just as a whirlpool in water is destroyed when one becomes agitated within the whirlpool of worldly existence. (65)
This defect known as "the whirlpool" is of the nature of passion (rājasa) and is a source of great fear; for by it, the mind of the yogin is whirled about, devoid of support, by various defects.
Due to the collapse of all supports, the quality of darkness (tamas) is known as delusion; by these [qualities], all divine births have their yoga destroyed.
The yogi, having wrapped himself in the white blanket consisting of the mind, is not repeatedly whirled about by most terrible calamities. (68)
One desiring perfection should contemplate the Supreme Brahman, making the mind inclined toward it, and should consume only sattvic foods. (69)

A yogi shall never attain perfection through those characterized by passion (rājasa) or darkness (tāmasa); rather, [he attains it] among those who are faithful, self-controlled, learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), and high-souled.
The yogi should beg for alms from those who have not deviated from their own duty; his food may consist of begged alms, barley-meal, buttermilk, milk, or even barley-gruel.
Ripe fruits and roots, or grains, oil-cakes, and parched flour—these are said to be the foods for yogins that bring about accomplishment.
Having recognized the time of death through its signs, the practitioner of yoga, being fully composed, should apply himself to yoga for the purpose of deceiving Time. (73)
And I shall describe the signs by which the knower of yoga recognizes death: a virtuous woman, wearing red and black garments, singing here of Yama; (74)
If a woman leads him toward the southern direction in a dream, he too does not survive; likewise, if one sees a naked mendicant laughing in a dream.

And seeing him leaping thus, one should know that death has arrived; for he who, seated upon a vehicle drawn by bears and monkeys, sings while heading toward the southern direction [is already dead]. (76)
He goes to drown in the ocean, or sinks in mud or cow dung, and does not survive; likewise, he enters his own river with hair, charcoal, ashes, and serpents.
Having seen himself in a dream surrounded by any of these, or by terrifying, hideous, and harsh men with uplifted weapons, he does not survive.
A man struck by stones in a dream shall meet immediate death; he before whom a jackal howls as it passes directly toward him at sunrise [shall likewise perish].
Whether his perception is distorted or limited, he meets with immediate death; he does not perceive the scent of a lamp, and likewise vomits fire at night.
He who does not see his own reflection in the eyes of others does not live; nor does he who sees a rainbow at midnight or an eclipse during the day. (81)
Upon seeing this, one should consider that his own life has reached its end; the nose becomes crooked, and the ears undergo depression and elevation.
The life-force of one whose left eye is leaking away has departed; when the face becomes reddish and the tongue turns black, [death is near].
Then the wise man should recognize that his own death is near, if in a dream he travels toward the south by means of a camel or a donkey cart. (84)
Even if she covers her ears while in the direction [of the sound], she would not hear the roar; she shall not live, for in such a dream, her husband is being covered over.
The door does not open, and the clear vision becomes blood-red; and he who enters a fire in a dream and does not emerge again. || 86 ||
Or his life may end by entering water; or he may be struck down by wicked spirits, whether by night or by day. (87)
Whether in their natural or transformed states, Yama and Antaka stand near him; likewise, they stand near the gods, the gurus, his parents, and those possessed of knowledge.
Having become a devotee, he does not live [long] if he subjects himself to censure and contempt; seeing such contrary omens, the knower of yoga [should act accordingly]. 89.
Having correctly established himself in dhāraṇā, he should become immovable in samādhi; if he does not desire death, then it does not come upon him.
Or, if one desires liberation, one should release [the breath] at the crown of the head (brahmamūrdhan). Furthermore, there are obstacles that arise both within the body and upon liberation.
O Pāṇḍava, listen also to those who approach the yogin: in the city of the Rākṣasas in the northeast, there is both a Yakṣa and a Gandharva.
In the eight [mandalas] of Indra, Soma, Prajāpati, and Brahmā, there are eight perfections (siddhis); hear them: the earthly and the fiery, || 93 ||
The intellect (mati) consists of the air-element, the ether-element, the mental, and the egoic; each is divided eightfold, becoming double and then double again in succession.
The first eight and the sixty-four at the end—listen to them as follows: stoutness, shortness, childhood, old age, and likewise youth. (95)
The nature of various species and the maintenance of the body by means of the four [elements]; the eight earthly siddhis are eternal, even without a portion of earth.

When the principle of earth (pṛthivītattva) has been conquered, and one abides in the northeastern direction, one’s dwelling is as if on land even in water; such a person, free from affliction, can drink up the ocean.
There is the attainment of water everywhere, as well as dry and liquid fruits; the body is supported by these three, or one may hold rivers in one's hand. 98.

The absence of wounds on the body and radiance—these eight are remembered [as the qualities of the sages]. These eight [qualities] and the following eight are recorded as being in the city of the Rākṣasas.
The creation of fire from one's own body, the freedom from the fear of its heat, the granting of power to the worlds, and the kindling of flames within water. 100.

The taking up of the fire with the hand, purification through mere remembrance, the restoration of one who has been reduced to ashes, and the sustaining of the body by means of both [the hands]—these are the powers. 101.
In the abode of the Yakṣas, there are sixteen and eight [deities] of fire; likewise, there is the state of moving with the speed of mind and the internal entry into living beings.
Carrying great weights such as mountains with ease, as well as lightness and heaviness, and the warding off of the wind with his two hands. (103)
By the mere touch of the tip of a finger, the entire earth trembles; by a single [mantra], the body is perfected—these are the accomplishments (siddhis) in the Gāndharva [Vidyā].
These twenty-four and these eight are the siddhis of the eastern quarter; there are thirty-two in the world of the Gandharvas. Listen now to what follows.
The production of a form devoid of shadow, the non-perception of the senses, constant movement through the sky, and the spontaneous cessation of the senses and other faculties [occur]. 106.

The perception of sound at a distance, the comprehension of all sounds, the grasping of their subtle elemental signs (tanmātra-liṅga), and the observation of all living beings [constitute the powers of hearing]. || 107 ||

There are eight [powers] consisting of wind in the realm of Indra, as well as thirty-two from the previous ones; these include obtaining things at will and departing according to one's desire. || 108 ||
Mastery everywhere, the manifestation of all secrets, the vision of saṃsāra, and the eight mental accomplishments. || 109 ||
And these forty [deities] are recorded as being in the world of Soma: Chedana (Cutting), Tāpana (Tormenting), Bandha (Binding), and Saṃsāraparivartana (Revolution of Saṃsāra). || 110 ||
The state of being pleasing to all beings, likewise the victory over the time of death, and the arising of ego—these eight preceded by the Prājāpatya [powers] are attained. 111.
Through his form, he effects the creation of the world, as well as its sustenance, the authority over its dissolution, and the setting in motion of the manifold variety of the worlds. (112)

This manifest world and nirvāṇa are clearly distinct from one another; the agency of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, as well as these eight states arising from the intellect, [are likewise distinct]. 113.
Fifty-six and likewise sixty-four—these are the qualities that prevail in the state of Brahman; this secret has been declared to you. (114)
These perfections of yogins occur either while they are living or upon the dissolution of the body; however, one must not form an attachment to them, for fear that a fall might occur.
Then, for the yogi who practices while having cast off these qualities, the eight supernatural powers arise, which bring about the perfection of yoga.
Aṇimā, laghimā, and likewise mahimā, as well as prāpti; prākāmya, and similarly īśitva, vaśitva, and others [yatra-kāmāvasāyitva]. (117)

Where there is the power to bring desires to their fulfillment while established in the state of Maheśvara, *aṇimā* is known as subtler than the subtle, and *laghimā* is remembered as being due to swiftness. (118)

Majesty (mahimā) is due to his being worshipful by all; attainment (prāpti) is that there is nothing unattainable for him; will-power (prākāmya) is due to his pervasiveness; and lordship (īśitva) is because he is the Lord. || 119 ||
Due to mastery, the seventh and supreme accomplishment is called "mastery" (vaśitā); it is the power of determining one's own desires, such that one remains wherever one wishes. || 120 ||
These perfections belong to one who has attained the state of the Lord; therefore, he is neither born, nor does he grow, nor does he perish.
He who attains liberation in this manner is declared to be "liberated," just as water poured into water reaches a state of oneness with it. || 122 ||
In this very way, the self of yogis becomes assimilated with the Supreme Self; knowing this result, the yogi should always practice yoga. (123)
In this regard, stainless yogis utter a simile for the sake of yoga: through contact with the rays of the moon, the sun-stone produces fire. || 124 ||
There is no such comparison for the yogin who, though alone, does not abandon [the world]: the kapiñjala bird, the mouse, and the mongoose dwell together in their own master’s house.
When [the body] is destroyed, their suffering departs elsewhere; that is the analogy for the ascetic, even though his body is like a lump of clay, with a mouth that is but a small part of it.
That instruction of the yogin creates a heap of earth-clods provided with leaves, flowers, and fruits by means of animals, birds, humans, and so forth. (127)
Having found a tree being stripped [of its bark], yogins achieve success; likewise, by observing the tip of a deer's horn shaped like a sectarian mark (tilaka). || 128 ||
Together with that, the yogin shall increase and attain perfection; having taken up a full vessel, he ascends from the earth.
Having observed the lofty path in this way, why was it not understood by the yogis: that house where he dwells, and that food by which he lives? (130)
The yogi should cultivate that knowledge which accomplishes the task and by which the goal is achieved for the sake of one's own perfection in yoga. 131.
This multiplicity of knowable objects is indeed an obstacle to yoga; for one who wanders about thirsting with the thought, "This is to be known, this is to be known. (132)
Even with a lifespan of a thousand kalpas, one would not attain the object of knowledge unless one has abandoned attachment, conquered anger, obtained [sufficient] food, and mastered the senses.
Having closed the doors [of the senses] with the intellect, one should fix the mind in meditation; one should consume sattvic food, not that which causes loss of consciousness.
He who indulges in this shall become a dear guest of Raurava. These three are the punishment of speech, the punishment of action, and the punishment of mind. (135)
He whose staffs are thus restrained is remembered as a *yati* who possesses the triple-staff (*tridaṇḍin*). People feel affection for one who praises his virtues in his absence. (136)
And living beings do not fear; this is said to be the characteristic of success. || 137 ||
Freedom from greed, health, lack of harshness, an auspicious odor of the urine and feces, luster, clarity, and gentleness of voice—these are indeed the first signs of the commencement of yoga.

Concentrated, devoted to Brahman, vigilant, pure, delighting in solitude, and having conquered the senses—the great-minded one shall attain this yoga, and from that yoga he attains liberation. || 139 ||

His family is purified, his mother has fulfilled her purpose, and the earth is fortunate because of him—whose mind is fixed on the Supreme Brahman, immersed in an ocean of bliss upon the path that leads nowhere else. 140.

He whose intellect is purified, who regards a clod of earth and gold as equal, and who dwells with equanimity toward all beings—that ascetic, having gone to that supreme, eternal, and imperishable state, is not born again. 141.
This secret of yoga has been declared by me; Gautama attained such a yoga as this. Therefore, O Pārtha, he established this Liṅga, which destroys all impurity through its mere sight and worship.

And whoever worships this Liṅga at night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, having bathed in the preeminent Ahalyā-lake and having performed everything with faith and devotion; || 143 ||
Freed from sin by that great service, he goes to where that sage Gautama resides. || 144 ||
O Pārtha, this majesty of the protected field has been set forth by me to you in summary form. Whoever hears all of this shall become purified; what more need I say? (145)
Whoever hears this supreme narrative of Gautama with devotion, having obtained sons, grandsons, and beloved things, shall go to the imperishable state.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Detailed Description of the Characteristics of Yoga within the Greatness of Gautameśvara," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme Liṅga known as Brahmeśa, by the mere remembrance of which the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice is obtained. || 1 ||
Once in the past, O Pārtha, Brahmā, desiring to create, performed severe austerities for one thousand and five hundred years.
Satisfied by that austerity, Śaṅkara, the Lord of Pārvatī, then granted a boon to him, the creator of the worlds, according to his own desire.
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā), delighted, joyful, and having accomplished his purpose, recognized the majesty of that sacred field and himself established a linga there.
And he dug a meritorious and auspicious lake named Brahmasaras, located to the east of Mahīnagaraka, which destroys even the greatest sins.
On its bank, the omnipresent Lord indeed established a great liṅga; there, it is said, the god Śaṅkara himself is personally present.
O Phālguna, there is a sacred site named Brahmeśa that is superior even to Puṣkara; having bathed there with devotion, a person should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
One should give gifts according to one's ability, especially on the full moon day of Kārttika; with a joyful mind, one should worship the Lord Brahmeśa with devotion.
His ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings; and whatever merit is found at Puṣkara or at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse, [is obtained here].
Whatever fruit is obtained by men at holy pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā, that same fruit one attains by bathing in this sacred site.
O Pārtha, listen to the most wonderful majesty of Mokṣaliṅga, which I attained after propitiating Maheśvara for the sake of the welfare of this sacred site.
O Pārtha, I then established the excellent Liṅga named Mokṣeśvara Hara, and subsequently dug a well with the tip of a blade of darbha grass.
Having propitiated Brahmā, the creator of the world and the supreme lord, Sarasvatī was brought forth from the water-pot of Brahmā. 13.
In this well of Mokṣanātha, for the liberation of the deceased of the worlds, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika—
Having bathed in that well, a man should offer a ball of sesame seeds intended for the deceased ancestors; he will certainly obtain the fruit of Mokṣatīrtha. || 15 ||
O Pārtha, no ghost is born in his family; of this there is no doubt. By the power of this sacred ford, the ghosts attain liberation.
Having bathed with great effort in the excellent Jayāditya well and having paid homage to Garbheśvara, a man does not sink into wombs again.
O Pārtha, this entire majesty of the protected field has been set forth by me for you through a concise application of yoga. He who hears this becomes completely purified; what more need I say? (18)

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Brahmeśvara, Mokṣeśvara, and Garbheśvara," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nārada said: Then the brahmins and Nārada, having propitiated Maheśvara, installed Śaṅkara in the meritorious Mahīnagaraka.
And for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, there is the supreme Kedāra Liṅga, which destroys great sins, located in the northern part of Atrīśa.
Having bathed in the Atrikuṇḍa and performed the śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules, and having paid obeisance to Atrīśa, he who beholds Kedāra [attains the highest goal]. || 3 ||
He shall never again drink his mother’s milk and shall become a partaker of liberation; then Rudra [revealed this] to the high-souled Nārada, O Blue-throated One.
Having given [the gift] himself, he himself remained in the auspicious Mahīnagaraka; a man, having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, beholds Nīlakaṇṭha.
Having paid homage to Jayāditya, one shall attain the world of Rudra; the best of men, having bathed in the well, worship Jayāditya.
There shall be no destruction of their lineage by the grace of Jayāditya. This, O Pārtha, has been told to you concerning Mahīnagaraka.
Having heard this entire narrative, one is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Nīlakaṇṭha," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Arjuna said: O Nārada, why is this a secret sacred field (guptakṣetra), and why is it hidden? Its power is so very great that it has not been praised by anyone at all.
Nārada said: O Pāṇḍava, hear here an ancient story concerning the cause of Guptakṣetra, and how this place became hidden due to a curse.
Long ago, on a certain occasion, the presiding deities of all the sacred fords went together to the assembly hall of Brahmā to pay their respects to him.
The deities of Puṣkara, Prabhāsa, Nimiṣa, Arbuda, and of the sacred field of Kurukṣetra and Dharmāraṇya.
And those [tirthas] of Vastrapatha and Śveta, as well as Phalgutīrtha, and likewise those of Kedāra and other sacred fields by the millions—‖ 5 ‖
They are the lords of the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean, of the Mahī and the ocean, of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and of the Sūkara [tīrtha].
The presiding deities of the rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā and Revā, and the presiding deities of the lakes, headed by Śoṇahrada; || 7 ||
All of them, having gathered together as a community, approached the great assembly of Brahmā, being stainless and desiring to know their own preeminence.
There, seeing that all the holy fords had arrived, the Grandfather rose up together with all the members of the assembly.
Having bowed down to all the sacred fords (tīrthas) with his palms joined in reverence, the Blessed One, his eyes wide with wonder, spoke to the holy sites.
Today our entire abode has been thoroughly purified by you; and we too have been further purified simply by the sight of you. (11)
Beholding sacred fords, touching them, bathing in them, as well as praising and remembering them—none of these can occur without supreme merit.
Even those who are possessed of great sins, fierce, and extremely cruel—they too are purified by sacred fords; how much more so those established in righteousness?
Having spoken thus to Pulastya, he commanded his son: "Quickly bring the guest-offering (arghya) for the sake of the holy ford, so that I may perform worship."
Pulastya said: "O Lotus-born One, countless sacred fords (tīrthas) are seen here; yet, as you direct me, my dear father, I shall offer a single oblation (arghya)."
There is a verse regarding the proclamation of the Dharma, because this is what is being sung: || 16 ||
If there were countless [deities] worthy of the arghya offering in the worship, then the arghya should indeed be offered all at once to the most excellent among them. (17)
Brahmā said: "O dear child, these words spoken by you are excellent and full of intent. Act accordingly; bring one *argha* offering with the utmost speed."
Nārada said: Then Pulastya quickly brought an excellent offering (argha), and Brahmā, taking it in his hand, spoke these words regarding the sacred fords (tīrthas): || 19 ||
"All of you together must proclaim one chief; I shall offer the guest-offering (arghya) to him, so that injustice may not touch me. (20)
The Tīrthas said: "We do not know our relative superiority among one another in any way. For this reason, we have come; having understood [the matter], you yourself should grant it. (21)
Brahmā said: "I do not know your superiority in any way; salutations be unto you! You yourselves ought to tell me of your own boundless greatness."
Where there is the Gaṅgā, Gayā, Kāśī, Puṣkara, and likewise Naimiṣa; Kurukṣetra, as well as the Revā and the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
Where there are hundreds [of tīrthas] beginning with Prabhāsa, what thought can we have regarding that? || 24 ||
Nārada said: When this had been spoken by the Lotus-born One, no one said anything at all; then, after a long time, Mahīsāgarasaṅgama spoke as follows.
"O Four-faced One, quickly offer this *arghya* to me; for not even a ten-millionth part of it can ever satisfy me. (26)
Because the earth was scorched by King Indradyumna, it melted into all its sacred fords (tīrthas) and became the river named Mahī.
And she is joined by me with all the sacred fords; therefore, I am renowned throughout the three worlds as being composed of all sacred fords.
And Guha, having installed the great liṅga Kumāreśvara, the Lord, was granted the status of the foremost among holy places by me, the Great-Souled One.
In ancient times, Nārada also established a beautiful place on my shore and granted it preeminence over all sacred fields.
Thus, by these three excellent reasons, let the offering be given to me alone; for even in a single portion of my virtues, my sacred ford is truly not equal to another.
When these words had been spoken by the King of Tīrthas, O Pārtha, descendant of Bharata, no one said anything at all, wondering what Brahmā would say.
Then the eldest son of Brahmā, Dharma, adorned with white garlands and unguents, raised his right arm and spoke these words: || 33 ||
"Alas! This is a grievous thing ill-spoken by the King of Tīrthas out of delusion; for even one's own virtues should not be proclaimed by oneself, especially among the virtuous. (34)
