He who, casting his own virtues upon others during times of prosperity, speaks thus out of egoism—he is indeed a Rajasic person, for such pride is loathsome. (35)
Therefore, because of this ego-sense, even though these qualities exist, this sacred ford (tīrtha) shall become unmanifest and its form destroyed.
It is renowned as Stambhatīrtha because pride (stambha) was displayed there; for even Brahmā immediately obtained the fruit of that pride—what then to say of others? (37)
When this was said by Dharmadeva, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; then, O Pāṇḍava, the Lord of Yogins and I quickly arrived.
Then Guha spoke these words at the assembly of the gods of dharma: "O Dharma, it was improper that this curse was given out of such audacity. (39)
Let someone say among all those holy places that exist: "If this confluence of the Mahī and the ocean does not deserve such sovereignty... (40)
Let alone the personal virtues that have been described by the King of Tīrthas; for who there could be called devoid of virtue, since virtue itself is false speech? (41)
"Alas! It is not fitting for the guardians; if even they act thus regarding matters without reflection, to whom shall the subjects go for refuge? (42)
When Guha had spoken thus, Dharma then addressed these words: "It is true that this confluence of the Mahī and the ocean is worthy. (43)

The preeminence of all sacred fords and even their ritual offering (*argha*) was obtained from the Grandfather (Brahmā). However, one's own virtues must never be spoken of; this is the constant vow of the virtuous. Even behind one's back, self-praise could cause even Brahmā to waver.

"Does he not praise himself while simultaneously hurling insults at others? Did Yayāti not fall from heaven to earth in former times? Whatever authoritative precedents were established by the wise Lord in the past—" (45)
These must be protected; what wise man would transgress them? For what purpose were we established by your father after he had given these instructions? (46)
He protected this very thing, and you ought to protect it as well; for if you, being lords, act according to your own authority.
"Therefore, let this supreme teaching be imparted by us. Having spoken thus, he then addressed Vṛṣa, who was desirous of releasing his own seal.
Observing the occasion, I uttered these words: "Homage to the Great Dharma, the creator of the universe, the high-souled one! (49)
"O Dharma, you who are eternally worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and who destroy all sins—if you should ever abandon your seal (mudrā), [then I shall depart]. (50)
Therefore, O Lord, how could there be existence for us? Do not destroy the universe! You ought also to show honor to Guha, the lord of yogis.
For he is indeed as worthy of honor as Śiva himself, being the direct son of Śiva; and the Lord Guha, your master, ought to honor you as well. 52.
Through the state of oneness between you two, this world may live in happiness; let not this curse bestowed by you be characterized by rejection.
And let favor be shown to the King of Tīrthas, O giver of honor! (54)

While I was speaking thus, the Lotus-born Brahmā praised me and said: "Excellent! What has been spoken by Nārada is right; O Dharma, act according to these words. Furthermore, honor Guha as well, for Guha is indeed our lord. When Brahmā had spoken thus, Dharma addressed these words:
Homage to you, Guha, the perfected one, the servant! O Lord Skanda, please attend to this petition of mine.
Because of this pillar, this great tīrtha will become unknown; it shall become widely renowned as "Stambhatīrtha. || 58 ||
It is renowned as Stambhatīrtha, which bestows the fruits of all holy places (tīrthas); whatever man shall perform ablutions and acts of charity here [shall obtain them]. (59)
And as it has been said, all its fruit will clearly manifest; for whatever fruit belongs to that new moon which falls on a Saturday— || 60 ||
Understand that this occurs during the pilgrimage to Mahīsāgara, as well as through ten pilgrimages to Prabhāsa and seven to Puṣkara.
The fruit of that [pilgrimage] shall be equal to eight [visits] to Prayāga, five to Kurukṣetra, and three to Nakulīśa. || 62 ||
And that fruit which belongs to Arbuda with six [villages], as well as that which belongs to Vastrāpatha with three and to Gaṅgā with five, shall come to pass.
The fruit of that shall arise from four [visits] to Kūpodarī; likewise, it shall be equal to what is obtained from six [visits] to Kāśī and five [visits] to Godāvarī.
"That fruit shall indeed be realized at Stambhatīrtha on the day of the new moon during the transit of Saturn. When this boon had been granted, Skanda then became delighted in mind.
Brahmā, composed in mind and possessed of immeasurable luster, offered arghya to Stambhatīrtha and granted it the status of being the most excellent among all holy places (tīrthas).
Having honored Guha as their protector, he dismissed the holy fords (tīrthas). Thus occurred this ancient account concerning the cause of Guptakṣetra.
Furthermore, O best of the Kurus, those Apsarases who were sent here by me for the sake of further success were also liberated from the form of crocodiles by you.
Since the entire dharma proceeds through various forms for the sake of protection, you and Kṛṣṇa have come into existence within this world.
Thus has this great fruit of all sacred fords been described to you; having heard this from the beginning, a person is liberated from sins.
Sūta said: Having heard this, the wise Vijaya, greatly amazed, offered his praise; then, having been dismissed by Nārada and the others, he departed for Dvārakā.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conclusion of Arjuna’s Pilgrimage," within the "Description of the Greatness of Mahīsāgara," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 58 ||
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, this most wonderful, purifying greatness of Guptakṣetra has been proclaimed; it is a great, incomparable majesty that increases one's joy.
Furthermore, regarding the previous glorification of the majesty of Siddhaliṅga, it was said that by its grace, the mother of the Siddhas shall attain perfection.
There was a virtuous soul named Vijaya, who through the assistance of Caṇḍila [attained his goal]. Who indeed was this one named Caṇḍila, and who likewise was he named Vijaya? (3)
And how did he attain perfection through the grace of Siddhamātṛ? Tell us this in accordance with the truth, for we have a great curiosity to hear it.
"Who would not feel curiosity in hearing the conduct of the virtuous? Ugraśravas said: "O Brahmins, this question has been well asked, even though it concerns a matter that is far removed in time."
I shall relate to you here the story heard from the mouth of Dvaipāyana: how, in ancient times, the Pāṇḍavas obtained the daughter of King Drupada.
Afterwards, with Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s consent, they settled them in Indraprastha; there the Pāṇḍavas were protected by Vāsudeva at one time.
Seated in the midst of the assembly, they engaged in various kinds of conversation, consisting of praises of the gods, sages, ancestors, spirits, and kings.
While this was being performed, Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīma, arrived there. Seeing him, the five brothers and the heroic Vāsudeva [stood ready].
Rising suddenly from their seats, filled with joy, they embraced him; and Bhīma’s son, bowing low and humble, paid homage to them.
Then, having been seated upon the king's own lap with blessings, he was affectionately smelled on the head and addressed in the assembly of people.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "From where have you come, my son, and where have you spent this time? Have you enjoyed yourself anywhere, or do you govern the kingdom of your maternal uncle?"
O son of Hiḍimbā, you have always acted kindly toward the gods, the brahmins, the cows, and the virtuous; this is pleasing to us and to Hari as well.
O virtuous one, all the forest of Heḍamba and those Rākṣasa soldiers of his, being protected by you, flourish while bringing welfare to the people.
I hope your mother, who did so much for our benefit, is rejoicing—she who formerly, while still a maiden, cast aside her pride and took Bhīma as her husband. (15)
Thus questioned by the King of Dharma, the son of Hṛdika smiled and said: "When that wicked uncle was slain, I was appointed [to his position]. (16)
Having established that kingdom in the [Buddha's] teaching and destroying the wicked, I wander about; my mother, the queen, is well and has resorted to divine asceticism. (17)
He said to me, "O son, always be devoted to the ancestors. Having heard these words of my mother, I have come here from the foot of Mount Meru.

With a mind bowed down by devotion, I desire to offer myself for the very purpose of paying homage to you, having been employed by you in some great matter, since this fruit [of my service] is so great. (19)
When a son always carries out the commands of his ancestors, he shall conquer the higher worlds and be born here possessed of fame.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus, the King, the Lord of Dharma, embraced him again and again and, with tears of joy and a voice choked with emotion, spoke to his son.
"You alone are our devotee and you also serve as our companion. || 22 ||
And for this very purpose, O son of Hiḍimbā, the virtuous desire sons; such sons indeed deliver them both in this world and the next. (23)
Necessarily, as is the mother, so shall the son be; your mother was deeply devoted to us, and you are just like her.
"Oh, how very difficult it is that my beloved daughter-in-law, the queen, performs! For she has disregarded her husband's prosperity and has taken refuge in asceticism alone. (25)

Surely there is not the slightest need for me to concern myself with my daughter-in-law’s desires or enjoyments, since she has set her sights on the welfare of the next world after considering the happiness of her son.
Even if she is of low birth, if she is devoted and gives birth to a child who is likewise devoted, I consider that very child to be of noble lineage; this is my supreme opinion. (27)
Having spoken many such various words, King Dharmarāja addressed Keśava and spoke these words.
O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, you know how this one was born from Bhīma; as soon as he was born, he became a youth of great strength.
Since birth and youth occur simultaneously for the eight classes of divine beings, his youth likewise appeared instantly.
O Kṛṣṇa, I am constantly anxious regarding a suitable wife for him; alas, where shall I find a fitting wife for the son of Hiḍimbā? (31)
Therefore, O omniscient Kṛṣṇa, you know even the three worlds; O Yādava, you ought to tell me of the wife suitable for the son of Hiḍambā.
Sūta said: Thus addressed by the King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), Janārdana meditated for a moment and spoke these words to the King of Dharma after a brief interval.
"O King, I shall tell you of a suitable and auspicious wife for him; she is currently residing in the beautiful and excellent city of Prāgjyotiṣa. (34)
And that daughter, O Pārtha, belonged to the Daitya Mura of wondrous deeds, who was a friend as dear to him as his own life to the Daitya Naraka.
And that terrible Naraka, who was equipped with an impenetrable fortress of nooses and was of wicked conduct, has been slain by me; you know all this in its entirety.
Then, when the Daitya Muru had been slain by me, his daughter Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā, being exceedingly powerful, came forth to fight with me.
Then, in that great battle, I fought her as she bore a sword and a shield with mighty arrows discharged from my excellent Śārṅga bow.
With her sword she cut my arrows, and that daughter of Mura, having approached, struck Garuḍa on the head with her sword.
Overcome by delusion, that Garuḍa became unconscious; then, for the sake of slaying him, my discus was raised.
Seeing the discus raised by me on that battlefield, the goddess named Kāmākhyā stood before me and spoke these words. (41)
"You ought not to kill her; protect her, O Supreme Person! For invincibility has been granted to her by me, as well as this sword and shield. (42)
Moreover, your intellect is incomparable and your power supreme in battle; yet, even after three nights, you have not conquered the daughter of Mura.
When this was said, I then spoke these words to the goddess: "I have now turned back; O auspicious one, do you restrain her."
Then Kāmākhyā embraced that devoted woman and spoke these words: "O blessed lady, desist from the battle; he cannot be slain by any means whatsoever."
Mādhava, who is invincible in battle, cannot be conquered by anyone; there has been no one, there is none now, nor will there ever be anyone who could defeat him in combat.
Or rather, O daughter, even Tryambaka is not capable of this, let alone anyone else; therefore, O auspicious one, pay homage to him who is to become your future father-in-law.
"Desist from this battle; this is clearly appropriate for you, for you shall become the daughter-in-law of this brother of Bhīma. (48)
Therefore, O blessed lady, honor Janārdana as your father-in-law; and you, O wise woman, should not feel grief on account of your father.
For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died; moreover, there are many who know this—tell me, by whom can it be prevented? (50)

Neither sages, nor gods, nor great asuras, nor men learned in the three Vedas, nor kings—whom does Death alone not strike down in due time? He who knows the higher and the lower is never deluded in this regard.
Indeed, death at the hands of this father of yours, Janārdana, is truly praiseworthy; for he has departed, liberated from all sins, to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus she was addressed by the one named Kāmā, and she, Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā, having abandoned her anger and composed her limbs, bowed down before me.
O bull of the Bharata race, I spoke to her with blessings: "Stay in this very city, honored by Bhagadatta."
"By me, by the Goddess, and by the Earth, Bhagadatta has been made king; he will offer you manifold honors, as if to his own sister. (55)
"And dwelling here, you shall obtain that hero, the son of Hiḍimbā, as your husband. Having thus consoled Queen Maurvī, I dismissed her.
She remained there in that city, while I went to the abode of Śakra; from there, having reached Dvāravatī, I was reunited with you. || 57 ||
Thus, this auspicious and worthy wife belongs to the son of Hiḍimbā; she who shone like lightning in the terrible battle known as Kāmākhyā.
Nor have I described the beauty of my father-in-law, for it is not appropriate for a virtuous man to describe the charms of all women. (59)
Furthermore, another condition was made by her; hear what it was: "Whatever man shall defeat me by providing an answer to my question," (60)
"Whoever is capable of this shall become my husband. And having heard this agreement, many Daityas and Rākṣasas [assembled]. (61)
They went forth for the sake of conquering her, but having been defeated, they were slain by her; whoever among them had gone toward her first never returned again.
If a multitude of moths dares to conquer such a bowstring as this, it is like a swarm of moths seeking to overcome the blazing radiance of fire.
Ghaṭotkaca, who possesses great heroism, shall certainly become his wife.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Enough with all her virtues for one whose single virtue is great; for what is gained by milk if it is mixed with poison? (65)
How could I, out of mere recklessness, cast aside the son of Bhīmasena—who is dearer to me than life itself and skilled in pure speech—merely because of your words? (66)
O Janārdana, there are other women as well in every land; you ought to name some excellent woman among those many.
Bhīma said: "The words spoken by Keśava are perfectly stated, profound in meaning and excellent; however, that which has been spoken again by the king out of affection does not seem right to me."

The prowess of a Kṣatriya would be truly difficult to accomplish only against a task that is hard to achieve, just as the might of a lordly elephant is displayed among herds of elephants and not among ordinary deer.
The self must be brought to renown in every way by the foremost of heroes; and how could that renown arise except through the performance of difficult tasks? (70)
For the protection of Haiḍambeya, O Pārtha, is not subject to one's own will; he by whom he was given shall protect him, as ordained by the Creator.
A wise person should exert effort in every way to ascend to a high position; if that is not achieved due to fate, it is not the fault of the wise one.
Just as Devavrata alone carried off the daughters of the King of Kāśī in the past, so let the son of Hiḍimbā alone obtain the bowstring without delay.
Arjuna said: These words spoken by Bhīma are based solely on human effort; though it appears weak because of its dependence on destiny, to me it seems exceedingly powerful. (74)
For Kāmākhyā, who spoke in the past, does not utter false words: "O blessed lady, the son of Bhīmasena shall take your hand. (75)
"For this reason, let Ghaṭotkaca go there quickly; this is what pleases me, O Kṛṣṇa—tell me, what do you think? (76)
Kṛṣṇa said: "Your words and those of the high-souled Bhīma are pleasing to me; for indeed, there is no one equal to the son of Bhīmasena in either intelligence or prowess. (77)
"My inner self knows that you have already obtained the daughter of Mura; therefore, let the son of Hiḍimbā go quickly. And what do you think, my son? (78)

Ghaṭotkaca said: "Indeed, it is not proper for one's own virtues to be spoken of in the presence of those worthy of honor; yet the excellent qualities of the sun shine forth spontaneously, like its very rays."
O ancestors, I shall act in every way so that the stainless Pāṇḍavas, through me as their son, will not feel ashamed in assemblies.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one rose and bowed to them; then, strengthened by his ancestors with blessings of victory, he desired to depart.
As he was desiring to depart, Janārdana, having greeted him, said this: "At the time of telling stories, you should remember me, the bringer of victory."

"By these means I shall increase your intellect, which is otherwise so difficult to penetrate, as well as your strength. Having said this, Kṛṣṇa embraced him and dismissed him with his blessings. (83)
Then the son of Hiḍimbā, possessed of great power, followed by Sūryākṣa, Kālākṣa, and Mahodara, reached the path of the sky and departed for that city named Prāgjyotiṣa at the close of day.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Ghaṭotkaca’s Departure for Prāgjyotiṣapura," within the Barbarika episode of the Kaumārikā section, in the first Māheśvara book of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Then he beheld a golden mansion with a thousand floors, situated in a great grove outside Prāgjyotiṣa.
It was filled with the sounds of flutes, lutes, and drums, and was crowded with ten thousand female attendants.
The area was filled with Bhagadatta’s servants, both those arriving and those departing, who asked their sister, "What do you desire? as they inquired after her.
Having reached that palace, which resembled a peak of Mount Meru, the son of Hiḍimbā beheld his friend Karṇaprāvaraṇā standing at the gate.
The hero spoke to her playfully: "O blessed lady, where is that daughter of Mura? I am a guest arrived from a distant land and wish to see my lover. (5)
Karṇaprāvaraṇa said: "O mighty-armed one, what use have you for that bowstring? O lover, millions of lovers have already been slain by it."
O Hero, having beheld your form—with its jar-like laugh and ever-erect hair—and having bowed at your feet, I stand as your obedient servant.
Therefore, O lover, rejoice with me and enjoy pleasures; I shall give you three beloved women as attendants for your three followers.
Ghaṭotkaca said: "O auspicious one, O beautiful lady, have you uttered words befitting yourself? These words shall not enter my heart again."
"O blessed lady, since desire is perverse, that upon which it is fastened does not bind it at all; what, then, can we do about that? (10)
"Today your mistress has been seen by me; either she shall be conquered and sport with me, or, if I am defeated by her, I shall go the way of former lovers. (11)
Therefore, let this be announced immediately to Karṇaprāvaraṇa, so that they may indeed honor the guest by the mere sight of him.
Having heard these words of the son of Bhīma, the night-stalker woman, faltering as she stood upon the roof-peak of the palace, spoke thus to Māurvī: || 13 ||
"O Goddess, a certain illustrious youth of immeasurable splendor, who has come as a guest of Love, stands at your door; grant him your favor. (14)
Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā said: "Let him be released immediately; for what reason do you delay? Perhaps by the conjunction of fate, my time [for his arrival] will be fulfilled. (15)
Having been addressed with these words, the maidservant approached Ghaṭotkaca and said: "Go quickly, O lustful one, into the presence of her and of Death. (16)
Having been addressed thus, that son of Bhīma laughed and, leaving his own followers there, entered his home like a lion entering a cave of Mount Meru.
Seeing flocks of parrots and likewise groups of pigeons, as well as sārikā birds intoxicated with passion, he also beheld those female servants.
By her beauty and youth, she was a source of delight even to Rati; she sat comfortably upon a swing, adorned with every ornament. (19)
Seeing her, who was like a flash of lightning, the son of Bhīma thought: "Aha! She has been pointed out by my father Kṛṣṇa as the one suited for me. (20)
This is only right, since the hosts of lovers have been lost in the past; for if the bodies of lovers were to waste away until their very destruction, it would be appropriate. (21)
"For the sake of amorous women, what counting can there be here for them? Thinking thus in many ways, the lover Bhīmabhū spoke.
O cruel one with a heart of adamant, I have arrived as your guest; therefore, perform for me that hospitality which is fitting for the virtuous and which resides within your heart. (23)
Having heard these words of the son of Hiḍimbā, she, whose heart was hardened by passion, was struck with wonder at his beauty and reproached her own foolishness.
"Fie on me, that I previously made such an agreement! Had it not been made before, he would have become my husband. (25)
Reflecting thus, she spoke these words to the son of Bhīma: "O gentle sir, you have come in vain; go back alive and happy once more. (26)

Now, if you desire me, then quickly utter a story; for if, after speaking a story, you cause me to fall into doubt, then I shall come under your power, or else you shall be slain by me while sleeping.
Sūta said: Having spoken these words, he gazed at her from the corner of his eye.
Having remembered Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, he began a story: "In a certain place, there was a certain young man with uncontrolled senses who had a wife. (29)
To him was born a daughter, and his wife passed away; thereafter, he protected and nurtured that young daughter.
When she reached youth, her limbs became manifest and beautiful; her waist was graced by swelling breasts, and her lotus-face was radiant.
Then his mind, its tether agitated by lust, abandoned its restraint; and that evil-minded man, embracing his daughter, spoke to her.
"You are the daughter of my neighbor; you were brought here by me and nourished for a very long time to be my wife. Therefore, O beloved, accomplish that purpose."
Thus addressed, she accepted those words as being exactly so; he approached her as his wife, and she likewise him as her husband.
Then, from that Madanarāsabha, a daughter was born to her. Tell me, does she become his daughter or his granddaughter? Answer this question of mine quickly, if you have the ability. (35)
Sūta said: Having heard this question, she reflected upon it in her heart in many ways.
And she could not find any way whatsoever to resolve this question; thus, defeated by the question, she resorted to her own power. (37)
And with both hands he struck the golden rope of the swing; thereupon, billions of exceedingly terrifying rākṣasas rushed forth.
Lions, tigers, boars, buffaloes, leopards, and deer—seeing those innumerable creatures running in fury to devour them—(39)
Smiling, the son of Bhīma struck his nails with his little finger and thumb; from that, twice as many Rākṣasas and others emerged there.
All those [arrows] made of bowstrings were devoured by them in an instant; and when his own power of weapons had been defeated, he then resorted to the power of physical force.
Rising suddenly from the swing, she desired to seize her sword; but as she rose, the son of Bhīma pursued her with speed, as it were.
Seizing him by the hair with his left hand, he threw him down upon the ground; then, placing his left foot upon the [demon's] neck and taking up a knife, [he struck].
With his right hand, he desired to cut off her nose; then the quivering bowstring spoke softly to Ghaṭotkaca.

O Lord, by means of your question, your power, and your strength, I have been conquered by you in three ways; homage to you! Therefore, release me; I am your servant, so command me and I shall perform that very task.
Ghaṭotkaca said: "If it is so, then you are released; show once more what strength you possess. Having spoken thus, he released her, and having been released, she bowed down and said: || 46 ||
I know you, O mighty-armed one, as a hero, the best among those endowed with power, the lord of all rākṣasas, and one of immeasurable prowess in the three worlds. (47)
For you, O Lord of the Guhyakas, are known as Kālanābha; you have been born on earth as the lord of sixty crores for the sake of protecting the Yakṣas. (48)
Thus Kāmākhyā spoke to me, and I remember all of that; this house, along with its attendants, has been given by me to you of my own accord. (49)
"Command me, O Lord of my life; what command of yours shall I carry out? Ghaṭotkaca said: "A marriage for him is by no means appropriate while he remains in concealment."
"O auspicious one, since my parents and kinsmen are still alive, carry me quickly now to Śakraprastha. (51)
"This is our family tradition that the wife should marry the husband; having obtained permission for that, I shall marry you. (52)
Then Mauryī informed her lord that Bhagadatta had arrived; having taken much wealth, she then sent off her brother.
Then, having placed Ghaṭotkaca upon her back, the blameless lady, accompanied by various provisions, set out for Śakraprastha.
Then, having been congratulated by Vāsudeva and the Pāṇḍavas, the son of Bhīma took her hand at an auspicious moment.
Having married her according to the supreme rites prescribed for both the Kurus and the Rākṣasas, he gratified the Pāṇḍavas with those riches.
Both Kuntī and Draupadī rejoiced exceedingly; they performed auspicious rites for him and for the son of Mādrī, who was gratified by the wealth.
Then, when the wedding was concluded, the king honored Ghaṭotkaca along with his wife and dispatched him to his own kingdom.
Having received the command with his head bowed, the son of Hiḍimbā, accompanied by his wife, returned to the auspicious forest kingdom of Hiḍimba.
Then, celebrated by the wives of the rākṣasas with heroic cymbals, he rejoiced in his own kingdom with a great festival.
Then, in the variegated forests and on the sandy banks of rivers, the son of Bhīma took delight with her, just as Rāvaṇa did with Mandodarī.
As that one of great splendor was thus sporting, a child was born from the tiger-like Rākṣasa Heḍamba, possessing a radiance like the rising sun.
As soon as he was born, he grew and in an instant reached youth; he resembled a mass of dark clouds, with a pot-shaped face and long eyes. (63)
With his hair and body hair standing on end, he bowed before his parents and said: "I bow to you both; for one who is born, the parents are the supreme gurus."
"Indeed, by doing what is pleasing to you both, I shall always be free from debt; I desire a name for myself to be given by you two. (65)
Thereafter, Bhemī embraced her son and spoke these words regarding what must be done for his ultimate welfare and advancement: || 66 ||
"O mighty-armed one, because your hair will have a barbarian-like appearance, you shall be named Barbarīka; you will be the increaser of joy for your lineage. (67)

O Brahmin, that which is your supreme and firm welfare is proclaimed in many ways by the foremost sages; therefore, let us go to the city of Dvārakā and ask Vāsudeva, the lord of the Yadu lineage, about it. (68)

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of Barbarīka," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Then the wise Ghaṭotkaca, having left Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā there, went through the air to Dvārakā, followed by his son.
And seeing that Rākṣasa approaching with his Rākṣasa followers, the warriors dwelling in Dvārakā raised a most formidable roar.
"In every village, nine hundred thousand well-equipped chariots have been stationed, thinking: 'The two Rākṣasas who arrive shall be struck down with arrows. || 3 ||
Seeing those heroes of the Yadu clan with their weapons grasped, Ghaṭotkaca raised his massive arm and cried out in a loud voice: || 4 ||
"O heroes, know me to be the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīma, who has come to pay his respects—he who is very dear to Vāsudeva. (5)
"Announce that I have arrived with my son before the Lord of the Yādavas. Having heard these words of his, they announced him to Kṛṣṇa.
The king said, "Let him come here quickly while he is in the assembly hall. Then they caused Ghaṭotkaca to enter Dvārakā.
Accompanied by his son, he too, beholding delightful forests, groves, pleasure-mountains, and palaces, arrived at the assembly hall.
There he paid homage to Ugrasena, Vasudeva, and Sātyaki, as well as to Kṛṣṇa himself, who was accompanied by Akrūra, Rāma, and others.
Embracing him as he fell at her feet along with his son, she seated them near her and, having bestowed her blessings, spoke these words.
"O son, tiger among Rākṣasas, enhancer of the Kuru lineage! Is all well with you in every respect? For what purpose have you come here? (11)
Ghaṭotkaca said: "O Lord, by your grace all is well with me in every respect. O Master, please hear the reason for which I have come."
"This son of mine was born of a wife instructed by a god; he will pose a question to you, so listen, for he has come from there. (13)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O child, son of Mūrvī, speak; ask whatever you desire. Just as Ghaṭotkaca is very dear to me, so are you."

Barbarīka said: Having prostrated before you, the primordial God, with my mind, intellect, and meditative absorption, I shall ask: O Mādhava, by what means may the welfare of a living being who has been born be attained? (15)

Some say that the dharma of excellence consists in sovereignty, renunciation, and enjoyment; some say it is self-restraint, austerity, and wealth; and others say it is liberation from enjoyments. || 16 ||
Therefore, O Supreme Person, among these hundreds of ways to attain the highest good, please tell me with certainty what will bring the greatest welfare for me and for this family. (17)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O child, the supreme welfare for each of the social classes has been declared separately: for Brāhmaṇas, austerity is the root, as well as self-restraint and Vedic study. (18)
The proclamation of the Dharma has also been declared by the wise to be a supreme good; however, it is proclaimed that for Kṣatriyas, strength must be established first. (19)
The punishment of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous; the tending of cattle for Vaiśyas, as well as agriculture and the acquisition of knowledge. (20)
The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born; living by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born. (21)
Delighting in his wife, supporting his dependents, pure, faithful, and devoted, he should not neglect the five great sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation.
Therefore, since you are born into a Kṣatriya family, do this—listen! First acquire incomparable strength, and with that, train him.
Protect the wicked and the virtuous alike, and thus you shall attain heaven; furthermore, O son, strength is obtained through the great favor of the goddesses.
Therefore, may you perform the propitiation of the Goddess for the sake of attaining power.
Barbarīka said: "In which sacred field, and who is the goddess, and how shall I worship her? Having made your mind inclined toward favoring me, please inform me. (26)

Sūta said: Thus questioned, the all-pervading Lord Dāmodara meditated for a moment and replied: "O child, I shall tell you of the sacred field where you shall perform that penance; it is known as Guptakṣetra, located at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. (27)
Therein, whatever various goddesses exist throughout the three worlds were brought together into a single unity by the high-souled Nārada.
There are four goddesses of the quarters and nine Durgās belonging to him; go and propitiate them, for their unification is indeed difficult to attain.
"O son, worship them constantly with flowers, incense, and ointments, as well as with hymns of praise and offerings, so that they may be pleased with you. (30)

When the goddesses are pleased, strength, wealth, fame, sons, fortunate wives, heaven, as well as the state of liberation and true happiness—none of these are difficult to attain; this which you have spoken is the truth. (31)
Sūta said: Having spoken thus to Barbarīka, Kṛṣṇa said to Ghaṭotkaca: "O Ghaṭotkaca, this noble son of yours is indeed very kind-hearted."
"Therefore, I have given you these two names, 'Suhṛdaya' and so forth. Having spoken thus, he embraced him and honored him with various kinds of wealth.
The Blessed One commanded Barbarīka for the sake of the hidden sacred field; he, having then paid homage to Kṛṣṇa, his father, and those Yādavas, [departed].
Having taken leave of them all, he proceeded to the Guptakṣetra; Ghaṭotkaca also, dismissed by Kṛṣṇa, went to his own forest.
Remembering the virtues of his son, he protected his own kingdom together with his wife; thereafter, the wise and noble-hearted one established a hermitage at Dagdhasthalī.
He worshipped the goddesses three times a day with ritual actions and meditative concentrations, constantly offering flowers, incense, and various kinds of oblations.
As he was propitiating them, the goddesses were pleased within three years; then, appearing before his very eyes, they manifested themselves by the power of that high-souled one.
"A strength such as yours is rare and does not belong to anyone in the three worlds; and they said, 'O one of great splendor, dwell right here for some time. (39)
"Through association with Vijaya, you shall indeed attain further prosperity. Having been addressed thus by all the goddesses, he remained right there.
Then a Magadhan Brahmin named Vijaya arrived; that best of the twice-born had traversed the entire earth, treading upon it with his feet.
Having acquired the power of knowledge in Kāśī, he approached for the purpose of spiritual practice; there he worshipped the seven liṅgas, beginning with Guheśvara.
He propitiated the goddesses for a long time in order to obtain the fruit of his knowledge; then, being pleased with him, the goddesses spoke these words to him in a dream: ||| 43 ||
"O virtuous one, accomplish the vidyā in the courtyard of Siddhamātā; this devoted and kind-hearted man will assist you. (44)
Then, having heard those words from within his dream, Vijaya arose, went to the Goddess, and chose that son of Bhīma’s daughter as his bridegroom.
Having heard the words of the goddess, he too resolved to provide assistance; then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the pure Vijaya fasted.
Having bathed and worshipped the Lingas, he also worshipped the goddesses individually; having performed his ablutions and observed a fast, Barbarika remained in the vicinity.
Then, on the first night, he went before Siddhāmbikā; having fashioned there a mandala in the shape of a vulva with nine lines, he proceeded.
Having driven eight stakes with their cords into the eight directions, he, wearing a black antelope skin and accompanied by Barbarīka, [proceeded].

Having tied his topknot and performed the ritual binding of the directions, he then undertook the procedure; in the center of the mandala, within a bright sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possessing three tiers (trimekhala), he acted.
Then, having handed over the sword made of khadira wood sharpened by mantras and having planted stakes all around, he spoke to Barbarīka: || 51 ||
"Remain pure and awake, reciting a hymn to the Goddess, so that while I perform this rite, no obstacle may arise. (52)
When the mighty Barbarīka had spoken thus and remained there, Vijaya performed these [acts]: withering, burning, and flooding.

Then, having assumed a comfortable posture and recited the mantra "Oṃ gurubhyo namaḥ" one hundred and eight times, and having prostrated before the gurus, he then began the ritual procedure for Gaṇeśvara.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme mantra of Gaṇapati.
It accomplishes all tasks, requires little effort, yields great results, and bestows all spiritual perfections.

Oṃ gāṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaiṃ gauṃ gaḥ—this is the seven-syllabled great mantra (mahāmantra). For this Gaṇapati mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) is named Gaṇaka, the deity (devatā) is Vighneśvara, the seed-syllable (bīja) is *gaṃ*, the power (śakti) is Oṃ; its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of worship, recitation, marking the forehead (tilaka), the fulfillment of mental desires, or for the fire-oblation (homa). First, the practitioner should apply the tilaka. With the mantra: "Oṃ gāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ," one should place unbroken rice grains (akṣata) upon the tilaka. "Oṃ gāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ"—this is the tilaka mantra. With the mantra "Oṃ gāṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ," one should offer three handfuls of flowers to Gaṇeśa. Here, with the root mantra (mūlamantra), one should offer sandalwood paste, incense, flowers, incense smoke, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), betel nuts, betel leaves, and so forth. Thereafter, one should perform the recitation (japa) with the root mantra. Having recited it one hundred and eight times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times, or ten million times according to one's capacity, one should invoke the fire for the sake of the oblation consisting of a tenth part (daśāṃśa-homa) by saying, "I invoke the fire of Gaṇeśa. Then, with the mantra "Oṃ gāṃ gaṇapataye svāhā," one should perform the oblation with balls of guggulu resin. This is the application and the ritual manual (tākalpa) of Gaṇeśa. Whoever thus accomplishes this supreme mantra amidst all obstacles, all obstacles perish and their heart's desire is fulfilled. (57)
Dākinīs, Yātudhānas, and terrifying beings such as Pretas [are subdued]; the destruction of enemies occurs, as does their subjugation. (58)

One who knows this *Gāṇeśvara-kalpa* shall also be victorious; having applied the *tilaka* according to the prescribed rite and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he shall succeed. (59)
Having offered one-tenth of the pills as oblations and worshipped Siddhivināyaka, he then performed worship of the Yakṣakṣetrapāla at night.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Gāṇeśvara Kalpa within the Mahāvidyā Sādhana," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, we have previously heard of the birth of Gaṇeśa; tell us now how Kṣetranātha was born—do indeed speak this for us who are listening.
Sūta said: When the inhabitants of heaven were being oppressed by the Daitya Dāruka, they prostrated before Śiva, who was seated with the Goddess, and spoke as follows. (2)
"O Lord, we have been oppressed by the terrible Daitya Dāruka, who is invincible even to the gods and asuras, and we have even been driven from our own abodes. (3)
That evil-minded one could not be slain by Viṣṇu, nor by Candra, nor by anyone else whatsoever, except for Ardhanārīśvara. || 4 ||
"Be our refuge as we are being tormented by him! Having spoken thus, the gods wept and cried out, "Save us! Save us! (5)
Then, overcome with great compassion, Pārvatī took the blackness from the throat of Hara and fashioned a single woman of great terror.
Having bestowed her own power upon her there, the auspicious goddess spoke these words: "Since you are exceedingly black (kāla), you shall be known by the name Kālikā."
"O beautiful one, quickly destroy the wicked enemy of the gods! Having been addressed thus, Kālikā, who utters a great roar, then approached him.
By that very roar, he killed him along with his followers, their hearts bursting; then the female spirit dwelling in the cremation ground let out a great shriek.
By whom even the three worlds were rendered destitute and as if dead; then the all-pervading Rudra, for the sake of the universe, assumed the form of a child.
And she arrived near him in the abode of the deceased as he was weeping; then, filled with compassion, she took the crying child onto her lap.
Kālikā suckled her breast while muttering, "Do not cry," but even as a child, he drank up the anger born of her body under the pretext of drinking milk.
She who had been the poison arising from the throat of Hara, so difficult to bear, became gentle at that time when Kālī had swallowed his wrathful nature.
Having performed his duties, even though he was but a child, he desired to abandon that state of childhood.
Then the gods, fearing that Kālikā might again cause them terror, said: "O child, do not act like a child; abandon such behavior and show mercy! (15)

The boy said: "There is no need to fear Kālikā, for she has been made gentle. If you have any fear, I shall create other children. Having said, "I shall create the sixty-four Kṣetrapālas," he created them from his mouth.
Maheśvara, assuming the form of a child, spoke to those who were in the form of children: "In the heavens there are twenty-five [worlds], and in the nether regions (pātālas) there are as many."

"Your dwelling shall be in the world of mortals (bhūrloka) for fourteen [years], as well as your protection; this very one, staying in the cremation ground, shall become your dog and your vehicle. (18)
Your food offering consists of black gram mixed with rice; and whoever shall perform any ritual act without first worshipping you [will suffer]. (19)
"That [offering] of his shall become fruitless, consumed by pretas and rākṣasas. Having said this, the Blessed Lord Rudra vanished right there.
And the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) remain stationed in their respective places as appointed. Thus has the creation of the guardians of the fields been described to you in brief. (21)
I shall proclaim the means of propitiation by which they become pleased.
Oṃ kṣāṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ. This is the nine-syllabled great mantra. || 23 ||

Having offered sandalwood and other substances here, and having presented sixty-four portions of *vaṭaka* cakes mixed with black gram and rice, as well as an equal number of lamps, leaves, and betel nuts, one should prostrate like a staff and recite this great hymn of praise. || 24 ||
Oṃ! To those with upward-pointing hair and deformed eyes, who are eternally of terrible form, with blood-red eyes and tawny gaze—to those guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas), I bow. 25.
Ahvara, Āpakumbha, and likewise Iḍācāra; Indramūrti, Kolākṣa, Upapāda, and Ṛtuṃsana. || 26 ||
Siddheya, Valika, Nīlapāda, Ekadaṃṣṭrika, Irāpati, Aghahārī, Vighnahārī, and likewise Antaka; || 27 ||
Ūrdhvapāda, Kambala, Khañjana, Khara, Gomukha, Jaṅghāla, Gaṇanātha, and Vāraṇa. || 28 ||
I bow to the guardians of the celestial fields, who are both matted-haired and hairless: Ṛkāra, Haṭhakārī, Ṭaṅkapāṇi, and likewise Khaṇi. (29)
Ṭhaṃṭhaṃkaṇa, Jambara, Sphuliṅgāsya, Taḍidruci, Daṃtura, Ghananāda, and another, Nandaka. || 30 ||
Phetkārakārī, Pañcāsya, Barbarī, Bhīmarūpavān, Bhagnapakṣa, Kālamegha, Yuvāna, and likewise Bhāskara. || 31 ||
I bow to Raurava, Lambauṣṭha, Vaṇija, Sujaṭālika, Sugandha, and Huhuka—the guardians of Pātāla.
Huṃkāra was present at all the liṅgas; Bhayāvaha was in the cremation grounds; Mahākṣa was in the terrible forest; and Jvālākṣa resided in the dwelling place.
Among trees there is Ekavṛkṣa; at night there is Karālavadana; Ghaṇṭārava dwells in caves; and Padmakhañja stands in the water.
Durāroha is at the four crossroads, as are the Kuravas on the mountain; Pravāha is in the waterfalls, and Māṇibhadra among the treasures.
I bow to those who, as the presiding lord of the field of mercury (rasakṣetra), are the destroyer in the sacrificial enclosures, and who remain pervading the fourteen worlds in this manner. (36)
Thus, I go for refuge to the sixty-four guardians of the fields; may they be gracious, may they be gracious, and may they be satisfied by my worship. (37)
In all undertakings, whoever, being pure, thus worships the Kṣetrapas, the Kṣetrapas become pleased with him and grant his desired object.
And Vijaya, understanding this ritual manual for the field (*kṣetrapakalpa*), worshipped according to the prescribed method; once it was accomplished, he praised him.
Then, having prostrated, he worshipped the goddess Vaṭayakṣiṇī; O brahmins, this was when she was formerly [invoked] by Nārada from the village of Kalāpa.
And along with them, a Brahmin widow named Sunandā was brought there by them, having arrived at that place on the shore of the earth to perform penance.
Performing the *kṛcchra*, *parāka*, and *atikṛcchra* penances, she observed two three-night vows dedicated to Sāvitrī during the months of Jyeṣṭha and Bhādrapada.
And likewise, O delighter of her family, she observed the month-long fast during Kārtika; having worshipped the seven Liṅgas, she always performed the worship of the Goddess.

He likewise performed his ritual bath at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean on the new moon day; thus, by means of these and many other constant observances of religious vows, [he remained steadfast].
Having shaken off her sins, she went to the world of Umā, where she was welcomed; and by a portion of herself, she was born on that very bank as Vaṭayakṣiṇī.
Hara, stationed at the Siddhaliṅga, being pleased with her, granted her a boon: "He who shall perform my worship without first worshipping her... (46)

"All that [effort] of his is fruitless," it is said; therefore, I must certainly protect her. Consequently, one should always worship Vaṭayakṣiṇī, who resides in the banyan tree, with flowers, incense, and food offerings, with devotion and with this mantra: || 47 ||
"O Sunandā, you who are worthy of being cherished, accept this worship from me; be gracious to me at all times, O Vaṭayakṣiṇī. (48)
Having thus worshipped, bowed to, and asked for forgiveness from that Vaṭayakṣiṇī, both man and woman always obtain all their desires. (49)
And the high-minded Vijaya, knowing this greatness, also worshipped with devotion the Vaṭayakṣiṇī residing in the banyan tree.
Then, having praised Siddhāmbikā, he recited the Aparājitā, the Vaiṣṇavī Mahāvidyā, together with its ritual practice.
O best of Brahmins, listen as I proclaim that Vidyā by the mere recollection of which all suffering comes to an end. (52)

Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva; salutations to Ananta, the thousand-headed one, who reclines upon the ocean of milk, whose couch is the coils of Śeṣa, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, who is clad in yellow garments. O Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Hayaśiras, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Trivikrama, Rāma, Rāma, O Giver of Boons, salutations be unto You! Salutations be unto You! [Drive away] the Asuras, Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Kumbhāṇḍas, Siddhas, Yoginīs, Ḍākinīs, and the planets headed by Skanda, as well as the lunar mansions, other planets, and others—slay them, slay them! Burn them, burn them! Cook them, cook them! Grind them, grind them! Destroy them, destroy them! Put them to flight, put them to flight! With the conch, the discus, the thunderbolt, the mace, the club, and the plow, reduce them to ashes! O Thousand-armed One, O Thou whose weapons are a thousand feet, conquer, conquer! Be victorious, be victorious! O Unconquered One, O Unobstructed One, O Thousand-eyed One, blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up! O Universal Form, O Many-formed One, O Madhusūdana, O Great Boar, O Supreme Person, O Vaikuṇṭha, O Nārāyaṇa, O Lotus-navelled One, O Govinda, O Dāmodara, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Destroyer of all Asuras, O Subduer of all beings, O Piercer of all sorrows, O Shatterer of all machines, O Crusher of all serpents, O Great Lord of all gods, O Liberator from all bonds, O Destroyer of all enemies, O Dispeller of all fevers, O Averter of all seizing spirits, O Pacifier of all sins, O Janārdana, O Bringer of joy to people, salutations be unto You! Svāhā! || 53 ||

Whoever recites, reads, hears, remembers, retains, or proclaims this Aparājitā, the supreme Vaiṣṇavī Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā), shall have no fear of wind, fire, thunderbolts, stones, or showers of hail; nor shall there be fear of the ocean, fear of planetary influences, fear of thieves, or fear of wild beasts. || 54 ||

In some places, there shall be no fear of the darkness of night, of women, of royal families, of poisons, secondary poisons, artificial poisons, subjugation, incantations for causing hatred, expulsion, killing, or imprisonment—provided these mantra-words are recited from the heart, bound [in ritual], and worshipped with perfected success. (55)

Namely: Homage, homage be unto you! O Fearless One, O Sinless One, O Unconquered One, O Unafraid One, O Immortal One, O Unvanquished One, O You who are perfected by recitation, O You who are perfected by remembrance, O Ekānaṃśā, O Umā, O Dhruvā, O Arundhatī, O Sāvitrī, O Gāyatrī, O Jātavedasī, O Mānastokā, O Sarasī, O Sarasvatī, O Dharaṇī, O Dhāriṇī, O Saudāminī, O Aditi, O Vinatā, O Gaurī, O Gāndhārī, O Mātaṅgī, O Kṛṣṇā, O Yaśodā, O Truth-speaker, O Speaker of Brahman, O Kālī, O Kapālinī, O You who instantly effect the gathering of limbs—protect, protect him who is on land, in water, or in the atmosphere; protect, protect him from the fear and calamities of all beings! Svāhā! || 56 ||
She whose flower withers, or if her embryo falls away; she whose children die, or she who is barren like a crow—she should maintain this vidyā, and she will not be tainted by these defects.
In battle, in the royal court, and at dice, his victory shall be constant; for she holds weapons in her hand and carries arrows in combat.
It is the constant destroyer of abdominal tumors (gulma), colic, and eye diseases, as well as the eradicator of headaches and fevers for all embodied beings. (59)

Namely: *Hana 2 Kāli, Sara 2 Kāli, Sara 2 Gauri, Dhama 2 Gauri, Vidye, Āle, Tāle, Māle, Gandhe, Vadhe, Paca 2 Vidye! Destroy evil; strike down bad dreams! Perform the counter-spell (*pratividyā*)! O Attractor, O Penetrator, O Jvālāmālinī, Ramanī, Rāmaṇī, Dharaṇī, Dhāriṇī, O Mānonmāninī, protect us! O Vāyavī, Jvālāmālinī, Tāpanī, Śoṣaṇī, Nīlapatākinī, Mahāgaurī, Mahāśrayā, Mahāmayūrī, O Adityaraśmi, Jāhnavī, Yamadaṇḍe, Kiṇi 2, Cintāmaṇi, Surabhi, Born of the Gods, Kāmadughā! May whatever task is desired be accomplished for me, Svāhā! *Oṃ svāhā, Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā, Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā, Oṃ svaḥ svāhā, Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ svāhā!* Wherever the evil has come from, let it go back thither, Svāhā! *Oṃ bale mahābale uāsiddhasādhini svāhā!* 60.
Thus, having become self-restrained through the concentration of mind, intellect, and meditative absorption, Vijaya accomplished this unconquered Vaiṣṇavī weapon.
O best of the twice-born, even for one who recites this constantly, even without the performance of ritual means, all obstacles shall perish.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Accomplishment of Mahāvidyā," in the Barbarika-episode of the Kaumārikā-khaṇḍa, within the first section, the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa, of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: While he was offering oblations of mustard seeds soaked in the resin of the *aśvattha* tree into a fire of *lākṣā*, using the principal mantras known as Balā and Atibalā, || 1 ||
When the first watch had passed, a certain woman arrived, wearing a single garment stained with blood, her hair long and standing upright.
With fierce eyes and white teeth, she who was terrifying even to fear itself, reached that sacrificial ground and let out a great roar as she wept.
Upon seeing her, Vijaya was instantly agitated as if filled with fear; but Barbarīka, remaining fearless, stepped forward to face her.
Then, embracing her neck, that hero, the best among the wise, wept twice as much, making a great sound like a thundercloud.
Seeing him, she was struck with amazement; yet, by the time she had even released her knife, his throat was so tightly constricted that she was unable to let it go.
And as her throat was being repeatedly squeezed by the powerful one, she uttered various cries like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Then, after uttering cries for a moment, she spoke in a low voice, "Save me! Release me! Thereupon, released by the compassionate one, she fell at his feet and said: || 8 ||
"I have come to you for refuge; I am your slave and your servant. Know me as the Rākṣasī Mahājihvā, who can assume any form at will. (9)
O Hero, if you grant me this life-offering so difficult to obtain—the one who dwells in the cremation grounds of Kāśī and who destroys the pride of gods and demons—then [I shall do as you wish]. (10)
"Therefore, I shall practice penance, granting fearlessness to all beings; in this matter, I swear by my own deity and by myself. (11)
"If I were to do the opposite of this, I would be reduced to ashes in an instant. Having spoken thus, the hero firmly restrained her with solemn oaths.
She too, being greatly delighted and released from her distress, departed for the forest; that hero, however, remained right there, sword in hand.
Then, at midnight, a great roar was heard, and a darkness arose with the luster of the Andhatamas hell.
Then he beheld a mountain with a hundred peaks and vast extent; it discharged various rocks and various lofty trees.
A great torrent of blood fell, resounding with the noise of various waterfalls; beholding the mountain in that state, the son of Bhīma remained undaunted.
Becoming twice as large, the mountain suddenly leapt toward the other mountain; then, having gathered up that mountain with his own body, he struck it down.
Then that mountain was shattered upon the surface of the earth; thereafter, he [the demon] possessed a body a yojana in height, with a hundred heads and a hundred bellies.
Emitting great flames from his mouths, Repalendra rushed forward; seeing him charging, the exceedingly powerful Barbarīka [stood ready]. (19)
Having assumed such a form, he rushed toward the roaring [elephant] with agility, skill, and great grace in the middle of the night.
They fought with nets of arrows like two clouds in the rainy season; with their bows broken they fought with swords, and with their swords broken they fought with their fists.
Like two mountains with wings, they fought firmly for a long time; then, having seized him by the armpit and whirled him around for a moment, [he threw him down]. (22)
He trampled it upon the ground and released what had spread out; he then cast it onto the shore of the Mahī-Sāgara at the southeast corner.
The village named Repalendra still exists today at a distance from there; thus was that one named Repala, whose prowess was equal to Vṛtra.
The lord of the cremation ground of Avanti, who was creating obstacles, was slain; having killed him, the hero Barbarīka stood once more. (25)
Then, during the third watch, she arrived from the western direction; resembling a mountain and emitting a great roar, she seemed to make the earth tremble with her feet.
Like a lightning bolt fallen from a cloud, she was known as Duha-druha; seeing her approaching with the splendor of the sun and fire, [he was struck]. (27)
Approaching with speed, Bhaimī ascended as if laughing; then, as she was rushing forward with force, he struck her on the snout with his fists.
He placed her right there, and she remained standing, greatly tormented; then, filled with rage, that malevolent woman let out a great cry and leaped up.
He swiftly hurled Barbarīka onto the ground according to his wish; then, having roared excessively, he delivered a blow with his foot.
The hero, seizing her feet, cast her to the ground with ease; then, as she rose again and ran toward him, he seized her.
Having struck him down with his fist, he crushed his throat; squeezing it like a wet garment, he swiftly caused him to lose his life-breaths.
Thus, in the place called Sīkottara, she who was born as a single-footed one in the cremation ground—the sovereign of the Śākinīs—was slain by Barbarīka.
Having slain her as well, he effortlessly hurled her toward the west; even today, a village named Duhadruha exists there.
Then Barbarīka remained there in that very manner for his protection; and then, in the fourth watch of the night, a wondrous Kṣapaṇaka arrived.
Shaven-headed, naked, wearing peacock feathers, and observing a great vow, he spoke these words: "Alas! O sirs, this is indeed an extreme hardship! (36)
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; why then is this fire kindled? For when the fire is offered oblations, there is great slaughter of subtle living beings.
Having heard these words of his, Barbarīka spoke with a smile: "While the oblation was being poured into the fire within the mouths of all the gods... (38)
"O wicked one, you speak untruth; O evil-minded one, you deserve punishment! Having said this, he suddenly sprang up and stood firmly upon his chest.
Having struck him with blows from his teeth and fists, he knocked him down; seeing him fallen on the ground with his face fouled by blood, he released him.
Regaining consciousness in an instant, he assumed the form of a terrible daitya and, out of fear of the son of Bhīma, fled and entered the opening of a cave.
The city named Bahuprabhā was sixty yojanas in length; he entered it suddenly, and Barbarīka followed after him.
Then, upon seeing Barbarīka, a roar arose from the leaf-clad ones (the forest-dwellers): "Run! Let him be slain! Let him be cut down! Let him be split apart! || 43 ||
Having heard that, nine crores of terrifying Daitya heroes, bearing various weapons, rushed toward the hero Barbarīka.
Seeing those crores of Daityas, the son of Bhīma’s son became enraged; suddenly closing his eyes, he rushed into their midst.
Then, with kicks of his feet, blows of his arms, and strikes of his chest, he sent some to the abode of Yama in an instant.
Just as an enraged elephant would level a forest of reeds to the ground, so did he slay nine crores [of beings] along with that Palāśin.
Then the Nāgas, headed by Vāsuki, having assembled, praised him with various words and spoke these kind-hearted words to him.
O descendant of Bhīma, you have performed the supreme service for the Nāgas, in that this Daitya named Palāśin has been sent to Yama along with his followers.
For by this evil-minded one, O hero, together with his followers, we have been tormented by various means and cast even lower than Pātāla.
"Therefore, choose from those nāgas whatever supreme boon you desire; we are all well-pleased with you and are ready to grant boons. (51)
Suhṛdaya said: "If a boon is to be granted to me, then I choose this: may Vijaya, freed from all obstacles, attain success. (52)
Then, saying "So be it," those who subsist on air were delighted and replied to him; and he, honored by the Nāgas, gave them the city and returned.
And passing through the middle of the opening, he beheld a great, radiant linga composed of all kinds of jewels, situated beneath a Kalpavriksha tree.
He beheld him being honored by beautiful Naga maidens; then, overcome with wonder, he questioned those Naga maidens.
"By whom was this Liṅga, possessing the splendor of the sun and fire, established? And what kind of paths are these leading out from the four directions of the Liṅga? (56)
Having heard these words of the hero, she, whose hips and breasts were large, spoke this with bashfulness and a smile, releasing sidelong glances from the corners of her eyes. (57)
By Śeṣa, the great-souled king of all serpents, after performing penance, this great Liṅga was installed here.
Bestowing all perfections through sight, touch, meditation, and worship, this path from the east of the Liṅga leads to Śrīparvata on earth. (59)
This path to the south, established by Elāpatra for the sake of reaching the Nāgas there, leads to Śūrpāraka on earth. (60)
This path to the west was created by the Naga Karkoṭaka for the purpose of reaching that place; it leads to the brilliantly shining Prabhāsa.
And this northern path, by which you stand ready to go, has been prepared for the movement of the nāgas by Airāvata. (62)
In the Guptakṣetra, the Siddhaliṅga goes to the Śaktiguhā; it was ordained by the high-souled Takṣaka that it should go there.
Thus has this been described, O Hero; now hear my petition: who are you that have just now gone behind the Daitya, and why have you returned here all alone just now? Tell us.
And we all, being your handmaidens, choose you as our husband; sport with us here upon these various grounds.
Barbarīka said: "I am born of the Kuru lineage, the grandson of the son of Pāṇḍu; known as Barbarīka, I have come here to slay that Daitya."
"And that sinful Daitya having been slain, I shall return once more to the surface of the earth; O ladies, I have no further business with you whatsoever. (67)
"Since I have constantly remained established in the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya)," having said this, he worshipped that liṅga and prostrated himself like a staff.
The hero ascended upwards while being gazed upon by them with timid eyes; then, having come outside, his face was clearly visible at that time.
With great joy, he beheld the victory over the eastern quarter; and at that time, Vijaya completed all his tasks.
Resplendent with a brilliance equal to the sun, he ascended upwards in an instant; then there fell a great rain of flowers from the sky by the gods.
The chief Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced; then Vijaya spoke these words to Barbarīka: || 72 ||
"O Lord of Heroes, by your grace I have attained incomparable perfection. Live long, rejoice long, dwell long, and be victorious long! (73)
For this very reason, the virtuous desire the company of the virtuous; for association with them is the truth that serves as the medicine for all defects. (74)
And you, take the ash remaining from the fire-oblation, which has a luster like vermilion, is free of impurities, contains small cavities, and is being replenished. (75)
This is inexhaustible; as you discharge it first in battle, it will destroy the bodies of your enemies—the very abode of death. (76)
In this way, your victory over your enemies will be achieved with ease.
Barbarīka said: He who performs a service without desire is called a virtuous man; what merit is there in the virtue of one who performs a service with desire? (78)
Therefore, give the ashes to someone else; I have not the slightest need for them. I choose nothing from you other than a glance from your face, made gracious and favorable toward me.
The gods said: "A great battle will take place between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas; then, if the Kauravas obtain the ashes situated upon the earth [as a boon], [they shall prevail]. (80)
"Then a great calamity will clearly befall the Pāṇḍavas; therefore, take this ash. He too acted according to those words.
The gods, together with the goddesses, honored Vijaya and bestowed upon him perfected sovereignty, as well as the name Siddhasena.
Thus that Brahmin Vijaya attained a success that is very difficult to obtain; and Barbarīka, having performed this, lived devoted to the worship of the Goddess.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Accomplishment of the Task," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Thus, while he remained there on the bank, intent on propitiating the Goddess and devoted to the worship of the seven Liṅgas, the delighter of Bhīma’s son [stood] there.
Then, after some time, the Pāṇḍavas, having been defeated at dice, arrived there in due course to bathe in the sacred fords.
Then, exhausted from the journey, those five with Draupadī as the fifth approached the goddess Caṇḍikā, who was situated to the northeast of the sacred field.
He sat down right there, and at that moment, the host of Caṇḍikā and Barbarīka beheld those heroes who had arrived.
But he did not know the Pāṇḍus, nor did the Pāṇḍavas know him; for from birth there had never been any meeting between the Pāṇḍus and him.
Then, having entered that place and approached the goddess, the Pāṇḍavas offered the funeral cakes and other offerings there; thereafter, being thirsty, they looked for water.
Then Bhīma entered the middle of the pit to drink the water; as he was entering, Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words to him: ||| 7 ||
"O Bhīma, having drawn out the water and washed your feet outside, you may then drink; otherwise, a great fault will befall you. (8)
Without even hearing these words of the king, Bhīma, his eyes agitated by thirst, entered into the middle of the pit out of a desire for water.
Having seen it, he resolved right there to drink the water; for the sake of purification, he washed his face, hands, and feet.
For whatever water has been drunk by men without having been washed out, the pretas and piśācas, having entered that very form, drink it. (11)
While Vṛkodara was thus washing his feet there, the one standing above then spoke these true words to his friend: || 12 ||
"O evil-minded one! What is this that you, fixed in sin, are doing? Why are you washing your face, feet, and hands in the Goddess’s pool? (13)
Since the Goddess is constantly bathed by me with this water, you have no fear of impurity or sin while pouring water upon her.
That which is called water smeared with impurity is untouchable even by men; tell me truly, how could that sin be touched by the gods? (15)
"Come out quickly from this pit and drink outside! If you are such a sinful fool, O wicked one, why do you wander among sacred fords? (16)
Bhīma said: "O cruel one, O lowest of Rākṣasas, why do you speak such harsh words? For water is indeed intended solely for the enjoyment of living beings. (17)
"The wise sages have also stated that bathing should be performed at sacred fords; they define bathing as the washing of one's limbs. Why, then, do you revile me? (18)
If drinking and likewise the washing of the limbs are not performed, then for what purpose are the acts of public welfare (pūrta-dharma) performed by those who are virtuous? (19)

Suhṛdaya said: It is true, there is no doubt about this, that one should bathe in the foremost of sacred fords; however, having entered among mobile beings, one remains outside among immobile ones. (20)
Even when entering into stagnant waters, that is not prescribed as a ritual bath, provided that the water has not been collected by devotees for the purpose of bathing the deity.
And where a lake is prescribed at a distance of more than a hundred cubits, this same sequence applies even when lying down: having washed one's feet outside [the dwelling], || 22 ||
Therefore, the ritual bath must be performed; otherwise, a fault is said to occur. Have you not heard the verse proclaimed by the Lotus-born One in the past? (23)
Those who discharge impurity, urine, feces, phlegm, spittle, tears, and even mouthfuls of water [into sacred waters] are equal to killers of Brahmins.
Therefore, depart quickly if you are thus one whose senses are unsubdued; for what purpose, O wicked-conducted fool, do you wander among sacred fords? (25)
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained, and whose every action is free from agitation, indeed obtains the fruit of the sacred ford.
Bhīma said: Whether it be unrighteousness or righteousness, I am simply unable to depart; hunger and thirst can never be restrained by me. (27)
Suhṛdaya said: "Tell me, why do you commit sin for the sake of your life? Have you not heard the verse that was uttered by Śibi? (28)
A man may live for even a single moment by means of pure action; he should not live even for an eon by means of an action that opposes both worlds.
Bhīma said: "Because of your crow-like screeching, my ears have become deaf. I shall certainly drink the water here; wail as much as you wish or wither away. (30)
Suhṛdaya said: "I am born into a lineage of Kṣatriyas who protect righteousness; therefore, I will never allow you to commit a sin."
Therefore, O wretched one, emerge quickly from this sacrificial pit!
"Otherwise, I shall quickly crush your head with pieces of brick! Having said this, he took a brick and hurled it at his head.
And Bhīma, having deceived her, leaped up and went outside; then both of them, possessing formidable prowess, began to revile one another.
Those two, who had reached the further shore of battle, both broad-chested and long-armed, and both skilled in hand-to-hand combat, fought with their arms as if they were two long hanging trunks.
They struck each other with fists, blows from the heels, and knees; then, after a moment, the Kuru prince was overcome by the Pāṇḍava.
Being thus diminished, Bhīma exerted himself again and again; yet he continued to diminish, O dear one, while Barbarīka grew even stronger.
Then, as if by sheer force, Barbarīka uprooted Bhīma and crushed him; enraged, he did so in such a way that it was truly marvelous.
Having thus taken up the one who was unconscious and quivering again and again, he set out to cast him into the great waters there for the sake of the ocean.
The Pāṇḍavas did not see this, as their vision was constrained by the Goddess.
When that hero of wondrous prowess had thus seized the chief of the Kuru warriors, it was a marvel to the gods in heaven as they beheld him from the expanse of the sky along with their goddesses.
Then, having observed Barbarīka who had gone to the shore of the ocean, the Blessed Lord Rudra, stationed in the sky, spoke.
O tiger among Rākṣasas, O mighty Barbarīka! Release this Bhīma, the best of the Bharatas and your own grandfather.
For he, while wandering on a pilgrimage together with his brothers and Kṛṣṇā, arrived at this very sacred ford (tīrtha) in order to bathe. || 44 ||
Therefore, the delighter of the Kurus deserves honor in every way; whether he be sinless or sinful, the grandfather is indeed worthy of worship.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of Rudra, he suddenly released him and fell at his feet, crying out, "Alas! Woe! Alas! What misery! (46)
"Forgive me, forgive me! he said again and again, striking his own head and weeping repeatedly. (47)
To him who was thus lamenting and fainting again and again, Bhīmasena embraced him, smelled the crown of his head, and spoke these words.
"We do not know you at all, nor do you know us from the time of our birth; yet, O son, your residence here has been heard of by Bhaimi and Kṛṣṇa. (49)
But for us, who are bewildered by various sufferings, everything has been forgotten; for it is evident that the memory of those in pain is utterly lost. (50)
Therefore, this suffering of ours has been ordained for all time; do not grieve, my son, for there is not even an atom of fault in you.
For every one who stands upon a wrong path is to be punished by a Kṣatriya; even his own self must be punished by the virtuous if it has set out upon an evil path.
What more need be said of my father, mother, friends, brothers, sons, and the rest? This joy of mine is exceedingly great; I am blessed, as are my ancestors. (53)
But since you have such a grandson—one who knows the Dharma and protects the Dharma—you are worthy of boons and likewise worthy of praise among these virtuous ones.
Therefore, having abandoned this grief, you ought to become composed.

Barbarīka said: "O dear father of fathers, you ought not to look upon me here, nor even to touch me, for I am a sinner, more contemptible than even a slayer of a Brahmin and unworthy of praise, O Lord. (56)
The wise declare that there is atonement for all sins; however, for one who is devoid of devotion toward his parents, no atonement whatsoever exists.
Therefore, with that very body by which I have caused distress to my father’s father, I shall cast it off at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
May I not be a sinner in other births as well; no one is worthy to turn me away from this resolve. (59)
"Since he who prevents atonement would be deprived of a portion [of merit]," having spoken thus, the powerful one leaped up and went to the ocean.
The ocean also trembled, [thinking], "How shall I slay him? Then, the fourteen goddesses of the Siddhāmbikā were there.
Having embraced and established her there, they sang together with Rudra: "O Lord of Heroes, there is no stain for a sin committed unknowingly."
This statement is declared in the scriptures; you ought not to act otherwise. And look, O sir, at this grandfather of yours clinging to your back! (63)
O hero, if you now abandon your own body while crying out "son! son! after me as I am on the verge of death, [then what will become of you]? (64)
Then Bhīma will also abandon that great sin of yours; knowing this, O high-minded one, preserve your own body.
But if you wish to abandon it, listen to these words regarding that as well: in a very short time, from Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī—
The falling of your body has been foretold; wait for that if you so desire, for, my child, the falling of the body at the hand of Viṣṇu is superior.
"Therefore, wait for that time with what we have requested. Having been addressed thus, Barbarīka also returned, dejected in mind.
He spoke these words of reproach to Rudra, the Goddesses, and Cāmuṇḍā: "O Goddess, you yourself know that [the world] is protected by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow."
Why was that disregarded by you for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas’ acquisition of land? And yet, this Vṛkodara was protected by you when he approached you. (70)

The Goddess said: "And I shall protect my devotee Kṛṣṇa from death; and because this great battle was fought by him in the service of Caṇḍikā, he shall become known by the name Caṇḍila and be worshipped by the entire world. (71)
Having spoken thus, all the gods and goddesses vanished from sight; Bhīma also took him and told everything to the Pāṇḍavas.
Filled with wonder, the Pāṇḍavas honored him again and again, and unweariedly performed their ritual bath at the sacred ford according to the prescribed injunctions.
Bhīma also installed a highly resplendent Liṅga where he had been liberated by Rudra; it is renowned as Bhīmeśvara. || 74 ||
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who worships Bhīmeśa at night is liberated from the sins of birth.
Just as these seven principal Liṅgas here, when well-worshipped, yield great fruits, even so this Bhīmeśvara Liṅga is highly venerable and removes all sins.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Bhīmeśvara," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book, within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.
Sūta said: Having stayed for seven nights at this sacred ford together with his brothers, the highly resplendent Yudhiṣṭhira prepared for his departure.

Having bathed at dawn in the clear light and having worshipped the goddesses and the liṅgas, he performed circumambulation of the sacred field and recited the hymn to the goddess; this is that which was always proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa as the prayer to be chanted during times of departure.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Goddess, worthy of worship, of great power, beloved sister of Kṛṣṇa, having bowed to you, I seek refuge in you through my mind, speech, body, and actions. (3)
O Ekānaṃśā, O Great Goddess, who bestows fearlessness upon Saṃkarṣaṇa and possesses a luster equal to the complexion of Kṛṣṇa; O Auspicious One, protect me like a son. 4.
"By you, in your unmanifest form, this entire universe is pervaded; realizing this, I have come to you for refuge—protect me, O Auspicious One! (5)
O auspicious lady, in all undertakings, I have offered my very self along with my followers to you; knowing this, please show me compassion.
Sūta said: To the king who was speaking thus with his hands joined in reverence upon his head, the son of Vāyu then laughed and spoke these words with derision.
O King, those who say of you, "This Yudhiṣṭhira is omniscient," speak in vain, for you do not know even an atom.
For who else among the foremost of the wise, the best of all those learned in the scriptures, would seek refuge with women, as you do with your straightforward intellect? (9)
For you alone know this, as it is proclaimed in all the scriptures: "This primordial nature (prakṛti) is inert and deluded, by which the world is utterly bewildered. (10)
O lord of men, the wise declare that Puruṣa is conscious and Prakṛti is unconscious; moreover, Prakṛti is dear to Puruṣa. (11)
O Yudhiṣṭhira of vain intellect, having yourself become that Puruṣa, you bow down to Prakṛti and call her "us"—at this, great laughter arises within me. 12.
One should never mount a vehicle while wearing sandals; for he who does so becomes as foolish as one who is devoted to the Goddess [yet acts thus]. 13.
O Pārtha, if your speech remains unrestrained like that of a bard, then for what reason do you not praise Mahādeva, the destroyer of Tripura?
Or, O high-minded one, having considered Maheśāna to be unperceivable, for what reason then do you not praise Puruṣottama, the scion of the Daśārhas? 15.
By whose grace we obtained Drupada’s daughter, as well as the kingdom at Indraprastha, and by whom the Rājasūya sacrifice was performed by you. (16)
