And you shall grant a place of residence in the worlds for the goddesses who are devoted to you; furthermore, those pustules which arise from wind, bile, and phlegm in children, you shall pacify with ease through worship.
And having climbed this peak, watch how the battle shall unfold.
When Vāsudeva said, "The Kauravas are running after us; let us go toward them," the goddesses then entered the sky.

Barbarīka’s head, having reached that mountain peak, underwent the funeral rites for the body on the ground, but not for the head. Then a great battle took place between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
Those such as Droṇa and Bhūriśravas who were slain within eighteen days, and when the cruel Duryodhana was killed at the end of the eighteen days; || 81 ||
In the midst of his kinsmen, Yudhiṣṭhira addressed Govinda: "O Supreme Person, we have been delivered from this battle. (82)
"O Hari, salutations to you, our very protector, O Puruṣottama! Hearing this, Bhīma spoke these words to him with indignation: || 83 ||
O King, why do you speak like a fool, rejecting me and calling that Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇa by whom the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were destroyed? 84.
"O Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira, having disregarded Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Phālguna, Sātyaki, and me, you speak thus; fie on you, O Sūta! (85)
Arjuna said: "Do not say so, do not say so, O Bhīma! You do not know Janārdana. Neither by me, nor by you, O Pārtha, nor by anyone else were the enemies slain. (86)
For in battle, I always see a man standing at the forefront, slaying his enemies there; I do not know who he might be.
Bhīma said: "O Pārtha, you are surely deluded; there is no other man here who is the slayer. If, however, it is your grandson who stands high [in prowess], then tell me, who indeed is he?"
Then, having approached, Bhīma asked Barbarīka: "Tell me, by whom have these enemies, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, been slain? (89)
Barbarīka said: "I saw one man fighting with his enemies; he had five faces on the left side and a single face on the right. (90)
On the left side, he has ten arms holding the trident and other weapons; on the right, he has four arms holding the discus and other weapons.
On the left he wears matted locks, and on the right a collection of crowns; on the left he bears ashes, and on the right he is smeared with sandalwood paste.
On the left he bore the moon, and on the right was the luster of the Kaustubha gem; from the sight of him, even I experienced great fear.
"Such a man as I have seen has never been seen before, nor any other who could slay them. When this was said, a shower of flowers of great splendor fell from the sky. 94.
The divine musical instruments resounded, and they indeed cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! The Pāṇḍavas were filled with wonder and bowed down to Puruṣottama.
Bhīma became embarrassed and heaved sighs; then his lord Keśava took him by the hand firmly.
Having said, "Come, O tiger among the Kurus," he remembered the son of Kaśyapa; then, having mounted Garuḍa, who appeared the very moment he was remembered, [he departed]. || 97 ||
Accompanied by Bhīma, he traveled through the sky toward the southern direction; then, having crossed the ocean, he reached the great mountain Suvela. 98.
Having seen a lake near Laṅkā, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words: "O tiger among the Kurus, behold this lake extending for twelve yojanas. (99)
"If you are a hero, then quickly bring some mud from its bottom. Thus addressed, the powerful one swiftly descended from Garuḍa into that water.
Traveling for a yojana with the speed of the wind, he saw no end below; then Bhima, having emerged with his strength broken, spoke.
"This is a very great and bottomless lake; having been swallowed by some of great strength, I have somehow emerged. (102)
Thus addressed, the radiant Kṛṣṇa laughed and tossed up the great lake with his thumb; it became half of that half.
Seeing that, he was struck with wonder and said: "O Kṛṣṇa, tell me, what is this? (104)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Formerly there was a night-stalker known as Kumbhakarṇa; when he was struck by Rāma’s arrow, the head of that evil-minded one was severed.
O Vṛkodara, this piece of his skull, twelve yojanas in length, was thrown down soft yet pulverized.
And those gods by whom you were held back are known as the Sarogeyas; they have been crushed by the millions by the rocks of Trikūṭa.
For these enemies of the world have been slain through strategic means. Let us go to the Pāṇḍavas, O Bhīma, for the son of Droṇa is indeed pressing hard.
Then Bhīma, having prostrated with the full devotion of his mind, speech, and body, said: "O Keśava, forgive all the evil deeds I have committed since birth."
"O Supreme Person, O Lord, be gracious to me, a fool. Then Hari, accompanied by Bhīma, said, "It is forgiven."
Returning once more to the field of battle, he spoke these words to Barbarīka: "O friend, wandering thus constantly throughout all the worlds," (111)
Worshipped by all the worlds, grant them the boons they have chosen; and this secret field, the most excellent among all fields, must not be abandoned.
"O resident of Dehisthalī, likewise forgive whatever misdeed I have committed. Having been addressed thus, the son of Bhīma bowed to them and departed at his own pleasure with joy. (113)

Vāsudeva, too, caused all the funeral rites to be performed. Thus, O Brāhmaṇas, the origin of Barbarīka has been described to you; now I shall proclaim his hymn of praise, by which the King of Yakṣas is pleased.

Victory, victory! O Yakṣa King named Sūryavarcas, surrounded by eighty-four crores; victory, you who are engaged in removing the burden of the earth, born from the womb of a Nairṛta through a mild curse; victory, royal swan in the lotus-belly of Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭa; victory, increaser of Ghaṭotkaca’s joy, named Barbarīka; victory, you who attained incomparable valor through the propitiation of the Goddess at Śrīguptakṣetra as instructed by Kṛṣṇa; victory, giver of victory and success; victory, Lord of ninety crores of those who devour the enemies of Piṅgalā and Repalendra; forest-fire to the flesh-eaters; victory, captor of the Naga maidens in the space between the earth and the netherworld; victory, crusher of Bhīma’s pride; victory, you who were active for a mere moment in the slaughter of the entire Kaurava army; victory, you who obtained the power to grant all boons through the favor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; victory, victory! You who are saluted by the Kali age, obeisance, obeisance to you! Protect us, protect us! Thus [he prayed]. 115.

O best of the twice-born, he who worships the Friend of the Heart (Suhṛdaya) on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in Śrāvaṇa, on the new moon day in Kārttika, and on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in Vaiśākha, with a hundred lamps and fried cakes—He is pleased with him.
Then the Brahmins and Nārada, having propitiated Maheśvara, installed Śaṅkara in the meritorious Mahīnagaraka.
And for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, there is the supreme Liṅga Kedāra, which destroys great sins, located in the northern part of Atrīśa.
Having bathed in this pool and performed the ancestral rites (śrāddha) according to the prescribed rules, a man should pay homage to Atrīśa and behold Kedāra.
He shall never again drink his mother’s milk and shall become a partaker of liberation; then Rudra, the blue-throated one, [spoke] to the high-souled Nārada.
Having granted the boon, he himself remained in the auspicious Mahīnagaraka; a man who bathes at Koṭitīrtha beholds Nīlakaṇṭha.
Having paid homage to Jayāditya, one shall attain the world of Rudra; the best of men, having bathed in the well, worship Jayāditya.
By the grace of Jayāditya, there shall be no destruction of their lineage; in their family there shall be neither disease, nor poverty, nor any blemish.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of wealth and grain, they enjoy many pleasures here and dwell in the world of the Sun.

Thus, O Brahmins, I have described this secret sacred field (guptakṣetra) in brief. Formerly, O twice-born ones, the extent of this field was declared by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) to be seven krośas, and it bestows the fulfillment of all desires and aims. 125.
Thus has been described to you the meritorious origin of the Mahīsāgara; by hearing it and by reciting it, one is liberated from all sins. 126.
The wise man who causes this supreme and most magnificent majesty to be heard, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Rudra. || 127 ||
If one causes the entire majesty of Guptakṣetra to be heard, one attains all sovereign powers and destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Whoever hears or causes others to hear the greatness of Koṭitīrtha and Mahīnagaraka becomes fit for union with Brahman.
Having bathed at Koṭitīrtha and performed the Śrāddha ceremony with diligence, one should give gifts according to one's ability; listen now to me regarding the fruit thereof.
Whatever merit is found in gifts given at all the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist in heaven, the netherworld, and the mortal realm—that fruit is obtained by men [here]. (131)
Whatever merit is obtained by performing sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha with the distribution of prescribed fees, and by the performance of all vows and austerities; || 132 ||
O Brahmins, that merit is obtained at Koṭitīrtha; of this there is no doubt. || 133 ||

This is indeed a purifier, always bestowing merit, conferring glory, removing sin, and supreme among the supreme; the person who hears this with devotion shall partake in merit and, upon the exhaustion of [their] karma, attain the same world as Rudra. || 134 ||

This [account] is auspicious, glorious, certain, and highly meritorious; it bestows heaven and liberation and removes the sins of men. A man who, being self-restrained and pure, hears this constantly, pierces through the sun and proceeds to the abode of Viṣṇu. (135)

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Conclusion of the Greatness of Guptakṣetra," in the Kaumārikā Section of the first Māheśvara Book within the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the first half of the glorious *Aruṇācala-māhātmya*. Victorious is the Yogin of Aruṇagiri, the lamp for all: he who bears the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) on his forehead, who has applied a tilaka of musk upon his brow, who wears a shimmering garland, whose loins are clothed in a glistening loincloth (*kaupīna*), who bears the king of serpents—difficult to overcome—upon his head, and who wears a digit of the moon. *Śrīmad-arūṇācala-māhātmya-pūrvārdhaḥ prārabhyate* (The first half of the glorious *Aruṇācala-māhātmya* is commenced). *Śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ* (Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa). *atha śrīmadaruṇācalamāhātmyapūrvārdhaḥ prārabhyate* (Now the first half of the glorious *Aruṇācala-māhātmya* is commenced). *lalāṭe traipuṃḍrī niṭilakṛtakastūritilakaḥ sphuranmālādhāraḥ Vyāsa said: Then the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest spoke to Sūta: "We are desirous of hearing from you the majesty of Aruṇācala."
Being thus addressed, "Tell us its greatness," Sūta spoke to those sages. Śrī Sūta said: "In former times, Sanaka questioned the Four-faced One (Brahmā) regarding this very matter."
Listen attentively; I shall now tell you that which, when heard with devotion, destroys the sins of men.
Formerly, Sanaka, standing with palms joined in reverence and bowing down, questioned Brahmā, the lotus-seated one, who was situated in Satyaloka.
Sanaka said: O Support of the Worlds, Lord of Gods, known through the Vedas, Four-faced One! By your grace, all-encompassing knowledge has come to me.
When the mirror of my mind has been cleansed by the power of devotion to you, all knowledge is reflected therein all at once through a single instruction.
Through the grace of your glances, O Teacher of the World, I have attained the untroubled knowledge of Śiva, which is the essential meaning of the Vedas and the Vedāngas.
O storehouse of compassion, O leader of the gods, there are Śaiva liṅgas on earth—divine, human, attained by siddhas, and elemental.
O ocean of compassion, tell me that which, by the mere remembrance of its name, destroys all sins and eternally grants the state of being identical in form to Śiva. (11)
May that imperishable Śiva-light, which is the support of the beginningless world and by seeing which one becomes fulfilled, be taught to me. (12)
Having heard these words of his, which were full of devotion and curiosity, the Blessed One, that treasure of asceticism, was pleased.
And the four-faced one, seated upon his lotus throne, meditated upon Śambhu for a very long time, his mind submerged in the ocean of internal bliss.
When he previously beheld Śiva, who consists of a pillar of light and has transcended all supports, he did not recognize anything at all.
Then, the Lord, in order to carry out the command received from Śiva, withdrew his heart from yoga and remembered his son Ānata.
With his body marked by horripilation born from the sight of Śiva, and his eyes filled with tears of bliss, he spoke with a faltering voice: || 17 ||
Brahmā said: Therefore, O son, having been reminded by you of my ancient [state], I meditated upon the yoga of Śiva and, out of reverence for you, remembered it once again.
Supreme devotion to Śiva has arisen within you through your many austerities; by that, my heart has been turned away as if in an instant. (19)
They purify the entire world through their unagitated conduct—those whose perpetual devotion to Sadāśiva increases at all times. (20)
Conversation, co-residence, play, and even mingling with devotees of Śiva, as well as seeing and remembering them, destroy all evil. (21)
Listen to this wonderful account of how, in ancient times, the splendor known as Aruṇādri manifested itself, filled with sincere compassion for Śiva.
Both Nārāyaṇa and I were born from Sadāśiva, who arose as superior to the universe and extended his resolve, thinking, "May I become many. (23)
Arising by their own inherent nature and disputing with one another, they never grew weary while fighting, for they were possessed of ego.
Then, beholding our mutually terrifying enthusiasm for battle, the Lord, the embodiment of compassion, reflected thus: || 25 ||
For what reason does this world-destroying battle arise between these two, who have fallen into dispute, each claiming, "I created it; I shall protect it"? (26)
At this moment, I myself must clearly observe these two who are utterly bewildered; if I do not restrain their battle, then there will be the destruction of the world.
"In the Vedas, my greatness is heard of as being superior to the universe; yet these two fools, their memory dissolved by anger, do not know it. (28)
Every living being considers itself to be exceedingly superior; that evil-minded person who does not recognize the superiority of others falls downward. (29)
If I were to set a limit for myself anywhere in the world, then, through the knowledge of that form, that Self would also come to me.
Having thus resolved within his own mind, Sadāśiva himself raised a pillar of fire between the two of us as we were fighting.
Having transcended all worlds, blazing like a fire on every side.
Then, due to its beginninglessness and endlessness, they both remained afflicted by their vision; beholding that blazing pillar of light, their resolve became weakened.
An incorporeal voice also arose before us both: "O children of deluded minds, for what purpose do you engage in this battle? (34)
Śiva alone will discern the disparity in the strength of you two; this form of Śambhu stands here, consisting of a pillar of splendor.
"If you two, being superior in strength, were to look at the beginning and the end [of this contest],"—having heard these words, they then desisted from the wrestling match.
I and Viṣṇu, possessing the power of movement, set out to search for it; [we beheld] the form of Śambhu consisting of a pillar of fire, devoid of beginning or end.
We two have resolved to look at it from beginning to end, just as two children desire to seize the reflection of the moon in the sky.
In that very manner, we both exerted ourselves to determine the extent of that splendor; then Viṣṇu, with great enthusiasm, became a boar of immense body.
And because he was searching for its root, he tore open the earth's womb; and I, having attained the state of a swan, flew up with great speed.
Desiring to see the upper portion of that head, I ascended into the sky; meanwhile, Mādhava dug down deeper and deeper until he had excavated the entire earth. (41)
Even after searching for many tens of millions of years, he beheld a column of fire appearing as if it were emerging from below.
Not seeing the beginning nor the end, he was distressed and overwhelmed; his fangs and strength were shattered, and the joints of his body began to fall apart.
Exhausted and overcome by thirst, Hari was unable to proceed; he was incapable of maintaining his incomparable form as a boar.
Even while resting, the Lord of Ramā became despondent; the one of immeasurable soul, his body exhausted, began to reflect.
"My glory having faded and weary from my ritual acts, I take refuge in Śiva, the protector; fie upon this great delusion of mine born of egoism! (48)
"By which I did not recognize myself as my own lord; for this [is the essence] of all the Vedas, of the gods, and even of the worlds. (47)
Śiva is the manifest root; how could he be the root of this? From him alone—who is devoid of beginning and end—I have arisen.
That I have begun this search for Śiva, who has assumed the body of an animal, is by the grace of my father Śambhu, whose bond of compassion is sincere. (49)
Once again, such an insight was gained by me through the awakening of my own self: that Śambhu, the Great God himself, desires to protect me. (50)
Immediately, there arose in him a self-born knowledge free from egoism: "I am no longer able to perform worship for this Teacher of the World. (51)
"I offer myself and go for refuge to Śaṅkara"—thus Viṣṇu meditated upon Śiva, his mind dedicated through praise. (52)
Through the grace of the Lord of Beings, I was once again cast down to the earth; and I wandered through the sky for many years as well.
With rolling eyes and drooping wings, overcome by exhaustion, I saw the Fire-god standing right before me, blazing higher and higher.

Having beheld a pillar of splendor resembling a massive linga, a Shaiva radiance worshipped by the gods, certain Siddhas born from a portion of that splendor said: "This is the splendor of Shiva. (55)
"Alas! Even now he wishes to maintain his feigned innocence toward me, who am making an effort to behold the eternal and supreme pinnacle of Śambhu. (56)
Even though his body was on the verge of falling, his ego had not yet departed; with his wings shattered, he became exhausted and his eyes grew bewildered.
"In the presence of this boundless splendor, this delusion will prove futile. Thus, with his mind thus agitated, Janārdana assumed the form of a boar.
He was indeed turned away by Śiva, who possesses sincere compassion; for such as these, there arises a multitude of tens of millions of gods, headed by Brahmā. (59)
At that time, the Blessed Lord Śiva, having entered into meditation upon his own self, desired to see the further limit of that [universe] beyond the atoms of fire.
"If he bestows his intellect upon him, his egoism will perish"—such were the compassionate words of those Siddhas as they spoke.
Having heard this, my ego shattered, I reflected within myself: "Neither from the knowledge of the mass of Vedas, nor from the practice of penance and visiting sacred fords," (62)
The knowledge of Śiva arises for him only through His grace; even when his pair of wings has withered away, his body remains indeed unshakable.
My mind strives again to grasp at my own ego; fie on me, who am overcome by the impulse of "I" and ignorant of the strength of the Self! (64)
Constant salutations to the Siddhas whose minds are dedicated to Śiva, by whose penance—attained through association with them—their inner disposition has been purified. (65)
I recognize this auspicious one standing before me as the cause of my own self; it is through the power obtained by his grace that we are endowed with such splendor.
All the gods shall forever have their enemies pacified, for they do not know the ultimate truth of him through even the great scriptures.
I sought refuge in that very Śambhu, who is distinct from the universe; then, having addressed Viṣṇu, whose eyes are like lotuses, I spoke what was otherwise unspeakable.
Having regained his body, he has taken refuge with devotion in Śiva, the moon-crested Lord. Oh, what a marvel has come upon those endowed with valor! (69)
Having heard of the great and immense mutual battle between us two, who were born from Śambhu and have taken refuge in the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), [the gods approached].
That very Śaṃkara, whose nature is immeasurable, then stripped away all our egoism by manifesting his own majesty.
He who proceeds to worship this Lord Sadāśiva—who is honored by the gods and consists of a pillar of fire—shall indeed become a boat for the ocean of worldly existence.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Manifestation of the Liṅga," in the first half of the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya*, within the *Māheśvara-khaṇḍa* of the first section of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Sanaka. || 1 ||
Brahmā said: Then, reciting the Vedas with all my mouths, I praised Śiva, having performed a mental worship filled with devotion.
Salutation to the Great Śiva, the sole cause of all the worlds; salutation to Him by whom everything is illumined and who constantly sustains it. (2)
This light, which pervades the universe, shines forth continuously; yet those devoid of Your compassion do not behold it, just as those blind from birth do not see the sun. || 3 ||
This stainless Bhūliṅga is indeed visible through the eye of inner realization; whether situated within or without, it is experienced by your devotees.
O Lord of Gods, this very form of yours, which is blazing like a mirror, is that which the yogi perceives as an undifferentiated form within his own self.
Or rather, the power of Śaṅkara is real, subtler even than the subtle; for there is nothing other than me, since even he is dissolved within me.
Though minute, you are a vessel of compassion and shall surely attain greatness; there is no one superior to you, nor even to me, who am dependent upon you.
Since my mind has been offered to you, it does not desire separation from you; how then could my speech proceed with the glorification of your majesty?

With matted locks exceedingly copper-colored from the purity of bathing at sacred fords, and with rudrākṣa beads placed upon them, he was like a fire with its flames.
He was radiant with a broad forehead marked by the triple lines of ash, complete with a white sacred thread and adorned with garlands of rudrākṣa beads.
Wearing two red bark garments, his body emaciated by ascetic penance, he was chanting many Vedic mantras that bring great pleasure to Rudra.
He spoke as if having attained the very same noble form as Śambhu; he was a treasury of splendor, full of compassion, like the sun manifest before one's eyes.
Beholding that great-souled elder who had taken refuge at the feet of Śambhu, Gaurī, with her palms joined in reverence, began to prostrate herself before him.
Seeing the Mother of the Entire World with her palms joined in reverence, the sage, wondering "What is this? and restraining his astonishment, bowed down to her.
Welcome, O Gaurī, auspicious one, Mother of the World, treasury of compassion! Oh, you have come here under a pretext to provide protection to your devotees.
"Ah! I believe that we previously understood this venerable matter only partially; thus, as if maintaining a sense of separation, we have come together with the disciples and others. (10)
O Goddess, if this display of yours were not your own manifestation of māyā, then how indeed could the manifestation of the phenomenal world ever come to be? (11)
Let alone my describing the entirety of your illusory play; it is impossible to determine it even by your own means at any time.
"Please sit upon this pure seat made of kusha grass, which is purifying; accept the water for the feet and the respectful offering (arghya) given by me according to the prescribed rite. (13)
When Ambikā was seated upon the supreme seat of darbha grass brought by her disciples, the aged sage, full of devotion, paid her homage.
Having offered the entire worship endowed with a spirit of devotion, and being permitted by Gaurī, he himself sat upon his seat. (15)
With the quarters of the sky washed by the moonlight of his teeth, his entire body covered in horripilation, and with tears of joy and a faltering voice, he spoke: || 16 ||
Oh, how great is the majesty of Lord Śambhu, of immeasurable splendor! Out of affection for his devotees, he has commanded you to protect his true devotee.
Nothing else remains to be attained, nor does anything else exist for you; O Mother, the Lord has manifested this greatness of devotion to demonstrate it. (18)
The account of Mount Kailāsa, the penance performed on the banks of the Kaṃpā, and the command of Aruṇādri—all this has been understood by me.
"O highly fortunate one, you have come here to this hermitage of devotees yourself. O embodiment of compassion, out of affection, please instruct us in what ought to be done. (20)
Having heard these words of the great seer who knows all things, Ambikā spoke out of curiosity, praising that great sage.
"O you of great majesty, Śiva himself, the God of gods, has commanded that you alone shall be seen by ascetics in the midst of them. (22)
You have reached the further shore of the Śiva-proclaimed Āgamas as well as the Vedas; through your asceticism, you alone are esteemed by Śiva among the devotees of Śambhu.
"I abide here by the name Aruṇācala," Śiva said. "The majesty of this mountain must be heard from your own lips. (24)
I have arrived to perform penance in the vicinity of Aruṇācala; by the mere sight of you, the Lord himself becomes propitious.
Conversation with a devotee of Śiva, hearing the glorification of Śiva, and the worship of the Śivaliṅga—these are the fruits arising from assuming a body in this world. (26)
Therefore, this majesty of mine should be heard from your mouth; through your clear instruction, you have become my father by virtue of your knowledge. (27)
Having heard these words of hers, Gautama, a treasure-house of asceticism, meditated upon Giriśa while recounting the majesty of Aruṇācala.
Whatever you ask again as if it were unknown, I recognize that to be none other than the Śaiva Māyā of all sciences; you yourself are that.
Alternatively, the hearing of Śiva’s majesty through the mouth of his devotee, as well as their instruction in the Śaiva path, is the cause of your satisfaction.

Just as the recitation of the Vedas brings the fruit of repetition for those who have studied them, so too does the chanting of the names of Śiva bring such fruit to those who speak and listen to it in this world.
Today all the austerities I have practiced have borne fruit, since I have heard and shall proclaim this majesty as instructed by Śambhu.
By the grace of Śiva and Aśiva, this wonderful majesty [has been revealed]. (33)
O lady of faultless limbs, listen to this great ancient narrative concerning the majesty of Aruṇācala, which is the cause for the destruction of all evils. (34)
Just as the Liṅga consisting of Aruṇādri manifested in ancient times, it is not possible to describe it again in its entirety even with ten million mouths. || 35 ||
The majesty of Aruṇācala was [revealed] by Brahmā, as well as by millions of other Brahmas, and formerly by Viṣṇu, Soma, Bhāskara, and Vahni.

He was worshipped by Indra and the other guardians of the directions for the sake of the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi), as well as by the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas.
He was worshipped by birds, divine sages, and perfected yogis, for the sake of removing various sins and for the attainment of various desired goals. (38)
This blessed Lord Śiva, the sovereign of the Mountain of Dawn (Aruṇādri), when propitiated, removes all sins upon being seen; when served, he grants all desires. (39)
Even when mentioned from afar by people as "Śoṇādri," it bestows liberation; its form, consisting of a pillar of splendor, is known as "Aruṇādri."
Meditating thus, yogis shall attain union with Śiva in their hearts; whatever has been given, offered in sacrifice, chanted, or whatever other austerity has been performed [becomes fruitful].
That which is obtained in the presence of Aruṇācala becomes inexhaustible. Formerly, Brahmā and Viṣṇu were born from a portion of Śiva’s splendor. || 42 ||
Possessed of ego, they fought with a mutual desire for victory; then, for the sake of quelling their pride, Sadāśiva, who is the object of meditation for yogis, [appeared]. (43)
Having attained a form consisting of the brilliance of fire, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, he stood in its midst, illuminating the ten directions.
Then, having assumed the forms of a swan and a boar, they went to the heavens and the netherworld respectively to see the beginning and the end of that pillar of fire.
Seeing them with dejected faces, the Blessed One, the treasury of compassion, appeared before them and granted the boon they desired.
Requested by him, the Lord of Gods attained the state of a stationary linga; renowned as Aruṇādri, he shines forth in perfect tranquility.
The fiery linga is constantly worshipped with the sounds of divine drums, the songs and dances of apsarases, and hundreds of showers of flowers.
In the past, the Lord was born from the navel of Viṣṇu as Brahmā, and he indeed created the worlds for the ninety-six Brahmās who have passed away.
Once, requested by Indra—who desired to create an obstacle to the asceticism of the yogins—Brahmā created a charming woman.
Beholding that lotus-eyed woman, who was perfect in the quality of loveliness, Brahmā became infatuated; his heart pierced by the arrows of Kandarpa, he lost his composure.
Seeing that Brahmā, whose seat is a lotus, desired to touch her, the excellent Apsaras bowed to him and, under the pretext of circumambulating him, wished to depart.
While she was devoutly performing circumambulation of this Prajāpati, his four faces emerged from all four directions in an instant.
That young woman, having become a female bird, soared into the sky; and then, seeing him approaching again in the form of a bird, she [did the same]. (54)
Seeking refuge, she took shelter in this Crimson Mountain (Śoṇādri), the crest-jewel whose foot has never been seen even by Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
"Protect me, O Lord of Aruṇādri, O refuge for those who have come for shelter!"—thus she cried out in distress, while at Aruṇācala, [the Lord heard her].
From that stationary liṅga, a certain hunter appeared, wielding a bow; having fixed an arrow upon his bow, he possessed the splendor of the sky filled with clouds.
Upon seeing Niṣāda standing before him, his delusion indeed vanished; thereupon, the Lotus-born One, with a gracious heart, became exceedingly humble.
Then he paid homage to the Lord of the Crimson Mountain, the refuge for all; "Salutations to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who brings about the destruction of all sins. (59)
To Śambhu, who takes the form of Aruṇācala, who is won over by devotion, and who brings about the cessation of karma for his ignorant devotees. (50)

"Or else, O Soul of the Universe, create another Brahmā for the creation of the worlds. Then, having heard those words of the distressed Creator, Śiva—
Becoming an embodiment of compassion, the one whose crest is the crescent moon said: "The time for you has already been granted by me; it cannot be turned back."
Who indeed, even while established as a sovereign, would not be afflicted by defects such as passion? Therefore, although situated at a distance, this [place] known as Aruṇācala [is the remedy].

Having performed the circumambulation in silence, O Soul of the Universe, be free from fever.

Having uttered these words, the lotus-born Brahmā then immersed himself in the lake and worshipped in due order the Great Lord Viśvanātha, the remover of sins, who was present there in the form of Aruṇācala.

Having worshipped this Lord of Aruṇagiri most clearly with ritual offerings, and having purified his mind through the yoga of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and other practices, this Creator, freed from all evil, then attained supreme sovereignty.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Brahmapuṣkara," in the first part (Pūrvārdha) of the Aruṇācala-māhātmya, within the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Gautama said: Formerly, in a kalpa, Nārāyaṇa was lying asleep upon the ocean of waters; reclining on his bed of Śeṣa, he did not wake at all for some time.
Seeing the universe filled with darkness, devoid of consciousness, and lacking all defining characteristics even at the end of a kalpa, the eternal sages were filled with despondency.
"Alas, how terrible is this form that utterly deludes the universe with darkness, by which even Viṣṇu has not yet awakened even at the end of the kalpa! (3)
Even the gods did not perceive that person who was full of light; how then could those who are subject to delusion attain peace from darkness?
Having thus resolved in their minds, they meditated upon the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, who dwells within the self, a stainless mass of splendor.
Then the blessed Maheśvara, a mass of splendor, being propitiated by the ever-wise who bowed down for the protection of the universe, became gracious.
Then, from Śambhu, who was composed of splendor, thirty-three crores of deities emerged from the rays of his sparks and stood firm.
Awakened by all the gods, the Lord of Ramā rose up; seeing that it was fully dawn, he reflected thus in his mind: || 8 ||
Due to the excess of darkness, I lay down at an improper time; however, for the sake of awakening, I personally beheld Sadāśiva, the supreme light.
He himself endeavors to perform the acts of creation for the world; what further task is there here for me, or for Brahmā himself? (10)

Bestowing grace upon him with side-long glances, she said, "Arise. Having risen, [he beheld] Śambhu, who was filled with compassion and bore the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.

Salutations to you, the Lord of the three worlds, who bears the qualities of the three forms; to you whose body is the three deities, who possesses the three eyes, and who is the enemy of Tripura. 16.
You alone are the Lord of the worlds; through your own portions consisting of the deities, you perform actions by your own will in the form of both cause and effect.
Having appointed me to protect the world and having utterly deluded me with your illusion, you neither wish to abandon your fault nor even your resolve.
What can I do? Having placed my burden upon you, whose form is the universe, I am indeed free from fault for sleeping at an improper time. You surely do not seek to find fault with me for this.
O Hara, O Śambhu, having observed the distress and remorse of Hari, the glorious Hara prescribed this expiation for Hari.
I abide upon the surface of the earth in the form of Aruṇācala; by the mere sight of him, the destruction of your darkness shall come to pass.

In the past, a boon was granted by me there to the former Viṣṇu. (23)
The rivers, the mountain torrents, and even the waters released from the clouds are seen to dissolve right there, by virtue of their being composed of internal light.
By granting sight to the blind, by providing the means for travel on foot to the lame, by the attainment of sons for those without sons, and by restoring the faculty of speech to the mute; || 25 ||

Having surveyed that mountain all around, Hari established the gods who dwell in the forests and the holy hermitages of the sages; and he stationed the Vedas, together with their auxiliary limbs and Upaniṣads, on every side in embodied form.
He created a hundred families of apsarases of divine form and commanded them: "Serve [him] with dances, songs, and instrumental music. (29)
Having bathed in this Brahma-lake, the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu performed a circumambulation of this highly honored Aruṇādri.

Bhāskara, a mass of splendor who was even oppressed by the asuras, worshipped Aruṇagirīśvara with devotion at the instruction of Brahmā.
Having immersed himself in the stainless, purifying holy ford created by Brahmā, he performed a circumambulation of this self-luminous Lord Aruṇādri.
Having achieved victory over all the Daityas without exception and performed the circumambulation of Mount Meru, he obtained supreme splendor that destroys the brilliance of others.
Overcome by the fire of Dakṣa’s curse, Soma, through the power of Śiva’s words, worshipped Aruṇācala and regained his original form once more. || 35 ||
Agni, though afflicted by the disease of consumption due to the curse of a Brahmin seer, became pure despite being impure through the service of Aruṇācala.
In ancient times, Śakra, having slain Vṛtra, Bala, Pāka, Namuci, Jṛmbha, Uddhṛta, and those Daityas who had obtained boons from Śiva and were lords of the world, [recovered his sovereignty].
Exhausted by his sins and having reached the end of the world, he propitiated Śambhu through austerity and was urged on by Śiva.
Having worshipped Aruṇādri, the lord of the gods became free from sin; and having performed the horse sacrifice, he gratified Śaṅkara.
Having attained the station of Indra, the glorious Śakra commanded a hundred apsaras, accompanied by the sounding of divine drums, to attend upon him.
Having commanded clouds of flowers, he constantly worships Śoṇādri with divine showers of blossoms and pays homage to him from heaven. || 41 ||
The remaining one, Śeṣa, having worshipped the Lord of Śoṇaśaila by the command of Śiva, attained the power of assuming any form at will while supporting the circle of the earth.
Other nāgas, gandharvas, siddhas, hosts of apsarases, and the guardians of the quarters, having worshipped him, obtained their desired boons. (43)
The mountain Aruṇa, the granter of all desired boons, was entreated from every side by all the gods who were prepared and desirous of conquering the Daityas and others.
With his form fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, the Sun, scorching with his brilliance, prepared to leap over Śoṇādri, the lord of the planets. || 45 ||
Furthermore, his chariot-steeds became exhausted and devoid of strength; he too was deprived of his splendor by the power of Goṇādrī.
He was unable to go to heaven because of the rays of the sun, which pervade all directions; however, by following the instruction of Brahmā, he propitiated Aruṇācala.
Out of affection for him, the All-pervading Lord granted him passage through the sky and auspicious horses; from that time forth, the Sun indeed [resided] at the mountain named Śoṇa.
He does not leap over it; rather, by circumambulating it clockwise, he causes the gods—who were previously deprived of limbs and ruined by Dakṣa’s sacrifice—to become complete again.
Having propitiated Aruṇācala, they obtained new limbs: Pūṣan his tooth, Śikhin his hand, and Bhaga his unimpaired eye.
She regained her sense of smell and her speech by serving Śoṇācala; and Bhārgava, whose eyes had failed, [regained his sight] from the tip of the blade of kuśa grass held in the hand of Viṣṇu.
Due to the obstruction of the stream of water for the gift of land offered by Bali, he went to Śoṇācala and performed an exceedingly difficult penance. || 52 ||
And having purified his soul while staying on the mountain named Bhāskara, he regained his eye through the service of the Lord of Aruṇācala, becoming the charioteer of the Sun.
A king named Pratardana became filled with devotion to capture a celestial maiden who was singing the praises of the Lord of the Crimson Mountain (Aruṇādri).

This region extending for two yojanas in every direction is known as Śivabhūmi; there is liberation for those who die there, and never indeed any dissolution [into rebirth]. (60)

At the Dāruhastapuṭa Tīrtha, he poured water for the thirsty one; at that Jānucakramaṇa [Tīrtha], the rogue longs for water.

Having himself taken hold of and beheld Aruṇādri, the great sage rejoiced like one who has regained his feet or recovered his very form.
Honored by the high-souled devotees of Śiva, whose eyes were wide with wonder, he, having regained his feet, departed as he had come.
The glorious Vālin, son of Śakra, was prepared to depart from the peak of Mount Śṛṅgavat in order to reach the summit of the Sunset Mountain.
He beheld the Aruṇa mountain, which is worshipped by the gods; having exerted himself to ascend upward, his strength exhausted, he fell to the earth. || 71 ||

The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the Godāvarī and the Sarasvatī, the Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, as well as the Śoṇa and that Śorṇanadī. || 98 ||
