There is a great sacred site named Saura, manifested in the northern direction; by bathing there, the pacification of all diseases occurs.
In the month of Vaiśākha, having bathed at Dinakṛt, the illustrious one attends upon Ātreya, joined by the Vālakhilyas and accompanied by the Vedas.
The purifying Āśvina Tīrtha is situated to the north-east of the Lord Brahmā; there the two physicians, the Dasras, were purified by immersing themselves in this place.
Having arrived here, bathed, and worshipped Śaṅkara, the two Aśvins reside in that auspicious place near the southern Śoṇa mountain. || 119 ||
The sacred ford known as Pāṇḍava bestows both worldly desires and liberation; for in ancient times, the Pāṇḍavas, who were lords of the earth, bathed there.
Then, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, Dhātrī arrived, bringing all kinds of medicinal herbs and fruits, and together with the gods, she worshipped Āruṇācala.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, the mighty Viśvedevas, having been dismissed, departed after worshipping the Lord of Śoṇaśaila to attend the sacrifice.
The Vaiśvadeva is a great sacred ford (tīrtha) situated to the north of Soma and Sūrya; by bathing there, one attains incomparable sovereignty over all beings.
A sacred bathing place (tīrtha) is visible all around in the beautiful eastern direction; here, in ancient times, Lakṣmī bathed and obtained the Supreme Person.
In ancient times, the holy river Skanda stood in the northern direction; having bathed here in the past, Skanda attained great strength.
In the western direction is renowned the supreme and auspicious Kumbhanadī; there Agastya, the pitcher-born, is eternally stationed.
The Gaṅgā is situated at the base, the Yamunā stays in the sky, and the river born from the Moon is at the summit; they all serve the Śoṇa mountain.
Furthermore, many sacred fords (tīrthas) have arisen on all sides; even Mārkaṇḍeya was unable to know their various divisions in the past.
Through many austerities, he gratified the Lord of Śoṇādri; and the lord of sages requested a boon from Him who was pleased. || 129 ||

Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Blessed Lord, Master of Aruṇādri, there are thousands of different types of holy fords (tīrthas) that are renowned and manifest; yet they are difficult to understand for those of limited intellect.
How could human beings on earth obtain the presence [of all these] in one place? For it would be impossible to attend to them individually. (131)
Having gone there, you whose splendor is hidden within, act in such a way that you are sought after by all the gods who are afraid even of touching the Crimson Mountain.
And I, having worshipped Śambhu on Mount Aruṇa through austerity, worshipped the subtle liṅga for the benefit of all the worlds.
Having conceived a divine celestial chariot fashioned by Viśvakarman and filled with various festivals, he further produced all eternal enjoyments.
The preeminent sages acquired various treatises on Dharma and, filled with devotion, performed all the rites dedicated to Śiva.
And having worshipped Śambhu, I employed seven beautiful maidens, born from the oblations offered into the fire, for the purpose of worship. (136)
In former times, kings who had destroyed hosts of enemies and regained their kingdoms worshipped the Lord of Śoṇaśaila individually with various enjoyments. || 137 ||

Worship this wondrous Lord of Aruṇādri, the bestower of boons, who is the mountain-form Śivaliṅga; he is the manifestation of the glory of experience, the remover of sins, pure, and whose name is beyond reach. 138.

Attain the supreme refuge of Aruṇagiri, who is worthy of protecting those who bow before him, who has dispelled all the world's impurities through his mere remembrance, and who is accessible to the fortunate through the accumulation of immeasurable merit. 139.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Various Tīrthas Situated at Aruṇācala," in the first part (Pūrvārdha) of the Aruṇācala-māhātmya, within the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Pārvatī said: How did the linga, which consists of fire, become approachable on earth? And how did it bring about the pacification for all living beings? (1)
Tell me how the sacred pilgrimage sites originated from the meritorious Aruṇa mountain, and how that mountain had all its limbs withdrawn.
Gautama said: In the Kṛta age it was a mountain consisting of fire; in Tretā, a mountain of jewels; in Dvāpara, a mountain of gold; and in the Kali age, a mountain of emeralds. (3)
When a fire-filled area extending for many yojanas had been established, the great sages performed circumambulations around its perimeter, and the fire was extinguished.
Requested by the gods for the sake of protecting the world, the glorious Lord of Aruṇādri became gradually pacified; thus Aruṇācala became exceedingly tranquil.
Then Gaurī said to the sage: "How did Aruṇācala become peaceful, or how did the gods pray to this Lord of Devas? (6)
Having heard these words of hers, Gautama spoke, praising her peerless devotion as she was one who knew the true meaning of reality.
Gautama said: In former times, being unable to approach the mountain in the form of Agni, the gods offered praise after worshipping him with the products of sacrifice.
O Blessed Lord of Aruṇādri, who brings welfare to all the worlds, though you are of the nature of fire, you are perfectly tranquil as light upon the surface of the earth.
"He who is copper-colored, ruddy, and even tawny, the most auspicious"—thus do all the Vedas praise you, O Śiva, whose form is the embodiment of well-being.
Salutations to the copper-colored, the ruddy one, to Śiva, the Supreme Self; to him whose true nature is known through the Vedas, to Soma, who is the embodiment of bliss. || 11 ||
O God, this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is your very form; it is seen as your form, like a treasury for the gods.
At the dissolution of the eon, it is appropriate for you to withdraw the means of water from the raining clouds and the many mountain torrents.
From you, the Supreme Self, the waters were produced; indeed, through the power of your manifold qualities, they carry out the creation of the universe. (14)
O Mahādeva, O Śoṇācala, O ocean of mercy, become cool; O Lord, become accessible to all living beings. (15)
Thus praised by all the gods who were bowed down in devotion, the Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees, immediately became cool and approachable.
The rivers and waterfalls began to flow again with abundant water; yet, even as the clouds rained, they did not take up much of that water.
Nevertheless, with a brilliance equal to hundreds of millions of rising young suns and world-ending fires, he became an object of approach for all living beings.
Having emitted the waters of the universe and the rivers through the outflow of his vital fluids, the God, having filled [all things], shines forth eternally.
By the power of their prayers, those various sacred fords (tīrthas) appeared all around for the sake of the guardians of the quarters, the gods, and the high-souled great sages. || 20 ||
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of his, Gaurī, filled with curiosity, began to inquire about the origin of all the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Pārvatī said: "O Blessed One, tell me in its entirety the origin of all the holy fords (tīrthas) that have arisen from Śoṇādri for the protection of the world."
Hearing these words of hers, and recalling everything he had previously heard from the Lord of the Mountains regarding the origin of all the holy fords (tīrthas), he began to explain them in full.
Gautama said: There is a great sacred ford named Aindra, which has arisen in the portion belonging to Indra; having bathed there in former times, Śakra dispelled the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Furthermore, the divine Brahmatīrtha has arisen in the south-eastern corner; having bathed here, Vahni cast off the sin arising from union with another's wife.
In the region of Yama, there exists a great sacred site named Yāmya; having bathed here, Yama cast off the fear arising from the Brahmāstra.
The great sacred ford Nairṛta shines in the southwestern direction; by bathing there, the sages attained victory over spirits and vetālas.
In the western quarter, the Vāruṇa Tīrtha shines forth; here in ancient times, Varuṇa obtained his own quiver after bathing.
For Vāyu, the sacred ford belonging to Vāyu shines forth here; having bathed there, Vāyu attained the majestic power of being the vital breath of the universe.
And in the northern direction here, there is that which is remembered as Somatīrtha; having bathed there in ancient times, Soma was liberated from the disease of consumption (yakṣma).
And here in the northeastern quarter, there is that which is remembered as Viṣṇutīrtha; having bathed there in ancient times, Viṣṇu was united with Śrī.
O Goddess, in ancient times Mārkaṇḍeya prayed to Śaṅkara: "O Sadāśiva, O Mahādeva, O God of gods, O Lord of the universe! (32)
O Blessed Śaṅkara, by what means might there be a gathering of many sacred fords (tīrthas) in one place? Please tell me out of compassion. (33)
Having heard these words of his, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, with a delighted mind, showed a means to the sage.
Maheśvara said: At all times during the hour of offerings, the collection of all sacred fords (tīrthas) arrives in my presence and serves me in a hidden form.
O great sage, you need not seek any other sacred site here; at the time of my offering, a multitude of sacred sites is seen.
Therefore, let this confluence of all sacred fords be constantly beheld by sages and all the gods, who are endowed with devotion, at the conclusion of the food offering. (37)
Thus, O Goddess, in former times the immeasurable Lord Śaṅkara instructed Mārkaṇḍeya on the sequence for visiting the sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas).
Gautama said: Indeed, all holy places (tīrthas) are present in the vicinity of Śiva; they are surely to be seen by men at all times during the hour of offerings.
Vows, sacred fords, austerities, the Vedas, sacrifices, restraints and the like, as well as yogic practices, all become visible through the sight of the Lord of Śoṇaśaila.

Having heard the words of the bull among sages, the daughter of the mountain king was delighted and said: "This network of sacred fords on earth that has been taught here by you is truly most wonderful."

O best among those who practice austerity, I have now attained my purpose through union with you; I have reached the entire network of sacred fords. Salutations to you, whose austerity is supreme! Even Śiva himself commanded me here to perform this very task.
How is it that this Lord Girīśa, though possessing a body of blazing great fire, remains here as the Supreme Lord in a tranquil form, to be worshipped on earth by the multitude of mortals? (43)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Various Tīrthas Situated at Aruṇācala," in the first part (Pūrvārdha) of the Aruṇācala-māhātmya, within the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Gautama said: Listen, O Goddess, to an ancient account: on Mount Kailāsa, I was commanded by Merudhanvī to go on a pilgrimage for the purpose of beholding the Liṅgas.
In Rudrakṣetra, in Kedāra, as well as in Badarikāśrama, in Kāśī, in holy regions, and likewise in the auspicious Śrīparvata.
At that time, I traveled to the holy cities, foremost among them Kāñcī, accompanied by sages, gods, merchants, and the most excellent hosts of yogis.
O highly fortunate lady, he beheld installed lingas and self-manifested (svayambhu) lingas here and there at the various sacred fords (tīrthas) in the presence of Śiva.
Accompanied by my disciples, I am wandering this earth, thus visiting all the sacred fords while remaining observant of my vows.
Performing austerities and sacrificial rites, traversing the earth, he remained ever united with the remembrance of Śiva and bowed down before the Śiva-liṅgas.
All the merits on earth have taken refuge in this region; here is the god Mahādeva, the hairless, three-eyed one.
I beheld the mountain known as Aruṇādri, which is a divine Liṅga; here, high-souled sages of firm vows have attained perfection.
Subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, the attendants of Śoṇādri were seen; I praised that great primordial Liṅga consisting of Aruṇādri.
Formerly, it was worshipped by the primordial Brahmā with his divine eye—that one who is copper-colored, ruddy, and tawny, and who is most auspicious.
Thus the Vedas constantly praise you, O Lord of Aruṇādri: "Salutations to the copper-hued, the beautiful Aruṇa, the auspicious Supreme Self. (11)
To Him whose nature is all the Vedas, who is eternal, whose form is immortal nectar, who is Time itself, who is moist with compassion, and who is an ocean of nectar to be drunk by the very sight—12.
O Lord of Gods, for you who are full of affection for your devotees, who are meritorious, and who are the destroyer of the cities, a vision of you bestows the fruit of all dharmas. 13.
Having already attained [the goal] on earth, you need not perform any further austerity anywhere; for you, this land of action has now been brought to a standstill.
Even the gods themselves pray for dwellings here under your protection; I have now obtained the fruit born from the accumulation of time. (15)
All the austerity performed by me has its fruit in the sight of you; such is your form, O Lord of Gods, which brings about such a wondrous manifestation.
He had never seen anywhere on earth a single linga made of stone that was as beautiful with its three corners perfectly joined by the sun, moon, and fire.
O Lord of Gods, your great body is seen in the form of the triple manifestation; it consists of the nature of the three powers and ordains the three periods of time.
That wonderful Liṅga of yours, whose body is a triangle and whose essence is the three Vedas, has been seen; you have assumed this expanded form for the sake of protecting the three worlds. || 19 ||
On a portion of the earth, there is seen that which is renowned as Śoṇādri; and for mortals who do not know it, merely by its sight— || 20 ||
The storehouse of feigned compassion abandons all enjoyments; a Linga devoid of worship is declared to be "void" (śūnya). || 21 ||
This [Liṅga], however, is always worshipped by the gods and bestows all boons; be gracious, O Śoṇācala Maheśvara, you who are filled with compassion! 22.
Save me, who am terrified of worldly existence and have sought refuge in you, O you who are kind to your devotees! This great and most wonderful form of yours is truly to be beheld.
"O ocean of mercy, O refuge of all, fulfill the purpose of me who has come to you for shelter"—thus was the Lord Śoṇācaleśvara praised by me. (24)
He revealed his supreme, divine form and said to me, "Come here; I am greatly pleased with your hymns and your supreme devotion. (25)
Right here, let your residence always be near me; and worship me constantly on earth with eternal enjoyments.
Perform penance and demonstrate here your greatness among all; [remember] you who formerly dwelt on the peak of Kailāsa, endowed with ascetic power.
I commanded that a portion of the earth at Śoṇādri be used to worship me; thus, my worship, honored by the Seven Sages, shines forth in heaven.
Likewise, engaged in perpetual worship, manifest yourself upon the surface of the earth; you are preeminent in austerity for the sake of the welfare of all living beings. (29)
On earth, worship me with reverence through the rites of worship prescribed in the Āgamas; for my divine great worship is indeed visible in heaven to the deities.
O King, you must cause [this shrine] to be manifested upon the surface of the earth; its greatness has already been described by me, just as I am Aruṇācala. || 31 ||
I am stationed upon the surface of the earth, and I am exceedingly pleased with you; for those who were previously rich in merit worshipped me. (32)
"Be superior to them on earth and manifest the worship of Śiva"—having been thus commanded, he who was devoted to Bhava bowed down to the Lord of Gods. (33)
I questioned the Lord of Aruṇācala, who was full of compassion, regarding this unattainable form of Maheśvara, whose nature is fire.
"How shall I worship him today with rites appropriate for the world of mortals? Or how may I fulfill this meaningful command? (35)
"O Illustrious One, who are approachable just as you are, please instruct me on the means. Thus was the glorious Lord Śoṇācaleśvara entreated.
The Lord, the soul of all and a treasury of compassion, favored me as I bowed before him; I, for my part, shall manifest the subtle lingas upon the surface of the earth.
"Perform my worship through the various rites prescribed in the scriptures; offer to me this subtle and wonderful Liṅga, which is endowed with five enclosures. (38)
"Worship the Lord known as Aruṇādri by means of the powers of austerity," having thus commanded the self-born, great, and pure [Brahmā], Mahādeva [departed]. (39)
Śiva revealed his form to me in the nature of a subtle liṅga; having beheld that pure, subtle liṅga which had risen up of its own accord, [he spoke]. (40)
Having attained my heart's desire while still possessed of all remaining obscurations, I again addressed the Lord Śambhu, who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge in him: ||| 41 ||
The forms described in the scriptures have become invisible; how then [can you see] your own forms, which are distinguished by various names? (42)
O Embodiment of Compassion, O Lord, O my Master, may you yourself know: who indeed would be your worshippers here, or what kind of temple would there be? (43)
How is the hymn of praise performed, how is the worship conducted, and who are the attendants here? How is the protection of the site to be ensured, and who are the guardians of oneself? || 44 ||
Or how does human worship increase for you eternally? Many gods have arrived; how can this be credible to men? (45)
"Be gracious, O Supreme Lord; command everything yourself. Thus entreated, the Lord himself, the Master Śoṇādrīśa, [spoke].
Then the Lord commanded Viśvakarman, who had arrived: "Create a divine city named Aruṇa, preeminent in its qualities. (47)
My divine temple, resplendent with clusters of great jewels, and the triple symphony (tauryatrika) along with all its ritual components—arrange all of that for me. 48.
The glorious Śiva, the Lord of Aruṇādri, whose form is compassion, spoke of the various names [of the deity], the sequence of worship, and the vow.
Listen to that from me as to who were created as attendants for the purpose of worship; listen, O Gautama, to my entire procedure for human worship. (50)
This great, incomparable linga, composed of splendor, which is seen here on earth for the welfare of all the worlds, [is that very one]. (51)
You should constantly worship the one known as Aruṇādrīśvara; on my northern side, Śakti, who is ever-rising, should be worshipped with joy.
Manifesting the majesty of his station, this king of the Aruṇa mountain, inseparable from his beloved, is known by the name Apītakucā.
Mahādeva, for the sake of the festival, is to be worshipped, surrounded by his consorts Bhoga and Suta; Śiva is the bestower of awakening upon the world of devotees, his hand granting fearlessness.
Holding a bow and an axe, with a perpetually serene countenance, Śambhu—the Lord of Umā and Skanda—is adorned with divine jewels.
Illuminating the worlds with her splendor and endowed with unimpeded glory, the beautiful Goddess Sundareśvarī is to be worshipped during the auspicious festival of Śakti.
Adorned with all ornaments and increasing the sentiment of erotic love, the youthful Gaṇapati, the delighter of prosperity, is to be worshipped in front. 57.
Adorning my presence with abundant and excellent foods and delicacies, she whose eyes were marked with red lines never left my side.
Let the supreme Śakti, whose purpose is the festival, be worshipped as she stands very near; let the glorious Mukharāṅghripati, an expert in the tāṇḍava dance, dance for her.
For the sake of the festival, Amṛteśvara should be worshipped before one's eyes, and the other highly fortunate Śakti, Bhūvināyakā, should also be fully honored.
At the gate are Nandin and Mahākāla, who shines like the sun before me; let worship also be prepared for all my devotees.
In the south, the Mothers should be worshipped together with Vighnaśāstṛ; in the southwest corner, Vināyakas who destroy obstacles should be fully worshipped.
Let Skanda, the wielder of the spear, be worshipped in the northeast corner; thereafter, the beautiful lingas are to be worshipped. (63)
Having fully worshipped my temple, which is the right-facing Dakṣiṇāmūrti, as well as the form marked by Viṣṇu in the west, endowed with the form of Agni; || 64 ||
In the north is the mark of the form of Brahmā; in the east is that which is joined with the deer-mark, endowed with all divine qualities and possessed of all powers. || 65 ||
Having worshipped the temple of the Lord of Apītakucā—which is endowed with all powers and surrounded by the wives of the guardians of the quarters—he approached his preceptor. (66)
For the sake of protecting the temple, [I invoke] the goddesses who are the mistresses of the divine manifestations.
Having fully worshipped Kṣetrapāla together with all his attendants, one should worship Aruṇagirīśvarī, who has come for the protection of her son. 68.
Kālī, various other deities who protect the ordinances, and diverse festivals of great splendor should be arranged every month. (69)
Create divine maidens devoted to the worship of Lord Śiva, skilled in the arts of dance and song, and endowed with beauty and good fortune.
Instruct your disciples—who are endowed with graceful charm, who grant desires, who are eternally pure, who are knowers of the Vedas, and who are resplendent with virtuous conduct. (71)
For the successful accomplishment of divine services, [he should employ] those who are fortunate, pure-minded, initiated, stainless, purified, and experts in the Śaiva Āgamas.

For the purpose of establishing the Śaiva practice during my worship at the beginning [of the rite], [I shall employ] those with mṛdaṅga drums, conch-blowers, lute-players, cymbalists, and flute-players.
Create goldsmiths who possess true knowledge and are proficient in the four branches of learning, as well as various Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are devoted to Śiva.
And four monasteries should be established for the residence of sages who dwell at the holy sites of the four directions, who are devotees of Śiva, and who are free from worldly desires. (75)
May the lords of sages dwelling among them protect my worship of Śiva; likewise, may the devotees of Śiva who wander for alms, as well as the Pāśupatas, protect it too. (76)
And let the others, even the disciplined Kāpālikas, always protect all those who are being born, those already born, and those yet to be born. (77)
This place of the mountain-dwellers must be protected, for its command is unimpeded; moreover, a great bakula tree, a divine plant, is seen here.
"Here let the devotees deliberate upon the performance of Śiva’s work; here my wealth is bestowed for the sake of attaining the Unseen Supreme. (79)
I shall hear the matter requested by my devotees, who stand before me, seeking that which grants inexhaustible fruit and must be protected by the servants of Śiva.
I shall accomplish everything that is agreeable to their minds; I shall forgive thousands of offenses, and they shall worship me.
Since this worship, though fashioned by humans, is declared in the scriptures, I shall accept all that image which is proclaimed in every sacred tradition.
"Having examined all the meanings of the scriptures as they are appropriate for the occasion, you should determine what action, when performed by my servants, would bring me pleasure. (83)
O Sage, having established the various modes of worship for the sake of protecting the world, a great worship should be performed with devotion on the full moon day.
Various sacrifices should be performed here by the thousands, as well as diverse acts of charity according to one's capacity, in his very presence. 85.
Those who give an unextinguished lamp in my presence attain this radiant form of mine; of this there is no doubt.
Those who offer me with devotion flowers born of water, flowers born of trees, or those produced from shrubs and creepers, shall become kings.
Standing before them in person, I shall conquer the enemies; for whichever king is preeminent in asceticism in whatever land, [I shall overcome him]. (88)
"Whatever beautiful thing is brought forth here by such-and-such prosperity, it grants me its origin; for even wicked-minded kings, having come into my presence, [attain this]. (89)
The devotees of Śiva will become exceedingly fulfilled; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these words issuing from the mouth of Śambhu, my impurities shaken off, I, bowing down, questioned the auspicious Lord of Śoṇagiri out of curiosity.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Majesty of Worshipping Aruṇeśvara," in the first part (Pūrvārdha) of the Aruṇācala-māhātmya, within the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Gautama said: O Blessed Lord, Sovereign of Aruṇādri, I desire to hear your names in detail, especially in this place worshipped by the gods.
Maheśvara said: O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, hear from me my principal names, which are difficult for those of little merit to obtain, yet always grant all desires upon this earth. (2)

Lord of the Crimson Mountain, Lord of the Red Mountain, Sovereign of the Gods, Beloved of the People; Protector of those who have sought refuge, Steadfast, and Increaser of the servants of Śiva. || 3 ||
The Lord of the Immortals, who bestows both female and male states, who fulfills the petitions of his devotees, and who liberates the wretched and the captive; || 4 ||
The Lord of the feet of Mukhara, the illustrious Mṛḍa, the Sovereign of musk, the witness who watches over his devotees, and the remover of the faults of his devotees. || 5 ||
Jñānasaṃbandhanātha, Śrīhalāhalasundaka, Āhavaiśvaryadātā, and Smartṛsarvāghanāśana; || 6 ||

The Lord of Dance, possessing the splendor of one who brandishes a sword while dancing with reversed steps; he who is fond of the Sāman chants, the destroyer of the Kali age, the embodiment of the Vedas, and the stainless one.
Jagannātha, Mahādeva, the three-eyed one, the destroyer of Tripura, the endurer of the offenses of his devotees, the Lord of Yogins, and the leader of enjoyments. || 8 ||

He is the child-form, the embodiment of forgiveness, the protector of dharma, and he whose banner bears the bull; he is Hara, the Lord of the Mountains, Bharga, and he who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
The ender of Smara, the enemy of Andhaka, the king of the Siddhas, the sky-clad one; he who loves the Āgamas, the Lord, marked with ashes and Rudrākṣa beads.
The Lord of Śrī, Śaṅkara, the Creator, the Sovereign of all sciences, the Sinless One; the Bearer of the Gaṅgā, the Destroyer of the sacrifice, the Immaculate One, adorned with serpents. || 11 ||
Aruṇa, Bahurūpa, Virūpākṣa, and Akṣarākṛti; he is without beginning, devoid of end, desirous of auspiciousness, and the self-effulgent Lord.

He is the embodiment of truth, consciousness, and bliss; the self of all, the sustainer of living beings, the one who makes even the union with women auspicious, the ordainer, and the one who has fashioned all that is beautiful.
The bestower of knowledge and the giver of liberation, he grants the desires of his devotees; he possesses wondrous majesty, is full of desire, is faultless, and is the granter of treasures.
Śūlin, Paśupati, Śambhu, Svayambhū, Giriśa, and Mṛḍa—these, O great sage, are my principal names here.
Recall other divine names mentioned in the Purāṇas; always circumambulate me and worship me with special devotion. (16)

"Since I am fond of circumambulation and have the form of the Crimson Mountain (Śoṇācala)," having been thus commanded by Mahādeva, O Daughter of the Mountain, I have made my dwelling here, worshipping Aruṇācala and never leaving this abode.
Gaurī said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, noble Gautama, lord of sages, tell me the greatness of the circumambulation of the Śoṇa mountain.
At what time, how, and by whom was circumambulation previously performed for the Lord of Śoṇādri, so that they attained the supreme desired state? || 19 ||
Brahmā said: Thus questioned, the sage Gautama spoke to the daughter of the mountain: "Listen, O Goddess, to the majesty as it was declared to me by Maheśvara."
Mahādeva said: "I am indeed Śoṇaśaila in person, manifest upon the surface of the earth."
All the gods, together with the sages, stand surrounding me on every side.
Whatever sins have been committed in other births, each and every one of them perishes at every step of the circumambulation.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and tens of thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices, as well as all sacred pilgrimage sites, are accomplished at every step for one who performs circumambulation.
For whom would success not lie ahead as they circumambulate the Moon-crested Lord—He who has abandoned all characteristics, who is devoid of activity, and whose birth is transcendent? (25)

The merit found in visiting all sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as the entire collection of dharma arising from all sacrifices and scriptural traditions, is truly obtained by performing the circumambulation of the Śoṇa mountain. 26.
By one step a mortal conquers the world of earth, by the second the intermediate space, and by the third the heavens, as he performs this circumambulation.
By the first [step], mental sin is destroyed; by the second, verbal sin; and by the third step, the bodily sin of men is extinguished. (28)
By one step, he shall wipe away all sins; by the second circumambulation, he obtains the full merit of all ascetic penance. (29)
There are thousands of leaf-huts belonging to great sages and perfected beings, as well as thousands of dwellings for the gods located here.
"O Siddha, I dwell here eternally before you, honored by the gods. Within me, a divine cave endowed with all enjoyments should be meditated upon. (31)
It is heard in the scriptures that my form consists of a pillar of fire, beginning with the color red; meditating upon this great liṅga of mine, one should perform circumambulation slowly.
Those who, meditating intensely upon this fiery Liṅga composed of the eight forms [of Śiva], perform circumambulation, shall utterly burn away their sins. (33)
Furthermore, for one who constantly performs circumambulation of the form of Śoṇācala, there is no rebirth; he certainly attains eternal immortality. (34)
The entire earth is purified by the touch of the dust of his feet—he who takes even a single step in circumambulating the Lord of Śoṇādri.
Bowing down to each direction, meditating, and praising with palms joined, he should perform the circumambulation slowly, keeping his hands unjoined with anyone else.
Just as a woman whose delivery is imminent should proceed without agitation, so too should one perform the circumambulation without hearing the sound of footsteps.
Having bathed, wearing pure attire, adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, and absorbed in the remembrance of Śiva, the wise man should take his steps slowly.
It was before the Manus as they moved forward, before the gods by the thousands, before the invisible Siddhas, and before others who had the form of wind. (39)
Reflecting upon the crowding of minds, the thronging of people, and the obstruction of the path, the wise devotee should advance slowly and step by step in a manner that is agreeable.
Alternatively, having proclaimed the names of Śiva with excellent songs and performing the dance of Śiva, he should circumambulate together with the devotees.
Or, listening to my majesty with single-minded devotion and respect, one should slowly perform circumambulation, overflowing with the essence of bliss. (42)
Filled with compassion and faith, one should wander everywhere, performing various kinds of gifts and meritorious services for those in need according to one's ability. (43)
In the Kṛta age, one should meditate on the Liṅga as consisting of fire; in Tretā, as a mountain of jewels; in Dvāpara, as golden; and in the Kali age, as an emerald mountain.
Alternatively, meditating upon a crystal form that is reddish and self-luminous, one is liberated from all sins and shall go to the city of Śiva. || 45 ||
Because it is beyond the reach of speech and mind, because it is itself immeasurable, and because it is fire, the supreme *liṅga* known as Acala cannot be attained.
Having meditated upon him and performed circumambulation, one should approach me directly; for the dust of his feet is the cause of freedom from old age and death for human beings. (47)
But he who assumes even a single form during the circumambulation of the Lord of the Crimson Mountain (Śoṇādrīśa) becomes an object of mutual longing for the mounts of the hosts of gods. 48.
While you perform the circumambulation of the Crimson Mountain (Aruṇādri) as your act of devotion, the celestial trees, such as the Kalpavṛkṣa and others, provide you with shade.
While the mortals on earth were performing the circumambulation of Aruṇādri, they were surrounded by thousands of gods, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and others.
Those hundreds of millions of celestial palaces, crowded with hosts, attend upon them as they perform circumambulations on the ground, [serving] by means of the dust from their feet.
The great path, which bestows the state of Śiva, has been seen as purified; by performing a circumambulation of the body, one becomes possessed of a celestial form in an instant.
Having attained a vajra-body, he cannot be assailed on the surface of the earth; even the gods, the siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis are eager for the power of traveling through the sky.
Invisible, they move about here and behold my presence; they observe my discipline and my devotion during the circumambulation.
Having seen it, filled with joy, she grants a boon to mortals; here in ancient times, the thirty-three gods performed a circumambulation.
In ancient times, all the planets, beginning with the Sun, having performed circumambulation, sat daily upon the path and each attained the status of a crore.
In every part of the entire world, all have attained lordship over the planets for that man who performs circumambulation on the earth on a Sunday. (57)
Having pierced through the solar orb and being liberated, he shall go to the city of Śiva; so it is for the man who performs the circumambulation of Aruṇādri on a Monday.
Having attained freedom from old age and death, he does not become unamiable on this earth, the man who performs the circumambulation of Aruṇādri on a Tuesday.
By performing the circumambulation of the Lord of the Crimson Mountain on a Wednesday, a man will certainly become a sovereign emperor, having attained complete freedom from all debt.
Having attained omniscience, he shall become a lord of speech; by performing worship on Thursday, a man becomes one who is saluted by all the gods.
By performing the circumambulation of Śoṇādri on a Friday, a man shall become a teacher of the world; indeed, by performing the circumambulation of Aruṇādri on a Friday, he attains this status.
Having attained great prosperity, a man who performs the circumambulation of the Lord of the Crimson Hill on a Sunday indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu.
Released from the afflictions of the planets, he shall become a conqueror of all; and likewise all the lunar mansions, together with their presiding deities, [shall be freed]. (64)
The merits of one who performs a circumambulation of me would swiftly depart; for me, the lunar days, the karaṇas, and the yogas here are of no account. (65)
The various auspicious moments (muhūrtas), planetary periods (horās), and gentle conjunctions that arise continuously grant their desired fruits to those who perform circumambulation of me.
For those who perform circumambulation of me, auspicious things arise constantly; the letter *pra* cuts away sin, and the letter *da* bestows what is desired. (67)
Through the syllable *kṣi*, karma is destroyed; the letter *ṇa* bestows liberation. [Those who are] weak, afflicted by emaciation, and overcome by mental and physical ailments—|| 68 ||
By performing a circumambulation of me, they are liberated from all evil deeds; for one who continuously performs the circumambulation of me with devotion using their foot. (69)
In an instant, O virtuous lady, I beheld the circumambulation of the three worlds, as well as the lords of the worlds, the lords of the directions, and those others who are the lords of causes.
Having performed circumambulation of me, they formerly became established in their kingdoms; and I too, accompanied by my attendants and joined by all the gods and sages, [remained there].
At the conjunction of the northern solstice, I perform my own circumambulation; my form is a fiery liṅga, renowned as Aruṇādri.
For the sake of the welfare of the three worlds, I shall perform circumambulation; having arrived here at the end of the supreme [age], Gaurī performs wonderful penance.
Having performed a circumambulation, that sinless woman of great asceticism will come to me again in the month of Kārtika, under the constellation named Kṛttikā.
Gaurī will perform circumambulation of me at dusk; that circumambulation is difficult for men of little merit to attain. (75)
Having beheld the Jyotirlinga and likewise offered prayers to the Goddess, that goddess named Apītakucā was attained by me in her company.
At the junction of the northern solstice, he will console all the gods, as well as the devas, gandharvas, yakṣas, siddhas, and even the rākṣasas.
There shall be a gathering of all those born of divine origin; at that time, those preeminent in asceticism who come to me and worship me [shall attain their goal]. (78)
They undergo atonement for the flood of sins committed throughout all their births; that day, occurring during the commencement of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), is difficult for men to attain.
Then, let human beings be fulfilled by worshipping my form, and let the rulers of the earth perform circumambulation of my divine [liṅga]. (80)
Standing before them, I myself shall personally defeat the enemies; for whatever king is more eminent in asceticism than the king of any given land, [I shall prevail].
He should have the foremost brahmins, learned in the Vedas, perform a circumambulation of me, constructing either a full mandala or half a mandala according to the rules of formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
"O Sage, standing ever before him, I myself shall ensure his stable kingdom and the total destruction of his enemies. (83)
One should never perform a circumambulation of me while mounted on a vehicle, knowing that my mind is intent on Dharma and that I am immersed in the conduct of Śiva. (84)
In former times, King Dharmaketu, having returned from the realm of Yama, desired to perform a circumambulation of me on horseback. (85)
In an instant, the horse became Gaṇanātha, worshipped by the gods; having released the lord of the earth, he attained the state of Śiva.
Beholding him again bearing the form of Gaṇanātha as his vehicle, he performed a circumambulation at his feet and himself became a leader of the Gaṇas.
From that time forward, Śakra and all the other gods, accompanied by Viṣṇu, perform circumambulation of me on foot alone.
A certain Siddha, having fallen from heaven due to the exhaustion of his ascetic merit at the appointed time, performed a circumambulation thereupon and regained his former status. (89)
O Lord of Gods, the blood shed from my foot as it stumbled during my circumambulation of the Creator is wiped away by the filaments of the mandāra flowers upon his crown.
On the great circumambulatory path, the footstep of men, though struck by fragments of stone, is sustained by the saffron from the breasts of Lakṣmī.
Having performed circumambulation of me, mortals always wander upon the peaks of the Jewel Mountain within the groves of wish-fulfilling trees.

Gaurī said: O you of noble vows, tell me the fruit for those engaged in ritual service, by which a person, having shown respect according to their ability, may indeed become successful in their purpose. (93)
The Sage said: O Goddess, listen; I shall tell you the fruit of ritual service (upacāra), which the Supreme Lord previously spoke to me out of compassion. (94)
Having fashioned webs of threads somewhere on this mountain, that spider, remembering his former births, enveloped me with its silken threads.
A certain elephant, overcome by thirst, released his ichor somewhere, tore off a forest sprout, and became a leader of the Gaṇas. || 96 ||
Worms rolling on my side, freed from all evil, all assume the appearance of perfected beings and go again to my world.
He who maintains even for a moment the flame of a lamp that is unextinguished, being himself self-luminous, attains a state of similarity with me. 98.
A certain Hārīta bird arrived at my side, having made its nest in a branch; like a firefly appearing as a lamp in the night, it has now attained liberation.
The cows, sprinkled by the streams arising from their remembrance of their calves, attained liberation at my side and took refuge in my world. (100)
A crow, greedy to seize an offering, was cleaning the area before me with the wind from its wing-beats; in an instant, it attained liberation.
The mouse, illuminating the interior of my cave by dragging along a multitude of jewels, dispelled the darkness and assumed my own form. (102)
Even the sages and the gods themselves pray to remain by my side to become trees providing shade, and not with the desire for rebirth.
For those who construct a gate-tower, a spire, a hall, a pavilion, or even a pond in front of me, the wealth of their desired goals shall be accomplished.
This Liṅga of mine, Agni-liṅga, which is forever unattainable by mortals, known as Anāsādyācaleśa, should be worshipped upon the surface of the earth. 105.
Nourishing the entire world, which is her own manifestation, through her glances, touch, and meditations, the Supreme Power known as Apītakucā is worthy of worship. 106.
The sole mother of all the worlds, who has attained eternal youth, she known by the name Apītakucā, is always to be served by those who desire youth. 107.
For living beings dwelling here in his presence, there is nothing desired that is difficult to obtain, whether in this world or the next. (108)
Worship the Lord of the Crimson Mountain, the repository of immeasurable virtues, the granter of desired boons, and the abode of all enjoyments. 109.
"O lady of virtuous vows, having attained your desire, you shall again take refuge in Śambhu; even this performance of penance is for the benefit of the world. (110)
Not only will your penance grant you your own desired fruit, but it shall also lead to the welfare of the sages who are practicing austerities.
Suspecting some other cause, the deities perform austerities; for the secret of the deities is inferred only by their fruit. (112)
O Goddess of the gods, through our long cohabitation and by observing your vow, we shall have attained our life's purpose; our fulfillment comes through your ascetic penance.
Having heard these words of the sage, which were pregnant with meaning, Gaurī, filled with curiosity, praised the great muni.
What other austerity remains to be performed? For you have already attained the vision [of the Lord]; this Aruṇādri has been seen, and its majesty has been heard.
Oh, how wonderful is the diversity of this earth, since it is seen to surpass even heaven, where the fiery linga of the deities, the bestower of boons, resides! (116)
Śiva has been propitiated by me and has revealed his own abode; here indeed, having worshipped Śiva, I shall bring the Teacher of the World under my control.
"May there always be an inseparable unity between me and you, O God; through the assistance rendered by you, may I become the Consort of Śiva. (118)

Thus, at that time, having reached an understanding with Gautama, she resolved to perform austerities with devotion; and with the sage’s consent, saying "So be it," she entered a beautiful leaf-hut out of piety.

With her delicate body and lotus-like eyes, her upper garment formed by her firm and lofty breasts, and possessing the luster of a sapphire, the daughter of the mountain shines like the embodied glory of asceticism with matted hair. 120.

Through numerous observances, specific austerities, and various yogic bonds attained during sacrifices, she brought the entire path of dharma as seen in the Vedas and Agamas to its state of fulfilled purpose.
Though performing various austerities, the slender girl never experienced weariness; rather, like some vine composed of emeralds, the young woman became exceedingly radiant.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Circumambulation of Aruṇeśvara," in the first part (Pūrvārdha) of the Aruṇācala-māhātmya, within the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Brahmā said: Then the gods, oppressed by the demon Mahiṣāsura, abandoned the earth and, being distressed, went for refuge to Gaurī while she was performing penance after bowing down to her. || 1 ||
Then, seeing those gods overwhelmed by fear, the goddess said to them, "Give me your assurance of safety," and asked, "What is to be done? (2)
Then the gods, led by Indra, with their palms joined in reverence, informed the Goddess of the fear they felt from the lord of the Daityas. || 3 ||
The gods said: "Surrounded by Apsarases, he sports happily in the Nandana grove; and in his own palace, he commands all the elephants of the quarters, headed by Airāvata."
Dwelling there for the sake of diversion with the women who have come to him, he enjoys the company of those headed by Uccaiḥśravas.
In his beautiful stables, hundreds of thousands and tens of millions [of horses] are seen; he desires a ram, the vehicle of the Fire-god, for the sake of mounting it as a son.
Having brought the buffalo of Yama, he loaded it onto a cart; having summoned all the supernatural powers (siddhis), he assigned them to the household chores.
He brought the entire host of apsarases for his own service, as well as whatever other object existed in the three worlds that was like a jewel.
Furthermore, one who is full of anger does not rest until he has seized what was not taken; and we, having become his servants, are constantly filled with fear.
Honoring his command, we perceive no other course of action; for the protection of those who have come for refuge is declared to be the fruit of asceticism.
This Daitya is difficult to conquer even for all those who are powerful; having obtained the rise of a boon from Śiva, he is invincible to both gods and Daityas alike.
Saying, "The ocean has been turned back by the blow of his horn," he constantly desires to please him with offerings of jewels.
Lifting up mountains with the tips of his horns, the exceedingly haughty one sports, smeared with the dust of all the crushed minerals.
"It is not possible for others to overcome his incomparable strength; you yourself must realize it by slaying him with your own splendor. (14)
This supreme power of Śambhu is seen here in female form; he must be slain by you alone, for he has indeed received a boon from Śiva.
O Goddess, we do not know anything of Śambhu’s activities; we must simply be protected at all times by you, the Mother of the World.
Having heard these auspicious words of theirs, who were afflicted by fear, the goddess, her soul serene, then spoke after granting them freedom from fear.
"O immortals, the protection of those who have come for refuge must be performed by me while I remain established in austerity; in due time, the enemy will become diminished."
"Having drawn out the great Asura by means of a stratagem, I shall slay him; for the killing of one who is innocent is not appropriate for me today. (19)
"Indeed, those who destroy the Dharma in the Age of Dharma become like locusts. Having heard those words, the gods bowed to the Daughter of the Mountain. || 20 ||
They all departed as they had come, fearless and with joyful hearts. || 21 ||
When those gods had departed, Gaurī, the lotus-eyed one, became the enchanting Śakti, endowed with splendor and possessing a slender waist.
That goddess established four excellent young ascetics (baṭukas) on the four mountains in the cardinal directions of Mount Aruṇa for the sake of protection.
When the Daughter of the Mountain arrived from the peak of Kailāsa, the four Mothers followed her, attending upon her.
Four attendants followed her: Dundubhi named Satyavatī, and likewise Anavamī, and Sundarī. (25)
"Release this weary guest who is overcome by hunger and thirst; let him see this Aruṇādri and no other," he said to them.
Having instructed those heroic and powerful commanders stationed at the boundary, the Daughter of the Mountain performed penance in the vicinity of Gautama’s hermitage.
While that slender-limbed lady was performing penance, no distress whatsoever arose; the clouds rained in due season, and the trees became laden with fruit. (28)
Animals that were naturally antagonistic abandoned their former enmity; the hermitage became a refuge for all creatures, dispelling their fear. (29)
Aruṇācala is protected by four heroic Vaṭakas stationed on the boundary mountains extending for two yojanas.
Not a single terror arose, nor was any manifestation of fear seen; there was no affliction by disease, nor any display of enemies.
All the sages, their purpose fulfilled, praised the daughter of the mountain; some extolled the abode of Śiva’s world, while others likewise praised the hermitage.
And that young Gaurī, performing severe penance day and night to bring satisfaction to Śiva, did not reach a state of satiety. || 33 ||
And Mahiṣa, possessed of great prowess, intent on hunting, roamed through the entire forest far from the Śoṇa mountain.
Accompanied by the army of the Daityas, he moved swiftly through the forests, slaughtering numerous herds of deer with his speed and devouring them.
Some deer, pursued by powerful and heroic archers and afflicted by fear, fled and entered that hermitage. || 36 ||
Following them, the sons of Diti were intent on killing those deer, but they were stopped by the heroic young brahmins who quickly cried out, "Do not go there! (37)
When the wicked dānavas then asked, "What is here?", the young brahmin students replied straightforwardly, "A maiden of beautiful form is performing penance here."
No one, however powerful, must enter this place frequented by sages; it is the site of the Goddess’s asceticism, a sanctuary that protects those who seek refuge. 39.
Having heard these words of theirs, the powerful and wicked Dānavas said, "So be it," and having quickly turned back, they reflected upon what ought to be done.
Having assumed the forms of birds through their illusory power, they entered the hermitage with reverence and perched upon the branches of the trees in the grove to observe what was happening here.
Furthermore, while she was performing penance in the Lāsita forest, which was filled with flowers of every season, Māyā was then seen by the soldiers of the Daitya.
Having observed her beauty and grace, and seeing that she was firmly established in asceticism, they were filled with wonder; they went and reported it to him. (43)
Afflicted by love and appearing as an old man, he then entered the hermitage; honored by her friends, he remained there as if his fatigue had vanished.
The old man asked them, "For what purpose is she performing this penance? They replied, "This young girl has been practicing penance here for a long time for the sake of her beloved's favor."
But that powerful lover was never pleased; at the time of the marriage ceremony, he did not grant her her desire as was appropriate.
By that unprecedented Lord, with great new implements fashioned and refined on the very spot by a potter born this very day, [the city was built].
With vessels filled with both fresh and cooked śāli rice, and with all such implements and such collections of materials. (48)
An assistance should be rendered by those whose majesty has never been seen before; once such assistance for her is accomplished, let her svayaṃvara take place immediately. (49)

Having heard these words of theirs, the Mahiṣa laughed and said: "I have truly obtained the fruit of my penance; this is established as the truth. Listen, O young ascetic girl, to all my prosperity! (50)
"I am Mahiṣa, the great hero, the lord of the Daityas, saluted by the gods; this entire triple world is held in my very grasp. (51)
O young girl, my true essence is that of a peerless hero through the strength of my arms; I am one who can assume any form at will and bestow all enjoyments.
"Accept me as your husband, the fruit of the penance of living beings; I shall fulfill everything for you with trees gathered from the Kalpa-trees."
Through my ascetic power, I first created Viśvakarman; through my ascetic power, I create thousands of wish-fulfilling cows in an instant.
With the nine treasures obtained and ever remaining at my side, the accomplishment of whatever object is desired is brought about instantaneously.
Having heard these words of his, she gradually remembered her divine nature; breaking her silence, she spoke to him slowly while smiling.
"I shall become the wife of one who is powerful; I have performed austerities for a long time. If you are indeed powerful, show me your own strength! (57)
Having heard those words uttered by Viracā regarding her own female nature, Mahiṣāsura roared out in anger, "Who is this that has been slain? (58)
Seeing Mahiṣāsura approaching with the desire to seize her, that maiden Durgā became unassailable, possessing a form ablaze like fire.
Beholding Mahāmāyā standing before him, blazing with light, he himself, in the form of a buffalo, grew until he resembled Mount Meru.
Repeatedly tossing the peaks of the mountain ranges of the clans with his two horns, he summoned his own army, which filled the intermediate spaces of the quarters.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, having prostrated themselves, worshipped Durgā—who was like the fire of universal destruction—with their own various weapons.
Then Hari gave her five weapons, Sadāśiva ten, and Brahmā four; yet she remained concealed by Māyā.
The guardians of the quarters, other gods, mountains, and oceans honored her with their own ornaments and weapons, making themselves invincible.
That Māyā, with many hands bearing a multitude of blazing weapons, quickly became Durgā, clad in armor and mounted upon a lion.
Unable to endure that splendor which filled the expanse of all directions, Mahiṣa fled upon beholding the terrible form of Durgā.
Then, seeing Mahiṣa fleeing because he was unable to endure her own terrible, blazing splendor, she reflected: || 67 ||
This wicked Mahiṣāsura must be slain by means of a stratagem; for in the forest, deer are brought down by hunters after first luring them with intoxication.
Having drawn him in by the words of messengers that are gentle yet strike at his vital points, I shall provoke his anger and bring him face-to-face in an instant.
For those engaged in unrighteous conduct, the hearing of words concerning dharma will immediately give rise to anger, which becomes the cause of the destruction of their own lives. (70)
Alternatively, if his mind is inclined toward righteousness and he becomes peaceful, then, through beneficial instruction, there will be no loss of dharma.
Those performing austerities must always practice the abandonment of anger, which is fruitful; the loss of dharma must not be tolerated, for that anger is indeed the supreme obstacle to austerity.
Having reflected thus, Gaurī, having mentally envisioned the sage who is the preceptor of the gods, dispatched him in the form of a monkey-faced messenger toward the Asura.
Go, O great seer with the face of a monkey, endowed with your illusory power; having awakened Mahisha, return quickly with this message. (74)
"Do not, O evil-minded one, oppress the Lord of Aruṇādri; for here, the prowess of those with wicked minds becomes invisible in an instant. (75)
For those possessed of devotion to Śiva, there is no affliction from the Kali age here, nor any torment by asuras, nor is there any inauspicious rashness. || 76 ||
O Asura, having attained the great rise of valor through merits earned in previous births, do not become like a moth in the fire of the Lord of Śoṇācala.
The powers bestowed upon you by Śiva through the strength of your former austerities would be consumed there instantly, like trees in a forest fire. (78)

In this place, there shall always be residence for those whose souls are devoted to dharma and who possess devotion to Śiva; however, for those intent on harming others, it shall be shrouded by hundreds of diseases.
Having attained incomparable sovereignty and other invincible powers, why, being of small intellect, will you go to destruction through your own faults? (80)
I have seen the maiden again; she is considered especially weak. Yet, because the Lord of the Crimson Mountain (Aruṇādri) resides within her, she excels this [other] one.
Alternatively, by means of various logical arguments or scriptures approved by Śiva, bring under control your own army—the mental fluctuations that are otherwise impossible to restrain.
"With my splendor, I shall in an instant consume that vast army of yours by which you, arrogant in your strength, oppress all the worlds. (83)
"Bring your entire army and station it before me with weapons ready; I shall immediately withdraw that creation by means of my own powers at this very moment."
O long-lived one, for you who are being cut down by a sword along with your army, liberation will occur right here; for who knows the intent of Śivā? (85)
Even when being restrained, a person impelled by prior karma performs actions involuntarily and experiences a corresponding fruit.
You too must indeed speak many compassionate words for the sake of turning him away from what should not be done and for his constant adherence to dharma.
Thus instructed by Gaurī, the monkey-faced sage, standing as a messenger before Mahiṣa, related everything she had said.
Having heard all of this, he too became overwhelmed by a surge of anger and began to devour him; but he [the other] departed by means of his power of illusion.
Then, having summoned his entire army, that evil-minded one commanded them—terrible to the world—to arm themselves with weapons and prepare for battle.
An incomparable army of troops, resembling the four oceans overflowing at the time of the end of the eon, surrounded Śoṇādri.
Then Gaurī, beholding the wondrous army of the Daityas, created many terrible hosts of spirits and radiant heroes.
Some emerged with a single foot, eye, or hand; some had hanging ears and breasts; and some had hands, feet, heads, bellies, and faces [all protruding from the same body].
I devour all this which is insufficient for me; I alone shall destroy the entire army of the Daityas without exception.
"What further task is there for you here? Behold and simply remain. "I myself shall fight here," they said to one another. (95)
While those hosts were speaking thus, the Blessed Lady blew her conch shell with her groups of Yoginīs in order to destroy that host of Daityas.
Beholding her in such a state as she approached, his soldiers, holding their weapons aloft before their master, displayed their own prowess.
The Daityas rained down showers of weapons in every direction; she, however, warded them off with arrows released from her bow.
With hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of chariots, lordly elephants, and horses, the invincible Bhūtas and Vetālas created by the Goddess fought.
The Mothers of various forms, the Ḍākinīs, and the hosts of Yoginīs were created; furthermore, by his splendor, Piśācas, Pretas, and Rākṣasas were produced.
By the invincible army created by the Goddess, the great asuras were in an instant devoured, pulverized, shattered, split apart, and slain. || 101 ||
And that goddess was seen, blazing and armed, having slain the asuras, while she was being gratified by throngs of dancing bhūtas who had feasted upon blood and flesh. || 102 ||
When she arrived from the peak of Kailāsa to perform penance upon the earth, certain Mātṛkās then came together for the protection of her body.
Dundubhī, Satyavatī by name, as well as Antavatī and another, Sundarī—these four attendants followed her. (104)
And Cāmuṇḍā, created by the Goddess, terrifying with her circle of fangs, clothed in the skins of Daityas and satiated with flesh and blood, wandered about. (105)

Adorned with jewel ornaments, dwell here, O Maheśvara; for the daughters of the gods and Gandharvas constantly come to you, O Īśāna.
Let them serve the Lord of Gods here with dance, instrumental music, and song; and let the Gaṇas, having become human beings, serve you day and night.
O Lord, by your grace, may this fragrant union of ours, which increases prosperity, be seen as the bestower of all goals. (8)
O Lord of Gods, may this body of mine, which consists of all mantras, be grasped here; may it be your service through your life-story, and may there always be devotion unto you.
May the thousandfold offenses committed constantly through both knowledge and ignorance be forgiven by you, out of regard for your devotees who have no other refuge. 10.
Having heard these words of the Goddess, Śambhu, the Lord of Śoṇācala, the bestower of boons, granted her that very boon she had desired.
Desiring to sport with Gaurī out of curiosity, Śiva himself addressed her, saying: "Hold this beautiful musk. (12)
Mahādeva said: A great Daitya named Pulaka, having assumed the form of a deer and performed intense penance, obtained from me a boon of most wonderful fragrance.
Having obtained the boon, he bewildered the celestial women with his own fragrance; likewise, having attained unrighteousness, he oppressed the entire world.
Requested by the gods, I summoned the leader of the asuras and commanded him: "For the sake of protecting the world, cast off this asuric body. (15)
Pulaka said: "O Lord of the gods, by your command I shall abandon this body. Having prostrated with a mind full of devotion, he spoke these words to me as well: || 16 ||
"O God, Lord of Gods, let this divine fragrance arising from my own body, which enchants the entire universe, be worn always with a respectful mind. (17)
Indeed, let this musk of yours always be celebrated in the world as that which produces horripilation and perspiration, and which increases the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa). || 18 ||
"O God of gods, Lord of the universe, he who bestows upon you belovedness and grants beauty, charm, form, and grace—such a one shall cast off his own body. (19)
He was always highly esteemed by the Goddess, who was captivated by his divine fragrance; for those who are born from a portion of me acquire that fragrance through my ascetic power.
"O Lord of Gods, let them dissolve into your form under the guise of being an ointment. When I had said, "So be it," that Daitya named Pulaka [acted].
Having entrusted his life-breath to me, he cast off his own body; thereafter, from that limb of his, there arose a wine of abundant fragrance.
Out of love, I supported with my hand your emaciated body, O Goddess of the lords of gods, which had been scorched by penance and adorned with a hundred peaks. (23)
"And now, extinguish this fever of my body caused by separation. Having thus praised the wonderful affection of Pulaka in many ways, [he spoke].
Mahādeva anointed Pārvatī, the abode of love, and smiling, the Lord questioned her who possessed the form of a woman.
Seeing that which had arisen from her hand, the Mother of the World asked, "What is this? and having bowed to the Lord of Aruṇādri, the Mother of the World spoke.
One should always contemplate the arrival of that flower which is held in one's own hand. || 27 ||
The Goddess said: "O God of gods, by your command, I have come from the peak of Kailāsa to Kāñcī, which has golden archways, in order to perform penance. (28)
Having obtained this supreme white lotus born from Lake Mānasa, which possesses unfading and heavy fragrance, I propitiated Mahādeva.
Whatever inexhaustible and tireless worship has been offered by me, it possesses uninterrupted great brilliance and is saturated with the ghee of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu).
It must be constantly observed and protected by kings; the characteristics of Dharma should be established with diligence for the sake of protecting the world. (31)
For the sake of accomplishing all desired goals and for my own pleasure, I have established the thirty-two dharmas for the protection of the world.
"Those who have come into her presence must guard her with great effort. Behold this radiant form of my daughter, adorned with every ornament and celebrating a festival of all enjoyments. (33)
Brahmā said: Having heard these words of the Goddess, Śambhu, the Lord of Śoṇācala, [spoke].
"So be it," said the Giver of Boons, and he granted every desired boon. "This glorious Śoṇācala, worshipped by the world, is now visible. (35)
He who [worships] this form of Śambhu, which exists as the Aruṇa mountain, shall always be surrounded by Gaurī, the bestower of boons, and by all enjoyments. (36)
All those on earth who hear this majesty of Aruṇācala behold it and pay homage, having achieved their life's purpose. (37)
All their perfections are ever complete: majesty, mastery of speech, beauty, and unimpeded strength. (38)
By retaining this greatness, they obtain the destruction of sin, the merit of bathing in all sacred fords, and the fruit of performing all sacrificial rites. (39)
And the vision of Śoṇādri bestows the grace of Sadāśiva. || 40 ||
Thus, by the command of Śiva, the Goddess arrived from the peak of Kailāsa; she attained liberation from her curse through the sight of Śoṇācala.
Although other very meritorious abodes of the Lord exist on earth and in heaven, Śambhu has become especially pleased here.
This Sadāśiva is directly perceived here in the form of Aruṇācala; he is the supreme splendor, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. || 43 ||
But this fiery liṅga, saluted by all the gods, is visible; therefore, this land is considered the field of action and preeminent for righteousness.
With their impurities shaken off by the splendor of Aruṇācalanātha, devoted men shall obtain happiness in every respect throughout the world.
For those who worship the Lord of Aruṇādri through circumambulations, prostrations, austerities, and observances, Śambhu has come under their control.
Śaṅkara is not so pleased by austerities, yogic practices, or gifts as He is by the sight of Aruṇācala, even if it occurs but once. 47.
The Vedas, along with the Itihāsas, eternally abide in heaven as self-existent; they, taking the form of mountains on all sides, praise the Aruṇa mountain.
The entirety of his majesty cannot be described by words, even by me or by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, even in hundreds of millions of years. (49)
The gods, headed by Hari, as well as the celestial trees beginning with the Kalpaka, always serve Aruṇācala while remaining in disguised forms.
The defect of the Kali age shall not affect him, nor shall there be the manifestation of mental or physical ailments, wherever the Liṅga known as Aruṇācala is fully worshipped.
Thus has all this been told to you—the life-story of this Aruṇa, which takes refuge at the feet of Śambhu and is difficult to attain even through the merit of a kalpa.

Sūta said: Thus, drinking with the pair of his ears that noble river of nectar—the story of the Lord of Aruṇagiri—which had issued from the mouth of Brahmā, the sage Sanaka obtained the fruit of his austerities. 53.

Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the latter half of the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya*. Vyāsa said: While dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, the sages spoke to Sūta. The sages said: "Tell us of that place belonging to Śiva which is the most excellent among all sacred sites. (1)
Sūta said: O sages, listen with reverence; I shall relate that which was previously heard from the mouth of Nandīśvara by Mārkaṇḍeya. || 2 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Nandīśvara, the greatness of Mādhyameśvara has been proclaimed by you; I too have grasped it all with a heart moistened by devotion and faith.
Nevertheless, O God of gods, O ocean of compassion, speak further to me as I, having shown due respect, question you once more.
There is nothing in these three worlds unknown to you, whether among all the Āgamas and Purāṇas, external or internal.
For men who are intent upon attaining the respective fruits of all their actions, the earth alone is distinguished as the ground for both heaven and liberation.
And you yourself previously declared that there are three kinds of fruits for men, distinguished as happiness on earth, enjoyment in heaven, and liberation. (7)
The first two [types of merit] generally diminish through the exhaustion of merit; however, the third does not diminish, because it is not dependent upon karma alone. (8)
The accomplishment of that [state] has been described by you as the domain of pure knowledge; furthermore, pure knowledge is difficult for all embodied beings to attain.
In what field or domain could that knowledge be perfected for all embodied beings merely through the worship of Śiva, without the study of scriptures and the like? (10)
Even regarding the practices of knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and conduct as taught in the Śaiva Āgamas, the intellect of embodied beings does not function with full clarity.
Tell me of that place, by the majesty of which even embodied beings with few observances shall attain pure knowledge. (12)
Let that place be described where even the simple-minded obtain the highest good by merely carrying ashes and rudrākṣa beads and remembering the Lord once. (13)
May that place where the welfare of embodied beings will be accomplished without obstacle, even by dwelling there unintentionally, be favored by me. (14)
Let that field be described where there is welfare even for those born of mixed castes, those who have entered the womb of animals, and even for stationary beings.
Having spoken thus, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, together with other great-souled lords of sages, fell at the pair of lotus-feet of that son of Śilāda, who was an ocean of all the scriptures.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of the Introduction to the Greatness of the Sacred Site," in the latter half of the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya*, within the first section (*Māheśvara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nandikeśvara said: O foremost of the devotees of Maheśvara, O sage, you have asked about that place for the welfare of all beings, both moving and unmoving.
For the birth of embodied beings in various wombs has been ordained by the Lord according to their respective karma. (2)
You have indeed served them for their own great benefit; otherwise, there would be no end to the cycle of worldly existence even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
For by means of very few actions and even limited knowledges, birth and death are attained again and again; through the mechanism of the waterwheel, they do not cease at all. (4)
How indeed could an embodied being, though detached from the union that is the entrance into a womb, be fit for rest without pure knowledge? (5)
The various regions have been previously described by me in connection with the relevant context; among them are the different sages and the dwelling place of Kṛttivāsas.
Some were on the banks of the Gaṅgā, some on the bank of the Sarasvatī; others were on the two banks of the Kālindī, and some on the shore of the Śoṇa.
Others [resided] on the banks of the Narmadā, others on the banks of the Godāvarī; some were on the banks of the Gomatī, and others on the slopes of the Himavat.
Some were on the shores of the ocean, others on various islands; some were at the mouths of rivers, and still others at the confluences of streams.
Some were on the bank of the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, others near the Tuṅgabhadrā; some were at Upaveṇī, and others near the river Śakti.
Some were on the bank of the Kāverī, others on the shore of the Vegavatī; some were on the Tāmraparṇī, and a few on the bank of the Muralā.
Some were on the banks of the Airāvatī, while others were desirous of setting out.

Some are on the banks of the Kanyā, some on the banks of the Kumārī, others near the Tamasā and the Varuṇā; still others are in the vicinity of the Mandākinī, others on the banks of the Śiprā, and others in the environs of the Sarayū.
Others were in the vicinity of the Vipāśā, others on the further bank of the Śatadrū; some were near the Carmaṇvatī, and some on the bank of the Bhīmarathī. || 14 ||
Some were near the Bindu-sarovara, others on the banks of the Pampā lake; some were in the vicinity of Bhairavī, and several were on the bank of the Kauśikī.
Others were on the banks of the Mālinī, others on the shore of the Gaṅgavatī; some were near Lake Mānasa, and some on the slopes of Mount Acchoda.

Some [say it was] at Indradyumna-saras, while others say at Maṇikarṇikā; some say on the bank of the Varadā, and several others say at Tāpī; others say near the Pātālagaṅgā, and still others say in the vicinity of the Śarāvatī. || 17 ||
Some were on the two banks of the Lohityā, some for a short time on its shore, others near the Vitastā, and still others near the Candrabhāgā.
Some were near Suralopa, others on the banks of the Payoṣṇī; some were on the bank of the Madhumatī, and others along the Pinākinī.
The sacred field of Vārāṇasī, purifying for five krośas, has been described; there the deity named Avimukta is worshipped by Viśālākṣī.
O Sage, know that to be Kāśī where Kapālamocana is located, where Kālabhairava resides, and where those who have died attain the state of Rudra.
Gaya and Prayaga have also been described to you as bestowing all accomplishments; indeed, it is there that the ancestors are gratified by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
And Kedāra has been heard of, wherein even the God, assuming the form of a buffalo, was slain by the Goddess—[a place] which brings about all auspiciousness for men. (23)
Badarikāśrama is a field that grants all accomplishments to men, where the three-eyed Lord dwells with the Goddess, worshipped by Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
For you have heard of the sacred field of Naimiṣa, where Maheśvara, known as Devadeva, resides, along with the meritorious Goddess who bears the deer.
The sacred site known as Amareśa is proclaimed to be the accomplisher of all goals; the Lord there is named Oṃkāra, and the Great Goddess is called Caṇḍikā. (26)
You have heard from me the description of that great place called Puṣkara, where dwells the god Rujogaṃdhi and the great sovereign lady Puruhūtā.
I have described to you that sacred place named Āṣāḍhī; there Haras is Āṣāḍheśa and the Supreme Goddess is Ratīśā.
And I have described to you the place known as Daṇḍimuṇḍī, where Mahādeva is Muṇḍī and the Supreme Goddess is Daṇḍikā.
That place named Lākula has been described by me as perfectly pure; it is there that Lākulīśa Hara resides, along with Anaṅgā Sarvamaṅgalā.
I have described to you the sacred site known as Bhārabhūti, where Śambhu is named Bhāra and the daughter of the Mountain is called Bhūti.
I have described to you the place named Arālakeśvara, where the trident-bearer is known by the name Sūkṣma, and the daughter of the Mountain is called Sūkṣmā.
I have described to you the great sacred field named Gayā, where the auspicious Śiva, known as Maṅgala, is the Great-Grandfather (Prapitāmaha).
The place called Kurukṣetra has been described to you, where dwells the goddess beloved of Sthāṇu and the god known by the name Sthāṇu.
I have described to you that supreme place named Kanakhala, where the fierce enemy of the cities [Śiva] resides, along with the fierce daughter of the best of mountains [Pārvatī].
O Mārkaṇḍeya, I have described to you the great sacred field named Tālaka, where the self-born Goddess and the self-born Supreme Lord reside.
I have described to you this great sacred site as Aṭṭahāsa, where the Sun-god, having worshipped the Lord, attained the fulfillment of his desires. || 37 ||
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, you have described to me the sacred field named Kṛttivāsa, which is the residence of Kṛttivāsa that is more praiseworthy even than Kailāsa. (38)
On Śrīśaila, Maheśa Mallikārjuna was worshipped by the goddess Bhramarāmbikā and by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) for the sake of accomplishing creation. (39)
On the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī is Śaṅkara, known as Kālahasti, who was propitiated by Vyāsa and by his mother, whose tresses were made resonant by bees.
In Kāñcī, the Subduer of Desire (Śiva), while staying at the foot of the single mango tree, was embraced by Kāmākṣī as she performed penance, and thus he became marked with a bangle.
There is a city named Vyāghrapura situated in the midst of the Tillika forest, where Patañjali attends upon the dancing Īśāna.
I have previously described to you that place called Śvetāraṇya, where Airāvata, having broken his tusk, resided there due to his worship of Śiva. (43)
I have mentioned the place called Setubandha; there, Rāghava installed the Lord known as Rāmanātha, the destroyer of misfortune.

The place of the Lord whose banner is the bull exists as a locus for the return of those who have departed; there, at the foot of a jambu tree, he has taken refuge for the sake of protecting the world.
"You have indeed heard that the Lord is eternally present in the field known as Vṛddhācala, along the river Maṇimuktā. (46)
I have heard of the most excellent place named Śrīman-Madhyārjuna, wherein Hara, the companion of Gaurī, is eternally present as the bestower of boons.
You have heard of Somatīrtha, which is presided over by Somanātha; there, for those who have cast off their bodies, there is no further bondage to worldly existence.
For you have heard of the sacred field named Siddhavaṭa, where the perfected ones worship the unsurpassed Jyotirliṅga.
Indeed, you have heard of that field known as Kamalālaya, where Śrī regained her life through the worship of the hair from the anthill of Hari.
You have heard of Kaṅkādri, where Hara is ever-present; even now, Brahmā and Keśava worship there for the sake of liberation.
You know the illustrious Droṇapura, wherein, at the end of the Kali age, the Lord of Pārvatī boarded a boat upon the agitated ocean.
It is heard that there is a sacred field named Brahmapura, where in ancient times Indrajit established Dhūrjaṭi on the bank of the Āryapuṣkariṇī.
The field of knowledge known as Śrīkoṭika is where the moon-crested Lord dwells; it dispels tens of millions of sins for those men who worship him there.
Having heard that Śiva is present at Gokarṇa, the son of Jamadagni, desiring to propitiate him, no longer yearns for heaven.
You have been told of the field called Tripurāntaka, where the Three-eyed Lord dispels the fear of hell for those men who behold him.
The sacred field called Kālāñjana has been described, where the Lord with the dark throat (Kālakaṇṭha) extinguishes the terrible fever of saṃsāra for his devotees.
