The sacred field known as Priyālavana is where the Lord of Ambikā resides; there, for the sake of one seeking milk, he bestowed the Ocean of Milk upon Upamanyu.
That sacred field where the moon-crested Lord Śiva was worshipped by Viṣṇu and Balarāma and granted inexhaustible fruit has been described to you as Prabhāsa.
You know Vedāraṇya, wherein the Lord of the Pramathas was entreated for the sake of liberation by Dakṣa, who had previously committed an offense.
You have heard of Hemakūṭa, the abode of the Three-eyed One, where men who practice austerities have no fear of rebirth.
There exists a sacred field named Veṇuvana, which destroys all sins; it is there that the auspicious Muktāmaṇi was born from within a bamboo creeper.
O Andhaka, you have heard of the place called Jālandhara; it was there that Jalandhara attained the status of Gaṇapati through his austerities.
"You have learned of the place called Jvālāmukha, which was described by me; there the goddess Jvālāmukhī worshipped Kālarudra. (64)
There is a sacred field named Bhadravaṭa of which you have heard; it is there that Heramba worshipped Tryambaka for the sake of prosperity.
The Nyagrodha forest was described by you as the place where Ugra, having engaged in a contest with Kālī, performed a fierce tāṇḍava dance.
You have heard of that sacred field known as Gandhamādana, where the worship of Mṛtyuñjaya was performed by the son of Añjanā.
I have proclaimed this place as Goparvata, belonging to Śambhu, where Pāṇini attained the preeminence among grammarians. (68)
Indeed, the sacred site known as Vīrakoṣṭha has been identified; it is there that Pracetas attained preeminence among poets through his ascetic penance.
It is proclaimed as the "Great Tīrtha," where you know that all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, were instructed by Śambhu.
I have described to you Mayūrapura, the sacred field of Maheśvara, where Hradinī was obtained by Vajrapāṇi while he was observing a vow.
The sacred field called Śrīsundara is said to be on the bank of the Vegavatī; it shines even in the Kali age by the power of the God of gods.
Indeed, you know that place called Kumbhakonam, where even the Gaṅgā manifests her presence during the month of Māgha for the sake of pacifying one's own sins.
You have heard of the place named Tryambaka, situated along the banks of the Godāvarī, where Guha obtained the spear that slays the demon Tāraka.
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, that place is known as Śrīpāṭala or Vyāghrapura, where Gaṅgādhara was worshipped by Triśaṅku for the sake of purification from his birth.
You have understood that sacred field known as Kadambapurī, where Śambhu, for your sake, destroyed Kṛtānta with his trident.
You have described to me that field called Avināśa, where the bull-bannered Lord, being well-pleased, bestowed his presence upon Paḍikaṇṭha.
O sinless one, I have described to you the sacred field called Raktaikānana, where Rudra, the bestower of boons, was born from Mitra and Varuṇa.
You have heard of the sacred field of Śrī Hāṭakeśvara situated in the netherworld (pātāla), where Vairocani worships the Lord in order to attain his own station.
As a constant attendant, you know Kailāsa, the beloved abode of Śambhu, where the Lord of Yakṣas worships the Three-eyed One with devotion.
The abodes of the wielder of the axe (Śiva) have been described by me previously; they have surely been grasped by you as well—what more do you wish to hear?

Having spoken thus, this son of Śilādā, his heart moist with the essence of compassion, touched with his hand the head of the lord of sages, the son of the sage Mṛkaṇḍu, as he bowed with devotion at his feet.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Description of the Various Śiva-Kṣetras Situated upon the Surface of the Earth," in the latter half of the Aruṇācala-Māhātmya, within the first section (Māheśvara-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O Blessed One, enough with deception toward me, who am solely devoted to you. Is there any disciple like me for you? Your own compassion is the witness in this matter.
Regarding the various fruits associated with the places previously mentioned by you, tell me, O Lord, that place where the attainment of all fruits occurs.
O Teacher, tell me of that by whose mere remembrance liberation is attained for all beings, both moving and unmoving, whether they are conscious or unconscious.
See, O Blessed One, that you do not favor me alone; for you are surrounded by all these sages for this very purpose.
By Pulaha, Pulastya, Vasiṣṭha, Marīci, Agastya, Dadhīca, Nakula, Bhṛgu, and Atri; || 5 ||
By Jābāli, by Jaimini, by Dhaumya, by Jamadagni, by Upayāja, by Yāja, and by Bharata Ārvarīvat.
By Pippalāda, Kaṇṭha, Kumuda, Upamanyu, Kumudākṣa, Kutsa, Vatsa, and Varatantu.
By Vibhāṇḍaka, Vyāsa, Kaṇvarīṣa, Kaṇḍu, Māṇḍavya, Mataṅga, Kukṣi, and Māṇḍakarṇi; || 8 ||
By Caṇḍakauśika, Śāṇḍilya, Śākaṭāyana, and Kauśika; by Śātātapa, Madhucchandas, Garga, Saubhari, and Romaśa.
By Āpastamba, Pṛthustambha, Bhārgava, Udaṅka, Parvata, Bhāradvāja, Dālbhya, Dānta, and Śvetaketu. || 10 ||
By Kauṇḍinya and Puṇḍarīka, by Raibhya and Tṛṇabindu, by Vālmīki and Nārada, and by Vahni and Dṛḍhamanyu.
By Bodhāyana and Subodha, by Hārīta and Mṛkaṇḍu, by the exceedingly sharp Durvāsas, and by Jālapāda Śakti; || 12 ||
By Kāṅkāyana Nadanta, Devadatta, Nyaṅku, Suśruta Āgniveśya, and Gālava Marutvata; || 13 ||
By Lokākṣin, Viśravas, Saiṃdhava, Sumantu, Śiśupāyana, Audgalya, Pathya, Cāvana, and Mātura; || 14 ||
[He was accompanied] by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Ekapāt, Krauñca, Dṛḍhagomukha, and Devala; by Aṅgiras, Vāmadeva, Aurva, Paṭañjali, and Kapiñjala. || 15 ||
[He was accompanied] by Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana, as well as Hiraṇyanābha, Satya, Vātāśana, and Suhotṛ.
With Maitreya, Puṣpajit, Satyatapas, Śālīṣya, Aiśīra, Nidāgha, Utathya, Saṃvarta, Śaulkāyani, and Parāśara; || 17 ||
[He was honored] by Vaiśampāyana, Kauśalya, Śāradvata, Kapidhvaja, Kuśa, Svārcika, Kaivalya, Yājñavalkya, and Āśvalāyana. || 18 ||
By Kṛṣṇa, Ātapa, Uttama, Anantakaruṇā, Amalakapriya, the pure Caraka, Kapila, and Kaṇāśin; || 19 ||
And you are being observed by Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as by other divine great seers, who are intent on hearing the answers to my questions.
You are the foremost among the followers of Maheśvara and have reached the further shore of all the Āgamas; since you pervade all the worlds, therefore, please grant us your favor. (21)
O Blessed One, we have been well-instructed by you alone; O Lord, this was already done by you previously—what else could possibly be required? (22)
The Supreme Lord is to be beheld through the divine Āgamas and Purāṇas—whether as Kātyāyanī, or Skanda, or the Blessed One, or indeed as you yourself. (23)
If we have devotion toward you, and if you have compassion for us, then you ought to show us favor by revealing this secret.

Thus addressed with humility by the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, Nandikeśa, his face smiling, spoke to him who was exceedingly uplifted and who had attained the perfection of a body through Śiva’s grace, having been satisfied by his prior devotion: "May your devotion to Śiva be supreme. (25)
Nandikeśvara said: "O Sage, I spoke to you in that manner for the purpose of testing your mind; had I not told it to you, to whom else would it have been told?"
Is there anyone else like you in this world so devoted to the dharma of Śiva, by whom, despite such a short lifespan, [this state] was thus made eternal through devotion?
For whose sake else, O Lord, did he, being enraged, restrain Yama—who is himself an executor of his own commands—by pressing him down with the big toe of his foot? (3)
"You alone must know all the Śaiva dharmas in their secret essence; you who were previously wandering like Time itself have now reached full maturity in your mind. (4)
By you alone, or by some other person, have I been thus served for a long time; in whom else besides you could I find such affection as this? (5)
I shall teach you that protected field, which is governed by the teachings of the Dharma; it is to be grasped with devotion by those who long for liberation through devotion.
Is that teacher a true guru who, though he himself is being respectfully questioned by his disciple, does not satisfy him with instruction? (7)
Having become composed in mind, place your eternal trust in this supreme secret of the Lord as it is being taught by me.
Remember the god who is the ender of Smara; worship him and study the teachings of Śaṅkara. Utter the syllable Om in a whisper; great welfare has come upon you.
O ascetic, in the southern region among the Draviḍas, there is a great sacred field named Aruṇa belonging to the one whose crest-jewel is the young moon.
Know that this place, three yojanas in extent, which is to be venerated by the Śiva-yogins, is the heart of that land, reaching into the heart of Śiva.
There, the Lord Śambhu himself has assumed the form of a mountain; known by the name Aruṇācala, he brings about the welfare of the world. || 12 ||
It is the abode of all the Siddhas, the great Ṛṣis, and the gods; it is also the dwelling place of the Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases.
He who is himself the Supreme Lord is to be honored even by the great seers, more so than Sumeru, Kailāsa, or Mandara.
The denizens of heaven envy even those creatures who belong to Him, for they have been deprived of their celestial abode and possess liberation obtainable without effort.
The wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) are not equal to the trees found there, which constantly honor Hara on the mountain with their leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Even hunters, whose sole delight is in violence, become infinite in number at this place by virtue of its form, attaining the fruit of circumambulating the Lord. || 17 ||
The clouds that move across its expanse and cling to its peaks consider themselves even superior to the Himavat, the father of the Gaṅgā.
Where the birds utter sweet notes and even the hollow bamboos resound, there the Yakṣas, Kiṃnaras, and Gandharvas attain a state that is difficult to reach.
Remembering this place, even fireflies attain the station of those who offer the *ārārtika* lamp-waving ceremony to the Lord at the onset of night during the dark fortnight.
The trees growing on her banks, constantly embraced by the river without hindrance, out of pride in their good fortune, treat the goddess Aparṇā with contempt.
Even the stars, upon reaching the tips of its lofty peaks, consider themselves to have attained equality with the moon.
On those ridges where all the deer constantly roam, they disregard even the arrow of Śambhu that rests upon his hand.
By those who move near his feet—even by the Śabaras for the most part—resemblance to Nikumbha and Kumbha is effortlessly attained.
What is the use of speaking at length? Even the trees, the animals, and the Śabaras who have grown up upon his body feel envy toward these two princes born of two mothers.
At whatever time lions, tigers, and elephants cast off their bodies there, they are surely honored by Śambhu of the Crimson Mountain for having granted him a dwelling place.
To the east of this mountain named Bhāskara, the mountain Vajrin is seen, where the wielder of the thunderbolt always resides and serves the Śoṇa mountain.
In the western direction, there is a certain mountain called Daṇḍādri; the son of Pracetas (Vālmīki) dwells upon its peak, serving the Aruṇa mountain.
To the south of Śoṇādri lies the mountain Amarācala; Kāla dwells upon its plateau for the sake of serving Śoṇādri.
In this northern region of Hari, the mountain Triśūla shines forth, its caves inhabited by perfected beings (siddhas) and protected by Śrīda.
Other kings as well, who have come from its very borders, and furthermore, the guardians of the quarters attend upon him on the riverbanks.
By him who constantly supports all the trees of the earth, they attain an abundance of prosperity even greater than through [his] propitiation.
When that Lord of the Mountain was beheld, the joy of both Menā and the Snowy Mountain increased all the more due to their shared relationship.
With his matted locks marked by the color of tree sprouts, this stationary Śambhu here is like the Lord himself in motion.
With the moon and the sun situated on its two flanks, the radiant peak of the mountain reveals to the worlds his state of possessing three eyes of light.
During the rainy season, that mountain, with its dark blue clouds beneath its peaks, shines resplendent as if bearing the Kālakūṭa poison upon its neck.
He who is the Lord of Mountains, possessing a thousand feet and a thousand heads, is described not only by the Śruti, but is also directly perceived.
It is not surprising that the streams of the celestial river were previously absorbed into his head; for even today, the Lord of the Mountain has many hosts of rivers clinging to his peaks.
He who, with autumnal clouds that have reached the horizon, imitates the preeminent bull mounted upon a bull. 39.
There, Śiva, whose dark-red body was firmly clinging to the tips of the mountain peaks, attained the state of a pillar through his immobility and the state of a formidable being through his density.
Because it is so difficult to traverse, it possesses a fierce nature even by name; for upon its ridges, lowly reptiles have made their dwellings. (41)
He vies with the lords of serpents, such as Takṣaka and Ananta; he has manifested himself through eight powers (vibhūtis) appearing on all sides from the corners.
It clearly manifests, as it were, its own eightfold form (aṣṭamūrtitā), since the rivers of the power of envy (īrṣyā-śakti) themselves flow within the iḍā and piṅgalā [nāḍīs]. (43)
In the center of Śiva’s peak flows the Suṣumnā, the river of lotuses, whose root and tip one must behold within the form of the pillar of light.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu took the form of two swans and became the stalk; and being entreated by them, Śambhu became present within that [stalk]. (45)
There, the lord of yogis, Gautama, took refuge in the one known as Aruṇācalanātha together with his wives for a thousand years.
Having performed intense austerities there in the past, the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain also directly manifested Sadāśiva by means of her penance.
There, the deity named Pravālādrīśvara was installed by Gaurī, who had obtained half of the body of the enemy of Manmatha (Śiva) as he became pleased with her.
The Liṅga bestows enjoyment upon men and leads them toward liberation (kaivalya). There, by the command of Gaurī, Durgā Mahiṣamardinī resides. (49)
Manifesting itself, it bestows the perfection of mantras upon the virtuous without obstacle; there, in Gaurī’s hermitage, is the ninth [site] renowned as Khaḍgatīrtha.
By bathing there even once, men’s five great sins are destroyed; and the Liṅga worshipped at Durgā is named Pāpanāśana (the Destroyer of Sin).
By a single prostration alone, there is the destruction of all sins. Therein, King Vajrāṅgada, whose essence was wealth, [fell] due to transgression.
Furthermore, through the greatness of that devotion, he attained union with Śiva; and by the mere circumambulation of it, Kāntiśālī and Kalādharu [attained their respective states].
The two lords of the Vidyādharas were liberated from the bond of Durvāsas’s curse; there is no sacred field superior to Śoṇādri, and there is no mantra superior to the five-syllabled one.

There is no dharma greater than that of Maheśvara; there is no god greater than Maheśvara; there is no knowledge greater than the knowledge of Śiva; and there is no scripture greater than the Śrīrudra.

There is no leader of the Śaivas superior to Viṣṇu; there is no protection superior to the sacred ash (vibhūti); there is no virtuous conduct superior to devotion; and there is no teacher superior to one who provides protection.
There is no ornament superior to the rudrākṣa; there is no scripture superior to the Śivāgama; there is no leaf superior to the bilva leaf; and there is no flower superior to the golden one.
There is no happiness greater than dispassion, and there is no state higher than liberation; there is no mountain equal to Aruṇādri, nor Kailāsa, nor Mandara.
Those dwellings are pervaded by mountains, yet he himself is Giriśa (the Lord of the Mountains). || 59 ||
Thus spoke the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, his mind filled with joy, to the son of Śilādāna; bowing to him again and again many times, he, with a heart full of awe, addressed him once more. (60)

"What specific actions lead to rebirth for human beings, and how indeed are those various [actions] heard to lead to hell? What is the remedy for each of them, and how exactly does that come about? Please tell me all this. (61)
Nandikeśvara said: A man endowed with the quality of pure sattva is difficult to find in this world; men possessed of the qualities of rajas and tamas are easily found.

Being of a sattvic nature due to his virtuous character, he shall attain the supreme good; for it was by the Creator that these various actions were ordained for the sake of experiencing their fruits.
Various kinds of hells have been created here and there; having become a partaker of the Mahāraurava hell, one may even be born as a donkey, a dog, or a pig.
After death, a man may become a Caṇḍāla due to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa; having been confined for a long time in the Raurava hell, he attains the state of worms, insects, and moths.
A twice-born man may incur the status of a performer of ritual acts through the drinking of liquor; and by seizing the property of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall attain the state of a Brahma-rākṣasa.

Whatever one may steal, that very thing shall become empty for him in another birth; furthermore, after having suffered torment for a long time in the Forest of Sword-Leaves (Asipatravana), [he shall experience the same loss].
A man who violates the bed of his guru shall become a eunuch, tormented by the servants of Yama with glowing rods of black iron.
One who violates another's wife shall dwell in the hell named Kālasūtra; one who sets fire to a dwelling shall dwell in the Ghora hell, and a giver of poison in the Sughora hell.
The slanderer shall dwell in Mahāghora, the reviler of the Dharma in Avīci; the betrayer of friends in Karāla, and he who is solely intent on violence in Bhīma.
In Saṃhāra he dwells as a most wicked person who conceals his sins; in Bhayānaka, as a liar; and in Asighora, he may even dwell as one who steals men, fields, water-wells, and so forth.

O twice-born one, he who delights in harming others is Vajra; he who eats meat is Tarala; he who betrays his mother and father is Tīkṣṇa; and he who corrupts the recitation of mantras is Tāpana. || 11 ||
The killer of a horse shall dwell in Nirucchvāsa, the killer of a cow in Dāruṇa, the destroyer of a fetus in Caṇḍa, and the perpetrator of the murder of a woman in Kukūlaka.
The stealer of a deity’s property, the one who burns with terrible terrors, and the thief of another's wealth—all these sinners indeed become messengers of Kṛtānta in hell. || 13 ||
They bind with nooses, strike with clubs, and pierce with stakes; there are herons with sharp iron beaks and great serpents with cruel fangs.
Kāleyas, tigers, and other predatory beasts bite them; they tear them to pieces with weapons and even burn their bodies.
They are dug into deep pits and beaten with whips; they are cooked in vats of oil and pierced by fine needles.
Indeed, the messengers of Yama drag the sinners along with burdens difficult to bear; the killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption, and the drinker of liquor shall have blackened teeth.
A stealer of gold has deformed nails; one who violates the teacher's bed has diseased skin; one who betrays the teacher suffers from epilepsy; and a defiler of the Vedas becomes a Caṇḍāla. || 18 ||
A false witness suffers from eye disease; one who eats before others has weak digestion; a stealer of knowledge becomes mute; and a thief of books becomes blind.
One who is devoted to another's wife becomes lame; one who reviles others becomes deaf; one who lacks proper conduct becomes a village pig; and a thief suffers from diseases of the tongue.

One who abandons guests and visitors becomes one with a goiter on the cheek; one who indulges in women on sacred festival days becomes a sufferer of urinary disorders; and one who eats forbidden food becomes foul-mouthed.

One who violates established boundaries becomes a slave; one who destroys tanks, gardens, or lakes becomes a donkey; one who fails to give what was promised becomes short-lived; and one who is boastful becomes a dog.
One who betrays Viṣṇu becomes a chameleon, and one who betrays Śiva becomes a mouse; having thus understood the fruit of such sins, one should perform expiation.
And that [rite] should be properly performed by the faithful in this field of Aruṇa.
Having thus heard of the manifold sufferings of evildoing men in the hells, he then fell at his feet and repeatedly entreated him for the means of their pacification.
Nandikeśvara said: Today I shall describe in detail the expiation for all great sins; listen with an attentive mind, maintaining a faithful conviction.
A slayer of a Brahmin, having reached Śoṇādri and immersed himself in the Khaḍgatīrtha, recites the five-syllabled mantra while wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads. || 2 ||
Having observed a fast and worshipped the Supreme Lord with self-restraint, he should feed Brāhmaṇas for a year, subsisting on alms and keeping his senses controlled.
One should perform special worship and service to the God with devotion; liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Even a drinker of liquor, dwelling for one year in the field of Aruṇa while maintaining his conduct as before, shall likewise worship Maheśvara.
One should bathe the deity with milk while reciting the Śatarudrīya; one is thereby swiftly liberated from the sin arising from the drinking of liquor.
One who has committed the theft of gold, having worshipped Hara with bilva leaves at Śoṇakṣetra and fed the Brahmins, shall be liberated from that difficult-to-overcome sin.
Having gone to Aruṇācala during the Kṛttikā constellation, one who was devoted to his teacher’s wife should become a practitioner of vows as before and [worship] with a thousand lamps.
Having propitiated Śrī Śoṇācala Śaṅkara for three months, one should give a decorated maiden to a wise Brāhmaṇa.
One should recite the six-syllabled mantra daily; by that, one is liberated from evil and shall dwell in the world of Śiva for as long as saṃsāra lasts—of this there is no doubt.
And one who has stolen another's wife, having restrained his senses in this sacred field, should worship Aruṇa-Śaṅkara for one month with fresh flowers.
One should bestow wealth upon the devotee of Maheśvara according to one's capacity; at that very moment, one shall be completely liberated from that sin.
Even a poisoner, having become a practitioner of vows in Aruṇakṣetra as before, is freed from the fault after offering an oblation of milk to the God.

Even a man who was previously a slanderer, if he becomes a practitioner of vows at Aruṇakṣetra and is devoted to the Vedas, should teach the foremost among the twice-born; thereby he shall become free from sin.

Even one who has set fire to a house shall, observing the vow as before, dwell for three months in the field of Aruṇa; for the pacification of that sin, he should construct a house and give it to a devotee of Śiva.
One who has reviled the Dharma, while observing a vow for a year in the Śoṇa-kṣetra, should perform sacrificial sessions and other rites according to his capacity for the pacification of his sins.
One who has committed patricide should remain in the field of Aruṇa for a month without indolence, and should bestow thousands of cows upon Girīśa and upon the twice-born.
During times of eclipses of the planets, having fed many twice-born brahmins, one should release a dark-blue bull; thereby, one shall be liberated from sin.
Even a killer of a woman or a killer of a child, having reached the field of Śoṇa, should give sesame seeds to the twice-born during the Vyatīpāta yoga for the destruction of his evil deeds.
In this Śoṇa-kṣetra, one who has restrained his senses and conceals his evil deeds should perform secret acts of charity; thus he shall indeed become free from sin.
A practitioner of vows who dwells for six months in Aruṇakṣetra, having abandoned false speech, shall become free from sin through the recitation of the hymn to Śoṇācaleśvara.
Having reached the Śoṇa region, which destroys the sins of wells and other such works, one should devoutly have tanks excavated there; thus, one will certainly become free from all affliction.
One who seizes a field should give a field to the deity for great fruit; even one who thorns at the grove should give an excellent garden to him.
One who has stolen a house should construct a new temple for the God; liberated from that sin, he shall attain union with Śiva. || 24 ||
One who harms others, by dwelling in the field of Śoṇa and gratifying the devotees of Maheśvara with wealth, shall undoubtedly attain the highest worlds. || 25 ||
Having eaten the flesh of animals and the like, the observer of the vow should propitiate Aruṇeśāna for three fortnights in the Śoṇa field with delightful offerings.
One who dwells in the sacred field of Aruṇa and worships Aruṇeśvara becomes sinless by thrice uttering the cry, "O Lord of Śoṇācala! || 27 ||
One who desires liberation should devoutly recite the mantra of Aruṇeśvara; whatever has been prescribed by him, that one should perform on foot alone.

By performing this, one will swiftly attain that auspicious state belonging to the Mountain of Dawn (Aruṇaśaila) in the event of lapses in what has been heard, or in the occurrence of great calamities and the sight of evil dreams. (29)
Even when there is an excess of passion, the wise should invoke Aruṇaśaṅkara; so too even one who has fallen from his caste and stage of life, or even one devoted to harming Śiva.
Dwelling for three days in the field of Aruṇa, one is liberated from sins; this is the earthly world of Śiva, the personified head of the Triple Veda.
This is Dakṣiṇakailāsa, which is the mountain of Varuṇa; in other fields of perfection, men attain supernatural powers through austerities.
By the mere remembrance of this, let the gradation be considered: that which is [attained] at Prayāga on the Gaṅgā, that which is at Kāśī, and indeed that which is at the Puṣkaras.
Whatever merit men obtain at the Karma-setu in Śoṇakṣetra, even more than that is obtained at Agniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, Vairāja, and Sarvatomukha. || 34 ||
A wise man should perform the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices at Śoṇācala; for what a man would gain by fasting for a single day in the Vāruṇa field [is equal to that]. || 35 ||

For him, there shall be the merit of a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts and ten thousand Sāntapana penances; moreover, he obtains the fruit of the sixteen great gifts (mahādānas) in the vicinity of Aruṇakṣetra.
When performed according to the Kalpa, they yield double the fruit. || 37 ||

Having thus heard from the mouth of Nandikeśvara the remedy for hell, the son of the sage (Nārada) praised him and requested: "Tell me the sequence of offerings appropriate for the days, seasons, years, and so forth. (38)
Nandikeśvara said: He who worships the Lord of the Crimson Mountain with red lotuses on a Sunday will certainly attain the great prosperity of a sovereign emperor.
Whoever worships the Lord of Aruṇādri on a Monday with musk and oleanders shall find a place of happiness in Satyaloka.
For one who worships Śoṇeśa with white lotuses on Thursdays, there will be a long residence in Janaloka together with the Siddhas.
On Friday, one should worship with *caṃpaka* and *mallikā* flowers; thus praised by the Brahmanical sages, one shall attain the world of *tapas*.
And on a Sunday, by worshipping Aruṇeśvara with jasmine flowers, even a most sinful person will never be destined for the realms of Yama. || 5 ||
On the first lunar day, one should offer an oblation to the God with milk-rice; he shall become prosperous with wealth and grain.
He who with devotion offers curd-rice on the second lunar day shall become most fortunate and excellent, and he will certainly become a drinker of the Soma juice.
And he who shall fully satisfy Śoṇeśa with cakes on the third lunar day, his health shall remain unimpaired throughout his entire life.
On the fourth [lunar day], he who offers to Aruṇeśa a full water-pot, heaps of grain, and other such gifts, shall have his heart's desire fulfilled.
On the fifth day, one should devoutly offer an oblation of rice cooked with mung beans to Śoṇeśvara; he who does so shall possess imperishable majesty.
On the sixth lunar day, one should devoutly offer rice cooked with jaggery to Śambhu at Aruṇācala; for him who does so, his lineage shall never decline.
He who offers sesame-rice to Śoṇeśa on the seventh lunar day, even if he be wretched, effortlessly casts off the state of being a debtor.
On the eighth lunar day, he who offers rice from the *rājaśāli* variety to Śoṇaśambhu shall have the world of kings brought under his control, even without rendering service to them.
Whoever offers wheat-rice to the Lord of Śoṇādri on the ninth lunar day, consumption and other such diseases shall never afflict him.
He who offers *karaṃbha* to the Lord of Śoṇa on the tenth lunar day shall always become a vessel of affection for all people. (15)
Whoever should offer oblations of flattened rice to the Lord of Aruṇācala on the eleventh lunar day shall be free from fear from any quarter.
Whoever offers soup and rice to the Lord of Śoṇa on the twelfth lunar day, his heart's desire shall be free from obstacles.
He who offers parched grain (saktu) to Aruṇeśa on the thirteenth lunar day will experience mental agitation, even if he is not fatigued. || 18 ||
Whoever offers various kinds of fruits to the Lord of Śoṇa on the fourteenth day, even if he be a fool, shall become perfected in the power of Sarasvatī.
Whoever offers a jackfruit to the Lord of the Crimson Mountain on the full moon day, for that person no eye disease shall arise.
Whoever, with devotion, offers roots, tubers, and other such items at the confluence of the Kuhū river to the Lord of Śoṇācala, his ancestors indeed become satisfied.
On the Aśvinī [nakṣatra], the devotee should give garments to Aruṇeśa; on the Bharaṇī [nakṣatra], he should also give ornaments to Aruṇeśa.
One should offer lamps under the asterism Kṛttikā, silver under Rohiṇī, sandalwood from the Malaya mountains under Mṛgaśīrṣa, and yellow sandalwood under Ārdrā.
One should offer musk under the asterism Punarvasu, camphor under Puṣya, saffron originating from Kashmir under Āśleṣā, and cold water under Maghā.
Betel-leaf on Pūrvaphālgunī, incense on Uttaraphālgunī, black aloe-wood on the asterism Hasta, and yakṣakardama paste on Citrā; || 25 ||
In Svāti, one should give a group of married women; in Viśākhā, a fan; in Anurādhā (Maitra), a pearl-umbrella; and in Jyeṣṭhā, cows as well.
One should offer strings of pearls at the base during Pūrvāṣāḍhā, a crown during Uttarāṣāḍhā, and precious gems during Śravaṇa, as well as a noble throne during Bhadrapada.
One gains a chessboard under Dhaniṣṭhā, clothing under Śatabhiṣaj, enjoyments under Pūrvābhādrapadā, and horses under Uttarābhādrapadā. (28)
Under the asterism Revatī, a man should offer a golden chariot to Śambhu, who is accompanied by Śoṇa; having performed a great worship, he should then present it.
He is especially to be worshipped among the zodiac signs beginning with Aries in the eastern direction, respectively with sinduvāra, kurabaka, kakubha, and pāṭala flowers.
With *kuṭaja* flowers, *nīpa* blossoms, *jīvantī*, *mallikā*, and others; with lotuses, *damanaka* plants, and *nadyāvarta* lotuses. || 31 ||
During both eclipses, one should devoutly bathe Śoṇanātha with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) while reciting the five-syllabled mantra.

One should perform the bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) during both solstices; one should carry out the rite of bathing with the six-syllable mantra using the products of the cow.
One should perform the rite of bathing the Lord of Aruṇācala with milk using the syllable Om (praṇava) alone, out of devotion, on both equinoctial days.
In the forenoon, Rudratulasī is recommended for the Lord of Śoṇādri; at midday, Kṛtamālaka; and in the afternoon, Mallikā. 35.
And at the rising of the sun, one should bathe the Lord Śoṇācala-Śambhu with the waters of a thousand jars while reciting the Śatarudrīya. (36)
Especially on Śivarātri, one who keeps vigil with restrained senses should worship with three-pronged bilva leaves, lotuses, and karṇikāra flowers.
One should worship Maheśvara on Śoṇaśaila for the sake of liberation with songs, instrumental music, and dances, according to the divine scriptural injunctions.
In the month of Pauṣa, the wise man should perform the Āgneya festival for the Lord, reciting the Vyāhṛtis while offering fresh grains, side dishes, and other foods.
And in the month of Vaiśākha, under the asterism Viśākhā, one should perform the Damanaka festival for this Lord of Śoṇācala according to the Śiva-tantras.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at dawn, the devoted practitioner, having performed the Prābodhika rite with Sāman chants, should perform a great worship (mahāpūjā) of Śoṇaśaila.
On Saturdays, during the Ārdrā nakṣatra, at the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the lunar nodes (parvan), and on Mondays and Sundays, one should worship the Lord of Śoṇādri according to the scriptures.
A devotee of Śoṇanātha should perform special worship even on occasions such as initiation (dīkṣā), the sacred thread ceremony (upanayana), marriage, and the birth of a son. (43)
Furthermore, on one's own birth-star, in times of prosperity or adversity, in moments of fear, and during both entry and departure, Aruṇeśvara is to be worshipped.

One should perform the worship of Aruṇeśa during the arrival of the circle of initiates (vraticakra), at the binding of the feet [of an enemy], in times of new prosperity, and during military expeditions against foes.

If one is extremely far away, one should meditate [on Śiva]; if one has reached the vicinity, one should see Him; and if one is stationed in the field of Aruṇa, one should worship Śiva at the three times of day.
"O child, what else shall I say?"—so it is said as he raises his arm: "There is nothing other than the Aruṇa-kṣetra that is sufficient for both heaven and liberation. (47)
By remembering it, the mind and ears are purified; by hearing it, the eyes; and by reciting it, the tongue—the Śoṇa-kṣetra instantly and completely purifies them all. 48.
In this great field of Aruṇa, those embodied beings who have obtained birth therein attain worldly enjoyment while they live, and liberation once their lives have departed.
Except for those who have already attained liberation, even for men of sinful nature, final emancipation shall occur here through the performance of the śrāddha rite.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā, Dvārakā, and the sacred field of Aruṇa—Arbuda excels them all; of this there is no doubt. (51)
To the son of Śilāda who had spoken thus, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu replied once more: "O you of exalted fame, I ask you again about this greatness; tell it to me. (52)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Rituals for Specific Desires," in the latter half of the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya*, within the first section (*Māheśvara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Nandikeśvara said: O Mārkaṇḍeya, by your asking for the greatness of Aruṇācala in detail, I believe you have placed a great burden upon me.
O high-minded one, it is only fitting that your mind is captivated by curiosity; for that man who does not know the life-story of the Lord of Śoṇādri is but a beast.
Or how could it be possible to speak, even by one who knows it in its entirety, of the greatness of Śambhu, who dwells on the Crimson Mountain (Śoṇācala), whose arising is glorious?
Or else, how could even this which has been heard be fully comprehended by those preeminent in wisdom, even though they are steeped in the flavor of the marvelous? (4)
Now, remember the wonderful conduct of the enemy of Smara; truly, my mind dances as if through the experience of supreme nectar. (5)
My intellect is simply unable to describe in its entirety the wondrous conduct of Śiva, which captivates the mind.
Nevertheless, O Sage, I shall proclaim according to my understanding this meritorious majesty of the Lord of Śoṇādri, part by part; let it be heard.
At the beginning of the Purāṇa-Ādideva Kalpa, the non-conceptual Maheśvara, by his own will, brought forth the entire universe once again.
Desiring to create and protect that manifested universe at all times, that primordial deity brought forth Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
The three-eyed Lord created Parameṣṭhin from his right side, and the God created Viṣṭaraśravas from his left side.
He joined Brahmā with rajas and Viṣṇu with sattva; thus both Virañci and Acyuta were appointed by the God of gods.
He exercises lordship over the creation and preservation of all the worlds; by his mind alone, he created ten Brahmins, beginning with Marīci.
And from his right thumb, the Creator brought forth Dakṣa for the sake of creation; from his mouth he produced the Brāhmaṇas, from his two arms the Kṣatriyas, and from his thighs the Vaiśyas.
And the lotus-seated one himself created the Śūdras from his feet; from Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, were born the Asuras and the Suras.
The Maruts, the serpents, the vultures, the Gandharvas, and the Apsarases, as well as Manu, from whose lineage this human race proceeds. || 15 ||
Having become various non-relatives and engaging in various activities, there arose here two kinds of lineages: the Ārṣa and the Kṣātra.
From Pulastya and Pulaha were born the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas; and from the sage Aṅgiras were born the sons headed by Utathya and Gīṣpati.
From Bhṛgu, Agni was born, as well as the ṛṣis headed by Cyavana; and from those led by Vasiṣṭha, the great ṛṣis were born, by whose sons and grandsons this entire world is filled.
Thus Brahmā filled this world with his own self-born sons; in the course of time, even through their great power, they forgot Maheśvara.
Even Acyuta, having married the daughter of Bhṛgu who dwells in the lotus, manifested in the world in forms such as the Fish and others, yet he did not remember the Lord.
Surely, having attained independence through the acts of creation and sustenance, Brahmā and Viṣṇu felt extreme pride; for what man would not become intoxicated by power? (21)
Nandikeśvara said: Between the two of them, who were deeply rooted in excessive pride, each thinking "I alone am the Lord," there arose a dispute born of delusion, even involving Virañci.

Exceeding [all others] in the transformations of his passion (rajas), appearing externally like a rising blue [cloud], and performing the creation of the universe, Virañci spoke to Viṣṇu out of pride: || 2 ||
Brahmā said: O Viṣṇu, how is it that you are superior even to me, your progenitor? Why are you so utterly deluded regarding the Grandfather of the worlds?
"O Keśava, having slain the two Daityas Madhu and Kaiṭabha who arose from none other than yourself, you, O deluded one, carry the pride of being the 'Foe of the Daityas'."
Even now, the hands of me, the Creator, who eternally create you alone in manifold ways, do not abandon the pain born of exertion.
For me, who am sinking into a great ocean produced by the water of my own exhaustion, not even a banyan tree has arisen; how then can there be a support for you?
In this great ocean conceived by me, a certain serpent flows; you are his support, and above you is the lotus, which is my seat.
Tell me, how can there be the arising of the quality of *sattva* in you, who are composed of *tamas*; do you, being utterly dull from the stupor of sleep, even know what *prakṛti* is?
O Janārdana, while you were sleeping in the ocean out of fear of the Daityas, how was this triple world, which is under my control, protected by you?
From my four mouths, the Vedas have emerged; my wife is Sarasvatī, whose nature is consciousness and who is my Śakti.
For by me indeed is this entire universe, both stationary and moving, created; and it is protected by my sons and grandsons, beginning with Indra.
Therefore, O Vaikuṇṭha, tell me: among those appointed by me, how indeed can you, a lord of the worlds, be superior to me?
Nandikeśvara said: While Brahmā was thus speaking with words of human pride, full of wrathful agitation, Nārāyaṇa also, smiling with disdain, spoke as follows.
Viṣṇu said: O Virañci, abandon your agitation; you indeed boast in vain. Understand this: you were born from the lotus of my navel.
"Formerly, when I cast off my yogic sleep, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were crushed by me; had they not been so destroyed, you too would have been utterly annihilated. (15)
Who else, indeed, could be the cause of creation for me, who by my own will assumed the forms of the fish and others in order to slay the Daityas headed by Somaka?
Those whose vision is obscured by passion do not see anything at all; what is it that can possibly be discerned by you, who are composed of passion? (17)
Indeed, my power, the dweller in the lotus, is inseparable from me; by her mere sidelong glance, the three worlds flourish. (18)
These are the elements, this is time, and even I am indeed the Self; what, then, exists within the three worlds that is devoid of me? (19)
O Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Guardians of the Quarters, and Manus, as well as I myself—contemplate this triad of worlds, Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar, as being under my control.
"By my own command, the power of creation itself remains established; so, for me, the lord of the three worlds, are you my elder brother or my equal? (21)
Nandikeśvara said: Thus, as their minds were blinded by delusion and they roared at one another, a vast period of time passed for them, like that of the universal dissolution.
At that time, there would be neither the rising nor the setting of the moon and the sun; the lunar mansions, the stars, and the planets all fell into decay.
The Maruts did not blow, nor did the fires blaze; neither the atmosphere, nor the earth, nor even the quarters of the sky shone forth.
All the oceans were agitated and the mountains trembled; the medicinal herbs withered away and living beings perished.
The regulation of time—consisting of fortnights, months, seasons, years, and so forth—has passed away; even the established order of day and night has met with destruction. (26)
Then Indra and the other guardians of the world, as well as Marīci and the other great sages, all considered the end of the kalpa to have arrived prematurely.
When such a great upheaval had arisen, impelled by the universal cry of distress, the Lord of Beings perceived that the world was born within ignorance.
And the Soul of the Universe, intent on protecting the world, reflected; with his internal vision, he perceived the cause of their delusion.
Having forgotten me, their master and the bestower of all sovereignty, these two, arrogant with pride, consider themselves to be the lords of the world.
Oh, how great is the power of delusion! Even though they know me perfectly well, these two, Druhiṇa and Acyuta, have become so arrogant toward me as if I were non-existent.
A person whose eye of the mind is defiled by the arising of the cataract of ignorance generally does not perceive a reality that has been attained and even praised. (32)
"Even though these two have committed offenses and are submerged in the ocean of delusion, they must not be neglected by me, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (33)
Having thus resolved in his mind, the Lord, that great ocean of compassion, desired to dispel the state of helplessness caused by Māyā for these two.

Oh, how great is the innate compassion of the one who bears the young moon upon his crest throughout these three worlds! For he has appeared from the midst of the ocean of delusion, even though Brahmā and Viṣṇu had already manifested themselves.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispute between Śiva and Viṣṇu," in the latter half of the Aruṇācala-māhātmya, within the first section (Māheśvara-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "Command me, O Lord, how the eternal Śambhu favored Vaikuṇṭha and Parameṣṭhin, who were blinded by delusion."
Nandikeśvara said: Listen; I shall tell you everything in detail, exactly as it is, just as the Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees, ordained out of compassion.
Then, while the two were thus disputing, there arose between them a pillar of light that blocked the opening between heaven and earth.
By the great yawning of that [being] who was splitting the cosmic egg, the atmosphere became intensely dark, as if it had been tossed upward.
By the splendor of that Jyotirliṅga, all directions suddenly shone forth, appearing as if they had been extended far and wide. || 5 ||
As if dried up by his intense, great flames, the oceans, having abandoned the agitation of their waves, returned to their own natural state.
In the sky, as before, the planets shone along with the hosts of stars, like certain sparks bursting forth from the pillar of light.
Stained by his blood-red splendor as if by red chalk, all the mountains bore the beauty of Mars and the sun.
The oceans, their aquatic creatures embraced by the intense reflections [of the sun], shone as if they were carved from blocks of ruby stone.
The trees shone as if draped with fresh clusters of coral, and the rivers gleamed as if filled with fully blossomed white water-lilies.
The earth appeared as if smeared with saffron, the quarters as if colored with vermilion, and the entire sky was seen to have become entirely crimson.
The shell of the cosmic egg became filled with that great light, like the skull-bowl of the hide-clad Lord (Śiva) filled with blood.
As that column of splendor thus continued to expand, the entire universe, both stationary and moving, assumed the appearance of dawn.
Having seen that wondrous fiery linga, the four-faced Brahmā and the four-armed Viṣṇu abandoned their mutual anger and each reflected within themselves.
Has this mass of the luster of the rubies on the hoods of Śeṣa and the other hood-bearing serpents burst through the earth and risen upward? (15)
Or are these twelve suns, whose appearance is normally found only at the end of an eon, risen simultaneously between heaven and earth? (16)
Or perhaps, due to the friction of clouds, they have spread across the middle of the sky and, meeting one another, fall swiftly upon the surface of the earth? (17)
Striking with his splendors at every moment, he increases, making the entire multitude of beings indistinguishable from himself.
Though blazing intensely, this [knowledge] does not lead to suffering; like fire, it does not consume even the beings closest to it.
Not only the entire world, but even my own body has attained a crimson hue through the transfer of his radiance—how wonderful! (20)
From what has this arisen? What is its root? What is its limiting condition? From where does it come? What is its material cause? And by what devotion is it manifested? (21)
What is the extent of this [mountain] on all sides—horizontally, across, and upwards—and how deep does it penetrate into the netherworld (pātāla)? What is its total measure? || 22 ||
My mind, eager to know all of this, repeatedly desires to fly up into the sky and plunge down into the netherworld. (23)
Thus, overwhelmed by the weight of their anxiety upon beholding the pillar of light, both Vaikuṇṭha and Parameṣṭhin were struck with wonder.
And Govinda, his lotus-face smiling, looked toward Hiraṇyagarbha and spoke with even greater pride: || 25 ||
Viṣṇu said: "O Brahman, for us two who desire to excel one another, this very truth has appeared as a touchstone for the sake of testing. (26)
It is certain that neither of us alone is able to know the beginning and the end of this mass of splendor, whose wealth is immeasurable. (27)
Whoever should perceive the root or the summit of this self-existent splendor, he alone is not inferior to us, nor is he even the lord of the worlds.
Nandikeśvara said: Thus, both of them, their intentions firmly resolved, exerted themselves against one another in rivalry to behold the root and the summit of that mountain of immense splendor. (29)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Effulgent Liṅga between Brahmā and Viṣṇu," in the latter half of the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya*, within the first section (*Māheśvara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 10.
Nandikeśvara said: Then Virañci, making an effort with the thought, "I shall see its peak," took to the form of a swan capable of traversing the path of the sky. || 1 ||
Viṣṇu, whose body is firm, assumed the form of a boar—a manifestation whose majesty was easily attained through the sport of piercing through the earth that sustains the universe.
Having thoroughly understood its root and being eager to turn back, this one with artificial stiff bristles struck the earth with his two tusks.

Tearing asunder the earth with his snout while facing downwards, the Great Boar appeared like a pillar of splendor bowing down; filling the netherworld with the deep throat-sound of his playfully grunting, he, possessed of great vigor, began to enter it. || 5 ||
Wherever he entered, there the jackal of deceit beheld that very same pillar of fire standing exactly as it was before.
From the fissure in the earth, certain serpents such as Śeṣa and others were seen emerging like sprouts from the pillar of splendor.
The primordial tortoise was seen by Acyuta, appearing like the root-tuber situated at the base of the golden mountain, having become its very foundation.
Not far away, at the foothills of the earth, the elephants of the quarters are seen standing as if bearing the burden of the world, their gait slow with rut and their forms majestic.
And that great frog was also beheld by the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu), upon whose back the entire, unbroken orb of the earth is established.
Adhokṣaja also beheld that foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), by whose grace even Śeṣa, Kūrma, and the others are able to bear the burden of the world.
These are Aṭala, Vitala, Sutala, Nitala, Talātala, Pratala, and Mahātala, in that order.
The lotus-eyed one beheld even the seven netherworlds (pātālas), and with wonder, he observed all those beings therein who possessed various forms.
He passed through the city named Bhogavatī as well as Vairocanī, and entered other, most inaccessible dwellings of the Daityas.
"This has been seen! This has been seen!"—with curiosity thus aroused, Mādhava, whose mind was still that of an innocent youth, began to search for its source. (15)
Even when pressed down from below by that boar into the depths of the ocean, that pillar of fire was seen to remain exactly as it was, without any change.
The earth alone was crushed and the ocean agitated; yet the root of that [earth] was not seen by Viṣṇu in the form of a boar. || 17 ||
Thus, for thousands of years, his mind utterly bewildered by delusion, Līlākroḍa was unable to perceive its root.
With its hooves shattered, its tusks crushed, its body mangled, and its snout broken, that earth-dweller experienced intense exhaustion.
As he sighed from exhaustion, that unrestrained pride of his perished at that very moment along with his desire to investigate its root.
Although his vow was not yet fulfilled, the lotus-eyed one was eager to turn back; nevertheless, he could not bear to move even a single step from his place.
For him, whose eyes were blinded by exhaustion as he remained within the depths of Pātāla, that very light once again revealed the path.
Although he had somehow or other crossed the ocean from its far shore, the deceptive boar sank into the outflowing sea of sweat-water. (23)
As if bound by a rope, Janārdana turned back with difficulty from that forest, following the column of fire with its continuous radiance.
Because I did not perceive the root of this treasury of splendors, the Creator likewise could not see its summit in any way whatsoever. (25)
I shall return from that place where the origin of this mass of splendors first occurred, and go for refuge to Śiva, the Lord.
For that God, who is superior to all, has been forgotten by me for a long time due to my eyes being blinded by delusion; therefore, such a bitter consequence has arisen. (27)
Having thus discerned this, the lotus-eyed one, freed from pride, quickly turned back and reached that very spot where the pillar stood, radiating with splendor.
Nandikeśvara said: Then, following that pillar of light, the Grandfather (Brahmā) leaped upward with speed toward the face of the sky, which is without support.
As he leapt up swiftly, the surging waves were checked by the force of his wings and were scattered, as if driven away by the winds.
Leaping far away with great speed, he did not come within the range of his eyes; only a very long, elongated streak was perceived in the sky.
Māyāmara appeared beside the pillar of light, like the moon moving near the clouds at twilight.
First, the path of the rising clouds was traversed; then the track of the celestial chariots; and after that, the orbit of the stars.
That bird named Kuhaṇa swiftly overpassed those exceedingly lofty abodes of the luminaries that move in the upper regions.
The speed of even the Maruts or of the mind itself, which possesses an exceedingly subtle form, was surpassed by that swan through its flight and other movements.
And just as the bird with weary wings flew further and further away, so too did he behold that column of splendor rising ever higher.
Having surpassed the seven layers of the Maruts and attained a state of wonder, he pierced the shell of the cosmic egg and gazed upon that blazing [fire].
Or how can one whose root is unseen stand before Hari, failing to release Śauri from his state of having an incomparable head?
For one whose vow has not been fulfilled, what is the use of these long-lived breaths? What, then, would be the appropriate means here; what is the task to be done, and what is my course?
Who will be the ally of Viṣṇu as he seeks to deceive? He is not even capable of overcoming an opponent through mere straightforwardness.
"Or he might insult me through deceit; for pride is the wealth of the great. While Brahmā was thus reflecting with a troubled mind, [the Lord appeared]. 13.
In the sky, not very far away, something stainless was seen: "Is this the digit of the moon? How has it come here? (14)
"Or perhaps it is a lotus stalk; how could such a thing exist in this ocean, in the sky?"—while he was thus in doubt, that [lotus stalk] arrived nearby. (15)
The lotus-born Brahmā did not realize that the *ketakī* petal was stale; yet, by the inherent power of its substance, it rose up with fragrance. (16)
Hiraṇyagarbha took a stainless petal of the ketaka flower; as soon as it was taken by him, it reportedly spoke, endowed with consciousness.
Ketaka said: "O sir, for what purpose do you seize me? Let me go, for I am striving for rest after having flown thus through the sky for a hundred thousand years. (16)
Nandīśa said: Seeing him thus increasing in strength, the lotus-born Brahmā became distressed by the exertion; his purpose utterly frustrated, he reflected deeply. (19)
Though he has taken refuge even in lowliness, being one who does not abandon his vow, where is that mass of splendors which has filled the cavity between heaven and earth? (20)
In this investigation of his, where can my human effort prevail? My wings seem to break, my vision seems to grow blind, my limbs seem to fall away, and I myself seem to sink down below. (21)
What more need be said? Along with the winds of my sighs, my very life-breaths now seem to be departing for certain.
May this knot of egoism and pride be severed from the mind; and may that rivalry with Mukunda perish quickly.
That pillar of splendor, which exerts itself even more than the vast expanse of heaven and earth, still maintains its height as it did of old. (24)
Neither I nor Nārāyaṇa am the cause of this mass of splendor; even further removed are the other gods, headed by Mahendra.
"I have no power to fall from here; therefore, I shall turn back"—having thus resolved in his mind, the Creator was filled with wonder. (26)
He addressed him, asking, "Who are you, or from where have you come? And the petal of the ketaka flower replied to that creator.
By the command of Śiva, I became a conscious Ketakī petal and remained for a long time upon the head of this Śambhu, who is the pillar of light.
Then, with the desire to dwell in the world of mortals (bhūloka), I arrived there.
Having thus heard the words of the ketaka fiber and having gained consolation, that Lotus-born One indeed spoke to him, saying: "Tell me, at what distance is the top of that pillar of fire? (30)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cleansing of the Upper Portion of the Liṅga by Brahmā," in the latter half of the Aruṇācala-māhātmya, within the first section (Māheśvara-khaṇḍa) of the Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. || 12 ||
Nandikeśvara said: Even the Ketakī flower spoke again to him with a laugh. The Ketakī said: "O fool, do you not know anything? Who are you, and why do you not [know] that? (1)
Who is capable of knowing that its measure is this much, wherein such millions of cosmic eggs are attached on all sides? || 2 ||
Ten thousand cycles of the four ages have passed since I fell; even now, it seems, the surface of the earth has not reached my middle.
Having paid homage to him as he was speaking thus, the Lotus-born Brahmā, casting aside his own ego, spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Brahmā said: O Great-souled one, it is indeed true; I am a fool, O Ketaka leaf! For I have indeed engaged in rivalry with Viṣṇu, who is Brahman. || 5 ||
Both of us have forgotten this majesty of Śiva, because we became excessively proud merely by the act of creating and protecting the world.
Let alone that shameful conversation; for even now I am not free from the rivalry I have bound myself to with the one who has Garuda as his banner.
For friendship is said to be formed by walking seven steps together; that is what you have with me.
Setting aside your unaccustomed disposition, you ought to show me favor; for both Viṣṇu and I have been [saved] from the ocean of delusion by the mere sight of the pillar of splendor.
The two of them, appearing like a swan and a crocodile, strove to dispel each other's equality, wishing to see whose root was superior and what state the other had reached.
I do not know what state such as this has come upon me, who am desirous of seeing its tip; alas, a thousand years have passed while I have been flying upward.
"I am utterly exhausted, as if deprived of my very life-breaths. By good fortune, O auspicious one, you have been found by me today as a support for those who are sinking. (12)
Therefore, fulfill this request of mine, your friend; for I am your friend by our shared conversation and your servant by our association. (13)
This prayer has been made by me with palms joined in reverence; you must act accordingly. If he sees the root [of the tree], then I am defeated by him. (14)
Or when I do not see it, even then I have attained equanimity; both of these states, my friend, are generally a source of great shame for me. (15)
Now it has come upon you yourself that you must avoid [this truth]; speak an untruth, for it is appropriate for the sake of a friend. (16)
Utter this single speech before the wielder of the discus; this Brahmā, in the form of a swan, is the very embodiment of the pillar of light.
I beheld that exceedingly lofty summit; I stand here as a witness to this, even by that moon-crested Lord who has attained the state of a pillar of light.
For he has been highly esteemed by his grandfather, who was like a father to him; therefore, this Viṣṭaraśravas is even greater than you. (19)
Having said this, "Let very great assistance be rendered by you to me. (20)

Nandikeśvara said: Thus further entreated by the Creator, even that Ketakī flower, moist with courtesy, spoke the entire word of Brahmā in the same manner to Viṣṇu, who was standing near the column of light.
Nandikeśvara said: Beholding Brahmā, he, possessing discernment, smiled twice as much as before and concluded, "He has not seen the tip."
"He alone, the God of gods and the Sustainer of all beings, is capable of showing favor to me, a deluded man, and of destroying the pride of this Creator," he thought.
I believe that my pride regarding the pillar of light—which I was unable to perceive in its entirety—has indeed vanished today, since devotion to Tryambaka has arisen within me.
Now that Great Lord (Maheśvara) is praised because he is free from pride—he, from whose right and left limbs we two have originated.
Even now, because his pride has not yet vanished, this Hiraṇyagarbha, having obtained a false witness, desires to thus deceive me. (5)
Therefore, today, he alone—Śaṅkara, who is capable of removing all suffering—is to be sought by me as my refuge. (6)
Likewise, for one who has committed an offense, who is ungrateful, and who betrays his guru—who else but Him is the protector? I praise that very Śaṅkara.
Viṣṇu said: Victory to you whose form consists of the earth; victory to you whose form consists of the waters! Victory to you whose form is the sun; victory to you whose form is the moon! || 8 ||

Victory to you, O one whose form is Vaiśvānara; victory to you, O one whose nature is the bearer of fragrance! Victory to you, O one whose form consists of the Hotṛ priests; victory to you, O one whose nature is composed of space! 9.
Protect me, O You who transcend the three qualities; protect me, O You whose form is Time; protect me, O You of imperishable sovereignty; protect me, O Mine of Compassion. 10.
You are the creator of all worlds, the protector of all embodied beings, and the destroyer of all creatures; who else exists besides you? (11)
You are subtler than the subtlest atoms, and you are greater than the greatest; pervading this entire universe, you exist both within and without.
The Vedas are Your breath; the universe is the manifestation of Your artistic power. You are that very same being, belonging to Yourself; O Lord, knowledge is Your very self.
The immortals, the Dānavas, the Daityas, the Siddhas, the Vidyādharas, and men; all living beings, birds, mountains, and even the peacocks—you alone are they indeed. (14)
You are heaven, you are liberation; you are the syllable Om, you are the sacrifice; you are yoga, you are supreme consciousness—O Lord, what is it that you are not? 15.
You are the beginning, the middle, and the end of all things, both stationary and moving; having assumed the nature of time, you impel the entire universe.
The Supreme Lord, the teacher beyond all, the auspicious one who bestows grace upon everyone—how can this very Dhūrjaṭi become manifest before my eyes? (17)
Having seen whom one attains refuge and achieves the supreme good; or rather, I praise that Abode as it was when first born, just as it is now. || 18 ||
"Having heard that, this Śruti will surely show compassion in every way"; having thus resolved, Vaikuṇṭha began to offer praise.
Having bowed down to that very Lord of the universe, the Supreme Ishvara, who is the pillar of light and devoid of beginning, middle, or end, he—though being forcibly restrained by Viranchi—smiled.
Śrī Viṣṇu said: Victory to you, O God, Great God, Vāmadeva, whose banner is the bull; O destroyer of Time, destroyer of the sacrifice, blue-throated one, whose crest is the moon! (21)
Victory to you, O Śambhu, Śiveśāna, Śarva, Tryambaka, Dhūrjaṭi, enemy of Smara, foe of Pura, Sthāṇu, Bhava, Maheśvara! 22.
Victory to you, O Lord, wielder of the axe, bearer of the trident, Paśupati, Hara! O omniscient Bharga, Lord of beings, Kapālin, Nīlalohita!
Victory to you, O Rudra, enemy of the sacrifice, wielder of the Pināka bow, lord of the Pramathas, bearer of the Gaṅgā, whose hair is the sky, lord of the mountains, supreme sovereign! 24.
Victory to you, O Bhīma, hunter of deer, wearer of animal skins, ocean of compassion! You indeed dwell eternally upon Kailāsa, O you whose seed is fire.
By your command, the wind blows, the serpent bears the burden of the earth, the sun and moon shine, and the cosmic egg floats upon the ocean. (26)
O Lord, by your command all the luminaries move through the sky; I and Brahmā are capable of the creation and preservation of the worlds. (27)
Having fashioned it for the sake of nourishment, the earth produces crops; yet that which is your own immutable boundary is not transgressed, for that is indeed your majesty.
How could I disregard you, who possess the extraordinary majesty of the great supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and are praised by other immortals? (29)
In times of prosperity we forget you, yet we remember you even in times of distress; you never feel anger toward your devotees, for your grace is ever-present.
When you desire to destroy [the world] and when you choose to favor it with devotion, then delusion and awakening arise for men as bondage and liberation.

Thus praised by the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), who stood with palms joined in reverence, while the lotus-born (Brahmā) was mocked and rendered arrogant by pride, the Treasure of Compassion appeared.
Nandikeśvara said: Having pierced through the pillar of light like the moon emerging from an evening cloud, he mounted the king of bulls, which was as white as the peaks of Kailāsa. || 1 ||
