Nandikeśvara said: At that time, having heard from somewhere that [the Goddess] was present there, Mahiṣāsura arrived—he who had treated the enemy of the gods with contempt and had destroyed Purandara.
Victorious over all the worlds and terrifying to the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, he was difficult to subdue even by all manner of weapons and missiles, owing to his boon.
He has become beyond the reach even of the most fierce curses; he is frequented by the Dānavas, Daityas, and Kauṇapas who are full of pride.
A defiler of the wives of sages and a destroyer of the path of Dharma, he was more powerful than Puloman, Namuci, and even Vṛtra. || 4 ||
A servant of Hiraṇyakaśipu, like another Hiraṇyākṣa, he reportedly dispatched a certain female messenger to entice her.
Then, wearing the garb of an ascetic woman, she spoke these improper words to Girijā in the very presence of her friend.
O timid one, why do you dwell here in this forest so full of terrifying beasts? You are better suited to sport in the delightful chambers of the inner apartments.
For what reason has your mind today, though in the prime of youth, become indifferent to enjoyments and fixed upon asceticism—a path difficult even for the gods to practice?
O lady of tender limbs, why do you sleep upon rough stones, having abandoned a bed made of swan-down with a canopy of pearls?
By good fortune, Śiva, who is rendered sluggish by his asceticism, has already been abandoned by you; indeed, there is no one else among the gods who is a worthy match for you.
However, there is Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas and protector of the three worlds; O fair-browed one, if you see him, you will surely abandon your asceticism in an instant.
What is the use of concealment? Indeed, having heard everything after a long time, that lord, afflicted by love, has dispatched me as a messenger to bring her here.
Perceiving that she was speaking such utterly contradictory and improper words, Vijayā understood the state of the Goddess’s mind and dismissed her.
And she, having made a vow out of extreme rage, assumed the form of a Daitya; going there and learning the news, she informed Mahiṣāsura.
Having heard all of that, his eyes becoming intensely red with rage, he approached, surrounded by tens of millions of Daityas, desiring to seize the Goddess.
With chariots, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers on all sides, he covered the earth, and with banners, he filled the expanse of the sky.
The sky seemed to burst asunder with their shouts and the sounds of musical instruments, while the surface of the earth split open from the stamping of the Daityas' feet.
Karāla, Durdhara, Vicaṣṇu, Vikarālaka, Bāṣkala, Durmukha, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and the Asura Amara; || 18 ||
Mahāhanu, Mahāmauli, Ugrāsya, Vikaṭekṣaṇa, Jvālāsya, and Dahana—these generals also set forth.
Hearing this clamor, the Goddess, apprehensive that her religious observance might be interrupted, commanded Durgā to slay the Daityas.
Having ascended the lion upon the secret glen of the Crimson Mountain, she was like Kālikā descended to the earth with her arms bearing blazing weapons.
With the corners of her mouth quivering and her sprout-like fingers twitching, she let out a lion’s roar as fierce as the thunder of a rain-cloud.
From their own limbs, the Mothers also wrathfully created thousands of Yoginī-circles, worthy of destroying the Daityas, for the pleasure of the Goddess. (23)
Some among them, possessing a ruddy luster, carrying staffs and riding upon swans, arrived with four faces whose lower lips were quivering with anger.
Some went forth in a rage, holding flaming tridents in their hands; with their ornaments jingling, their foreheads marked with the *paṃsa* sign, they rode upon bulls. 25.
Others emerged by the hundreds, accompanied by their armies and mounted on peacock-vehicles; they held spears, staffs, and gestures of fearlessness in their hands, and possessed six faces.
Mounted upon their Garuḍas with great fury, they went forth bearing conchs and discs, like the sun and moon from the sky.
Likewise, those borne by tigers, possessing the luster of blue lotuses, set forth, carrying maces and plows with their trunks which emit deep, gurgling roars.
With thousands of eyes red with rage, riding upon white elephants, and wielding hundreds of millions of sharp-edged spears, other supreme goddesses set forth. (29)
Some, mounted on horses and resembling flashes of lightning, rushed forward; bearing swords and shields, their faces were tawny with rage.
And those sixty-four crores [of Asuras] forcibly obstructed them outside the hermitage, just as the rays of the sun block masses of darkness.
Then, between the circle of Yoginīs and the army of the Dānavas, a terrible battle commenced, with hand-to-hand combat and hair-pulling.
The crests of the Daityas, shattered by the arrows released by the Yoginī, covered the surface of the earth on all sides like flowers growing upon the land.
Rivers of blood flowed forth, with locks of hair clinging like water-moss; they were filled with rolling elephants like pāṭhīna fish, stirred by the Cupids who were the lotus-faces of the goddesses.
Mounting the trunks of the elephants like female goblins ascending palaces, they shone forth with fierce dances, drinking wine of blood and flesh.
The hosts of yoginīs sport with skull-cups shaped like ḍamaru-drums, filled with the wine of the blood of wicked asuras and the heroes of the daityas.
Likewise, flocks of herons avoided the entrails, fearing they were nooses; and even though they were hungry, the jackals abandoned the meat because it was pierced by arrows.
The dust of the earth, raised by the agitation of battle, was laid to rest by the nectar from the mandāra blossoms scattered by the perfected vidyādharas. (38)
The horses of the enemies, struck by the arrows released by the heroic yoginīs that remained embedded in their bodies, were like porcupines with their quills bristling from excessive indignation.
Some were struck with staffs, others with sharp spears, some with javelins; others with discuses, some with plows, and a few with hundred-edged axes.
By the swords of the yoginīs, the lords of the dānavas were slaughtered until they reached total extinction, with the exception of their own commanders.
Brāhmī herself, having arrived in person after a long time, slew Karāla with her blazing, formidable staff in a battle she had prepared.
Māheśvarī, having engaged in battle for a very long time with her trident, became exceedingly wrathful and swiftly severed the head of Durdhara.
Kaumārī struck off the head of the Asura Cikṣura with her spear, and Vaiṣṇavī severed the crown of Vikarāla with her discus.
Vārāhī swiftly severed Bāṣkala’s head with her mace, and Aindrī quickly struck Durmukha with her thunderbolt, depriving him of his life.
Because she whose name is so renowned was free from fault, he [Śiva] cut off Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa with the edge of his discus.
The two heroes Pracaṇḍa and Cāmara, Mahāmauli and Mahāhanu, Ugrāsya and Vikaṭākṣa, as well as Jvālāsya and Dahana. (47)
Kālanemi and the other asuras followed Mahiṣāsura as he marched in anger for battle, just as they once followed Vipracitti.
Wearing helmets, equipped with excellent quivers, and wielding bows, the chariot-warriors—adorned with raised armlets and bearing fluttering banners—reached the field of battle.
Filling all directions with terrifying lion-roars, they rushed toward the circles of Mothers while raining down volleys of arrows.
Having engaged in battle with those powerful ones, they, being unable to withstand them, sought refuge with the goddess Durgā, who is mounted upon a lion.
Having spoken thus of the invincibility of that wicked-souled illusory buffalo, all seven Mothers praised Durgā, the Goddess, in this manner.
O Goddess, in the form of yogic sleep (yoganidrā), you sportively conceal yourself within the lotus-eyes of Viṣṇu, just as a bee hides there for its own purpose.
O Mother, Madhu and Kaiṭabha did not delude him in that manner; how then did Viṣṇu slay them with their very permission?
O Goddess Kauśikī, if you had not been born as the death of Śumbha and Niśumbha, how indeed would the sovereignty of the world-protectors have come to pass? (55)
O dweller of the Vindhya, what fruitless austerity could have been performed by the Vindhya mountains, wherein even friendship with the Kirāta women may be obtained by you?
O Mother, the Kāpiśāyana wine, which was offered as a gift by Kubera, has surely been drunk by you along with the juices of the Daityas and the restrained humans. (57)
O Mother, you manifest as the power of creation of Brahmā, the power of sustenance of Viṣṇu, and even the power of destruction of Rudra. 58.
Born from Yaśodā and Nanda, you shall be known by the name Ekānaṃśā; you will provide assistance to Hari in the destruction of Kaṃsa and the other demons.
You are knowledge, you are the Great Illusion, you are Lakṣmī, and you are Sarasvatī; you are even the goddess Pārvatī, O Durgā—what indeed do you not become?
Nandikeśvara said: By means of this hymn, Durgā herself, being pleased with the Mothers for the battle against Mahiṣāsura, granted them fearlessness and then set forth.
With a fierce spear-head he struck off the chowrie, with a small sword the great crown, and with a skull-topped mace the great jaw.
[He struck] Ugravaktra with an axe, Vikaṭacakṣus with a spear, Jvālāmukha with a mallet, and Dahana with a club.
Having slain Mahiṣa, she herself fought with wrath at his front; with a joyful heart, she let out a most terrible lion’s roar while wielding her discus.
Then, overcome with extreme indignation, the demon Mahiṣāsura pierced Durgā with arrows in the forehead, the breasts, and the shoulders.
Then Durgā, with great fury, struck the lord of the asuras on his arms, chest, and face with razor-sharp arrows possessing blazing tips.
Then the Daitya struck Durgā with three arrows in the face, five in each of the two arms, and two in each of the two eyes.
With one arrow Durgā struck the charioteer, with eight the horses, with three the bow, and with four she cut down his banner. 68.
Then the lord of the Daityas, standing on his chariot, hurled at Durgā a Śataghnī weapon of blazing form, resembling the staff of Death.
While the gods cried out "Alas! Alas! and the circle of Mothers fled in terror, Durgā playfully seized her as she was rushing toward them.
A sword, a goad, a noose, a bhuśuṇḍī, a small dagger, a spike, a spear, a mace, a discus, a javelin, a shield, and a hook.
He hurled a battle-axe, a bhindipāla missile, a sharp-edged spear, and a club at Durgā, like a cloud at the end of the world hurling a thunderbolt.
Seizing the very weapons thrown by her enemies as they fell upon her, she broke them at will with her hands, just as a female elephant breaks stalks of sugarcane.
Even the lion, difficult to approach, tore with his fangs that which was marked by the tip of the tail, while striking with his lotus-like claws.
Becoming a lion for a moment, a boar for a moment, a tiger for a moment, an elephant for a moment, and a buffalo for a moment, the Daitya fought with Durgā.
Then the buffalo, exceedingly provoked, struck the lion and the goddess repeatedly with his two sharp horns. (76)
For a moment he stood in the midst of the sky, for a moment he reached the surface of the earth; for a moment he was seen wandering through the quarters, and for a moment he vanished from sight.
Requested by the circle of Mothers, the smiling Durgā tore asunder the Dānava Mahiṣa with her unfailing trident.
Even as the Dānava fell with a loud, rattling roar, [Viṣṇu] forcibly placed his foot upon the seat of the demon's shoulder.
Then, seizing by the hand the severed head of that enemy of the gods, whose life had departed from being throttled by her neck, she danced.
Thus, when the demon Kāsarāsura—the sole thorn of all the worlds—was crushed by Durgā in battle, the gods danced, the great sages rejoiced, and the clouds rained down divine flowers.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Oh, such is the wickedness of the Daitya Mahiṣa! Oh, such is the prowess of Durgā, the remover of misfortune! (1)
When Mahiṣāsura had thus been slain by that Bhadrakālī, what did the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, who was established in penance, do?
Nandikeśvara said: Immediately thereafter, holding the head of the Daitya with one hand, she bowed to Gaurī while wielding a sword with her other hand.
Then, beholding her dancing with joy, the Goddess, whose teeth illuminated the sky, spoke to her with a gaze moist with compassion.
O dweller of the Vindhya mountains, you have performed an exceedingly difficult feat; by your power, my ascetic practice has become free from all obstacles.
Now, O you whose conduct purifies the world, you ought to cast this impure and terrifying buffalo head from your hand.
Thus addressed by Gaurī, Durgā, her mind filled with loathing, shook her hand repeatedly in order to strike him on the head.
"O Goddess, let a new sacred ford be created that destroys sin; by bathing in it, O Durgā, there shall be atonement."
Thus addressed by Gautama, Durgā, fearing misfortune, split the stone slab with her very sharp sword.
Then, from that rocky surface split open as far as the netherworld (pātāla), water with surging waves gushed forth, pure like a virtuous mind.
Today, she too, having uttered that unsurpassed mantra—“Obeisance to the Lord of the Crimson Mountain”—into those deep and purifying waters, [entered].
The Liṅga that was situated on the neck of Mahiṣa fell to the ground; it became established upon the bank under the name Pāpanāśana (the Destroyer of Sins).
Then Durgā, her sins washed away by the waters of the sacred ford, emerged; and then the head of Mahiṣāsura fell from his hand.
Having performed circumambulation and bowed to the Lord who destroys sins, she stood before him, greeted by Gautama and Gaurī.
Having thus observed her, who was visibly intent upon sin, Pārvatī, the daughter of the Mountain, spoke to Dīrghatapas.
In the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura, she directly gave her own consent; oh, this Vindhyavāsinī [assumed] the wicked form of a buffalo! 16.
Having seized it, he ate this auspicious linga of his; therefore, O best of sages, tell me what atonement I must perform as well.
Gautama said: O Goddess, you who cause the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire universe; meditation upon you alone is the destroyer of all the sins of the worlds. 18.
Moreover, even if you have spoken thus relying upon worldly custom, for even a boundary established by oneself is not transgressed by the great. (19)
O Mother, I shall now describe a certain practice that washes away the impurities of the internal organ; please grant your attention. (20)
This Aruṇādri is the mountain of fire itself, concealed [from view]; it blazes with its own light on the night of the full moon of Kṛttikā.
O Kātyāyanī, you must perform service to that [liṅga] and practice austerities; by beholding its light, everything you desire shall be accomplished for you. (22)
Having been addressed thus by Gautama, from that time forward this mother became formidable; yet she was indeed a devotee of Śiva and remained devoted to the worship of Śiva.
She performed penance, taking her station in the midst of five fires; standing between four flames, she fixed her gaze upon the sun.
The daughter of the Lord of Mountains shone like a golden needle; she appeared as if drawn forth by the long, outstretched cords of Pārvatī’s love.
That auspicious lunar day, the full moon of Kārttika, arrived; then, at the end of that day, on the peak of the Śoṇa mountain, [he stood].
A certain light, whose majesty was free from all limiting conditions, was beheld by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the others who had approached for that purpose.
It was being worshipped on all sides by gods accompanied by divine sages; it required no fuel, no oil, and was not produced from a wick or a vessel.

Beholding the Great Lamp, Pārvatī was struck with wonder; then, having performed circumambulations and bowing at every step, the daughter of the mountain, being highly pleased, praised the Lord of Aruṇādri.
Salutations to you, whose bow is Mount Meru, who dwell on the mountain Kailāsa, who are the son-in-law of the snowy mountain (Himavat), and who take the form of the Crimson Mountain (Śoṇa).
Salutations to the Lord of Aruṇācala, the embodiment of compassion, who is worshipped by the gods beginning with Varuṇa, and who possesses the splendor of the rising sun. || 31 ||
Victory to you, O Moon, whose crest is adorned by the daughter of Jahnu; you who have captivated the hearts of all the wives of the sages with your beauty! 32.
Victory to you, whose power of love is augmented by union with the Daughter of the Mountain; O Master, expert in the repeated play of the expansive manifestation of Māyā-Nārāyaṇa!
Victory to you, who perform the ecstatic *tāṇḍava* dance accompanied by the twilight; victory to you, worshipped by the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and vidyādharas! 34.

Victory to you, O father of Heraṃba! Victory to you, O lover of the six-faced one! Victory to you, who are prayed for by the daughter of Himavat! Victory to you, who are difficult for kings to attain! 35.
Having praised him thus, the bull-bannered god, seeing the goddess with her eyes fixed repeatedly upon that light, dissolved out of a pretext of compassion. (36)
Having set aside his own form and assumed an exceedingly beautiful one, and having mounted a divine bull, he beheld this auspicious Śivā.
Having thus abandoned all her sovereignty out of excessive pride and set herself to asceticism, the Lord of the Mountain proceeded once more to console the innocent daughter of the King of Mountains.
Nandikeśvara said: Then Brahmā was with Sarasvatī, Mahāviṣṇu with Padmā, Śakra with the daughter of Puloman, and the other guardians of the quarters as well.
The hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Vasus, the gods as well, the thirty-three crores of divine assemblies, and other groups of sages too [were present]. (2)
The eleven great Rudras, the twelve Ādityas, as well as the Bhairavas, Piśācas, Vetālas, and Kaṭapūtanas; || 3 ||
The yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, and bhūtas, as well as others who are servants of Śiva—all of them were filled with contentment, though they were enveloped in hideous forms and attire.
Surrounding Maheśāna, they arrived by the thousands; having seen that proclamation of the heroes made by the Yoginīs and the Dānavas.
Seeing the God who had manifested his presence—terrifying like the end of a kalpa and bringing joy to Umā—all were overcome with extreme wonder.
With her hair standing on end, her face perspiring, and trembling, she—possessing full breasts—abandoned the pain of separation from him that had been deeply rooted for a long night.

She placed her eyes upon his toes; then, having descended from the bull and taken her by the hand, Śiva, with a beauty of body, face, and neck suffused with a smile, spoke thus out of affection: 8. She placed her eyes upon his toes; then, having descended from the bull and taken her by the hand, Śiva, with a beauty of body, face, and neck suffused with a smile, spoke thus out of affection:
Śiva said: O Goddess, why are you thus distressed without any apparent cause?
"I have joined my palms in supplication so that she may be propitiated by all; do you not know our oneness, which is like that of moonlight and the moon? (10)
O Queen of the Gods, this such innocence of yours has been established since time immemorial; O Daughter of the Mountain King, where is this body of yours, so soft as a *śirīṣa* flower? (11)
Where indeed are austerities and meditations appropriate for one such as I? I am Nārāyaṇa, you are Lakṣmī; I am Brahmā, and you are Sarasvatī.
You are Vāruṇī and I am the lord of serpents; you are Rohiṇī and I am the Moon; you are Svāhā and I am the bearer of oblations; I am the Sun and you are Suvarcalā.
You are the Ganges and I am the ocean; I am Mount Meru and you are the fertile earth. You are Śacī, the daughter of Puloman, and I am Indra; you are Rati and I am the god of love, Kāma.

You are Buddhahood, and I am the king of kings; you are tranquility, and I am the wind; I am the lord of the ocean, and you are its wave; you are primordial nature (prakṛti), and I am the spirit (puruṣa). 15.
You are knowledge (vidyā) and I am that which is to be known; you are speech and Pārvatī is its meaning. I am the Lord (Īśvara), and you are my very portion, existing in the form of my command.
Since you are the Lord who ordains creation, preservation, dissolution, and grace, you should not make a distinction between us two as you would toward an ordinary person.
O Goddess, you who have assumed a body by your own will, you constantly agitate me—whose nature is consciousness and light—as if you were fruitlessly jealous of me. 18.
"The remedy for what has been seen by me is now being performed by me"—having said this, the Lord sat down and seated her at his side.
As if hiding Gaurī within her own body out of modesty, the two bodies of those two, merged through love, attained oneness.
Due to its proximity, it was perceived as if possessing two distinct meanings at once: one half white as camphor, the other half pinkish-red like vermilion.
That body of Śiva and Śivā, having attained oneness, became wonderful: in one half were locks of hair, while in the middle of the necklace was a key.
The body of the moon-crested Lord was adorned with a crescent-moon garment; it was enchanting, graced by a single anklet, an ear-ornament, and a necklace.
The body of Ekapiṅgala shone with a single breast; and having given it to the Goddess for the sake of her abode, Vāmadeva spoke to her: ||| 24 ||
O Goddess, let there be no room for anger toward me hereafter, since you have departed for asceticism, leaving Guha who seeks your breast-milk.
Therefore, dwell here near me under the name Apītastanī; [worship] you, the goddess Apītastanī, the Lord of Śoṇādri, and me as well.
May all people, having propitiated her, enjoy both worldly pleasures and liberation; for this Goddess Durgā, the slayer of Mahiṣa, is born from a portion of you.
May this very place be present here, bestowing the perfection of mantras upon men; for by bathing even once in this meritorious Khaḍgatīrtha, [one attains these fruits]. 28.
May this Lord of the Coral Mountain be the remover of all diseases for men, the destroyer of all sins, and the eradicator of evil. (29)
May this [account] bring about great prosperity for those men possessed of devotion and faith; and let this Gautama, O Goddess, be the recipient of your grace. (30)
May these seven Mothers, the sole mothers of the seven worlds, grant [their favor] to those who practice penance according to its rules throughout the worlds as long as the moon and stars endure.
From this day forward, may the Śāstṛs, the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, and the Baṭukas also grant their presence for the prosperity of the worlds.
"Let them always maintain their presence right here in Aruṇakṣetra; here in Aruṇakṣetra, I dwell, known by the name Aruṇa. (33)
You too, O Goddess Aruṇā, must remain here, moist with compassion; for it is because of you that the two deities, Aruṇa and Aruṇā, grant their presence to those who desire [their favor]. (34)
Therefore, in this field of Aruṇa, all supernatural powers (siddhis) are easily attained. || 35 ||

This act of propitiation of the Lord of Śoṇagiri was performed by the daughter of the Mountain King; whoever hears of it shall cast off his enemies and attain both heaven and liberation with ease. (36)

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva’s Praise of Pārvatī," in the latter half of the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya*, within the first section (*Māheśvara-khaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, a compendium of eighty-one thousand verses. 21.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: "O Lord, O Blessed One, eternal bliss of Śiva, O Aṇḍikeśvara! I have been delighted by you with the nectar of the majesty of Śoṇeśa."
How did Vajrāṅgada, the king of the Pāṇḍyas, commit the transgression regarding the Śoṇa river? And how, through that very devotion, did he again attain prosperity? || 2 ||
How were the two lords of the Vidyādharas, Kāntiśālin and Kalādharin, who had been pierced by the curse of Durvāsas, protected by Śoṇa and Śambhu? (3)
Nandikeśvara said: "O son of Mṛkaṇḍu, you have attained the true fruit of long life, since this most steadfast devotion of yours is directed toward the Lord of Beings."
I shall relate the account of Vajrāṅgada and Udanta, as well as that of the two Vidyādharas, from which arose the glory of the Lord of Śoṇādri, who became highly honored in the world.
In ancient times, there was a king among the Pāṇḍyas named Vajrāṅgada; upon the pillar of his arm rested the earth like a statue.
He was righteous, a knower of justice, profound, generous, and patient; he was peaceful, disciplined, wise, devoted to the vow of monogamy, and accomplished.
Devoted to the worship and adoration of Śiva, illustrious and the best among those possessed of virtuous conduct, he—having conquered his enemies—ruled the earth from the Bridge (Setu) to Kedāra.
Once, while wandering on horseback under the pretext of hunting, he entered a vast forest extending as far as Aruṇācala.
There, having seen a certain musk deer of intense fragrance, he out of curiosity set his horse after it.
Pursued by him, that deer, swift as thought, circumambulated Mount Śoṇa from left to right and then fell down. || 11 ||
Then that king, though his vital strength was broken, wandered about until he grew weary; deprived of his luster, he fell from his mount like one whose merit is exhausted falling from heaven.
Afflicted thus by an unknown cause, as if by a *mātaṅga*, the king did not recognize himself for even a moment, like one possessed by a spirit.
And he thought: "What is this causeless upheaval of my being? Where indeed has that mount, my horse, suddenly gone? (14)
While he was thus overwhelmed by anxiety and his knowledge had become ineffective, the sky suddenly appeared like a mass of matted hair streaked with flashes of lightning.
While he was still looking on, having cast off their animal bodies, the horse and the deer quickly attained the state of moving through the sky.
Wearing crowns and earrings, adorned with necklaces and armlets, dressed in silken lower and upper garments, and garlanded, the two shone resplendently.
And they spoke to the king, whose mind was drawn by wonder, as if removing with the masses of rays from their teeth the darkness born of his distress. (18)
"O King, enough with despair! By the power of the Lord of Śoṇādri, know that this new boat has appeared for us who have reached such a state. (19)
Then the king, having somewhat recovered his composure, spoke to them both with palms joined in reverence and full of humility. (20)
"Who are you two by whom such an affliction as this has been inflicted upon me? O auspicious ones, speak! For the protection of the distressed is indeed the virtue of the great. (21)
When he had thus asked his question, Kalādhara, pointed out by the radiant one, spoke to the king who was filled with wonder.
"Know this, O King: for we two were formerly lords of the Vidyādharas, possessing mutual affection like that of Spring and Madana. (23)
Once, however, we went to the penance grove of the sage Durvāsas on the side of the Golden Mountain (Suvarṇādri), which was difficult to reach even for the mind.
We beheld that holy garden enclosure, radiant with flowers, which served as the means for his ascetic practice and the propitiation of Śiva. (25)
Although we were well-disciplined and possessed the intellectual faculties appropriate for perceiving reality, we entered that garden, eager to gather flowers.
Out of affection for that place, he, radiant with beauty and exceedingly proud, moved about repeatedly, striking the earth with his footsteps.
But I, there, deluded by the excellence of the fragrance of the flowers, placed my hand upon the blossoming blooms, being of evil intent. (28)
Then Durvāsas, a mass of asceticism blazing like a sacrificial fire, stood upon a seat of tiger skin at the base of a Śāṇḍilya tree.
With his lower lip quivering incessantly from the intensity of his indignation, and his broad forehead made formidable by the knitting of a fierce frown; (30)
